It can add themes like modern day weaponry, tilesets, and music, along with entirely new character options.

RPG Maker VX Ace is a truly Pokemon and old FF style rpg maker.
However there are some major limitations that prohibit the program from getting even more popular. So you need to have a check list if you want to buy this program.
First, the code language is ruby. I am a programmer myself, but I have a little knowledge about ruby so it may actually be useful to have the code language as ruby, but i deeply doubt that the majority of the gamers do know or will learn about the ruby code language. Program is indeed designed to let you games without programming but  if you are serious on making a game, you will eventually need scripts. Trust me.
Secondly, graphics. There are limitations on the tileset number in a map, and there is only two layers for tiles. You have a good c layer tile that you need to put on top of a d layer tile? Nope. Only through placing an event. Also events dont auto shape according to tiles touching it. With events its three layers, but you cant put an event on another from the program but only in game. So , even if something you want is possible, it takes long time.
Again, graphics. You need to find more graphics. There are good sites and people who put most of their time on this, but still you spend a lot of time searching on the internet. And if you do not find what you like , like me, editing...
Events, there are limitations and required stuff that we only acquire from custom scripts. You want an event to follow the player? Fine. Event following another event? Custom Script. You want light effects? Custom Script. You want regional events so you dont need to put the same event 100 times? Custom Script.
So before you buy it, you need to have many checks in the list below;
1. Do I have experience with other game making programs?
2. Do I know ruby?
3. Do I know Japanese (for the pursuit of graphics)?
4. Do I have experience with an image editing program ? (even paint is sometimes sufficient)
5. Did I play a pokemon(2d ones) or an old ff game?
6. Am I ready to spend most of my time on stuff that are not included in the program? (like image editing, searching graphics and scripts)
7. Can I spend dozens of hours just for a game of couple minutes?
8. Am I serious?
Actually 8 is the only thing that matter , but if other conditions are not met, I would not recomment this program for you. There are other programs.
If you are serious, I would like to recommend you the game To The Moon, it is said to be made from this program. That will show you the extent of RPG Maker VXA.

Hostile Waters: Antaeus Rising is a 2001 strategy game, similar to the original Command and Conquer, where you create and use a variety of ground and air defense units, collect resources, while battling an enemy on an island in the ocean. The story puts you in the middle of a world rebuilt after a war that nearly destroyed everything. The people of this new world once again find themselves in a conflict, this time against the leaders of the old world who escaped into hiding after losing the war.
The story is pretty good and would make for an interesting reboot with a modern look. As a real-time strategy, it's actually pretty fun. The voice acting is decent and the game looks good for a 2001 release, but definitely outdated by todays standards. The game utilizes a 3D map, which is a nice change for RTS games released around the same time. The controls are different than I expected for an RTS. I usually like to micromanage my units, but with Hostile Waters: Antaeus Rising you don't have that ability. There are an array of different units you can create, each with their own abilities and shortcomings, Unlike more popularly known titles such as the Command and Conquer games, in Antaeus Rising you have the ability to individually upgrade units with armor, shields and so on.
All in all, while it might be a bit dated, it is a decent RTS and is worth picking up if you are into old school Real Time Strategy games. Personally, I would like to see this on a reboot list at some point in the future.

So far I'm really enjoying this game. If you are a fan of the series, or just a fan of tower defense games in general, try this out. It's free to play, and worth the try. However I do have a few problems with this game, mainly the massive grind for not much reward. After you complete all the missions is the campaign, which it doesn't take much time to do, you just begin grinding for levels and gear on the same maps. Another thing is the gear drops. As of right now I just switched out a mythical shield, supposedly the second best class in the game, for a green powerful shield, the second lowest class in the game, because it was legitimately better. Personally, I don't like this. You get a ton of drops each round (thankfully they fixed that but it's still pretty bad). I get about 2-3 bags full per map, and I tend to rely on the colour-coating so I don't have to look through every item. But when I can't rely on the colour ratings, it doesn't make sense to me. Especially when that piece of equipment looks like trash. My shield looks like a piece of wood with vomit on it, and when I'm a fairly high level and have played the game for a while, I find it annoying. Again it's just a nit-picky thing, but I feel it should be fixed. Other than those two things though I find it a great game. If you can get past the grind, and bad drops, it's a great expansion to the already amazing dungeon defender's.

I love these types of games.
And I loved this one as well, at first.
The challenge is nice, unfortunately, there's somethig very broken.
After putting 18 hours in to building up a village, I started running out of food.
A village of ~300 people, with 100 farmers, and 30 hunters, and 9 fully staffed pastures couldn't produce enough food to sustain itself.
I tried to stop the colony from collapsing, but failed.  I figured it would stabalise itself after enough of them died, but when I dropped to 100 adults, with 70 of those guys being farmers, I still couldn't feed everyone.  Eventually the people stopped dying, but I had to move 30 people to hunting (in addition to the 70 farming) and that didn't leave enough for firewood, so once that ran out everyone froze to death.
70 farmers and 30 hunters couldn't feed themselves, and their ~50 children.  I'm not sure how that's anything OTHER than broken.  (Unless you are SUPPPOSED to die?)
I spend the next 18 hours trying to work off of a save from shortly before the collapse (from which there was no recovery) and tried building out all fishing, tried making my 14 farms, and 4 orchards have a more efficient route, and tried running hunters, tried shutting down the pastures.  No combinition was enough.
If you play this, know that once food production drops off, you'll never get it back.

This "game" isn't even really a game, the only factor of it that seems even slightly game-y is that it's iteractive, but that interaction ultimately plays no role in anything you do, that point is actually hammered home a few times through dialogue, that no matter what you do, nothing changes. So it's not even like The Stanley Parable where you can at least DO something, even though it amounts to walking in different directions, at least that had some divergence, there was none here. I could have just watched someone do this and saved myself £5.59, this essentially could have been released in the form of a video and contentwise it really only serves the purpose of being a documentary about the games created by a person who may or may not even exist and what we can learn about them from said games.
Not only that but we aren't even given the chance to form our own opinions before the narrator outright tells us what the game is meant to indicate, Davey pretty much shows you a game and tells you what it communicates as if that's THE way to understand it. Long term this is revealed to be the point, that he was employing dogmatism to see a person the way HE thought they should be seen, but simply confessing a fault doesn't make it arty or significant in any way, it would make about as much sense to update his Facebook status to "There's more to a person than you might think there is".
As for the section at the end where he decides to just stop narrating and let you move around with no idea what the point of any of it is, that just had me wondering why he even bothered, now not only was the game communicating nothing, the narrator was communicating nothing too, what am I supposed to be getting from this? Imagine that as you read this review I just trail off and don't finish reviewing but expect the empty space where my review WOULD go to speak for itself, that's what it was like to me.
Overall I have to say that I was thoroughly disappointed and was constantly expecting something, ANYTHING to happen that would make me THINK or even just perplex me, but nothing, I just walked, constantly looking for some divergence and finding none, walking from point A to point B and then to point C and on and on because I was powerless to go anywhere else. The narration only served to give me some guy's opinion on the area I was walking through, but I could get that by just asking a friend what they thought of it. It was visual, it was audial, but I DID nothing, I had no agency, no autonomy, I could not truly actuate, the walking may as well have been automated, footage taken and the video uploaded to YouTube.
One thing I will say in its favour though, the voice acting is great, but that was yet another thing I preferred about The Stanley Parable. Even though I've lost the magic of being surprised by The Stanley Parable after discovering all the endings or finding them online I can still enjoy showing a friend and seeing their reactions when playing it for the first time. If I was to show someone this I'm sure they'd just be bored.
The question really is, what did the developer WANT me to think? What did they EXPECT me to think? What did they see me DOING? Every player's experience of this will be different only in that they will FEEL different about it, there's not just no replay value (I didn't expect any from a story-driven walking simulator, obviously) there's not even any play value, someone can just describe the game content and there you have a suite of the same emotional tools at your disposal.

As my village began to grow once more I felt the shattered fragments of my soul beginning to piece themselves back together. However, six fishermen in a village of seven people was not enough, and I quickly learned this as I watched all my young adults starve once more. I still had two people left. As they progressively had more and more sex and my incestual village was for the third time repopulated I knew what I had to do. Farms were the only way out. Now I have a monopoly on the cabbage industry, and even now my 4000 cabbages each harvest is not enough to sustain my village of twenty people. THis game is a wonderful look into what it's really like to be insane. I had a great deal of fun simply watching the inmates perform their rituals along with what the game had to really offer, which was a lot of atmospheric scares. But more on that in a moment. I like the objective approach this game took with the inhabitants of Mount Massive, most of them are trapped in their own little world, either too broken to be in touch with reality, or too tortured to realize the reality around them. some even help you in their skewed and twisted ways. especially the main plot point: Father Martin; while he's the main reason you are trapped in the asylum as long as you are, he's also a good chunk of the reason you stay alive. a good chunk of the people want you dead for various reasons, so there's still your danger of getting skewered.
the game is rather atmospheric and relies a lot on opressiveness, capriciousness, and atmospheric and story tension to scare you a lot more than it uses jump scares. I never understood the rejection of jump scares: I know they are cheap, but sometimes the confusion and high intensity is necessary to break you out of the cautious lull you set yourself into. jump scares can be used to enhance an experience without relying on them and this game does a good job of doing that.
the story was a wonderful walk into the dark recesses of the human mind and it's depravity. I was almost convinced the scientists found something they shouldn't have with their deep hypnosis trials. it was a decently profound story with a great deal of necessary unanswered questions for the mind to ponder... untill the last fifteen minutes of the game.
once you decend the elevator into the laboratory, the game quickly changes from a deep psychological horror, to a cheap, clear-cut, action thriller. it's like they hired a different storywriter for the last part who thought any supernatural elements absolutely must be explained in full technicolor detail as to not let anyone believe in the silly ghost stories of the inmates. the game does an absolutely marvelous job of making you believe you just might be an inmate yourself. then strips it way with talk of nanomachines and a cheap as free chase sequence. truly, the last ending of Outlast completely tarnishes what should have been a great story to keep playing again and again.

The earliest incarnation of multiplayer FPS couldn't have had a better start. Surprisingly
still holds up today and i'm
! Even though the online multiplayer is long dead but i already expected that from the get-go given the age of the game and the plethora of other more popular FPS.
Luckily you can still play against bots and you can set a high difficulty which provides a decent challenge if you're so inclined to enjoy this game again. You can pick from the basic game modes like deathmatch, capture the flag, assault, etc. and you get to choose from a good range of maps.
But by far, my favorite thing about Unreal Tournament are the pre-loaded modifiers which create a whole new element to gameplay that still keeps me coming back i.e. zero gravity, one-shot kill, etc.. At the time this came out it was awesome and IMHO it still is! I still have clear memories burned deep of hours spent just zoning out on the maps and the soundtrack... oh the feels!
Maps like Facing Worlds for Capture the Flag, and Morpheus for Zero Gravity Deathmatch are the prime reason why i went ahead and purchased Unreal Tournament on here and i can't tell you how happy i am that it runs like a dream!
Funny enough, as much as i played the early multiplayer FPS's like Unreal Tournament and Quake 3 Arena... there are still a number of maps that i never touched on here. Definitely rectifying that!
If you want to see where the origins of multiplayer FPS came from and actually be able to enjoy it in a visual setting that still holds up, you need to just get this game and have a go at it.
Mind you, it's easy to dismiss Unreal Tournament given its age and how today we're used to better graphics, and the concept of multiplayer
isn't so acceptable nowadays when the alternative of playing online is available, but it's really not too shabby at all! Definitely worth it for you to give it a try!

After years of waiting since backing on Kickstarter I'm left disappointed. The game's length, quality and amount of content are severly lacking.
A Hat In Time is a return to 3D platforming collect-a-thons of yore, akin to what the recent Yooka-Laylee sought to bring back. It cribs heavily off of Super Mario 64 and Sunshine while adding it's own unique spin on things and it mostly succeeds. However, the game super inconsistant in quality and game design and kinda grew stale quickly.
Let me start with the gameplay, the Kid controls fairly well with controls being very responsive and giving you a lot of moves to play with and make your way around the levels. However, certain things get really frustrating because the camera isn't that great, sometimes it's really hard to hell where the Kid is in the middle of a jump because you might not be able to see your shadow and the wall climb/jump is terrible. If you jump towards a wall you'll run up a bit and you have the option to jump off or just slide down the wall. Jumping off the wall leads to a really, really small jump that almost doesn't get you any height and you can't control the direction of it at all, it's always perpendicular off of the wall. You also don't get your double jump back after doing this which you probably should since it'd help.
Most of your moves come in the form of different hats that you knit after finding bundles of yarn, it's pretty interesting but there's no method to this progression. Every yarn bundle looks different, one representing each of the different hats. Once you get a new yarn bundle, you now have a "blueprint" for that hat and any subsequent bundles of the same look just count as a "plus one" on your yarn counter, meaning that any other bundle, no matter what it looks like will contribute to the creation of any hat. It doesn't take long to find every hat bundle and just make all of the hats (if you've been good on finding the bundles). Also, a lot of the hats don't have much of a purpose. One of the first ones you get allows you to run faster, but it's not that much faster and really isn't worth using. The last hat in the game allows you to stop time briefly, but it only has a single use for the entire game and I can't think of any other reason why you'd want to use it. The hat powers are great, but they're not well untilized.
Onto the levels, there's only four and they're not that great. The first level is quite large and sprawling with a lot of visual interest. The second one takes place in a movie studio and has some clever ideas, but nearly every mission is it's own secluded section that's incredibly short. The third is a large forest with a lot of barriers you have to take down but when you do, you're left with a largely empty creepy forest without much in it and it can be confusing to navigate because everything just looks the same. The fourth is an utterly massive level that takes place on the peaks of themed mountain tops but the whole level is "free roam" without any interesting missions or characters to interact with you're left to your own devices to find the various timepieces yourself. It feels pretty lazy. There is a fifth "level" is just the final boss area which is incredibly short, think of the area right before Bowser in Super Mario Sunshine. Other than that there's also several small secluded challenge levels that are all themed exactly the same and really don't have anything to do with the levels they're attached to.
Content: There just isn't enough of it, at 2~ hours of game time I managed to beat the final boss with only optional mopping up to do if I cared to get the 100%. I played for four more hours trying and managed to get to 90% and I won't be going back because I'm already bored of the experience. Also, a lot of the collectibles are pointless, I have all of the hats so all of the extra yarn is pointless to collect and everything else is just cosmetic items that don't even count towards your completion precentage. I believe there's 40 "timepieces" (think Stars in Mario games) and you only need 25 to beat the game.
The good: The music is great (though a lot of it takes heavily from Mario and Zelda), the game has a good art style and stays fresh enough for you to beat it.
I do like the game, don't get me wrong but as someone who spent $15 to get 2 copies I feel like $30 is waaaay too much for what A Hat in Time has to offer and for that I can't recommend it. Definitely get this on sale though if you love 3D platformers.

Okay, arlight. So I didn't play the game for awhile because it became slightly repetitive. But when they recently added new areas and updated old ones as well as adding a slew of gameplay features and a much better hud I wanted to play again. I was not dissapointed. The game has gotten much more difficult. Having to start out again in the mystery lake area was a good choice. It made me really unlock the other areas once again and I still really want to check out the third area which I have yet to get to. This last playthrough I did reminded me of one of the first times I played. I nailed the first area and did my usual route but I didn't find the rifle in any of the usual places. This forced me to go to smaller areas which when before I played were not inhabited by wolves and now were. One thing I learned very quickly is that the wolves are now faster than you are. This is a good thing because before you would meet a wolf and then you'd just run away from then for a couple minutes until they lost steam or were to far away to be chasing you. Now wolf encounts require more thought a precision like losing line of sight with the wolf or trying to sneak around them. So as I was saying I was trying to find the rifle and couldn't the last place on my route was the abondent water treatment building because its the last interior before the ravine. Now usually this part would be easy because I have a rifle and ammo so I can just shoot the wolf and methodically scavenge the building. Because I didn't I had to do a cat and mouse with the wolf darting from throwing my flare at to going back to scavenging. This is also one of the places you can find the rifle and it was my last chance. Sadly I couldn't find it. I tried scouring his den area but was met with aggression and ulitmately I left the treament building with only 13% of my health. I sneeked passed another wolf which was wating right out the door for me and headed to the ravine. In my playthroughs from before this was a small section and that as there to create atmosphere and also to get you ready for a completely new enivroment. It was short but now I found that it was quite long and at this point fatigue had been setting in and I was on my last leg. by the end of the ravine area I was pratically crawling and hoping that it wouldn't get cold. Of course it did but I knew if I could just make it to the trailer I would be fine and sleep all this tire and cold out of me. It was truly a heatbounding moment. having to slowly walk towards the trailer which was in my line of sight as my health slowly ticked down for 9 to 8 to 7 to 6 to 4 and finally 3 at which I made it to the cabin and only to find that me going to sleep the one thing both my character and me as the player was trying to do led to untimely death. I just stared at the screen not being able to believe that once again 2 1/2 hours had gone down the drain. But the game was able was execute my failure with exellent precision and care (by the way I was playing on the hardest difficulty).

Best RPG game/RPG maker out there, requires little to no coding experience and only a basic computer to make simple small game. If you bother to learn coding it opens up potential for more creation, fun and diverse games. I'd say a good 25-30 hours or more needs to be put in to start making a game that works and plays like an actual old skool RPG. The more you fiddle and break things the more you'll be able to make as you'll find your skills improving. You can create good little basic games with the game content included but you'd need to learn a bit of coding and play with events then download DLC to make advanced stuff. Anyone with a Photoshop or artist back ground as well will certainly open up more potential. RPG Maker VX ACE will appear to newbies and hardcore developers but only the hardcore ones will stay long term with it.
Those who can computer art/design/draw will have a massive advantage as you can create your own sprites, pictures and movies. Anyone with good maths skills will be a wizard at creating damage formulas and making enemies and battles come alive, if not community forums are your best friend.
There is plenty of content and DLC to help you make games out in the community some free but the best stuff is quite expensive starting from £5 up to £30. Check Humble Bundle and Steam sales often though!
It's a very powerful tool but you'll need time to learn and adapt, just be aware this is for making top down birds eye view RPGs not your typical 3D hack n slash or MMO type games. Think Pokemon, Breathe of Fire or Phantasy Star type games from the SNES and Genesis era with battle sequences and repetitive music and sound :-D
There are quite a few good selling RPGs made with this game/tool on Steam and you are commercially licensed to sell stuff. Just check any content you download has authors permission to use for profit and don't go copying Final Fantasy thinking you can make scratch from that :-D
To summerise I've been making an RPG for about a year now which involves 2-3 hours work a week and I'm getting near to a finished product. Basic games can be made in a weekend.....

I love these types of games.

The challenge is nice, unfortunately, there's somethig very broken.
After putting 18 hours in to building up a village, I started running out of food.
A village of ~300 people, with 100 farmers, and 30 hunters, and 9 fully staffed pastures couldn't produce enough food to sustain itself.
I tried to stop the colony from collapsing, but failed.  I figured it would stabalise itself after enough of them died, but when I dropped to 100 adults, with 70 of those guys being farmers, I still couldn't feed everyone.  Eventually the people stopped dying, but I had to move 30 people to hunting (in addition to the 70 farming) and that didn't leave enough for firewood, so once that ran out everyone froze to death.
70 farmers and 30 hunters couldn't feed themselves, and their ~50 children.  I'm not sure how that's anything OTHER than broken.  (Unless you are SUPPPOSED to die?)
I spend the next 18 hours trying to work off of a save from shortly before the collapse (from which there was no recovery) and tried building out all fishing, tried making my 14 farms, and 4 orchards have a more efficient route, and tried running hunters, tried shutting down the pastures.  No combinition was enough.
If you play this, know that once food production drops off, you'll never get it back.

Outlast... A brilliant game, horror in its purest form.
Amnesia was the only real scary game in existance before this game was released and now there is a game that takes the crown of the king of horror.
In Outlast you play in feet of a journalist called Miles Upshur.  You receive an e-mail from an employee at Mount Massive Asylum which is owned by the company Murkoff Corporation.  Of course you dont find out the source of the tip Miles Upshur received until the DLC content was released where the source of the tip is revealed.
The game progresses through as you are forced further into the asylum by those who reside inside, at first one of the inmates overpowers you and throws you out the window then you're discovered by another inmate who ensures that you do not leave so that you can be his witness.  Throughout the game Miles Upshur sees many things and goes through intense pain while being chased by many other inmates who wish to kill him.
This game is a great horror game, jumpscares are very well done and the ambience is very good.  This game is in the same vein as Amnesia with the fact that you have no weapons and you're only abilities of surviving is running away and hiding from your enemies.
There are not many things to fault about this game but almost all games has faults and one of the problems with this game is that it can get a bit of repetitive with the main threat you face in the game, a man known as Chris L. Walker.  The moments when Chris is pursuing you it's basically just hide and hope that he doesnt check the locker that you hide in.
When it comes down to it all, this game is still a great game and the repetitiveness of the Chris L. Walker moments are not enough to make this game disappointing at all, this game is a must buy for anyone looking for great horror games.

Because, though the idea of using the Telltale approch of game-design to tell a noire story is a really good idea, and the game seems to have a decent enough story from what we can see right now, the execution is not good at all.
I hate to point at the graphics, especially when talking about a small indie team, but you have to be clever with the money you have. The game is mainly about talking to people and investigating. Either you have money up the a*s and can pay for performance capture like the L.A. Noire of this world, or you don't and you go for a stylised art direction, like The Walking Dead or The Wolf Among Us. Both approch will let you convey emotion, but one necessitate a big budget not to fall in the uncanny valley. Blues and Bullets goes for the "realistic" approch, but the models are not detailed enough, and not well animated at all. It feels like watching a cutscene from a really old game, except you have to look at faces a lot in this one. It's kind of jaring that they chose that kind of technic, when cell-shading mixted with the well done black&white art direction would have been a far better choice.
If I take a whole paragraph to explain that, it's because when combined with the okay but not great voice acting, Blues And Bullets asks you to pass a big cringe curve to actually get into it. Which is a shame because the art direction, the music, and some aspects of the story and gameplay work as intented for the most part. It's not a mechanic heavy game, but it gives enough to do to stay in the story...if you don't get weirded out by the models and their robotic animation.
TL;DR
I feel that I'm being really arsh on this one, but despite the fact that the project seems dead, I would have loved to love it. Unfortunately as it is, I would play any other Telltale's game over this one, especially The Wolf Among Us. And for a more polished investigation story, I would play L.A Noire, the Still Life games (or even Deadly Premonition...okay it's not polished but the cringe curve is worth it).
Hard yet fun, promise that it wont dissapoint you ;)

I write this guide whilst in the mists of shaking, I have been sick the past few days and the tightness in my chest caused by the game makes it even harder for me to breathe and calm down, but I will never forgive myself if I don't complete my thoughts on the subject.
I think i want to start by stating that this is a very spoiler intensive review, and while I recommend the game, I strongly recommend waiting on whether or not you intend on playing this game before reading it, and more to the point on whether or not you feel spoilers would be okay in a subject such as this.
Now despite saying this I want to share my experience with the game a little bit before the review proper. I had watched Silent0siris's playthrough of the game before the game was gifted to me, yet despite knowing everything that was coming up, this game hit me harder this time than the last time. In an effort to further understand and disect the game I spent my entire personal playthrough of the game taking screenshots (almost stated photos) of scene I felt were either beautiful or powerful enough to make note of.
Here is where the spoilers start so I recomend closing this review or finding another if you do not wish to continue:
I felt aweful for doing this midway through. there are times where the game demands silence, by which I mean it doesn't out right ask you, but through it's message you find yourself for a loss for words many times. I experienced this first through Silent0siris's playthrough, but much stronger in my own, where I felt like scum for taking screenshots to savor the moments. I think
explains what I mean in a way...
Still the most interesting thing to me are two of the many images I found myself taking near the end.
I find to be one of the most powerful messages in this game, to the point of preserving it straigh.
However
has got to be the single most powerful image in the game proper.
"Why" you ask?
Seeing as I've been skirting around describing the game propper, I guess I'll start with a little more skirting.
But it seems




















(and yes every word links to a different image there)
But why?
Well it all starts with a bug... an accident in programing that quite possibly meant so much more, something that "Coda" (person or character or idea previlent in the game, down to the point of being the main subject of the game, so to speak) latched onto.
This, FINAL scene is made in tribute to coda's work... So why does it reverberate through so many people's hearts to the point of wanting, nay, NEEDING to ensure this connection is real, needing to doccument this moment in time, however brief however fleeting? Because the game isn't about Coda.
The premise of this game is one of the narator and their connection with a game developer named Coda, who's work, he feels should be shared. (Interesting to note, the word Coda is defined by webster's as either a concluding part of a literary or dramatic work, or something that serves to round out, conclude, or sumarize and usually has it's own interest)
Throughout the game we're taken through Coda's work, from his first counter strike level, to his first solo game, and onward and onward to coda's final game, being fed thoughts and answers deconstructing the pieces as we play them, as the author tries to analyze and share HIS experience with this developer. Though... to most this lacks any humor, and for good reason, because at the exact same time, the narator is sharing(albeit subtly) his inner demons being worked through from an angle of game design.
So here we are, an outside party being walked through a series of games, related losely via concept emotion and mostly developer, while at the same time being told stories about the developer, and the narator's connection with said developer. Here we are, common plebians, uneducated masses sitting through conversations of game design, choices, growth,
anxiety,
Loss...
The narator let's us into a very intimate place... as he tries to understand what it was that he did wrong to sour his relationship with coda... going so far as to fully admit that he's doing it again, he's sharing coda's work without permission (a statement that resonates with MANY a viewer) in an effort to better understand this game developer, and more to the point, why the games he made affected him so.
And this is part of why that image so many people want to share and save do that very thing: because for a moment, we watch as a man we can only assume is broken by anxiety and loss do the very thing that hurts him so much, in an attempt to understand why.
I can't help but wonder how long that last scene alone took to create... and how difficult it was for him to keep creating onto near infinity that maze we see at the end. I tried to reason it away with "oh it's only three dimensional for a little bit, then it's an algorithm that completes the rest and or repeats itself onto infinity" ... part of why i wanted to doccument that maze myself was to try and catch a sign of cheating.. repetition... and it's all... very unique...
I find myself wanting to believe he worked on it, on each wall delicately placing it in attempts to better connect with his now distant friend I find myself wanting to believe that he's doing it as some sort of self imposed punishment, some sort of self imposed retribution for having once again shared coda's work despite coda's wishes.. and it's at that point i find myself torn for many reasons.
One of them being whether or not coda exists... or more importantly whether or not I WANT coda to exist. as a concept i almost feel that the message loses weight, and there is very a many sign that points towards coda infact being a concept, but if coda is real our narator is hurting coda once again with his actions and attempts to connect once more to him... But I feel it makes me connect with him more...
The messages this game provides are very powerful. Go play it.

Outlast is one of those games riding the wave of the 'No Weapons, first person, sh*t your pants' survival horror games. And that is by no means a bad thing in the slightest.
The asylum you're thrust into is dark and atmospheric and you're always unsure where the next bad guy is coming from. Be it a deranged, aimless patient, or a calculated, blood thirsty scientist psychologically toying with you, you're always kept on the edge of your seat. Armed with only your trusty reporting camera, you'll be relying on it's infra-red vision to navigate the labarynthine hallways, sewers, basements and gardens; you'll feel utterly lost and naked without it (trust me it happens). Your only resources are the batteries to power your camera (which deplete at an alarming rate) and your wits. You'll have to sneak, sprint, and solve puzzles in order to get out of the asylum alive and find out exactly what is going on.
The pacing of the game is excellent and there's never a dull moment; the intrigue generated by the carefully crafted story will push you to endure the constant jump scares, persistent feeling that SOMETHING may be following you and the constant fear that your batteries will deplete down the next pitch black hallway.
This is defintely up there as one of the scariest horror games I have played and I'm debating whether to put myself through another playthrough on the hardest difficulty; because we humans are strange like that.

Kind of a mixed-bag where your enjoyment of this will come down to how much you like the combat and the character interactions.  I found both enjoyable enough to overcome most of the game's flaws.
First off, the port is really good.  There are arbitrary resolution options, easy and well-done keybinding, instant switching of button prompts upon switching from keyboard to game controller, graphic options and I didn't suffer one crash while playing Zestiria or experience any kind of framerate issues.  The UI is solid and doesn't have any glaring issues. This is a very pleasant surprise for a Japanese series's PC debut.
Zestiria also has a lot of small touches that make it easy to play.  For example, you can save anywhere.  The game calls it a quick save, but it's a permanent save you can use anywhere and doesn't delete after loading it.  You can also line-skip dialogue and cutscenes, which is great for fast readers and for when you just want to hurry along a cutscene without just straight-skipping it.  If you die against a boss, you can just retry the fight immediately after being given a chance to rearrange your equipment/party instead of having to load a save and make a run back to the boss.  Another big thing with Zestiria is you get a bunch of dumb costume accessories that have a ton of editing possibilities and all costume changes are reflected in-game.  This is always a cool thing.  All this adds up to a hassle-free experience and I give the dev team a lot of credit for these features.
You'll spend a ton of time in combat, so let's talk about that a bit.  Zestiria decided to have battles not transition to an imaginary plane but instead take place in the current environment.  Honestly, I don't really see the advantage to this gameplay-wise, other than as a testing phase for future implementation,  It makes getting a feel for the whole battlefield practically impossible and also can cause the camera to spaz out at times.  While I didn't find the battle camera to be as problematic as most (like 90% of the time it was a non-factor), there will be times when it gets caught on a corner or you get too close to an enemy and it just starts to wig out.  Other than that, the game uses a pairing system called armatization that lets you combine characters, mainly to exploit elemental weaknesses, which are a big thing in Zestiria.  Bosses can be problematic though, as they tend to get incredibly aggressive when weakened and it's extremely likely you'll get a full-party wipe in a matter of seconds a number of times.  I liked the combat and found it mostly satisfying with the above issues plaguing it a bit.
The character interactions are one of the main draws of the series and it's really good here.  The skits and humor are mostly well-translated, particularly all the puns.  At times the translation gets a bit too meme-y/referencey at times but on average, it's a very good adaptation.  The biggest problem character-wise is that non-party members might as well be non-existent and don't do anything to make you care much about them.
The story is bad, and this is coming in with low expectations for it.  The first two-thirds are kind of boringly generic, but not really holding the game back or anything, then the last third of the game comes and suddenly there's a huge emphasis on the story and it's just bad and there's a lot of it.  Even things like quest design start to fall apart, like there are numerous times where the game sends you to some place, only to arrive there and then immediately be told to leave and go someone else.  The home stretch of the game also arbitrary locks some fast-traveling locations so you end up just trying to power through it to get back to killing stuff and doing sidequests.
Dungeon and music is uneven.  The parts of Zestiria that feel fully cooked, like the entire middle section of the game, have some decent design, like the shrines for example, and really cool, uninterrupted music.  Other areas, like most random ruins and transitional areas, are rather copy/paste with unmemorable tracks.  The team really dropped the ball by not having Sorey's theme be the generic overworld music because it rules and is insanely underused in the game.
The last negative is the equipment system, which is terrible unless you love micromanaging between a bunch of screens.  They tried to reinvent the wheel here and just messed up.  I won't bother to explain how poor the implementation of it is, but thankfully you can largely ignore it as long as you're playing on the higher difficulties.
All in all, if you're interested in JRPG's for the PC, this is a pretty solid choice, especially considering how slim the pickings are.  Yeah, it's about 15 hours too long and the story and equipment system are poor, but ultimately I found it a fun game to play, especially once you get your primary party, all the way through the shrine trials.  There's a lot of replayability here due to how the series handles new game+ features, as well.  So if you're looking for a combat and character-oriented JRPG, Zestiria is probably one of your best bets on PC.

Ein Shooter der sich stark von anderen Spiele im selben Genre unterscheidet.
Man erkennt sofort,dass die Deckung dein bester Freund ist,da man schnell sterben kann und im Vergleich zu anderen Shootern nicht viel aushält. Man muss also vorallem im Muliplayer taktisch handeln,um so Erfolg zu erringen. Die Waffen wurden verdamt gut dargestellt,weshalb sich zu anfang das Treffen und schießen als kleine Herrausforderung entpuppt. Die Maps im Multiplayer sind rießig,abwechslungsreich und die Atmosphäre ist düster und übermittelt den 2. Weltkrieg gut, um den es hier geht. Du kannst zwischen unterschiedlichen Klassen wählen,womit jeder andere Waffen und Fähigkeiten hat,wie es in vielen Shootern üblich ist. Man kann ebenfalls Panzer fahren,was zwar das einzigste ist,jedoch gefällt es mir als Fußsoldat sowieso besser. Seid dem neuen Update kann man auf Seiten der Alliierten (Amerikaner) oder den Japaner kämpfen. Im Singleplayer ist es jedoch anders man kämpft zu erst, auf der Seite der Wehrmacht (Deutschen) und dann darf man die Kampagne der Alliierten (Sowjetunion) spielen. Es exestiert keine wirkliche Geschichte,man bekommt meistens einen Plan wie genau man vorgehen muss und dieser wird von dem Sprecher erklärt, was ganz nett ist,jedoch keine wirkliche Story bietet. Die Aufgabe ist es entweder anzugreifen, oder zu verteidigen. Mit der Zeit steigen wir auf und erlernen neue Fähigkeiten, wie zum Beispiel befehle zu erteilen oder Artillerieunterstützung anzufordern. Wir dürfen/müssen in einigen Missionen Panzer fahren,was ich aber persönlich ziemlich langweilig fand und die Fußsoldaten wie im auch im Multiplayer den Panzern vorzog. Ab und zu werden einige echte Briefe vorgelesen und die Aufträge werden interessant erzählt. Es ist nicht besonderes,aber für einen Tag macht es Spaß in realistischen und schwierigen Gefechten gegen die mittelmäßige KI zu kämpfen. Es ist einer meiner lieblings Shooter und ich hatte einmal mit dem durchspielen der Story Spaß und wurde unterhalten. Den Multiplayer spiele ich auch ab und zu und vorallem gefallen mir die schwierigen und atmosphärischen Gefechte.
Es sollten sich das Spiel nur die Leute holen,die auf herrausforderne Shooter stehen und nicht viel wert auf eine gut erzählte Story legen,sondern mit einfachen Spaßfaktor zufrieden sind.

Just Cause 2 has a great Demo but DO NOT let it mislead you. I downloaded the demo, and spent a good amount of time messing around, exploring, shooting some bases, and just basically wrecking havoc. If you have some time to kill, download the free demo and play away. That is about where the fun stops.
Allow me to break it down.
Graphics 3/5. The graphics are okay but even at the highest settings look more like The Sims laughable graphics, rather than a serious FPS game. They leave much to be desired, and the cutting/bad transition with movement in the game is horrendous. You will drive straight and seemingly go through the car in front of you.
Campaign. 1/5. SHOOT THESE 14 GUYS, BLOW UP EVERYTHING ON THIS BASE. WASH RINSE REPEAT. The story is not fluid, no character development, and it is just so damn repetitive. There is nothing fun about it, Within my first 20 minutes of playing the full game I had enough money to buy anything I wanted, but what was the point? The weapon upgrades are terrible, and you cannot unlock new weapons. No point to play.
Customization 0/5. I hope you are sensing a trend with this game.
Replayability. 0/5. After playing the demo you have played the ENTIRE game. No point in buying it and wasting your time doing the exact same thing over again. The map doesn't open up until you "discover" new places, so expect to be hijacking planes and cars to fly/drive to pointless places just to, you guessed it, shoot some guys and blow some stuff up.
Would I Recommend? HELL NO. Save your money, play a better game like H1Z1 or something along those lines.

Okay, arlight. So I didn't play the game for awhile because it became slightly repetitive. But when they recently added new areas and updated old ones as well as adding a slew of gameplay features and a much better hud I wanted to play again. I was not dissapointed. The game has gotten much more difficult. Having to start out again in the mystery lake area was a good choice. It made me really unlock the other areas once again and I still really want to check out the third area which I have yet to get to. This last playthrough I did reminded me of one of the first times I played. I nailed the first area and did my usual route but I didn't find the rifle in any of the usual places. This forced me to go to smaller areas which when before I played were not inhabited by wolves and now were. One thing I learned very quickly is that the wolves are now faster than you are. This is a good thing because before you would meet a wolf and then you'd just run away from then for a couple minutes until they lost steam or were to far away to be chasing you. Now wolf encounts require more thought a precision like losing line of sight with the wolf or trying to sneak around them. So as I was saying I was trying to find the rifle and couldn't the last place on my route was the abondent water treatment building because its the last interior before the ravine. Now usually this part would be easy because I have a rifle and ammo so I can just shoot the wolf and methodically scavenge the building. Because I didn't I had to do a cat and mouse with the wolf darting from throwing my flare at to going back to scavenging. This is also one of the places you can find the rifle and it was my last chance. Sadly I couldn't find it. I tried scouring his den area but was met with aggression and ulitmately I left the treament building with only 13% of my health. I sneeked passed another wolf which was wating right out the door for me and headed to the ravine. In my playthroughs from before this was a small section and that as there to create atmosphere and also to get you ready for a completely new enivroment. It was short but now I found that it was quite long and at this point fatigue had been setting in and I was on my last leg. by the end of the ravine area I was pratically crawling and hoping that it wouldn't get cold. Of course it did but I knew if I could just make it to the trailer I would be fine and sleep all this tire and cold out of me. It was truly a heatbounding moment. having to slowly walk towards the trailer which was in my line of sight as my health slowly ticked down for 9 to 8 to 7 to 6 to 4 and finally 3 at which I made it to the cabin and only to find that me going to sleep the one thing both my character and me as the player was trying to do led to untimely death. I just stared at the screen not being able to believe that once again 2 1/2 hours had gone down the drain. But the game was able was execute my failure with exellent precision and care (by the way I was playing on the hardest difficulty).
Would recommend!

Full disclosure: I backed the Kickstarter for this game when it was first announced.
And also full disclosure: me backing or not, this game is an absolute diamond.
It feels like a perfect love letter to the collect-a-thons of old, as well as bringing back that feeling you had as a kid while you were playing Super Mario Sunshine.
The character is an absolute thrill to play as, since she controls so well that, obstacles course or not, you want to continue jumping around! And the level design fits this perfectly; there's a billion different ways to get from point A to point B, and the dev team clearly put a lot of effort into making sure that each one was as rewarding as the last.
Even better, the boss fights ALSO take full advantage of Hat Kid's abilities to manuever, as each one is a wonderful test of how well you can navigate using your abilities.
The soundtrack is also absolutely stellar, with plenty of different selections that all fit the mood their going for. If I have an oppurtunity, I'm definitely going to grab this on vinyl.
All in all: the characters are lovable, the settings are wonderful, the soundtrack is killer, and the aesthetic is an absolute treat. I would recommend this to anyone who likes to have fun when they play video games.
Seriously, it's that good.

Well done to the producers too, they made this game very scary, but not so scary that people wouldn't buy it because of the fear level. Now onto my opinions of this game. As you can probably already tell, I'm a fan of this game. I loved every second of it, the excitement, the fear, the horror. I do agree with people who say this game could've been way more horrifying, but at the same time I feel like the developers got it right with the plot, difficulty, build-up to scary moments etc. I also really liked the notes and documents system and the variety in the enemies (variants). Now with the Whistleblower DLC, I really want to say I enjoyed it more than the main game, but I'm just not sure about it. But for a horror game, it has an excellent story. The story and exploration mixed with the notes and documents made me feel like I was immersed in every situation, which, I think, the developers of all horror games should strive for. All in all, Outlast is a very pleasurable encounter for those of you that enjoy being frightened so much that your mind will scream in affliction and writhe in agony due to the malevolent nature of this game. 8.5/10

Possibly one of my all-time favorite games.  I have bought this game 3 times by now, for one reason or another.  The story is rather unique and the setting you find yourself in is like few others I have ever seen.  The fact that this game came out in the age of giant PC game boxes and has continued to be sold non-stop even up until today is saying something in and of itself.  However, the feel of the game and its re-playability have been key reasons for why I just keep coming back to it.  From the ability to hot-seat from the carrier that houses your brain (which if you try to look around in some of the internal views, you might catch a glimps of) to any one of your combat vehicals, it offers multitudes of ways to experience each of the unique levels.  Even the pilots' AI's are differnt in their appoch to how they handel each type of vehical.  Be it hellicopter, hovercraft, tank, or buggy; as well as what they will do in combat... even their prefered weapons can become something of a deciding factor from one fight to the next depending on the enemies they are facing and who is on their wing.  Compared to most modern feel-alikes, the part that stands out most for me is the ease with which you can command your forces in the field be it from the live interface or the tactical map.  The only down side I could think of is the one mission where stealth is required, where in you fail if your forces are detected before a particular objective is completed.  Thankfully its only one mission and after you finish it, you never need worry about it again.  If any other levels give you trouble, feel free to ask for tips or tricks.  By now I more or less know them all.

Let me start off by saying this game is a MASTERPIECE. It brings back so much nostalgia and so many good memories of the good old days of 3d platformers. It's like Banjo Kazooie, Super Mario 64, Psychonauts, and all the beauty of platformers had a baby. Okay, now into the review.
POSITIVE:
It starts off with the most adorable story and light hearted tone. You start in Mafia Town and it's not colorless drivel, it's a world full of color and enemy types, collectibles, vaults, different mechanics and characters. It's the perfect introduction to a game that's so simple, yet can be brought into the speedrunning and complicated scene so easily, just like SM64. You start off with the Kid's Hat, which lets you see objectives; It's so helpful to see where you're supposed to go, yet you have so much freedom it's grand. You can gain up to 5 more hats as you progress, all with their own special mechanics. For example the sprint hat lets you run and the brewing hat lets you throw explosive potions. Even these two hats have so many applications, and it's just the beginning. Oh! And I almost forgot. This game controls exactly like SM64, Super Mario Sunshine, or Super Mario Galaxy would. It has a double jump, a dive, dive cancel, wall jumps, and the mechanics just keep getting more and more complex. For example slowing down time and using a grappling hook. Speaking of the grappling hook, there are badges in this game that you can equip (Up to 2 and 3 of them in the late game) that give you new and different things you can do. Again, for example there's the Item Magnet Badge which attracts nearby collectibles and the Hover Badge that saves you from taking fall damage. There's also negative or trash Badges that give bad effects. For example there's the 1-Hit Hero Badge that makes your HP sink to 1. These negative badges are merely to add challenge to the already rough 3d platformer. Plus, there's a plethera of "Time Rifts", aka special hidden stages, like in SM Sunshine. At the end of every level and rift there's a Time Piece (Or a star in Mario language) which you can use to unlock more acts and worlds. Also at the end of every Time Rift there's a slot machine that gives you cosmetics and tracks, making it able to customize your game, your character, adding your own flair to things. So far as the games' length and replayability, I played the game for a solid 14 hours and I still haven't found everything or completed all the achievements. Character-wise, they're all so lovable and they all have their own personality. Like Mustache Girl, who wants to be the hero of the story and destroy evil. (Mostly the Mafia) The controls are very tight and responsive, and if you mess up your inputs, the game most definitely punishes you. The soundtrack is beautiful and suits the game so very well. Now enough of my rambling and onto the negatives.
NEGATIVE:
I've searched almost every corner of the maps and I've seen only a few glitches and bugs. Which in this day and age is good, yet doesn't mean it's acceptable. I've seen a few T-poses and missing textures, but nothing terribly game-breaking. There's also a lack of explaining advanced mechanics like the speed boost if you cancel your dive when you hit the ground. Plus there's no application for some things, and even if not, sometimes it's only a one time use thing. There's a lack of different physical weapons not counting hats. There's an excessive amount of yarn to the point where it's not even rare. Also everything important glows like a thousand suns, which is nice for newbie players but it's definitely not necessary. I'm not going to talk much about the swimming mechanic because it's literally never used, but it definitely needs some work if it's meant to be a part of the game and not just an instant death.
SUMMARY:
This game is a must get for platformer lovers and fans of the mario franchise.

World Design: 10/10
AI: 9/10
Dialogue: 7/10
Story: 7/10
Gameplay: 10/10

text:
If you frequently browse the internet, you've probably heard of this game. Just about every YouTube let's player out there has taken a crack at it, and fans everywhere request it and proclaim it's supreme scariness to the world. Of course, there is also an equal and opposite reaction to this positivity from fans, with people saying it's an overplayed, overhyped jumpscare-fest that doesn't deserve the attention it's getting. Having been intrigued by the game after watching Markiplier play it, I downloaded the demo, and was compelled enough by the experience to quickly purchase the full game. After having completed the main game and the optional sixth night (and unsuccessfully attempting the infamous 4/20 mode) I believe Five Nights at Freddy's is a wholly worthwhile experience and a damn scary game to boot, but not perfect.
Five Nights at Freddy's is an incredibly unique approach to horror compared to most of its contemporaries. The typical formula for indie horror games these days is running around some abandoned building or tunnel system, possibly while collecting items, and being chased by a monster, with a few jumpscares along the way. These games are based around making the player do something they don't want to do: put themselves in danger of a monster. Five Nights at Freddy's, on the other hand, draws horror from making the player do nothing. In this game, you are a night guard at Freddy Fazbear's Pizza, a Chuck E Cheese-esque establishment, but the twist is that the animatronic characters get a bit "quirky" at night, and by that I mean they move around and try to brutally murder you. You have nothing but a camera tablet and two door lights to keep track of them, and doors to keep them out. Simple, right? Wrong. You see, your power is limited, and using the cameras, door lights, and closing the doors drains power. You have just barely enough power to make it to 6 AM, when your shift ends, so you need to use your tools to survive only when absolutely necessary.
This is brilliant, as the player has all the tools they need to survive, but they are forced not to use them, as running out of power causes a blackout, at which point the titular Freddy will come to execute you. This is as much a strategy and tower defense game as it is horror, as you must figure out the best way to ration your power while also keeping the animatronic ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s off your back. In fact, calling this game a horror game is almost a misnomer, as it’s more of a paranoia simulator. You know they’re coming, but you don’t know when, and you go crazy trying to keep yourself from shutting both doors because you know you can’t afford to waste that much power. Still, the game is not unfair. It rewards players for remaining calm and using their resources intelligently, and with this and some knowledge of the animatronic robot’s patterns, you can easily succeed.
This, however, is where the game’s biggest problem arises, as once you’ve learned all the game’s tricks, which doesn’t take too long, it becomes predictable, and predictability is horror’s number one enemy. As such, once you get the game down, while the game doesn’t become any less challenging, it becomes a lot less scary. By the sixth night, nothing the game did even fazed me, and I reacted to any deaths I had with frustration rather than fear. Also, the game is rather short. If you don’t die, you can beat it in just under an hour, and even if you die constantly it’s not likely to last more than 3 hours, even with the optional sixth night (4/20 mode will add at least several hours of extra play time if you decide to attempt it, though). Still, this isn’t a big deal, as the game is only five dollars, and in my opinion, the scares and unique challenge this game provided while it lasted is well worth that price. If you’re not sold, though, I’d recommend trying out the free demo, or waiting until the game goes on sale. However, I recommend you don’t watch any let’s play footage, as this game is best going in blind.
On a side note, the presentation of the game is solid. The graphics are early 90’s pre-rendered 3D style, and while they don’t look that great, the game still manages to convey a solid atmosphere with them, and it almost helps the scares, as this game, being about animatronics, takes great advantage of people’s fear of the uncanny valley, and early 90’s 3D was no stranger to things that looked real but not quite. The sound design is simple but effective, and does a good job of keeping you tense and paranoid (the deep laugh that plays when Freddy moves still fills me with dread). The voice acting from the former security guard (or whatever he is) who calls you throughout the week is good enough to make him seem like a real character and maintain the atmosphere, even if it’s nothing particularly noteworthy. Overall, the game focuses less on impressing with flashy, high-budget effects and lets the mechanics drive the scares, which is exactly how a horror game should be.
Score: 8/10

But Zestiria, they don't really work so different from each other (At least as far as I know).
Hopefully the next 2 Tales Of games in development will turn out better. Please don't make this mistake again. I'm ok with a party member leaving, but give us enough different people to replace them with. Two humans just doesn't cut it.  Still a great game but there are better Tales Of games out there for people getting into the series.
*Edit*
I have now beat the game.  I'd say it's the best game for 2015.  But still not as good as Graces F or Hearts R but still great.  Now I'm trying to find things to do post game outside of the DLC (I do have it though).

Ein Shooter der sich stark von anderen Spiele im selben Genre unterscheidet.
Man erkennt sofort,dass die Deckung dein bester Freund ist,da man schnell sterben kann und im Vergleich zu anderen Shootern nicht viel aushält. Man muss also vorallem im Muliplayer taktisch handeln,um so Erfolg zu erringen. Die Waffen wurden verdamt gut dargestellt,weshalb sich zu anfang das Treffen und schießen als kleine Herrausforderung entpuppt. Die Maps im Multiplayer sind rießig,abwechslungsreich und die Atmosphäre ist düster und übermittelt den 2. Weltkrieg gut, um den es hier geht. Du kannst zwischen unterschiedlichen Klassen wählen,womit jeder andere Waffen und Fähigkeiten hat,wie es in vielen Shootern üblich ist. Man kann ebenfalls Panzer fahren,was zwar das einzigste ist,jedoch gefällt es mir als Fußsoldat sowieso besser. Seid dem neuen Update kann man auf Seiten der Alliierten (Amerikaner) oder den Japaner kämpfen. Im Singleplayer ist es jedoch anders man kämpft zu erst, auf der Seite der Wehrmacht (Deutschen) und dann darf man die Kampagne der Alliierten (Sowjetunion) spielen. Es exestiert keine wirkliche Geschichte,man bekommt meistens einen Plan wie genau man vorgehen muss und dieser wird von dem Sprecher erklärt, was ganz nett ist,jedoch keine wirkliche Story bietet. Die Aufgabe ist es entweder anzugreifen, oder zu verteidigen. Mit der Zeit steigen wir auf und erlernen neue Fähigkeiten, wie zum Beispiel befehle zu erteilen oder Artillerieunterstützung anzufordern. Wir dürfen/müssen in einigen Missionen Panzer fahren,was ich aber persönlich ziemlich langweilig fand und die Fußsoldaten wie im auch im Multiplayer den Panzern vorzog. Ab und zu werden einige echte Briefe vorgelesen und die Aufträge werden interessant erzählt. Es ist nicht besonderes,aber für einen Tag macht es Spaß in realistischen und schwierigen Gefechten gegen die mittelmäßige KI zu kämpfen. Es ist einer meiner lieblings Shooter und ich hatte einmal mit dem durchspielen der Story Spaß und wurde unterhalten. Den Multiplayer spiele ich auch ab und zu und vorallem gefallen mir die schwierigen und atmosphärischen Gefechte.
Es sollten sich das Spiel nur die Leute holen,die auf herrausforderne Shooter stehen und nicht viel wert auf eine gut erzählte Story legen,sondern mit einfachen Spaßfaktor zufrieden sind.

For fans of the Tales of Series, I have to leave this footnote to begin with. Zestiria plays dramatically different than what you are use to. Although the changes at face value don't seem that different, it certainly will be a culture shock to say the least. I enjoyed Zestiria all the way through, it was well written and a welcome return to the series. If I could point out one flaw I would say that it feels like it's lacking something. Compared to the previous Tales of Titles there is quite a bit less game to play. The major cities are smaller, some minor characters had more buildup than party members, and some party members disappear due to plot reasons and never reappear again. Previous Tales of Titles have done the disappearing party member sure, but they always returned in time for the end of the plot. Unfortunately Zestiria doesn't do this, and at least to me, it kinda feels like I was cheated just a bit. Now don't get me wrong, Zestiria is a fantastic game, I enjoyed every moment of it. However it falls flat when compared to its predecessors. I’m glad to see the Tales of Series get a reboot, and I'm excited to see more. But we should demand more. Buy this game, play it and enjoy. But make sure you remind the Development team what you want. Remind them of the standard they have set in the past, so with the money they get from Zestiria, they can get this reboot back to the quality it should be.

Take Thy Throne is a very enjoyable, charming, and unique 2D Sidescrolling Tower Defense mutliplayer based game with a lot of potential.
It has a few game modes available right now, such as the Tutorial, Take Thy Throne, Capture the Flag, and Dragon Slayer.
In Take thy Throne, your objective is to get to the enemy’s fortress and defeat their king to win the game. In Capture the Flag, a flag is spawned somewhere on the map and you must find it, and bring it back to your fortress to score a point for your team. In Dragon Slayer, you must keep killing dragons until one player’s lives are depleted.
There are multiple classes to choose from, and each serves a different purpose, and plays differently. One example is the Helper class whose main job is not to fight off enemy attackers, but  to mine ore, and chop wood to provide resources to expand or fortify your fortress.
The developers are very kind and diligent with updates, and are hard at work to continually improve the game, and to promote it as much as possible with new maps, new classes, and recently the addition of achievements, and trading cards. There’s plenty of new content to come such as Dragon Wars, Team Deathmatch game modes, and maps, only to name a few.
The main problem with Take Thy Throne right now is lack of players online. As it's a fairly new game, word of mouth and advertising needs to take place, and really promote the game so more people can come online and enjoy the game. Right now, I'd recommend getting a group of friends to play the game, as it is hard to get into games with other players right now or try asking around on the forums to see if other players would like to play with you.
After some more improvements, and more players coming online, I can really see this game taking off, and really attracting a more wide and diverse audience

Fantastic game based on an incredible concept, made by a team that clearly has a lot of passion for their work. Backed this on kickstarter a long time ago, and got access to the beta a few weeks ago and have had a absolute blast in both the campaign mode, and the endless survival mode.
While the game itself is incredibly fun, and the reason alone for me playing and enjoying the game so much, I think it could benefit from more weapon and enemy diversity, and certainly from the addition of a level editor. The levels included are already very simple, but well-thought out, and I think allowing players to make their own, and really harness the true potential of the Matrix-esque gameplay would add a lot to the long-term replayeability.
PROS:
+ Great art style and sound design
+ Very satisfying core gameplay loop
+ Great level design
+ Good level diversity
+ Great replayeability w/ challenges and Endless mode
CONS:
- No level editor
- ~2 Hour campaign

SUPERHOT was reviewed with a code provided by the developer.
SUPERHOT is the most innovative shooter I’ve played in years. SUPERHOT knows this. SUPERHOT even makes a joke out of those exact words at one point during the game, but it’s the truth. There wasn’t a single moment in SUPERHOT where I wasn’t having my mind blown in some way, be it from finding a new way to ruin an enemy’s day or one of the many mid-level fourth wall breaks that elevates SUPERHOT from being something much more than just a stylish shooter and into the realm of pure first person genius.
Sadly, SUPERHOT is short. I had beat SUPERHOT‘s story in just under two hours, and you only unlock new ‘challenge modes’ to play once the main game is complete, most of which are just modifiers for the existing story levels. SUPERHOT is truly a genius shooter close to rivaling legends, sadly cut down by its minuscule running time.

Wow! This game really got to me. I just finished it and wanted to write this review while things were still fresh in my mind (and before reading anything else that my change my thinking on what I just experienced.) This game is narrated by the creator of the Stanley Parable, and is a showcase of short games made by a developer friend of his, because the friend was too introverted and reclusive to let anyone else ever see them. But it ends up being a commentary about the creative process and the validation we all seem to need from others for the various endeavors that we undertake. The narration and music are used to good effect, and the surreal and sometimes eerie environments that you traverse through in the game really get you into the lonely and sometimes disturbing head-space of the developer friend. I have to admit that when I got to the end of this game, I was left scratching my head a little about what I had just experienced; where I ended up at the end was not where I thought I'd be when the game started. My guess is that if you liked The Stanley Parable, that you would probably appreciate this game on some of the same levels. There really isn't much humor in this game like in TSP, but there are definitely multiple levels of narrative and meta-narrative that will feel familiar.
My advice: go into this game knowing as little about it as possible and hopefully not having heard much about it at all. I bought the game knowing that it was made by the creator of the Stanley Parable, and that's about it. That was all I had to color my expectations about the game and I believe the game will give you a much greater experience for not having any preconceived notions about what is to come.

Banished is a game that makes me happy to play it. It is a surprisingly logical and realistic city-builder which is both complex and simple at the same time.
You start the game with a handful of exiled people and you need to build a city for them. It is as simple as that but you manage this game to such detail that you become increasingly engrossed within it!
The interface is the most simple thing I have ever seen - highly intuitive! You can order your workers to collect wood, stone, or coal from the forest, in order to build things. But the beauty of this game comes when you need to assign your people to various jobs. You manage how many people spend time nurturing the forest so you don't run out of wood, compared to how many are cutting wood so you don't all freeze to death in the winter. You manage how many people are building new buildings or if they're going to spend this summer fishing because your food reserves are low. You spend hours waiting, hoping for a merchant to pass by because you desperately need some medicine - but that specific merchant doesn't carry medicine!
It is that involvement with your people which I find extremely engaging and so much fun! And this is only reinforced by the fact that you can see your characters' names, age, and sex if you click on their houses (or on them but they move pretty fast). This means that I spent my entire game watching over this one child waiting for her to grow up and see what she becomes - she ended up being a miner in winter and a farmer in summer. I built her her own house and now she has two kids who can go to school!
The game also runs very smoothly, I have had no bug or crashes happen to me, sometimes the weather slows the game down but that is about it. The only downside I can think of is that the interface does not zoom in and the text is quite small and hard to read. That may be a serious problem for some and I hope they fix it soon!

This is one of the best games of all time.
A seamless blend of tactical RTS and vehicle simulator, it pits you, a naval carrier/factory and a crew of dead soldier stored on computer chips against a mad Cabal of arms dealers and evil politicians hellbent on making war against a world that has been completely demilitarized. Your journey takes you through a chicane of 20 islands in the South Pacific as you investigate and dismantle the Cabal's operations.
The storyline, written by famous comicmaker Warren Ellis and narrated by legendary Doctor Who veteran Tom Baker, is very deep and engaging, and makes you genuinely care about both your crew and vessel, and the helpless world you are protecting. I won't give away any spoilers but suffice it to say there are far worse things hiding in those islands than 20-year-old tanks and gunships, and by the end you'll experience quite a few genuinely scary moments.
The gameplay is, as I said, quite seamless, without a single bug. Steam integration could be better however: the Overlay isn't working so you can't take screenshots and it doesn't log your game time (which is why it says up there that I've played 0 hours of it), and as of yet there is no Steam Cloud support. We can only hope. However, the root game is quite well-rounded and optimized. The AI, especially that of your uploaded soldiers, is competent without making you feel unnecessary; there's always a situation where you're better off taking the wheel yourself. Graphics-wise, quite amazingly, the game looks rather good, especially given how old it is, and it will run without a problem on any machine.
You have absolutely no reason to deny yourself this amazing game.
100/10 Recommended!

I'm not ashamed to admit that seeing this on the store page managed to raise a smile, along with more than a few happy memories of this absolute gem of a game from back in the day. Despite having this beauty on what we old timers refer to as a 'CD', (look it up kids!), I could not resist picking it up right away.
Any game that puts you in direct control of a nicely varied selection of modular vehicles then sets you free to cause mayhem and destruction throughout a well written & voiced campaign mode is worth a look. Steadily escalating your capabilities in a brilliantly paced way that ties directly into the plot throughout will make it well worth your time.
Adding to this tapestry is an ever increasing rosta of varied AI wingmen which all work under and alongside you to their own unique strengths and personalities. Making the very means of their inclusion a major plot point & using them to add some character to the overall campaign is a great touch. An early example of these would be your typical grizzled tank commander who will chew you out if given anything less than an artillery cannon to pound his enemies into dust with.
Yes, the characters are often familiar, but very cleverly done as this serves to guide you as to where they would be best suited on the battlefield. When put into their prefered roles, they truly do shine. Showing off some incredible ai for the day, they will carry out their roles with an impressive degree of independance. With their battle chatter and relevant feedback to you and each other adding yet another layer to their realism, they help make your typical mission feel extreemly vibrant and organic.
If only you could provide the player with an unbelivably intuitive command system for said wingmen, allowing you to issue on-the-fly instructions to these guys & gals.. who would then act on those orders in a contextually sensible way the likes of which are rarely seen even today. Yeah, you can do that. Want that hovertank to guard your resource collecter? 3 buttons. Transport chopper to bring your laser turret to high ground? 3 buttons. Deranged chopper pilot to provide you air support? Well you get the idea. All easilly done whilst blasting enemy factories/dodging missiles/going sightseeing.
Not a fan of sending commands whilst in the thick of it? Relax and enjoy the accessable yet thoroughly satisfying command overview screen where you can issue units waypoints, co-ordinate attacks, set up resource gathering, construction queues, and transport duties etc from the comfort of your very own holo-map thing.
get back into the thick of it and blow the absolute hell out of stuff whilst you watch your masterplan unfold around you.
The sheer ambition behind this game managed to light a fire under me all those years ago, a fire which has been rekindled by simply seeing it on the store front. A genuine classic which I would put up on a pedestal beside the likes of Deus Ex & would not hesitate to recommend to anyone. If for no other reason than to get a good idea of what a game created by true talent and vision can -and should- feel like.
My only gripe is the lack of options to extend the life of the campaign after that first, (awesome), playthrough. Oh, and I'd absolutly
for a good multiplayer mode :)
