Let me start off by saying this game is a MASTERPIECE. It brings back so much nostalgia and so many good memories of the good old days of 3d platformers. It's like Banjo Kazooie, Super Mario 64, Psychonauts, and all the beauty of platformers had a baby. Okay, now into the review.
POSITIVE:
It starts off with the most adorable story and light hearted tone. You start in Mafia Town and it's not colorless drivel, it's a world full of color and enemy types, collectibles, vaults, different mechanics and characters. It's the perfect introduction to a game that's so simple, yet can be brought into the speedrunning and complicated scene so easily, just like SM64. You start off with the Kid's Hat, which lets you see objectives; It's so helpful to see where you're supposed to go, yet you have so much freedom it's grand. You can gain up to 5 more hats as you progress, all with their own special mechanics. For example the sprint hat lets you run and the brewing hat lets you throw explosive potions. Even these two hats have so many applications, and it's just the beginning. Oh! And I almost forgot. This game controls exactly like SM64, Super Mario Sunshine, or Super Mario Galaxy would. It has a double jump, a dive, dive cancel, wall jumps, and the mechanics just keep getting more and more complex. For example slowing down time and using a grappling hook. Speaking of the grappling hook, there are badges in this game that you can equip (Up to 2 and 3 of them in the late game) that give you new and different things you can do. Again, for example there's the Item Magnet Badge which attracts nearby collectibles and the Hover Badge that saves you from taking fall damage. There's also negative or trash Badges that give bad effects. For example there's the 1-Hit Hero Badge that makes your HP sink to 1. These negative badges are merely to add challenge to the already rough 3d platformer. Plus, there's a plethera of "Time Rifts", aka special hidden stages, like in SM Sunshine. At the end of every level and rift there's a Time Piece (Or a star in Mario language) which you can use to unlock more acts and worlds. Also at the end of every Time Rift there's a slot machine that gives you cosmetics and tracks, making it able to customize your game, your character, adding your own flair to things. So far as the games' length and replayability, I played the game for a solid 14 hours and I still haven't found everything or completed all the achievements. Character-wise, they're all so lovable and they all have their own personality. Like Mustache Girl, who wants to be the hero of the story and destroy evil. (Mostly the Mafia) The controls are very tight and responsive, and if you mess up your inputs, the game most definitely punishes you. The soundtrack is beautiful and suits the game so very well. Now enough of my rambling and onto the negatives.
NEGATIVE:
I've searched almost every corner of the maps and I've seen only a few glitches and bugs. Which in this day and age is good, yet doesn't mean it's acceptable. I've seen a few T-poses and missing textures, but nothing terribly game-breaking. There's also a lack of explaining advanced mechanics like the speed boost if you cancel your dive when you hit the ground. Plus there's no application for some things, and even if not, sometimes it's only a one time use thing. There's a lack of different physical weapons not counting hats. There's an excessive amount of yarn to the point where it's not even rare. Also everything important glows like a thousand suns, which is nice for newbie players but it's definitely not necessary. I'm not going to talk much about the swimming mechanic because it's literally never used, but it definitely needs some work if it's meant to be a part of the game and not just an instant death.
SUMMARY:
This game is a must get for platformer lovers and fans of the mario franchise.
Graphics: 9/10
Sound: 10/10
World Design: 10/10
AI: 9/10
Dialogue: 7/10
Story: 7/10
Gameplay: 10/10
Overall: 8.9/10
This game is beautiful, rich, and smooth.

One of the finest games to have ever been made, RAGE really did make one heck of a strategy game here. Back in 2000 I picked up the original boxed copy for a mere £10 when it was brand new, the reason I bought it was because in PC Review they said it was a modern day Carrier Command (my favourite game of all time on the PC - 1988), since Carrier Command I have always wanted another game similar to it and RAGE provided a similar experience in a different mould.
Carrier Command was about you taking a Carrier that can create Mantas (planes) and Walrus' (amphibious tanks), you were to travel from island to island and capture them for resources in order to then track down the enemy carrier and destroy it, you need to be aware though as the enemy carrier can also do the exact same thing as you can. Hostile Waters is very similar in the regard that you travel from island to island in order to prepare for destroying the enemy carrier however unlike Carrier Command you don't have any freedom going in between islands, instead each island is a mission.
In both Carrier Command and Hostile Waters you have to go on the islands and recover resources, this is where the games similarities move apart, Carrier Command has supplies sent straight to you depending on what you require at any given moment, short of missiles? Order them from a nearby island and it will be shipped straight to you, in Hostile Waters you instead only receive resources by harvesting them from destroyed objects.
Where Carrier Command is clearly focused on the sea, Hostile Waters makes the island missions superb fun, each island can have bases or something else entirely, having the right preparation in order to carry out your mission is essential and the AI becomes pivotal. Thankfully the AI is brilliantly done, if they're in trouble then they don't just stay there, they'll do what they can to take down the enemy, out maneouvre them and even retreat. The battle chatter makes the missions even better as the AI have conversations between themselves, it makes the feel very real.
Using the mission map to plot out AI behaviour is a breeze to do and it makes you more of a commander than a pilot so you tend to let the AI do what they like to get things done. If you want to take control of their vehicle then that's possible too.
Some of the latter missions are dearthly and really requires you to plan ahead as you will be turned to sushi, having said that though it's not impossible but once you've completed the game you will have perhaps the biggest smile on your face.
Buy the game, play the game, live the game. If I could give a score out of 10 it would be 11!
If you haven't played Carrier Command at all then I highly recommend that too.

This is one of my favourite PC games of all time.
It's pretty much a forgotten gem, which is a great shame. It is a unique game that manages to combine strategy with blowing chunks of metal out of people. It's possible to manually control everything, manually gather resources (like a strategy game), manually shoot at people who would shoot at you (like a dumb tank shooter). Alternatively, you could leave it to the AI and plan your attacks out, just like a strategy game.
This game therefore turns the strategy genre on its head, allowing you to have more direct control over your units. You can have the AI do all the boring stuff, taking land vehicles from the carrier deck to the actual land and then go looking for resources, while you take control of the aircraft taking people out.
As the game goes on, you get cool upgrades, new weapons, armour, different units, all kinds of stuff. You get more AI characters to control your ever growing army, and you'll end up with some intense battles against the hordes of... well, hell if I know. The story is a bit weird. The gameplay is where it's at.
I haven't played a game like this. It's a shame really, this game is really innovative and I would have enjoyed a sequel. Unfortunately, the developers went out of business. Kind of a shame, they started off in my birthplace.
You won't regret buying this game if you like explosions or strategy. Oh, a small bonus since you read this far: hold down the right mouse button when you are in the Antaeus construction room and move your mouse. Ahh, I love random attention to detail!

*Still in early game as of time of writing*
Tales of Zestiria is thus far proving to be a really good PC JRPG. At the time of launch however it has suffered major bugs but kudos to the Steam forum admin who was taking feedback and giving progress on fixes as well as another user who provided his own fix (the individual even helped me personally which was great) but fortunately now the game is pretty stable. It does only run at 30 fps but I don't mind it and sadly it was developed with 30 in mind so increasing to 60 sounds like it wont happen.
The start of the game isn't very promising, just a warning. It starts out with the same story we have all heard before, hand-holding tutorials, and slow-narrative pacing. Give it time though; the game does improve in all those areas. Combat opens up as you get your party together (most of the games party joins in the first chapter of the game), the narrative and characters become more developed and interesting beyond their trope-like first impressions, and the combat becomes very easy to learn, difficult to master.
As of right now, my biggest complaint has to be equipment and items. They are overly complex to the point where it breaks pacing. Same name items now may have different stats, they can be fused which could make them better or worse, you have a skill sheet too thats tied to equipment that stacks in different ways with each other, etc. I find myself having to stop and take several minutes at a time trying to min-max my equipment trying to figure out what it will mean, what will work, what wont, etc. and it isn't any fun. True, previous games it was boring simple how they were mostly just flat stat upgrades but it was quick and to the point. Here, I'm several hours into the game and I'm still confused how it all works and it's throwing off the pacing where I'm trying to cure a plague from a town only to be stuck wondering why I have a locked skill on my spear because I missed that note on page 13/80 on how equipment works.
So far I would say the game is great dispite the drawbacks. The bugs are mostly squashed with fixes available, and the item system I hate can thankfully be mostly ignored (once I figured that the stats at this point weren't that big a deal it helped my enjoyment immensly) and I'm becoming more invested in the story now. Pretty solid so far, would recommend.
Also on the note of DLC, the game currently has several DLCs in the form of costumes primarily but theres a $19.99 DLC that consists of cheats essentially. Pretty lame but avoidable.
UPDATE: After playing for a while now my opinions haven't changed much but I did start to find myself get into a rhythem and I'm still have fun, so despite the faults it's pretty good overall.

This is one of my top games, often my favorite game, and I will tell you why:
1. It is very difficult for a FPS.  That's a good thing because you must develop real skills to master the realism settings used by most servers.  Awareness, making accurate fire, and taking appropriate cover is more important than reflex, and this attracts a more mature and serious type of gamer than the average FPS out there.  The point being that it provides a more rewarding experience for not providing instant gratification, and this keeps out many lame and immature players.
2. It is a Wargame.  Wargames incorporate game mechanics which simulate real military conflict.  RO2 rewards teams with players who coordinate with their squad members, rewards competent squad leadership, and has a 'commander/team leader/platoon leader' position to coordinate squads, reinforcements, and artillery.  Its very satisfying when it all comes together, and it often does because of the active and serious multiplayer community.
3. Looks good and plays well.
Buyer be informed, the single player campaign is ok, and helps you learn the gameplay and how to control the AI players as a squad leader, but the main event is the online multiplayer game.
If you like WW2 games, FPS games, or Wargames, RO2 is a game for you.

SUPERHOT was reviewed with a code provided by the developer.
SUPERHOT is the most innovative shooter I’ve played in years. SUPERHOT knows this. SUPERHOT even makes a joke out of those exact words at one point during the game, but it’s the truth. There wasn’t a single moment in SUPERHOT where I wasn’t having my mind blown in some way, be it from finding a new way to ruin an enemy’s day or one of the many mid-level fourth wall breaks that elevates SUPERHOT from being something much more than just a stylish shooter and into the realm of pure first person genius.
Sadly, SUPERHOT is short. I had beat SUPERHOT‘s story in just under two hours, and you only unlock new ‘challenge modes’ to play once the main game is complete, most of which are just modifiers for the existing story levels. Still, what there is to play is some of the best FPS gameplay I've ever seen.
SUPERHOT is truly a genius shooter close to rivaling legends, sadly cut down by its minuscule running time.

Fallout 3 is a good game, but it is a bit lackluster. Let's take a look at the pros and cons...
The quests have variety and don't get too boring. Although the minimap and compass is confusing and can be hard to navigate certain places. Certain stretches of land don't have too much happening aside from the occasional NPC, enemy, or location. Fast travel is useful and is going to be used a lot over the game. Another problem with the game is certain places lack more sidequests or interaction with a community after there is a major choice made. A good example of this is Megaton, the first town you encounter. After making a big decision, there is only 1 meaningful sidequest and doesn't give any attention to the town or characters, aside from Three Dog mentioning it on the radio.
Gameplay is solid and with addition of VATS, it does stand out. Don't take VATS seriously, as in it is pretty goofy looking now, but I don't really mind it. Good variety of weapons and armor, so I think they nailed this pretty well. Another complaint is that the game doesn't become challenging. The AI is dumb, they don't hide or take cover from fire. After getting a couple of solid weapons, the gunplay is pretty consistent and no major challenges, not even from the main enemies. The only truly terrifying threat were the Deathclaws, and they are the hardest enemies. However, Deathclaws don't come up in the main quests so you are going to have to look around a bit to see them in action. There is a TON of content available, so that is a plus.
The RPG elements are solid, but there is no "moral grayness" going on, which would be MUCH more interesting. Most choices are blatantly good and bad and you can tell which is which. The Karma system is implemented and tells you if you are a "good" person, or a "bad" person. Depending on how you look a this, it can be a negative since it doesn't let you truly think about what is the best course of action. I don't think it bothered me, so it didn't ruin my experience too much.
Let me tell you straight up, THIS IS NOT OPTIMIZED. It will not run unless you install modifications. After installing them, it runs pretty well, even on a potato computer like mine. The gameplay is smooth and I encountered no lag. Besides the game not running at the beginning.
Fallout is known for its post-nuclear setting and RPG elements. I think the game nails the aesthetic well, but the color palate is lackluster, with only shades of grey, green, and brown. There is also the radio, which is spews out old 40s and 50s songs or patriotic American songs depending on the radio you listen to. You can also hear the effects of your actions on the radio, so it is a great addition to the atmosphere.
People say New Vegas is better and the best modern Fallout game. I have not played NV yet so I cannot tell you if it is better or improved on the problems in Fallout 3.

Despite not recommending this game in review, I do think it had some good things to it.
This is a negative review because I want my opinion clearly visible as to flaws with the game that might stop a purchase.
The game is fun, it's story driven and the combat is actually extremely deep once you find all mechanics to it. (Upon playing 50 hours. It's not extremely deep, but fun)
The flaws to this game is mainly the lack of replayability and decisions.
This game constantly has NPC's say.. "Choose, do this or this"
You'd think this would mean you can make a decision that effects the story, but no.
Your character makes that decision on his own. The developers basically mocking you with the fact that there's a decision, but it means jack♥♥♥♥♥♥to you.
In the first 50% of the game, there is only ONE decision YOU can make. That your character doesn't make for you.
This decision to either build a bridge and night, or day.
If you build it at day, people look at you funny for being so powerful, then the same cutscene plays from if you built it at midnight exactly.
This decision effects nothing ingame.
You can argue that the game isn't about decisions, but then the game shouldn't clearly represent a decision to you as if thay planned to add ingame decisions, but rushed it out instead of making the decisions actually be in the game. None of the other Tales of games gave you these fake, illusions of decisions. It's only this game and it's horrible.
NOW. To anyone who says "This game isn't about decisions, yada yada yada"
The game CLEARLY makes it apear you are making decisions. The game clearly depicts choice and that your character needs to choose to do something, how ever you don't get to make the decision at all. This is probably due to a rushed game. Why else would NPC's literally tell you to decide between two options CONSTANTLY, only to have there not be a real choice.
There was one decision in the entire game, fix a bridge at night or day (Keeping spoilers out of this) Literally, choosing to do it right away in daylight adds 3 seconds to a cutscene. The same cutscene you'd see at night with different lighting. The end.
This game is fun, but disappoint as all hell with decisions MOCKING you with their existence, not allowing your input on what happens.
I will also bring up a very random sidenote.
The 3d models ingame are often hit or miss. The main protaganists walk animation makes him look extremely constipated. (Look it up, you'll have a really good laugh)
The main character is easily the worst model in the game.
The 3d models of npc's all over the game aren't animated. In cities there are 100's of npcs that dont even have idle or breathing animations. They are dolls.

I can most definitely recommend this game to anyone interested to a good JRPG.
It does look decent enough on PC. Not as good as huge engines, but it is very serviceable, light and can probably run on a toaster.
The style used looks good and allows the game to look nice and will probably age well, kinda like Vesperia.
Anime cutscenes are pretty awesome and very well made, a nice step forward compared to previous Tales of games.
A special mention for the Music/OST, as it's just amazing and probably the best soundtrack I've had the pleasure to play with for the past 10 years.
During my playthroughs there were absolutely no occasions where I'd just want to turn off music, whereas in other games it eventually comes down to that.
Gameplay is pretty nice. Might seem overwhelming at first, but normal/simple difficulty settings do not really punish you so you can learn the Fusion stuff at your pace and still progress within the story.
Once you get the hang of it though, it's a very huge and flexible system that allows you to customize your characters however you wish.
The setting and environment is very well established throughout the whole game, and with bits and pieces here and there, the story never feels overwhelming.
Actually, as far as the storyline goes, all we're given are indications, sometimes pressing due to urgency, but most of the times we have a guideline to follow, and that's really how it should be, considering this is supposedly an open world game.
I absolutely loved the side-quest system. As you run around the game, you might find some interesting dialogues. At that point, if it's anything interesting, you can further expand on them by talking to your companion, and then you'll have the option to follow through and complete.
There's no stupid quest log, exclamation marks or other crap to mark it a quest, one of the worst additions of the past 10 years (Thanks WoW!).
It all feels very natural and flows within the game without any issue whatsoever. I had no trouble getting all the sidequests done, at my pace and time, without having to check any quest logs or anything else.
As the story gets to its ending, we're given a decent ending and a follow-through DLC episode (for free if you snag it by Nov 18).
Overall I like what they've done with the setting, story and everything game wise. It's not perfect, but it's still one of the best JRPGs I've played in a long while.
Sure, there are many disputes about many things, but it's still quite worth playing (and I disagree with many of said disputes. Just ignore them, some people have way too much time and nothing to do).

Refunct? More like refund! Hahaha…ha. Nah but seriously for a couple of quid this game aint bad, theres really not much to it though. I suppose its essentially a parkour game, where you jump and bounce off walls to reach higher platforms. They turn green as you land on them and essentially the point is to touch the top of every platform by standing on buttons. This makes more platforms appear for you to jump your way over to. There are a few things that mix things up, elevators and tubes to enter.
Its an insanely simple game, taking me less than an hour to complete fully. The only challenging part was one of the optional collectibles which took some thinking on how to get to. Other than that its not difficult by any stretch, but I don’t think its supposed to be.
I have the feeling the game is essentially fodder for speedrunners to try and blast through as quick as possible as moving efficiently is something you could perfect after some practice. Its more of a colourful relaxing game to those who arent into that kind of thing, good to unwind to I suppose. It is weirdly satisfying to colour all the tiles and there's definitely fun to be had on the way.
Is it worth the price tag? Ehhhh… Yeah just about I guess. A penny more and I’m not sure I could recommend it. I completed it in 48 minutes and I don’t see much reason to go back. Its the sort of game that would benefit from the ability to create user made maps.

I am really happy to own Red Orchestra 2. Unlike most WW2 era games, it stands out. There is a lot of depth and realism packed into an otherwise standard genre that’s been covered a hundred times before. Smart gameplay choices and a clearly dedicated group of developers have given this game more than meets the eye.
Red Orchestra 2 is such a fun multiplayer game. I just want to emphasise that before I continue because I’m constantly thinking about when I can continue playing it again. It’s more than just your standard WW2 shooter that pits two teams against one another and whoever kills the most, wins. Tripwire Interactive have considered other aspects of warfare during the Second World War, to make the game feel genuine, realistic, and most important of all, unique.
I’ll start with the basics. The game is built to be realistic and therefore features a minimal hud, no crosshair, different stances, and even a “scare factor” (but I’ll get into that later). As you move around the battlefield, your character pants and bobs and holds their breath before shooting at the enemy. There’s a decent ADS(aim down the sights) system that is effected depending on which stance you are in, standing, crouching, or prone. You have to manually check the amount of bullets in your weapon and manually reload when you’re dry. You can use cover to hide or peak,  and sprint while crouched to give yourself more cover whilst moving. All these basic functions add intensity to FPS multiplayer that is unmatched in all other games I’ve played.
The game has incredibly large maps to further emphasise the realism that you’re on a battlefield and there are many ways to approach the situations in front of you. You actually have to think about things tactically instead of just running in there and hoping for the best. There are good areas to run to, and bad areas to avoid.
It’s a very team oriented experience. You get to rush trenches with your friends, you get to defend church towers with them, crawl in the mud with them, and a lot of the time get killed with them. The element of teamwork is key to success so if you have a bad team, you’re going to have a bad game. Depending on which team you choose, you can hear different dialogue between your friends and your own character. If you play on the Russian team, everything the German team says will be in German and vice versa if you’re on the German team. The vocal reactions between your character and your teammates is really a great little addition to the realism. They automatically let you know what’s going or express how they’re feeling about things that happen around them. It all makes for a very visceral experience.
So now I will move onto the star of the show, something I like to call the “scare factor”. There’s a little bar above your stamina meter that lets you know how mentally stable your character is. As you get shot at or witness teammates getting killed, this bar will drop, your vision will blur, and your weapon will shake. Even when the artillery comes raining down on you, your characters starts shaking and you feel truly helpless. I love this, it really captures the intensity of war and makes me feel as though I’m right there with him.
The graphics are incredible, utilizing an enhanced version of the Unreal 3 engine to make some of the most atmospheric battlefields I’ve ever seen.
Red Orchestra 2 is not for everyone. It’s a realistic war experience, not COD. Of course there will be many who won’t like it at all, but I’m not one of them (despite the enjoyment I get from COD). If you’re looking for something different and certainly something to remember, this game is for you :)

Tl;dr: Towerfall is one of the best local multiplayer games ever made.
The one thing that stands out about Towerfall is how it utilizes simplicity to an amazing extent - basing the whole game on one simple mechanic of shooting arrows. Sure, different arrows and other powerups keep it fresh, but the core design is so strong - playing without any powerups in a simple map doesn't get boring after the 5000th round. Adding to the variety are the modifiers in Versus mode, which just adds to the number of hilarious deaths.
But make no mistake - multiplayer is very competitive with the *right* opponents (and this is one reason which may put off people - there is no online multiplayer). The game is a good example of easy to get into, hard to master. I'm fortunate enough to have friends who're also into this game, so I've had some pretty tough competition to level up.
The Quests are where Towerfall is at its weakest, but the weakest sections are still pretty strong. The game technically isn't long - if you're good at the game it'll barely take you 4 minutes per level to beat it in Normal without retries. The length, however, comes from the retries. But really, the feeling of beating Ascension in Hardcore mode after the 400th try is priceless.
I'm a bit conflicted about the Dark World expansion though. It's definitely a good expansion, adding 4 new characters and (effectively) 4 single player quests with a restructuring of how quests are played (different arenas as opposed to different rounds in the same arena in the original) - but I'm not sure whether that justifies the price. Multiplayer is almost the same, just with more maps and characters (and since there are no character-specific abilities, that doesn't mean much).
So basically, main game - must buy. Expansion - should buy.

Utterly brilliant, unique concept. Easy to play, but difficult to master. Love the minimalistic-but-detailed art style. Your enemies shatter into hundreds of individual fragments of glass upon death, and firing your gun will cast dynamic shadows that make the game feel incredibly stylized and polished. Can't say I've ever played something I'd refer to as a Puzzle-Shooter before, but this game is insanely fun! Hell yeah I'd recommend this game! The story might only approximate to 2 hours, but there's SO much more. A vast number of challenges, an 'Endless Mode', and more! Even the main menu contains little minigames, etc. Not to mention the fact that perfectionists like me will repeatedly play the same level over-and-over until I nail a perfect run without getting bored. The concept of being behind a computer, behind a computer, is just genius. It's like a combination of Mirror's Edge's art style with The Matrix/Max Payne's bullet-time. Slowly watching a bullet soar past your head as you slice someone in half with a katana feels overwhelmingly badass. There's just so many positive things I could say. Buy this game!

I must admit, I was lured in by this game's interesting Noir art style, the low price tag, episodic format and promise of a rich storyline. However, after only my first session, I can already tell that this game is a great disappointment.
The black-and-white noir aesthetic that seemed so appealing in the screenshots only serves to mask jilted and wooden animations, which in turn highlight the lackluster and sometimes laughable voice acting. The most heinous crime however, is the gameplay, which turns what might otherwise have been interesting tactical TPS encounters into dull and unbelieveable shootouts on rails.
Ultimately, it's clear that this game tried to emulate Telltale's format of dialogue-driven gameplay with meaningful choices affecting an extended storyline, and even though this game isn't buggy or lacking in production values, the strong artwork doesn't make up for the dreadful animation and voicework, the strong concept doesn't make up for the poor gameplay, and unfortunately the whole experience hinders the storytelling to such a degree that you very quickly stop caring about the outcome.
If you like multiplayer battles in Total war, this is a must-have.

I fell in love with Super Mario Sunshine.  This reminds me of that, in all the right ways, from the creative settings through the insanely annoying secret levels, to the seemingly endless array of hidden secrets that are right in front of you.  It's even got the appropriate jaunty music (and I adore the way the music slows down to a crawl when you sit on a chair to admire the view.)
And on top of that it's got half-a-dozen really funny stories that are well-written and stuffed with clever jokes (the first part of Murder on the Owl Express is hilarious.)
Sure, the camera is as annoying as in any of these games (the tree in the spooky village almost made me give up in despair), and the controls are occasionally annoying (when she jumps off the top of a wall-climb and plummets to her death... again.)  But they are minor issues in a game that's as fun as this one is.
We're suddenly in a golden era of PC 3d cartoon platformers, and I couldn't be happier.  But the competition is going to have to work hard to push this one off the top of the pile.

I'm a bit torn.
On one hand I felt compelled and intrigued most of the way through, but on the other hand the game lacked the impact and interactive elements that The Stanley Parable had. The payoff at the end felt severely lacking and I kind of saw the 'twist' (of course there is one) coming. The emotional weight of the story didn't really hit me very hard, which was surprising to me, since I very much identify with the problems being portrayed.
There's absolutely NO meaningful interaction in this game, whereas with The Stanley Parable - even if it was merely the illusion of choice, there was still some value in going different paths.
I did notice some glitches along the way that had me restarting a level once (I actually thought it was done on purpose for a few seconds), which is kind of shocking, considering the deliberately low quality level design.
Overall I enjoyed my few hours with it (it's about 2 hours long). If you have money to spare and you enjoy pressing W (sometimes S) while taking in absurd scenery, listening to a story you have no control over, I'd say give this a go. If, however, you haven't played The Stanley Parable, that is a much better and more interesting game in this genre, and you can safely give this one a pass.

I think this game is quite interesting, however some components felt a bit off.
Lets start with the Pros:
1. Combat (Granted it is good for the most part, I felt fighting magic casters>4 is near impossible. I play on Insane atm. Cons:
1. AI sometimes is extremely stupid(walk infront of enemy with 10% health, stops to cast heal and then dies from enemy attack, etc etc)

3. Story is a bit cheesy esp with the whole "im gonna save the world" from the start [after tutorial town]. Also extremely predictable. Perhaps this is why it is a typical fantasy story game. However I didn't really find out until I died to one the first time and I didn't save for a while. Not really a pro/con but I wish they tell you these things before you die to one.
Overall I give this game 7/10.
If you are in it for the story, I don't recommand it [you'll probably stop playing after 5-15 hrs after seeing how bad the story is]. Otherwise the other things within the game will keep you occupied for a long time and it is fun to fight through the battles & some fun humors from some of the characters.

A Hat in Time is one of this year’s best 3D platformers.
The level design is great. Hat Kid controls smoothly and allows the player to navigate the worlds with ease. Its heavily nostalgic of early collectathon games. As you progress you create hats using yarn you find throughout each world. Each hat has its own unique powers which allow you to further explore and complete levels.
Each world bleeds personality with great visuals; no two worlds are alike. Exploring is rewarded with hidden yarns to unlock hats and some hidden levels that give you timepieces.
The story is quick to the point, get back all your lost timepieces. The characters you meet along the way our well written, humorous, and have some top-notch voice acting.
I REALLY love the soundtrack of this game. It’s upbeat, swingy, and makes you want to dance along. Each piece fits the level well.
I managed to 100% the game in 12 hours. While some might not think thats the longest, I thoroughly enjoyed every minute of it.
All in all, its one of my favourite games of the year, and I would it to recommend anyone looking for a good collectathon game, or even just a good platformer in general.

This is a difficult game to review. Partially because it is so lacking in what could be called gameplay - anything that would justify the title of a game. The creator could have just as easily released the audio track of the narration and comunicated as much story, as much meaning.
It is also difficult because so much of the game is so willingly self-defeating and self-effacing that any critiscism you make of it feels like water off a duck's back. A wet duck's back. A soaking wet water-boarded duck.
And yet I am compelled to review, possibly because I felt like I had sat through an hour and a half of an interactive medium that asked no real interactivity of me other than to simply witness.
I felt like an audience member asked to sit in for the sake of appearences, such was the lack of interactivity on any level. This is, presumably, the author's intent as the subject is about the inability to communicate. Or mabye it is bad at communicating?
The game is a pedestrian tour through solipsism, with brief stops for onanistic wonder at a simple puzzle involving two doors.
This is a game without redeeming qualities that hides behind its intellectualism, hoping that by asking enough questions and posing enough points for you to ponder that you will be wowed into agreeing with it, to loving it in order to be in on the joke.
I found myself dissapointed on every level.

I am really happy to own Red Orchestra 2. Unlike most WW2 era games, it stands out. There is a lot of depth and realism packed into an otherwise standard genre that’s been covered a hundred times before. Smart gameplay choices and a clearly dedicated group of developers have given this game more than meets the eye.
Red Orchestra 2 is such a fun multiplayer game. I just want to emphasise that before I continue because I’m constantly thinking about when I can continue playing it again. It’s more than just your standard WW2 shooter that pits two teams against one another and whoever kills the most, wins. Tripwire Interactive have considered other aspects of warfare during the Second World War, to make the game feel genuine, realistic, and most important of all, unique.
I’ll start with the basics. The game is built to be realistic and therefore features a minimal hud, no crosshair, different stances, and even a “scare factor” (but I’ll get into that later). As you move around the battlefield, your character pants and bobs and holds their breath before shooting at the enemy. There’s a decent ADS(aim down the sights) system that is effected depending on which stance you are in, standing, crouching, or prone. You have to manually check the amount of bullets in your weapon and manually reload when you’re dry. You can use cover to hide or peak,  and sprint while crouched to give yourself more cover whilst moving. All these basic functions add intensity to FPS multiplayer that is unmatched in all other games I’ve played.
The game has incredibly large maps to further emphasise the realism that you’re on a battlefield and there are many ways to approach the situations in front of you. You actually have to think about things tactically instead of just running in there and hoping for the best. There are good areas to run to, and bad areas to avoid.
It’s a very team oriented experience. You get to rush trenches with your friends, you get to defend church towers with them, crawl in the mud with them, and a lot of the time get killed with them. The element of teamwork is key to success so if you have a bad team, you’re going to have a bad game. Depending on which team you choose, you can hear different dialogue between your friends and your own character. If you play on the Russian team, everything the German team says will be in German and vice versa if you’re on the German team. The vocal reactions between your character and your teammates is really a great little addition to the realism. They automatically let you know what’s going or express how they’re feeling about things that happen around them. It all makes for a very visceral experience.
So now I will move onto the star of the show, something I like to call the “scare factor”. There’s a little bar above your stamina meter that lets you know how mentally stable your character is. As you get shot at or witness teammates getting killed, this bar will drop, your vision will blur, and your weapon will shake. Even when the artillery comes raining down on you, your characters starts shaking and you feel truly helpless. I love this, it really captures the intensity of war and makes me feel as though I’m right there with him.
The graphics are incredible, utilizing an enhanced version of the Unreal 3 engine to make some of the most atmospheric battlefields I’ve ever seen.
Red Orchestra 2 is not for everyone. It’s a realistic war experience, not COD. Of course there will be many who won’t like it at all, but I’m not one of them (despite the enjoyment I get from COD). If you’re looking for something different and certainly something to remember, this game is for you :)

I love the Tales series. Every single game in the series I've been able to play has been incredibly compelling from start to finish, and really felt like more than the sum of its parts. Sadly, Zestiria is the exception to that latter part. It's every bit as compelling as most of the series, yet while every element of a Tales game is present and correct, each feels severely undercooked.
The game's characters are perhaps its strongest points, but still fails to reach the bar set by most of the previous games I've played in the series, coming out just ahead of Graces F. The best Tales game feature a protagonist who is both interesting and develops in something other than power as the plot progresses. Yuri and Luke were great examples of this archetype. Jude was not, but Milla as a joint protagonist meant it didn't matter. Sorey (this game's lead) is a bit of an Asbel (from Tales of Graces) - he's simply not interesting. He exists to be the protagonist. There is a hint of potential for Sorey: he grew up surrounded by Seraphim, human-like creatures most humans cannot see. He's never met another human, but is thrust into a great adventure. The stage is set for an nice traditional "small town kid in big city" sort of arc, then completely ignored from about 2 horus into the game. Sorey pooters from place to place, doing as he is told by exposition with little agency of his own.
The rest of the party are thankfully a bit more interesting. The best three characters elevate the weakest, and the interactions of even the weakest characters are still enjoyable to see. Edna steals the show overall, toying with the gullability of the other characters and often coming close to breaking the fourth wall with some sarcastic quips. Lailah's sudden switches from seriousness from serious to carefree are well handled rather than jarring. It's a shame that unlike games like Vesperia, we never learn much about most of the cast. They're slaves to the plot, and not a lot more.
Speaking of that plot, it's all over the place. It's obviously inspired by Arthurian legends - a sword in a stone, round tables, and so on. Yet it doesn't really go anywhere. It's a typical chosen-one-versus-evil plotline for the most part, with few twists. The main antagonist is absent for a huge portion of the game - we're told of their existence, but most of the game sees you trundling about the world Getting Stronger (TM every JRPG ever). For the first third, the game feels as though it *is* building to a reveal, only to send you on a Zelda like quest to 4 temples for the next third and completely ignoring any sort of ongoing buildup altogether, until someone suddenly realised they needed stuff to happen and abrubtly kicks the story into gear again via a bunch of confusing flashbacks leaving me completely confused.
Combat in Zestiria is an interesting one - it's got depths in spades, that much is for sure. You know this, because for the first few horus of the game it resembles a continuous information dump in the form of popup windows explaining things, never to be seen again. It's compeltely bemusing at first, especially as many of the tutorials aren't exactly relevant until later in the game when you have more skills and party members to make use of. A lot of the complexity is wasted on encounters that feel like processions anyway.
The core is split in two - the first half sees you control a single character in real time. You can perform dodges and attacks in chains of four. Each uses up some spirit chain (SC), which at a basic level recharges when you're not attacking. To reduce the waiting and encourage aggressive play, successful attack dodges refill SC. You can extend action chains beyond four by spending part of your Blast Gauge (BG) to do a special sort of atack, itself refilled by guarding and dodging. It's a cool system that generally rewards agressive battles.
The second half is the Armatus - spending a BG to combine your controlled character with another party member. You get super powerful elemental attacks, lots of health and it looks awesome. The bigger your combo when you activate it, the more damage you do initially. Sadly, after the combat clicks, we get the procession I mentioned above: for every encounter, your partner with the Seraph matching your enemy's weakness, build a combo then Armatize to win. BG is so plentiful, there's little reason not to Armatize to ease through fights quickly. And you'll want to, because you'll be fighting a lot.
Part of this constant fighting is due to the dungeon design, which apparently exists in 2 types. Story dungeons are at least reasonably unique, especially the elemental temples. They have a few interesting puzzles here or there, and are pretty good fun to get through. However, many are visually similar - there's far too many long hallways and open rooms and not a lot else outside of the elemental temples, and little in the way of interesting visuals. The side dungeons are worse: cut and paste collections of corridors and open spaces that go on, and on, and on. They're dull trudges from easy fight to easy fight, that get longer and longer as the game goes on.
The visual blandness in dungeons is a shame, as the game can look quite pretty outside of them. The pre dungeon field areas are almost universally home to interesting layouts and fun to explore. Initially gloomy, restoring blessings makes them look alive and beautiful. Pendrago's exterior is a real highlight. It makes entering the average dungeon a disappointment, because it means another hour of trudging through corridors.
Finally, the skill system. I mentioned the barrage of tutorial popups earlier, but the undisputed champion of poor explanation is the skill system. To attempt to explain it, each piece of equipment will boost two stats, and has four slots for skills. Each skill has an element and a group. Each element corresponds to arow on a grid, and groups correspond to a column. Equipping gear fills in your skill grid with the skills on the equipment. The idea is you equip gear such that you fill in 3-in-a-row, 5-in-a-column, or stack multiple of the same skills. This boosts their effects, and bestows powerful bonus skills - fill in the first column for a character, and all stats get a 20% boost. You can fuse together items of the same type to combine their skills and improve their stats.
It's a cool idea, but hamstrung because the amount of grinding it will take to deliberately make rows and columns makes it far more effective to just equip whatever gear gives the right character the right stats and treat skill matches as a happy accident. Mechanics are in place to boost drop rates and the chance of dropped gear having specific skills, but it's not a fun prospect fighting the same enemies over and over hoping that the right type of gear will drop for the right character, with the right skill for hours at a time, knowing that you'll get stronger gear eventually anyway and have to do it all again.
So that's Tales of Zestiria. Recognisably a Tales game, and there's fun to be had for JRPG fans. But aside from some cool ideas (seriously, battles taking place on the overworld/dungeon itself rather than in a seperate arena is a great touch), the entire game feels sorely undercooked.

The simplicity of the controls in LIMBO perfectly complement its intelligent and varied puzzle design. Unlike in fellow artsy platformer Braid, the puzzles are not immediately challenging to comprehend; instead, the conundrums in LIMBO encourage noticing detail, becoming familiar with the odd logic of the world, and sometimes throwing yourself to the void without fear.
Each "level" is almost modular in design, with checkpoints generously placed. It's clear that LIMBO is intended to be an experience; an example of art, rather than simply a masochistic rite-of-passage.
Even so, LIMBO is not without challenge: dozens of gruesomely-silhouetted deaths are all but guaranteed on your first time through; but LIMBO's level of forgiveness makes true frustration rare.
Though it may feel somewhat short (at about 3-6 hours in length), and despite being a bit artsy-fartsy for some tastes, LIMBO is presented with a polish, certainty, and subtlety that makes its unabashed gloominess a joy.

First off, i'd like to point out a major issue you need to know before buying this game.
RPG Maker VX Ace runs in an extremely small 640x480 window that's hard to see on most large computer screens. There is a hidden fullscreen option but it stretches everything to fit your screen, has an awful framerate, and just overall looks bad. While that may not seem like such a bad thing, once you buy the game and are stuck leaning towards your screen just to see your character sprite, i'm sure you will change your mind.
This is just the beginning of the problems with RPG Maker: VX Ace.
Another large problem with this game in my opinion is the lack of in-game custom tilesets and sprites. Don't get me wrong; you can create your own characters and tilesets, but hence the word "in-game". If you were expecting RPG Maker VX Ace to be that easy, then you are wrong. There isn't an in-game tile creator so in order to import custom tiles and sprites you have to make them inside of a photo editing software, which not everyone has. Even then, RPG Maker requires sprite sheets and tilesets so you can't make individual graphics; They have to all be an exact size in an exact order. This makes downloading a template almost required for every graphic in your game; and it gets pretty annoying.
The level designer is not bad. You have some tiles that you can click to select and place on a square grid and it feels alright. The action mode is surprisingly fun and easy to use that adults and children of all ages should be able to easily understand.
RPG Maker VX Ace is both efficient and inefficient. Most of the program is easy as it looks, but some of the most vital parts in creating a great RPG game does not follow that same efficiency. If you don't mind having to squint to see your finished game, and are willing to download a few templates and plugins for photoshop, maybe this game will be good for you. But what I know is for sure, is that it came close to being a fantastic RPG creating experience. It just didn't quite make the cut for me.

Even after almost 20 years, the original UT remains a satisfying run-and-gun arena shooter with a ton of quirky weapons and interesting levels. There's no questioning it's harder on the eyes than its competitor from the era, Quake III, but it also had more gameplay modes, more features, and better bots than Quake III did, which is why it captured my attention in a way the admittedly purer shooting experience of Quake III never did. The sequels certainly each had their merits - who doesn't love running people over with the absurd vehicles in 2004? - but the 1999 original will always hold a place in my heart, both for nostalgic and earnestly-held gameplay reasons.

One of the best things about A Hat in Time is how the character plays. It's just so fun to bounce around as Hat Kid, climbing up walls, throwing potions, changing your hat in real-time to use different abilities. They put a lot of effort into the fluid controls, and it shows. There's so many fun techs and abilities you can use to jump, climb, and dive your way through the levels.
Some people criticize the length, but those are the same people who rush to 25 Hourglasses required for the ending instead of getting a 100% clear file. This can easily take you about 20 hours, and don't forget that they're adding more worlds as free DLC due to a stretch goal reached in the Kickstarter.
All in all, A Hat in Time is one of the best indie games I have ever played, and I can whole-heartedly recommend it to just about anyone.

At its core, Just Cause 2 is a pretty bog standard sandbox game. The gunplay is serviceable, and there's plenty of scenic vistas to visit. The grappling hook even adds some interesting twists to the standard formula, and makes getting around a bit more fun than it might otherwise be, although it is slightly clunky at times. If this were the full experience I came out of this game with, I would probably give this a recommendation.
Unfortunately, there are some definite issues with the design of the game. There's three types of collectibles, and entirely too many of each of them, which makes trying to 100% the game a dull slog. You pretty consistently feel underarmed, especially if you're playing on higher difficulty levels. A lot of the areas are very samey, and there's a lot of repitition in missions.
Even with all that, though, I could have still had fun with the game, at least enough to suggest buying it when there's a good sale. I quickly reached a point where any fun the game might have provided just completely evaporated. The game has a tendency to toss escort missions at you like they're candy. Now, I don't have the level of hatred for escort quests that some people have. They can be done well. Not in this game, however.
Escort missions in this game follow this pattern: Advance, find some enemies, hope you can kill them before they AI becomes suicidally inept, repeat until the mission is over. Sadly, the ally AI will usually give you about five seconds before running out of cover to get shot down by a hail of enemy gunfire. Sure hope you can get instant headshots on half a dozen enemies, otherwise it's only a matter of time before your allies are whittled down to nothing and the person you're escorting gets shredded.
Up until these escort missions, I was having a pretty good time playing this game. The absurd ally AI accompanying the preponderance of these missions just left a sour taste in my mouth. I was lucky enough to get this on sale with all the DLC and the original Just Cause for about $4, and I already feel I overpaid. Maybe others have had a better experience, but personally, I can't recommend purchasing the game, even with a substantial discount.

).

Third: the music. The music is AWESOME. You can even collect different types of versions of specific songs. Mafia towns song has bit of italian vibe to it. The spooky Subcon Forest has some scary melodies in it. They did really great music for the game. I really love the music of chapter two.
Fourth: The gameplay feels just right. The controls aren't overly mapped, so you can play it with a controller. They feel just nice and comfortable. The visuals give some great punch to some actions like throwing explosives or punching a critter with your weapon.
But for such a great game, there are also some flaws, like sometimes spazing cameras or a bit too annoying wall climbs (only in small spaces). But those are tiny flaws, which don't even affect the game all too bad

HONEST REVIEW:
I have been in contact with the developer of this game, Studge.
He is possibly the most down to earth and polite developer I have ever known and it's good to see that there are developers that don't just make games as money grabs and they still put true effort into their games.
I will update my review if I come accross anything that I haven't covered in this review already.
Firstly, the music is designed very well, it is very immersive for a pixel art medieval game. The sound effects along with the music fit in well and it adds a nice atmosphere to the game.
Secondly, the graphics of the game are well suited for this genre of strategy platformer. It is clear cut and is appealing to the eye. The colour palette of this game is well thought out because it creates a very good atmosphere for this chirpy yet serious pixel art game.
Thirdly, the gameplay, controls and UI. The gameplay is refreshing, it is nice to see a platformer that can achieve this, you feel a sense of importance when you win a game because of how a match is fought out. You can upgrade your player thoughout the match with multiple upgrades that can help him in the battle which is nice to see. The controls are responsive and you can bind your own controls which the developer of this game added after this was a sought after thing. And the UI, I really like how clear the UI is however the only thing I can bash it for is the minimap, the minimap is a bit constricting because you can't see the terrain of the map, it's only the towers and you. But I have been talking to the developer of the game and he seems open about proposals for changing elements of the game.
Apart from the minimap the only other problem that I have with the game is the connection to multiplayer games, at the moment I haven't had many problems as I was able to connect to some but not others. The developer of the game is getting this fixes ASAP and he is currently finding out what the problem is.
Another thing constricting it at the moment is that there is only one map to choose, however the developer is thinking about developing another type of map for the game possibly in an upcoming update.
In conclusion, the game is only £2.79/$4.00 and for this price I would highly recommend buying it and getting your friends to get it aswell as it can be quite fun with a large group.
TLDR:
Pros:
Developer is open about his game and is open for suggestions for his game
Music and sound effect are immersive and add to the feel of the game
Graphics suit this type of game
Gameplay is refreshing
Controls are responsive
UI is clear
Well price once multiplayer is fully functional
Cons:
The minimap on the UI needs some improvement because it doesn't show terrain
Multiplayer is on and off at the moment
Only one map at the moment
*REMEMBER*: The game is still in it's early stages so it is constantly being improved and I will update this review along with the progress of the game.

So, I've been around the block with the Tales series since 1999 after playing Tales of Destiny. With the series constantly hanging around the Playstation consoles while also having some appearances on Nintendo systems and one appearance on the Xbox 360, a PC version of a Tales game was something I thought would never happen. But here I am reviewing the first Tales game to appear on Steam. If anything, the game itself, while flawed, isn't as bad as people made it out to be, particularly during the original Japanese PS3 release of it, and as a PC port, does put its best foot forward despite some issues.
The Tales series isn't really known for pushing system specs to the limit, but the visuals do have a vibrant look to them with small details of leaves blowing in the wind in the fields.
With the music of Graces & the two Xillia games, I did feel like Motoi Sakuraba was pretty much phoning it in for those installments. Zestiria was a huge improvement in the music department this time thanks to Go Shiina contributing tracks alongside Sakuraba. While I actually hold the unpopular opinion that Go Shiina's previous soundtrack contribution to the series, Tales of Legendia, isn't really all that great, his talent really shines for me this time with some great dungeon music.
The story had some controversy because of how one particular character was handled. After seeing it for myself, it was nothing to really freak out about. The story itself, for better or worse, does follow typical Tales quality (I did enjoy it though). The character are likable and engaging, though it's also on the typical Tales quality, for better or worse.
Now, for the highlight of the series, its real time battle system. It's like a simplified fighting game, moving the character, linking attacks together to combo the enemy in real time movement. This time, the battles are done on the same exploration screen. However, there's issues with the camera, specifically if the area you're in battle at happens to be a narrow corridor. The camera will be too zoomed in for you to assess the battle field until you move into a better location. There's no way to rotate the camera during the battle (the best you get would be in the menu). It's not enough to condemn the game, but it's going to be an issue at certain times. The battle system is still as fun as ever as you combo the enemies to grind for experience & money.
As far as the PC port is concern, I'll deal with the elephant in the room and say that it's a bummer that it was locked at 30 FPS but I was able to live with it. Outside of that, the port does have the graphics tweaking option that is supposed to be there, along with keyboard & mouse support to the point where you can navigate the menu using the mouse cursor.
Overall, the game was not as bad as it was made out to be. The story is pretty much not high literature and can be enjoyable alongside the characters with the typical Tales quality. The battle system still shines as bright as it ever has despite some issues. If you can handle that this PC port locked the framerate at 30, I can still give this a recommendation.

Rather than asking why would I recommend this software, the better question is why would I not?
Granted, my thoughts on the software is a bit biased because it was a part of my childhood (RPG Maker for the PS1), but RPG Maker is still a great software for those wanting to brave that which is game development and make their own old-school RPG they've always wanted to growing up. The software is easy to use, and there are many resources available both here on Steam, the official site, and on the internet.
Now keep in mind, like with most development tools, you'll need art, music, and sounds. Assets to make your project unique and stand out from the stock assets included with the software. There's also the programming side, which involves understanding Ruby and how it functions in RPG Maker if you want to do more than use scripts created by other people for battle systems and such. This is the real work, and with enough time and effort anyone can make something great.
Just to give you some idea, look at Corpse Party. Created with RPG Maker in 1996 on the PC-9801, it was popular enough for two remakes (one on windows while the other on the PSP and iOS), two sequels, adapted into four manga series, even being used in a theme park attraction in Japan.
Now I'm not saying that everyone that buys these products can make something that explodes into something like that, but there's always that potential to make something great as long as you're serious about it.

Superhot is a first person shooter with a very interesting and satisfying mechanic
The main focus of Superhot, is that time only moves when you move. Fortunately, the game constantly keeps things fresh, so the time mechanic doesn't feel gimmicky or boring.
You and you enemies both die with one bullet, which makes things quite intense, and prevents the time thing from being too overpowered.
The game gives you a wide range of moves to make you feel like a badass. You may throw your gun or any random object like a statue at an enemy to temporarily stun them. In doing so, they will also drop their weapon. That gives you a chance to take the weapon and kill opponents, or just beat them to death while they're vulnerable.
There's a decent variety when it comes to weapons. Katanas, pistols and shotguns are just a few. The great thing is if you can use them, be sure that they can be used against you.
The game is very stylized. Enemies shatter into small crystal-like pieces, and text flashes on the screen as if you're playing an interactive trailer. There's no HUD, so even when you run out of ammo, your only indication is AFTER you have gotten ready for a shot, and pulled the trigger. The text will tell you you're out, and you have to discard the gun. It all makes for some really intense fights.
The game can actually be quite slow-paced at times. Almost like a strategy or puzzle game. You need to minimize your movements to avoid forwarding time much, or zig-zag dodge bullets.
At the end of every level, you have a chance to save a replay in case you did something cool.
There's actually quite an interesting story that I don't want to go into, because it's best unspoiled. Don't expect a focus on story, but it's nice that it's there.
The main game was quite short. Took me about 2 hours to beat, but there are a lot of challenges that increase replay value for you, and an endless mode where you can put your skills to the test. The gameplay is satisfying enough to make me want to go through and complete those.
Overall, it's such an awesome game. It's incredibly satisfying, and makes you feel like an action hero. If you like the look of it, then you have to play this game, I've never seen anything like it before.

The game is presented to the player using only grayscale colours, ambient noise and without any (explicit) story. And yet, I found the immersion to be immense. You play as an unnamed boy in search of your sister in the world of LIMBO. LIMBO is not a friendly place, especially not for a child on his own. We have been insensitised to death by games. But this game goes where no other games dare go: the death of children. The boy constantly has to keep his guard up, because death lurks around every corner. In this dangerous world such a boy is extremely feeble and as death inevitably gets his grip on him it is extremely discomforting to see it happen. The developers described this game as requiring "trial and death." No matter how many times you die, it feels as horrible as it did the first time. This grim game brings no joy, and yet I strongly urge you to experience it. You will not have experienced anything like it. Games are rarely ever described as art, but this it. This is art.

This game is a cascade of emotions.
There are moments of genuine surprise and laughter at a good joke, amusement from the communal way that everyone can join in on a light-hearted joke and take each other's lead, clever wit, playful banter, sharp hecklers and sharper roasters.
There are wonderfully moving and highly proficient musical performances, as well as jaw-dropping displays of talent from lightening-fast rappers and rhythmically complex beatboxers.
There are people who actually engage in debate and challenge each other to employ their critical thinking skills.

At its core, Just Cause 2 is a pretty bog standard sandbox game. The gunplay is serviceable, and there's plenty of scenic vistas to visit. The grappling hook even adds some interesting twists to the standard formula, and makes getting around a bit more fun than it might otherwise be, although it is slightly clunky at times. If this were the full experience I came out of this game with, I would probably give this a recommendation.
Unfortunately, there are some definite issues with the design of the game. There's three types of collectibles, and entirely too many of each of them, which makes trying to 100% the game a dull slog. You pretty consistently feel underarmed, especially if you're playing on higher difficulty levels. A lot of the areas are very samey, and there's a lot of repitition in missions.
Even with all that, though, I could have still had fun with the game, at least enough to suggest buying it when there's a good sale. I quickly reached a point where any fun the game might have provided just completely evaporated. The game has a tendency to toss escort missions at you like they're candy. Now, I don't have the level of hatred for escort quests that some people have. They can be done well. Not in this game, however.
Escort missions in this game follow this pattern: Advance, find some enemies, hope you can kill them before they AI becomes suicidally inept, repeat until the mission is over. Sadly, the ally AI will usually give you about five seconds before running out of cover to get shot down by a hail of enemy gunfire. Sure hope you can get instant headshots on half a dozen enemies, otherwise it's only a matter of time before your allies are whittled down to nothing and the person you're escorting gets shredded.
Up until these escort missions, I was having a pretty good time playing this game. The absurd ally AI accompanying the preponderance of these missions just left a sour taste in my mouth. I was lucky enough to get this on sale with all the DLC and the original Just Cause for about $4, and I already feel I overpaid. Maybe others have had a better experience, but personally, I can't recommend purchasing the game, even with a substantial discount.

This is a great game.  It's a combination of telltale-style light adventure, detective investigation, and some arcade shooting.  It has great camera work and voice acting, and the script is far better than average.  It has some nice takes on cutscenes and flashbacks which avoid you having to sit passively and watch.  For example, one is a gunfight using words from the narration as cover.  The game takes place in a fantasy ganster city that is inspired by history, though some details are changed.  For example, the floating Hindenburg (or possibly a tribute) is now gigantic and a lavish hotel.
In this game, Al Capone is alive and relatively healthy after his jail term.  His granddaughter has been kidnapped, and Capone recruits a retired detective to find her.  Weird cultists and violent murderers are involved in some way.
So, it's a beautiful game, and I like it very much, which is why I'm recommending it.  However, it has some problems which will be deal-breakers for many.  They aren't for me, but I'm going to discuss them so you will be informed.  First, the game is incomplete.  Two episodes have been released at the time of this review.  The game has a huge vision and (apparently, speaking as an outsider) a tiny budget.  There was a long time between episodes one and two, and it's been a long time since episode two with no news.  I personally am only buying episodes one at a time because of this.
Secondly, the controls are very sluggish.  We can say the main character is a man who never hurries, but in truth the character's movement is very restricted, and it can be difficult to get him where you want him to go.  Investigating crime scenes requires you to move in front of hot spots with the left stick and then move the right stick until you are directly facing the clickable area.  You can see the button prompt, but you can't use it until you are in exactly the right place, which gets frustrating.
Thirdly, there are some smaller issues.  Don't expect accurate history from the game.  And, prepare for accents that are all over the map.  It helps that the game is not set in a real city, but I was still annoyed that only one character sounds close to being from Chicago.  The game really earns its age rating, so don't expect the violence to be stylish.  It's pretty gross in spots.  Finally, the animation is not great, just okay.

Plot +
Voice Work +

Detective Mechanics  +
Pacing/Immersive Techniques +
Rampant Gore +/-
Animation -
Unfinished Game -

Inaccurate as Nonfiction -

A Hat in Time is one of this year’s best 3D platformers.
The level design is great. Hat Kid controls smoothly and allows the player to navigate the worlds with ease. Its heavily nostalgic of early collectathon games. As you progress you create hats using yarn you find throughout each world. Each hat has its own unique powers which allow you to further explore and complete levels.
Each world bleeds personality with great visuals; no two worlds are alike. Exploring is rewarded with hidden yarns to unlock hats and some hidden levels that give you timepieces.
The story is quick to the point, get back all your lost timepieces. The characters you meet along the way our well written, humorous, and have some top-notch voice acting.
I REALLY love the soundtrack of this game. It’s upbeat, swingy, and makes you want to dance along. Each piece fits the level well.
I managed to 100% the game in 12 hours. While some might not think thats the longest, I thoroughly enjoyed every minute of it.
All in all, its one of my favourite games of the year, and I would it to recommend anyone looking for a good collectathon game, or even just a good platformer in general.

How do you recommend a game without revealing almost a thing about it?
Reviewers often struggle with how to write about a game as spoiler-free as possible. With most games, you can describe gameplay, graphics, music, and other aspects of the content in vague, generalized fashion. I am kind of at a loss to how to that with The Beginner's Guide.Professional reviewers have an established level of trust and a track record that allows the gamer to at least gauge whether a recommendation on a game probably means they will also like it. I'm a nobody, so I am not afforded that. But I would still be doing anyone reading this a disservice by spoiling a single aspect of The Beginner's Guide.
In its simplest form, this is another walking simulator by Davey Wreden, the man who made The Stanley Parable, one of the most highly regarded walking simulators of all time. Walking simulators carry a stigma about them. One of the earliest popular walking simulators I ever played was Myst, a game that came out in 1993. Criticisms of Myst at the time almost perfectly mirror the criticisms some express towards them today. The debate of "is this even a game" is nothing new. It is not some new question players are suddenly arriving at since Dear Esther, Gone Home, and the rest brought the genre back in vogue.
The player at the end of a walking simulator can, at least in my opinion, identify if the game was successful based on a simple question: could the content be conveyed as well through another medium such as a book or a movie, or was the interactive aspect of a video game vital to the content? To that end, the video game format is even more necessary to The Beginner's Guide than The Stanley Parable. Like The Stanley Parable, there is narration over the course of the game. This time it is provided by the author. However, the narration and the content are at odds with each other, increasingly so throughout the game. What the player draws from that is ultimately up to them, as you will reach the end of the game the same way no matter what.
To be blunt, this game may resonate with you in some important way, and it may not. That is not to suggest that this is meant to be a complex narrative. Rather, the game is about delivering some very direct, personal messages through abstract means. It is as much about the messages it is trying to convey as the difficulty in the means of conveying them. It is both an existential crisis in electronic form and a simple statement of "do with this what you will." And what you draw from it depends on the player. Whether you're an artist, game creator, or just a fan of video games, there are different aspects of the content that will be more relevant to you.
My greatest recommendation for The Beginner's Guide is to read as little as you need to before playing it. That is not so much about avoiding story spoilers, but because this is an experience every gamer should have for themselves. Take the opportunity to develop your own thoughts on it before reading the interpertations of others. Once finishing the game, whether you like it or not, your time will have not been wasted. One would be hard pressed to come away from the game without at least a few thoughts on it. My Steam play time was 80 minutes, and at $9.99 (currently discounted at $7.99), that is a valuable use of your equivalent lunch money.

I don't like giving short reviews that just say "I don't like it" but... there's really nothing else to say about the game because there's nothing else in the game to talk about.  There are achievements for getting big enough chains, but outside of that, there's literally nothing to strive for, you just match things because you've been trained to match things by other matching games up until you realize the game has no feedback and doesn't care, and you shouldn't either.  Some of the other reviews call this "relaxing", but I honestly never felt Bejeweled was terribly stressful enough to start with that it required a version with no levels, win, or lose condition.
