This game suffers from a few design issues. Much of this game consists of overly large areas with high ceilings, but said spaces feel empty when there's little but one or two enemies to occupy them. The cities look all too uniform, with no real distinguishing features to set them apart from one another, and this only gets worse inside building-dungeons, where the color schemes of the walls/floors/ceilings are so similar that you feel like falling asleep just looking at them.
The game is locked at 30FPS, and this doesn't have much effect on the game. However, there are times when it's quite noticable, like in the animations of distant enemies, as well as a close up few enemies with particularly fast animations (bats for instance). Minor graphical glitches are evident, but not more than you'd expect from a new release. Aside from that, it performs well. As an added bonus, the game supports resolution scaling tools like NVidia's DSR flawlessly.
That said, this game is a worthy successor to the "Tales of..." series (as well as a solid JRPG, something Steam is short on), and while it isn't my favorite of the lot, I feel like my money was well spent here. There's plenty of things to collect around every corner, from stat-boosting herbs to equipment-improving creatures called Normins. Difficulty can be raised or lowered at any time, and range from child-friendly levels to unfairly difficult.
And in true JRPG fashion, don't sink too much love and grinding into the Aerith, because she leaves you at the end of disc 1.

Spoilers for like the whole game ahead.
Ok, so, for starters, I guess for the elephant in the room: YouTuber JonTron has a voice role, and the dev team has been quiet about it so take that as you will. Even though JonTron is a terrible person, it's not a dealbreaker for me, though a statement by the devs would really be appreciated. I do wanna put that out there as a disclaimer, though, so people are informed.
With that out of the way, this game is really good. The best thing about it is probably how varied it is. Every world has a vastly different mission structure: Chapter 1, Mafia Town, is pretty straightforward initially, but after you're "done" with it and beat the Mafia boss, it gets more open, especially with it containing a Mission you need a Chapter 4 powerup to beat. Thankfully, the game tells you on the Mission Select Screen if you lack something you need to progress. Chapter 2, Battle of the Birds, takes place in a few more linear areas as opposed to Mafia Town's island. Additionally, there's two paths, each for a movie director who wants to make the best movie, and your perfomance in those levels determines who wins, which impacts the boss fight at the end of the chapter. Chapter 3, Subcon Forest, has mostly linear missions, but the world is probably the most open (and sometimes confusing) of the game. The catch here is that you have to sign contracts before you can access missions, so you have to commit to what you do. Chapter 4, Alpine Skyline, is completely open with no selectable missions and isntead only a "Free Roam" option. You can get the 4 main Time Pieces in this world in any order. Chapter 5, Time's End, is only a linear gauntlet with one level.
Chapter 1, 2 and 3 are all very good, with Chapter 2 being the best in the game due to the variety. You have to solve a murder mystery on a train, gain a penguin fanclub and run away from a deadly parade. Chapter 3's dark undertones (for instance, there's a noose trying to talk you into suicide and an absolutely terrifying haunted mansion) make it a close second, though, with it mostly being held back by the confusing and samey layout. You definitely learn it, but it's unintuitive compared to Mafia Town or Alpine Skyline. Alpine Skyline has some really nice challenges, but it feels like it's missing something, especially near the end where it just kinda... ends without a boss fight. Chapter 5 has a nice premise of everyone being prosecuted for their alleged crimes and it has some nice callbacks, but it ultimately feels a bit too generic compared to everything else. The final boss also isn't as good as the previous fights, especially with both Chapter 2 and Chapter 3 having amazing boss fights, Chapter 2's being one of the best bosses I've seen in some time due to the way it calls back to the previous chapters while also just being really fun. The final boss has this nice twist with the enemies being aware of their deaths creating health, but both the Chapter 2 (a time bomb from a previous chapter gets tied to you) and Chapter 3 (you paint the boss blue with his own attack so he becomes vulnerable) bosses had better twists.
Sprinkled throughout the game are time rifts, which have to be discovered before they can be found in the stages. Each stage has 2 blue time rifts and 1 purple time rift. The blue ones are unlocked as you progress whereas the purple ones are unlocked by assembling artifacts that are sprinkled throughout the levels. Their position is hinted at with a photo of their location. While that is a pretty cool idea, some photos are a bit too generic so it's pretty hard to find those rifts. Blue rifts lead to Super Mario Sunshine Secret Stage-esque platforming-centered stages which are usually pretty fun, whereas purple rifts lead to exploration-based stages where you have to find crowns to progress. The latter also contain pages, which you can collect in order to get some backstory for the characters. I would prefer it if the pages were counted by stage instead of globally, since some of the rifts can have a lot of stages so it's tough to know where you missed a page.

While CSS and CSGO are both great games and I don't see no reason as to why you shouldn't buy Counter Strike Source, I would like to point out the pros and cons of CSS (At least based on MY thoughts and preferences) while comparing it with CSGO to help you decide which one you should buy.
Pros:
1.Lets get this one out of the way. Definitely feels way more fun than CSGO in general.
2.Gunplay plays out smoother and the recoil of the weapons plays a big part on that. (CSS has random recoil while CSGO has preset recoil for each weapon)
3.Customizable...A LOT. With a little basic knowledge of the engine, you can add your own custom models, materials, sounds, etc etc. And even some new modes using sourcemod or other plugins. (Sure as hell beats CSGO's skins, which are paid...)
4.More variety on custom servers (DM, Surf, Zombie, Zombie escape, etc)
5.Its rather more casual than competitive, which is what I prefer.
6.Better bots (In my opinion and experience)
7.Less toxic community (Including kids, russians etc), but that doesn't mean its toxic free! (All the ♥♥♥♥♥♥s moved on to CSGO)
8.You can tweak your server settings when starting a map, rather than starting a match with preset settings, and having to fiddle with the console.
9.Hitboxes, while they are a bit big and got some complaints, I feel like they fit right in the game and are way more responsive than CSGO's hitboxes.
10.Snipers feel damn fine to use in this game
11.No CZ 75, No R8, No Mag 7, No Sawn off, No negev, No tec 9 etc etc. CSS has the original weapons from CS 1.6 and thats it. (This includes the fact that there is one M4, instead of CSGO, which has 2)
12.Guns are tweaked just about right. Each one feels balanced and deserves the stats that it has.Not too OP, and not too♥♥♥♥♥♥ Yeah, even the glock, believe it or not.
13.Suprisingly, less hackers.
14.I think the maps in CSS are more fun to play, rather than CSGO variants.
15.Gamebanana and other sites have a gigantic collection of custom maps for the game.
16.No weapon skins. (Instead you can get a buttload of cool custom models and reskins)
Cons:
1.Less active community than CSGO.
2.Servers with "premium" features (Only Premium users have access to AWP, Auto sniper, have 150 health etc etc) are common.
3.No official servers like CSGO. (Most servers will be in a way or another, modified and not vanilla, at least the ones with players in it)
4.66 tick servers.
5.Graphics are a bit dated.
6.No lobby system.
7.No matchmaking.
8.Hostages can be killed, which can lead to exploits (Although hostage killers do get punished so its not common to kill hostages)
9.Wallbanging is drastically reduced and less effective
In conclusion, I think Counter Strike Source is a better game than CSGO. Hell! I think its the best in the series.
If you're a casual player like me, you should get this. If you like competitive, I think CSGO is your choice (Although you can find clans who host competitive matches in CSS, which are awesome)

I purchased the season pass last year when Episode 1 was released, and did not regret the decision. Episode 1 was a slow burn, with multiple scenes of gritty noir along with some psychological nightmares that suggest our hero, Eliot Ness, is still traumatised from his time on the force. The game is thick with noir influences, using a black and white color scheme with harsh reds splashed in for effect. The voice acting is mostly solid, particularly from Ness and Capone. I appreciate the ability to scour crime scenes, although I wish Ness moved a little quicker. After playing Episode 2, I'm still excited I chose the pass, although I have to say that waiting a year between episodes is a bit of downside. At a little over two hours of gameplay per episode, waiting a year between is ridiculous to say the least.
Pros:
- Compelling, gritty crime story that mixes cultists, gangsters, and real-life figures.
- Fantastic aesthetics, good graphics, good controls.
- Voice acting is above average, characters are interestingly written and acted.
- Heavy noir feel mixed with alternate history settings, like a zeppelin nightclub and a Russian submarine.
- Decisions have actual consequences in game.
Cons:
- Main character moves slowly in certain areas, making exploring sometimes a chore.
- Might have to turn up the brightness/contrast somewhat, as the heavy black/white scheme can make environments confusing to navigate.
- Long wait time between episodes (thus far).
Overall, I'm anxious to see where this goes story-wise, and to see just how deep the psychological rabbit hole of Ness' mind dives. A solid 7/10, but please, please please please release the next episode sooner. A year between releases is just too long to maintain interest.

This game is easily one of my favorite games of all time, just everything about it I love. Bethesda really nails the whole post-apocalyptic feeling, because everything just feels empty and deserted. These days the game looks pretty ♥♥♥♥♥♥ and even back in 2008 when I first played this game, I didn't think it looked that impressive (Dem Mods though). I admit that I'm a little spoiled by New Vegas, so the mechanics in FO3 don't feel quite as good as they do in New Vegas, but using VATS and the gameplay itself is excellent. I enjoyed all the songs in the game, but I really wish they would have added more, especially with all the DLC this game has. The karma system is something I feel all RPG's should have and while some of the decisions you make don't really affect things as a whole, it's still nice to have multiple choices to the quests you do. Audio as a whole is excellent (as stated with the music) but it just feels limited with the amount of the voice actors and the songs on the radio, the quality is definitely there though. I honestly could keep going on why I love this game so much and there is a lot of stuff I haven't even seen yet (DLC and Mods) but there is one big issue that makes me question this version in particular. On Windows 7, this game would crash at least every hour for me and sometimes it would be even worse. You would think with a game as popular as FO3, that Bethesda would at least fix something as big as this is, but they haven't. I have played this on Xbox 360 before and it maybe crashed 1 or 2 times (it's pretty sad when the console version of your game, performs better than the far superior PC). If you can deal with the technical issues, then you're in for one of the best RPG's of all time, up there with games like Mass Effect 2, Dragon Age: Origins, Skyrim, and KOTOR. Regardless of any of the negative things I said about FO3, I think one of the most important aspects of any game is fun and if I can sit and enjoy a game for extended play sessions for weeks and keep coming back to it after I already beat it before, well I think that's what every game should strive for.

text:
"POST CRASH LOG DAY 5:
My sleep cycle got messed up while exploring, and I was forced to leave my shelter at 4AM in order to pace my fatigue and hunger with my distance from a safehouse. So I leave the trailer I had shacked up in, walk out into a foggy, dim haze only to slip off a slope and land on the ground below, suffering a sprained ankle. Even worse, mere yards away was a (presumably) cold and hungry wolf, growling and looking me dead in the eyes. The wolf approached, and with my ankle injured I wasn't able to outrun. With the wolf approaching more and more rapidly, I hastily take out my nearly broken hunting rifle, load it with the only bullet in my bag, and just as the wolf pounces I pull the trigger, hitting it right in the head, an instant kill. With the wolf dead, I calm down a bit, only to realize that, in my panic, I had run outside in -20 degree (celsius) weather, and I was suffering terribly from the cold. With no way to see through the fog, and a sprained ankle, no weapons, I was bound to die. Yet I brought myself to start limping forward, slowly. I slowly began to weaken, my condition getting worse and worse as the minutes passed. But just as all hope was lost, I faintly made out the shape of a tall structure. AN ABANDONED WATCHPOST! I crawled up the winding stairs to the top, and collapsed upon a shabby bed in the corner. After regaining my senses, and warming up a bit, I threw a log in the wood stove and warmed up with a can of beans and a much needed drink of water. There was still a long day ahead."
I've had my eye on this for a while and I decided to give in and try it out. The game is early access which I've had 50-50 opinions on, due to buying into games that have still not really delivered.
When I dropped into the sandbox mode(Only mode available so far), I felt a bit uneasy about this game as well. Highly stylized but low realism, it just seemed like another walkabout. But then as I figured out the mechanics, got mauled by wolves, froze to death, and walked off a cliff shattering my ankles, I REALLY got into it.
The atmosphere is FANTASTIC. Once you start playing for a while, your mind goes into overdrive trying to think up a survival plan, looking out for danger, managing your vitals, and deciding if the space in your bag will be filled with food or materials. The gameplay itslef is not at all exciting, but the mood shifts from calm, to panic, to dread, to fear, back to calm in the space of a single minute.
Fantastic, and it's still being worked on and improved. Definitely recommend, even in early access.

Well this is my first review on steam, so I hope it helps some people out. For starters I haven't played many tales titles at all so this won't be a review affected by nostalgia glasses. I haven't finished the game yet but I can tell it is a great game. The combat system is something different for those like me who haven't played tales games before so it brings a fresh perspective and feels NEW. The characters are pretty likeable although some will get on your nerves a lot(I'm looking at you Lailah and Alisha). Thing is when you play this game don't expect a very twisted or surprising story. If you've watched any shonen anime you'll see that all the characters are pretty stereotypical but not in a way that takes away from the game.
The story is basically your typical hero who can claim a special power no one else can because he's pure hearted and decides to do the typical pure hearted thing and save people. Sorey as a character is... well pure. He's really just your typical nice guy who wants to help people and can't understand why bad people are bad. It's kind of uplifting actually.
As as far as the game sytem goes the UI is neat and pretty manageable. The only major cons I found were the stupidly complex game mechanics like battle actions and support talents and runes on your armor, which pretty much decide which stats increase and which status effects you resist; the other con was the grinding..... I don't mean for levels because grinding for exp is something I'm used so it doesn't bother me but rather for grade(required for getting a lot of the benefits) and gald(money..). It's hard initially to get any useful amount of grade or gald but gald comes faster later on.. Grade not so much.
So those were my grievances with the game, but pros more than make for slight annoyances which are in no way game breaking. So my pros:
- Neat and easy UI.
- The Combat system.
- Switching between characters in battle, just makes things feel so dynamic.
- Zavied, Rose and Edna( Characters you meet a little a late into the game but who are some of my favourite characters)
- The story while a bit predictable is still pretty interesting.
- The skits that play in game during events and such.
- The tactical play required when you're underleveled or at higher difficulties( fun for me.. maybe not so much for others)
- The length of the game more than justifies the price.
- Replayability if you're a completionist.
So all in all..,I approve this game.

I used to play the Stronghold series games years ago. I loved watching the town around my castles grow. The peasants planting food and harvesting. Hunters chasing game and candlemakers gathering wax from the beekeepers. That wasn't the focus of the game however, as there were dangerous enemies building siege weapons and preparing for war against you whilst you did the same. There was an "endgame" whereby you were destroyed, or your armies proved victorious against your enemies.
Banished has no endgame. The townbuilding aspects are certainly more detailed than those of stronghold, but not by a whole lot. It does seem difficult at first and your first few towns will likely fail. Mine did. Wooden houses for instance use way more firewood than stone ones. Don't even bother with them.
The thing is, once you figure out the "formula" of what to build first and where to prioritize, the game becomes easy and repetitive. Even the achievements are really a matter of patience than any kind of challenge. I play at maximum speed almost exclusively and on the hardest difficulty and starting conditions and it's still rather tame.
If you enjoy advancing a settlement from Colonial times to the modern Era, play Tropico 5.
If you enjoy Colonial town construction and enemy forces to destroy, buy one of the older Strongholds.
If you enjoy building detailed and rather pretty Colonial Era settlements that never really evolve or go anywhere, never become part of something bigger, where you create your own story, this game is for you. I enjoyed it, but have little reason to play it anymore.
Sidenote, there are some great mods for this game, but none so far address the lack of "endgame" content.

《Today I begin a new life》
　　Today I shed my old skin which hath, too long, suffered the bruises of failure and the wounds of mediority.
　　Today I am born anew and my birthplace is a vineyard where there is fruit for all.
　　Today I will pluck grapes of wisdom from the tallest and fullest vines in the vineyard,for these were planted by the wisest of my profession who have come before me,generation upon generation.
　　Today I will savor the taste of grapes from these vines and verily I will swallow the seed of success buried in each and new life will sprout within me.
　　The career I have chosen is laden with opportunity yet it is fraught with heartbreak and despair and the bodies of those who have failed, were they piled one atop another, would cast a shadow down upon all the pyramids of the earth.
　　Yet I will not fail, as the others, for in my hands I now hold the charts which will guide through perilous waters to shores which only yesterday seemed but a dream.
　　Failure no longer will be my payment for struggle. Just as nature made no provision for my body to tolerate pain neither has it made any provision for my life to suffer failure. Failure, like pain, is alien to my life. In the past I accepted it as I accepted pain. Now I reject it and I am prepared for wisdom and principles which will guide me out of the shadows into the sunlight of wealth, position, and happiness far beyond my most extravagant dreams until even the golden apples in the Garden of Hesperides will seem no more than my just reward.
　　Time teaches all things to him who lives forever but I have not the luxury of eternity. Yet within my allotted time I must practice the art of patience for nature acts never in haste. To create the olive, king of all trees, a hundred years is required. An onion plant is old in nine weeks. I have lived as an onion plant. It has not pleased me. Now I wouldst become the greatest of olive trees and, in truth, the greatest of salesman.
　　And how will this be accomplished? For I have neither the knowledge nor the experience to achieve the greatness and already I have stumbled in ignorance and fallen into pools of self-pity. The answer is simple. I will commence my journey unencumbered with either the weight of unnecessary knowledge or the handicap of meaningless experience. Nature already has supplied me with knowledge and instinct far greater than any beast in the forest and the value of experience is overrated, usually by old men who nod wisely and speak stupidly.
　　In truth, experience teaches thoroughly yet her course of instruction devours men's years so the value of her lessons diminishes with the time necessary to acquire her special wisdom. The end finds it wasted on dead men. Furthermore, experience is comparable to fashion; an action that proved successful today will be unworkable and impractical tomorrow.
　　Only principles endure and these I now possess, for the laws that will lead me to greatness are contained in the words of these scrolls. What they will teach me is more to prevent failure than to gain success, for what is success other than a state of mind? Which two, among a thouand wise men, will define success in the same words; yet failure is always described but one way. Failure is man's inability to reach his goals in life, whatever they may be.
　　In truth, the only difference between those who have failed and those who have successed lies in the difference of their habits. Good habits are the key to all success. Bad habits are the unlocked door to failure. Thus, the first law I will obey, which precedeth all others is --I will form good habits and become their slave.
　　As a child I was slave to my impulses; now I am slave to my habits, as are all grown men. I have surrendered my free will to the years of accumulated habits and the past deeds of my life have already marked out a path which threatens to imprison my future. My actions are ruled by appetite, passion, prejudice, greed, love, fear, environment, habit, and the worst of these tyrants is habit. Therefore, if I must be a slave to habit let me be a slave to good habits. My bad habits must be destroyed and new furrows prepared for good seed.
　　I will form good habits and become their slave.
　　And how will I accomplish this difficult feat? Through these scrolls, it will be done, for each scroll contains a principle which will drive a bad habit from my life and replace it with one which will bring me closer to success. For it is another of nature's laws that only a habit can subdue another habit. So, in order for these written words to perform their chosen task, I must discipline myself with the first of my new habits which is as follows:
　　I will read each scroll for thirty days in this prescribed manner, before I proceed to the next scroll.
　　First, I will read the words in silence when I arise. Then, I will read the words in silence after I have partaken of my midday meal. Last, I will read the words again just before I retire at day's end, and most important, on this occasion I will read the words aloud.
　　On the next day I will repeat this procedure, and I will continue in like manner for thirty days. Then, I will turn to the next scroll and repeat this procedure for another thirty days. I will continue in this manner until I have lived with each scroll for thirty days and my reading has become habit.
　　And what will be accomplished with this habit? Herein lies the hidden secret of all man's accomplishments. As I repeat the words daily they will soon become a part of my active mind, but more important, they will also seep into my other mind, that mysterious source which never sleeps, which creates my dreams, and often makes me act in ways I do not comprehend.
　　As the words of these scrolls are consumed by my mysterious mind I will begin to awake, each morning, with a vitality I have never known before. My vigor will increase, my enthusiasm will rise, my desire to meet the world will overcome every fear I once knew at sunrise, and I will be happier than I ever believed it possible to be in this world of strife and sorrow.
　　Eventually I will find myself reacting to all situations which confront me as I was commanded in the scrolls to react, and soon these actions and reactions will become easy to perform, for any act with practice becomes easy.
　　Thus a new and good habit is born, for when an act becomes easy through constant repetiton it becomes a pleasure to perform and if it is a pleasure to perform it is man's nature to perform it often. When I perform it often it becomes a habit and I become its slave and since it is a good habit this is my will.
　　Today I begin a new life.
　　And I make a solemn oath to myself that nothing will retard my new life's growth. I will lose not a day from these readings for that day cannot be retrieved nor can I substitute another for it. I must not , I will not, break this habit of daily reading from these scrolls and, in truth, the few moments spent each day on this new habit are but a small price to pay for the happiness and success that will be mine.
　　As I read and re-read the words in the scrolls to follow, never will I allow the brevity of each scroll nor the simplicity of its words to cause me to treat the scroll's message lightly. Thousands of grapes are pressed to fill one jar with wine, and the grapeskin and pulp are tossed to the birds. So it is with these grapes of wisdom from the ages. Much has been filtered and tossed to the wind.Only the pure truth lies distilled in the words to come. I will drink as instructed and spill not a drop. And the seed of success I will swallow.
　　Today my old skin has become as dust. I will walk tall among men and they will know me not , for today I am a new man, with a new life.

This is a great software to use for starting out on building something, I'd highly recommend buying this when on sale if you're curious on what it can do and don't wanna spend a lot. though the program does have some cons it's still great.
Pros:
+Pre scripted
+Pre Rendered graphic sets (enemies, tiles, characters)
+Built in character generator
+Pre composed music
+Comes with a manual and pop up info boxes if you get lost on how things work
+Can easily import your own content into your project
+Scripts are easy to apply and find
+Set tabs for everything you may need for a standard RPG
+Customizable title screen with title name on the background (Draw Title)
+Custom resources for fan made games can be easy to find
Cons:
- Scripting requires Ruby 3 (no HTML5 or Java)
- Most DLC Isn't worth what it's priced
- typos in the armours tab ("Leather Hap")
- Character Generator Face graphics come out odd and creepy looking
- Character generator clothes and Neck don't have matching graphics
- Standard battle system is similar to Dragon Warrior and will need multiple scripts to change (Yanfly Battle system scripts)
- RTP Music is mostly either too happy sounding or too sad sound mainly in the title theme songs
- A lot of people use RTP character graphics in their games so making a game from pure 100% RTP may not be that good of an idea.
The manual can be of great help especially if you wanna know what the software is compatable with as far as Video format, picture size (544x416) or even how to script in actions, over all I'll give this software a 7/10
though the software offer so much that so much is what people will more and likely use making being unique hard to do unless you're willing to learn a new coding language (CSS is used with Ruby so if you know CSS then that takes some work out of things)

I've been using the RPG Maker games since RPGM'95.  I've had every version at one point or another.  And I can say, without a doubt, that VXA is my favorite to use.  The ability to customize each tileset with the liquid, walls, and details you want makes life so much easier.  Need magma in your town, but want a healthy forest growing from it?  No need to open Photoshop.  Just make yourself a new tileset in the database, and volcano-forest away.
As an added bonus, there are tons of free resources available on the internet - tutorials, music, tiles, characters, battlers, everything.  Seriously, you name it, and it's out there.  And if it isn't already out there, you can commission someone to make it for you (unless you can make it yourself, which is time-consuming, but not impossible).

The first time i saw RPG maker was with the orginal playstation. yes, back in the 90/200s. for the most part, it's the same thing. But what i want to address are the people reading the negative reviews.
Yes, the software has it's drawbacks, but most of them can be worked around. so i'll address them by typical problems
the sprites are smaller than those in XP but you don't have to stay with the Chibi style of sprites. You can, in deed use XP sprites in. It takes a little bit of work, but can be done. You are not locked into the stock sprite maker either. Game character hub will help. sprite creator 3 is really good too.
The game resolution is small; however, you should look at Yanfly channel. There is a  script that will allow you to make it a little bigger.
You are not restricted to the tile base system of building maps or their low resolution. Learn photoshop or any other digital design software. Illustrator will be helful for sprite creation and map creation. if you don't know a program like photoshop, then don't expect too much.
I stress this. Learn the way things are built in RPGMVXA! Learn how to build your own maps in photoshop and get those to work inside the maker. learn how the tile system works and how you build your own tiles to make the maps more interesting. Learn how the icon system works to make custom icons or replace the current ones. .
So in short
- Learn to script or use YanFly. I highly recommend Yanfly as you can make even a  Zelda like on map fighting game if you wanted
- Learn Photoshop or some other softwear. this is where the entire thing opens up and allows you to do much much more than the maker allows you to stock.
- Learn how to get your custom graphics in the game. things go by faster and there is more flexability.
- If you don't want to use their sprites? Don't. but you need to learn file sizes and what the maker can read and can not read.
This is an amazing game maker and can create just about any 2D RPG or even side scroller if you can imagine. and with the massive amount of Makers that are coming out, this is more or less the future of game creation. If you are too lazy to learn how the softwear works, then you wont be creating things that could wow people or look different from what everyone else is creating. This goes for design or art softwear. You need to take the time to learn this system. it's mostly file management. If you can do that, you can create some amazing games. If you are looking for quick gratification, you'll get that, But you'll also be one of the people who says "i don't have the flexability i want" with this.
Also, as one noted in the reviews. Making a game takes time. You can build your game on your own but it will take years.  If you have a team, it'll be shorter but you have to manage everyone. If you want to make a massive Final Fantasy like game, you can do it. But you need to take into consideration your pactiance, artistic talent, speed of learning organization and desire to create something, then make your game to your abilities and as you use it more and practice, things will get better and easier.
I recommend this with no reservations. It's an amazing piece of softwear and as i'm an Art Teacher, I am currently teaching this softwear to highschool students and their project is absolutly amazing.

EDIT: This is an old review made long ago. Unfortunately, it seems that the company making this game has floundered, as nothing has been heard from them since September 2016. The game is well-made, but unfortunately, it seems that it will remain forever incomplete.
Blues and Bullets brings the noir-style detective story to fresh new life in an episodic series. The game is set in an alternative version of 1950s America. In the game, you play as Elliot Ness, the former founder and leader of the Untouchables and the man who took down Al Capone, who is now retired and runs a diner called Blues and Bullets. You are contacted by your old adversary, who has been out of jail for several years now, with a new mission: his granddaughter has been kidnapped, and since he can't trust the police, he wants you to investigate. Before you know it, you are mixed up with ritual murder and strange cults.
The gameplay is a mix of a few different styles and genres. Most of the game relies on making decisions about what to say or do in a certain situation; some of your decisions will have a lasting impact on the storyline, while others can alter Ness' personality or add new dialogue and background to the story. There are a lot of objects to interact with in every environment, but when you walk around, you can't move the camera, which can make it hard to appreciate the detail and depth that the developers went to when they crafted the world of Blues and Bullets. Also, invisible walls will prevent you from exploring areas that are off-limits, which some might find annoying.
There are also segments where you have to examine crime scenes for clues (which are presented in all their glorious, gory detail) and place them in a deduction board to solve the crime, a mechanic seemingly borrowed from the Sherlock Holmes adventure game series. While this system is challenging and fun, it's not possible to solve the crime incorrectly (attempting to put the wrong clue in the wrong place will not work), so there's no real pressure to it.
Combat and action sequences are relatively rare. Most of the action uses a simple, cover-based shooter mechanic, while hand-to-hand combat uses quick-time events. The shooting system is good, and pretty fun, but the QTE can be a mixed bag: they are relatively challenging without being too difficult, but making one mistake will force you to start the whole sequence over again.
The voice acting and animation in this game are both superb, and the story line and characters are worthy of a real TV series. However, the biggest complaint I have with this game are the graphics. This is probably my own fault for playing this on a Macbook Air 2013, but for me, the game runs pretty slowly most of the time, particularly during some of the gunfight sequences, and I have a problem with color blur. Adding a graphics menu to the game might help a little.
Summary:
Pros:
—Intriguing storyline
—Diverse characters and excellent voice acting
—Beautiful original soundtrack
—Diversity of moral choices encourages replayability.
—Fun shooter mechanic
—Crime scene investigation sequences encourage puzzle solving and challenge deductive reasoning
Cons:
—Lack of graphics menu
—Slow gameplay (probably just me)
—Use of QTEs may be frustrating to some
—Lack of checkpoint saving feature means that if you quit in the middle of a scene, you have to do the whole thing all over again

Spectacular battle arena-type game focused on fast-paced bow and arrow oriented combat, with mechanics that are very approachable and, for the most part, easy to figure out on your own. The relative transparency of its mechanics does not, however, mean that it is an easy game to master, with its tight controls, twitch counterplay mechanics, and well-crafted, deceptive arenas. A notable feature is the added dimension of screen wrapping - players or objects that pass through the bottom of the screen will come out through the top, left side through the right, and vice versa. Should you decide to pick the game up, you will soon discover what a devilish thing this can be.
The game is split into three modes: Versus, Co-op, and Trials. The Versus mode pits 2-4 players against one another in one of three different sub-modes, all focused on killing the opposing players, with a large number of game modifiers available that change the games in a variety of ways. There are a large number of stages available, some of which have to be unlocked through various means. Co-op mode (perhaps more aptly called "Quest mode", as it can be played and enjoyed perfectly well as a solo experience) is a mode that pits you and a friend (up to three friends in the expansion's version of co-op) against waves of different enemies on each of the themed maps. There's not much more to it than that, but it is enjoyable and provides for some challenge if you're going for achievements. Lastly, Trials is a time trial mode that challenges you to destroy a number of dummies as quickly as possible with the tools available in each stage. It's somewhat maddening, but engrossing for the obsessive.
Overall there is little about the game that I can fault. The most notable flaw is its lack of online multiplayer, the exclusion of which may well have been intentional, as the game appears to have been constructed to strongly encourage getting together and duking it out with a group of friends. Even so, I would recommend it as a singleplayer game due to its inherent charm and the challenges it provides in its Quest and Trial modes, although I imagine a lot of people would disagree with me on this point. I'm just a sucker for a good challenge wrapped into a neat little package. I expect I will be returning to this game many times in the future.

Now for the actual review.
Fallout 3
The result of Interplay going bankrupt and selling their acclaimed franchise to Bethesda and made into an Open World FPS/TPS-RPG hybrid.
Well, let's see...
Your dad's Liam Neeson
You've been raised in a bomb shelter
He leaves without warning
Everyone is trying to kill you now
So you leave
Hoping to find him using your particular set of skills.
That's the plot of the main quest.
How much that matters is up to you, because the game is completely non-linear and you can just run around killing stuff and nothing else if you feel like it.
Combat is not amazing

One skill you have is called VATS, this makes up for the otherwise lacklustre mechanics because it's so satisfying to watch something come apart limb by limb in slow motion.

It's a world worth exploring, full of lore, cool and entertaining characters (look for two high functioning ghouls in a Metro station), lots to do and endless amounts of mods to keep to you playing and entertained for ages.
Is it a perfect game:
Absolutely not.
Is it fun and worth more than you pay for:
Yes, Absolutely.
I think everyone should at least try this game and see what they think about it, even though I personally think NV is better, but that's a story for another day, but I think everyone should play both these games and make up their own minds, or just to get a kick out of enemies coming apart in slow-mo.

I believe gameplay is the core of a good game; you don't want to be in a world if being there isn't fun. Now the biggest incentive for keeping having fun in that world is the immersion you can experience in it.
On both those aspects Fallout 3 excels. It is a very good FPS with progression or a complex first person RPG, you can pick which style you like best, and you experience one of the best most immersive post-apocalyptic worlds ever created.
From the rumbles, to the surviving inhabitants for the Capital Wasteland and their culture, this game has much and more to offer as we unwrap the aftermath of DC 200 years after a nuclear war. And, in spite the fact it invites you to wonder how you'd make it in this world (or wouldn't) , it is also full with great humor.
There are a few problems with compatibility with Windows 8 and later, but most I faced were because of Alt-tabbing. Haven't experienced any random crashes and haven't used any mods or patches so far. Vanilla install from Steam and it is impossible for me not to highly recommended it.

I burst through the door just to slam it shut behind me again. These asylum "patients" are out of their minds! Brandishing weapons that are no more than rusty pipes and knives, they chase me from room to room eating at my conscience and forcing me to fight through my primal fear.
I scan the room pitch black room. A few lockers and bed. Not much for hiding places, I'll surely be found. This is it, my last breaths. I jump as the shoulder of a patient slams against the door as he, or it, cackles wildly. Into one of the lockers. Now. I fling open a locker door and quietly close it behind me as the patient breaks down the door. I can hear his manic, erratic breathing. He scans the room, and heads right to the lockers. I'm forcing myself to keep my breathing steady, and to hold my bladder in check. He opens the locker right next to me, and slams the door shut. He walks out of the room mumbling something about ghosts. I let out a sigh of relief and nearly cry at my good luck. Why did I ever decide that this creepy asylum was worth reporting on? I flick on my camera's night vison, and quietly exit my hiding place. I forge on, into the run-down asylum. Anything for a story.
The graphics are realistic, the sounds are terrifying, and the fear is real. You can't blow through this game without stumbling around in absolute darkness. I'm not kidding. Most of rooms and areas are so dark your screen is just black. The game forces you to scavenge for batteries and use your camera, usually taking you off the path you want to go and into a pitch black room with a body hanging from the ceiling. The inhabitants of the asylum are jumpy, violent, and scared. It's not uncommon to walk down a hall just to have a door, that's slightly ajar, slam shut scaring the bejesus out of you. If you're walking down a dark hallway, your night-vision camera can pick up the reflection of an inhabitant's eyes before they materialize on your camera. By then, it's almost too late. Halfway through the game you drop your camera and have to go down into the basement to find it, just to have it surrounded by patients. After you pick it up, the screen on the camera is cracked and the display flickers at times. You'll find yourself running for you life, you'll feel ice cold sweat sliding down your forhead and back, you'll want to turn on all the lights in your house, you probably won't go to bed the same night you play it, you'll be talking yourself into the next session whether the fear is worth the rush, you'll sit stock still and barely breathe as you hide from the asylum's monstrosities (and you won't even know it). You will scream, you will hit the pause button in panic, you will get addicted to the rush, you will talk yourself into exploring to find classified documents. This is nightmare fuel (I've had a few), this will raise your blood pressure, and you will be coming back for more. Amnesia doesn't compare. This is the real deal. This is on another level.

I used to play the Stronghold series games years ago. I loved watching the town around my castles grow. The peasants planting food and harvesting. Hunters chasing game and candlemakers gathering wax from the beekeepers. That wasn't the focus of the game however, as there were dangerous enemies building siege weapons and preparing for war against you whilst you did the same. There was an "endgame" whereby you were destroyed, or your armies proved victorious against your enemies.
Banished has no endgame. The townbuilding aspects are certainly more detailed than those of stronghold, but not by a whole lot. It does seem difficult at first and your first few towns will likely fail. Mine did. Wooden houses for instance use way more firewood than stone ones. Don't even bother with them.
The thing is, once you figure out the "formula" of what to build first and where to prioritize, the game becomes easy and repetitive. Even the achievements are really a matter of patience than any kind of challenge. I play at maximum speed almost exclusively and on the hardest difficulty and starting conditions and it's still rather tame.
If you enjoy advancing a settlement from Colonial times to the modern Era, play Tropico 5.
If you enjoy Colonial town construction and enemy forces to destroy, buy one of the older Strongholds.
If you enjoy building detailed and rather pretty Colonial Era settlements that never really evolve or go anywhere, never become part of something bigger, where you create your own story, this game is for you. I enjoyed it, but have little reason to play it anymore.
Sidenote, there are some great mods for this game, but none so far address the lack of "endgame" content.

So I've immersed myself once again in the world of the JRPG. And I found myself... slightly entertained, but not as well as I'd have preferred.
So the pros:
This game was clearly made with the Tales of spirit. Sure some of the things are downright cliche, while others might give you a chuckle. My favorite was an obscure bit you see early on - some gossip you pick up is along the lines of "Another fistfight has broken out. This is why we can't have nice things!" New game plus, this still caused a chuckle.
The elements are expected, but you still get a curve ball here and there. Some promises you make you CANNOT keep, and the emotional blow of that can be felt. It certainly resounds with waking up from complete innocence, and taking on the mantle of responsibility.
There's a wide range of ways to battle it out, and you can choose what stats and skills matter to you.
Cons:
The battle system. I hate the way both the companion AI works, as well as the staggering mechanics. The use of a 3D ring looks nice but there are so many things that kill it. To elaborate:
A wide ring for enemies to run around in, and they seem to target your allies randomly. If you choose to go after an opponent, you can find yourself running back and forth in the circle, missing your first strike, then chasing them again. And some enemies can just teleport to a different spot in the ring.
Your companions suck. If you go against an opponent with even an inkling of power, be ready to micromanage their health, because a brief sneeze from the boss will kill them. A lot of the time I found myself facing an enemy 1 on 1. Which is fine, I still won, but your companions will never get smarter. This only gets worse on chaos dificulty.
In a baffling display, the devs decided to make optional arenas where one (or two) of the main characters fight waves of enemies. Only with a wide circle, you constantly find yourself getting stun-locked by enemies off the screen, or dodging looking for an opening where there is none. One stun lock in the the wrong place, and your enemies will chain stun you as they all lunge at you, making your health drop in large chunks because your character quite literally can't move, dodge, or do anything to mitigate damage. The worst case of this happening occurs in an optional sidequest, where you face off with another main character and their companion. You are meant to win, but I found myself scratching my head in anger as I constantly got locked in place and went from 100% health to 0% with no recourse. That said, the game is passable on standard difficulty.
On to equipment. There are 50 different effects for equipment. That's right. 50. Each piece can have 4 effects. These effects can be the same, and thus stacked, or different. You can mix these effects by fusing equipment. Some equipment can have an effect slot filled up with a special doubled version of the effect, or even a tripled one. Sometimes when fusing equipment for skills, a character must wear it to multiple battles to unlock the effect. If these locked effects are on equipment that is fused, those effects will be treated as nonexistent and disappear. With me so far?
So, say, you want a sword with 4 "attack + 4%" effects, to maximize damage. You have to fuse sword after sword, in hopes of gitting the correct effect slots. And did I mention that fusing equipment makes the base stats of the equipment go up? So you probably want to fuse your swords for max attack. You can fuse an item up to 99 times, then make it into a special "blessed" version, which can be fused 99 more times. Every time you fuse, those effects will most likely change.  See where I'm going with this? It could take days, months, weeks to get the perfect sword. You might never get it. It would be beneficial to have a system where you simply pull the effect out of equipment, then put it in when you need it, but that DOESN'T EXIST. SO GIVE IN TO THE DESPAIR.
There are 8 characters that you can play with in the game. You will ever only have 6 at a time. Two of the characters become essentially unusable, including one who honestly would have been better if the devs didn't give up on them halfway through the story.
Like most main villians, this main villian is interacted with in 3 scenes in the game. The rest of the time it's just implied he's somewhere evil doing evil things. His henchman have motives that are UNCLEAR AT BEST. Including a girl who constantly attacks you because you are doing exactly what he wants you to do. Confused yet? I certainly am.
The music is good. The skits are great at times. The plot twists are MEH at best, but you get a good sense of a game that acknowledges what it is and owns it. And I can't fault that.
All in all, 7/10, would kill my friend's brother again.

It's not a game... It's a piece of art. I cannot think much of it right now because i just finished it. It gives a mass of dots to a person playing, the dots aren't connected, but the player is is connecting it after getting all the dots. Game is very emotional and challenges you to get the author. The answer is unexpectable.
*Spoilers might be there*
The game starts with a simple project of a Davey's (this collection author) friend Coda. It is a simple cs 1.6 map and Coda is showing, that the map is something unique, because some things are misplaced, unnormal. It surely was something that fascinated Coda to create new games... A way to express himself. Some games are cryptic or/and can't be beaten. Actually, there's no goal except of seeing everything you can achieve. In one level, you're trapped in a room. After removing walls you can see tons of labirynts all over around you. Coda was expressing his anxiety and shyness. Game with nice and warm house cleaning made you feel comfortable, soon it was starting to get irritiating after doing the same thing all over and over again, preventing from making it house all simple and clean. Just like your live. It cannot be perfect as you struggle with problems and people. The game with the island represented Coda's forced decisions, because he felt it was socially right to lie and be an actor in his own life. He has shown that he is very cryptic, hidden in himself. This game overall is about one person's growing anxiety and hate towards others. He felt that he was forced to do something, to be socialised, because other way he would be left.. Alone. The one way doors represent the time going forward, not being avaiable to change the past. Like you write a book, you cannot simply remove the text that was in the middle of the written book. You would have to force it, making it unnatural for that person's mind. Desperation, depresion, anxiety, loneliness, need to be loved by someone who would understand him. By only playing this game, i understand that Coda is best described by those words. He just felt fullfilled when he was making games, he had someone to show the game, he had a reason to do the games. Not popular reason to make money or fame, but it was his way to describe his own mind. He isn't easy person to come around. Surely, he isn't. He felt his decisions were forced and he couldn't describe himself in the outer world. The world wanted to change him, but he didn't let it happen. It's sad and good. I hope Coda got someone who would be with him and percieve the world just as he does.
Also the game overall is nicely done. The narration is very emotional and it makes you feel like you were listening to a live person, not a recording. The music is also great.
I am also a little game dev or maybe a passionate programmer. I didn't release anything big or special, but my mind isn't as open inside as Coda's. I hope people will understand the game and it will help them understand them.

Tales of Zestiria sits on my mind oddly. First and foremost before you read this reveiw I am going to openly admit that I have never played a Tales game before and that this was basically the best title to start the series with since I only have a 360 and my PC. So longtime fans of this series that for whatever reason are reading this reveiw keep in mind that i'm completely new to this series.
TL;DR VERSION AT THE BOTTOM.
I'll go into gameplay and mechanics first and this might be lengthy so prepare:
The gameplay is honestly really fun and exciting. Not only do battles start without any loading and takes place right where you encountered the enemy (giving it really good immersion) but they also have this really hectic and fast pace feeling to them. Firstly the battle zone is surprisingly big (unless you get caught in a corner, narrow corridor or god forbid doorway) so you have a lot of room to move around to cast spells or to heal party members or to simply recouperate your SC. Now what is SC? Well it's basically the limiting factor put onto you to keep you from just steamrolling everything. You see, instead of giving you a mana bar to limit your spell casts and giving your basic attacks infinite uses they give you SC which is drained with every action you do besides blocking and running. While this might sound very annoying at first I actually think it's a brilliant system since now I can freely cast spells and combine them with my basic attacks to have insane combos. Also since even your basic attacks drain the SC they don't need to make your martial artes (basic attacks) weak or underwhelming compared to your hidden artes (basically the spells.) In fact with some characters it's actually more pleasing and satisfying using martial artes instead of hidden artes (Sorrey and Dezel). This is even more apparent when you use the armatus which is basically a superform in this game and apparently a new feature in the Tales games. When you use the Armatus two of your characters that are linked together will combine and make a stronger form that has it's own moves but has the combined stats of both previous characters. However as I said everything you do drains SC and because of this you must control how much you do in a short amount of time otherwise you'll find yourself in the middle of a group of enemies without anything to do and just take a bunch of hits.
I would go into the other mechanics but I'll sum up the gameplay and battle system as interesting and strategic since there is a lot of things you can do in a single battle to rack up some massive damage and combos. However it should be noted that there's no way to control the camera and there can be times where it seriously ♥♥♥♥s up.
The atmosphere in this game is quite lively and colorful. It has clear contrast so that's its really colorful without being too bright and annoying and this really fleshes out a lot of the areas since almost everything sticks out by itself while also blending in with the background. The towns could use a bit more work on them but ultimately still feel like they're actual towns and cities. Open feilds (my favorite areas honestly) are suprisingly big and gives you a sense of vastness and that you're actually traveling across the continent. This is enhanced even further with the draw range of the game. They really seemed to take the time to make sure that everything physical in these areas would look good both near and far which again makes it hard to tell where the wall of the area is without looking at the map which I believe is good. Dungeons however are painfully straight forward and small. You'll find yourself kinda bored and unexcited about what you have to do there when you're not fighting the mobs.
Now the chracters and story is what kind of makes this and oddball for me. On a personal level I like a few of the character Edna being my favorite closely followed by Alisha. However there are a lot of archetype characters that are pretty unamusing sadly with a few of them painfully stereotypical (I'm looking at you Dezel). While on the other hand you have characters that simply don't act accordingly to what they do (specifically Rose) and then you have Laliah who is just queer, sometimes I really like her and other times I find her annoying or stupid. This gives the party a schizophrenic feeling and gives the player obvious favortism. I always try to use Edna and Laliah as much as I can while keeping Mikleo and Dezel on standby unless I need them or they simply make the battle easier.
[SPOILERS IN THIS SECTION!!!]
As far as the story goes it's...well...it could be better honestly...a lot better actually. It's pretty stereotypical and can be summarized as a more cliche version of Ocarina of Time without the time travel and more characters which I can deal with and even enjoy since a lot the of character interactions can be funny. However one character in the game pretty much ruined the entire story for me and that's Rose. You see before you meet Rose it's implied and almost blatantly explained that only the Sheperd can use the armatus however within literally 10 minutes of interactions with Rose it's established that she can use the armatus too which really breaks the whole story. You see apparently Dezel was messing with her mind and body since she was little so that he could use her as a vessel for the armatus however this made her very easily controllable when using it and also gave her the ability to see and speak to seraphim as well. Now the biggest problem I have with this is that it makes no freaking sense on how or even why she uses the armatus. Okay maybe she does have a lot of resonance but the reason why the Sheperd can use it is because his power is linked and intertwined with another Seraphim. Not only that it's up to the human to use it in the first place so how is it possible for a seraphim to force her to use the armatus and is the reason why she can use it at all when it requires the human to say their name and to give them access to it. The explanation for her power was really weak and story breaking but going even further beyond that is that she joins the party for literally no reason whatsoever other than "sure, why not." and everyone just goes with it from there on.
Well that was pretty lenghty.
Ultimately I would recommend this game. I find the combat fun and exciting and it makes it a blast to grind through. The enviorment and atmosphere can be beautiful and colorful and the interactions between characters is quite charming.
TL;DR VERSION
Fun gameplay. Good graphics. Good atmosphere. Some characters are good others are bad. Story is cliche and not really good but neither is it really bad. Dungeons are too linear but feilds are great. Camera can be really stupid sometimes. I'll give this game a 7-8/10.  It could definitely use some work in a few places but the gameplay is the best part and it's really fun.

I'm a fan of tough games and Banished is certainly not easy. The idea is simple; you're given a few families, a little bit of gear, and you must build a thriving city. Your enemy, at first, is the environment. You'll quickly realize, however, that your enemy is actually the people you want to protect.
I decided to run with this concept and to fight against some of the silly things my citizens did and found the game to be enjoyable! These settlers like to stop harvesting food so they can walk 300 blocks home to eat the same food they were harvesting. They walk right past the materials they need to construct a house for their children to live in so they don't freeze to death. They walk all the way across the map to get a tool when there are 500 in storage next to their own home. The list goes on and on. Because of this, I swear my citizens are suicidal.
I decided to not make it so easy for them! They'll die when I dang well decide they can die! In over 100 hours of game play I learned how to control my own population growth. I learned how to get people fed when they didn't want to eat. I learned how to keep them warm when they refused to wear a warm coat. I swear its like I'm raising a two year old. I need an airplane spoon mod that makes buzzing sounds when my food count is low!
In a weird twist of fate Banished casts your ally as your nemisis. If you enjoy an unforgiving challenge then I definitely recommend giving Banished a shot! If you think the ai should do all the work for you, steer clear.

This is a rather good game that falls just short of being a great "Tales of" game.
TLDR; If you like JRPGs, you'll probably enjoy this quite a bit, if you're used to "Tales of" JRPGs, this will fall a bit short, but will still be quite enjoyable.
Overall, 7/10.
First off, I've now beaten it, and about 40 hours seems quite long but, in my experience Tales of games run about 60, so it was a bit shorter than i was used to. Overall, the experience was very good but just lacking a few places.
The characters were quite enjoyable and had great chemistry, but they didnt really grow all that much through the plot, minus the main character. Everyone else was just kinda there for the ride, but never really had a proper arc. Though, most of the party members were also not really given a conflict to overcome, they started and ended without much change. This really is a shame, because there were a great deal of interesting dynamics that could be explored, particulary with the Main Character and his squire's relationship.
The combat system is good, though a bit more shallow than other Tales of games, it's still very good though. Though the ally AI can be a bit lacking. There are more than a few attacks with a limited range that your allies will just kinda wander into and get killed, making the more challenging bosses more annoying than hard since you're usually on your own. There's also no mp gauge, instead something called SC. SC buids at a rather fast rate by just guarding or standing still, so you have to pause occationally, but never actually run about of the ability to heal or use other artes, this made items basically pointless, though than using them to overcome the AIs occationally thick-headedness.
The equipment system. This is probably the only part that I just dont like. The idea is cool but there's just too much going on. Equipment has different skills attached to it that give bonuses, and there are a ton of them. But the same piece of equipment can have different bonuses, and you can fuse equipment, there's a mastery rank (which i still dont fully understand the importance of, other than making fusion cheaper), certain skills give additional bonuses if you have more than one or line them up on the skill grid. It's just needlessly complicated to me. It reminds me of Tales of Vesperia's system, but made more obtuse. This also means that a great deal of equipment will just be useless to you, since even if its stats are better, you've got some skill line up that makes what you've got technically better.
Music is stellar. A bit corny at times, but the corny-ness is usually warrented when it occurs. Quite a few of the dungeons have excellent music going in the background that makes running around much more pleasant. There's quite a large amount of variety to it, but I don't think I found any part of it to be out of place.

Environments are kind of lack-luster. The style and layout of the dungeons are very similar, with some being very close to copy and pasted. It's a shame, but it doesnt feel like they put a lot of care into the individual dungeons, with some being pretty much pointless other than some possibly useless equipment you can find. The towns dont fair much better, most only being 2 or three areas to explore. It's rare to go into a house in town besides the in, so there's actually very little to explore in each town. You typcially just get 2 main areas, an inn, and a temple/church/etc to go into.
Plot is fairly standard Tales of, presenting you with situations but not giving you some magic trinket that solves everything, making for some intersting moments. Again, the issue is they dont go very far with it, the plot really doesnt get much deeper than it presents. You're told you're gonna fight a final boss, and that's exactly what you get. No twists or turns to it, not necessarily a bad thing, but it lacks depth in places. There are some points where you're asked to make a decision, but the choices end up being pointless, with either the same result most of the time, or you just doing every option anyway.
Overall, I did enjoy myself, but finished the game feeling like they didnt put as much effort into this as they did previous tales of games. On the other side, Xilla and Xilla 2 both came out not too long ago, so maybe this was a rush job. The games since Graces f have been all over the place quality wise, so who really knows what this means.

Godus Wars seems like an attempt by the developers to start fresh with Godus after it tanked. It didn't work. In this game, you play as a god commanding followers to take over a planet. You do this island by island, region by region. At the same time, another god is attempting to take the islands, so you need to fight them off. Progress is incredibly slow, it would take at least four hours to take the first island, let alone the entire planet. Each land-grabbing battle is a very simplified RTS. You sculpt the land so your followers can build abodes, and produce units once you have enough. Then you can destroy the opponent's energy supply to win. In the first 90 minutes, no other gameplay mechanics came up. Units barely respond to commands, and it's difficult to gauge whether they'll follow the paths you carve out for them. Often, they'll go a completely roundabout way to where you need them, taking twice as long. Killing the enemy god in battle does not actually kill the god, you still need to fight them in every region of the island. There’s a key system adds nothing of substance to the game. You use keys to unlock regions of land to attack, and earn keys for successfully attacking. The whole game is incredibly boring, and suffers from almost everything the original Godus did. Do not play this game.

Red Orchestra 2 is a realistic first-person shooter. Guns behave realistically, with bullet drop and spin taken into account. The game also takes away many of the elements of a traditional HUD, like an ammo counter, forcing players to remember, or manually check, the approximate number of rounds that are left in the gun's magazine. When reloading a weapon, the character checks the weight of the new magazine and determines if it is heavy (full or close to full) or light (empty or close to empty).The game's first-person cover system allows players to hide behind all objects in the world to avoid gunfire. While in cover, players can peek out to take more accurate shots or fire blindly. However, the shape, size and, composition of the object changes its effectiveness at protecting the player. Smaller objects may not cover the player's entire body, and some may not stop bullets. Health does not regenerate over time or by use of medical equipment, but non-fatal wounds must still be bandaged so no more health is lost through blood loss.
There are tanks in Red Orchestra 2, with more vehicles to be added in after the game's launch. The interiors of each tank are fully recreated with either a human or AI manning each station. The level of detail was described by Tripwire's president John Gibson as rivaling or exceeding tank simulation games. Because of the extensive work required to recreate each vehicle, which Tripwire estimates to take three months each, the game launched with two tanks: the German Panzer IV and Soviet T-34. Two more tanks and two troop carriers are in production and will be added to the game for free shortly after launch.
In June 2011, Red Orchestra 2's developer, Tripwire, announced they would be taking an aggressive, three-pronged approach to proactively deal with cheating. Red Orchestra 2 would be using a combination of three anti-cheat services; VAC along with Punkbuster and a related service called PBBans. Server operators can choose to use any or none of these services. Tripwire later clarified that Punkbuster for Red Orchestra 2 will have three levels of protection so server operators can optionally make it more or less aggressive in kicking players. A Beta was initiated early on the development process with several phases. First, the Family and Friends Beta for family members and friends of the Tripwire Interactive Staff. Then the Beta moved on to include long time clans from Red Orchestra: Ostfront 41-45 and clans new to the game. After this stage, the Beta was opened for anyone that had pre-ordered the Digital Deluxe Edition of the game, which gave the added bonus of participating in the final stage of the Beta.
Some mod teams were given early access to the SDK and have been developing mods. These mods include Grabenkrieg The Great War: 1914-1916, a mod about World War I, In Country: Vietnam, a mod about the Vietnam War, and Karelian Front, a mod about the Continuation War. There is also the CGT mod that adds classic gametypes such as Capture The Flag and Search & Destroy to the game. The full SDK was made available in January 2012.

If the controls don't make you rage-quit first, you'll enjoy a fairly interesting storyline and an inspired take on the hard-boiled Frank Miller aesthetic. Certainly worth giving the first episode a shot if you're into detective stories or urban fantasy. I'll be getting the season pack.

I originally bought Outlast from the Steam Summer Sale 2014 for £4 and it was the best purchase of the year! This game brings hype in every part of the game and the jumpscares are really well planned.  Then comes the story.
The games takes place in a Blood Thursty Asylum, you take control of Miles Upsher, a Journalist trying to get a story worth printing. But is it easier than he thought?
As for the comparison of Amnesia, it has the same game mechanics apart from the fact that you can vault over objects inbetween running from the most fearful characters of gaming. You will find that you will be running to save you're life and continue the story!
On a scariness level -Outlast suceeds as for being a good comparison to Amnesia. The lighting in different parts of the game gives you a more horror feeling and a more realistic thought as you continue. The sound affects with the creepy music that plays when getting chased is a good example to watch where you are going.
If I had to make one complaint about the game then that would be the length. For a horror game it is very shortened down and as for the scary experience that you have throughtout the game, it only lasts for a few hours on a normal based difficulty. Thats where the DLC comes in to action. The Whistleblower DLC adds a new character and longer storyline to play when you have completed the original!
The DLC - called Whistleblower - The Whistleblower DLC is a great add-on for the game. It adds a nice, new and longer story for people that want to carry on playing Outlast and have already completed the Original game. On Whistleblower you play the character "Waylon Park". This game is a sequal to the Original but Whistleblower storyline stretches out from the Original in the ending.
As it stands - Outlast is my favourite all-time horror game for me, it has all the scary features in it for me. Jumpscares are perfect along with the Sound effects. Hope they make more awesome horror games like this

This game is by far the best JRPG game I've played since 2013 but don't get me wrong here. Not every aspects in the game is excellent so let me go straight to the point.
->Gameplay: The best part about the game is the combat mechanics. It's a real-time-based combat system and it has a lot of common aspects you can find on well-known JRPG games but this one is much better. You can do more than just upgrading your equipments, attacks can reach wide or far, various attack combos, multiple options for your battle strategy and many different enemies with their own special ability. The game gives you large amount of info about the battle mechanics as you progress and some features of the combat is locked until you reached a certain part of the story. Overall, it's excellent.
->Graphics and animation: From the studio who made Fate/Zero, you know this one will be great, and it's superb in my opinion. Not much to say about this part though. It's locked to maximum 30 fps since it's a Playstation port but the beautiful environment and scenes is more than just enough.
->Story: The plot is great, chearful and has scenes that wants you to at least chuckle but it has some cliche that you find on a typical action anime. It's not average but many (not most) of them are not new and suprising. You can tell what's about to happen next in some scenes. All in all, it's exceptional.
In the end, the game is very excellent in terms of its visual and gameplay and the story is as enjoyable as you would expect in my opinion. I would gladly recommend this to any JRPG fans out there especially for those who never played this series before.

Those who have described this as a key finding simulator aren't wrong. The game consists of five keys and two combination locks. Gameplay is limited to looking for a key (the only object you can pick up, and one of about five types of objects you can interact with - the others being notes, lockers, doors and combination locks); finding the key; opening a door; and looking for another key. There are only two puzzles to solve - one which is solved by opening doors, and one which I guessed and solved in about 30 seconds. That second puzzle may have been the most challenging part of the game.
The game wasn't without atmosphere - most rooms were dark and grungy, except, inexplicably, the bright and clean gymnasium. At tad clichéd, but workable. The two minor jump scares did nothing for me, but maybe someone else will have more of a response. Notes scattered throughout the game tell the basis of a story.
Controls were a bit flakey - at times it would say to use the mouse or the keyboard to interact, but only the keyboard would work. However, prompts always led you through the possible interactions, which amounted to click, click and drag, or work with your inventory. There was a small bug with items (keys, as there was nothing else to pick up) not always appearing in the player's hand when selected from the inventory, but that was harmless enough.
Overall, a very short introduction to what might prove to be a bigger key finding simulator. Perhaps if other parts of the game a released there will be something there, but this single part isn't worthwhile. It has some atmosphere but almost no gameplay.
