When I think JRPG, I feel the general standard is Tales/Persona/Star Ocean series (though there are obviously much more). I think:
"The dungeons I explore will have daunting creatures, puzzles, and treasures."
"The sights I will see as I explore this world on an adventure will leave me breathless."
"The characters will leave an impression on me."
"I will grow stronger as I engage in combat with my enemies."
"I will eventually settle a final battle with the evil overlord."
"I will slowly take in a great story."
Typical tropes and expectations I have in most jrpgs and tales games.
How is Tales of Zestiria? It's a new world from the Tales series, but does it measure up to its predecessors?
Short answer: Yes.
This is a minor spoiler, but the controversy surrounding this game isn't really centered around the game itself, but the marketing. They marketed a heroine, introduced her as the heroine, but suprisingly sidelined her at one point in the game in favor of a different character who remained in his party 90% of the game.
The reason fans are bothered by this is the dlc. They released dlc to give an epilogue surrounding the now benched heroine. In essence, they ask you to buy the game with the expectation of an adventure with her, but they take that away to leave you wanting more of her, then telling you to pay for it. Some fans have accused them of plotting this from the beginning to make a shameless cash grab over fans.
Having said that, I fully support the game. The characters were fantastic, the animated sequences were wonderful, and the cinematographer made sure most scenes were nicely animated.
I kinda like how they didn't force a romance onto the player, the devs even said "It's up to the player who he believes is the main heroine." A cop-out of admitting the main heroine, but not a bad one.
The art, however, I found lacking. I'm sure it's because there's some attachment to the PS3, but the sights I was hoping to see when I peered over long cliffs were horrendously dissapointing. You can see the polygons of the sky as it reaches a floor: the surface of the earth obscured... masked in white blurs that pass for clouds. This wasn't the only case, the textures were extremely low effort, the repetitive green shading made me a bit bothered as I walked through a grassy field. Their use of colors is sloppy and repetitive at best.
But the animations for the characters were well polished. The characters body movements during cutscenes were all well done, so while the art might be sloppy, the animations were wonderful.
30fps is an issue, one I am upset with, but future tales games should see framerate increases as this is the last one the ps3 will encumber.
The gameplay was OK. It was fun to equip weapons and armor, fusing them for stronger variants, gaining AP and using battle actions... I found a few things innovative and fun with the combat, but I began to feel nothing but dread to every random encounter near the end. The monsters are EXTREMELY durable. there were normal creatures by the end of the game that had about 35,000-50,000 hp, and you would encounter them in waves of 2-4 each battle. The problem being at level 56 I was able to get a single characters normal combos to do 1.2-1.5 k damage. The danger I felt from the enemies was almost non-existant, but the tediousness of tapping my attack button over and over to finally kill monsters was tiring at best. Sometimes the enemies become completely immune to damage and staggering for a short period of time, and regardless of artes or regular attacks nothing you do will break through, even sometimes when it's not guarding.
WIthout spoiling much of the story... I thought it was fairly great! I liked seeing Sorey grow from a bumpkin to a leader, gaining allies and friends... The story did have minor inconsistencies: hellions are seen by random ppl in the field, but at one point in the game they cant see the spread of the disease which is a hellion, and they cant see their fellow humans as hellions sometimes. There were moments where I could only pause wondering what context they were writing parts of the game, such as the first reunion of Alisha and Sorey, where the fact that he joined their army to avoid her potential execution as a hostage didn't seem to come up in their conversation. She didn't seem to even know he fought in the war. For the most part, try not to look into it, and just make up whatever excuse you can to forget the minor oddities and you'll find the story is very good, even if it could use a moment of revising.
TLDR;
Pros
-Good story
-Animations, movement, expressions
-fun dungeon crawling
-memorable characters
-nice lore
Cons
-Graphics
-30 fps
-tediousness of super-durable random encounters, especially if you're in the epilogue dlc.
-inconsistent story bits.

Writing a review sure may take longer that the one playthrough of Refunct, but it shouldn't discourage you.
This game sure looks barebones when you look at each of its elements separately. Graphics are very simple, goals are clear and uncomplicated, controls standard for the FPP game, and the world itself is just few cuboids with random objects sometimes in between. Despite all of this, Refunct shows how great and engaging game you can create with such small amount of resources.
The tone of the game is also really refreshing. Music is cheerful, colors bright, and gameplay flowy and responsive. Even achievements contribute to the great happy-go-lucky feeling that you get playing this. It's amazing and impressive that you can get such a positive vibes from the such small game. Refunct likes you. It wants to make you happy and it's suggesting you to feel better about yourself... Without usage of any sort of plot or mechanics other than running and jumping.
In short... This game is cute and you should probably play it... especially when you are feeling down.

This tool is absolutely PERFECT for making retro rpgs and can go far beyond that scope thanks to the possibility of creating scripts inside the engine itself. A more than decent RPG creator for those looking into producing this sort of thing. It indeed as it says is powerful enough for big time creation however I would not exactly call it simple to use. It does take some getting use to but eventually you'll be able to put together what you always wanted to.
You will more than likely go through the creation of several test games before you start any serious projects as there is a lot to explore when making something with this software.
The only downsides for RPGMVXace I think are two things. The only available combat system without intersystem programming or third-party content is first-person enemy attacking turn based fighting. I personally would like to explore some new systems when it comes to making the combat of an RPG as most of the time it is the heart and soul of a game. You can of course change it to a top down team on team combat look or on field action fighting RPG with the effort put in. However it is an issue that it takes so much time to make it anywhere near so.
Secondly the expansion packs are not auto install as this is a developers program they expect you to implement the DLC yourself. This can not only be time consuming but a serious pain in the♥♥♥♥♥♥if you don't know what you are doing. Again it has a positive of giving you the option to sort how you want your DLC to be implement ed yourself however it is far to difficult for what it is worth.
I personally have used this editor alot, my hours don't say it all as I was subjected to using a non-steam copy for quite a while until I got the money to actually buy it on here. However I do have some knowledge on how to use the program after just a few hundred hours use. You can always look at options to speed this process such as tutorials and guides on the internet and broaden your horizon with things you can make with third party content. I myself learned how to do most of this stuff over time and am now able to use the software to the extent I would like. Because of this I am now able to develop a decent indie RPG game which has been my goal from the start.
Essentially purchase this software if you ahve the dedication. I'm not in anyway saying do not buy it if you don't have the time, it may just take a longer to understand what you are doing but by all means you can still have fun messing around with it and you can easily develop a fun small game for your friends to try out.
RPGMVXace is a steam essential for people that love their RPGs.

I do not really review episodic titles without having all episodes at hand with a complete walkthrough. With Blues and Bullets I did an exception as the title with its heavy noir atmosphere kept calling me. "A Crowd of Monsters" made an interesting and enjoyable game and I'm sure we'll hear more about them in the future.
In the center of the game we have Eliot Ness who is based on the real Eliot Ness - an agent who enforced the Prohibition in the early 20th century and was famous for being part of the so-called Untouchables, a group tasked with getting Chicago rid of its corruption and - most notably - putting Al Capone behind bars. Here, the story is fictionalised - Eliot has already retired when he gets a visit from one of Capone's henchmen. The kingpin wants to bury the hatchet and offers the agent a job most unexpected: finding his granddaughter as Sofia Capone was kidnapped.
The game is completely monochrome to provide full immersion into its noir-esque world - safe for some objects / areas that stand out due to their vivid, red colours. These either highlight story-related (important) characters or interactable objects or just represent cosmetics (such as Eliot's red tie). Flames also appear in their natural colour - still, I found the game a little dark so I suggest you increase the brightness a little. Too bad there are not many graphics options in the menu - they could have really toned down on the lens flare.
The accompanying music and voice acting are both excellent. Eliot's voice I immediately recognised - he is voiced by none other than Doug Cockle (Geralt of Rivia in the Witcher series). The rest of the cast are also really good - the game offers a film-like experience and the slow but interesting detective sequences get replaced by fast-paced shoot-outs with exploding barrels and Tommy gun wielding goons.
The game is similar to any Telltale games: we interact with objects, pick between conversation options and sometimes make choices. Unfortunately, similarly to any Telltale games we are almost always led to believe that picking the other answer during our next playthrough will yield different results. Another Telltale similarity - the main menu shows our choice in each chapter and we can check how we fared compared to the rest of the gaming community.
I didn't like how the camera worked in the game. It moves along a set route which limits the places we can go. It makes it a tad bit difficult to notice all the interactable objects. A little more freedom in the detective sections could have been better. As for the detective sections - each episode contains a relative big section with explorable rooms. Interacting with each object and their parts (e.g. opening a suitcase and checking its contents by rotating it in every direction) allows us to complete the board; Eliot's questions that should be answered by picking the right clue.
This is a great game! I do not believe we have many in the noir genre; for Blue and Bullets many talented developers and artists assembled. The game, at this point, has only one letdown for me: the release date of its episodes. Episode 1 came out last (2015) summer while the 2nd one only this spring. And we have 3 more episodes to go on. At this rate this does not bode well; hope they can cut down on the difference and bring the series to full fruition this or early next year.
PS: The the rest of the episodes (3-5) will be reviewed later after their release.

Yukie: A Japanese Winter Fairy Tale:
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

Far in the north is a little village that hasn’t experienced the four seasons for many years. This village has been cursed to an eternal winter by the beautiful demon, Yukie. A man with striking blue eyes is determined to avenge his father’s death, along with that of four of his ancestors. To do so, he’ll have to face and beat the demon Yukie. It’s the story of Yukiji.
Yukie: A Japanese Winter Fairy Tale is a visual novel where you experience the story through the eyes of Yukiji, the hero of the tale.
When you start a new game, you’ll be able to decide whether you want to hear the Japanese voice-over or just read the dialogue. As I am not from Japanese background, I chose to read the text. However, I must admit that having the voice in the background gives the game more authenticity. The game itself is presented in scenes, which take between five and twenty minutes to conclude. They can become longer if you keep dying in the battle scenes. As you progress through the sequences, your character will find the graves of his ancestors, which are identified by a Katana (sword).  Take this sword and you will to acquire additional attacks, as well as the ability to move faster, and a parry move.  You’ll also find out more about the story.
The gameplay is fairly simple; depending on the scene, the Hero will either move from left to right, or right to left. Every 10 to 20 seconds a text will appear briefly to continue the story. Some of the scenes will have battles against wolves, hawks, crows and other animals, as well as against additional characters featured in the tale. The battles are based on sounds; you’ll have to identify the sound that represents your enemy. The trick in the battle is to strike at the exact moment that you hear the specific sound. In the later battles, your opponents will fight back and the battle will be won according to how quickly you react against their strikes. To successfully parry an attack, you have to click the appropriate arrow on your keyboard at the precise moment that a small square appears to the right or left of the opponent.  Occasionally, Yukiji will receive additional health points after winning a battle.
The story is pretty good; I deliberately haven’t gone into it in detail because it’s far better for you to experience the story and its highlights yourself.  In any visual novel, you need to have a break from reading; in this case that break is provided by the battle scenes. It’s a nice idea that the reader has to react to the sounds and reflexes in order to parry attacks - it definitely make the game more enjoyable.
The artwork is pretty nice and the soundtrack is great. I think the mechanisms, especially the parries, could have been more accurate.
Positives:
~~~~~~~
-	Interesting story and characters
-	Easy to read
-	Nice artwork
-	Great soundtrack
-	Trading cards.
Negatives:
~~~~~~~~
-	No achievements
-	Mechanisms could have been better
An interesting Visual Novel with combat scenes based on reacting to sounds and reflexes.
6/10

+Nice sound track

+Lots of co-op levels with two difficulties each
+Linux port
Mixed
+/-Controllers are recommended
Cons:
-No online multiplayer
The keyboard controls are fine for this game, but since you are hopefully going to have at least two people sitting at the same desk, controllers are recommended (unless you want a keyboard in your lap, that is). The lack of online multiplayer is almost an improvement to this game, since it actually forces people to sit in the same room together. Reminds me of the good old days of N64 and PS2/Gamecube.
The bottom line is, if you don't have friends living nearby and you don't have at least one controller, you probably shouldn't buy this game. But if you have those things, this game is a blast.

I keep walking, seeing a wolf in the distance, I sneak past, only to discover a logging camp, with three trailers. "Awesome" I think, as I make my way through them. I find a lantern, some lighter fluid, jerky and a soda. I sleep on one of the beds for a few hours before having to go back at it.
Day 2:
I continue down the road, coming across train tracks. I can see a bridge in the distance, so I make my way to it, only to see a dam down the river. I enter it, warming up instantly. I take a second to eat some jerky and drink my soda. First time I've felt safe all day. As I go to search through a locker, I hear something behind me, and as I turn and look, a wolf, someone able to open doors, has made it's way in, and is now eating my foot. I died from blood loss and shock of a wolf being so damn crafty.
10/10 would get jumped by a wolf again.
Edit:
Would love to see a game mode where there's someone hunting you as you're trying to survive. Fires and such give away position, as does maybe foot prints in snow. As scary as wolves are, but stuck in the dark knowing someone could be behind me with a knife sounds terrifying.
Fun and creepy :3 Worth the buy!

There are a lot of good reviews out there already, so I'm not going to repeat most of them... In short, this game is an awesome experience! I never was a fan of survival type of games but ever since I started playing this I'm hooked! Great atmosphere, graphic style that fits perfectly and a learning curve that's not too steep but doesn't hold your hand either. One of the greatest things about it I think is how one event or incident can turn the balance. On my current playthrough I thought I wasn't even going to make 24 hrs. I started in the dark, had used my flare, no weapons, got attacked by a wolf and was left with 9% condition in the middle of a blizzard. I made it to the camp office found enough food and first aid to get me back to 100% and all of the sudden was in great shape... A couple of important lessons I learned:
- When you make a fire, clicking on it opens the menu to cook stuff, melt or boil water or to add wood.
- When making a fire outdoors you need to be very careful not to stand to close to it, you will get killed (happened to me on my second try, when I made it to day 19 and still had plenty of food and ammo.)
- When you select "Forage Wood" while you're inside you can select tinder or reclaimed wood and you will get it inside the location you are. When you do the same thing while outside you get to pick tinder, softwood (cedar, great for fires) or hardwood (fir, needed to repair the rifle, hatchet and knife).
- You should not go out when your condition is under 80%, when above you can easily survive a wolf attack, but below and you may get killed.
- When you fight of a wolf that had you pinned down and it runs away you can follow it's blood trail and often find its dead body. Just make sure you take care of your wounds first and that your condition is high enough, otherwise rest up first and look for the body later.
Definitly recommended!

This is a fabulous example of how video games can be art.
*Graphics*
You play a silouhetted young man in a dreary, monochrome landscape. The art is expertly done through use of contours which accent the game's dark mood. There is a good level of detail among the silhouetttes, and the faded background and midground also have things that are rather creepy when you notice them (bodies hanging, etc). I find the art to be stylish yet economical, and the animations realistic.
*Gameplay*
Your only options are to move around and push/pull items, and yet, there is a feeling of flexibility as you wander through the world, in which you confront huge spiders, brain eating slugs, people trying to kill you, and a good deal of machinery. A lot of the game revolves around puzzles, which start out fairly simple and utilize more physics and logic as you go along. I was also surprised by the game's gore- body parts flying around as your hero dies for the nth time.

I don't even know how to express what I think about this game after having just finished it. A variety of emotions and experiences, even perhaps a few epiphanies. The only thing I can write definitively for myself, is that it really made me look at games and game design as another personal form of self-expression. I will be paying more attention to the details in games that I play, rather than rushing through and devouring all the content. It will only take 2 hours of your life to complete, like watching a movie, but a little more interactive, and cheaper than going to the cinemas too. If you are the creative type, I would definitely recommend you give this a go!

Outlast Whistleblower Update
Outlast Whistleblower is the prequel to Outlast, and pretty much continues the trend and atmosphere experienced in the base game. If you were a fan of the first game's intense a atmosphere, and scare teasing you will enjoy the DLC.
It tells the story of a Waylon Parks The Whistleblower who informs Miles of the atrocities happening in Asylum. There are more than a few nods and mentions to the base game, which will keep the fans happy and provide plenty of 'Aaaaaaah I remember...' moments.
There's just something about the Outlast series that I really like. I'm not sure if it's the presentation, or the sense of hopelessness mixed with the strong desire to survive the main characters have. Perhaps it's something to do with how I always come away feeling like the engine and experience would make the ideal 'Alien' survival game.
If Alien: Isolation is anywhere near Outlast in terms of presentation, story, style, sounding and lightning they'll be onto an instant hit with me.
That feeling of slowly pacing yourself through the corridors of Mount Massive, peeking your head around the corner to scout the junction. Your heartbeat rising as you see a suspected insane inmate ready to tell you a secret... the sound of chains... the musical ques all work together to create a really gripping experience.
I'm not one to scare easily, but this game (and the DLC) got me a fair few times. Not only with the well timed and scripted jump scares, but with the sense of panic that can (and will) takeover as you scramble away from foes determined to cook, fix or marry you. It's one of the few games were you CAN'T fight and flight is your only friend. Running and scramble over objects, squeezing through gaps and hiding in lockers or under beds has never felt so 'real'.
The realism is another aspect that works so well for the game. I felt like I HAD to go slowly, I didn't want to run and announce my arrival and position with the heavy stomps of footsteps.
It's not only the speed of the game, it's the First-Person sway and bobbing. I know some people aren't a fan of the simulated movement of the head however it works so well in Outlast and really helps you believe you're the protagonist.
Overall Outlast - Whistleblower DLC is well worth the time, especially if you played the base game. Sure it has similar elements to Outlast, but that's the beauty of it for me. Play this in the dark.

On the night before christmas a stared at the door, Eager and yet fearful of the battle to come...
Within the beast made of steel and concrete my nemesis awaited my return, for this time i was armed and howling for the taste of this abominations blood.
I prepared myself with water and wolf meat (a small smile graced my face thinking he wont like the smell of his own kind on my breath) then i chaecked my rifle and supllies then headed inside.
Through the passage i walked feeling the crisp air and the breath of fate down my nape, keepijng all corners covered as eased my way through, i lit a flare and tossed it into the corner beside me for ambient light and not to scare off my prey.
As I sat waiting, rifle trained on the top of the stairwell that lead to the bowls of this cold tomb of many time before, i heard the faintest of noise coming from that direction, i aimed and waited longer.
Then all of sudden quiet as the night and darker than any moon-less sky the black fur and glaring teeth of fluffy appeared, calm and steady it moved watching the room but not noticing me at first, more interested in the flare beside me.  He then noticed me kneeling in the opposite corner, i raised my rifle and steadied my breath hoping for a clean kill.
One round out. hit fluffy in the broad of its chest but not enough to kill. A large whelp came from the beast as it span around and ran back down the stairs. knowing i had wounded it was a relief but the battle was still not over.
I got up and walked gingerly to the top of the stairs, eyeing every aspect of that passage, noticing the blood trail on the floor i slowly followed it down the stairs, they turned right and thats when i heard a large growl...
diving across to the far side of the stair platform and slamming into the wall i see fluffy charging at me with all its might.
I raise my rifle pray for an accurate shot under the commotion, squeeze off my last round in a blur of movement Hitting fluffy directly in the head and it keeling over on its side...Dead.
That night i feasted well on the flesh of my enemy and foe of many lives lost. the taste so sweet was fluffy that i forgot to check my surroundings for items, and within the dark found plenty of ammo,food and equipment to last multiple sun rises.
As i left the Dam so cold and daunting i realised that now I'm ready to take on anything this wilderness can throw at me. whether it was cold, starvation or beast alike.
All that remained was the footprints in the snow and a song in my heart for it was christmas day and had survived another Night.
i recommend this as a must buy for anyone who loves survival games and those who enjoy a challenge of their own wits under pressure for if you make a bad call in this you will lose your life :)

I've been playing Tales games since about 2007 with my first game being Tales of the World: Radiant Mythology. Ever since then, I've played most of the releases that came out in North America.
Tales of Zestiria uses a rehashed updated engine from Xillia. People still load in as you progress in fields and towns. The combat is in the real world, “real-time” I suppose. However, because of the PS3’s limitations as this game was made for THAT and the PS4/PC releases being ports. The game engine was made to always being 30fps compared to Xillia’s 30FPS Overworld/60FPS in battle. The 30FPS lock means that there will be slowdowns in certain scenes, but not too much. It doesn’t detract from the experience if you have hardware to keep up with the game’s demands. Anything that isn’t a potato should run this game.
The acting in the game is pretty amazing. Everyone in this game put their hearts out and long hours when recording for this game. Having Kira Buckland as Edna, Robbie Daymond as Sorey, and the mighty Kirbopher/Chris Niosi as Dezel made the game a sure treat to listen to.
The game overall as a whole gets repetitive at some points and sometimes flat out boring in some dungeons like the Water Trial Dungeon. I recommend playing about 1-3 hours at most per session to not get burnt out by this game to fully enjoy what it has to offer.
Also, don’t be fooled by promotional artwork of the game. Alisha, the first female character you meet, accompanies you for about 1/4 of the game before being suddenly kicked out in favor of Rose, the second female character you meet early in the game. Alisha returns at some points in the game, but it’s clear that the development team at Namco Bandai dropped her during development for a different character, but didn’t want to rework the entire game. They also called in Ufotable for anime cutscenes and probably didn’t want to pay them again for changes.
Overall, the game to me feels like a 7-8/10. It’s not a bad game, it’s not the best either. But it’s a fun game with great characterization and acting. Is it worth the $49.99 price tag? Sure, but if you get it for cheaper, it’s an absolute steal.
10/31/2015: I beat the game. The game's closure is really lackluster in my honest opinion. It was terrible. Wouldn't mind bumping this game down to 6-7/10. For a game in 2015, this game is worse than Xillia/Xillia 2 and pretty much every Tales Series game out there. Probably even worse than the hated Symphonia: DoTNW.
11/1/2015: Doing all of the sidequests gives more closure to some of the characters. Particularly everyone except Mikleo and Sorey, who had their closure time during the main story in Lastonbell. The Post-Game Epilogue DLC "Alisha's Story" started out as perhaps an interesting tale for Alisha. However, this DLC is just another dungeon with like 6-7 floors of the same crap with Monsters that are usually all resistant to physical attacks, making you want to just play Rose instead of Alisha. The story is meh, started out great, then it just feels tacked on and like it was so out of character for everyone to tell Alisha what's going on. It feels like that the developers really hated Alisha and only had her for contracting reasons and tried to appease to the fans they♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off by kicking her out of the game like 2-3 hours in the game.

There are a lot of people who say that this game isn't scary, or at least isn't as scary as it's hyped up to be. That's fine. What makes something "scary" is subjective, after all. Even if you don't have a fear of animatronics or don't react much to jumpscares, the one thing that I think we can agree on is this: The tension in this game is very high.
Managing only one resource--power--seems simple enough but the room for error dwindles as the difficulty increases each night. Even if you know each character's behavior and how to monitor them, the speed with which you have to address them ramps up and you're bound to make more mistakes. Meanwhile, the atmosphere is doing its best to unnerve you to a higher degree as you progress. The noises in the game aren't so bad on their own but the last thing you would ever want to hear while checking the cameras is footsteps in the hall or Freddy's laughter, regardless whether or not they indicate an actual threat.
Throw in some hallucinations and Foxy channelling Usain Bolt and you're almost done with Night 3.

Unity horror games are a dime a dozen. For a lot of them, a dime is also all they’re worth.
is yet another Unity-based horror game. It shows promise, but isn’t there yet.
As a divorced alcoholic, your ex-wife calls to tell you that your daughter has run away, and because you’re a divorced alcoholic, you’re clearly a great father, and decide to go track her down and bring her back home.
You head to St. Mary’s School, where “believing in kids, gods gift” is apparently their poorly worded and grammar lacking motto, and your journey begins. You must find a key to open a door, which will give you another key to open another door, and once in there, you’ll get a
, nah just kidding, another key.
Eventually, chapter one ends. And you’ll be scratching your head.
What is annoying is that Episode 0, which I imagine would’ve been a quick prelude to the game, was a cutscene that was about 90 seconds long. Why was this considered an episode? Why couldn’t the cutscene play at the beginning of episode one, like the vast majority of games?
For an indie game with what I’m assuming is a small budget, the music is fairly decent. There’s not much variation to it, but it isn’t grating enough to become annoying.
The acting is surprisingly good. The protagonist definitely sounds like he’s an alcoholic, and has that gruff, harsh voice of someone who no longer really cares.
The graphics are okay. I’ve seen worse. While they get the job done, there’s a fair amount of artifacting, with objects popping or weird lighting effects that defy the way lights fall. Your character’s animation is also very stiff, the worst being when you answer your phone, and your arm slowly raises from your side like some sort of battery powered animatronic that’s in need of a battery change.
They’re horrible. Strafing is absolutely atrocious. If you try to combine walking or running while strafing, good luck with that. There are no options to change sensitivity, either.
All of the keys you pick up are what appear to be unmarked metal keys, as shown in your inventory. Yet when you open your inventory, most of the keys have a description of what they’re for. “B1 Bathroom Key” or “Office Key”. With no markings on them, and we’re assuming this guy isn’t part of the staff, because he clearly isn’t, how does he know which key opens what? Any sort of suspension of disbelief is shattered.
Throughout the game, there are many journals to read. When you see one, it’ll have the exact same text and be labeled the same, yet when you actually use it, it’s different text. That text is also very small, and it’s actually much easier to read what’s on the paper before you interact with it. Odd design choice and/or lack of…
It doesn’t exist. A wheelchair that rolls across the hall in front of you, yet the wheels don’t actually move. Story notes that are identical. Music that doesn’t always sound positional (such as the gramophone in the gym). Also, at some point for no reason, my flashlight went out and I couldn't turn it back on. Does the flashlight have a limited battery? If so, that should be portrayed somehow, perhaps with him banging the side of it, hoping it doesn't go out, or just flat out say you have limited time with it. If it's not intended, then it's a very odd bug.
In its current state, the game is a bit below average. It’s not horrible by any stretch, and there’s definite promise, but it has a way to go. Controls should be updated to be less clunky, some proofreading wouldn’t hurt, and most of the design decisions need to be fleshed out.
Try it if it’s in a bundle, or a giveaway. As there’s currently only one episode available (as of this review), which can be completed in about 40 minutes or quicker, there’s not much here for your money (ignore my play time; I finished it before cards unlocked, and it sat idling for a bit to finish). Once all episodes are released,
all episodes are released, it might be worth a second look.

At it's heart, Banished is a simple game, but it is not easy. I have found it very difficult, at least at the start of a new game. It feels like, to me, getting everything almost perfect is critical to the survival of your people. Don't think I'm complaining, though! Getting a city to flourish is so incredibly satisfying, all the more so because it doesn't happen every time. There is a real sense of accomplishment watching your city grow.
However, it also means that problems you encounter are very difficult, sometimes impossible, to overcome. This game really teaches you that hindsight is 20/20. I would advise having a few different save files.
City management games can easily become tedious, but Banished has never felt so. There are definite stages. The founding of your city is, as I said above, the more difficult. Once your resources are sufficiently built up, you enter a stabilization phase, building population and expanding your city. The endgame is mostly trading for unrenewable resources, and can get a little monotonous, but it takes a while.
Banished is a truly beautiful game. The graphics are detailed without being overdone. I've never had lag or framerate issues. The soundtrack is similarly engaging, without being distracting.
The controls are a bit odd, but comfortable once you get used to them.
The Workshop is full of useful or fun mods, addressing balancing/peeves or creating new buildings.
All in all, 7.5/10.

I am usually quite ambiguous when it comes to evaluating games; even the most critically acclaimed game may fall down into the mire from the right perspective (looking at you FO4). However there are a select few games which I would consider "Must Plays". Games so important and timeless that - provided you have any interest in the genre what-so-ever - you have to own. Oblivion would be such a game for the open-world genre, Dawn of War for the RTS genre. Why? Neither game is perfect by any means, but they are landmarks, marking turning points and signifying a leap forwards.
The FPS genre could have a number of games put forwards for this presitgious honour, but for reasons which shall soon become apparent, the only real contender is Unreal Tournament.
UT99 as it shall be referred to from here on, marked the modernisation of a format which had been in the making for several years. Quake 3 Arena was a popular alternative but play Quake 3 now, and while it is still thoroughly enjoyable, it feels old. It still has the terrible animations, the clinically un-atmospheric environments, the soapy aftertaste of a game lacking in passion and excitement.
UT99 put all of this right. The levels were beautifully designed and characterful, with each and every square inch dripping with details and offering a plethora of combat options. Every weapon had its own personality, there was no progression or advancement from one to the next; just a change in options. Even the characters each had sparks of life in their eyes. But what really set it apart from the rest of the pack was the music. Without the music, UT99 would have been a great game. But the soundtrack elevated it up to the prestigious podium of mastercrafted perfection.
UT99 set new standard for combat, level design, graphic capability, combat scale and bot intelligence. However it's use of  musical scores changed the way games would be designed forever. UT99's stablemates in its year of release almost uniformly did away with soundtracks, save for the occasional musical score. In the year following its release, soundtracks became more common, especially noticable in games like No One Lives Forever and Hitman. Go forwards just one more year, and games such as Halo and Serious Sam join the fray. Both very different games, but what do they have in common? Iconic soundtracks.
UT99 is a fundementally vital game for the advancement of the FPS and the arena shooter, and it deserves its place in the halls of fame (and your library) for that alone. However the next time you notice the musical atmosphere in a game, remember that you have this game to thank.

I remember when RPG Maker first came out.  It wasn't that great.  This is very much not that RPG Maker.
VX Ace is a pretty damn powerful piece of software for creating all kinds of games.  It's got a huge library of pre-made assets to draw from (more with DLC).  It's got scripting with LUA for all kinds of cool tricks.  I've used it to alter the interface of my games and muck with some spell effects and such, but I've seen total-conversion type platformers and fighting games and all kinds of crazy stuff made with VX Ace's engine, thanks to the scripting.
Even if you don't know LUA, though, if you have any kind of urge towards game design, you may wanna check this out.  Granted, it's not really what professionals use (try LOVE or other programs for more serious entry-level stuff).  But it's really easy to get into the nitty gritty and just start Making a Thing right away with VX Ace.  It'll help you start paying attention to details of event flow and triggers, doing database work, level design, character design, you can even write your own music and import it as .ogg files, do your own pixel art if you want.  Or just use what they include.  But you'll probably get sucked into wanting to do more and more for yourself from scratch so that your pet projects really shine, and that's a really cool and fun way to develop some new interests and creative projects that you probably didn't even know you could do!
Self-improvement can be fun!  But uh, it's not cheap either.

First, before the review, I enjoy this game but cannot recommend it until it is finished. It has been ages since it started development thus may never actually be completed.
Godus Wars, formerly Godus, is two games in one. In one game you modify the world making yourself a colony more powerful than all others thus end up taking control of the entire landscape. In the other game you conquer the world using the exploration mechanics of Godus.. which I can’t figure out how to actually start playing.
In Godus you sculpt the landscape thus making it easier or more difficult for your people to navigate resulting in either safety or increased migratory potential. You sacrifice your followers or even use the exploration features to conquer new worlds for resources. You also gain extra resources from treasure chests. These resources you may spend on your tech tree, gifts, shrines, settlements, or powers to give your people the greatest chance of survival.
In Godus Wars.. I imagine you use the exploration feature available in Godus to conquer areas for keys, items, and other resources. After you conquer an area you gain resources to spend further upgrading your populace. I have no way to verify this because in its current distribution Godus Wars doesn’t seem to work thus this explanation is a more in depth explanation of the exploration features of Godus.
Sadly, the creators gave up on Godus Wars for now and the main developer moved to a different project then left his game development company who owns Godus Wars completely… so the game is, in my opinion, unlikely to ever be finished. Its original vision is gone and the direction it will be taken if finished is probably different than the creator intended.
Due to my previous statements I’ll have to give Godus Wars a 80 out of a possible 100. It’s a good game that will probably never be finished and I think that 80 is fair and would be a relatively average rating among those who review it. Godus really is a very good game and is bound to be great if ever finished.

A Hat in Time is a good game, it's not a great game or an amazing game, but it does some things right. And for every thing it does right there's an issue holding it back from being the best it can be. I'm going to recommend it but I'm mostly going to talk about the issues I've had with the game, because I think if the developers put a bit more work in they could have easily made a great or amazing game.
The raw platforming, without abilities and without enemies around, is very enjoyable. The controls are very responsive and you're always looking for new place to try and jump to. The Hat abilities themselves are also all quite good and blend into the gameplay well, but there's nothing you can do with Hat Kid that hasn't already been done before, everything she does she does well enough and a bit different enough that you don't mind. It never really feels like a cheap knock-off game. There are downsides though. The character controls are camera relative and the camera does tend to move on it's own in strange and unpredictable directions, this means you'll be holding a direction and expecting your character to go in it, only for the camera to move you an inch to the left, causing you to whack your head on a fence and bounce off, plumetting to your death. All of the automated functions like homing attacks, grapple hooks and tight ropes are character relative too, meaning if your character is facing the wrong way because the camera moved on it's own mid jump you're going to miss the prompt for the next thing and also, plummet to your death. The tightropes in particular are very interesting, since many times I've lined up the ropes perfectly only to go straight through them, where my sloppy or rushed jumps that I think I've missed end up magnetizing me to the rope. This hit and miss situation makes the segments where you have to bounce from rope to rope extremely frustrating because you have no idea what's going to happen. Though they space these sections out fairly far apart so you don't frustrated with them, making these things distance based instead of character relative would make these problems go away.
The levels are all well done, the worlds are vibrant and have their own stories and the characters in them have their own personalities and motives that get revealed to you as you progress through an area. As you unlock new hat abilities new areas open up to you with lots of hidden goodies to collect and the stories tend to draw you in just enough that you don't mind doing a bit of backtracking every now and then. There's an unusual reliance on stealth mechanics in the game, where you have to dodge vision cones or get sent back to the start of an area, over traditional fighting. The main reason I think is just that the combat mechanics aren't really there. As you explore a level there aren't really any enemies to fight. In fact fighting is very much optional, for a very large chunk of the game unless you need to chain homing attacks to get somewhere. There are specific combat abilities you can unlock that you never really need and there's a slot for 'weapon' on the character screen that I don't think you ever have to use, because after the first mission you get the only weapon you're going to use for the rest of the game. It's a bit disappointing that they give you a cool lazer beam attack that you never have to use. The boss fights don't require you to use any of your hat or badge abilities either, they have very simple patterns that after a tiny bit of trial and error you can get down straight away. I'm sure you can use your hat abilities to make them even easier but I never felt like I needed to. The bosses as characters are great and they are enjoyable as a result of them characterizing their villains quite well, but the fights themselves are underwhelming.
It's a fairly short game, I have 32 Time Pieces and I've played about four and a half hours or so, about a quarter of that time was spent backtracking through things I've already done to track down whatever I need to progress forward. I haven't finished the game yet but I have unlocked all 5 worlds and 100% completed two of them already. I probably have maybe one or two more hours of gameplay before I've completely finished everything there is to do. Though the smaller worlds and backtracking aren't that terrible, as the worlds themselves are packed full of detail and lore that just makes them a lot more fun to play around in. It's just a shame there isn't more levels. Hopefully at some point there will be, either through DLC. Or mods, as there is full mod support for the game.
Overall A Hat in Time is a good game and worth picking up if you want to play a 3D platformer, just be aware that it's very much a 3D platformer and not much else. It sticks to what it's good at like glue and I think that rigid approach to the level design and gameplay is what lets it down. Not so much just more combat but better combat or even just a reason to fight anything at all would have been very nice. Also with all the hat abilities you get it, you never really find yourself having to quickly switch between them which is a real shame, since the straightforward level design doesn't just bring the game down but it's also a large part of why it's so easy. Outside of their specific usage scenarios inside the areas you find them in and a few others, you basically never have to use them. The game is called A Hat in Time and you never really have to worry about what hat you're wearing until something glowing a certain colour is blocking your way. It does feel disappointing when you have a cool wizard hat that lets you shoot explosions and you basically only use it to clear crates once or twice a level.
Even though my very presitigious Steam review has been fairly negative, A Hat in Time is worth it if you have a young child and want to get them playing games or you just need to scratch that platformer itch. Just don't expect it to really do much else.

This is a fabulous example of how video games can be art.
*Graphics*
You play a silouhetted young man in a dreary, monochrome landscape. The art is expertly done through use of contours which accent the game's dark mood. There is a good level of detail among the silhouetttes, and the faded background and midground also have things that are rather creepy when you notice them (bodies hanging, etc). I find the art to be stylish yet economical, and the animations realistic.
*Gameplay*
Your only options are to move around and push/pull items, and yet, there is a feeling of flexibility as you wander through the world, in which you confront huge spiders, brain eating slugs, people trying to kill you, and a good deal of machinery. A lot of the game revolves around puzzles, which start out fairly simple and utilize more physics and logic as you go along. I was also surprised by the game's gore- body parts flying around as your hero dies for the nth time.

Go to where you installed Steam, and go down SteamApps\common\Fallout 3\Fallout3.exe
Right-click, go to properties, click compatibility, and run the compatibility troubleshooter.
Check the box that says "Run this program in compatibility mode for" and select what it says. Try Windows 7.
HOW TO RUN DLC:
Start the launcher, but don't go fullscreen. Select "DATA FILES" and check all the boxes, and the click OK.

Outlast Whistleblower Update
Outlast Whistleblower is the prequel to Outlast, and pretty much continues the trend and atmosphere experienced in the base game. If you were a fan of the first game's intense a atmosphere, and scare teasing you will enjoy the DLC.
It tells the story of a Waylon Parks The Whistleblower who informs Miles of the atrocities happening in Asylum. There are more than a few nods and mentions to the base game, which will keep the fans happy and provide plenty of 'Aaaaaaah I remember...' moments.
There's just something about the Outlast series that I really like. I'm not sure if it's the presentation, or the sense of hopelessness mixed with the strong desire to survive the main characters have. Perhaps it's something to do with how I always come away feeling like the engine and experience would make the ideal 'Alien' survival game.
If Alien: Isolation is anywhere near Outlast in terms of presentation, story, style, sounding and lightning they'll be onto an instant hit with me.
That feeling of slowly pacing yourself through the corridors of Mount Massive, peeking your head around the corner to scout the junction. Your heartbeat rising as you see a suspected insane inmate ready to tell you a secret... the sound of chains... the musical ques all work together to create a really gripping experience.
I'm not one to scare easily, but this game (and the DLC) got me a fair few times. Not only with the well timed and scripted jump scares, but with the sense of panic that can (and will) takeover as you scramble away from foes determined to cook, fix or marry you. It's one of the few games were you CAN'T fight and flight is your only friend. Running and scramble over objects, squeezing through gaps and hiding in lockers or under beds has never felt so 'real'.
The realism is another aspect that works so well for the game. I felt like I HAD to go slowly, I didn't want to run and announce my arrival and position with the heavy stomps of footsteps.
It's not only the speed of the game, it's the First-Person sway and bobbing. I know some people aren't a fan of the simulated movement of the head however it works so well in Outlast and really helps you believe you're the protagonist.
Overall Outlast - Whistleblower DLC is well worth the time, especially if you played the base game. Sure it has similar elements to Outlast, but that's the beauty of it for me. Play this in the dark.
Just make sure your other half doesn't burst through the door 2am in the morning, turns the lights on and scares the crap out of you...

Tales of Zestiria owns all of the good features of a "Tales of" game, and a few new pitfalls that are fairly balanced out.
First, the pros:
+Story is excellent, as always
+Setting can be absolutely beautiful
+Characters are great, dynamic, and all of them are witty and humorous
+The gameplay is addicting and fun
+The battle system allows for some really kickass combinations and moves
+New features to the game are integrated well
+The Battle Skills system is a bit revamped, and it's actually better for newer players while still easy for veteran players
Cons:
-This port is not perfectly optimized for PC, and can have issues still
-Some textures are lackluster, even with high settings
-While the anime cut scenes are flawless, the "skits" can have off-time audio/visual (common to "Tales of" games in general)
-The Battle System is so heavy with features, mechanics, and stats that you're basically learning how to play the game for a majority of the game itself. The "Monoliths" that are spread throughout the game are an ongoing tutorial that begins to drag forever, and it can be VERY EASY to forget many of the helpful features due to their sheer number. Some refinement could have been used to make the game simpler, though as stated above these features and mechanics are at least integrated well. The big IF here is whether or not you have the ability to coordinate your battle and your character(s) like a symphony orchestra conductor.
Overall, this is an excellent game that is barely held back by any of its trivial flaws. If you're looking for a lengthy action-RPG with excellent story, you can't go wrong here. Also, it's an RPG on Steam. Buy more of these, and Steam will have more of them. This formula has worked so far!

I'll start off by saying this review is in no way influenced by the developers decision to not give steam keys to people who purchased the game in the groupees bundle...  Even though I went ahead and purchased the game, I still think the Developer has an obligation to people who already purchased the game to provide them with a key.... enough on that subject...
Where to start with One Final Breath, it looks in the trailers to be your prototypical First person horror experience..  The graphics are decent, not the most impressive but very passable.  The game play is your typical search the random dark place to answer some burning questions or solve some type of question.  This game isn't an exception as you are tasked with finding your daughter who has run away from home.
As you explore the abandoned St. Mary's school, you'll find scattered notes left behind to help you piece together the history and get some back story on the building.
The first part in what will eventually be a five part episodic game.  So my review could change as future episodes are released (if they are released)  Ultimately it still remains to be seen what the developer has to offer in the future with this game.
Some negitives I've taken from the game... it's too dark with no options available to brighten it up.  Dubious audio quality with no option to turn on Subtitles.  Seems to be a key hunting simulator thus far.  In fact when it comes to in game options non exist..  Prior to starting up the game you can alter a few settings but for a game like this you should really be able to have on the fly changes.  The audio is either missing or needs to be made more clear/ or turned up as my character made numerous references to sounds which I didn't hear from my speakers or headphones..  The spelling, well this one isn't a deal breaker but still.... what is a WONG key?
Also about 40 minutes into my playthrough the screen became transparent, then slowly went dark, the mouse cursor was stuck in the middle of the screen and I couldn't control it, attempts to move the mouse were meet with the cursor thrashing back and force in a one inch hidden square.  I was unable to do anyting at all, I eventually had to ctl, alt, del out of the game then manually close it out..  It wound up costing me the 39 minutes I had played...
The positives..  the atmosphere is fairly unnerving, even with the above mentioned sound issues.  The art style is rather unique and sets it apart from alot of the other FP horror games flooding the market.. The story seems engaging and interesting for the most part.  Provided you care to seek it out from the various scraps of paper which lay around.  The map layout is fairly simplistic to remember (not overly complicated to increase)  the puzzles are simple.
I would have to not recommend this game currently, this may change provided the developer goes back and attempts to fix some of the bugs and glitches I mentioned above, and at the bare minimum includes some type of settings in the game menu.  Subtitles would also be very beneficial, especially for people who are hard of hearing like myself...

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding cheese cake recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1 cup digestive plain sweet biscuit crumbs
3 tablespoons sugar
3 tablespoons melted butter
40 ounces softened cream cheese
1 cup sugar
3 tablespoons flour
1 tablespoon vanilla
1 cup sour cream
4 eggs
Directions:
For The base:.
If you're using a dark pan, preheat the oven to 350. If you are using a shiny pan, 375.
Combine the crumbs, melted butter and 3 tbsp sugar well and pat onto the bottom of a 9 inch springform pan. I also like to very very lightly butter the sides of the pan so that the cheesecake will not stick later on.
Bake for 10 mins in your preheated oven and remove. Let it cool while you prepare your batter.
For the batter:.
Make sure everything is at room temperature.
Combine sugar, cheese, flour and vanilla in a big bowl and mix on medium speed till well combined. Don't forget to scrape the bowl as you're doing this.
Mix in the sour cream till its incorporated well. Then, add the eggs one by one, mixing well after each addition.
Pour the batter into the springform and let it bake for 1 hour and 10 minutes After the baking time, turn off the oven and leave the door ajar. Let the cake cool in there for about 1 1/2 hours.
Remove the cake and let it cool thoroughly. Refrigerate overnight.
Release the sides of the springform.
Eat.

Disclaimer: I haven't finished this game yet, this is very much a first impression. Don't get your knickers in a twist if I get something wrong or leave some example out Everything you read here is subject to change.
A Hat in Time is a platformer funded by kickstarted developed by Gears for Breakfast.
It very much wears its influences on its sleeve. The gameplay harkens back to a time where 3D platformers were a total blast to control (Think SM64/Sunshine and Banjo Kazooie). Even though A Hat in Time is supposed to be a successor to the 3D platformers of the late 90s and early 2000's, the amount of games and other media this game takes from is much larger. Those well-read in game trivia from back in the day will notice references left and right that might evoke a smile, or a sigh of exasperation depending on how immersed you like being.
Gameplay: Pretty damn good, but a bit of polish could have done wonders
A Hat in Time controls far better than the average PC game in its genre, but it still doesn't have the polish that you'd expect from a Nintendo or Rare classic. Hat Kid has many of the same moves as Mario from Sunshine, but she doesn't have quite the same weight to jumping that made Sunshine such a joy to control. Combat especially feels quite stilted and awkward, Hat Kid has limited options for attacking in the air, which can lead to some awkward situations in more challenging levels. Still, despite my problems with the movement mechanics in AHiT, I still had tons of fun moving around the game world.
Presentation: I really shouldn't complain, but here goes anyway.
A Hat in Time, visually speaking is a mixed bag. While many areas have had layer after layer of visual polish, some areas look flat out lazy in comparison. Character animation ranges from pretty good to pretty bad at times. While Hat Kid has a very appealing design, many supporting characters look like they were stock assets taken from an old Dark Basic game (The owls particularly offend me). I have my complaints, but AHiT will look completely fine to most people.
On the other hand, the music and sound design here is top-notch. The music will dynamically change depending on where you are in the game or what you're doing. You'll hear instruments be swapped out, the music slow down, or speed up. The songs themselves are quite catchy and evoke the rich sounding music that was present in Super Mario Galaxy. The voice acting, unfortunately, needs work, but the game thankfully gives you an option to have characters mumble like Banjo Kazooie, so I can't be too hard on it.
Verdict: If you dearly miss the days where 3D platformers had actual depth and complexity to them, and Yooka Laylee left you sorely dissapointed, then A Hat in Time might be just what you've been looking for. Especially if you can't afford Mario Odyssey or a Switch. However, if you're like me and constantly nitpick an otherwise fine game for how it's different to what it claims to be, you may be dissapointed yet again.

A Hat in Time is simply amazing. The controls are fantastic, and it very rarely felt like Hat Kid (the game's adorable protagonist) wasn't doing exactly what I told her to do. Platforming is the core of every level, and the game gives you plenty of tools to move about in a myriad of ways, whether it's diving in midair to get extra distance or swingingly effortlessly with a grappling hook.
The characters are amazingly endearing, to the point where I can't get them out of my head. The entire game is fully voice acted (with some barely-there exceptions). I found myself enjoying the voices, but if you don't you can simply turn them off, or even convert them to Banjo-Kazooie-style mumbling noises! Every interaction is full of humor, and I found myself laughing out loud on multiple occasions.
The music is also phenomenally catchy, with each track fitting the stage perfectly, and multiple instrumentations that fade in seamlessly depending on where you are in the level. A Hat in Time's composer Pascal Michael Stiefel deserves major kudos, and I hope to see him in many more games in the future.
I think the one criticism I would have of A Hat in Time is that its first world, Mafia Town, is a bit rough around the edges. The character models seem a bit messy, and there are cutscenes in those levels that seem like they're missing animations. The game's presentation improves massively after that, and I was absolutely in love with the final world. The boss encounters are also amazingly fun and high-energy, in a genre that generally suffers from slow and boring boss fights.
I highly, HIGHLY recommend A Hat in Time, especially if you fondly remember the tight platforming of Super Mario Sunshine or the constant humor of Paper Mario: The Thousand-Year Door. At $30 it's worth every single penny, and two additional chapters are on the way as free post-launch DLC. Forget the memory of failed Kickstarter promises and buy this game!

The Beginner's Guide is one of the more interesting gaming experiences I've had this year. The game is narrated by it's developer Davey Wreden and tells the story of one of his friends who used to make small games. The game is essentially you playing though these games with Davey's commentary analysing what he thinks the games mean, and you're encouraged to give it some thought yourself.
To say any more about the game is to spoil it, and this is a game to play unspoiled. It's not going to be for everyone - especially with the overwhelming success of The Stanley Parable, people might come into The Beginner's Guide expecting more of the same, and they could be disappointed. However, if you go into the Beginner's Guide knowing what it is then I think you'll enjoy the experience. At its core, The Beginner's Guide is a short, interactive, emotional story told through video games that you can and should play in one sitting that will leave you thinking once the final game has been completed. If that sounds like something you'd enjoy, then The Beginner's Guide is for you.

As a big fan of the Tales of... series, my excitement for this game maintained its high ranking throughout the year. Finding out it was going to be on Steam definitely interested me, and I have to say that the inclusion of more platforms proved to be a good decision.
In general, Tales of Zestiria returns to older Tales of... formulas and improves upon the newer battle systems introduced in Tales of Graces, Tales of Xillia, and Tales of Xillia 2. I would honestly say this game contains a good mix of new and old Tales of... games. Tales of Zestiria contains a much more open world than Tales of.. games of late, which was nice to see after the linear world of Graces, Xillia, and Xillia 2. I actually felt like I was exploring vast areas in Zestiria, which really added to the experience. Unfortunately, the world in Tales of Zestiria still feels smaller compared to older Tales of... games, as I don't feel as I'm venturing throughout the world, moreso venturing through a continent. However, this drawback stems from the style the developers are going for, so it's necessarily a system needed to be perfected, rather than a flaw in this particular game.
The battle system in Tales of Zestiria certainly expands on Tales of Graces rather than Tales of Xillia, as evidenced by the lack of TP or another MP-based battle system. In addition, A-Artes and B-Artes return as Martial Artes and Hidden Artes for humans, and Hidden Artes and Seraphic Artes for Seraphim. This makes the battle system seem awfully familiar to Tales of Graces, and really, it's a fun system. In addition, the game allows Seraphim and Humans to combine, creating a stronger playable entity which will completely destroy certain enemies. This game isn't easy unless you master this battle system, so the overpowered entity really assists the difficulty curve. Unfortunately, the camera definitely does not agree with many battles, and while the seamless transition from field to battle is nice, I don't believe the game was ready for that transition until the camera issue was solved.
The overall gameplay system also really expands upon itself, mainly stemming from the fusion system. The fusion system in this game, which allows one to work with different skills, really expands upon the battle system. The goal to becoming stronger in this game lies more in what skills one has, rather than how much attack or defense a certain piece of equipment holds. Until one learns this system, the game can be penalizing on harder difficulties.
There's so much more I could talk about, but really, it all comes down to personal preference. Tales of Zestiria really boils down to whether one wants to have a fun time playing an RPG with a fun action battle system, or not. While I found the story to be entertaining, I can see why many don't care for it, as it's a commonplace Tales of.. game story. However, the characters are enjoyable to watch, the story was fun to watch unfold, and the gameplay was phenomenal. I definitely recommend this game if you enjoyed any other Tales of... game, or if you enjoy real-time battle systems.

I found this little game during a steam sale and though I'd give it a go.
At first I was loving it, reminded me of the early Settlers games before Ubisoft got their hands on Blue Byte and completely ruined the essence of the games for ever.
You start with a few banished settlers and a few supplies. It's then down to you to manage your settlement, find resources, build the right kinds of resource buildings, and make sure that you have enough homes for a growing population. Your little people will age, settle down with another and have children. Who will need to be schooled so they can become more skilled workers and be more efficient at the the jobs they end up in.
There's a thriving modding community making new resource buildings and user tools and for a while the game is lots of fun.
However... as your town grows, so does the strain on your CPU. It's very resource intensive and I don't think the developers have made the game scale up very well.  I have a high end 8 core CPU, 16GB ram and a top end graphics card... but once the town hits 500 or so residents. Thinks start to slow down, 600 and frame rates are dropping sharply. 800 and it's stuttering along from time to time and every time it autosaves... the game simply stops until it completes.
There's also no end game... No goals to achieve. Once you've got a town up and running, feeding itself and your population is stable. You can only choose to leave it ticking over like that, or grow it further.
After a while it simply becomes very boring to play.  I've not picked it up in months as a result.
However... whilst I am not recommending the game. It's not an expensive way to kill a few hours. Just don't expect any longevity from it.
Who knows, many it will continue to be developed and they'll make you able to trade with other settlements or build an army to attack other towns... Like you used to be able to in the original settlers games.

I've come back to this game after a couple of years to give it another try one day when I was bored and looking for something to kill a few hrs.
There have been improvements to the game, it's certainly been better optomised. Same rig as before and I can now grow larger villages... But if you like to speed things up like I do when letting things idle along... It's once again slows to a crawl. keep it at 1x or 2x speed and it's good for towns of around 1500 unless you want to makes things go a little quicker.
It's alo still got a massive flaw in it... the balance between stable & unstable populations is such a thin and fine line that you cannot tell when a cascade failure is going to happen.
There I was going along with around 1400 adults, 300 students and 4 hundred children... with food productions hitting 70-80,000 a year and always being left with an excess of 20-30,000 come harvest time... then within a year and an adult growth of jut 20 or so people... students and children roughly the same. I'm suddenly facing starvation.
I grow more crops, make more farmers... still each year I can't make it throgh to harvest without 10-20 people dying of starvation. I close down the schools to give my woking population a huge boost, put those extra 300 people to work growing food... it's still not enough. In one year the produce required by my villagers jumpers from 40-50,000 to 75-80,000 without much in the way of a population change.
Then I start getting issues where I'm suddenly not producing enough tools.. even with 16 blacksmiths hammering away producing steel & carbon steel tools... the lack of food affects other industries... all of a sudden my fish pnds drop production by 40-50% without any drop in workers... 48 fisherman can't produce enough fish for the village, 130+ herdsmand with 30 fields of all types of farm stock can't produce enough meat to feed the village.. and over 600 farmers and more than 60 fields cannot produce enough food.
I'm careful about how I build homes and markets for my settlers... each home is easily within distance of resources, work and food. Yet for no reason a worker will move to the other side of the village and can barely get to work before they leave to get food.
Fields that were once harvested well before late autumn came, now have food laying around unpicked and wasted. if they picked it all... I'd be hitting closer to 100,000 units of food.
So I start buying in tools and extra food with all of those extra goods I'm making... selling bricks and roof tiles, warm coats, pottery... everything except food.  I'm buying in thousands of food units... It's still not enough. Every year 20-30 die and only 10-15 become adults... Soon my children start to grow in numbers whilst my adults reduce... It's a cascade that then starts to become a little worse each year... I start praying for the children to die.. but these muppets keep having more and more of them. Soon adults are dropping in larger numbers... 500 kids and 1500 adults.... 520 kids and 1450 adults... it compaounds the problem... more die... more are born. Within less than a generation I have a population that is 40% children... I can't afford to start educating them again because that compounds the problem even further.
It becomes a never ending cycle of doom... then it reaches a critical juncture... In spite of buying in thousands of carbon steel tools... suddenly... the number of people without tools starts to rocket... 10, 20, 30, 40... 150, 200... 300... that means less work getting done... more starvation, more deaths.
But it's impossible to recover from... these little rutting rabbits cannot keep it in their pants long enough to stablize the population... Their loins and their seed are the very seeds of their own undoing.
In short... whilst you can grow bigger villages... the balance is so b0rked that's it becomes impossible to provide stability. Every village no matter how big or small... is essentially doomed to oblivion.

One Final Breath is a fantastic game that reminds me of Tell-tale’s style of gaming and storytelling. This makes for a compelling game that keeps you engaged and coming back for more.
The game runs in Unity, which is a great game development architecture which allows for a rich and deep gaming experience.
The graphics of the game are nothing to boast about (in comparison to a triple A title), but that’s a positive – especially as it means that you could run this game on almost any given rig. The frame rate is a constant 60 fps, the controls are simplistic and suitable and the game itself runs well and bug-free in my experience.
The game features an involving storyline, with a rich narrative told through good voice acting and cinematic to match. This is perhaps the strongest element of the game and is carried through well into gameplay. The episodic nature of the game is an interesting choice and keeps you coming back for more content, especially if you like playing narrative games in long bursts (like me)!
I would love for a more in-depth graphics options being built-in to the game’s menu, and a general expansion of options – for example subtitle options, key rebinding and so on. This would make more sense being made accessible in-game rather than through a launcher. It’s more of a convenience thing.
All-in-all, this is a great game for those who love dynamic storytelling and compelling gameplay. Definitely recommended!

Well, straight up, I have to give this game kudos for trying to stand out at least a LITTLE in the current rash of first-person, "non-combative" horror games being foisted on the market...yes, there does seem to be THAT many of them of late!  First of all, there's the rather wacky "detective"-style monologue of our booze-happy protagonist, which while a little on the "inappropriate" side for a game whose primary aim should be SCARING us, is at least...er...yes, "different", I suppose.  Secondly, the slightly cartoon-ish graphics are...well, again, DIFFERENT!  You may be getting the impression by now that I'm not necessarily using the word "different" to imply "genius", but points to the devs for vaguely trying and all that jazz.
Then there's a lot - and I mean a LOT - of things in this which are all-too-familiar to those of us who buy every second first-person horror game that comes out.  A lack of a flashlight*, which doesn't so much add to the atmosphere, but makes searching around for keys and what-not a bit of a chore.  And did I say KEYS?  Yup, lots of THEM in this game, too.  You know you're in for a key-heavy game when you attempt to open the door to a public bathroom and are told, "I need to find a key to open this bathroom".  Thank ♥♥♥♥ it isn't that hard to gain access to a public toilet in the REAL world (unless you're in France).  What else?  Well, the sound effects drop in and out and seem unfinished at best; some of the "animations" (e.g. our character raising his phone to answer it) are lifeless and robotic; there's oodles of doors which you not only can't unlock, but indeed can't seem to interact with any more than you could a perfectly featureless brick wall; keypad panels next to doors which are almost impossible to successfully interact with...and so on and so forth.
There's some other distinct lacks of originality which I noticed, but these are really more observations than complaints, as I generally eat this kinda thing up for breakfast in all honesty.  How about a school with weird "overhangs" from a hospital, such as wheelchairs with ghostly spinning wheels...sound familiar?  How about said hospital crossing over into an asylum?  Spooky little girls with black hair?  No...none of that rings any bells for you?!  Man, you really don't watch too many horror movies or play too many horror games, do you?!?
Alas, almost everything that I've stated thus far might be eminently forgiveable, if this game didn't commit perhaps the cardinal sin of any self-professed "horror" game...that is to say, it just ISN'T THAT SCARY.  Sure, it's a tiny bit "spooky", and yeah, there's a couple of very minor and faintly effective "jump scares" up its worn sleeves, but nothing even remotely inspired.
I guess it goes without saying that this game isn't QUITE as good as it looks in the screenshots.  But really, what should I expect at this stage?  We should all know by now that any game whose Store page makes you go "♥♥♥♥ me, that looks ♥♥♥♥ing AWESOME!" is probably going to fall substantially short of expectations, unless it has words like "Outlast" or "Amnesia" in the title.  I only have myself to blame, really.  I really should know better.  Oh well.  No doubt there'll be another game just like this in the Store by this time next week, and unless the price is suitably outrageous, I'll probably be a♥♥♥♥♥♥and buy that one too.  Sigh.
Now, I see you're waiting anxiously for the PUNCHLINE to all I've said thus far?  C'mon...you know it already.  You've looked at the Store page.  You've heard my testimony thus far.  And you've had a glance at my playing time.  What you maybe DON'T know is that I have a tendency to pause things for short periods whilst I go off and do other (quite possibly more productive) things, like visit the toilet (the one in my flat, which I definitely don't need a key to gain access to).  So yes, sure enough...IT'S A VERY SHORT GAME.
Now, granted, it still has a few "episodes" to go, and I believe I'll get these for "free" down the track as part of my mighty four dollar expenditure.  But unless future episodes are substantially longer, it's still going to be only a few hours in length, tops.  In all sincerity, such things affect my opinion of games very little, as long as they're high quality games for whom the short length seems more than justified given the narrative being told (see "Among The Sleep" for one such example).
