Disclaimer: I haven't finished this game yet, this is very much a first impression. Don't get your knickers in a twist if I get something wrong or leave some example out Everything you read here is subject to change.
A Hat in Time is a platformer funded by kickstarted developed by Gears for Breakfast.
It very much wears its influences on its sleeve. The gameplay harkens back to a time where 3D platformers were a total blast to control (Think SM64/Sunshine and Banjo Kazooie). Even though A Hat in Time is supposed to be a successor to the 3D platformers of the late 90s and early 2000's, the amount of games and other media this game takes from is much larger. Those well-read in game trivia from back in the day will notice references left and right that might evoke a smile, or a sigh of exasperation depending on how immersed you like being.
Gameplay: Pretty damn good, but a bit of polish could have done wonders
A Hat in Time controls far better than the average PC game in its genre, but it still doesn't have the polish that you'd expect from a Nintendo or Rare classic. Hat Kid has many of the same moves as Mario from Sunshine, but she doesn't have quite the same weight to jumping that made Sunshine such a joy to control. Combat especially feels quite stilted and awkward, Hat Kid has limited options for attacking in the air, which can lead to some awkward situations in more challenging levels. Still, despite my problems with the movement mechanics in AHiT, I still had tons of fun moving around the game world.
Presentation: I really shouldn't complain, but here goes anyway.
A Hat in Time, visually speaking is a mixed bag. While many areas have had layer after layer of visual polish, some areas look flat out lazy in comparison. Character animation ranges from pretty good to pretty bad at times. While Hat Kid has a very appealing design, many supporting characters look like they were stock assets taken from an old Dark Basic game (The owls particularly offend me). I have my complaints, but AHiT will look completely fine to most people.
On the other hand, the music and sound design here is top-notch. The music will dynamically change depending on where you are in the game or what you're doing. You'll hear instruments be swapped out, the music slow down, or speed up. The songs themselves are quite catchy and evoke the rich sounding music that was present in Super Mario Galaxy. The voice acting, unfortunately, needs work, but the game thankfully gives you an option to have characters mumble like Banjo Kazooie, so I can't be too hard on it.
Verdict: If you dearly miss the days where 3D platformers had actual depth and complexity to them, and Yooka Laylee left you sorely dissapointed, then A Hat in Time might be just what you've been looking for. Especially if you can't afford Mario Odyssey or a Switch. However, if you're like me and constantly nitpick an otherwise fine game for how it's different to what it claims to be, you may be dissapointed yet again.

Well, I am sort of torn on this one, to be fair, I would five it about 40 percent. The game resembles a big eintopf of washed out cliches from noir movies, spiced up liberally with the red pepper of the genre - blood, namely quite revolting sadistic scenes. I am not trying to moralize or something, I can see them justified sometimes, like in the Silent Hill series, but here the game just does not provide any good reason to stomach them.
The esthetics and the main protagonist are straight up borrowed from the Sin movie, the anthagonist in the episode is borrowed from the cover of the SW:KOTOR 2 game, the constant noir whining is borrowed from Max Payne, and I have seen the thug-intellectual character somewhere before too, only I don't recall where exactly.
The strongest point of the game are probably the investigation scenes where you examine a scene and try to find clue and reconstruct what has happened. The problem is you can achieve it by mindlessly clicking on everything and then trying all the combinations. Then you have the story and the dialogues borrowed from Telltale games that try to create the illusion of important decisions. And lastly, there are very mediocre shooting gallery scenes which are just bad, and the game would be better without them.
The graphics are barely functional, and the black and white style helps to hide the fact that there are barely any textures on the objects. Despite that, the game has some glaring performance problems even on very modern hardware, which is quite unfortunate, especially since it also crashes occassionally. I never judge a game just by how it looks, but the barely adequate graphics combined with outright wooden and stiff animations sometimes really detract from the playing experience, especially during conversations (facial animations), and during the shooting sequences.
If you love noir movies and are an avid consumer of cliches, change the verdict to Yes. For me, however, the game left a foul aftertaste. It's not that it is strictly bad, but it is too mediocre to leave a lasting impression.

The Beginner's Guide is one of the more interesting gaming experiences I've had this year. The game is narrated by it's developer Davey Wreden and tells the story of one of his friends who used to make small games. The game is essentially you playing though these games with Davey's commentary analysing what he thinks the games mean, and you're encouraged to give it some thought yourself.
To say any more about the game is to spoil it, and this is a game to play unspoiled. It's not going to be for everyone - especially with the overwhelming success of The Stanley Parable, people might come into The Beginner's Guide expecting more of the same, and they could be disappointed. However, if you go into the Beginner's Guide knowing what it is then I think you'll enjoy the experience. At its core, The Beginner's Guide is a short, interactive, emotional story told through video games that you can and should play in one sitting that will leave you thinking once the final game has been completed. If that sounds like something you'd enjoy, then The Beginner's Guide is for you.

A Hat in Time is simply amazing. The controls are fantastic, and it very rarely felt like Hat Kid (the game's adorable protagonist) wasn't doing exactly what I told her to do. Platforming is the core of every level, and the game gives you plenty of tools to move about in a myriad of ways, whether it's diving in midair to get extra distance or swingingly effortlessly with a grappling hook.
The characters are amazingly endearing, to the point where I can't get them out of my head. The entire game is fully voice acted (with some barely-there exceptions). I found myself enjoying the voices, but if you don't you can simply turn them off, or even convert them to Banjo-Kazooie-style mumbling noises! Every interaction is full of humor, and I found myself laughing out loud on multiple occasions.
The music is also phenomenally catchy, with each track fitting the stage perfectly, and multiple instrumentations that fade in seamlessly depending on where you are in the level. A Hat in Time's composer Pascal Michael Stiefel deserves major kudos, and I hope to see him in many more games in the future.
I think the one criticism I would have of A Hat in Time is that its first world, Mafia Town, is a bit rough around the edges. The character models seem a bit messy, and there are cutscenes in those levels that seem like they're missing animations. The game's presentation improves massively after that, and I was absolutely in love with the final world. The boss encounters are also amazingly fun and high-energy, in a genre that generally suffers from slow and boring boss fights.
I highly, HIGHLY recommend A Hat in Time, especially if you fondly remember the tight platforming of Super Mario Sunshine or the constant humor of Paper Mario: The Thousand-Year Door. At $30 it's worth every single penny, and two additional chapters are on the way as free post-launch DLC. Forget the memory of failed Kickstarter promises and buy this game!

This is a very good game builder that comes with plenty of resources. While it doesn't come with a tutorial, it does have helpful windows that pop up when you have your cursor over something. The price might be a little high, but the power of this program is pretty good.
There is even a workshop for this program, which is a nice bonus. This program is meant for beginners. If you want something that is more advanced, try a full production program or code your own game.
I recommend holding off on this program for when sales are around. $70 is a bit much, but it's worth the grab when a sale is happening.
I bought this during an indie sale from Humble Indie Bundle. That was literally the cheapest bundle I ever saw with games and DLC. Having already bought it from their website during a sale, I bought it again because it came with games and content. The big winner was that you even got Steam keys for the program, games and DLC. I couldn't refuse such a bargain.
If you are looking for a free way to make a game, Game Develop is out there with video tutorials and can code in different formats, but comes with very little resources to build a game on.
The other optin is Blender, a 3D rendering program that can do videos and games. There are tutorials, but finding an up to date tutorial is a challenge since the program tends to update faster than the tutorials can be completed. It's free, so you can give it a try if you want. Keep in mind that you have to design everything from scratch or download other people's work, which you have to make sure you have permission to use in a game you plan to license in the future.

What a great game, honestly. I've been anticipating this game since I've first heard about it several years ago, and the wait has been well worth it.
Presentation is amazingly cute and charming, with memorable characters across the board, an adorable art style, great soundtrack and actually quite funny gags. Worlds are good and varied if laid out a little confusingly at times. The actual levels and challenges in the worlds are a take on the Mario Sunshine formula of collect-a-thon trinket hunting, but are as a rule several times more creative, unique and sometimes more complex than platformers of a similar kind, ranging from anything to an ordinary fetch quest with a small spin or two to elaborate stealth sections to a portion where the game basically turns into a lighthearted horror game, trying to solve puzzles while stripped off your powers and stalked by what appears to be some demonic queen roaming in her manor. It feels like every other world/level throws a new gimmick or elaborate gag into the core gameplay, and it keeps things fresh to the point that I could binge entire worlds without a semblance of being even remotely exhausted or bored with them. Even the boss fights are really cool in this, which tend to be the weak point of most 3D platformers of a similar jib. Fairly challenging, prone to catching you off-guard with how elaborate and lengthy they are and actually quite hectic, they round out the more straightforward platforming challenges and less confrontational on-off gameplay gimmicks.
Beyond some tiny tidbits like the worlds not being as expertedly laid out as they could be and the camera behaving a little unruly at times(it's still perfectly serviceable for the most part, camera isn't your nemesis this game. Just feels a bit jank at times), I just wish it was a little longer. Game has 4 main worlds with about 5 or so acts(and some hidden platforming mini-levels) each and 1 final world that serves as a final parcour section to the final boss and the boss fight itself, and while many acts tend to actually be quite long for what they are, and I haven't quite finished everything yet, it all just feels over a little too soon. I heard there's free DLC worlds on the way though, so I suppose my plight may only be temporary, and besides it isn't really the game's failing that it's short(I reached the final boss and did a bit of other stuff before actually fighting it with 8 hours, which is fine, really), more that it's good enough that you'd like more.

After purchasing the game I watched a 20 minute lets play video of it online and then dived right in. It was very entertaining i expanded my village made farms and gathering huts, built bridges and houses. Keeping everyone well fed and warm was a challenge. My village was struck by a devestating famine due to my inexperience and poor city planning. My population was decimated and i was having a blast the whole time deeply immeresed in trying to pull my village out of the hole it was in. That first game lasted 20 hours and it was a pleasure. I then started a second game. I decided that the optimal strategy would be to build a large amount of farms and at all times (apart from winter of course) have roughly half my citizens working those farms. My population grew at a rapid rate and within 5 hours i had a relatively large bustling city and virtually no one had died from anything other than old age. When city builder games get to this point there in trouble, they have to have a way to keep you immersed and the immersion begins to fall apart when a simple strategy of having half your citizens working farms completely removes all challenge in the game. The situation got worse when i worked out that firewood was the optimal trading currency and that i could exchange it with the traders that came relatively often for pretty much anything. My city prospered and grew, constant exchanges of firewood for food with the traders and half of my citizen working the farms caused my food stockpiles to grow at a ridiculous rate and i eventually needed literally hundreds of barns to store it all. At this point one thing could of saved this game.
RISKS AND DANGERS AND PROBLEMS EVERYWHEREEE!!!
- where are those wild animals lurking in the forests ready to devour your citizens and the invasions of barbarians ready to wreck even the most prosperous villages. The disaster mechanic in banished could of served this purpose and made the game riveting . But they did nothing. In my 30 hours of play time i didnt see a single tornado, one or two fires sprouted up but they were quickly quenched by the 3 or 4 wells i had scattered around. The first time that a popup appeared telling me one of my farms was infested with crop ruining bugs i merely deleted said farm and built a new one. And the tiny loss of food meant nothing because of my ridiculous stockpiles of food. I got so excited when the popup saying two of my citizens were infected with some kind of disease appeared. But nothing happened they just went to one of my two hospitals and were cured. I got bored and moved on. If you look at the reviews for this game youl find that over 75 percent of them have less than 50 hours play time. This game will entertain you for one or two short games before you work out that having half your citizens working farms will solve alll your villages problems.
In summary the graphics are nice, the interface is smooth and it has that one more turn addictive feel you get from civ games. This game could easily have become my number no.1 most played steam title. So it is with a heavy heart that i rate this game unfinished and broken at the core. However if the game is on sale for 75 percent off then by all means buy it for that first glorious game.
BUT ONLY IF YOU CAN HANDLE IT BREAKING YOUR HEART !!!

Napoleon: Total War is an excellent addition to the Total War ranks. It corrects many of the mistakes made by Empire, while still retaining the Napoleonic grand strategy feel. There are fewer nations, and your world map is almost entirely gone, limited to the more tried and tested method of a European map.
Even as a scaled-down version, Napoleon is far more playable than Empire. The game seems far more polished than Empire, with the politics and government branches greatly developed from older titles like the first Rome and Medeival II. Still, the politics, while more intricate, has not detracted from the ultimately military conquest feel of the series, merely added anther effective tool to your arsenal.
As a great admirer of the modding community I am pleased to observe that modds exist for Napoleon that enable you to play as any of the minor nations - the vanillia game only enables the larger powers - and even allows you to play as Ireland, which didn't exist as a soverign state at the time.
The campaign is excellent, and the option also exists to skip the grand strategy and play Napoleon's most important battles, each unlocking the next until you finally see can you succeed where the 'little corporal' failed and defeat Wellington at Waterloo.
I have no hestitation in reccommending this to any Total War fans, and especially those who played 'Empire' and felt that the attempt at grand global strategy took away from the traditional feel. This game is the perfect middle ground between the glory days and the heights that 'Empire' aspired to.

This was my first Tales game and I have to say I rather enjoyed it. The story held my attention and did surprise me at times, but the witty banter of the skits in-game and at discovery points gave me quite a bit of joy. The combat system was at first hard to pick up, but once you read the in-game help, you start to get the hang of it. This game really does emphasize RTFM.
Pros:
- Decent story with some interesting characters. The skit events are where characters really shine and can be very humorous.
- Combat system seems easy to learn, hard to master.
- Story will take about 40 hours to beat. NG+ is available and powering up the Lords in the game allows you to "buy" carry over skills which can power up your character in the next game.
- Good music.
Cons:
- Can be very grind heavy to unlock items and perks, but that's to be expected.
- Side missions are not tracked and need to be hunted down (some may consider this a good thing), but your NPC companion on the travel map does offer some guidance.
- Have to obtain the Alisha DLC from the Bandai Namco site, which requires creating an account.
Meh:
- Sheer amount of mechanics in game is overwhelming. But everything can be followed up in the in-game library/manual.
- Some points in story lock you out of backtracking until progression.
- One of the characters you get at the start of the game leaves after about the 2nd chapter or so of the story. She returns very briefly somewhere during the climax but then never rejoins the party. Frustrating, since they have their own gear/items in the game that do not get used by any other character.
- Some story side battles and skits are tied to very specific progress points, so missing them requires a new playthrough.
If you enjoy a fairly solid JRPG, then this game is a good buy. Some of the DLC stuff is purely cosmetic, but the Alisha DLC is very required for getting more story out of the game.

I first saw this game and was skeptical of the strange graphics and strange everything really. However I had some extra pocket change from buying games and decided why not. I was certainly in for a treat.
Not let me get the cons before going into the pros just to get them out of the way
-The Sounds
Sounds is few and far between when it comes to this. Guns, voice acting and certain sounds that must be activated and one song that plays everytime a new day comes and pig noises/ splatter from the gore. So sometimes you can get hit from pigs that you wouldn't have known were there unless you used your eyes and which I have almost died many atimes from this issue. While yes the graphics isn't on par of that of modern games but given the price I'd say it's fine. However i'm fairly certain that a potato that was gutted would be able to run this. Which is certainly a good thing.
-Replay value / Things to do.
I felt these things are very similar so I put them in one. As you can probably tell it isn't a huge game by all means. I've only played two hours and almost unlocked everything in the game on day 30. While it may bring in a new enemy every week or so and have bosses there really isn't much to say about the unlocks as each are as basic and basic goes and once you unlocked all the items then it just get's a bit boring and may need breaks to get to the high plains. As I Said im perhaps a quarter through and I have almost all the unlocks.
Things to do is once again few and far between. There are several options to kill the boars and use them for personal gain. First is probably going to be the most used is the grinder. The grinder is essentually you currency. The way it works is if you kill a boar you can shove it's body by melee or by running over it if it exploded in peices. It will grind the peices and suck in anynear by giblets that were once the pigs. The grinded meat can be used to make items such as ammo. In which I will go on about it in my positive side. But for now you get the concept.
Next is the electric fence. This is probably going to be your least used. The Electric fence is a fence that is posted in a circle in the middle of the map and can be activated by a switch on a wall of a small shack. This basically makes it so anything that is in the circle and or in the rims of the electricity will be made into bacon. The good thing is that it is good to killing a group of boars but it will turn into a statue of ash and will break apart when touched. When using the fence you cannot use the remains of the boar for items like ammo as it needs blood to charge. I usually use it once a game a day and never touch it again. Also. The skeleton boars aren't affected by the fence. cos you know....They dont have flesh.
The water pump
The water pump is your only source of health and is limited to the amount of uses it can have. So using it when you most need it is vital. However there are two pumps. If one runs out then another can be used but be warned once you use it up you cannot heal any longer.
You might be thinking Is that all? Yes. yes it is. This game is very, very, very small but I can see that future improvements could be made.
Now on to the pros.
- Gameplay.
This game is♥♥♥♥♥♥stinkingly fun. I never knew how fun it could be shooting pigs and boars before untill I played this. While it is very small it is very fun on it's own. Bringing in silly bosses, mini bosses and strange boars and pigs that you may have never thought could be a thing until now. I love it.
-Grinder Rewards
As explained flesh apeases the machine and gives you items for slaying and inserting the flesh of the pigs and boars.
But it gives more that just that.
Grenades are the second unlock you get from this and dosen't take much to get it. However it is equally the most useless out of the rest of them as the rest as some passive or gives ammo. However the grenade can be used to cook (If you ever played cod or really any game with grenades where you can hold them to wait the timers) to get a better chance on hitting your target but in my opinion it is one of the worst items on there.
Boars milk is basically a speed boost which can be awesome at times and makes it easier to dodge targets like minibosses.
I forgot the names of the rest but there are stuff that makes melee damage basically insta kill non boss characters and ect.
-The story.
The story is quite funny and makes no sense but because game.
The story goes like this. There is a farmer who has been betrayed by his pigs and boars as they pinned him by the wall by pitchfork and knawed off his left foot. So he wants to get revenge by supplying you with weapons to destroy them with.
(Also shoot the guy so he talk but make sure he talks per hit so let him finish his dailog before shooting again and he will give you a suprise ;} )
Co-op
Yes, it's a thing. Never tried it but it is certainly a thing.
-Dosen't break the bank
This could easily be a 5 dollar game is it had a bit more to it. However it is only a single dollar. In this case it is worth every penny.
-Guns
For god sake you are killing pigs with aks, revolvers and even paint ball guns. What isn't there to like about this?
Bosses/minibosses
Silly, cute and funny. The bosses can be difficult at first but can be easily defeated. However bosses take a bit more than just blap blap shoot bang. As key areas can mean more damage.
- Revenge Day
Tired of the relentless pain the pigs have caused you? Do you just wanna slaughter the♥♥♥♥♥♥outta pigs in an over kill of a match? One day per week which is at the end of the week a thing called revenge day comes. You have infinate ammo, Explosive rounds, and insta explode anything that moves. This is great for farming blood in the grinder for (Practically) free items. Also if you shoot an exploded peice of a boar you can shoot it up in the air and juggle it by continuously shooting it and if you keep it up for a certain amount of time it will explode into fire works. This can be done easily on revenge day. You dont get much but pride on how long and how far you got it to go up before it exploded.
There is more to explain but it seems if I went further than I would ramble on about how this is actually quite good for it's price.

What can I say?
This is in fact a serious program and it's great for anyone who wants to start making their own games and learn the basic logic behind programming (without the need to be a programmer) and small game development as a whole. The possibilities to customize how your game looks and behaves are ENDLESS.
There is some learning (I estimate that it's about 50 hours to learn the most important things + quite a few complicated ones), but there are TONS of guides. You don't even need to have skills in Ruby, because there are also TONS of scripts out there that contain the option (part of the code) you're looking for. And as for code, you can customize ANYTHING in it... at your own risk...
You want to create a 640x480 jRPG with a MAD amount of possibilities? Use this program. Of course anything else can also be created but I would not recommend using this for anything other than RPG's, adventure games and visual novels.
Also please note that games created with RPG Maker can only work on Windows OS, and I think that this is the biggest downside of this program. Other than that I cannot think of ANY reason not to buy it.

What to say about RPG Maker VX...
Want to try your hand at making simple, easy-to-make classic RPG-style games? Then get this software. While it's price-point is a bit high, if you invest enough time into it and persevere, you'll learn a heck of a lot. Some of the things you learn can even be applied to other game development/coding programs (if you go in deep enough, naturally). I've even made a few different small projects in the software, although they weren't really anything worth showing to the public.
In short, if you're new to game development and want to start with something that has a wide-range of resources, tutorials and help from the community, buy this.
If you're looking for a heavy, in-depth development program for making 3D games, this isn't for you.

Blues and Bullets is an episodic alternative history noir game developed by A Crowd of Monsters. The first episode was released in July 2015 with the second due to be released in March of 2016.
I will keep this review updated with each chapter I complete.
Gameplay takes place in third person as you control Eliot Ness, the police officer who caught and locked up the great, Al Capone. Eliot has now retired from being a cop and runs his own diner, called Blues and Bullets.  This game reminded me quite a bit of L.A Noire as you search for clues for a crime. There is only one crime scene to investigate in this episode but it is a gruesome one at that. There is a small element of gun play, which is very basic at best; it is done via an “on rails” mechanic similar to that of Time Crisis or Blue Estate. The gun play so far has a very small part to play in the game overall.
Graphically, the game is represented in a black and white noir style visual. This art style just looks awesome, whilst the graphics themselves aren’t stunningly good, the black and white tricks your eyes into thinking it is better looking than it actually it. The animation is slightly on the poor side, but nothing that can’t be ignored.  Eliot is voiced by none other than Doug Cockle (the voice of Geralt from the Witcher franchise), and the rest of the voice acting is all done to a very high quality.
I was completely hooked onto the story right from the start of the game, there isn’t a slow ramp in excitement like most adventure games like this, and you get right into the nitty-gritty from the get-go. The ending of episode 1 leaves you wanting more as the plot takes a huge turn of events. There are plans for there to be another 4 episodes released, I am hoping they speed up the development cycle of them, as I think 9 months between episodes is a bit too much in my opinion.
There isn’t any aspect of difficulty in episode 1, the only real puzzle can be completed with just a matter of trial and error and the gun play scenes have checkpoints at every corner so even if you do die, you don’t have to replay a whole lot of content. I am looking forward to see how they make the gameplay elements of this game have more of a challenge in future episodes.
Episode 1 took me just about two hours to complete; this was with finding all interactable objects throughout the scenes to get an achievement. I found out at the end of the chapter, that finding all of these objects unlocks a “Bobble head” mode, which is always a classic cheat mode that used to be included in game. It will be interesting to see whether you can activate this mode in future episodes or whether it is only to be used in episodes you have already completed!
Sadly I did have a couple of technical problems with Blues and Bullets. I suffered two random crashes of the game that took me straight back to desktop, with no error message or warnings. There were no signs that the game was suffering performance issues, it did only happen when completing a scene, never mid gameplay. Thankfully the game saves at the end of each scene you complete, but this does leave room for game save file corruption.  The game can be played with keyboard and mouse; normally for third person view games I opt for a keyboard and mouse controls, especially ones with any form of gunplay, sadly I could not do it with Blues and Bullets. Firstly the onscreen controls do not show any keyboard controls; only Xbox controls. Secondly, the cursor in game has a fairly big glitch where it just shows as a blank white square. You have to move your cursor to the bottom right hand corner of the screen for it not to be visible even when using a controller.
To sum up, Blues and Bullets is so far a very interesting adventure game that has a lot of potential. Hopefully the technical problems are cleaned up before the next release of the series comes out. If you are a fan of the Noire themed films and games, this game is definitely going to be for you. It’s a fairly quick paced game which is something that a lot of adventure games can’t boast about so even the casual players amongst you will definitely get some enjoyment here.
If you are on the fence about the game still, you can purchase just episode 1 for £3,99 which should give you a good amount of content to see whether you will enjoy the rest of the series, provided the developers don’t change it drastically or you can purchase the complete season for £14,99. Right now I would be completely happy paying £14,99 for this season, it does a lot of things right and the only negative points are technical problems which will hopefully be patched in the future.

Episode one was released in July of 2015. Now the Second is set to release in March of this year. That's eight months between each episode.
I can understand if they have a small team, and they likely do. I'm not new to the episodic format. I'm usually waiting on Telltale Episodes all the time and played Life is Strange episodes as they released. I just find eight months to be a bit excessive.

First of all, I am going to admit I do have a bias on this game already because living in Northern Canada and getting a game on surviving in it already makes it 10/10 for me. But, I digress and will try and keep this fair.
The Long Dark was recommended to me by a friend and I have to say, I am not disappointed by it. I loved the artstyle from the get-go because it's minimalistic and aesthetically pleasing but it may not work for everyone. For example, the buildings have an almost comic-book style to them which I enjoy but your mileage may vary. As for the actual gameplay, it's very easy to get into - very straight forward on what you have to do - but it gets very difficult very fast.
For example, I kept assuming you need a fire going when you rest so you don't freeze to death (using my real world logic) but this seems not to be the case. Within the first day I used all my accelerant and tinder plugs and no idea what to do after. I went out to forage, got hit with a blizzard and died. Cue clucking of tongue and an annoyance to make it past the first day.
But I admit, once you get the hang of it, it does become fun. Some people may not find calorie counting and foraging wood and lighting fires to be all that exciting mind you. Which this game has so if you want something more fast-paced, this probably won't do it for you. But for me, taking notes on what I'm doing, planning for the day or even just poking around outside for a minute and running back to shelter is fun. The fact that it's located in the wilderness of Canada - a place used rarely in games - just makes it better and I cannot wait for the Story Mode.
Overall, again, I give it 10/10. The game is getting more content as the days go on so that's a big plus as it has changed from when I first downloaded it.
Also, Jennifer Hale. I mean... that right there. Alone.

This was my first Tales game and I have to say I rather enjoyed it. The story held my attention and did surprise me at times, but the witty banter of the skits in-game and at discovery points gave me quite a bit of joy. The combat system was at first hard to pick up, but once you read the in-game help, you start to get the hang of it. This game really does emphasize RTFM.
Pros:
- Decent story with some interesting characters. The skit events are where characters really shine and can be very humorous.
- Combat system seems easy to learn, hard to master.
- Story will take about 40 hours to beat. NG+ is available and powering up the Lords in the game allows you to "buy" carry over skills which can power up your character in the next game.
- Good music.
Cons:
- Can be very grind heavy to unlock items and perks, but that's to be expected.
- Side missions are not tracked and need to be hunted down (some may consider this a good thing), but your NPC companion on the travel map does offer some guidance.
- Have to obtain the Alisha DLC from the Bandai Namco site, which requires creating an account.
Meh:
- Sheer amount of mechanics in game is overwhelming. But everything can be followed up in the in-game library/manual.
- Some points in story lock you out of backtracking until progression.
- One of the characters you get at the start of the game leaves after about the 2nd chapter or so of the story. She returns very briefly somewhere during the climax but then never rejoins the party. Frustrating, since they have their own gear/items in the game that do not get used by any other character.
- Some story side battles and skits are tied to very specific progress points, so missing them requires a new playthrough.
If you enjoy a fairly solid JRPG, then this game is a good buy. Some of the DLC stuff is purely cosmetic, but the Alisha DLC is very required for getting more story out of the game.

i really enjoyed this game and i'm really happy to see tales on pc!
that being said, i don't know if this is something i'd recommend to a newcomer to the series. if this does end up being your entrypoint into the series, it's good to know that this game is quite unlike any tales game prior.
the story is really fun and interesting. it leans a bit on the cliched side, with the bulk of the story basically being a Chosen One situation, but the game focuses more on the people you meet rather than how wonderful and great you are for being the Chosen One. it delves into a lot of questions of morality and, although perhaps not exploring them as deeply as one would hope, it is still a very satisfying experience.
the combat is pretty good. for those familiar with tales of graces, you'll likely be rather familiar with the basics of this combat system. rather than having HP and TP (essentially magic power), you have HP and a Chain meter, which allows you to perform basic actions such as attacking, casting spells, using special attacks and dodging. this meter refills over time, and at a decent pace, so it's not frustrating or debilitating by any means. i'm just personally not a fan of replacing TP with something that recovers over time and also governs the use of regular attacks. that didn't really restrict me from enjoying the game, though. i really enjoyed it
something i don't like at all is the equipment skill system. every piece of equipment in the game starts out with one or more skills attached to it. by combining these skills with other skills, you can get a variety of other effects as a result. this sounds cool, and at first i thought it would be, but it gets annoying later on. the equipment fusing (and thus, skill fusing) system makes little to no sense and basically encourages desperately clinging on to old, worse equipment in the hopes that you find something with better skills. the worst case scenario for me was early in the game when i had a skill bonus that gave me +20 to all of my stats. this sounds great! but then any time i get a new piece of equipment, i can't equip it, because even if it raises one of my stats, it would cancel out the stat gain from the bonus skill. it's very confusing and i can't really do it justice in essay form, but i really did not like it. it was a nice idea, and i welcome experimentation, but i do hope this does not make a return in later games.
i also have to give this game a special credit for its use of music in cutscenes, boss fights, and dungeons. with the addition of go shiina as a composer, there were some extremely unexpected songs that really stood out amongst the usual sakuraba pieces that are in the game. that's not to say i dislike sakuraba's work by any means, but it's incredibly refreshing to hear another style in the game. what stood out for me the most is the music for the wind/water/fire trials and the music for the tiamat battle, which i won't go any further into here.
as i said though, there's a lot in this game that makes me very hesitant to recommend it to first time players of the tales series. it is very unconventional, and while that's often something i would applaud, i don't feel they were necessary changes. for instance, your HP is not tied to your level, but rather how many bosses or side bosses you've beaten. i didn't find this to be an issue personally, but i've heard a lot of people say it's not very fun for them. it's a personal thing, i suppose. the game also has a lot of wide open areas with a character whose top speed is a slight powerwalk. sure, there are skills to increase speed, but that's only for about 20 seconds after a fight, which can often be something you're not looking to get into when exploring a new area or walking through low level ones for the umpteenth time.
so if you're going into this game as an introduction to the series, keep in mind these changes. i highly recommend trying out another game in the series if you're on the brink of enjoying it but its oddities are holding you back. personally i would say try tales of vesperia or tales of symphonia (which will be released on steam in 2016!).
if you're experienced with tales games and you think the changes aren't bad or you just want to try and see for yourself then i absolutely recommend the game. this is by leaps and bounds the best looking tales game there ever has been, but there's so much more to it than just flashy graphics and breathtaking landscapes.
TL;DR it's a good game but be wary that it is somewhat unconventional

You're tasked with clearing a farm where boars and other livestock have gone crazy and grown quite resilient (possibly undead): your only company in all this is the farm owner who seems to be quite happy with being stuck on a wall with a pitchfork in its chest.

Blood and Bacon is pretty polarizing when it comes to enjoying it as you'll either appreciate its simple, gory, shoot-a-ton-o-stuff mindset or dislike it for its basicness, repetitiveness and toiler humor. There's really no way around it as you'll be doing mostly the same thing for most waves (that is, shooting purcines until they die/ gib/ explode while trying not to be gored to death): some variety can come from armored enemies that you must shoot in the back or bosses that require a bit of strategy but that's all.Said repetitiveness is also made stronger by the overall lack of different enemy models and the fact you'll be seeing the same two bosses types over and over every ten days with- at most- only slight changes in how they work.
As for what it does right well, the game is extremely easy to pick up and play and the fact each day is so short means you can give it a quick go even if you have little time. The toilet humor can be funny at times- if you're ok with that brand of humor ofc- and the huge amount of gibs/ blood on screen is as amusing as it is satisfying to see after you've managed to clear a particularly hard day. While basic the gameplay can also be quite challenging especially when playing solo as certain enemies can kill you in a few hits if you let them get too close: same goes for bosses as they'll require a good amount of concentration to succeed.
For me Blood and Bacon was a fun yet slightly dull and somewhat forgettable experience, an one trick pony if you wish: but for a dollar I feel I got enough enjoyment from it to justify its purchase hence my thumbs up. As for you well, it's quite decent if you're looking for something silly to play in short bursts, even more so with a friend.

This is a JRPG maker, to state the obvious, but I'm just gonna move ahead to the pros and cons because I know you probably just wanna know how the program is.
Pros:
-Easy to figure out once you get the feel of it.
-Provides a sprite and face maker.
-Lets you import your own pictures to the title screen, and even textures to make maps. (you can import music, sounds, etc too)
-Controls are simple, so you wont need to adjust any of them to fit your game.
-Personally, I found the folders easy to navigate. When you have a new game, all the needed folders are there. Audio has its own subfolders to separate sound and music, and other folders have the same feature. I found this useful.
-Event making is the easiest thing in the world to do with this program compared to others.
-If you don't know scripting, that's fine. Event making is there to help.
-Quick events are also helpful. Instead of figuring out how to make a shop NPC, there is a quick event for it. The same goes for doors/traveling.
-You can edit the entire battle system, and its enemies. Even the attack animations are editable.
-It gives you a lot of preset sprites, faces, music, and other things to work with if you dont already have resources. It's a good place to start from scratch.
With all the pros, this seems like an amazing program- and it is- however, it has its cons.
-It takes getting used to, and you may need multiple tutorials on certain things. Trust me, it wont make sense at first.
-Sometimes, the controls will glitch on a play-test, and you'll need to reboot it multiple times (I've had this problem before)
-The sprite/face maker can be limited, as it only has one facial camera pose and preset items to pick from.
-If you expect to make games like Witch's House and Ib with this in a few weeks after getting it- don't even bother buying this. You'll get frustrated when you find out that it takes a lot of work and tons of time.
-Scripting is a pain, just use the event maker in-program.
For a short summary:
This is a very powerful JRPG maker, and you can do a lot with practice, patience, and some tutorials. Previous experience in making games is not needed to use this, so you can learn with it. It will take a lot of work, but it pays off. Don't expect the most beautiful graphics you've ever seen until you've hit an advanced level of scripting, graphic map making, and other fields.
I give it a rate of about 7/10, because although it has its cons, I've had the most ease with this program than any other. I definetly recommend this to anyone looking for a simple start in game making.
Note: if there is anything you need help with when trying to make a game, contact me on Steam. I can't help with scripting or making graphics for you, though.

Despite the sometimes unfair reputation that the RPG maker series gets, I will reccommend this to anyone who is interested in creating games, either for a hobby or a commercial endeavor. It is true that there are a lot of poor RPG maker games that remain restricted to what the base engine provides (think default menus, sounds and mapping) but with enough creativity and commitment toward your project there's lots of scope to create a quality game with unique mechanics.
The engine itself is easy to understand, the menus are fairly intuitive so you can pick up most basic skills by just playing around. Most people argue that this is why the RPG series can give way to such low quality games, because it is comparitivley simple to create events and to get what you need your game to do. However the simple systems in place, with creative thinking, can be used to create much more in depth gameplay.
If you have experience in scripting languages or would like to learn at an entry level, RPG Maker VX Ace uses the Ruby Language, which is a fairly easy to start out with. You can use scripts to change many elements of gameplay and add extra depth to your game. Even if you have little interest in scripting, there's a whole community that build resources including scripting to help you add to your project. Many of which are free providing you credit the author.
The art assets are also highly customisable, provided you have a decent graphics editor such as Photoshop or GIMP, you can make beautiful tilesets, characters, maps and menus. Similarly if you lack the skill or patience to create such things, the community also can provide free assets for you to use. Of course there's paid DLC too, for the more hobby orientated user.
The music and sounds are also highly customisable, you can incorporate them in many ways throughout your project. If you are skilled enough you can use your own music and sound effects, or as before use what the community provide. Again, there's paid DLC to fill any gaps you may have in your soundscape.
To sum it up, RPG Maker VX Ace is very accessable but has all the basis for making a sturdy game. Regardless of whether you are a hobbyist or someone hoping to make a Commercial game, your creativity is really what determines how well your game turns out, RPG Maker gives you that sturdy foundation from which to build upon.

------------Original Review----------------------
Blues and Bullets (BB for short) is one of those games that are so unique that you wouldn't forget. I highly recommend this game as the gaming experience is just fulfilling and its uniqueness alone would make it something worth trying.
In a sentence, BB is a sin-city-graphic-styled, point-and-click, linear, violant noir game.
BB is definitely developed for adults and if it was a movie it would be rated R, so I don't recommend any minors to play this game.
To start with, I've been long awaited a game with the black and white and red graphics style like sin-city, it's just deep, beautiful, and very contrasted. As you play, you feel like you're watching a movie instead of just playing games--the visual experience is very satisfying.
BB is an episodic point-and-click game. It's quite linear, almost like a visual novel. Basically, it means that no matter what option you make, it wouldn't really affect how the story goes. There is little action/shooting involved in the playing. But that is what this game is focused on--the story.
As a noir game, the themes of BB--revenge, "good ol' cop", justice, duty--seem very cliche. But on the other hand, it is very well executed. Although there is only one episode available as of now (Feb.12, 2016), I'm very attracted into this story. There are some other potential themes as the story develops, such as race and religion, and I am looking forward to it very much. Bottom line, when I finished the first episode, I really liked the story.
The game isn't finished yet, as four more episode are to be released, the second episode is set to be released in March 2016, which is about half year after the first episode, if I remember it correctly. So, if you are impatient to finish games, you probably want to wait for the full release. But in my opinion, every episode is worth the wait, so I personally would rather play one episode and wait for the next.
The game has little replayability, since it's focus is on the story, I finished the first episode in around 100 minutes, so you're probably looking at around 9-10 hrs of playing time, worth the money I'd say.

So I've bought all 5 episodes during the Lunar Sale for around 12€. I should have read the news, which said, that only episode 1 was out, but whatever. Let's get started -
as far as possible. Please read the verdict at the end. There you'll find the conditions under which I can recommend buying this game.
Before I go into detail, I have to bring up one thing that's been bothering me from the moment I started the game: the very limited options you have. There's only around 6 resolutions (none of which is fitting my monitor presets), you can't fiddle with AA leaving ugly edges everywhere ruining the atmosphere in the process and so on. You are only allowed to roughly adjust options for your system which is really lame, since every PC is different and you have no control over how smooth your game is running. Mine had framerate drops every 20 or so seconds, which is obviously annoying to say the least.
The art style of the game will remind you of classics like Sin City with its unsaturated colors but red. Maybe overused, but a fitting style for this game. It underlines the somehow depressing atmosphere of the game. Unfortunately, this atmosphere is ruined by the insufferable camera managment. It is okay to force a certain view of the situation on people. But I've only found it acceptable if not necessary in point&click adventures, where you are usually not navigating around a 3D world. In Blues and Bullets the camera changes in the direction the player is supposed to go (see "hand holding" later on) and it feels horrible when you want to track your way back, because it feels you really have to force yourself against an invisible wall, that only breaks after a few seconds of stubborn walking against it. Why not give the player the option to actually use the mouse and look around to enjoy those gorgeous ambients and surroundings you guys created? Why not only limit this artsy stuff to cutscenes? That would suffice big time! Let's see some improvement, please.
The walking speed itself is atrocious - like a snail on weed you waddle forward. You can "run", if you want to call it running, but it won't make much of a difference. This is something I'd like to see fixed as well. Those two aspects and a missing mouse control make it far too easy to work through the game, objects of interest scattered around the game world are not only displayed at once, but you are lead to them through the camera presets. There is a lot of holding hands going on just with those mechanics, unfortunately.
This game features a detective story, which is neat. Personally, I love detective stories and am fond of point&click adventures. This is, where the game shines but also leaves potential. As you investigate you gather different clues which are - within an extra ingame menue - displayed as a pin board, which obviously represents those used in police investigations. As you collect clues you have to sort out which clues go where on the board. For that, categories are preset ("course of events", "used weapons", and so on) and unfortunately the number of clues is preset as well. It would be nice to not know how many clues you can (and indeed need to) find for one specific field of investigation. This way your story would maybe have more holes than be a clear picture of what happened. This is not a must have, but you have to be punished somehow for not sorting everything out correctly, otherwise the game would be even more linear.
Investigating objects reminds me of L.A. Noir, where you get a clear view of the object and you can interact. Again, it is just too obvious (a big red eye appears and fades in at a certain point) where to click to progress, which could also be done more subtle.
A true detective has to get into firefights. Those are nothing but painful. You as a player are only able to cover or shoot with such a slow and unresponsive mouse that it is scary. There are not many action scenes you go through, but you are being navigated by a script, meaning you can't run yourself. For my taste, this is not mandatory for this game. Why not let the player explore at least a bit? There is so little exploration as it is, why not let us run and gun around when we have the chance to?
What I also liked, were the choices you could make during dialogue. Those were either spontaneous, just a choice of going about things (rude, friendly, sarcastic, etc) or even game-influencing. The last one I admire, because it would mean, that there are, in fact, consequences from your choices. This I can't confirm for sure as of yet, since in ep1 there might not be consequences yet. Those may as well occur during the following episodes, which would be very promising.
Dialogues themselves often feel petty and from time to time even absurd. It is not necessarily the voice acting, but the content and how it is presented. To be fair, during ep1 there is a clear rise in quality of those talks, which puts me at ease for future episodes.
Last but not least the story: It is a mix of reality, fiction, mistery and crime, which is interesting to say the least. I would go as far as to say, that it is a creative approach in story telling. Yes, story telling, this is the main focus of the game, which makes it feel like a movie for the majority of the time. I am okay with it - I mean, I put up with it, because it does it quite well. Not overwhelmingly perfect but well. There is some kind of character development and there is a nice mistery behind the story with character conflict and ominous people and circumstances, which get a grip of the player.
Overall, I would only recommend Blues and Bullets to players who enjoy a more "talkative" game with little to interact except crime scene action, which might be the most playing you will be doing. It is really linear with a movie aspect and nicely staged scenery lasting around 1 hour and 10 minutes, which is short. So short, that you should only consider buying during sales. I payed around 2.40€ per epsiode, which is the limit.

This game is in early alpha and is already better than many games I've played. No game breaking bugs, no strange occurrences, no texture/mesh issues (at least ones that can't be blamed on my spotty internet) and it's fun! The only major issue I've seen is it has some balance issues. However, those issues are in your favor so it's not frustrating.
Dungeon Defenders II is exactly like the previous title, except free. You play as one of four heros to build towers and defenses to make sure your (usually) crystal is spared from getting destroyed by invading monsters who want it for reasons not totally mentioned (early alpha). You can build said character however you see fit. Want them to be a wall of defense while your friends fry, electrify, and explode them? Would you rather take things into your own hands or let your towers do the work? Slice them? Shoot them? Or...uh...magic them? You can do this solo but it's more fun with other players. I'd imagine it's even more fun if you play with friends and can communicate with your talking. It's also probably easier.
There're quite a few levels to play, and all look amazing. Each level has it's own spawning routes and challenges. Sadly, the monsters never change so it might get boring killing the same goblins and orcs over and over and over again. The good news is, they often die before you get a good look at them.
As I said earlier, this game has balance issues. Enemies die, maybe, too quickly for the games own good. Right now, it might get boring. The developers try to alleviate this by adding excursion modes with increase the difficulty but a good party of four can still find it a push-over. Right now, though, I think the devs have other things on their mind and to do list than increase the difficulty. I'm sure that'll happen later on as the game gets pushed to an official release. Either that or archers are OP! For now, enjoy the slaughter of your enemies and dance in their dropped blue mana crystals! There's still the issue with having way too much equipment drops from mobs but I believe there was an auto-sale option in the first one so I'm sure the sequel will have it in time, as well.

Dale Hardshovel HD is a good puzzle game. The controls are simple: you move the artifacts horizontaly with the mouse. You need to match the artifacts, in pairs of 2 or 3 artifacts, in the given time to be able to complete the level.
A little more info about matching: for the matching to count they have to be next to each other in a "stay" position...if you swipe an artifact over more artifacts and there is one of same model under it won't count as a match. Also if an artifact is on the moving platform and another of same time on the ledge near the moving platform when they will be next to each other it won't count as match.
The complexity of levels differ based on the things you'll find in them: from movable blocks that will help you to get over holes, spikes that will destroy your artifacts, blocks which dissapear after you passed them a number of times to teleporters, moving platforms(which can't keep more than one artifact at a time), magnets and switches.
As a side note, for long play sessions the soundtrack may become a bit annoying because it gets repetitive.

This is one of the best 3D platformers I've played in a long time. Tight controls, great abilities and creative level design.
"How does it stack up to Yooka Laylee?" you might ask.
Well, in terms of level design, humor and characters, it surpasses Yooka Laylee in several points, or at the very least matches it. The catch? The game is WAY too short. Only 5 levels and only 40 hourglasses to collect, 24 of which are needed to beat the game. However, the sheer amount of mission variety is staggering, and the attention to detail in every level is marvelous. You never seem to be doing the same thing twice. If I had to compare it to an existing game, the overall mission structure is like a heavily abridged version of Super Mario Sunshine, complete with platforming levels in a void.
The character cast has an incredible amount of heart and soul in it. Even the bad guys are immensely likable. The Cook Mafia has to be my favorite band of crooks in the history of video games. Hat Kid herself doesn't have much personality beyond "cute and happy" during most of the gameplay, but her character becomes more apparent in her diary entires, relic descriptions and the way she comments on various world objects.
The bosses are easily the most challenging aspect of the game. They're fast, have a lot of attacks, and the fights can go on for ages with no midpoints if you die. Some of them can even get you in a stunlock, which is quite infuriating.
Overall, A Hat In Time is a solid little gem, with its biggest problem being that there isn't enough of it.
+ Great level design
+ Great controls
+ Great characters and humor
- Way too short
- Some bosses can stunlock you
PS: How on earth did this get only a Pegi 7 age rating?! The mansion in Subcon Forest will traumatize more children than the haunted piano in Super Mario 64 ever did.

Cons:

Overall, this is a great software for anyone interested in making a game, whether for personal or commercial use. If you are planning on purchasing it, however, I would wait for it to be on sale.

I must start with I totally dig alternate reality historical fiction. I also greatly enjoy film noir. Mix those two together with a design style that is lovingly ripped from Sin City and this purchase was a no-brainer. I've only played the beginning episode (I'm not sure the others have been released at this point), but I am hooked and ready for the rest of the story.
I will keep this brief and spoiler free.
Playing as Eliot Ness, retired from the police, you are hired by Al Capone (stay with me, this is an alternate reality, remember?) to find his kidnapped niece, Sofia. That's the basic beginning plot and that's as far as I'm going to go with the story.
The gameplay is straight adventure fair. Easy for anyone to jump in and play. You basically use one button to interact with everything. This works very well. The fighting elements of the game are very well realized. There are QTE events as well as more arcade-like gunplay sequences. For those who fear arcade-like sequences, take heart as they are not difficult, but are very well staged to make Ness feel pretty bad-@$$. Also, choices you make affect what happens later in the game. So far, the choices I have made seem to have little effect, but some of it was a very nice touch, so kudos to the writers!
Speaking of stage, this is where the game shines. The sets are stunning. The black/white/red color scheme is used to great effect. Every scene looks absolutely gorgeous and feels like a film noir. This is also partly due to the game designers choice to lock the camera. While I find this a bit annoying, I understand why they did this. They can control the camera angles so that each scene is presented at its best and they keep the noir theme running throughout. This is a narrative story, afterall.
And what about the story? So far, the writing has been excellent and the story has got me hooked. The only minor gripes are that the acting does not always live up to the writing. Al Capone is a bit ham-fisted, a bit too over the top. Some of the secondary characters feel less like professional actors and more like friends that chipped in to lend their voices to an indie project. But the actor who plays Ness truly shines. He is perfect, and that's the most important thing.
While the set graphics are absolutely out of this world, the character design and execution is a bit hit and miss. Ness, again, is beautifully realized. But some of the other characters do not quite have his definition, they feel like they were created in far less time and do not quite sit in the scenes as well as he does. All of the character animations are a bit stiff - it is clear they were all motion captured, but there's something missing to truly elevate the animation to AAA level. Lastly, the facial expressions are sorely lacking in this game. This is a game where you are talking to a number of people and their reactions and expressions can really help to engage the audience even more. Unfortunately, everyone looks like they have all been recently shot up with Botox.
Alright, but if these graphics seems so terrible, why are you giving it a thumbs up? Because the game is fantastic! My comments on the animation are minor quibbles. The animation isn't terrible, most people may not even notice. I work in 3D for a living, so these are things I notice. This game is about story and atmosphere and it does both BEAUTIFULLY!
My minor gripes with the game do little to tarnish it. Anyone who enjoys a good story and phenomenal atmosphere owe it to themselves to pick this game up.
EDIT: I almost forgot to mention one of the coolest mechanics of the game, when Ness goes into "detective mode." The designers did a really nice job utilizing a simple one-button ui while still keeping it completely engaging. You encounter a grisly murder scene and are given an opportunity to deduce what happened. You search the body, the rooms, in order to gain clues which you then place on a virtual crime board (essentially, Ness is piecing it together in his head). It is extremely well designed and a lot of fun to play through. It's also quite a disturbing scene visually - but so brilliantly done.

Outlast is a really cool horror game. It's smart, polished and stable; it's quality, it never disappoints. Its setting makes it feel like the first Resident Evil seen from a first person perspective (and without guns, obviously).
Outlast isn't that terrifying; the mechanics are easy to understand and once you've figured out what creatures does what, you more or less know what to do to survive. You will spend quite a bit of time crouching in the dark, trying to save what little battery you've got left on that camcorder and in that regard, it's a game of patience. Most creatures will kill you in one blow (at least, in Hard mode) and you will have to pay attention to what their routines are, where they are looking, etc., lest you find yourself quickly dead. Creatures also have a good hearing so even in panic, you will learn to refrain from running.
However, the phases through which creatures are stalking you tend to get repetitive; like I said, a lot of time is spent crouching in the dark. During these moments, your character starts panting loudly, effectively preventing you from concentrating. The game, also, inflicts on the player a lot of trial and error: you enter a new place, you get spotted, you die, loading..., you walk two more meters, you look around, get spotted, die, loading... etc. There's sometimes a great deal of distance between two save points, forcing you to replay the same ten minutes again and again - and that is annoying. Fortunately, it is rare and, also, as you understand how the game works, you get ballsier, your risks become more calculated, and you die less.
I said the gameplay tended to get repetitive, but the game has some excellent surprises, including changes of setting, poignant musical moments, and offers some really fast-paced sequences. It's never boring, it's generous with the player, and the story and the fate of the main character really make you eager to know what's coming next.
All in all, I recommend Outlast. Any horror fan will enjoy it!

If nominating this game in freaking TWENTY-SIXTEEN for a steam award *(Steam being something that did not exist until 2003) doesn't speak volumes for the high regard in which I hold this game, I'm not sure if anything else I say will convince you.  But here goes:
Multiplayer:  Is insane.  And very customisable, especially given it's age.  So if you want to put 24 players into a map designed for a max of 6 and make every weapon a rocket launcher, go for it.  Want every gun to insta-kill and every player be invisible?  This game invented that.  Don't have even teams?  Put a few bots in, they have an option to scale their difficulty to that of the players.  Low-gravity & optinal item power-ups?  These are options from a game that was made in 1999.
Single Player:  Arguably as good as playing multiplayer, and that's BANANAS.  There are 5 different tournaments to win (1 for every play-mode, Deathmatch/Team Deathmatch/Domination/CTF/Assault) and that's plobably about 10 hours of gameplay already.  Assault in particular is like finding there's a rumpus room in a house you've been living in for a year and only just found out about.  Then there is also custom games where you can fill any map with AI players.  These bots can be customised to have names, favourite weapons, be aggressive or cowardly, more accurate or less accurate, and to have varying awareness levels.
Weapons:  Best fps weapon design...maybe ever?  Every weapon has an alternate firing mode, and some have extra features on top of that, while still being completely accessible to a new player.  Take the Rocket Launcher;  Click fire once, fire one rocket.  Hold it down and it will load up to 6 rockets and fire them in a spread. If you follow a target for a few seconds before firing, your crosshair will change and that means you're locked on and your rockets will be homing. Hit right-click and you get a capped rocket instead that acts like a grenade.  Hold it down and it will load up to 6.  This is a single gun, and I'm not even joking when I say it's not overpowered, because every single weapon is just as deadly in it's own ways and thay all combine to be a ton of fun.
This game, at the time I write this, is less than $5.  Give it a shot.  I promise that if you look past graphics which are polygonal but far from unwatchable, this game will impress you.

Those of you that enjoy city builder games or even RTS games, will definitely get something out of playing Banished. The game will require a certain amount of micro management as well as detailed resource management. Getting your merry band of settlers to a point of productivity and stability is a thouroughly enjoyable and at times, rather challenging experience. Once your town is stable and secure in terms of housing, tools, clothing and food production you might feel there is little else to do. Various new challenges and problems are waiting if you opt to continure to grow, build and increase your population and town further.
How would I improve the game?
I would've like to have seen a 'Guardsman' job role to perform a specific role of protecting the population. You can opt to have 'random disasters' occur from time to time... Perhaps the occasional raid from Bandits/Pirates/Looters would've been a fun and welcome addition.
It also seems strange how all the building take place on the same horizontal level, and there seems to be no scope for building on slopes, hill sides and/or mountain tops.
Overall 7.5/10

People are too easy on games like this.
This game and Amnesia: A Machine for Pigs were released simultaneously, and were competing games -- having played both, I can pretty succinctly say that both are not worth your money.
The first thing to note about Outlast (and AMFP), is the fact that it's short. Like, really short. You can beat this game in two hours short.  This is a huge problem for the game, and it's only further complicated by the fact that the game itself is fairly easy.
Another issue that this game has is that it's plain old boring. The majority of the time, I was walking around and waiting for the next Jump Scare. Otherwise, I was completing a fetch quest and avoiding easy to dodge goons. And when I finally finished it, the last level was a massive kick in the balls to good horror writing.
If Outlast came out before Amnesia: The Dark Descent, perhaps it would be considered a stepping stone for a great game. But this is 2014, and this is a 2-hour adventure with a crappy ending. If you like horror games, you might want to check this out, but it's not the game that people have been praising it as.

So far, it has been delivering the "Tales of" experience that I was looking for... Regular combo sytem is indeed oversimplified, but it compensaets with all the Armatization options, giving you much more attacks to work with.

But the most important thing... The characters are hilarious and, more than once I feel that I'm watching a really funny anime (playing in Japanese BTW)...
So, in the end... Recommended. Buy it. And hope that Bandai Namco brings more Tales of games to the PC.

The Long Dark is a true survival experience, though not like most other survival games, The Long Dark boasts a beautiful world that will leave you speechless, behind this beautiful world lies a disturbing world in which you have to overcome hunger, thirst, cold and fatigue, you must hunt for food or scavenge nearby buildings for clothing and other survival
equipment, you must either fight or sneak past wolves to help you navigate your way through this unrelentless world and look for a place to rest and find food.
Melt snow for water, use purification tablets or boil the water to make it safe to drink, heat up coffee or cocoa for extra warmth and cook food for added warmth and fatigue, loot vehicles and corpses for extra supplies and cut the meat from an animal carcass for even better food, go fishing in the nearby lake or take your chances at the dam, everything you do has an advantage and a disadvantage, stay indoors and the wolves will circle the area or you'll run out of food, stay out too long and they will hunt you or you'll freeze to death.
In The Long Dark you are tasked with the goal of surviving for as long as you can, hunt the safe house or explore the world in this beautifully built world with atmospheric sound and superb voice acting from David Hayter (Metal Gear Solid) and Jennifer Hale (Mass Effect) who both gave you audio clues to whether or not you are Cold, hurt or hungry, as well
as when it's getting Dark or Light.
The Long Dark is an indie title developed by Hinterland studio with some of the crew who have worked on some triple A titles such as Mass Effect to name one of them, they are constantly updating the game to bring new features, items and maps, The Long Dark currently has 2 maps which can be explored on one save by travelling past the dam, both maps
are visually stunning and are full of danger with a lot to explore.
My verdict on The Long Dark is that it's a stunning game with some of the best voice actors, the gameplay is amazing and will have you playing for hours on end and is a true survival experience.
