One of the weaker mothership Tales of games in the series, right next to Tales of Symphonia 2. Continuing the tradition of introducing something really cool in its previous mothership title (in this case, Xillia/Xillia 2's dual raid battle system), but choosing to not take any of its successful elements and incorporate new experimental elements that is rather shakey in its introduction. It did take Graces F's/Destiny's unique style shift battle system, but severely limiting its options through poor choices, one of which was initially not displaying a numerical value of SC required to attack with a specific move while in battle. This makes judging the cost of which combos you want to pull off to a rather vague sense of estimation, though this can be helped by just keeping your SC high (admittedly not a good design choice though).
The premise so far for the initial story is interesting, but only for the first 2 hours of the game. You play as Sorey (or later Rose), the main character and the chosen Shepard who pulls out the sacred sword (AKA Excalibur) and is given the task of purifying the world of yomas and unify the human and seraphim race into cohabitation. There's a few parts of the story here and there that try to emulate a moral choice, something Xillia 2 did well, but only because it had a silent main character. Zestiria's main character has a clear personaility and when picking a choice, it didn't seem to have much impact as the character simply brushes it off with an ugly "EH" kind of feeling. Gee, for a hero, you're kinda hard to like. The moral choices presented are also pretty weird, for example, you can fix a bridge with earth magic, but you are given a choice, do you want to fix it in front of the people in distress to try to be a hero symbol, or do it when everyone leaves? I choose the "look really cool in front of everyone" and only ONE PERSON reacted with an "oh, okay". Then everyone tells me I was wrong to try to inspire people that there is hope in piety because they would instead take me for a monster that is trying to help them. Goddammit, what do you people want from me.
PROS:
- Utilizing divine weapons as a focus, your human characters can basically temporarily fuse with your seraphim party members to create a new combat form depending on fusion members, something akin to Digimon. Pretty neat, but I wish the fusion character actually looked different for each form, rathern than just a colour pallete and weapon change.
- Dual audio! Never bad to have a choice, especially when it lets me run away from awkward English dub, its usually a hit or miss on the voice acting charts (such as Abyss and Symphonia being superior in English over Japanese).
- Pretty decent PC port, was rather shakey at the start, but easily fixable if you look around. Japanese games rarely have good PC ports, so this was a surprise.
CONS:
- A weird varying degree of difficulty at the start. Normal enemies are incredibly easy fights that they last only 12-16 seconds on moderate difficulty, but boss fights demolish you in 2-3 hits and take a lot longer. I tried to remedy this by bumping up the difficulty on the field for normal encounters, then down for boss encounters, but not all boss fight encounters are obvious. Difficulty level need some proper balancing to make them fun by lasting long enough, but not ridiculously hard, especially with AI party members.
- A horrible, horrible, horrible equipment system. Equipment now have random stats and random skills within a certain algorithm that makes it a chore to choose. Not only that, you'll have to do a weapon crafting system by basically fusing the same weapons to make it better, though not all combinations are an improvement as it doesn't display what skills the gear would get until after. Frustrating.
- Has chosen the poorly done road of forced party members, limiting customization, strategies, and playstyle. You HAVE to have two human characters in your party to fight as a full four, otherwise you will only fight with two. This is pretty annoying, especially when the one human female keeps leaving at random points in the game (and later on NEVER COMING BACK, what the hell, I thought you were the heroine that wants to get their hands dirty to help save the world). I just want my magic knight class back.
- No jumping in combat. Yep. Goodbye super awesome aerial combos.
- Characters aren't really likable, they're pretty stiff and stereotypical in their archetype. Hell, Graces F had one of the worse stories, but better (well, selectively) characters that are much more well liked. Jade is top tier husbando material and Pascal is top tier waifu material that forgets who you are.
- Combat now happens in where you encountered the enemy, rather than taking you to a seperate closed off, but cleared area. This makes it a seamless transition, only...not all areas of the game is designed for combat. More often than not, your camera will get stuck in a wall and you will be forced to look at the ground. Camera control is absolutely rubbish, it completely focuses on your target, rather than zooming out to have view of both your character and the target, leaving you sometimes to be lost, camera stuck in the wall, or the ground, or all of the above.
- Skits (where characters talk amongst each other on certain situations or points of the story) seem to have been cut down significantly, only happening at save points or map points of interest. Kind of lost the flavour of character interaction and development.
Overall, there's a lot more in the cons section than the pros, but thats only because I've played Tales of games since I was a kid, I had a lot of experience of which one were good and clicked with me and ones that didn't, so don't let the small pros to cons ratio fool you. The game is okay, a solid 6/10, kind of bueno, but nothing that will ever top Tales of Symphonia, Vesperia, or Abyss, the latter being my most favourite for its characters, story, and character development (please play the PS2 version, the 3DS adds nothing but a smaller screen to look at). This game is worth looking into, but probably better to pick it up at a sale, spend the rest of your money on previously mentioned Tales of games for a better experience.
P.S. Namco Bandai, please learn how to properly manage your promotional materials, falsely advertising that Alisha is the main heroine then ditch her in favour of someone else and then blaming the fanbase for their misconception is bad, especially when she was everywhere with Sorey when the game was first announced. The game characters even thought they had started to develop romantic feelings for each other, so much as to visit each other's room at night. If thats not misleading, then I don't know what is.

To review The Long Dark, you are either best waiting until the game is completed in it's development OR explain what it is right now and comment on it's progress as time goes on... I'm going to attempt to do that.
As of now, The Long Dark is in it's alpha testing phase, with no storyline, however holds 2 huge wilderness maps, in 3 different difficulties as a man or a woman. There are no zombies, no bad guys, just you and nature and of course, wildlife. At the moment it's a total survival sandbox - exploring, looking for supplies, weapons and clothing to help you fight the Canadian wilderness.
The Long Dark is hands down the loneliest game I have ever played, and the fact it's a sandbox and nothing else at the moment, it adds to the atmosphere. The visuals are stunning, the voice acting is very professional, the animal AI is fantastic, and to be frank, if this is the game at its alpha stage, I can't wait for the full experience. Right now, the achievements are the closest thing to a 'quest' or a 'mission' because the majority monitor your survival time. So far, I've lasted just under 14 days...
2014 has been an excellent year for games, especially new and indie. This is definitely a favourite, and if this is what Hinterland Studio have got in mind as an Alpha test, they are going to become a big deal, even if this is a one hit wonder. They are not messing around with this one.
Get it.

Ok I want to write a negative review; specifically for people who see this product and say "hey I can do that."

While the resources provided are nice any music or character sprites per made are of course copyrited to the product. You will have to do a good deal of resource creation if you wish to release a game.
Finally, I would like to stress that making a computer game takes a TEAM of dedicated individuals on average, several months. If you think your going to buy this product today and put a game out by yourself next week, or even next month then think again.
All this being said I would still recomend this product; but specifically.
-To someone cutting their teeth in game design
-Who plans to do this, or want to explore this for a career
-Who has an intermedeite knowlege of computers and graphic design
There are several solid games out there made by this engine; but they were made by some very talanted people and often groups who had the money and time to invest in a long term project.

Fallout 3 is an excellent game. It's beutiful for it's time, it's truly open world, and you can play any way you want. The character customization system is very diverse, allowing you to be a multitude of different races, styles, and ages! I personally ran around a badass asian with punk rock hair. The combat system is completely epic, as it allows for fast paced action, or slower paces action depending on your personal playstyle! You can use Vault-Tec Assisted Targeting System if you like, it allows you to select certain enemies to fire at, aswell at specific parts of their bodies.
The storyline is particularly one I enjoyed. (SPOILERS AHEAD! SKIP TO NEXT PARAGRAPH IF YOU HAVENT PLAYED YET!)
You start off as a wee litle baby. You learn how to walk, you costumize who you are, and you have a birthday party. You wake up on your 19th year to find that your father, James has left the vault. You make a daring escape and chase him down. While doing this you meet a multitude of different people, and explore many places! For example, on your quest you are put in a radio tower which was put back into function by an eccentric DJ names Threeee Dawggg. (Three dog.)
He tells you that in order for him to help you find your dad you must help him fight the, "good fight". So you end up going to the capital of Washington DC! Here you battle genetically modified humans who had the "FEV" virus put into them, in order to retrieve a transmitting disc for Three Dog's radio. I always do this as afterwards it permitts you to listen to the radio anywhere in the game!
The gameplay is astounding, allowing for beutiful graphics or easier to run graphics. I reccomend at least 2 gb of ram and a somewhat decent processor. This game is simply wonderful to sight see in. There are tons of side quests to partake in. (SPOILER:) For example, in one of them you must help Lucy West send a letter to her family across the wasteland. You find out her family was killed violently by her brother Ethan. You can resolve that quest in a multitude of ways.
Overall, this game is amazing and will swallow at least a month of your life.

Five Nights at Freddy's is an indie point and click game done up by Scott Cawthon. The story revolves around a lone security guard, Mike Schmidt, working the graveyard shift at Freddy Fazbear's Pizza. With the business struggling and closing down by year's end, no one's going to come by and rob it... It's the animatronics you need to protect yourself from. You must last through your six hour shift with limited battery power, and the advice from your colleague on the shift before.  You can find my playthrough below, take a look.
The premise of the game is highly simple, you must last six hours (approx. 10 min) on the Night Shift with limited power in the building. To defend yourself from the four animatronics (Bonnie, Chica, Foxy, and Freddy Fazbear) you've only your camera network to keep an eye on them, lights near your doors to check for them, and your heavy-duty security doors, all of these taking up your power on use. You do not have a weapon, you cannot run, you must sit there and wait for your shift to end.
Five Nights at Freddy's takes a different spin on the horror genre; instead of pushing you through tasks you do not wish to perform, you must wait and observe your environment in order to protect yourself. Fail, and you'll be met with a final jump-scare, in which poor Mike Schmidt will join Freddy Fazbear's Pizza forever, stuffed into an extra Freddy Fazbear suit. Everything in this game is tailored not to frighten you, but to stress your mind and alertness which will make you afraid of anything with your hyper-awareness.
Everything in this game is tailored to that goal, from the clever, predatory enemy AI, to the sound and character design, subtly pushing in horror elements to the once thought innocent anamatronic characters.  Despite causing terror, these subtle changes and movements of your enemies ramps up your own paranoia, especially as Foxy is introduced, and the enemy AI becomes signifigantly more difficult as the nights progress, Freddy himself becoming extremely aggressive and attacking your door on the Fourth and Fifth nights.
Don't be expecting highly in-depth gameplay here like Amnesia or Outlast; with Five Nights at Freddy's the less-is-more approach does fantastic wonders. No background music makes the animatronics noises only ever more noticable, minimal ways to protect yourself only ramps up your fear, and the limited means of protecting yourself only makes those five nights even more harrowing. After the first five nights, a super difficult sixth night is unlocked, and after that a custom night is opened (which many people have been playing at max difficulty level in an effort to be '4-20' night, the ultimate Five Nights at Freddy's experience).
For the game's low cost, Five Nights at Freddy's comes highly reccomended for anyone looking for a good casual game, or a hard-core scare experience. I certainly reccomend it to anyone looking for a great indie-horror experience.

A Hat in Time is a solid 3D platformer. It controls very well. It really doesn't do anything new, though. The concept of moving a little character around a 3D world was novel and exciting back in the '90s and oughts, but now it's nothing special at all. I think that most of the game's appeal is in its high visual production values, amazing soundtrack, and straight-up heartwarming cuteness. Those elements alone might be enough to hold peoples' attention for a couple of weeks. You may get some more mileage out of the game by exploring the growing library of user-created content like new hats and levels. At some point, though, if you've double-jumped through one level, you've basically double-jumped through them all. In a world with more games than free time to play them, I'd only recommend paying $15 to $20 for a game like this.

Refunct is a nice entry into the "relaxing simple games" indie subgenre. It's incredibly short, but I got it for less than a dollar and found it to indeed be very pleasant and relaxing, so no complaints here. Basically, you make your way across platforms hitting switches which unlock more platforms, while trying to make sure you touch all the platforms at least once. I would love to see some expansions for this with new courses, since the basic premise has so much room for growth -- I liked the way it introduced new ways of using the course, but there was so much more you could do with them, plus so many more potential ideas -- what about an ice level where you can get up speed to jump further, but also slide where you land? What about a course that's all uphill, getting progressively higher and making falling a bigger risk? So much potential! (This is also the type of game that's ripe for community-sourced courses.) If you've got an hour to kill and want to listen to pleasant music and just kind of chill, this is totally worth picking up.

This is what I wanted Yooka Laylee to be. I do feel I should maybe give Yooka Laylee another shot, perhaps a few patches here and there will make that game more enjoyable... but this game was just fun. It hooked me without much effort and made me remember what I liked about this genre.
Is it perfect? Of course not, it has a few glitches... one even screwing me out of a yarn collectable. Some jumps feel a bit wonky... but I can honestly forgive that. I guess the biggest differences between Yooka Laylee's flaws and this game's flaws it that I was still overall having fun.
One big reason is the game oozing with personality. Like we've wanted, the dialogue is fantastic, with some nice jokes here and there to keep me interesting.
The controls felt smooth, the starting abilities were just enough to have fun early on without feeling like I would have fun later, and the areas I've explored so far have as much personality as the NPCs.
I might expand my thoughts after finishing the game, since this is just me casually having fun... but I'm posting this review for one big reason. This game is just fun. If you were disappointed with Yooka Laylee like I was and just wanted a fun casual experience, this gave me that nostalgic feeling of the N64/Gamecube platformers all over again.

The first aspect of this game I noted was how lovely it was. Not that it was a platformer, or highly rated, simply that it was lovely. I was in no way disappointed. The music evolves and changes as you progress further in the percentage of blocks stepped upon, soothing and falling under the category of 'emotional' music. Whether you're above the water's surface, looking out at the sky, or diving down below the water and looking at the sunken 'city' of blocks, there's beautiful colors and the way the day and night cycle changes and effects shadow and hue is just gorgeous.
Playwise, it's very smooth. The jumps are intuitive, as are the controls. Yes, they aren't explained, but it led to some 'eureka' moments of figuring out something, whether a little parkour puzzle or simply that water didn't kill you. All of the stressful aspects of 'challenge' that other platformers have aren't present, it presenting intelligent challenges instead of ones that kill your character or make you restart your progress in some way. There being no risks is oddly refreshing. It's not a game you have to rush.
While short, it's a suitable distraction and has replay value if you're having a bad day. The combination of the color palette, the music, and having to focus on the jumps means this game can help pick up moods. I would definitely recommend it, and enjoyed playing it. Something about raising a sunken world and making it green is just attractive, no matter how simplistic the game is.

For any games, once one discovers a dominant strategy that can be repeatedly utilized to win any possible scenario, then there is no point in continue playing it.  The dominant strategy for Banished is this
1) build a gathering hut in a large forest, prioritize-build it while the others go gather wood, stone, and iron in ANOTHER forest, put four people in it after it's finished.
2) build a forester lodge beside the hut when enough wood and stone are gathered, put four people in it after it's finished, switch laborers to focus on stone and iron
3) build enough houses to house the families, construct woodcutters, then either a taylor or a blacksmith, depending on whether you need more clothing or tools.
4) build other buildings as resources come in, but always leave a surplus of food of around 100xpopulation, 10xpopulation of firewood; 2xpopulation of clothing and tools is recommended if playing conservatively.
5) priortize houses as they are important for growth. They are where babies are made, and 30-something siblings living with their 70-something parents ain't going to make kids.
Even on small mountaineous map with harsh climate, on hard difficulty, presumably the hardest starting scenario, one can double the population by year 10 just by doing the above, and get to 50 by year 20 is not out of the question.  The dominant factor for this game is the availability of space for more housing, balance against the food production buildings and wooded areas for firewood.  Variables like education and chapels are merely cosmetics that increase the efficiency of space, but not necessarily needed to grow your town.  As for natural disasters, since your town is likely separated into several parts by bodies of water, and as far as I can tell fire doesn't go through water, and tornados don't wreck more than one part of town, if one has enough of a surplus, one can easily rebuild and those are not game-changing disasters.
So survival is simple.  If you like a game that you can play while playing another game on another computer, this is recommended.  This is a solved game; but people continue to play tic-tac-toe even though it's analytically uninteresting, so others may differ in opinion.
Edit -- this is an evaluation of the vanilla game; perhaps with mods there will be enough complexity to make it less linear.

Note: Haven't beat it yet but at last boss. I may edit this if anything changes my opinion after that. Recommending it 'cause I am enjoying myself, even with the negative points.
Story: Disappointing. The last tales game I played was  Tales of the Abyss. Coming from that, this story is vanilla, plain, generally doesn't rock the boat. There's a couple of interesting plot revelations, such as a certain villain origin. Some plot points or lore isn't fully explained, and leaves me wondering where in the game that missing information is. Just not as indepth as I was expecting. That aside, there are some really funny scenes and it wouldn't be a Tales game without some cheesy moments as well.
Combat: Fun. Took me half way into the game to get the hang of it, as I prefer button smashing to smite my enemies. But that can only carry you so far. Later bosses require you to dodge and pay attention and I got more enjoyment by taking a more active role in combat. Free raises from your battle partners is awesome. I abuse that feature to the max. Also, I thought it was cool to have the battle take place on the field map. Which explained the HUGE maps.
Equipment: I liked upgrading my gear, but I got a good set of skills on mine and was loathe to lose them, so I haven't been fusing same name equipment together that much. Apparently gear bonus is more important than actual level. More fuses = better stats, new bonuses/skills on them (depending on base skills).
Music: AWESOME. I want the soundtrack. Shut up and take my money.
Traveling: Great that I could quickly travel from save point to save point. Bad that at times that was disabled and I was forced to walk with no explanation as to why. Thought the game had a bug the first couple times it happened. Oh. It's supposed to happen. Great. An auto-run feature would be nice when transversing large open lands.
Special abilities: Fun. The power of them really ramps up when at least two characters have the same ability (there are exceptions where the power doesn't stack, like food prep) . I would like to be able to choose who else gets which abilities when staying at an inn.
Visuals: I thought they looked really nice. Sometimes, there's a graphical error that flickers on the screen during some cutscenes (distracting and annoying) or just when running through a town.
Dungeons: There are some cookie cutter dungeons. Outdoors, underground. Outdoors, you're funneled into this rat's maze with walls on either side. Doesn't feel very wilderness to me, more like all the scenary was spent on the wide open maps, leaving these guys with the leftovers. Underground ones all look and act like the same set of ruins/caves with different textures. That part reminds me of the Hack.Sign game dungeons.
The 'mainstory' dungeons are better and much more interesting, it looks like more care went into their design.

TowerFall Ascension is an arena type game. This game was released in March 2014, after initially being released as an Ouya exclusive in 2013 (snarf). It is now on PC, PS4 and Mac/Linux.
TowerFall's arena type gameplay focuses heavily on archery. The game has two modes; firstly the single player - the aim is to kill targets around each stage either by stomping on their heads, or by shooting them with your bow before a timer runs out; this leaves to plenty of replaying of levels in order to better your score and to beat your best time.
Where TowerFall really shines is in the multiplayer mode. Up to four players will fight in a battle royal environment. Your aim is simple, kill or be killed. Each player has a limited amount of arrows to do it in too, so you can't just spam fire and hope you get lucky. You are able to replenish your ammo by picking up rogue arrows shot by yourself and the others though, meaning things can get very frantic. Throughout the stage, there will also be various different power-ups spawn, such as special effects on your arrows or shields - these all add to the extremely fast paced gameplay.
The graphics and art style, yet again have the pixelated theme, but they are still all really well drawn out and it looks very pleasant. Each of the arenas that you are fighting in also look amazing too, some will be set in the jungle, others in a poorly lit cave, they all look gorgeous.
Single player in TowerFall Ascension is easy; you can easily clear the stages in less than an hour. Where the difficulty ramps up like most games is the multiplayer. It will only be as difficult as your opponents are, as they are they only thing that can kill you; you don't need to worry about the environment playing tricks against you.  It will take you a few hours to get to a point where you are competent in games; it can be very frustrating though.
I have been playing TowerFall for almost eight hours now; I would say that this is a game to play in small chunks. Bring it out when you have friends over for an hour of almost archery style Super Smash Bro fun, but any more than that, and you may find yourself getting a little bored.  This is certainly a game to keep installed due to the replay-ability though.
The game supports resolutions up to 1080P, which I suppose is all you need for a pixel style game like this and it is highly recommended you play this game with a game pad; keyboard controls would be a nightmare.
To conclude, I am going to simply recommend TowerFall Ascension; its a game that not everyone will enjoy, and is almost certainly made with couch multiplayer in mind. If you don't have friends who also own this game, don't get it, the single player is not worth it. If you can find a group to play with, sure its worth the £10,99 because of the fun fast paced gameplay you'll get out of it.

Rating: 8.5/10
What is it?
First Person Survivor Horror
The Good:
+ The games main objective is to scare the living crap out of you and it succeeds on so many levels. The combination of music, atmosphere, graphics all lead up to a very frightening experience.
+Great atmosphere. The game takes place mostly in an Asylum.
+Graphically, the game is gorgeous. The game makes good use of darkness, forcing you to use a camcorder with night vision to help navigate the environment.
+ The gameplay although basic gets the job done. You have no method of combat so you have to rely on stealth, running, peaking around corners to avoid enemies.  The focus is on exploration and solving basic puzzles.
+ Music is very well done, really adds to the horror element.
+Decent story, most of it is done through records scattered around the levels.
+Good length for the type of game. It doesn't wear itself out.
The Bad:
-The biggest problem I found was that the game relies on the same puzzles throughout most of the game. I.e Find 2 switches, levers, buttons to progress. Overtime it doesn't feel 'natural' to the setting but it starts feeling repetitive.
-The AI can feels a bit wonky at times. It becomes hard to predict when they come after you and when they don't and what triggers it.
Conclusion
If you've played Amnesia or Slenderman you should know what to expect with this game. The goal is to get absorbed into the world, and try and survive until the end. Your ultimate enjoyment is going to depend on how scared you are going to be and how interested you are in the story.  The length isn't a big issue, as I was able to complete the game in roughly 4 hours. Its a solid length for the game as anything longer and it would start feeling very tedious. I highly recommend this game if your looking for a  good horror game.

The Whack-a-Mole of the horror genre, Five Nights at Freddy's plays unlike any spooky game you've ever seen. While the player never once moves from their office, and while each level is only a couple minutes short, the game is deceptively simple--spending your nights at Freddy's actually demands both strategic thinking and fast reflexes. Using just a simple mouse-only interface, very little animation, and some clever design, this game not only creates a superb atmosphere of suspense, but also manages to be quite challenging. All in all, I'd say it's well worth $5.

I have continuously played this game since the original release of RO2. This game definetly resides somewhere in my top 1-3 favorite games of all time. Hands down the best WW2 FPS game that i would consider "current" although it is several years old. Prepare to be killed quite often and depending on your nature prepare to feel major frustration as well!! As you adjust to the game and release your self from the" CoD / Battlefield franchise grip" and into the mechanics of this game, with time it becomes quite rewarding!! You should begin as a rifleman and play this position for at least a couple of months to get the basic jist of game play and learn to aim and shoot in game.  And while your new and learning the game  your deaths arent as costly such as they would be playing a Squad Leader or better yet a Team Leader. Being that this game revolves around team work at the squad level in order to accomplish goals as a whole, it is wise to learn each position well before jumping onto an established server. The community tends to grumble when a sub par skilled player is leading the team to a Lose.  which brings me to the only frown i really have with this game..  The gaming community while having many great people who are very helpful in it , is full of people who talk alot of trash over the Voip system. it can get annoying at times. I see this as a set back in a team based tactical FPS... but humans will be humans unfortunately and there isnt much you can do to change that other than running a private server. The more time you spend playing the more rewarding it becomes as you learn the maps and how to stay alive longer between each respawn. The gaming community is alive and strong . It is rare at any time of the day for me to be unable to find a populated server worthy of playing! So come on!! , Join the rest of us  and get in the war!! We got some territory to take!!!!  A few gaming  tips while you are a noob...1) dont throw nades til you actually know how to throw them,,,, all you will do is kill teammates. 2) learn to  differentiate between team uniforms and the way they hold their weapons when running. each team is different intentionally to help you . 3) look at your map often!! 4) Dont run into falling arty.... you are just wasting precious tickets!! Note: Haven't beat it yet but at last boss. I may edit this if anything changes my opinion after that. Recommending it 'cause I am enjoying myself, even with the negative points.
Story: Disappointing. The last tales game I played was  Tales of the Abyss. Coming from that, this story is vanilla, plain, generally doesn't rock the boat. There's a couple of interesting plot revelations, such as a certain villain origin. Some plot points or lore isn't fully explained, and leaves me wondering where in the game that missing information is. Just not as indepth as I was expecting. That aside, there are some really funny scenes and it wouldn't be a Tales game without some cheesy moments as well.
Combat: Fun. Took me half way into the game to get the hang of it, as I prefer button smashing to smite my enemies. But that can only carry you so far. Later bosses require you to dodge and pay attention and I got more enjoyment by taking a more active role in combat. Free raises from your battle partners is awesome. I abuse that feature to the max. Also, I thought it was cool to have the battle take place on the field map. Which explained the HUGE maps.
Equipment: I liked upgrading my gear, but I got a good set of skills on mine and was loathe to lose them, so I haven't been fusing same name equipment together that much. Apparently gear bonus is more important than actual level. More fuses = better stats, new bonuses/skills on them (depending on base skills).
Music: AWESOME. I want the soundtrack. Shut up and take my money.
Traveling: Great that I could quickly travel from save point to save point. Bad that at times that was disabled and I was forced to walk with no explanation as to why. Thought the game had a bug the first couple times it happened. Oh. It's supposed to happen. Great. An auto-run feature would be nice when transversing large open lands.
Special abilities: Fun. The power of them really ramps up when at least two characters have the same ability (there are exceptions where the power doesn't stack, like food prep) . I would like to be able to choose who else gets which abilities when staying at an inn.
Visuals: I thought they looked really nice. Sometimes, there's a graphical error that flickers on the screen during some cutscenes (distracting and annoying) or just when running through a town.
Dungeons: There are some cookie cutter dungeons. Outdoors, underground. Outdoors, you're funneled into this rat's maze with walls on either side. Doesn't feel very wilderness to me, more like all the scenary was spent on the wide open maps, leaving these guys with the leftovers. Underground ones all look and act like the same set of ruins/caves with different textures. That part reminds me of the Hack.Sign game dungeons.
The 'mainstory' dungeons are better and much more interesting, it looks like more care went into their design.

Napoleon: Total War is a turn-based strategy game that starts during the Napoleonic era. Playable factions are the great powers in Europe at the time. Unlike to Empire: Total War, the map in Napoleon: Total War is quite small and contains of only Europe.
Best strategy is to ignore your enemy's army all together and to blitz his regions. His troops will disappear entirely if you have conquered all regions of your enemy's home theatre. Two new mechanics were introduced:
1. Your troops will slowly replenish its soldiers in your own and friendly territory.
2. Weather: Don't attack Russia or other cold regions during winter or you will lose a lot of men.
+ factions have a lot of regions
+ Each faction has different units that look great. Check out France and its late game elite units
+ battlefield map is actually fun unlike to Empire: Total War's
+ a lot of mods that improve on the base game
+ research tree
+ If you conquer a region, you can sometimes decide to liberate the people, to annex the region or to force a protectorate on them.
+ Much better optimized than Empire: Total war
- the AI is very bad on the campaign and battlefield map.
- barely any naval invasions
- fort battles are broken
- there is sometimes an odd sound bug on the campaign map. can't believe it's still in the game!
- The campaign map contains of only Europe, which left me craving for more.
- protectorates rarely get attacked by your enemies. So you can abuse the mechanics and make factions like Venice a protectorate in order to secure your flank, which will be safe forever.
It's sometimes difficult to decide if you want to play Empire or Napoleon Total war. Empire has a bigger map and more factions, but Napoleon is overall more polished, runs better and has a much better unit variety.
Replay value: Average (the campaign map is too small to keep the player interested)
Rating 8/10
Recommendation: Yes

I love this game to pieces, no question about it. Tales of Symphonia was my first and my favourite, and always will have a special place in my heart, but that didn´t make me think any less of this game. It´s such a good game.
The game runs smoothly and has a good range of settings to fiddle with, both in graphics as well as controls, despite the 30fps lock. My mid-range PC ran the game on medium settings without any problems. And even though controllers are probably the best choice for playing a game like this, keyboard and mouse are fully supported and have customisable key bindings for those who can't or don't want to play with one. Also, the music is good overall, with some truly standout orchestral tracks in places. As for the voices, I personally found the English dub to be surprisingly good and not annoying at all to listen to, though the Japanese voices are also included, if that is what strikes your fancy.
Even though the story felt a little bit less twisting and turning compared to earlier games, it is still a fairly in-depth and enjoyable experience and the localisation is funny and amazingly well done with a lot of attention to detail. The characters are likeable and have some great interaction, both in the main story and throughout the various skits, and the absence of any major technobabble is an especially refreshing change from the norm for the series, though hearing about malevolence might get a little bit annoying after a while.
The battle system is interesting, and a little more in-depth than usual with gear fusion taking a higher priority than the ordinary level grinding. You can get through most of the game without delving too deeply into it, but fiddling with gear, the right stick commands and titles are definitely something worth looking into if you´re planning on playing on higher difficulties. The AI in itself isn´t as customisable as in earlier games and the camera can be a little bit annoying at times in battle, but I didn´t find either to be a huge problem in single player and I think the seamless battle environment and the sheer fun of the real time battle system more than made up for it.
It´s still an incredibly fun game regardless and I wouldn´t have it any other way.

The first time you get your hands on this product, you'll be like "Holy ****! am I playing Dark Souls?"  Don't worry, because when you actually take some time to play around with rpg maker, you'll be like "Pfft, what is this? Final Fantasy VI?"
In all seriousness.
This product becomes so easy to use once you get the hang of it!
And it's so simple too!
Want to make an NPC? No problem! Just create a new event, select the sprite, make the script for the character (right-click dat big empty space), and edit the dialogue. Easier done than said!
Random encounters? Yes! Very easy to make!
Wait, wait, what if I want to make a jumpscare game? No problem. You can make images appear! Just don't get your hopes high on a FNAF rip-off
Can you sell the games you make? Hell yah!  Why do you think it's called RPG Maker? And There's no catch! Royalty free!
Pros
-Easy to use
-Recommended for people who want to sell their first game
-Recommended for devs who are just starting out
-No complicated scripting required for a good game
-Importing your custom content like sprites is a walk in the park
-Legit fighting system
-Asking price isn't as high as compared to other engines like Cryengine or UnityPro
Cons
-Resources you get when you buy RPG Maker is actually really limited unless you buy some of the DLCs
-DLC bait (although the DLCs are really great)
-Not the engine you'll want to use if you want to make the revolutionary, next gen, 2D RPG game
-You can easily make visual novels here, but not recommended. It'll end up being bland
What are you waiting for? Go buy this now!

I teach a survival simulation course to children and adults.
I work at a camp where we have a variety of programs that we offer to grade-schoolers who come and take field trips at our site. Among the fun ones like "Log-cabin Building" and "Pioneer Cooking" is "Survival Simulation". What does that look like? Very similar to this game. We are open in the spring and the fall and are in the northern United States and often find ourselves doing this in the snow. As a matter of fact, on first looking at it, I was convinced that some items had been taken from my manual. But that was silly. Smart survivalists all say the same basic things.
Before I take the children out, I give them a quick lesson on all the things they will experience in the simulation. How to find water, how to find or create tinder, kindling and fuel for a fire, what a fire needs to live, what we need to live, how to build a lean-to, how to find what direction the wind is coming from, how to build an S.O.S. signal and how to create a splint, stop blood loss and treat shock. Pretty rushed though, but that's OK because we are going outside and going to practice everything that I just showed them.
So, at our camp, we have "The plane crash" in a wilderness area (no houses around sorry) and the burning wreckage is going so hot and heavy that the survivors only have time to grab five items out of a long list of things that was on the plane. We are looking basically for them to chose: Matches, Knife, Metal bucket, Rope, Tarp and not choose things like: Flashlight, Popcorn, Toilet paper, and the like. They only have a few minutes before the plane catches all the way, and then sinks into the bog.
The main good news during my Survival Sim is that there are no wolves. Not real ones at least. The pretend ones come later. We do, however, put them to the test. There are around ten children usually and they are given fifty "Life Points" per group, each child accounting for five of those points. I will give them twenty minutes to find water, get a fire going and bring their water to a boil. Fire accounts for: Light, Heat, Ability to melt and boil water, Ability to cook food, Safety, Ability to dry wet clothes, and most importantly: Hope.
If they fail at the first task the rest are ultimately harder. And I take away half of their Life Points. Then I have them search for food, erect a shelter, someone "has an accident" and breaks their leg and bleeds everywhere and goes into shock, and then I have them build and S.O.S. and get into the shelter before the wolves come.
Usually around half of the children die. But we go inside out of the snow and discuss what happened and they write down the things they did that were successful and the things that were not.
All of that prepared me for The Long Dark. In the game, I found myself learning new and inventive strategies that I did not know I was able to invent. I felt as if I were a child and the game makers were myself, being patient and ever so helpful. Wait. No. There was no help. Only the savage fangs of the wolves. And the snow. The long dark? The long snow-blind, wolf-infested, frozen-soul dark. Dark and dirty... And damn cold.
My first experience with this game was my wife screaming from the other room. "Oh my gosh honey! This is totally you!" she went on and on. She was so happy to have found something that looked like I would play it over and over. That was two weeks ago. It was to be my Christmas present... Heh. I've been enjoying it a little early.
Enjoying it? Obsessing over it? Living it? I caught myself looking up dog-food prices the other day. On the top of my review, it shows how many hours I have played of this game. Does it really reflect the thirty hours I've spent scouring maps and watching youtube videos? No. You ♥♥♥♥♥rdly hour-counter. How dare you scoff at my lack of total commitment! I love this game and have recently purchased it for my brother and one of my closest friends.
Do I recommend this game? Yes. Only if you want to live.

I've used RPG makers since around 2007 or 2008 I think when I was introduced to RPG Maker 2000 translated by Don Miguel. I made a whole bunch of garbage and even completed some games as well which is not something you see me doing today. You can even check out one of the games I made
if you're seriously interested or
(Thanks, Steam for censoring me again. Learn to be helpful. It's bulls-h-i-t.
Sometime later, I downloaded the demo for RPG Maker XP and had no idea what I was doing for some reason. I remember screwing around with it a lot until I managed to make an enemy fightable. Sometime later, I cracked VX as it's incredibly overpriced.
Then Ace. When I first saw it I said that I can just find some scripts to do whatever this update is capable of, but since it was a hell of a lot cheaper to buy on here I decided to just get it anyways.
I'd say it's probably the best RPG Maker I've used yet. Really. I like the ability to make title screens in the editor itself instead of making some piece of crap on paint. Seriously, I've only managed to make one good title screen on my own...with someone else's art.
Another great addition is the ability to customize the battle backgrounds. You can choose the floor and the background to whatever you choose. Want a field of organs floating in space? You can do this. Want a throne room inexplicable sitting on top of clouds? You can do this as well. Perhaps a diabolical king decided to do this with his fancy magic to make his final fight all the more epic, or maybe some giant monster exploded and now you're fighting on its flesh as it rockets into space.
Another new feature that you may find useful is the ability to use an example map. You could be incredibly lazy and import an entire city into your game, or be more original and edit it to something else and save time.
Back in RPG Maker 2003, there was the option to generate dungeons. You choose the walls and the floors and add some details in a generic maze style. This is in VX Ace as well, just without the details part. Just make sure the map is large enough, otherwise it will generate a small room and nothing else. As with the example maps, this is a good way to save time and edit a map less to make your game.
I remember when I was making a game on VX and I found a script to have certain enemies fade away slowly like in a Final Fantasy game such as Zeromus. In VX Ace, it comes ready with a boss-fade effect for when you kill an enemy. There are three fade effects to choose from, although I have been able to make a crumbling effect in 2000 by having a boss disappear immediately and be replaced by a tiny dot monster to prevent combat from ending and then have a terrible MSpaint animation of the boss crumbling away pixel by pixel. It's not too bad actually, but I'd like to see more fade options. Perhaps a way to customize your own since it's always satisfying to see the final boss have their own special way of being destroyed (looking at you, Sephiroth).
There are more features to talk of, but I'm sure that's enough to give a good example of what this update contains. Yes, I recommend it. But wait for it to be on sale. It does it all the time.
EDIT: Some more time using this program and I can say that this is pretty lacking in graphics. Sure, the community has made lots of stuff, but I definitely prefer the variety Don Miguel's RTP for RPG maker 2000 provided. There's much more to make your games with and I challenge you to prove me otherwise.
On top of that, the way the game handles MIDIs is very poor. First off, it has its own soundfont. The soundfont has a weird reverb to it and it generally doesn't sound very good at all. Then, if you initialize  MIDI at start up, it takes much longes to load the game. These are MIDIs! It makes no sense! Maybe t's the soundfont, though.
Another thing it really lacks is animations. First of all, the weather is limited to rain, snow, and "storm". There are a few weather scripts from the community, but I've not seen a sandstorm one which really sucks. The snow is also really weak. I wanted a blizzard, but I couldn't get one. The battle animations are also lacking. There are no bow animations. Why? Previous RPG makers have had arrows, why not this one?
The character maker is a bit lacking but not too much of a problem. There's no option to make a sprite with a hood, so I had to make a character have a red hairstyle flatted on the top and have him not face the player or to the left or the right.
Finally, there is no key item menu that can be brought up via event. I wanted to be able to open up a special window with key items by talking to a crystal so that the player could select a key item. If the right one were to be selected, it would trigger something. There's no option. I saw something on it, but it shouldn't be so needlessly complicated. Maybe there's a script that implements it. Who knows?
So do I still recommend this? Yeah, I guess. Get it as cheap as you can, for sure. 70 dollars is insane especially when you consider the DLC. It's certainly not worth that much.
EDIT: Changing this to not recommended. I just can't recommend this at all anymore. There are barely any resources, and the tiles that are there are just squares that inconsistently fuse with eachother. I just can't see a way to make a good map with it. Just use 2000 and Don's RTP. Much more resources to use.

This is a very interesting, engrossing, but flawed in some aspects game. The noir astmosphere is extremely well done and grabs you into the world. The artstyle of being all grey with only the color red standing out makes it visually striking. The story is just beginning but has me intrigued. There is only one section in the game but at this section you must look for clues at a murder scene and put the pieces together for yourself. It's not really that difficult but it's a good start. Doug Cockle as private detective Elliot Ness is good casting and everyone else does a decent job as well.
As for the flaws, while the artstyle is very good graphically it's nothing special. Not terrible but not great either. Lip synching is also inconsistent with the character models mouthes not always lining up with the words they're speaking. The biggest issue I have is with the controls. I used a keyboard and I was limited to moving with the W S A D keys for walking and only E is used for observing items of interest. Five Nights at Freddy's is a simple game that banks on jump-scares.
Each animatronic character that you have to monitor in this game has its own personality and behavior. You have to learn these to begin to predict where to monitor and when and at what points to toggle the door locks and lights. This requires many play-throughs to get it right.
The thing that makes this game worthwhile, to me, is how much they were able to do with such a limited tool set. There's really no animation. You're just looking at still images through a camera that pans side to side. Instead of animations, cameras black out momentarily. You only ever see still images. And yet, you still get this quirky story with a game play that requires replays and observation to eventually master.
If you're looking for a real horror or survival game, this isn't it. If you're looking for very deep game play, this isn't it. If you're looking for two or three hours of trying to beat-the-pattern with the occasional startle (even after the tenth time, I still get a little jolt), then it's worth grabbing. I got it at half price and it's worth that. I think the default five bucks is just about right at the limit of a reasonable price.
I just find it so damn clever how much they did with so little. If you're uncertain about the game, it's still worth looking into at a lower price point.

This game is a must-buy for Tales Series Fans and Newcomers alike!  I have compiled a short abrievated list of pro's and con's for those looking for a quick read.
TL;DR - Great addition to the Tales series!  Best combat system in a Tales game thus far (albeit the random camera issues).  Great story and cast but not as captivating as Tales of Symphonia/Vesperia's characters.
PROS:
- Amazing combat system.  Very fun to fight and has a rock-paper-scissors skill mechanic which makes even normal encounters fun every single time. It's so fun that you won't even want to run away from field monsters!
- Unique Bosses.  Each and every boss has a different strategy that must be employed in order to defeat them effeciently.  Unless you are playing on a low difficulty, simply mashing buttons in the bosses's general direction won't cut it.
- Fantastic Music.  Very immersive and will make you want to find the OST on Youtube! This game has one of the best soundtracks out of any of the Tales games. Yes, I said it.  Admitedly, most Tales games have pretty epic music.
- Incredible Dialogue.  Every important scene is voice acted, and all skits are voice acted!  And there are a TON of them. Tales of Zestiria allows you to choose whether you want the Japanese or English voices.  In my opinion I'd say the English Voiceovers are incredibly strong and fitting for each of the characters.
CONS:
- Camera Issues.  Yes every review you have read has stated this.  Why, you ask?  Because of the nature of  the combat system the camera sometimes zooms too far in or zooms into a corner causing some frustrating gameplay issues.  But, this has happened to me only about 10 times in my 30 hours of playing the game thus far.
- Storyline.  [NO SPOILERS]  The game makes you feel attached to one of the supposed main characters in the game then they suddenly are no longer there anymore.  In addition to this, the storyline has a lot going on and can be a bit confusing at times. Especially for those new to the Tales series.
- Items.  This game has fewer items than in previous Tales games and also does not provide pictures for the items.  This is not that big of a deal, due to the game's unique equipment fusion system, but sometimes it leaves more to be desired.
ENDING COMMENTS:
If you love the Tales series, you will like this game!  If you're new to the Tales series, Tales of Zestiria is a fine introduction.  Give the game time to get started; it takes about 4-5 hours of gameplay to really get immersed into the story.  The combat system is epic and every battle is unique and fun to play.  There are some minor flaws in the game, but they are easily overlooked.  Happy Sheparding!

To get steel tools you need a coal mine and you need to upgrade a blacksmith. To upgrade a black smith you need a brick maker. A brick maker requires a shore house. An advanced economy is a complex economy. There are many other technology routes that can be taken or explored, while ignoring others. What you can't build out can buy from traders. I'm going to gift this game to some kids next Christmas who'll love it -- and unwittingly introduce them to "economic geography".

I've been waiting for the "Tales of" series to come to Steam for a while, and I have to say they picked a great entry to launch the franchise through Valves service.
Tales of Zestiria is an engaging, fast paced JRPG that creates an experience that is both fresh and distinctly "Tales of". The world is large, and there's a surprising amount of freedom to tackle quests and tasks. Combat is engaging, intuitive and fun. Although you may get lost in all the large amount menu's and stat boosting options. Mind you since there is a lot of ways to modify and build up characters through gear fusing, stat stacking, you can easily find different strategies to give your party the edge they need to cut through a battle.
Story wise it's fairly clean cut. The hero is your true blue virtuous goodie goodie, and that's not a bad thing. Mind you it's his journey and growth that really make it interesting as he struggles with finding balance between self sacrifice and enjoying life. The cast is likeable even if there is no character that really steals the show I still found myself wrapped up in their antics.
The game is great for offering both english and japanese voice acting... and although as an anime fan I usually watch in Japanese I've played it for the most part in english since sometimes dialogue between characters can occur on the fly, during battle, and sometimes you can't focus on ready small text boxes while in combat. That said the english voice acting did grow on me. I think that's a relatively good sign for the quality of the voice work.
I'm sure it was no coincidence that Tales of Symphonia was put as part of the pre-order rewards. Tales of Zestiria pulls a lot of it's style and tone from that classic Tales entry. So if you enjoyed that game, then Zestiria is also for you.

RPG Maker VX Ace is software meant to help facilitate users in creating that RPG they have in mind. It's not without it's complexities, however, and they are there.
Back when RPG Maker for the PSX came out, a friend and I got it. We had to have it mailed to us, since no stores sold it. I honestly don't remember how, since it was before I was really on the internet. In any case; it was weeks of anticipation, for what equated to a memory-card hogging, confusing system of software. I think the best we did was have an event that was basically an arena, where one monster at a time would walk to you and start a fight. It was a lot of money for something we quickly found kinda...hard.
Today, though, we can use a keyboard and mouse! Other then that, it's still hard. Like really hard. Not because it's challenging, but because it requires not only putting things together, but learning EXACTLY how to do it. To some, it comes naturally, it's fun, and they put out a couple games. You can find them on the marketplace, too, and play and enjoy them!
But be honest, do you buy RPG maker to play RPGs? No. You buy it to work. You buy it as a swiss army knife with a few thousand different tools, with a house to build. It's all there, but you need to learn how to use it...and that's without worrying about content (Want a sprite not there? You can make it, but it's work!)
I wonder how many people bought it without making even a simple, but complete game. Count me in!
Why, yes, I do have over 2000 hours. It's because my main way of working on my own project is by keeping RM open all the time. Staring at me.
"...Hey. It's not done yet."
"Yea, I know. Here, I'll make a skill I had in mind. That's something done."
"Good, good...I'll be here when you want to make something else."
I've found that RM's forums and Youtube in general have been very helpful. But be forewarned. You're not buying a game. You won't have a great, or even good game just kinda...fit together. You're buying work.
In short, I love procrastinating, and RPG Maker VX Ace is a really fun piece of software to tinker with.

Blues and Bullets is one of those games that, despite essentially being pieced together from other games, manages to make it work on its orn merits. At its core it plays like a modern Telltale game, mainly involving dialogue and choices, but it also takes notes from LA Noire in its aesthetics and occasional shooting, while the investigation gameplay is heavily remniscient of Sherlock Holmes: Crimes and Punishments, in which you search crime scenes for evidence and then piece them together on an evidence board yourself. The graphics sometimes have a bit of lack of polish, being an indie game, but the art style does a pretty good job of of covering the flaws, and the somewhat stilted character animations are made up for by the generally pretty good voice cast, particularly thanks to the voice of Doug Cockle (probably better known by his real name, Geralt of Rivia) as the main character.
The premise is an alternate history story about Eliot Ness, one of the real-world investigators responsible for the arrest of Al Capone. The story isn't exactly as grounded as its real-life inspiration would suggest, and certain scenes feel oddly out of place compared to the rest of the game, but for the most part it's well-told and pretty interesting so far, and left me looking forward to the next episode. The first episode spends a lot of its time setting up the story, so it feels somewhat linear, but it opens up enough later on to suggest that further episodes will do better with the pacing. Overall Blues and Bullets does a pretty good job for a first episode from a new studio, and while it is somewhat risky to buy an episodic game from a non-established developer, I thought it was worth giving it a try.

That was definitely an interesting experience. Whatever the motivation was, whether it was a true story, an exercise in self-finding, a way to process successes and failures in life, a way to deal with anxiety; it really doesn't matter. Everyone will interpret and experience this in a different way, will relate it to themselves in a different way. If anything that is the most important aspect.
Everyone is different. Everyone deals with problems, with setbacks, and with success in a different way. Some people enjoy being in the shadows, in the background, others need to be the center of attention, need to be the on the social stage of life. Some play a role, wear a mask every day, others are the way they are, and what you see is what you get. Artwork of any kind has always been a way of self-expression, and also a way to tell a story, to express oneself, a way to work out issues. Ultimately, true artworks inspire, invoke thought and creativity and speak to the audience. If something ticks those boxes (or even only one of those), then it's a piece of art.
For me personally, I can certainly relate to a good number of the aspects and events you can experience playing this. One review said that this could easily have been a YouTube video documentary; true, it could have been, but isn't that where the main difference is? When you watch a movie, a TV show, a documentary in a movie theater or on television, you're a passive observer with no real influence. Events play out, and you take them as they are. Playing a game, you at minimum get the illusion of making choices, you are an active part in the narrative, even if you follow a linear path.
In a way, this game, in one way or another, conveys at least the important insight that we can only learn and know as much about a person as that person is willing to let us know about them. It's a matter of trust that has to be earned and developed, because the more we open up, the more vulnerable we get.
I quite liked the main sentiments from the Matrix movies that apply here, too:
Ultimately I think what we should take away from this game, and perhaps as an important guide is this: Whatever you do in life, make sure it's something you (at least somewhat) enjoy, something that challenges you, something that makes your life worthwhile, and maybe even something that allows you to make a difference; even if it's only a small amount. And something else: If it feels right to take a risk, even if you logically think it might be too dangerous, perhaps you should take it once in a while.

This game has some plusses and minuses. While I have only bought the first episode (and am buying the rest), there are a few things I wanted to comment on. Not all are good or bad.
1) I like the historical angle of it. It feels like 1920's Noir with a pleasant and interesting twist. I like the exploration of "what if", and I enjoy this aspect of the game. If you are a history nerd like I am then you may enjoy seeing the different twists and turns in that regard.
2) Odd graphical glitches. I at one point failed a quick time event, and someone stabbed me to death with what I can only presume to be their mind. Their hand moved, but the knife moved much faster and stabbed me to death before their hand reached me. Also, there were times when the dialog and mouth motions were out of sync.
3) It feels like this company is trying copy Telltale Games' format in a lot of ways. While I am a big Telltale Games fan (so I enjoy this play style), it is a little too exact.
4) Some of the dialog is written in a stilted manner. I know this is nitpicking, but this kind of surfaced for me most when I encountered a janitor at one point, and every dialog option had him saying "my good sir". It felt awkward. The voice acting is pretty good, though.
5) Story is interesting enough to keep me going. It's definitely worth playing.

As Godus Wars currently stands, it is a nice casual Real-Time Strategy game.
I would like to see more unit variety (melee units, for example) and building types. They should bring back the need to harvest crops and mine for ore - making it a little more of a traditional RTS.
While the game is free for people who already own Godus, I don't think this game would stand up as a purchase for newcomers, it is just too bare bones as it is right now.
They should also find a way to eliminate the need for two windows being open when playing the game - it's just clunky and I can't think of many games that need this.
To conclude, I would like to see the game build on unit and building variety and find new ways to make the game more strategic and less casual (maybe introduce a 'Hardcore' mode, for people who want a more traditional RTS experience - adding all the elements that fans of the genre have come to expect).

B&B is a stylish simple adventure game with elements of CSI-style investigation where you inspect a crime scene for clues and assemble the clues into reasoning trees, bits of cover shooter, bits of QuickTime event (QTE) timed button pushing, bits of important decision points, all delivered in some pseudo-monochrome but with blood red still blood red unique visual look, all wrapped up with some ultra noir in an alternate history, in an 5-episode arc. It is one heck of a ride for the first episode, as there's enough action to make things exciting while the noir alternate history look kept you interested.
Right at the beginning, the game started in a weird disturbing way. You control a little girl who, along with other kids, were held by a cult for unknown purposes, and you're trying to engineer an escape, which ultimately failed. Then you transition to Elliot Ness, the original Untouchable. After Al Capone went to jail, you retired to a quiet little diner in Santa Esperanza while watching out for family of your former team, many of whom were killed by Al Capone's henchmen. Then an unexpected visitor came in: bringing a gift from 20 years ago... An unspent bullet you left with Al Capone...
Then the game transitioned into a cover shooter, as you shot your way into Al Capone's house by killing his crew, first with your own revolver, then with a captured Tommy gun. There's an in between QTE action where you capture the gun (or die). Once you confront Capone, you get to make several dialog choices and a major decision (there are five major decisions in this episode), but the end result is you walk away without killing Capone, and Capone let you walk away.
Back in the present, Ness was invited, apparently by Capone, to visit the Hindenburg Zepplin, now a part of the Ryan Hotel empire... and Capone wanted to hire Ness... as an investigator. Capone's granddaughter Sofia is missing... Some bogus uncle, with forged documents, took her away. Capone suspect one of his old henchmen.  Both Capone and Ness knew where to start... the forger in town.
Without spoiling the rest of the game, Ness and Capone's second, Milton, had to conduct an investigation and follow leads, which can include bluffing, hand to hand combat, investigation, and one heck of a surprise cliffhanger for Episode 2.
The cover shooter is a bit on the slow side, but quite workable as this is rail cover shooter (more Time Crisis than Gears of War) and not very difficult. Same with the QTE combat, as that gets automatic reload should you fail.
All in all, this is a very stylish adventure game with an art style that SCREAMS "noir" and a bit over the top, with some disturbing themes and an alternate history that is simply reminiscent of our own history, but does not follow it directly. The ending should dispel any such notion. You should definitely give it a try, even if it's just the first episode.

I've never been a fan of the Fallout series. Never understood the principle, story and gameplay. This however changed, when I picked up this game.
The fourth instalment in the series, Fallout 3, is what I would describe as a story-driven RPG shooter. There is something that many games cannot replicate which this game does amazingly and that is the feeling of guilt. The Karma system aswell as the detailed emotions of people in the game ,displayed thru their dialogue, can be really manipulative. For instance, at the start at the game, you're already given a very hard decision. If you were to kill the Overseer ,his daughter Amata would be.. dissapointed in you. You had your own reasons the kill him, and he had his, but then you feel that remorse and guilt after you realise what you've done.
The gameplay mechachics and RPG element are also very well done. The Perk and S.P.E.C.I.A.L. system make the game more rewarding once a player focuses on leveling something specifically. Weapons don't seem overpowered and underpowered, as they scale up acordingly with the progression of the player. Controlls are easy to get used to and are generally comfortable.
The one and only con about this game is how um-optimized it. This usually results in frequent crashes and performance loss but mods and tweaks can help you with that.

I am a big fan of strategy games, and European history, and this game effectively allows you to run your own medieval settlement and watch it grow into a sprawling city. This game, is just pure magic. I waited for 5 years on this game, and well, it didn't disappoint.
I never backed the game, but i have been closely following it since its very early days, when Mekucube (at the time known as Mechatheslag) was posting small little updates almost every day on his youtube on what progress he had made, be it a small little area to test in, to picking up a water melon and holing it above Hat Kid's head. I was also a slacker backer and played during the beta, i sadly didn't back the game during the original kickstarter, and i regret not doing so.
Now, enough gushing over old stuff, its onto the actual review.
This game, is just from start to finish, full of charm, cuteness, and emotion, every time i booted up the game i got this huge grin across my face (and not just excitement that its actually here), a grin of happiness. This game knows what it wants to be, and it did just that, giving so many memorable characters such as the Mustache Girl, the Mafia, Snatcher, Conductor and so many more. Each character in the game was unique and different from one another, and no two characters are alike, even each mafia member you can talk to has something different about them that makes them memorable. The writing is on par with Paper Mario: The Thousand Year Door (and with TONS of references to it as well)
Next up, Art direction, and oh my god this game looks AND sounds fantastic. It Just oozes with an adorable feeling that makes you giddy at everything you see. The art style is remincisent of the Wind Waker, and it shows, and giving itself its own identity too boot. The game feels fantastic to look at, and also each act of each world has its own title card, which gives you a LOT to look at in between levels. And dont get me started on the music, its just filled to the brim with so many good tracks. Shoutouts to Pascal and special guest Grant Kirkhope, you guys made an OST i can just listen to for hours... which is 5 hours long in total. Great job to them. The voice acting as well is Top notch, everyone delivered their lines oh so well i could feel the emotion they put into each and every line.
Now, how does it play? Well, it plays like Super Mario Sunshine, but a LOT more movement based. Hat Kid feels so good to control that never once did I ever feel like the game took control away, or that any mistake that I made wasn't my fault. Now the main gimick of the game, is Hats. With each hat you gain new abilities, and you can even swap them on the fly too for some extremely fluid switching. and this game wouldn't be a collectathon if it didn't have collectables to nab. You go around, collect Pons, Yarn, badges, other things, and your main plot macguffin, Time Pieces. You can Jump, Dive, wall jump, swing, attack, and so on. Hat Kid's movement options would make even Super Smash Bros. Melee professionals be envious. Theres never one way to get to your goal, and how Hat Kid moves is just right. And if you want to swap from keyboard controls to a controller, its super quick and you dont have to change any settings, it automatically switches over to your gaming preference (and theres Gamecube controller support!)
Now, if i have only a SINGLE complaint about this game, it would be the length. Its short. and I mean, SHORT. only a good 5 hours if you go for everything, while my hours at the time of this review say otherwise, 15 of them were during the beta.
All in all, I HIGHLY reccomend this game if you were a fan of gamecube era styled games, and its well worth your $30.
Thank you, and have a good evening~

Tales of Zestiria is another excellent action rpg from Namco. You take control of Sorey, the Shepard, on a quest to bring the Seraphim back to humankind.
Load times are nearly non-existent in game and the world map of the game feels like an instance more than it does a general overview! The combat system has taken a great stride in depth too. You can make your weapons better by combination as well as special effect adding. Spending time looking around at the scenery not only rewards you with additional cutscenes and story, but you gain AP for every landmark or story movie. By doing all of this, they've really made it hard to feel like you aren't doing something constructive even just wandering around aimlessly.
Here is where I have to mark the game down a bit. The game runs at a constant 30fps, so it looks choppy compared to other games I've recently purchased. I've also seen texture issues in the graveyard at Marlind...flashing textures loading as solid colors. Graphic settings are limited, and V-Sync literally does nothing. In game, at least they let you customize your players look.
There is nice stereo separation, and atmosphere awareness. When you are in an area that is supposed to be spooky, they do a good job making it feel that way. The same goes for a lively area. You'll hear nearby voices in busy markets and water sounds when you are close to rushing water. There is no lag or sounds that seem particularly out of place.
Now here is where the game gets really in-depth. You have your general equipment that you'd expect to customize, but also: fashion (accessories and outfits), weapon skills, martial artes, saraphic artes, titles, support techniques (including treasure finding, money finding, snack creating, and more), battle techniques, and weapon enhancement.
Tales of Zestiria is a great RPG with fun combat. If you like anime you'll likely be into this. If you like action rpgs with combo systems you'll likely be into this. While it hurts right in the master-race to only get 30fps on my beast of a PC, it doesn't take away from how excellent the game is.

That was definitely an interesting experience. Whatever the motivation was, whether it was a true story, an exercise in self-finding, a way to process successes and failures in life, a way to deal with anxiety; it really doesn't matter. Everyone will interpret and experience this in a different way, will relate it to themselves in a different way. If anything that is the most important aspect.
Everyone is different. Everyone deals with problems, with setbacks, and with success in a different way. Some people enjoy being in the shadows, in the background, others need to be the center of attention, need to be the on the social stage of life. Some play a role, wear a mask every day, others are the way they are, and what you see is what you get. Artwork of any kind has always been a way of self-expression, and also a way to tell a story, to express oneself, a way to work out issues. Ultimately, true artworks inspire, invoke thought and creativity and speak to the audience. If something ticks those boxes (or even only one of those), then it's a piece of art.
For me personally, I can certainly relate to a good number of the aspects and events you can experience playing this. One review said that this could easily have been a YouTube video documentary; true, it could have been, but isn't that where the main difference is? When you watch a movie, a TV show, a documentary in a movie theater or on television, you're a passive observer with no real influence. Events play out, and you take them as they are. Playing a game, you at minimum get the illusion of making choices, you are an active part in the narrative, even if you follow a linear path.
In a way, this game, in one way or another, conveys at least the important insight that we can only learn and know as much about a person as that person is willing to let us know about them. It's a matter of trust that has to be earned and developed, because the more we open up, the more vulnerable we get.
I quite liked the main sentiments from the Matrix movies that apply here, too:
Ultimately I think what we should take away from this game, and perhaps as an important guide is this: Whatever you do in life, make sure it's something you (at least somewhat) enjoy, something that challenges you, something that makes your life worthwhile, and maybe even something that allows you to make a difference; even if it's only a small amount. And something else: If it feels right to take a risk, even if you logically think it might be too dangerous, perhaps you should take it once in a while.
