The Beginners Guide..
The Beginner's Guide is a narrative video game from Davey Wreden (the creator of The Stanley Parable), it doesn't last more than an hour and a half and that is with exploring everything in decent detail.
I can honestly say, out of all the games I've played through in my time, very few, if any have left me feeling so shaken, so deep in thought, so empty and so full of questions. This beautiful piece of art, resonated with me so strongly, and though I may say this quite a bit, you need to experience this game. Do not look through screenshots, do not watch the trailer, just buy it and experience it. Keep in mind it doesn't have any great overall objectives, no real goals, it just requires you to walk, look, listen and open your mind.
: At the end of the day, this is not something you can really explain as it will feel different for each person who plays it. It's really a game about projection. You see and feel what you want to in a lot of things.
The main premise of it, however, is the former Stanly Parable creator befriends this person named Coda, someone who he takes such a deep interest in because of the games he makes. The narrator explains how he feels about each of his creations, his interpretations and so on. This seems to be piecing the puzzle of this Coda character together, about what they are dealing with.. He goes on to share his work to get external opinions for Coda and this leads you further down the rabbit hole or realisations.
That is all I will say with regards to story.
: One thing I honestly enjoyed so much is the different styles in which this Coda character uses. How his style changes and progresses. Sometimes getting so much more into detail. It really feels like you can see and feel his progress in making games. From very stock standard Counter Strike like maps, to quite quaint and detailed sceneries. They do not disappoint at all, and it's nicely optimised to run on even the lowest quality of computer.

This is not a game for everyone. In many ways, it's not much of a game. You really can't die and won't fail. (In the rare instances you can fail, you get infinite tries). It's more of an interactive story. You experience a number of games created by a person name Coda and try to figure out what's going on in the head of this strange game developer. That's the main premise. That said, it's brilliantly well-done, and I suspect many people will reflect on it and see themselves in it one way or another. I'm glad I played it. I imagine people will be comparing to the Stanley Parable. I doubt this has anywhere near the replay value. The game does have a conclusion of sorts, and I think it speaks for itself. If you don't like "non-game" games, then this probably isn't for you. If you like more artsy/experimental stuff, I'd strongly encourage you to give it a try at least.

This program will not make you an instant game developer. It has a lot of built in functionality and a lot of great features, but to make something good you're going to need some artistic capability (for character/object/sprite design), a lot of patience, and a willingness to learn. Even with such a great toolset, game development isn't easy.
That being said, RPG Maker takes a lot of the more tedious aspects out of development. You don't have to do much coding (but you will probably need to pick up a little bit of Ruby to customize your game), you don't need to make many common sound effects (they provide rainy noises, dungeon echoes, etc), and you can playtest at any time (which is insanely useful for bug hunting).
If you're serious about developing something then give this a shot. If you're just going to try it for a few days, get frustrated, and quit, then don't bother. You're going to have to spend dozens of hours on anything you make with this, even with the headstart it gives you.

I remember buying this one from a Humble Weekly bundle a while back, even paying extra to get a special tileset to make cyberpunk games out of. It might have been worth the around $7 that I payed for it, but definitely not the $69.99 they're asking for it. Here's why:
1) The resolution is locked at 640x480. This isn't really that big of a crime when you think about it, since 640x480 is a very comfy resolution for an RPG and a really large resolution would mean that too many tiles would be displayed on screen at once, but what makes this bad is that you can't go fullscreen in a way that's not stupid, which ruins immersion a little bit but more importantly prevents upscaling on larger monitors, meaning that people with really large native resolutions might be stuck on what is basically a postage stamp to them.
2) The tiles are locked at 32x32. If you just wanted to make your original game work around smaller tiles for whatever reason, tough luck!
3) I tried and couldn't find a way to make it so that whenever you start a new project, they don't already make half the game for you and fill your attacks and items databases with prefabs. Manually deleting all the pre-made items and attacks every time is annoying. It's a good feature for people that would make fantasy-themed RPGs, but if you wanted to make something else then deleting these large amounts of pre-made things every time is tedious.
4) Everything that this thing does, GameMaker can do better, and for free. In GameMaker, you can make the resolution or tile sizes be anything you want. Of course, there's more coding involved when using GameMaker, but considering how much Ruby scripting you'll have to do in RPG Maker to do anything that would make your RPG a bit unique in terms of features, this isn't really a problem.
Overall, just go with GameMaker for making your RPGs. There's slightly more to learn, but consider how much more the FREE edition does than the $69.99 RPG Maker.

I am not a new player of Trackmania, a long time ago I had played United Forever and I was absolutely found of this game.
Recently, I just heard that there was a new Trackmania which was going to be released, I hadn't heared about Turbo and I was so happy to be able to replay a serie that I thought was dead.
So yeah I really enjoyed this game and I'm gonna make a review of what my experience was like :
So, first, I'm tired of these peoples complaining "The interface sucks, it's ugly as hell" . This argument is just false because this is just a question about personal tastes. They are also complaining about the fact that it is difficult to understand, where I do not agree simply because I hadn't any problems understanding it.
Second, the difficulty, yeah, I agree the game is really easy until red tracks, but I do not think it is that bad, It makes the game way better for new players because it gives them the time to adapt to the controls until the finally get to the hard tracks. So the difficulty curve should need a higher difficulty overall, I totally agree on that point but it makes the game good for newcomers, which is why I think it is good enough.
Third, the editor, I absolutely need to find a way to play united again because I hear that Lagoon's editor is not as good as the one from United, but from what I remember, the editor was really good in united but I can't see in any ways why it is better than the one in Lagoon. The one in Lagoon even has mixmapping and airmapping which are both awesome features that weren't in United Forever.
Fourth, the game lacks community. YEAAH, cannot say anything against that, it is rare to find a server with at least one person in. So yeah :| Lagoon definitely lacks a community
Fifth, Lack of split screen, no, the game doesn't lack split screen, it just lacks the campaign maps, you can still play on your own maps. Because of the kind of recent Maniaplanet 4 update, the campaign tracks are lacking in splitscreen, so, yeah, huge bad fact about the game, but It's not like you can't play split screen, you can still play in your own maps, wich I loved to show to my friends.
So yeah I hoped this review helped you and I really do hope you will enjoy the game

Been hearing about this Trackmania series for years, and finally decided to check it out.
The game, at its heart, is a series of time trials on short courses, with very appealing visuals, sounds, and physics. I love how it strips away all the usual racing game elements - like story, dialogue, car choices, tuning, etc. It's just a pure racing experience, which is a joy to play.
However, Trackmania 2 Lagoon is one part of a larger game "system" called Maniaplanet, which is very confusing at first - though once you wrap your mind around it, it all kind of makes sense.
Besides Lagoon, there are a number of other racing environments, such as Stadium, Canyon, and Valley - each of which you need to buy separately - bu they're all kind of mixed together on Maniaplanet. There's also a first-person shooting game system mixed in as well.
I started off with the demo, which I eventually discovered was a free version of all the games, where you can only play one "channel" at a time. But, this means you can play Trackmania for free as long as you want, but just one channel at a time. So you may need to wait awhile before Lagoon comes up.
You can design your own courses. And there are public server where you can race online with others on a series of player-designed courses. The more I play, the more I am discovering about this whole system.
But anyway, just the solo time trial mode in Lagoon is well worth the price.
Don't let all the complications of the interface keep you away... the game itself is pure addictive video game pleasure.

I purchased this game during a sale for seven dollars, and I can say wholeheartedly that it was worth every penny. I knew little about the game, and merely read the description which honestly described my dream game. I am a big fan of strategy games, and European history, and this game effectively allows you to run your own medieval settlement and watch it grow into a sprawling city. The game is much more realistic than its peers: having random disasters (plagues, crop failure, famine, fire and more) and many small details making the game really stand out. The game is difficult to master, yet the failures and experienced had in the beginning make the eventual mastering of the game more satisfying. The game has more crops and buildings than other RTS city-building games that I've played (Tropico, AOE, Towns), and more professions as well. So far I've not gotten a settlement with more than sixty people, but I'm still learning the game. I recommend this game to all strategy game enthusiasts like myself.

You know, Banished could be a great game, could be...
Banished is a city building game where you go to the most basest needs of your people, food, shelter, and happiness. You build up from a colony of about 6 families. They reproduce with no ability to explore the family trees or relationships which is kind of a missed point, it's always more fun to explore the founders of your town, and build up a back story for the families if you feel particularly literate. But it's really not a deal breaker, just a seemingly small addition to the gameplay that could open up alot more game time for some people.
The basics are simple, you start with a cart/barn/small town depending on the difficulty level and proceed to build up your own banished colony. You have to start with getting these families gathering some basic resources Wood, Stone, and Iron. You do this by zoning resources to gather and people that are available to work will start to chop trees and mine rocks after processing the request with their own free will, which works great right at the start here. Once you got that you start to build houses to shelter your families.
This is where the game turns to hell, now that you built six houses for your six families, they start to stock the houses up with food, and this is where you made your mistake. Because they will start to pile as much as the first house will hold, then the second house, then the third house, by the fourth or fifth house the starting cart is out of food. No, it's not an issue of the cart not having enough food. It's just that the arbitrarily picked first families in houses have a stock of food in their house that they just aren't willing to share, so families four, five, and six starve to death.
So, let's try that again, except this time, screw giving them shelter, we need to get some food production going heavy before we can trust them to share food, but by the time you actually get enough resources and time to build about two fisheries, a barn, and 3 houses, winter comes and kills all the unlucky souls without firewood. And because we were busy making sure we had enough food to stop the greedy morons from hoarding it in their house and not sharing, we forgot to get a woodcutter to make firewood so by the end of winter you're lucky to have the hoarders survive.
Ok, again, THIS time getting a forester, woodcutter, fishery, and six houses up, gets that woodcutter built right as winter is starting and LUCKILY we can make it. Cool, we're going along great, and because we really didn't need all six houses to house the people we had the families grow well inot the base set of housing without ever needing more. And I mean that, cause my fishery, gathering hut, and hunter's lodge were not enough to sustain the village. The Foresters and Woodcutters are doing fine, but I look over and see the food low Icon floating over one of the houses. I just figured it was a minor issue cause "hey the other houses have plenty of food, so it has to be a fluke!" I ran out of tools before I could get a blacksmith built, waiting on stone to finish getting collected.
But this is how stupid these colonists are! The Foresters and Woodcutter hoarded all the food in their house, then all the gatherers and fishers died of starvation, while these idiots were eating fine. So now the town had nobody to get food, I informed my miners to switch out of the mine to go fish, but wouldn't you know it, they pathed around for about an hour and died of starvation too, with food in their own house. Karma kicked in and almost immediately dropped a tree on two of the foresters.
The worst part, you can't directly tell a particular colonist what to do, you have to watch them fail at figuring out what they should be doing, watching them say "I'm starving to death, but I'll walk past the food in my house to put down this one Iron I'm holding, then go stand at the dock and die of starvation."
It's just bad game design, you've got to have a superb AI system that has that self preservation of "Shoot this family ain't sharing their food with me? SCREW THEM I'M GONNA STEAL IT THEN" Or you have to give me control of things like how much food they're allowed to hold in their house, telling a unit to stop what they're doing to go eat, or tell them to stop walking to the cart when there's a barn full of food right here.
This game is essentially a heap of missed potential, a game with free will (which in itself not a bad thing) but is plagued with AI issues, and even pathing mistakes, however the pathing tends to do pretty well for itself. Ultimately it's a really fun Idea, and somewhat fun to tinker with. But I will not recommend this game, due to a lack of logic (I start with a cart of potatoes but I can't grow them? I have to buy potato seeds?) lack of sense (these colonists were clearly banished because they're idiots) and lack of gameplay, aside from desiging your old style colonies, with a FTL Inspired, unfair series of events, but not even in a fun way. I never felt that my colony died because of my poor planning, I usually felt that my colonists didn't have the will to live from the onset.
Stay away cause it will make your heart ache for a game that could have been something special, but you will only find it to be filled with a different kind of special.

In short, A Hat in Time is a short jump back into the feeling of playing a collectathon back in the days of yore. It truly captures the essence of the whimsical fun of the genre when it was in its hayday, and while the collecting aspect is short and sweet, it is more than worth the wait for those who followed its development, and in the 15 hours it took me to get all the hourglasses, it has earned a spot as one of my favorite games of all time.
To briefly cover what the game is- not that anyone bothering to read this doesn't know the basics, its a game I would say is most similar mechanically to something like Mario Galaxy- there's a few levels, you pick which hourglass you're going going after in that mission, and you go get it, though they constantly mix the forumla around a little for each level. In some, you'll run over a fairly open and large level searching for loose objectives, more like Donkey Kong 64, for example, while in others  you follow the simple mission structure of a game like Mario Galaxy. Beyond collecting the 40 hourglasses- the main collectable of the game- there's also yarn to find in hidden corners of each world for making hats, but not much else, and green orbs you use to buy little badges- basically, interchangable powerups.
First, the good. The game is abundant with charm and characters that are the perfect amount of over-the-top, the music is top-notch, and while I found the level design a little hit-or-miss with me personally, I never stopped having a great time. The gameplay is smooth, fluid, and well animated. The graphics strike a particular chord with me, and each world tends to mix it up enough to keep the visuals interesting and diverse. While I might just be a huge softie, I was surprised to say I felt geniune emotion throughout- a childish joy through most of the game, getting teary eyed at a few times near the end, and one mission in particular that spooked me pretty darn good from the visuals and sound design alone. I could gush for quite some time, but the short of it is, the game is just pure fun- the visuals are fun, the sound design is fun, the music is fun, and the characters are just fun, and the game rarely tries to be anything else. It knows exactly what it wants to do and hits the target dead on at almost every single point.
That being said, I do want to mention a few faults of the game. The main secondary collectable, yarn, is used exclusively for hats, but there's a very limited number of hats in the game, yet yarn is fairly abundant. While I did a fairly thorough job of searching each level, I never felt I was ever NEEDED to. It felt excessive and just a little tacked on. By the end of the game, I had just under 20 extra yarn never used for anything, and collecting it had long since started feeling pointless, especially as the game doesn't track this collectable in any way to scratch that completionist itch of getting that pretty little "100% Complete" written on you game file. That being said, it doesn't detract from the game much, but for those of you who, like me, search every inch of every world and expect some reward for doing so, you'll find yourself wanting. That being said, that's the only thing I could complain about- a small, easilly ignored blemish, besides a small number of visual hiccups I experinced early on that never really detracted from the game in any real way, at least not in my experience.
Over all, A Hat in Time truly feels like the best version of the collectathons we all remember through our rose-tinted childhood glasses- it takes all the good from those and mixes it well with the polish we expect of a modern game. It's short, but its incredibly sweet, and filled with an undeniable charm I doubt many can resist, and perhaps most importantly, it is a game that knows exactly what it wanted to be, and hit the nail squarely on the head. It is absolutely one of my favorite games of all time, and it was well worth the wait.

I remember buying this one from a Humble Weekly bundle a while back, even paying extra to get a special tileset to make cyberpunk games out of. It might have been worth the around $7 that I payed for it, but definitely not the $69.99 they're asking for it. Here's why:
1) The resolution is locked at 640x480. This isn't really that big of a crime when you think about it, since 640x480 is a very comfy resolution for an RPG and a really large resolution would mean that too many tiles would be displayed on screen at once, but what makes this bad is that you can't go fullscreen in a way that's not stupid, which ruins immersion a little bit but more importantly prevents upscaling on larger monitors, meaning that people with really large native resolutions might be stuck on what is basically a postage stamp to them.
2) The tiles are locked at 32x32. If you just wanted to make your original game work around smaller tiles for whatever reason, tough luck!
3) I tried and couldn't find a way to make it so that whenever you start a new project, they don't already make half the game for you and fill your attacks and items databases with prefabs. Manually deleting all the pre-made items and attacks every time is annoying. It's a good feature for people that would make fantasy-themed RPGs, but if you wanted to make something else then deleting these large amounts of pre-made things every time is tedious.
4) Everything that this thing does, GameMaker can do better, and for free. In GameMaker, you can make the resolution or tile sizes be anything you want. Of course, there's more coding involved when using GameMaker, but considering how much Ruby scripting you'll have to do in RPG Maker to do anything that would make your RPG a bit unique in terms of features, this isn't really a problem.
Overall, just go with GameMaker for making your RPGs. There's slightly more to learn, but consider how much more the FREE edition does than the $69.99 RPG Maker.

Awesome game if it is the first Total War game you played that involved ranged firearms.
I have played Rome Total War and got a bit bored of the conventional hand-to-hand, compact method of combat. So I bought Napoleon Total War and was not left unimpressed.
The camera movement is astounding and the gameplay is very diverse and challenging (both campaign and multiplayer).
You will have to adapt to different strategies and means of movement, as well as positioning of your troops.
You will be forced to make effective decisions and strategies in order to ensure your success and victory over the enemy (tip: outflanking your opposition is an INTEGRAL part of the game).
As with the visuals it is AMAZING. The environment truly gives you that 'Napoleon' ambience (if you know what I'm saying) to your battles. With the soundtrack it's not as good as the music in RTW, but the fife and drums that soldiers march into battle listening to truly gives battles a completely different and unique atmosphere (tip: 'FN+DEL' or 'Insert' allows you to go on the selected unit's first person view so that you can experience what it looks and sounds like).
Overall, it's an absolutely breathtaking and immersive game. It places you in the shoes of both the soldier and the general controlling the battle. I highly recommend it if it is your first Total War game that involves ranged fighting, or if it is your first Total War game.

After having used this software for over a hundred hours, the best piece of advice I can offer anyone is to scale your expectations back - and I mean way, WAY back. No words can describe how disappointed I am with RPG Maker after spending countless hours watching tutorials, reading guides, experimenting with concepts, editing with GIMP, all to create nothing useful or something just barely functional. I simply did not realize how limited the software was. Even after I discovered what it could do (or more accurately, could not do) I scaled back my expectations constantly only to hit a roadblock again and again. By far my biggest critique of the software is the bare-bones nature: you can make a Final Fantasy game with it, and by that I mean the FIRST Final Fantasy, aka the one that is probably older than you are. The mechanics are all at least 25 years old, resulting in:
-No in-house method of creating a game map (as in, a reference map you can press a button to show where you are in the world)
-No in-house method of editing Sprites or Tiles (I had to use GIMP software for that)
-a mystifyingly limited number of tiles you can use to build a map with (after using GIMP to put together a custom tile set, I exported it to the game only to discover i could only use a fraction of the tile set because Enterbrain imposes a limit on tile sheet sizes…when I discovered that, I swear a small part of me died.)
-Needlessly complicated methods to get around the tile limit (like parallax mapping and some outside scripts)
-No in-house clock
-Way, way too heavy reliance on outside scripting to do even the most basic of things that RPG's have already been using for decades.
-Arbitrarily small limits on things such as stats or item amounts (true, you may not use every slot to create items, but why take the chance to limit the developer? Go ahead and set the limits sky-high, it is not that hard)
Think of an RPG, any RPG: what mechanics did you like about it? chances are, RPG Maker cannot do that. Did you like the Psynergy or Djinni system of Golden Sun? Too Bad. Did you want to make a game with multiple skills in it to level up without the use of scripts, as per Runescape or the Elder Scrolls? Nope. Did you hope to implement a monster capture system like Pokemon? Not Happening. Did you like the flashy Summons from the early Final Fantasy games this software is failing to live up to? Not a chance. Do you like to actually watch your characters on the battle screen fighting the enemy like in…almost every RPG ever made? Without scripts, you will be stuck in a soulless first person mode and will never see your characters sprites in battle. Are you awed when your enemies use your own nuclear attacks against you, or unleash their own unique abilities to show you that you are not the only person with show-stopping special effects? Enemy sprites are static and use utterly no animation when they attack. Want to change the default walking or running speed?... Actually, I still have not found a script that could let me do that.
This software may be useful for veteran programmers, but for those new to the field, stay far, far away. Now, admittedly the community has made incredible scripts that dramatically improve the experience, but fans had to do that, not the developer. I might even go so far as to say that I think some of the fans put more effort into improving RPG Maker than Enterbrain itself did actually making it. Ultimately, I cannot recommend RPG Maker VX Ace to anyone.
TL;DR
Do not buy (or at least wait for a sale), you will be disappointed.
3/10

Picture yourself in a winter wonderland with nothing but some torn up winter clothes and some flares. You begin looking for shelter. You find a lakeside village. While avoiding the wolves, you find a ton of food, a knife, new clothes, tools, water, and firewood. Now you leave the village to get away from the wolves. You notice a cabin on an island in the middle of the lake, so you head for it stopping at little ice fishing huts on your way there. Then a blizzard hits. You take shelter in the nearest fishing hut. You set up camp in there. Fire up the furnace, place down your nap sack, and begin fishing. 1 day passes. Everything is alright. 2 days pass. Your water is getting low but you can always boil snow. Day 4... no more wood. You begin searching but your food and water supply can't keep up with you. Your clothes are now rags... Day 5... a blizzard hits but you never see it because you don't wake up...
That's the furthest I've made it... Good luck and btw start practicing your speed mouse clicking. The faster you can click the less likely you are to die from a wolf attack. I've survived wolves with only 1% condition... yeah this game is not your average survival game. It's intense. It gets your heart pounding. "Do I have enough water? Food? Wood? Clothes? AHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHH!" Just don't get comfortable cause that's when you die from dehydration or the freezing cold.

Having played a good few hours of Banished so far, I've got to say: this is a good game. Not great, but good. Overall, my impression is that it's still very much a work in progress.
Banished draws you in and easily sucks away hours of your life as you concern yourself with keeping your villagers alive and building them a stable and, above all, sustainable home. There is a real sense of accomplishment in transforming three families and a cartload of basic supplies into a thriving community of hundreds of villagers.
However, a few times now I have got to the point where it seems I have achieved all I can in the game. Others who have played Banished might recognise it; you have built up most of the viable land on the map, stabilised your population, and backed it all up with a steady supply of food and resources. What is there left to do? Apart from sitting behind your monitor and appreciating all that you've built, honestly, not much...
Once you have built all the 'civic' buildings (which can occur relatively early on) there is little left to achieve besides marginally increasing the population. That gets old rather quickly. There is the odd 'disaster' which occurs, but there is little you can do to directly combat those. Instead, you simply wait for them to run their course and rebuild, if necessary.
I feel Banished is crying out for a deeper level of complexity in order to increase its replay value. Building up larger communities should come with the societal problems which typically arise from them. I once saw one of my villagers met his end because he was "stabbed". An incident like that should trigger an event which leads to your society choosing its own justice system. And why don't the citizens protest after a stonecutter has been crushed by a rock for the umpteenth time? Those feel like missed opportunities to me.
In short, I feel that with a game like this you should be able to eventually control its society and politics a bit more to give each settlement its own 'flavour'. I'll be keeping a keen eye on the future development of this game in the hope something like that will be added.

Combining three of my most favourite things, film noir, jazz and occultism, Blues and Bullets got me hooked from the very first scene.
On first glance, this noir thriller seems like any of those episodic adventure games, and gameplay-wise, it doesn't stand out of similar titles. You control Eliot Ness, hardboiled detective by the book, in a very limited game world full of invisible walls and hotspots usually highlighted already from a large distance. From time to time you get to make your way through simple rail shooter passages and a very well presented hunting for hints at a crime scene. But Blues and Bullets doen't shine with it's gameplay (seriously, Eliot's jogging animation is killing me), but with it's sin-city-esque art style, the authentic voice acting, the melancholic and groovy music and it's (sometimes not) lovable characters, the movie-game manages to captivate it's audience. And yes, Blues and Bullets should be seen as a movie, as the game is fairly simple and consists mostly of cutscenes. Keeping that in mind, you will have a good, while short, time with this gripping story of a laconic detective slowly getting involved in the bizzarre doings of a mysterious sect.

An incredibly fun, addictive, competitive, well-balanced, and surprisingly deep game. My family is playing it constantly, every day. I also find it quite fun to play through co-op levels as a solo player.
One word of warning: the game is a bit pricey just by itself, but to really get the most out of it you'll very likely want the expansion. The expansion's features are fully integrated into the core game, but if  you try to use them it'll tell you you have to buy the DLC. :-p
Without the expansion, you can only play co-op with 2 players, each of whom has a fixed number of lives. The expansion adds co-op levels for up to 4 players, but there's no lives store - if a player dies, another player has to revive him, and if all players are dead the game's over (continuing is possible). These worlds can also be played solo mode with fixed lives, and unlike the core game worlds you can continue if you die on a particular level.
The versus mode is quite fun, and does a great job of balancing skill levels without dampening the fun (if you're winning, you get fewer arrows, and if you're way behind you start with a shield). The number of interesting outcomes for a battle seems quite high, and I find myself saving replay GIFs regularly. Neat little details abound, such as the way you can knock someone's hood or hat off if your arrow merely brushes through their hair instead of hitting them squarely. Occasionally some odd tweak will appear unexpectedly in a co-op level, and some of these lead to unlockable new characters you can play as.

TL:DR, Good game, lacking content but that should change with the stretch goals. If your a fan of collectathons, I'd recommend heavily.
I love this game. I always have liked games like Super Mario 64 and Super Mario Sunshine and this game feels just like those. It is charming, it is easy to jump into, the characters are likable, and it's overall a really good game. However, there are several issues I see with the game though too.
As of now, I have collected all of the time pieces (this games equivalent of stars) in around 16 hours and while there is some other collectables that I have not gotten yet (some hat styles), the game feels too short. The time I did spend in Hat in Time was really good, I was laughing at parts and it has some really good characters, but that doesn't cover up that it felt lacking in content at times. Another area where the world falls a bit flat is the optimization. While my computer isn't the best (i7, 8GB of RAM and integrated graphics), some parts I had frames below 10 with all the settings down completely. While I dont expect this game to be optimized perfectly, some parts just felt like they could be cleaner.
However, these downsides don't take away from what this game currently is and what will soon come to it. Co-op mode, a 6th and 7th chapter, new game+ are all things that are coming soon and I am looking forward to it. The voice acting, which in most games I can't stand, was good and helped give a better understanding to some of the characters. While there aren't that many characters, all of them are well done. The snatcher, the character introduced in Chapter 3, is easily one of my favourite characters in games in general.
Overall, the game has plenty of potential, but as of now it feels lacking. As a fan of these types of games, A Hat in Time is a great and I would recommend it to anyone who is interested in platformers or collectathons.

-The sensitivity does not have many options

Other than these small gripes, this game is perfect for people who are skilled in FPS games and want to play casually while also perfect for people who want to play more competitively and improve their skill.

-Better customization for crosshair and HUD
-Voice chat (it might be there and i just havent found it yet ¯\_(ツ)_/¯)

TL;DR: Its a good game for casuals and competitive people and i see a long lasting future for this game.

This is an enjoyable RPG, although the main quest storyline leaves something to be desired. It leaves me wondering about the logic of certain story elements and leaves me scratching my head due to a lack of information and background. But the world is filled with character's stories and information that helps scratch this itch. I like that it doesn't coddle the player, making you feel like you actually have to struggle to survive, especially near the beginning of the game.
It's also nice that it doesn't automatically tell you how to get somewhere or where you need to go on certain missions, it makes you explore and find stuff on your own (and on occasion, to the wiki--which is old school fun). It is a nice change of pace from the trend of dumbing things down to the point of sucking the life out of it). The more you explore the more you find out and the more you want to know.
Another element that is nice is the choice system. Things you do in the game have realworld impacts that change the game forever.
As gameplay progresses it does become easier and easier to "game the system" and get what you want out of it, but in a way this is good because it frees you up to focus on other game elements. At a certain point, money, ammo, and equipment are just not a problem at all and you can even spare some for quick cash if you want to. The need to loot is a little high, but this is a genre staple when it comes to gameplay. FO3 is not exception.
In my opinion mods are a must for this game in 2017. The graphics are extremely dated and certain game mechanics could use some work, but thankfully solutions to many of these issues are a few clicks away. The 2k and 4k visual overhauls make the game a beauty and really adds to the quality and playabilty, even bringing it up to some modern titles. Add in an ENB, some NPCs, maybe a bit of wasteland overhauls to bring in some sickly looking trees and other plants, etc., and this game can look great!
Don't pay attention to the fact that it says that I only have 11 hours of play time, once I started using FOSE it stopped tallying my play time in Steam (I guess it isn't as integrated into their platform as titles like Skyrim).
To this day, FO3 is still a great title and definitely worth playing.

Just Cause 2
Open World Third-person Shooter
Avalanche Studios
Square Enix
is an open world action game developed by Avalanche Studios and published by Square Enix in 2010. This is the first of many reviews to come about the latest installments of franchises that are coming back in the near future.
You play as Rico Rodriguez, one of the Agency's main operatives, as he is sent to the island of Panau to oust Panay from office, as well as track down and assassinate his old mentor, Tom Sheldon, who the Agency fears has gone rogue after disappearing during the regime change. In order to find Sheldon, Rico allies himself with the three dominant criminal gangs on the island: the Roaches, an organized crime syndicate, the Reapers, an insurgent Socialist militia and the Ular Boys, an ultranationalist rebel group that espouses traditionalism and opposes foreign influence.
The story is over-the-top and the dialogue is really cheesy. The story serves only to justify you being a terrorist who destroys power plants, ventilation systems, dams, military bases and many more objects. Save for a few moments in the 7 Story Missions, it is not memorable.
Even though it has been 5 years since the game was first released, it still looks damn great on PC: the island is colourful, the explosions are vibrant, the draw distance is long and the water feels realistic. The only things that have always been the problem with the game are the facial textures and animations. Other than that, you will have a gorgeous experience that will run at 60fps even on a toaster.
The goal is to cause as much chaos as you can by destroying military facilities and everything related to that. Right from the get-go you can explore the 400 square miles of Panau, discovering the 368 locations, engaging in high-speed chases by water, plane or car, hijacking enemy vehicles to crash into oil rigs... There is a lot of variety in what you can do and how.
The big game changer is the grappling hook, which can be used to gain speed while using your unlimited parachutes, to pull enemies from ledges, to attach a speeding vehicle to the ground so that it flies in the air, to attach an enemy to the ceiling and turning him into a human piñata, and so on. You can also carry three weapons (two sidearms, one big gun) and both grenades and sticky bombs.
There is the black market, which can be used to order and upgrade weapons and vehicles, or as a way to fast travel. But I strongly recommend that, because each time that you go from one place to the other, you are bound to find an hidden collectible, a new location, or a new badass vehicle that you hadn't tried already.
The side activities that you complete for the gangs are very similar to one another, and usually consist of escorting someone, finding an object in a base or destroying a base or two. There are also races that are varied and very fun to play.
The game is a ton of fun, and you won't regret the time you'll spend with it.
The game tends to be very challenging even on the easiest settings, thanks to strong and numerous enemies that will pursue you, as well as an unforgiving checkpoint system in the missions.
The soundtrack is hugely underrated, but really strong and energizing, while the voice acting is one of the cheesiest since the original Resident Evil. But since it seems like they made that on purpose, I'll let it slide.
The sound effects are great, with clear distinctions from one gun to the other, and with some hugely satisfying explosions.
A huge map, tons of collectibles, multiple missions and 50 Steam achievements are bound to make you play this game for a long time to come, especially if you are waiting for Just Cause 3's release.
Overall, this is a phenomenal game to play, with an amazing open world, fluid and varied combat, multiple collectibles, strong soundtrack and beautiful vistas. This is a game that I love, and I strongly recommend buying to everyone who loves action games. Glory to Baby Panay!

I haven't even made a complete game with this, but it's still very intuitive and simple for beginners.
It may be a bit expensive for it's asking price, but it's a simple RPG builder that is actually quite flexible. The games you make with it all follow the same engine unless you want to tweak the script to make your game a bit more different. I highly suggest you learn how to do so if you want to make a more unique game.
Map building is fairly easy, and it's also quite easy to set up events. Although it is a long process, modifying and changing the database is pretty essential to making your game and it's set-up is pretty easy. It's interface is very simple and intuitive, making it easy for non-programers to understand and use.
RPG Maker isn't entirely flexible beyond Role-Playing games, and while people have made commercial games out of it, it's definately not the best tool to get the job done. RPG Maker VX Ace is also NOT on the Mac, as it's code was mainly built for Windows. Some of the DLC packs are also too expensive for their asking price and is much more worth getting it on sale, or just building your own assets from scratch (If you have that talent).
But add in trading cards, Steam Workshop support and a large seperate online forum with a cool community, and you've got a software that's worth owning if you ever wanted to build a RPG game.

Five Nights at Freddy's is a first person scare game that puts you in the position of a night watchman forced to stay alive five nights in danger of animatronic plush characters walking around. Your job is to survive from midnight to 6 AM.Its not a horrifying game, but the scares are done through the building tension of knowing the animatronics are out to get you and seeing where they are.
The gameplay is simple, you are literally stuck in your one screen office, you can look left and right, when you point your mouse down, a series of monitor comes up that lets you look at one camera at a time. You click each camera individually and you'll see areas of the pizza place and where the animatronics are.
There are two blind spots and those are directly to the left and right of your office, so there are two buttons. One button is for light to check what's directly outside your door. The other is the door button for when something is right outside your door! You have a door and a light on each side. You can't see both doors at the same time, which can result in jump scares.
So why not just lock the doors and giggle at the fluffies trying to get in? The challenge to this game is that each night starts you at 100% power. Every moment drains your power slowly, every time you look at the monitor drains your power. When you turn on a light, that is more power too. Plus, the doors are magnetic, so using them really drains your power. Once you are out of power, everything turns dark and well its virtually game over.
As the nights go on, there will be different animatronic characters you will be warned about. You will get phone calls at the start of every night explaining things. How certain animatronics will act, such as the fox will run at you if you don't check your cameras.
For $5 it is a good diversion, even if the game is pretty dumb feature wise. New game or continue. No options, but at least you get to continue at the day you failed. A big plus is that the same night can still feel different. So there is a lot of replay, but keep in mind it is a quick game that is one screen with cameras in rooms. I bought it in a $2 bundle, you can too.

Tales of Zestiria is a classic JRPG. It reminds me of JRPG titles such as Dragon Quest and Final Fantasy. On top of the classic JRPG components, Tales of Zestiria added some new elements, such as narratives, customization, and a polished battle system.
Story: The story moves at a pretty nice pace and keeps you engaged. A lot of characters interaction, as well as dynamic events happening in the world around you.
Music: Beautiful BGM. The Japanese voice acting is great as well.
Art style: Great designs. A lot of details on the characters and the surrounding world.
Battle system: The battle system feels a bit awkward at first, and may take some time to get used to. Overall, the battle system keeps the battle at a fast pace with nice flashy effects.
One downside though is that the battles feel a little bit too easy; most of the battles can be won by smashing the buttons. For that reason, I really recommend setting the difficulty to high when you're comfortable.
TL:DR: Great story, music, characters, and polished battle system. However the gameplay is not very challenging. If you are a hardcore RPG fan, you may be disappointed by the easiness of the game. That being said, I still really enjoy my time playing Tales of Zestiria; and I would definitely recommend it.
A good pick-up for any JRPG fan. It is also a good entry title for people new and trying to get into JRPG. However, don't get it if you're looking for a challenging hardcore RPG experience.

Get this game right now if you like survival games, you will definitely get your money's worth at full price and it often goes on sale if you're cheap. I myself love survivals a lot and have had this game for a while. It can be a bit challenging, but half the fun with any survival game is that it challenges you.
+ Really beautiful art style. Amazing looking for how simple it is.
+ Being able to survive for a long time has a really rewarding feeling that is hard to get in many other survival games.
+ Game is very stable despite being an EA title. I honestly don't recall running into a single bug and it doesn't require a top notch PC to run.
+ 3 difficulty levels have been added, no longer are you forced into one difficulty.
+ Lots to explore if you want to. Quite a large world, but you don't have to play all areas if you don't want to, though I'd say that's half the fun. More maps coming as well.
+ Steam workshop allows for player made language packs.
- Can be very easy to get lost if you're not 100% familiar with the map you're playing on.
- Sometimes you get really crappy spawn luck and you either have to try to deal with it or start over. This is pretty much not an issue on easiest difficulty as resources are so common and wildlife doesn't attack.
- No tutorial yet, so some things can be sort of confusing at first.
- No customization at all, which is a con for me since I do love customizing things.
- When you die, it's over, you have to begin anew.
= Very little music, which could be good or bad depending on the person playing. I don't mind it so much, it helps to hear stuff around you.
= Sometimes the sound effects are a bit irritating because of the repetitiveness, but overall they're not too bad.
= I'm not a big fan of the inventory/conditions/crafting interfaces, but they're functional.
= The environment can be very cruel, even on easiest difficulty. This can be a big con for people new to survivals and not good at managing themselves in-game. To me it's just part of the game, though, so at worst this is a neutral point for me.
= Map setup doesn't change each play through, other than actual items you pick up (though some locations have exclusive or almost guaranteed spawns so they need to be checked for certain items). This can be both good and bad because it makes the maps predictable once you're used to them, which hurts replayability a little, but also allows replays to go smoother.
= No story mode for the moment, but that is in development.
= Development has been a bit slow lately, but it's not a huge team and there's a lot to do in the game in it's current state, so I would still argue it's still a worthwhile buy.
---

It's a great local multiplayer game. One of those 'easy to learn, hard to master' type deals. The mechanics are solid, it controls well, and once everybody is familiar with it you can have some incredibly intense and fun games with your buddies. Luck plays a big part early on, but once you get the hang of it, your deaths are very rarely anybody else's fault but your own.
At its best the game is satisfyingly choreographic - players leap and grapple from ledge to ledge, shots collide mid-air, arrows can be dodged (and caught mid-air) with the right timing, corpses are pinned to walls, and the instant replay at the end of each round allows you to enjoy the sheer frenzy of what just happened at your leisure.
Look up some multiplayer gameplay videos for the game on YouTube, those are going to be the best gauge of whether or not you're going to enjoy what's on offer here.
Ignore the reviews complaining that the single player isn't strong. This is a multiplayer game. If you bought it for the single player, it's your own fault that you're not enjoying it. It's a bonus there's even a solo mode included in the game.

Towerfall is one of the local multiplayer indie games that I've ever played. I have seen veteran gamers and people who don't play games both get hooked on Towerfall after playing just a few rounds. It is that accessible and easy to get into. But that's not to say that it's easy - it'll take countless hours of gameplay to understand the subtle tactics which will allow you to compete at high levels of play.
The art style and presentation of the game is beautiful and nostalgic to anyone who grew up with games from the SNES era in the 1990's. There is no online multiplayer but the developer has explained why many times: the game is too fast to facilitate satisfying and fair online gameplay. With that said, you will want to be playing this with friends locally because that's the way that it's meant to be played.
Recent updates to Towerfall have brought so much value to the game. I recommend getting the Dark World expansion pack, even more so now that it adds Steam Workshop support. Not only is there a whole new world of user-generated Towerfall content to enjoy, but the way that all of this new content is integrated into the game is brilliant.
If I could only have one local multiplayer game on Steam, I would probably choose Towerfall. Get some friends together and play Towerfall.

This review concerns Episode 1. For Episode 2 review, see here:
In a world where you can find hotels in the sky and mob bosses in submarines..., well, eeer, let me rephrase that. In a world where Eliott Ness stepped down as a cop and opened a diner, he's contacted by an old friend to help him to find a member of his family. But it seems that the clues are pointing you towards something more darker than it seems...
The game is an episodic one, so only the first is released now and setting the story. The opening is showing children captive of a strange sect/cult/maniac. You're taking the control of a little girl first before switching to Ness. Even if for now, the plot needs more explanation (because it's the first episode), you're directly thrown into that dark world and waiting for more after that cliffhanger.
And the gameplay is similar to Telltale: you choose your answer, you make decisions that will influence the story (though I'm waiting for the rest of the episodes, because I've chosen to be the gentle and helping player and not the bitter or bad one). You have also some Quicktime Events, though they're not the core of the gameplay.
But contrary to any Walking Dead or The Wolf is Among Us - I don't know for the other series -, you're also having some shooting sequences (you cover, you aim, you place your crosshair on the bad guy and you shoot) in a pure rail shooter ambiance. You have also the Clue Mode and the Investigation Board when you need to find what happened earlier: you look at the clues, you find the number required in order to be thorough and you're putting the right clue in the right place on your Investigation Board (though I don't know the English name as my interface was in French).
The real strong point is probably the graphics: everything is in black and white, apart for every item that may be in red (blood, carpets, lipstick, clothes, etc etc..). Even at one moment, you get a rail shooter sequence between words that appear! Everything is made to put you into a dark ambiance. The soundtrack is also very good, very '40 - '50.
And I'm very impatient to discover the second episode. That game has a huge potential. It's really enjoyable, even if you're not in an open world. But you get hooked by everything.
Definitively a must-have!

This game was so worth it!
I got it on a whim looking for a local co-op game and found *the* local co-op game. The first night I got it, I played with one friend. Then two. Then we get all four of us playing. By the end of the night we all needed a cup of tea because we'd been screaming at the screen and each other and having a great time.
The co-op is completely customizable. It's hilarious how much you can screw with the game by dictating starting gear or setting changes. My absolute favorite is to include ghosts so that when you die, you're a ghost trying to get out other players. Also? There's three different multiplayer modes--head hunter, last man standing, and team deathmatch.
The single player is why I avoided the game at first. I'd seen a review saying that the single player was terrible. And actually, it's not bad. It can be single, or you can have your friends help you through the campaign. I couldn't imagine beating it alone because it's hard with just me and a partner, but I'm sure it's doable. There isn't a *ton* of content, but it's enough to have a good time, for sure. We're almost done with normal mode all through the campaign (on the last level of the expansion) but then we'll have to go back through on hardcore.
What really makes the levels interesting is the bosses. They're cleverly difficult and there's a different way to beat each one.
Finally, the expansion is great. It unlocks some cute aesthetic changes and adds another five or so levels of gameplay to the campaign. So whether or not it's enough content to typically warrant a $10 purchase, we wanted it so bad we bought it anyway.
All in all, it's been a great investment! It's set me on a hunt to find all the great local co-op games. This is certainly one of the best I've found.

Today, many games are received well, but few are remembered. Simply being "good" is not enough to make it as a "classic", and the telltale sign of a classic since time immemorial, is that the game starts amazing and remains amazing even as it ages. It's a quality that transcends even nostalgia.
Unreal Tournament (UT99), is one of those few "true classic" games. It's a genuine classic; among the pinnacle of shooters not only of its time, but of all FPS games ever made. The sheer versatility of the game engine, its incredible array of mods, the incredible depth and value of content that comes with just the base game...I do not exaggerate one bit when I say that nobody makes games of this quality and value anymore.
It isn't perfect, no game is, but in a game market historically plagued with style over substance design, UT99 managed to give us both in every way that matters. Single Player? LAN? Traditional net?
All available in half a dozen modes, with stellar AI support that only a tiny handful of games (let alone shooters) even attempt.
If there is any criticism I have of this game, it's that the Steam version is -NOT- the complete Game of the Year Edition, as it's missing the entire 2nd CD of content.
Much of the missing content can be found online for free as core updates or updates to mods.
(though you will be missing some Chaos UT maps; for some reason, their last version of Chaos UT99 didn't include all the maps in the GOTY edition. It's a shame because two phenomenal CTF maps are missing, and one of those also has one of best music tracks in UT:GOTYE)
Getting the game to run on newer computer systems requires only a little effort (I'm running on Win10 without issue), so barring GOG, there's no reason to not have this in your library.

I haven't even made a complete game with this, but it's still very intuitive and simple for beginners.
It may be a bit expensive for it's asking price, but it's a simple RPG builder that is actually quite flexible. The games you make with it all follow the same engine unless you want to tweak the script to make your game a bit more different. I highly suggest you learn how to do so if you want to make a more unique game.
Map building is fairly easy, and it's also quite easy to set up events. Although it is a long process, modifying and changing the database is pretty essential to making your game and it's set-up is pretty easy. It's interface is very simple and intuitive, making it easy for non-programers to understand and use.
RPG Maker isn't entirely flexible beyond Role-Playing games, and while people have made commercial games out of it, it's definately not the best tool to get the job done. RPG Maker VX Ace is also NOT on the Mac, as it's code was mainly built for Windows. Some of the DLC packs are also too expensive for their asking price and is much more worth getting it on sale, or just building your own assets from scratch (If you have that talent).
But add in trading cards, Steam Workshop support and a large seperate online forum with a cool community, and you've got a software that's worth owning if you ever wanted to build a RPG game.

VX Ace is truly an incredible program with the capability of turning your ideas into a reality. The program is simple to learn and within a few hours of learning the basic layout you can begin creating your own game and content. Like many things in life, you get what you put into it. The more hours you log, the better and more expansive your game can be. Whether your interest in VX is simply for fun, as a hobby, or you desire to create games for a living; VX Ace is a great starting point and can help teach you the ins-and-outs of game design. Trying to learn the entire program on your own can prove difficult though, (however, not impossible,) and it is recommended that you seek online tutorials or forum help. Your game can be as small or as large as you like it to be, and limitation is almost only set by your imagination and ambition. Within my second day of using VX Ace is was creating fun cut-scenes to share and show to my friends. If the idea of creating your own game appeals to you, this is a must-own product.

I'm not a fan of survival horror games, but this one is surely something.
Gameplay can be described with one sentence: "walking
in the darkness simulator".
QTEs are well placed and not frequent, although they surely looks way too simplified (they's mostly "shake you mouse not to die" type).
Screamers (yeah, there are screamers in this game, what did you expect from survival horror game?) would be predictable if they weren't so surprising almost every time. The guy who placed them this way surely did a good work.
No unneccesary pazzles, but the constant "You'll need the key to open this door"-messages are pretty annoying.
But the thing I liked the most and why I do recommend this game - it's a graphical part.
It's a little bit too dark, yes, but it's just enough gory and, well, it's surely impressive. Yeah, the part where there are guts all over the floor isn't new, we've seen enough of this in Dead Space and Quake 4, but other than that, well, let's just say this game is very atmospheric and immersive. Main characters were done very well and they're very believable.
: Immersive, interesting horror game with interesting ending, but main campaign is a little too long (DLC doesn't have this problem).
If you're fan of survival horror games and liked Manhunt, Slenderman, F.E.A.R., Dead Space and Quake 4, grab it without any doubt.

First of all, you can tell already that my play time is very limited. However, after only an hour and a half of playing (most of which was spent curled up in a corner trying to regain some piece of sanity) I feel like I have had enough of an experience to play the game (as well as the Xbox One edition, of which I've played about two hours more).
GRAPHICS
This game is beautiful. There is no other way to put it. Even running on the lowest graphical settings, the game looks fantastic. Obviously on ultra, the graphics are amazing, but even so, at the lowest settings, the game looks like three times better than Amnesia. My only gripe in the visuals, however, is that the character models look to be less tetured and dull. While yes, there are a few exceptions, it would appear that the majority of the inmates of the asylum had very minimal effort put into them. Still, what truly makes the game shine is the intense setting, where the immersive graphical settings make the game all the better. Make no mistake, this is one of the best horror environments of all time.
SOUND
As most horror games, Outlast nails the sound design to the perfect pitch. Loud screams, faint creaks, authentic audio clips, and an incredible soundtrack force players to immerse themselves just by their ears. I would never tell anyone to turn off the sound, as it is indefinitely the best part of the game.
GAMEPLAY
Surprising to me was that this game plays like a modern FPS reminiscent of Battlefield with mantling, climbing, jumping, and overall feeling as though you have the body. However, there are no weapons; your only equipment is in the form of a camera and batteries. While that was a cool function in the game, I will say that there is a bit of a let down, as Outlast suffers largely from the same reasons as the original Dead Space. Most levels feel like a Point A to Point B objective and back again. While yes, there are places where things get a little switched up, I was disappointed by the repetitive nature of the game. However, the terror is more than enough to compensate. This is where I believe this game succeeds where Amnesia failed. You never feel safe in this game. In Amnesia, I never felt like I had to peak out from a corner or hide, because for the most part I could sprint by the monsters with no problem. In Outlast, however, you feel completely defenseless and terrified. Heart-pounding moments where you are chased in the dark by a single crazed lunatic give you chills down your spine. When I saw the massive hulking inmate chasing me, I remembered saying &quot♥♥♥♥♥♥SHIT♥♥♥♥♥♥SHIT♥♥♥♥♥♥" The game is tense and filled with unexpected and massive scares.
STORY
Obviously the story is what's important in a game like this, right? True, but it's weak. Most of the plot points I've seen are either generic and mashed from other horror media, or the game takes a cliched turn where I find it hard to suppress a groan of contempt. The story isn't particularly original or standoutish in the grand scheme of gaming, but small plot twists and the horror of the game in itself keep players intrigued and on their toes.
VERDICT
You may be wondering after reading this review why I don't recommend this game. Why did I say that? Because the game scares me so badly that I have to take breaks from it that can last for days on end before I get the balls to come back and continue on. This is a marelous game, and it has probably scarred me for life despite the entertainment value. So, what do I rate this game, despite some of its minor downfalls?
9/10

Where am I?

Picture yourself in a winter wonderland with nothing but some torn up winter clothes and some flares. You begin looking for shelter. You find a lakeside village. While avoiding the wolves, you find a ton of food, a knife, new clothes, tools, water, and firewood. Now you leave the village to get away from the wolves. You notice a cabin on an island in the middle of the lake, so you head for it stopping at little ice fishing huts on your way there. Then a blizzard hits. You take shelter in the nearest fishing hut. You set up camp in there. Fire up the furnace, place down your nap sack, and begin fishing. 1 day passes. Everything is alright. 2 days pass. Your water is getting low but you can always boil snow. Day 4... no more wood. You begin searching but your food and water supply can't keep up with you. Your clothes are now rags... Day 5... a blizzard hits but you never see it because you don't wake up...
That's the furthest I've made it... Good luck and btw start practicing your speed mouse clicking. The faster you can click the less likely you are to die from a wolf attack. I've survived wolves with only 1% condition... yeah this game is not your average survival game. It's intense. It gets your heart pounding. "Do I have enough water? Food? Wood? Clothes? AHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHH!" Just don't get comfortable cause that's when you die from dehydration or the freezing cold.

Get this game right now if you like survival games, you will definitely get your money's worth at full price and it often goes on sale if you're cheap. I myself love survivals a lot and have had this game for a while. It can be a bit challenging, but half the fun with any survival game is that it challenges you.
+ Really beautiful art style. Amazing looking for how simple it is.
+ Being able to survive for a long time has a really rewarding feeling that is hard to get in many other survival games.
+ Game is very stable despite being an EA title. I honestly don't recall running into a single bug and it doesn't require a top notch PC to run.
+ 3 difficulty levels have been added, no longer are you forced into one difficulty.
+ Lots to explore if you want to. Quite a large world, but you don't have to play all areas if you don't want to, though I'd say that's half the fun. More maps coming as well.
+ Steam workshop allows for player made language packs.
- Can be very easy to get lost if you're not 100% familiar with the map you're playing on.
- Sometimes you get really crappy spawn luck and you either have to try to deal with it or start over. This is pretty much not an issue on easiest difficulty as resources are so common and wildlife doesn't attack.
- No tutorial yet, so some things can be sort of confusing at first.
- No customization at all, which is a con for me since I do love customizing things.
- When you die, it's over, you have to begin anew.
= Very little music, which could be good or bad depending on the person playing. I don't mind it so much, it helps to hear stuff around you.
= Sometimes the sound effects are a bit irritating because of the repetitiveness, but overall they're not too bad.
= I'm not a big fan of the inventory/conditions/crafting interfaces, but they're functional.
= The environment can be very cruel, even on easiest difficulty. This can be a big con for people new to survivals and not good at managing themselves in-game. To me it's just part of the game, though, so at worst this is a neutral point for me.
= Map setup doesn't change each play through, other than actual items you pick up (though some locations have exclusive or almost guaranteed spawns so they need to be checked for certain items). This can be both good and bad because it makes the maps predictable once you're used to them, which hurts replayability a little, but also allows replays to go smoother.
= No story mode for the moment, but that is in development.
= Development has been a bit slow lately, but it's not a huge team and there's a lot to do in the game in it's current state, so I would still argue it's still a worthwhile buy.
---

Okay so to start of this review let's just say that I originally thought "Eh once you've played a telltale game you've played all there is to play of this genre.". Well if I had a time machine and duct tape I would go back in time to that moment and tape my mouth shut. This game is a story telling masterpiece thus far, Episode 1 left me wanting more with it's unique twists and turns. Now with all of the things this game gets right it does get some things wrong so lets talk about those the first thing is the graphics/optimization. This game runs on the unity engine and that probably wasn't the best choice, but even in light of that fact it looks decent. The only problem is that if you're like me and have a 4k monitor you aren't going to be able to play it in 4k resolution. I'm sure that the devs are working to better optimize this game, but as of this review that is a problem. Another slight problem is the camera and the controls the camera is fixed and this is fine, but sometimes it causes the controls to act and feel a bit clunky there was one section in episode one at the docks where the camera bugged and it caused the main character that you control to walk backwards (Even though I was pressing the walk forwards key) until he got unstuck. Like I said the problems that exist are small and easily dealt with, but I feel like they are worth mentioning. Last thing I'll mention in this game is the art design even on the dinky 1920 x 1080p resolution I'm playing it on, the greyscale/monochrome (there are some reds but mostly black and white) is just beautiful the overall art design in this game is fantastic, but at the same time I feel that it's held back immensely due to the unity engine. other last thing (I lied in the last sentence) I feel that it's worth mentioning that this game does a better job in my opinion than telltale does in providing some in between options for some of the necessary choices in the game and I like that and I think telltale could (To quote telltale's the walking dead season 1) take a page out of Blues and Bullets' book. So to wrap this up I don't recommend many games, but if you're like me and are truly obsessed with the Noire genre and pay more attention to story rather than graphics I would reccomend buying this game.

Laughable. Not in the snarky "haha, this game is so bad, X would Y" sense laughable. In the sense that it tries to make a noir-ish detective story meets grisly cult-inspired murder story meets alternate history 50s story, but fails at doing any of that in a competent way.
Dialogues are silly. Scenes are set up in a very amateurish way, mostly abusing the good old fly-by camera games loved to use in late 90s-early 00s, to the point that it sometimes feels like an actual person recorded the flyby with noclip and smoothed mouse. Visuals and animations try hard to look cool in the black and white plus red style, but looks outdated and "meh". Interactions are painfully slow and don't feel meaningful at all. Future episodes might redeem this, but so far it doesn't seem like they will, at least in any way that will also work with competent storytelling.
I honestly kept foing through the game after initial shock of the "is this for real" kind only to see if it gets any stupider. It does. And the game might actually be interesting in the "is this seriously released as a paid product in 2015?" kind of way. Unless you value your time and money, of course, and spend those on something better.
Oh and from the technical perspective - it ran fine for me, but don't even bother trying to play it with kb+mouse if you have a gamepad, as the mouse is there just to say that it's supported, the game doesn't use it in any actually good way (like, say, Telltale games do).
Overall, it really feels like a student project that tried to become something more, without the developers having skills, budget and experience to make it something more.

I have only played the first episode but so far it's been an excellent game. Noir adventures are my jam but even if you aren't a fan of the genre I'd recommend this for the incredible graphics, music and story. The game starts off in a suspenseful situation and you're given the whole timed decision consequence scenario that is well known among Tell Tale games. Though I haven't really seen any deviation in how the story plays out through different choices. The story plays out rather quickly as you can be in a calm conversation in one episode then thrust into a fight some couple minutes later.
There's a few gun fights that play out simply in an aim and shoot, also featured are a few quick time action events. And if by chance you do happen to die the game is very forgiving and restarts right before the event. In addition there are also detective-esque moments where you will have to piece together what happened at a crime scene. There isn't any side quest deviation but you do have branching paths of Eliot Ness and another individual which slowly become connected.
Despite the monotone graphic style with sparing use of red there are incredibly detailed and vibrant environments.The episode played out in just over 2 hours and the game does leave you at a bit of a cliffhanger at the end but it gives you enough stuff packed in the episode so that it's never boring. The music and voice acting also does a great job of getting into the feel of the era. It's as polished a game as you would expect from any of the top tier developers. I did experience a little bit of lag at certain areas but nothing that hindered my playing too much. With the intriguing plot this game and stunning visuals you'll be happy about trying this one.

While I agree somewhat with the positive reviews, I put this game on the shelf for a year.  I figured that fan feedback would help fix it, and that the game company would fix some of the issues with the game.  Apparently, it hasn't happened.  This is a non-exhaustive list of really, really stupid things about the game, which were present a year ago, and which are still present now:
1.  Workers who do not have any work to do in their profession, do not do logical things.  For instance- Builders need stone, iron, and wood to build a house.  If they run out of materials, they do not start collecting those resources.  You would think that would fall under the perview of building.  Not to these guys!  They'll stand around twiddling their thumbs, waiting for you to manually instruct them to collect the materials on which they are short.
2.  Citizens are absolutely senseless about their house selection.  For instance, if you build a mine on one end of the city, and a farm on the other, it's perfectly possible that the citizen who lives near the mine, will decide that he's the farmer, and vice versa.  Sometimes this causes issues, because the little peeps in your game get cold, and their primary source of warmth is their own house.  Sometimes they will freeze to death, just because they live too far from work.  There is very little you can do about this.
3.  Very few strategies are viable.  Games like this aren't fun, when you have to follow an exact formula, every time.  There's really no room for experimentation.
So in summary, I can't recommend buying this game at full price, nor playing it vanilla.  I shelved it for a year, and there has been NO significant update to the AI.  They still act like they're a city full of kids from the special olympics.  Maybe when it's on sale for dirt cheap, if you want to explore the workshop for mods that un-stupid the little morons that live in this imaginary world, you might buy it.  Don't pay $20 for it, though.  In fact, don't even pay $10.  Wait until its price is in the single digits, if you are at all interested in playing this semi-broken game.

Five Nights at Freddy's is an open world, action-adventure video game developed by Rockstar North and published by Rockstar Games. It was released on 17 September 2013 for the PlayStation 3 and Xbox 360, and is scheduled to be released in Q3/Q4 2014 for Microsoft Windows, PlayStation 4 and Xbox One. The game is the first main entry in the Five Nights at Freddy's series since 2008's Super Mario World. Set within the fictional state of San Andreas (based on Southern California), the single-player story follows three criminals and their efforts to commit heists while under pressure from a government agency. The open world design lets players freely roam Freddy's Pizzeria, which includes open countryside and the real city Froddy's house (based on Los Angeles).
The game is played from a third-person perspective and its world is navigated on-foot or by vehicle. Players control the three lead protagonists throughout the single-player mode, switching between them both during and outside of missions. The story is centred on the heist sequences, and many of the missions involve shooting and driving gameplay. The player character's criminal activities may incite a response from law enforcement agencies, measured by a "wanted" system that governs the aggression of their response. FNAF Online, the online multiplayer mode, lets up to 16 players explore the open world and engage in cooperative or competitive game matches.
Development began in 2009, soon after the release of Chucky Cheese's. The development team envisioned Five Nights at Freddy's as a spiritual successor to many of their previous projects, such as Call of Duty: World at War and Team Fortress 2. The game's use of three lead protagonists is a break from series tradition—a design choice from the developers to innovate on the core structure of its predecessors. As part of their research for the open world, the developers conducted field research around California throughout development and captured footage for the design team. Development duties were shared between many of Rockstar's studios worldwide.
Following its announcement in October 2011, Five Nights at Freddy's was widely anticipated. It was acclaimed by many reviewers, with praise particularly directed at its multiple protagonist design, open-ended gameplay and technical advancements. Critics were polarised by a scene depicting torture and the game's treatment of women. Some labelled the game inherently violent and misogynistic. Five Nights at Freddy's broke industry sales records and became the fastest-selling entertainment product in history, earning US $800 million in its first day and US $1 billion in its first three days. It won year-end accolades, including Game of the Year awards from several gaming publications.
