Outlast has proven to revive the nearly  dying genre of horror in the video game universe. It takes cliches of asylums, mad doctors, and German folklore, and turns it into a masterful experience of horror and suspense. I cannot begin to describe the feeling of adrenaline that pumped through my heart as I ran from these mutated genetic lunatics. The plot has taken risks in including the cliches I have mentioned above, but it had not hindered the story. The plot, while at first seems cliche, actually became increasingly interesting as the game went on, and by the end I was craving the answers to what happened with PROJECT WALRIDER and the Murkoff Corporation, and the dead Doctor Rudolph Wernicke. The ideas of science of this game seem to be classic science fiction, bringing back memories of pleasent nostalgia.
As a horror game, Outlast has revived my love for the Horror genre. It takes the aspect of Amnesia: The Dark Descent, that being that one cannot defend one's self from enemies, and tosses the player into a world of uncertainty and hope of escaping the Mount Massive Asylum alive. Never have I been more frightened of figures in the dark. Another interesting aspect of the game is the choice of a camera as opposed to a flashlight. A very interersting way to go, but it makes sense if one looks at the game's  basic plot. Eventually, batteries become your goal next to that of escaping the Asylum, and planning an escape route and hiding place if there is an enemy nearby becomes another objective. The Horror genre over the years has suffered greatly, primarily with the major decline of Silent Hill and Resident Evil, and the more shooter route that Dead Space took with its sequels. This game takes aspects from those games in their prime, along with some tactics of Amnesia, and meshes it together, weaving a wonderful and intriguing tale of the Mount Massive Asylum, the Murkoff Corporation, and PROJECT WALRIDER.
Overall, the game is what I claim to be one of the best of the new age of Horror. If they makes sequels, I will most certainly purchase them.

Namco Tales used to alternate which team makes the next game. Team Symphonia and Team Destiny. Out of the more recent titles, Team Symph made Symphonia, Abyss and Vesperia. Team Destiny made most of the hand helds or things that never got localized. Team Destiny's first localization was Tales of Graces F.
If you like Tales of Graces, this is the perfect game for you. If you like Symphonia, Abyss or Vesperia more than Graces, then you're going to hate Zestiria.
And by that, I mean, if you love horrible story lines and a stupid Pokemon-weakness combat system, this is the game for you.

Today I am reviewing an Indie-horror game called Outlast.
In this game, you play a man named Miles Upshur, a freelance journalist who has the balls to get into any situation. An anonymous tip sends him to a mental hospital which is named Mount Massive Asylum (I know, it's a stupid name for an insane asylum). This specific asylum is owned by a company which is known for it's corrupt dealings. And has been rumored to be doing secret experiments inside the asylum itself. Upshur finds this rather interesting and decides to go to this hospital and prove whether said experiments do take place. Or not. When things quickly descend into darkness, Miles becomes more eager to get out of the building, with his sanity intact.
When I first bought this game, I was excited to play it. I'd finally bought a game which only gave you limited supplies, complex puzzles and things to be afraid of. I bought it, it ran faster than  I would've expected first off. I honestly believed it would be rather slow, perhaps it's because I play it in a windowed mode, maybe not.
As soon as the first chase began, I was excited, I loved the thrill of knowing that the one thing your were fighting was always behind you. And you had to do whatever you could to hide whatever was chasing you. The puzzles were fairly frustrating, I had some trouble with certain bits. There was always something stopping you and you never got all the hints at first which gave the player more to discover.
The atmosphere showed clearly how such a game like this should be portrayed. And it shows it realistically. For these events could actually take place in the modern day world. It had graphic scenes which not many horror games actually let you view for instance Amnesia or Slender. The fact that it's at night time (which most horror games are) makes it even more gloomy than what it should be perhaps. The dismembered bodies and the disturbing faces makes the horror game a much more memorable experience, whether you like it or not.
Now for the cons: A few things bothered me about this game. Only a few, trust me, there are more pro's than there are cons.
I found it rather annoying how the batteries used to charge the camera ran out in a couple minutes or so, only when you're using night vision, thank god. And they had only ever shown up where convienent, not in some random place, only where you'd most need it if you're lucky.
And I found it kind of stupid that when you're in a place, hiding from the current antagonists, when they see you, they go in the same route every time, they never mixed it up a little. And I noticed that if you were hiding under a bed in a room which had numerous amount, the game tries to make you heart pump by having them go to the bed beside, in front or behind you. And I found it annoying how they'd always go to the same places when looking for you, it all seemed rather robotical.
Finally, this is only my opinion by the way, it isn't the same for a number of people. In my opinion IT WASN'T SCARY! I know what you're thinking now, "what?! how could he not find it scary? it was scary as ♥♥♥♥!" Well my opinion is, it's not scary buddy. I have played the entire game and this is a game which is supposed to be filled with jumpscares, I only jumped ONCE. ONCE. I was kind of amazed myself. It wasn't a game which kept me awake at night thinking about it. It was a game I found exciting to play when I was being searched for or chased after. I bought the game expecting myself to♥♥♥♥♥♥my pants. Well, that didn't happen. At all. But I didn't like it for the frights, I liked it for the thrill.
So here are my pros:
1. Thrilling game.
2. Gives complex puzzles which you actually have to use your brain to figure out.
3. Gives a unique atmosphere which makes the game independent from other games.
4. Has a realistic feel which can make you think if this is possible.
5. Lets players with lower graphic laptops or PC's join in (if you dare).
6. Provides challenges which gives you the rush that every horror game needs.
And here are my cons:
1. Supplies are used to fast.
2. Items and information only shows up where convienient.
3. Enemies don't stretch their minds when looking for the player.
4. Tries to make you afraid they'll find you, but doesn't exactly succeed.
5. Not scary enough to fill my lust for horror.
I recommend this game for anyone who is looking for a fun ride in the horror genre and can handle seeing disturbing images, I would say it's for the people 16 and up. But if you got the guts then 12 and up.
So, in the end. My rating out of 10 for this game will be 7.9.

The puzzle platformer genre is one that is ever-changing, dynamic. It is a medium that is as static as a flowing river. This makes it incredibly difficult to stand out. Many games, developed with passion by optimistic teams end up falling in line; just another brick in the wall. This is the thin line between theory and practice, and the thick reminder that the gaming industry - despite encouraging and thriving off creativity and art - is a hungry, unsatiable beast. It is in the end, a business.
At face value it seems Chariot may have fallen victim to this. The graphics aren't game-changing, the gameplay is familiar to say the least. It is a far cry from "revolutionary" in what consumers have now associated the word "revolutionary" with. However, in its own little way, it has revolutionized the genre.
The eponimous chariot is singlehandedly responsible for the main premise, and unique selling point of this game. Your objective is to push, pull and drag the chariot from Point A to Point B. That's essentially the whole game. However, the fact that you can't directly control this chariot is the point.
At first unpredictable and volatile, how the chariot reacts to your sprite becomes natural the more you play, and strictly speaking the physics MAKES SENSE. It's not the BEST, and it's not REALISTIC, but it makes sense. The main concern about the physics engine, and the game in general, is that the chariot can sometimes clip objects, or flail across the screen like a ragdoll. Still not sure what causes this, but you can probably imagine what I mean. It happens in a lot of games: something clips an object, gets stuck inside of it, starts erratically moving back and forth and then gets flung across the gameworld. It's reminiscent of getting whacked by a Giant at level 1 in Skyrim. That said, it doesn't happen all that often, but the fact that the main flaw affects the main premise of the game, the main object of the game (hell, it's even the title!) is concerning. It's possible that his only happens on co-op, which my wife and I play exclusively.
Overall decent game. It is slowly making a name for itself through familiar territory, with a familiar pretty much everything, save for one unique take that is different enough to warrant the existence of this game.

This review will be for Chapter 1.
Graphics-wise, the game looks like LA Confidential, but feels darker. The textures are detailed enough, but the animation can get a bit unrealistic at times.  For the best graphics experience, go to Options and make sure the graphics settings are set to your native resolution. When I started the game it chose a lower resolution for me and I didn't realize it until I had finished the game!
The game plays like a TellTale adventure game (e.g. Walking Dead). You partake in dialog choices and there are a few real time action events where it's basically a Simon Says reflex test to press the correct keys within a certain time. There's also a shooting mode where you get to aim and shoot at certain targets.
An  interesting feature this game has is a clue-deduction system. There is one murder scene where you collect clues and finally link them all up in a kind of mental branching whiteboard. It's quite easy really, once you have all the clues. Much simpler than in the Sherlock Holmes Crimes and Punishment version where the wrong clues can lead you to the wrong conclusion. The game will block you from using the wrong clue.
Story-wise, it's pretty good for a crime mystery but I feel Chapter 1 is too short. However it's got me interested enough that when Episode 2 comes out I'll definitely play it.
Conclusion: Decent game, unique look, but I think it's still not as good as The Wolf Among Us's Chapter 1. Although I enjoyed it, I'd advise buying only Chapter 1 first to see if it's to your taste.

Absolutely amazing, and equally peaceful city building / management simulator.
Aside from surviving natural disasters, There is no actual combat in the game, no aggression aspect to it.
All you can do is sit down, zone out to the chilled-out medieval music in-game and start building / planning away.
It's not for everybody, chances are you'll be bored staring at people you can't directly tell what to do / waiting for something to happen. It's all up to what you're looking for in your game. I bought this to be able to zone out without having to go through the intensitivity of simulating combat / any such thing. And that's exactly what it does.
I usually start playing this game, and only two or three hours later do I snap out of it, save my game and repeat that process the next best time I feel like doing so.
Summarized, it's a great game to play when life is a little rough on you. There's no real stress factor other than you just having to make sure your people have what their little simulated hearts require. :)
I'd give Banished a 8/10 it's not perfect, and requires a certain kind of mood/mentality, but when I'm looking to de-stress myself this is the perfect game to do so!

Firstly I have to say I really wish there was a "neutral" rating on Steam.
As echoed by other reviews the game, in principal, is great.
The brutality of seeing half your population die from disease, starvation or freezing to death is remarkable. You concentrate on getting food stocks up but take your eye off the ball and forget to chop/collect wood for heat and everyone dies. You concentrate on fire wood and building warmer homes forget to add more crop fields and the all die.
The game is ruthless and you need to be on top of everything.
That said once you have a sucessful formula the game just fizzles out with little reward. Rinse and repeat....add a stone house for a 34 year old farmer and the 11 year old girl(?) to live in which will usually result in her dying at child birth (creeps me out). then add another crop field to boost the food resrve for the extra population etc.
There are no goals (apart from surviving), you can do nothing more than add stone structures so no room to upgrade further or research better methods of farming (i.e irrigation etc) The building selection is small and once you have everything,again, it becomes more of a chore than fun.
Don't get me wrong I do like this game but could be so much more. The modding community is great and adds a little variation to the game but again there it ends.
As stated before a "neutral" button would be better for me but due this I have to ,unless there are more updates and mods, say NO I would not recommend this game due to it's overall lack of content. I hope I can edit this review in the future if the devs/modders can add more depth and expand on what is, essentially, a good survival/city builder.

As a player who've used this tool since RMXP (It's still a relatively new version). After making a small game project with my mates in the circle (which takes around 50 hrs, though it didn't work out quite nicely XD), I absolutely stands with my point that this IS the first tools you would use to make a game if you wanna make an classic RPG.
Compare this to old version, in this case RMXP, the way you create events and draw maps became much easier than XP. The important part is that, If you want to make some special effects with RMXP, chances are you will need to learn some basic script writing skills. VX Ace, while you still needs to for some fancy effects, provides basic effects and add-on without learning how to write a script. Which is a very good news for the first time user.
A very good tool, very friendly to the first time user. Highly recommended to newbie developer who are into classic RPG games. and yeah, I forgot to say that if you get more into it, I promise you that  using scripts will enable you to make a game that's far more than an RPG to begin with.

Now that's off the chest, I'll summarise my points in brief.  Been playing just about every Tales' game released thus far, except maybe the ones on Nintendo DS.  Shame more of the games aren't localised.
Pros:
- Tales game on PC. If you know the series, you know it's got an awesome battle system.  ToZ improves on this greatly by integrating combat directly on the map, and it works quite well!
- Really like how there's a bigger emphasis on strategy elements during combat. Given less items available compared to previous games, and the "SC" bar completely replacing the MP bar (kind of brought back from "Tales of Destiny 2 for PS2's SP bar". Button mashers will hate this, but I like a good challenge where you have to actually think how to mow down your foes!
- 2560x1440 res works very well with this game.  Port to PC has been rock-solid so far, even recognising my Xbox 360 controller.
- Controls remain the same as of "Tales of Vesperia" and later, so no real learning curve there.
- Voice acting is superb. I think I quite prefer the English cast over the Japanese cast to be honest.
- Go Shiina's contributions to the ToZ soundtrack is PHENOMENAL. I quite liked his work from "Tales of Legendia" and "Tekken 5: Dark Resurrection", but it's a shame he didn't do more of the songs.  (And I say this as a Sakuraba fan).
Cons:
- The Armatization stuff kind of reminds me of that visual novel, "Princess Waltz", where the male human protagonist combines with another character with special abilities, but otherwise retains the same general appearance between different characters. Kind of felt a bit like a pallette swap for the most part aside the subtle additional accessory.
- I found some of the cutscenes' sound quality was quite poor on the lower registers - those with a critical ear will be able to pick out the MPEG-like compression quantization artifacts in some of the audio.  Not a huge problem but noticeable when the rest of the game is crystal-clear.
- Sakuraba needs to retire.  Seriously.  He needs a creative break.  Even reusing one of the boss tunes from "Tales of Vesperia" seemed lazy enough, but considering he writes far too many songs that sound like him but generic enough to not be memorable in their own right.
- 30fps. Not that it affects gameplay at all, but I like silky-smooth animations, not arbitrary film-like frame rates.
- Japanese audio mode does not retain the original theme song from the Japanese ToZ release back in March. Why? (Copyrighted licensing distribution barriers I guess).
TL;DR, you like JRPG's and the "Tales of" series?  Get this game.  If anyone's expecting something along the lines of Skyrim or <insert AAA title here>, this game is NOT for you.

If you're looking for a good scare, Outlast is certainly the game for you. I cannot say enough good things about it. The atmosphere is phenomenal and extremely well put together. Paired with the music and sounds, it can't get any better.
As for the actual gameplay, Outlast needs a little thinking involved. You shouldn't expect for everything to be clearly marked for you. Outlast does, however, get a little repetitive - grab your three items to unlock this or fix that and you advance, all the while a monster patient is lurking around. It can get to feel a little repetitive, but if you're like me, you won't exactly notice. You'll be too busy trying to keep yourself alive and complete the objective. One downfall I did notice, besides the repetitveness, was the length. I've realized that most modern horror games aren't incredibly long, and this game follows the rest. I do wish there was more story to find, more gameplay, and a change in pace - i.e. reduce the repetiveness and try something different with the flow of the game, which is something we can hope for in Outlast 2.
Outlast was a terrifying experience for me. There are gruesome cutscenes, jumpscares, and chase scenes. The characters are certainly twisted individuals. You can almost feel the pain, fear, and adrenaline that rushes through Miles Upshur, the protagonist in the story. His emotions are very well conveyed to the player. Not only Miles's emotions, but the various patients' emotions, as well. Plot twists, unexpected events, perfectly conveyed emotion, and a fantastic story really add to the game's atmosphere.
This is a game I will recommend one hundred times over. Very fantastic game with great features. It can certainly send chills up your spine.

[Ofcourse, it is best if you hook your laptop up to your TV so that you aren't all crowded around a tiny screen :) ]
The Darkfall DLC is also totally worth the price -- It adds a whole lot of powerups to the game and really changes the way you would play it. To end, I can't stress how amazing this game is and how me and my friends spend most of our time talking about Dodge cancelling, or some amazing kill that we had the night before. This game. Just... Yes. So much yes. It's a breath of fresh air in a survival genre that has come to almost solely exist as "Fight to survive against zombies!" (or cannibals a la The Forest) to see one that is simply "Try to beat the environment." It seems like a simple challenge. Houses to loot, food and wood to be found... And then the wolves show up. You'd probably seen them in the distance a few times, but the sheer terror when one decides to take interest in you is almost palbable.
This is a game that sweeps you away in a torrent of emotion, adrenaline, and thought. The solitude, while not much at first, becomes so present that it alters your view on the game entirely. Found a few frozen bodies the first day, didn't think much of them. Looted what I needed and moved on. By the third day, I found one sitting at the bottom of a decently steep drop off of a hill, curled up against the rocks. Couldn't help but think that he'd probably left to find help or supplies, fallen and broken or sprained his ankle, then curled up to the rocks to avoid the biting wind to no avail.
Every little thing changes the longer time goes by. The granola bars and sodas you find en masse early on become huge victories. Every small mistake you start beating yourself up over.
Me personally, I keep screwing up on the fourth day. Here's to hoping for day five and to a long life for The Long Dark! 10/10 would recommend to anyone who enjoys survival at its finest.

Short: A must-have classics of videogaming. Still totally worth playing today.
Why to buy it: Historical masterpiece. Perfect for relaxation. It helps to find peace and emptiness after a hard day at work. More efficient than meditation, sauna, or sport.
Long version:
Unreal Tournament has something magical. It has been years since its original release, and still, it's amazingly good and definitely worth playing. For those who do not know this ultimate legend of FPS, let me introduce it in a few lines :
Most FPS have tried to find a neat story to keep the player into the game. Then someone came and said: "Hey, guys, why do we care with a story? Don't we play only to shoot and have fun, after all?" And so came Unreal Tournament. The idea is that you are a gladiator in a futuristic universe, with some interesting background with appreciable ties with the Unreal universe. So you are in an arena with guns spread everywhere, and if you are killed, you just instantly respawn and continue the fight. It means there is no break, no searching for the way forward, for stupid opening buttons. You just fight and fight and fight endlessly, until you win the match. The experience was, and still remains, an extremely intense one. Videogame here is at its greater height, even if it's shear violence and barbarousness.
Now, is it still worth today? The graphics have aged, for sure, but the level design was so good, that it doesn't matter a lot. They did not try to build magnificent open spaces areas in a luxurious nature: Most arenas are confined basements, and this is the kind of decor which cannot be much prettier today than it was seventeen years ago. Gameplay is still pretty much perfect. Weapons are sufficiently hidden so that you have to find out where they are while trying not being killed by those who already have them, and there is a good diversity of them. Everything was well-balanced then, and it has remained so up to now, as equilibrium never ages.
What feels like the twentieth century, however, is the AI if you play solo, especially in Assault mode, where your team keeps following you, backing you up in the most useless manner. That means that if you are almost at the objective, and you die, you return to the starting point, and your team, instead of finishing what you were up to, just left the enemy base to greet you in pack at your respawn place.
To end this review, I will tell you some personal story I have with this game. In my youth years I was often bullied by a big tough guy; but one day we spoke and, I don't know really how, we ended up by him lending me his Unreal Tournament game. I enjoyed it a lot, and now that we had a common enthralling to share, we became good lads and he never bullied me again. Peace among people can be achieved through cathartic  videogaming, it would seem.

This application is exactly what any RPG fan needs with a few pointers.
1. You will not make money making a game. You can sell a decently built game, but the time taken to complete a good one is insane. Fun, but do not put time into this thinking it'll print money.

While the price is high and the learning curve can be a bit steep, RPG Maker VX ACE is a great piece of software for those who wish to create their own RPG game. It's been used to create various kinds of games too, from Visual Novels to platformers, it's possible to do almost anything if you know how. Just be aware that just as Painttool SAI or Photoshop is a tool to create art, RPG Maker is a tool to create a game. What you'll be doing in RPG Maker is a project that will take time and effort, not a game that is to be played to gain achievements.
It should be noted that, without a plan or basic concept, you may not find your money's worth when using RPG Maker. (Especially at 70$+) You might be half-way done and feel as though it's hopeless and you should give up because nothing is working right. Don't do it! Press on!
This is the very reason that I highly stress the the "Learning Curve" point. While this software does have easy to use tools and interface, you will need to learn the basics if you want to program even a quarter of what your creative mind has thought up. You will likely not be able to make something as fancy as "The Witch's House" or "IB" from the get-go.
You'll be browsing forums for answers to many questions and scratching your head trying to think up how to make simple events run the way they are supposed to. Still, once you master the basics of RPG Maker, a floodgate of new ideas can open up and you will realize that RPG Maker is indeed a powerful program.
To summarize though, don't jump into the program unless you're comitted to learning it. Just like a game, you need to master the controls and the game lingo before you can master the game. Have a basic idea or plan ready, so that you have direction to follow as you learn how to use RPG Maker. Be aware that there are many tutorials (both video and readable) out there to help you and when things come to a standstill there's forums for support!
Finally, keep in mind that while your first game may not be a million-dollar blockbuster, it's proof of how far you've come and you'll only get better as you go!

It is totally worth checking out if you like horror games.

First off I'm recommending this game because there isn't a neutral option, and a non-recommendation seems harsh. It's not a bad game, but it isn't as good as I hoped.
This game has potential, but feels rushed. This isn't my first Tales of game, and it isn't my worst experience. Tales of Symphonia 2 still holds that title. This game however doesn't even come close to my favorite, Tales of Vesperia. This story rockets by at lightening speed, and by the time an area is done you barely understand whats happening. Some aspects are dwelled on for far too long, and others come and go faster than Vanilla Ice's career. This makes characters seem schizophrenic. One scene they're serious and cryptic, then the next they're bubbly and clingy. The main mcguffin is "purity", but it's purity in this bizarre christian sense. One moment that stood out as weird to me was when Edna made a comment about the main character "guilt tripping a woman into making the first move", the main character then gets yelled at about "maintaining their purity". This raises so many questions. I can't be the hero anymore if I shoot a load? What are the logistics of human-seraph relationships? Would this be considered cheating, or polygamy?
With all that said the story does have some fun story bits. If you like JRPGs, and Tales of it definitely has it's moments. They're just no where near as good as some of the previous games. Character interaction is as good as ever, and will bring a smile to your face. I'm seriously hoping it gets better later.
Next the game is tutorialized to hell, and back. I'm 6 hours in, and STILL getting tutorial messages. This combat system is needlessly padded, and complex. I've just started smashing buttons because this is worse than a fighting game. All the combos, artes, elements, combined forms. It's trying to evolve the combat system, but all it does is confuse it. The combat system works, but it definitely takes a time investment to learn everything.
This is a knit pick, but while the art in the game is great, why does the combined forms (I can't remember the made up name for it) turn Surey into a transvestite? Seriously, he grows hair about 5 feet long in what appears to be a pony tail, and wears a dress complete with high heels.
At 6 hours in this is really a first impressions, but as I said my first impression is neutral. I'm gonna keep playing it, but it hasn't sucked me in like Tales of Vesperia, or Tales of the Abyss. I'm hoping it gets better.

It didn't take all that much effort to get it to work on Win10, I think I had to like fiddle with the compatibility options in the Properties of the .exe or something. Not a huge deal. Anyway, I just didn't like the game. It's supposed to be open world, but I felt like I was getting railroaded the whole time.
Maybe it's my own fault for just following the directions for the main quest, or maybe I just don't know how to play the game 'right'. The dialouge felt overly binary, there's "good option" "evil option" and sometimes "neutral/noncommital option" if you get lucky. I wanted to play as a sneaky dude who wears light armour and steals things, but I kept dying until I put on the super heavy bulky power suit thing. Should that just be something I should have expected, being in a bombed out wasteland? I'm not usually a fantasy sort of person, but I enjoyed Skyrim a lot more, probably because of this very example. I wanted to play as a sneaky guy who stabs people in both games. At the beginning of Skyrim I was presented with three main choices, swords, magic, or sneaky. I chose sneaky because I like to steal things and then run/sneak away because I'm a scumbag. At the beginning of Fallout 3 I was presented with two choices: gun or baseball bat.  Running around for a couple hours expanded my options to gun, bat, mines, or laser gun. My issue is that they all feel like the same choice: in the end I'm just running around eviscerating fat green dudes with various weapons.
The steam page says something about "every situation can be dealt with in many different ways". I just didn't see it. Raider camp, shoot & loot, moving on, evil green martian giants, shoot & loot, moving on, etc.
Maybe I'd be more forgiving if the atmosphere didn't seem so desolate. I know I'm in a post-nuclear-war place here, but green fog on grey building isn't the best color scheme to have to look at for a couple hours. In other open world games the reason I like exploring so much is to see all the cool different places there are. In Skyrim I found a cave with a giant tree in the middle of a Yellowstone-esque geothermic desert, and a castle of evil doom in the snow, and so on. Every place felt different to look at. In Fallout 3 I'm trudging a wasteland of brownish dirt and green sky to a concrete rubble maze of grey walls and green sky and everything is always grungy and dirty.
I did have one part of the game I loved. The vault with the
That part was my favorite part of the game, because I had to figure out exactly how to
I had to problem solve, instead of just shooting anything that shows up on my radar as a red flag thing.
TL;DR: everything felt predetermined and everything looks green and grey

I first discovered A Hat in Time in early 2013, back when Mafia Town was just a dock, a white building, and a few NPCs.
When the Kickstarter launched a few months later, I made an account just to support this amazing-looking revival of the collectathon genre. It was like the combination of my all-time favorite games. It was too good to be true.
I was overjoyed seeing the project's success, and every video I watched of the alpha just made me more eager to play it.
Eventually, I caved and bought the beta, which I loved because it respected and rewarded the player's will to explore. I could venture out into the sea of Mafia Town past its frightening robotic shark to find secrets hidden in the islands on the horizon. I could surprise myself by venturing into suspicious drain pipes and ending up in secret areas. And I had a great appreciation for how much the badges, such as the parasol and the portal, deepened gameplay.
What made A Hat in Time so special to me wasn't the bosses or the exploding train stage. (Those were actually the weakest points of the beta for me.) What I cherished was the freedom and the thrill of discovery.
The development process on Twitter fascinated me. Chapter 4, originally called Sand 'N' Sails, particularly interested me, because it looked to be a more condensed version of the Great Sea in Wind Waker. Roaming freely in a desert looking for villages and hidden caves while staying hydrated so you don't die of heat stroke? What a cool change of pace!
The end of the beta filled me with intrigue as it hinted towards a greater story. Seeing Hat Kid grown up really made me wonder just how great a role time travel was going to have, and what connections Hat Kid might have with other characters in the story, like Mustache Girl or the terrifying Queen Vanessa.
Cut to release day. I'm anxious to begin. I play for 6-7 hours and beat the game with around 25 timepieces.
I'd like to say I loved the game. I'd like to say that I was charmed to bits by all the silly dialogue and unique environmental details, and that each chapter was better than the last.
But I couldn't help but feel underwhelmed. The final game is missing something. Something the beta and even the alpha had.
The freedom and thrill of discovery have been neutered.
There are fewer abilities than there were in the beta, and the abilities that exist are very context-sensitive, forcing you to switch hats regularly.
The Time Rift areas are now inaccessible until you unlock them, and the game shows you where they are.
The green orbs are less fun reskins of Star Bits from Mario Galaxy in that they're sometimes required to open new missions despite being unlimited, replaceable collectibles.
Hat Kid can't swim underwater anymore, and for that matter, she can't swim much at all.
Remember when Hat Kid could ride on fireworks? That's been ditched, too.
That neat and tense part of Queen Vanessa's Manor where you learn to strategically time the flashes of cameras to defeat shadows is gone.
Chapter 4 is now frustratingly streamlined for a so-called "free roam" chapter.
It's as if the head developer was suddenly afraid of people breaking his game or getting stuck, and he took every measure to prevent that, even if it meant ditching some really cool stuff. The game is less interesting because of it.
If there's anything I wish had been changed from the beta that wasn't, it's the absurd number of duplicate rewards that serve little to no purpose. It'd be one thing if they counted toward 100% completion, but as it stands, they're useless glowing balls that set off my Obsessive Completionist Disorder.
Most of the game's "good moments" are purely cosmetic things, like the damages bill that steepens as you travel through Dead Bird Studios, or the friendship meter when Hat Kid and Mustache Girl high-five. Yes, these moments have their charm, but in my eyes, all they do is add some seasoning to the spoiled meat of the game.
Almost every mission in the game consists of the same few elements: bounce on tightropes, swing on grapple hook targets, and find the next platform to jump on. Beyond that, there's minimal mechanical variation, especially compared to most other games in the genre.
Frankly, in the end, I don't think this game knew what it wanted to be. It tried to be too much at once, and there's a sense of dissonance as a result.
For example, there are quite a few times when the game takes a long pause, like while riding an elevator or a zip-line. They're the kinds of long pauses that are right at home in a long, casually-paced RPG, but for a relatively short, fast-paced action platformer like this, it's jarring and somewhat irritating.
There were multiple times during my playthrough when a new act would open, and I put it off because I didn't want to do it. Navigating the foggy maze of trees that is Subcon Forest was never fun to me, because everything looks the same. The penguin acts in Battle of the Birds were obnoxious and artifically lengthy. Chapter 4, which is easily the chapter I hate most, I stayed away from as much as I could due to its highly inefficient navigation system, lazy theming, and infuriating enemies.
Aside from a few unnatural difficulty spikes, A Hat in Time is an easy game, which is not necessarily a bad thing; but when it's "stroll through the park" easy, it's concerning. Hat Kid feels virtually weightless, is tight to control, and has bizarre horizonal jumping range, trivializing anything that would pose a captivating challenge with the controls of a 3D Mario game. If you do die (which happened for me when I touched hazards I couldn't even see), there's no lives system and checkpoints are frequent. There's hardly any risk versus reward to keep you on your toes.
I knew in advance Chapter 5 was going to be a one-act final confrontation, and considering how impressively dark Chapter 3 is, I was expecting the game's last stand to be truly threatening. Turns out it's a hackneyed final area with a clichéd final boss fight that's all flashy effects and sappy exposition with not much of a fight. It comes out of nowhere without any buildup, too. And to top it off, the ending feels basic and incomplete. Normally this wouldn't bother me in a self-proclaimed collectathon, but A Hat in Time is more of a story-focused adventure game, so it's a shame it doesn't have any of the emotional resonance, complexity, or delicate pacing of your average story game.
A Hat in Time is the first game in its genre that I don't feel inclined to revisit. Most of the replay value is the scripted kind, where the game gives you dialogue options and they might each lead to a slightly different reaction.
It might sound like I hated everything about the game, but that's not true. I started out enjoying myself, and the end boss of Chapter 3 is an honest treat and the highlight of the game. But in the end, it felt very "manufactured" to me and was sometimes a real chore to play.
All the beauty of this game is in its polish instead of at its core. It reeks of missed potential.
It genuinely pains my heart to say that.
A Hat in Time has all the ingredients of a truly great game, but the recipe has all the wrong serving sizes, and it ultimately left a bitter taste in my mouth. I feel emptier than I would have felt if I'd just skipped it.
---
People seem to like bringing up that I prefer Yooka-Laylee, as if that somehow invalidates my criticisms.
My argument is that if you removed all of A Hat in Time's cutesy charm, you'd be left with a lot of straightforward, run-of-the-mill platforming missions with a few cool boss fights mixed in.
Yooka-Laylee is clearly the less polished and less detailed game, but it has all the things I think A Hat in Time lacks: gameplay variety, rewarding exploration, lots of freedom and replay value... I just find it to be a genuinely more fulfilling experience.
This isn't to say A Hat in Time is bad, but I'd only recommend it at one third of its $30 price.

Even in Alpha, The Long Dark is already in my top 10 favourite games. I am anxiously awaiting updates and story mode, which is not to say that the sandbox is lacking; it's a free-roam wilderness survival game (right up my alley) with elements of suspense without being an in-your-face horror game. The art style is really great: simple, but still beautiful. I am so grateful for the ability to play as a female-representing character! Plus, it's cool to have a survival game set basically in my back yard - Fallout is great, but I've never been to DC or the Mojave. The Long Dark really allows me to put myself into the game, which is a cool added bonus. Obviously this doesn't apply to most - I know.
There are some issues, of course. The wolves (the only "enemies" in the game) seem pretty overpowered, though this may be on purpose. I have only once survived an attack, and I think I just got lucky, as on my first hit the wolf ran away whining. The other times, whether or not I have an axe or a knife and 100% condition...it hasn't mattered. I frantically click-mash and in a second I am dead. The first few times it was cool - I like challenging games - but now it's getting a bit tiresome. I think it'd be cool to have some sort of "peaceful" mode later on, where your only challenges are the elements (just staying alive long enough to find food and shelter is a challenge on it's own in the beginning, especially if you spawn at night in the middle of nowhere). This would allow for more adventuring and less running from building to building to escape ravenous wolves. Then again, maybe it'd take away the challenging aspect that I like so much. I'm not sure.
Also, sometimes the audio gets choppy, but that might just be my computer.
TL;DR, for an alpha, the game is amazing. Suspenseful, beautiful, relateable free roam survival game with so much potential for the future. Right now, wolves seem overpowered, and the audio does some weird stuff, but overall one of the best games I've played in the past year or so.

I have played this game longer than any other. This is because this game has the best multiplayer if you want the ultimate realistic hardcore FPS experience.
The soundscape is excellent. Weapons sound very realistic, whether near, far, or inside a building. Weapon handling (accuracy etc) are still the best I have ever seen in any game (much better than ARMA series in my opinion). There are some neat gameplay mechanics that simulate suppression, and reward teamwork and discourage camper score-whoring. This is probably the only game that really models suppression. Don't bother with the single-player though, its rubbish and the AI is dumb.
When it was released back in 2011, it was rough around the edges with lots of bugs, but now in 2014, with continuous support from the devs, virtually all the problems have been ironed out, and it now runs very stable.
Being realistic and brutal, this is very unforgiving to noobs (and CoD players). Only 1 rifle bullet is needed to kill. Noobs spawn, run forward, and get killed by enemy artillery, or a tank 300m away, or a sniper 200m away, or a machine gunner 150m away, or a maxed out assault trooper 5m away, and never see it coming. Being realistic, machine guns are almost just as accurate as sniper rifles, but it is slightly harder to spot prone enemies without the scope. I am usually the machine gunner, and by a round's end (20min) I may have killed over 80 of them and only died 5 times. That's how ruthless this game is. This is arguably both the game's biggest strengh, and its biggest problem.
This game uses a leveling and unlock system, but it is still quite fair on new players. While fully levelled guns will help (with slightly reduced weapon sway, recoil, reload time, magazine size etc) it is still only 20% of your effectiveness and the remaining 80% is down to your tactical awareness, teamwork, and most of all, your individual skill. That is the most important thing. If you are naturally good, you will start out quite well and only get better as you level up, but if you are not so good at aiming with a mouse, you might always struggle.
The online community is more mature than in most other shooter games. We still get the occasional 12 year old, but not too often. As of Dec-2014 there are still a good range of servers and a good volume of players online (about 1500 sunday night, 300 monday morning). At peak times there are about 5-10 servers with 64 players, and some servers occasionally go over the 64 player limit. The most I have seen is 85, that was epic. In 800 hours of gameplay I have only seen 1 incident of hacking (the artillery hack), and that one was patched out by the devs within days. So, this game has a virtually hack-free environment.
So, this game is too brutal and realistic for many, but if CoD or Battlefield is not cutting it for you, I recommend you try this.

4) The soundtrack is enjoyable considering you will spend a few hours at a time playing the game.
Unless the devs are planning on releasing a very large patch for the game sometime soon, I don't see a future for game unfortunately.
I do though recommend this game for people who enjoy this genre but also warn that the game will become fruitless and just another addition to your steam game list.

After completing the game I knew I just had to come back and edit my review. Don't worry this updated review is going the be spoiler free.
I got this game after seeing not only the video, the price, but also the number of positive reviews.
After playing it for a short time I became hooked. I just had to play this game to the end and I did. Blood and Bacon is an addictive and fun arena style wave shooter. You play as a hired gun with one job at hand to rid the farm of an army of undead hogs.  As you progress new weapons and items unlock, and at the same time enemies get bigger, stronger, and grow in number. After so many days you will encounter a boss battle. Each boss battle becomes more intense and challenging making victory feel more rewarding. With the number of options from all the unlockables players are able to come up with various combinations of how to handle each day.
As for story it stays very simple and instead focuses more on the gameplay. That isn't a bad thing if you are a fan of games like Doom, or Serious Sam. The music is very catchy and really gets you in the mood to play. The graphics are closer to classic shooter style from the N64/PS2 era that just fits the theme of the game so well. In honestly it's more of a breath of fresh air compared to other modern games. The game has an art style that I haven't seen since Conker's Bad Fur Day. In all honestly it's just another reason why I enjoy this game so much.
After all that said I still highly recommend this game. It's not only addictive but also a great time killer. So if you have the shekels to spare please pick it up. You can't go wrong with this one.

The player is free to roam the game's open world, not having to focus on the game's storyline. Progress in the game is measured with Chaos, which is earned by completing missions, destroying government property, collecting items for the factions and reaching 100% completion in settlements and military bases. Chaos unlocks new agency missions and stronghold takeovers. Chaos and stronghold takeovers expand the factions' area of influence, which unlocks faction missions and race challenges.
Initially, the player must acquire weapons and vehicles in the field. Early in the game, the player encounters a black market supplier, from whom weapons and vehicles can be purchased, with an option to have them delivered to the player's location via helicopter. As more Chaos is gained, additional weapons, vehicles, and the extraction option become available on the black market. All weapons and vehicles on the black market have parameters that can be upgraded in several steps, by building upgrades with weapon and vehicle components found within the game world. There are over 2,000 parts that the player can acquire.

I've been playing Dark World a lot. I've cleared all stages on Legendary without continues. Going to try for no death runs next.
I love everything about it. I've mostly only played solo but I'm glad there's 4 player co-op now. My only request would be that the two campains are merged allowing for 4 player in the Ascension Quest. The problem would be unifying the difficulty system and reseting everyones achievements so I can see why it wasn't done, I still think it would be a nice addition.
I don't miss the scoring system. All the stages have an achievement for clearing the highest difficulty with no deaths, this being the highest achievement pretty much made the scoring superfluous. Additionally the game now tracks fastest times which I think is a much more easily understood and meaningful measure of skill. Speed runners rejoice! The Dark World campaign isn't overly long and be cleared on the easier difficulty in around an hour, but those who enjoyed playing for gold skulls in the Ascension Quest will get a lot out of playing for the harder achievements.
Prism arrows I think are designed to affect high level competitive play, where no one misses a dodge catch, in which case it makes a significant change to the meta game. Trigger arrows are fun but damn is it easy to SD with. There is such a huge number of arrow varieties now that adding more might start to subtract from what makes each arrow interesting, as well as increasing the barrier of entry for newcomers. Haven't had a chance to play much versus yet but the Dark World content should make a great addition.
Also love the additional Trials stages. It's a part of the game I didn't expect myself to take so much pleasure in, but once you start aiming for the red pearl dev times the mode becomes a kind of rewarding puzzle game, though it does play havoc on my RSI and I fear my controller will crumble in my hands before I ever clear them all.
All in all I love every bit of TowerFall and can't wait to see what Matt works on next, TowerFall or otherwise.

I have never written a review for a game before, nor have I posted on any game forum. And yet, for this game, I have now done both.
The Long Dark is everything I could ever want in a survival game, and I can hardly contain my excitement as I know more is coming from the amazing Devs that actually interact regularly with the players via the forums, taking in all suggestions and feedback.
In the Long Dark as it stands, there is only a survival sandbox mode. You are dropped in the frozen Canadian northern tundra after a worldwide geomagnetic distaster. The isolation you feel, the helplessness, hits you IMMEDIATELY as you are spawned into a frozen tundra with no goal, no map, and few belongings. Survival is not as easy as it may at first seem. Resources are scarce, and the struggle to even stay warm and fed day by day is a real challenge as you scavenge house to house, area by area. Beyond that, there are wolves. Oh my, the wolves. If you don't freeze to death, starve to death, or die of dehydration, the wolves, or the subsequent blood loss from wolf attacks, WILL kill you. The only question is one of when.
As far as actual gameplay, I am very pleased. Crafting is fairly straightfoward, and the wolf struggle system is intuitive enough once you know what to do (although Hinterlands has promised many tweaks to this system in the future to fine tune it). You have to constanlty repair clothing and any tools you use, as well as watch your hydration, hunger, and fatigue levels. the controls are fluid and the menus are simple enough for anyone to understand immediately. I personally love the simplistic graphics as they are, and the sounds, ambient and otherwise, are overall very good. Nothing is more terrifying that hearing a wolf howl in the distance, and nothing is more comforting than hearing the crackle of a warm fire as you cook meat or boil water.
All in all, I'll end with this. Although at the moment I am currently clocked at 11 hours, I will be playing many, many more.

I have played this game longer than any other. This is because this game has the best multiplayer if you want the ultimate realistic hardcore FPS experience.
The soundscape is excellent. Weapons sound very realistic, whether near, far, or inside a building. Weapon handling (accuracy etc) are still the best I have ever seen in any game (much better than ARMA series in my opinion). There are some neat gameplay mechanics that simulate suppression, and reward teamwork and discourage camper score-whoring. This is probably the only game that really models suppression. Don't bother with the single-player though, its rubbish and the AI is dumb.
When it was released back in 2011, it was rough around the edges with lots of bugs, but now in 2014, with continuous support from the devs, virtually all the problems have been ironed out, and it now runs very stable.
Being realistic and brutal, this is very unforgiving to noobs (and CoD players). Only 1 rifle bullet is needed to kill. Noobs spawn, run forward, and get killed by enemy artillery, or a tank 300m away, or a sniper 200m away, or a machine gunner 150m away, or a maxed out assault trooper 5m away, and never see it coming. Being realistic, machine guns are almost just as accurate as sniper rifles, but it is slightly harder to spot prone enemies without the scope. I am usually the machine gunner, and by a round's end (20min) I may have killed over 80 of them and only died 5 times. That's how ruthless this game is. This is arguably both the game's biggest strengh, and its biggest problem.
This game uses a leveling and unlock system, but it is still quite fair on new players. While fully levelled guns will help (with slightly reduced weapon sway, recoil, reload time, magazine size etc) it is still only 20% of your effectiveness and the remaining 80% is down to your tactical awareness, teamwork, and most of all, your individual skill. That is the most important thing. If you are naturally good, you will start out quite well and only get better as you level up, but if you are not so good at aiming with a mouse, you might always struggle.
The online community is more mature than in most other shooter games. We still get the occasional 12 year old, but not too often. As of Dec-2014 there are still a good range of servers and a good volume of players online (about 1500 sunday night, 300 monday morning). At peak times there are about 5-10 servers with 64 players, and some servers occasionally go over the 64 player limit. The most I have seen is 85, that was epic. In 800 hours of gameplay I have only seen 1 incident of hacking (the artillery hack), and that one was patched out by the devs within days. So, this game has a virtually hack-free environment.
So, this game is too brutal and realistic for many, but if CoD or Battlefield is not cutting it for you, I recommend you try this.

I first discovered A Hat in Time in early 2013, back when Mafia Town was just a dock, a white building, and a few NPCs.
When the Kickstarter launched a few months later, I made an account just to support this amazing-looking revival of the collectathon genre. It was like the combination of my all-time favorite games. It was too good to be true.
I was overjoyed seeing the project's success, and every video I watched of the alpha just made me more eager to play it.
Eventually, I caved and bought the beta, which I loved because it respected and rewarded the player's will to explore. I could venture out into the sea of Mafia Town past its frightening robotic shark to find secrets hidden in the islands on the horizon. I could surprise myself by venturing into suspicious drain pipes and ending up in secret areas. And I had a great appreciation for how much the badges, such as the parasol and the portal, deepened gameplay.
What made A Hat in Time so special to me wasn't the bosses or the exploding train stage. (Those were actually the weakest points of the beta for me.) What I cherished was the freedom and the thrill of discovery.
The development process on Twitter fascinated me. Chapter 4, originally called Sand 'N' Sails, particularly interested me, because it looked to be a more condensed version of the Great Sea in Wind Waker. Roaming freely in a desert looking for villages and hidden caves while staying hydrated so you don't die of heat stroke? What a cool change of pace!
The end of the beta filled me with intrigue as it hinted towards a greater story. Seeing Hat Kid grown up really made me wonder just how great a role time travel was going to have, and what connections Hat Kid might have with other characters in the story, like Mustache Girl or the terrifying Queen Vanessa.
Cut to release day. I'm anxious to begin. I play for 6-7 hours and beat the game with around 25 timepieces.
I'd like to say I loved the game. I'd like to say that I was charmed to bits by all the silly dialogue and unique environmental details, and that each chapter was better than the last.
But I couldn't help but feel underwhelmed. The final game is missing something. Something the beta and even the alpha had.
The freedom and thrill of discovery have been neutered.
There are fewer abilities than there were in the beta, and the abilities that exist are very context-sensitive, forcing you to switch hats regularly.
The Time Rift areas are now inaccessible until you unlock them, and the game shows you where they are.
The green orbs are less fun reskins of Star Bits from Mario Galaxy in that they're sometimes required to open new missions despite being unlimited, replaceable collectibles.
Hat Kid can't swim underwater anymore, and for that matter, she can't swim much at all.
Remember when Hat Kid could ride on fireworks? That's been ditched, too.
That neat and tense part of Queen Vanessa's Manor where you learn to strategically time the flashes of cameras to defeat shadows is gone.
Chapter 4 is now frustratingly streamlined for a so-called "free roam" chapter.
It's as if the head developer was suddenly afraid of people breaking his game or getting stuck, and he took every measure to prevent that, even if it meant ditching some really cool stuff. The game is less interesting because of it.
If there's anything I wish had been changed from the beta that wasn't, it's the absurd number of duplicate rewards that serve little to no purpose. It'd be one thing if they counted toward 100% completion, but as it stands, they're useless glowing balls that set off my Obsessive Completionist Disorder.
Most of the game's "good moments" are purely cosmetic things, like the damages bill that steepens as you travel through Dead Bird Studios, or the friendship meter when Hat Kid and Mustache Girl high-five. Yes, these moments have their charm, but in my eyes, all they do is add some seasoning to the spoiled meat of the game.
Almost every mission in the game consists of the same few elements: bounce on tightropes, swing on grapple hook targets, and find the next platform to jump on. Beyond that, there's minimal mechanical variation, especially compared to most other games in the genre.
Frankly, in the end, I don't think this game knew what it wanted to be. It tried to be too much at once, and there's a sense of dissonance as a result.
For example, there are quite a few times when the game takes a long pause, like while riding an elevator or a zip-line. They're the kinds of long pauses that are right at home in a long, casually-paced RPG, but for a relatively short, fast-paced action platformer like this, it's jarring and somewhat irritating.
There were multiple times during my playthrough when a new act would open, and I put it off because I didn't want to do it. Navigating the foggy maze of trees that is Subcon Forest was never fun to me, because everything looks the same. The penguin acts in Battle of the Birds were obnoxious and artifically lengthy. Chapter 4, which is easily the chapter I hate most, I stayed away from as much as I could due to its highly inefficient navigation system, lazy theming, and infuriating enemies.
Aside from a few unnatural difficulty spikes, A Hat in Time is an easy game, which is not necessarily a bad thing; but when it's "stroll through the park" easy, it's concerning. Hat Kid feels virtually weightless, is tight to control, and has bizarre horizonal jumping range, trivializing anything that would pose a captivating challenge with the controls of a 3D Mario game. If you do die (which happened for me when I touched hazards I couldn't even see), there's no lives system and checkpoints are frequent. There's hardly any risk versus reward to keep you on your toes.
I knew in advance Chapter 5 was going to be a one-act final confrontation, and considering how impressively dark Chapter 3 is, I was expecting the game's last stand to be truly threatening. Turns out it's a hackneyed final area with a clichéd final boss fight that's all flashy effects and sappy exposition with not much of a fight. It comes out of nowhere without any buildup, too. And to top it off, the ending feels basic and incomplete. Normally this wouldn't bother me in a self-proclaimed collectathon, but A Hat in Time is more of a story-focused adventure game, so it's a shame it doesn't have any of the emotional resonance, complexity, or delicate pacing of your average story game.
A Hat in Time is the first game in its genre that I don't feel inclined to revisit. Most of the replay value is the scripted kind, where the game gives you dialogue options and they might each lead to a slightly different reaction.
It might sound like I hated everything about the game, but that's not true. I started out enjoying myself, and the end boss of Chapter 3 is an honest treat and the highlight of the game. But in the end, it felt very "manufactured" to me and was sometimes a real chore to play.
All the beauty of this game is in its polish instead of at its core. It reeks of missed potential.
It genuinely pains my heart to say that.
A Hat in Time has all the ingredients of a truly great game, but the recipe has all the wrong serving sizes, and it ultimately left a bitter taste in my mouth. I feel emptier than I would have felt if I'd just skipped it.
---
People seem to like bringing up that I prefer Yooka-Laylee, as if that somehow invalidates my criticisms.
My argument is that if you removed all of A Hat in Time's cutesy charm, you'd be left with a lot of straightforward, run-of-the-mill platforming missions with a few cool boss fights mixed in.
Yooka-Laylee is clearly the less polished and less detailed game, but it has all the things I think A Hat in Time lacks: gameplay variety, rewarding exploration, lots of freedom and replay value... I just find it to be a genuinely more fulfilling experience.
This isn't to say A Hat in Time is bad, but I'd only recommend it at one third of its $30 price.

Like SimCity type games, but wish there were more "reality" based ramifications to allowing your city to become unbalanced?  Well, in this game your settlers starve to death.  Or stop having babies.  Or freeze to death.  Or...well, there are a lot of reasons why you will need to learn how to keep your settlement balanced.
You will need to havest resources like lumber, stone, iron, coal, etc.  You will need to combine them into other resources and products.  Find some berries?  You can eat them (which will feed your people) or turn them into an ale (which will make them happy).
You can turn the regular houses into stone houses so that they are warmer, though they can still burn down in the even of a fire (build wells!).  You can start trading to get access to the animals and plants that you didn't find on your own.  These plants and animals give you access to more resources that you can use to make better clothes, or other types of food/drink.
This is a game that will steal your life away from you, hour by hour.  You will fail in the beginning.  Your settlement will starve or freeze and you'll watch helplessly and try anything you can to stop it, but it will go until the only people you have left alive are too old to have children, and then they will die as well.
You'll try a new settlement the next time and get a little farther, but then you'll build too rapidly and forget to stockpile firewood right before winter.
The third settlement will be wiped out by disease and fire.
The fourth will be stable up to a point, but you'll struggle to expand.
The fifth is where you'll succeed.  And you'll as happy as your citizens.

They were going to kill Jalandar.
Lilliani remembered how she had once spent her mornings in front of a fire with the other children. She had grown with them, with the village. She lost herself in the many memories she had of the rainy Autumns and breezy Summer evenings. She could see the faces of her friends. Rolan, Allysa, Isbel and Jalandar. The memory quickly turned bitter and painful. She looked up at the path upon which Jalandar was to be led to the site of his execution. He had been flogged the first time, and marked so that the others would know what he had done. Now, he was marked for death.
The snowy wind cut across Lilliani's face. She winced and recoiled back, covering her weathered face with her ragged shawl. She could barely keep warm in her coat,  which hung awkwardly across her shoulders. It was heavy, and covered her frame unevenly. The frigid air cut like daggers into Lilliaini's body through places where the stitch-work had begun to fail. She pulled up her coat gingerly and hugged herself tightly.
The villagers gathered around the town-center. They were hardy men and women, who had faced many difficult years. Through each of them, they had endured, and found within themselves a grim, yet lively resolve which held the village firm.
It was different now. Too many had been lost and many more were sick. The physician had run off on the second day of the plague and had taken most of the herbs which had been scavenged in the sparse woodland to the east. They had nothing and could do little more than comfort those that died weeping. The fire that followed took the main storehouse which held all of the food meant to bring those that remained through the Winter. Jalandar was among the first to throw water at the flames. There weren't enough hands to put out the fire.Finally, the traders, many of whom likely heard of the plague, stopped coming. The trader's bell had not made a sound in months. Thus, the end lumbered forth inevitably and grotesquely.
The elders had begun to refuse food when the snows began to fall. They died first. Children followed. Bereft parents, along with the remaining elders and those too sick to work, were the last to receive rations. Soon, they would be bereft no longer. Several tried to steal food, causing the overseers to call forth harsh punishment against those who sought to avoid starvation more than others. Jalandar was among them. He had stolen for his wife, who was left weak following an illness.
The doors to the town hall creaked open, coming to a stop and hanging loosely on the hinges. Two men came out, holding Jalandar by his arms. He was a pathetic sight. His clothing was in tatters and his face was gaunt. He looked down at the ground as he was marched forward with no particular haste. The villagers had all turned to look at the condemned young man. Lilliani felt pity, and also anger. They all suffered. Jalandar knew this. He had accepted his fate. As he was led to the square, a silence had fallen over the stifled murmurs. The overseers stood waiting for the condemned. As he was led before them, Jalandar stared at the overseers with a small amount of condescension. Lilliani tried not to show emotion. She had seen death. She had seen friends die. Lilliani lost herself for moment, before coming back to see Jalandar looking at her. He was on his knees now. Lilliani closed her eyes, thinking of how quick it would be. He deserved at least that. She pulled herself away from what was come.
Lilliani came back with a start as someone pushed past her. There were many headed to the crowd growing by the neglected dockyard. Lilliani rushed towards the growing chaos. People shouted and pointed, and pushed each other. A few nearly lost their balance and fell into the cold waters. She tried to see what was causing the commotion. From the south, there was a soft silhouette. As Lilliani strained her eyes trying to see past the heavy snowfall, something made itself manifest. Laborers began to hurridly shift about. An overseer was shouting orders. The sound of a bell turned into a booming reverberation which seemed to shatter reality.

The power of this software is insane, especially making this type of game. If you want to make a small project you should be able to do so with little help or tutorials, but if your looking to make a blockbuster, it takes a lot of research, tutorials, youtube videos, and browsing around communities. Which brings up another good point, they have a tremendous community that is very helpfull, and if your looking to make a game your not selling you can grab all kinds of free add ons and pre wrote scripts. That is also a question i always see, can i sell my game that i made? Everything included in this software is royalty free, and same for any script you write yourself so you can definately sell your game but its gonna take some work to make it unique and not look like everyone elses games. Besides making top down rpg's i have played with this software and made platformers, mystery games, side scrollers, and straight cut scene 16 bit sequences. I believe this software is well worth the money for the power you get, and the simplicity of having scripts built in for you to use. ive tried other brands like unreal engine, unity, and a few others and they were just way above my level. i did have to learn a lot, but it is completely doable. After 5 small projects im doing a mega project with a friend and we have like 6 hours of gameplay (hoping to get in around 50) , that took us around 200 hours to make. i dont even have the game done but i have an amazing sense of accomplishment. I'm not just saying pick this up on sale , i'm saying its worth full price plus more, and if you sell your game this could be priceless.   There are 2 or 3 games currently built by this software that are under steam greenlight now, check em out!   11/10

RPG Maker has been a series I have always enjoyed, all the way back to RPG Maker on the PS2. However, if you want to get this because you want to be a game developer, you might want to look elsewhere. RPG Maker isn't really for anyone serious about making games. It's a decent tool to get your feet wet, but that's it. It's very specialized, and with that specialization comes restrictions.
If you just want to play around and make a simple game, then by all means, this is a great engine for that. But if you want to do something increasingly complex, this engine can fall short. Yes, you have the ability to do quite a lot via RGSS, but if you're competent enough to do that, it might be a good idea to look into more advanced engines.
Only main complaint about VX Ace specifically is that the mapping system is significantly worse than it was in XP. But, that's partially due to the graphic style change as well.
Oh and don't buy the DLC. I got them via a bundle and I can honestly say that they're mostly garbage, simply because they do not mix with the standard resources and there isn't enough content in the DLC packs to make their own resource library.

Limbo is best described as an extremely well-crafted artsy experience. The visuals are simple, yet incredibly detailed. The atmosphere is spot-on both visually, and audibly. The controls are simple: move, jump, interact. This is a puzzle game with no instructions. You will need to think about how you use the few things that are around you in order to progress. The game definitely “out-smarts” the player from time to time. There is no real “action” in this game… it starts off very calmly, slowly teaching you new mechanics. Later on, there are a few instances of puzzles that rely on precise timing of your actions, which can be a bit aggravating at times. The auto-save system is very forgiving. The entire game can be played seamlessly from start to end without any visible loading (unless you die.) The game will likely take about 3-4 hours on your first play-through, but doesn’t really have any replayability, unless you want to find the hidden eggs (which are cleverly hidden.)

But what about at night? Ever wonder what happens after hours? Do the animatronics just remain turned off? Do they keep singing throughout the night? Or do they step off of the stage for a while and freely roam around the resturant? Well, I don't know about Chuck E Cheese, but I do know that you don't want to be caught after hours at Freddy Fazbear's Pizza.
Think you have the guts to stay put in your security office long enough for the sun to come up before you get stuffed into a Freddy Fazbear suit? Don't worry! After all, it's only a six hour shift from Midnight to Dawn! Oh, and don't use up too much power too quickly. Freddy Fazbear's Pizza isn't raking in as much cash as it used to and power gets pretty costy. I wonder why? Maybe it's because of the bite of '87...
Anyway, your first few nights should be a breeze. Just check those lights and cameras, and only close the doors when neccessary. That $120 isn't going to earn itself, now is it? See you at the end of the week (hopefully)!

Blues and Bullets already screams crime noir from the title alone, but does it really have the guts to delve into its inspired roots or is the title simply misleading? Rest assured that this episodic adventure game from a Spanish team really picks up and shows promise in a genre long forgotten by gamers. Right off the bat in the first scene alone, the game has this stark contrast between black and white with touches of red dotting in once in a while. It's poignant and nostalgic and serves the setting well but mostly it's to mask the really crude texture work hidden in the darkness and the poor shadow work, though this isn't made with a big budget, so it's understandable. What the game gets right in the first few minutes it's the score. It's noir soul basically but the tracks in this game are very powerful and more fitting with the dark undertones of the game. The protagonist, Elliot Ness (who seemingly sounds too much like Geralt of Rivia) is your typical down on his luck detective with a love for violence and whiskey. It's typical in films and tv but seeing this sort of character in gaming with as plenty of backstory is rare and it's breath of fresh air to walk in his shoes. The writing also follows up on the positive side with it being relative to the genre once more. Sardonic quips and comebacks mixed with self hatred and dark comic saturate this game, and it works fantastic. Each character has their own identity though they have yet to be fully fleshed out since this is the first episode. The dark nature of crime noir gets a notch up in this game with one particular sequence being bathed in blood and gore so caution for those weak in the heart, this is not a game for fun.
The mechanics in contrast to this game however reveal the weakest aspect of the game. I understand that there are limitations given the small company, but even moving the character felt sluggish, shooting (while not an important aspect) was incredibly stilted and uneventful, and the animations range from passable to awkwardly stilted. The choices made in this game have yet to bear fruit, but I doubt I will be making a second run till the next episode fans out since you pretty much play the same scenes through and through. The games I can compare this most to are Life is Strange and The Walking Dead since they too were episodic and focused on your choices. Blues and Bullets is instantly captivating and compelling from the start and rears you into an adult tale of missing children and violence that has me excited for the next episode.
+ Dark, superb writing, brings out the distinct characters
+ Powerful soundtrack that evokes the noir feel
+ Atmosphere and visual design is top notch
+ Pacing is excellent, has me pumped for the next episode
+ One of the better usage of the Unity Engine, considering its saturation of the market
- Sluggish movement, animations, and shooting mechanics
- Game performance is subpar, my decent machine failed to keep a consistent 60fps
FINAL THOUGHTS: This game really surprised me. I didn't expect to enjoy as much as I did, which considering I really ignored the adventure genre. But the non-technical aspects of this game, are on par with the likes of Life is Strange (my current GOTY), though I have to say the writing for B&B is better.

I picked up "The Long Dark" on a whim. I saw it on sale for ten dollars during the Steam Exploration Sale, and I thought that it wouldn't hurt to give it a go. Being a novice with survival games such as "The Long Dark", I didn't know what to expect.
What I can report is that this game is nothing short of excellent.
Currently playing on a save file where my character has survived for 77 days straight, I can attest to the fact that I have pretty much seen it all. The game starts with your player being dropped into a random location in either one of two predetermined regions. The regions are interconnected, however, so you do have the freedom to move between the two maps currently offered (that is, if you can find you way between them). Your only goal is to survive in the harsh Canadian wilderness, and that is something much easier said then done. You will have to be patient and use cunning in order to most effectively exploit the resources at your disposal. Looting houses for supplies and finding fresh water and food when your on the brink of death is one of the most satisfying feelings I've ever experienced in a video game that is as intense as "The Long Dark" is. Your character can only hold so many things, however, so learning to store some of your provisions in a safe place and carrying only what you need is vital to your survival.
Other environmental factors such as the harsh weather and wolves must be accounted for. There is a rifle in the game, but you will most likely find without any ammo (a resource that needs to be discovered separately). Until then, caution is the name of the game as you attempt both to avoid the unforgiving Canadian weather and try to slip past wolves undetected. Few things are effective in even scaring the wolves off temporarily, and their eerie howls and snarling growls that ripped through my headphones as I ran towards my safehouse contributed towards one of the most tense and scary experiences in any video game I've played. The wolves themselves may not seem to pose a lot of danger, but as you survive day after day and week after week, the thought of a single one of them attacking you (resulting in your permadeath and the loss of all of your save progress) can be a devestating thought. But sneaky maneuvering is of the utmost importance when encountering one of the beasts.
"The Long Dark" is one of the most impressive games I've played in a long time. It's atmospheric, intense, and very, very addictive. It breaks with traditional, forumlaic gameplay in exchange for a much meaningful respite from the big and brash gameplay of many AAA titles nowadays. The sound design is excellent, the art design feels purposeful, and the user interfaces are very easy to navigate. With the Steam Christmas sale arriving soon, I have no doubt that Hinterland Studios will be dropping the price on this masterpiece. And that's only one of many reasons you should pick up "The Long Dark".
