They were going to kill Jalandar.
Lilliani remembered how she had once spent her mornings in front of a fire with the other children. She had grown with them, with the village. She lost herself in the many memories she had of the rainy Autumns and breezy Summer evenings. She could see the faces of her friends. Rolan, Allysa, Isbel and Jalandar. The memory quickly turned bitter and painful. She looked up at the path upon which Jalandar was to be led to the site of his execution. He had been flogged the first time, and marked so that the others would know what he had done. Now, he was marked for death.
The snowy wind cut across Lilliani's face. She winced and recoiled back, covering her weathered face with her ragged shawl. She could barely keep warm in her coat,  which hung awkwardly across her shoulders. It was heavy, and covered her frame unevenly. The frigid air cut like daggers into Lilliaini's body through places where the stitch-work had begun to fail. She pulled up her coat gingerly and hugged herself tightly.
The villagers gathered around the town-center. They were hardy men and women, who had faced many difficult years. Through each of them, they had endured, and found within themselves a grim, yet lively resolve which held the village firm.
It was different now. Too many had been lost and many more were sick. The physician had run off on the second day of the plague and had taken most of the herbs which had been scavenged in the sparse woodland to the east. They had nothing and could do little more than comfort those that died weeping. The fire that followed took the main storehouse which held all of the food meant to bring those that remained through the Winter. Jalandar was among the first to throw water at the flames. There weren't enough hands to put out the fire.Finally, the traders, many of whom likely heard of the plague, stopped coming. The trader's bell had not made a sound in months. Thus, the end lumbered forth inevitably and grotesquely.
The elders had begun to refuse food when the snows began to fall. They died first. Children followed. Bereft parents, along with the remaining elders and those too sick to work, were the last to receive rations. Soon, they would be bereft no longer. Several tried to steal food, causing the overseers to call forth harsh punishment against those who sought to avoid starvation more than others. Jalandar was among them. He had stolen for his wife, who was left weak following an illness.
The doors to the town hall creaked open, coming to a stop and hanging loosely on the hinges. Two men came out, holding Jalandar by his arms. He was a pathetic sight. His clothing was in tatters and his face was gaunt. He looked down at the ground as he was marched forward with no particular haste. The villagers had all turned to look at the condemned young man. Lilliani felt pity, and also anger. They all suffered. Jalandar knew this. He had accepted his fate. As he was led to the square, a silence had fallen over the stifled murmurs. The overseers stood waiting for the condemned. As he was led before them, Jalandar stared at the overseers with a small amount of condescension. Lilliani tried not to show emotion. She had seen death. She had seen friends die. Lilliani lost herself for moment, before coming back to see Jalandar looking at her. He was on his knees now. Lilliani closed her eyes, thinking of how quick it would be. He deserved at least that. She pulled herself away from what was come.
Lilliani came back with a start as someone pushed past her. There were many headed to the crowd growing by the neglected dockyard. Lilliani rushed towards the growing chaos. People shouted and pointed, and pushed each other. A few nearly lost their balance and fell into the cold waters. She tried to see what was causing the commotion. From the south, there was a soft silhouette. As Lilliani strained her eyes trying to see past the heavy snowfall, something made itself manifest. Laborers began to hurridly shift about. An overseer was shouting orders. The sound of a bell turned into a booming reverberation which seemed to shatter reality.

Okay, so this is going to be a VERY, VERY,
deep review on the game, primarily listing ways the game can improve and become even more amazing.
Okay, so I look at the game and think 'well this is interesting'.  And it was very interesting.  A game that focuses heavily on realistic survival?  That was something I wanted to try (particularly for 'research' for my own game ideas but that's beside the point)
Booting up the game I turn down the settings to make it easier to run on my computer.  After doing that, I take the time to explore, gather a few supplies, and spend a bit of quality time with the project.
Allow me to explain why this game is so engrossing by example.
I open my eyes, and before me lies vast expanses of white, broken only by the occasional trees and the long grey expanse of road that lies before me.  Taking a quick moment to go through my supplies and check my condition, I set out on the street, not sure of where it will take me.  The only background to my journeying is the soft fall of snow and the crunch of my footsteps as I walk, alternated with the quiet 'tap, tap,tap' my boots make when I cross from snowy ground to concrete.
In the distance, I catch the sight of a small settlement, and make my way over, hoping I might find someone to clue me in on where I am, or at least where I should go.  Then, out of nowhere, I hear a howl to my left.  My head snaps in the direction of the noise, and right there in the distance the black outline of nature's embodiment of enmity stands on its four legs, ever so conveniently facing the wrong direction to find me.
I loose no time, even if I'm not seen, dashing inside.  Once indoors, however, I find that I'm completely alone.  There's no point in calling out, the building is too small for anyone to hide in.  Instead, I start looking around.  Maybe I'm stealing, maybe I'm not, but right now my stomach is rumbling and my throat is parched.  I need food and water.  Now.
Thankfully the tiny cabin is somehow warm enough to fight off the cold outdoors, so after I take a moment to stamp my feet and shake off the outside chill, I start sifting through the place.  In the crates I find a tin of sardines, some matches, and a can of condensed milk.  Not bad, but in the locker I find some small tools and, more importantly, soda and an energy bar.  Score.
Without a second thought, I rip into the energy bar and down the soda in moment, satisfying my empty belly.  A winter coat lies hidden in the other locker, and I immediately put it on, feeling the warmth of my body becoming more solid, more
.
And now, I make for the door.  Maybe there's someone in the next building.  But as I step outside and move on, the creeping feeling of loneliness begins to set it.  I cannot shake the idea I'm all alone out here, and, seeing the houses on the two islands in the distance, the howl of the wolves in my ear, the creeping, crawling feeling of the cold setting into my bones, the food turning to lead in my stomach, I grit my teeth in preparation for my journey to live.
My journey...into
This is what the game does to you.  As you play, you gain the sensation of being a part of someone's story.  Even without story mode (which honestly does feel a small bit unnecessary for this game, though some win goal of some sort would be cool) you begin to settle into the character's situation.  In short you BECOME the character.  His plight is yours, when he succeeds you feel like parading around in victory, and when he dies you beat on your desk with a cry stuck behind your teeth as if you cannot accept what just happened.  (BTW my first death was, pretty much literally, sleeping to death.  As stupid a move as it sounds.  Note to self: don't sleep past the fire going out.  Ever)
That said, there are several ways to improve this game.  It is by no means perfect, however it is still a fantastic game.
I will be focusing on the major, core elements that should be added/fixed for the game.  (primarily added)
First off, there needs to be an alternative method to create fire other than matches.  This puts a time limit on the sandbox mode that is COMPLETELY UNACCEPTABLE.  You should be able to craft a fire-starting kit (I mean everyone knows you can rub a couple sticks together, but there's also a way to make that method even more effective).  In addition you ought to be able to craft weapons and other gear you can use to help you survive.  A spear, a shank, just something other than a knife you can use to keep yourself alive.
You should be able to make bait for your snares to lure over animals.  This is something that, while not necessary, is incredibly helpful and makes getting animals a bit easier, as you can set your traps up to attract the creatures and make it easier to catch them.  Sometimes a bit more ease is also realistic.  You should also be able to salvage cars for parts like metal and such so you have more access to them, this in turn is also realistic, because you'd need a tool to do it, but on the other side this would allow someone to make more repairs on their gear.
Speaking of cars, we not only should be able to strip them for parts and supplies, but maybe also be able to fix them up and, after siphoning some gas from other vehicles and making sure they work right, ride them around to make travel a bit easier.  Or at least make them a bit warmer!
And, on the subject of gas, I would like to be able to fix up a house and power it up again with the proper resources.  But that ought to be a long-term goal, like a finishing objective or something.  A thing to actually PURSUE other than survive.
A side addition would be some form of multiplayer mode.  Think Dark Souls.  Communication through action.  That would provide a more engaging element for when people don't want to survive on their own, while not entirely depcretiating the core single player value.
Perhaps we could also add the ability to capture animals as pets.  Like a wolf.  If you catch an injured wolf or trap it, then care for it and keep it alive over a long time, eventually the animal could warm up to you and become your partner.  You have NO IDEA just how emotionally investing that would be.  Spending hours and hours in game befriending and working alongside your animal partner only to have him die defending you, or rushing to save him/her from an attacking wolf and being just in the nick of time, or even just having him laying at the foot of your bed waiting for you to get up and start your day.  That stuff is GOLDEN for this game!  I cannot emphasize just how much more engaging this feature would make the game.  (if you cannot tell, I really want this in game).
One thing you could probably fix is decay.  Food should be able to be preserved either by being frozen or using salt or something similar.  This would allow it to last much, much longer and give players a way to keep food around for longer periods of time, since they cannot really use all of it right away, and while this prevents some of it going to waste, it at the same time teaches players to keep around ways to preserve their food for later use.  Not to mention things cannot always be fixed, so if something gets too badly damaged it should be, in some form, irreparably damaged.  While this would make things more difficult, it would also force players to focus more on keeping things in good condition and making sure that they don't waste anything.  This would be a good thing to patch into the game.
Finally, there ought to be some way to craft portably.  This is not necessary, but being able to just sit down and make something you need is a very good thing.  It lets players be mobile, though other things like repairing your tools and making big stuff, like big traps or cages, should be limited to the crafting tables.
That is all, thank you.

An episodic adventure game set in an alternate version of the 50's that will appeal to Telltale games fans. You play as Elliot Ness, former leader of the famous Untouchables and search for... Al Capone's grand daughter, who has been kidnapped. Game plays almost exactly like The Walking Dead or Game of Thrones - you interact with objects, make a lot of difficult choices and take part in some quick time events (and even shootouts). You may feel the low budget from time to time, but apart from that, the game is top notch.
First of all it has a fantastic atmosphere - you are not sure if everything is happening for real, or if it is some kind of delirious dream. In this alternate reality, the famous Hindenburg zeppelin has been turned into a hotel floating above the city of Santa Esperanza (by a guy named... A. Ryan; Bioshock, anyone?), hight tech submarines are stationed in the docks and gruesome murders are being commited by a cultist of an extraordinary strength, who is able to torn victims arms with his bare hands. There is also a case of missing children, that have been abducted by a strange sect, whos members are wearing bird-like masks. Story looks very promising and dense.
The graphics are nice as well - developers know how to operate lightning, depth of field and colors to create something unique and intriguing. Voice overs are ok as well - the performance of two main characters is really good and pleasant to hear. Music is awesome, though it has almost nothing in common with blues.
The first episode lasts for about two hours and features several choices that will have consequences in the future. You can buy it for 5$/€ and it's totally worth it. If you like it, get the rest of the episodes without paying twice for the first one, as there is Episodes 2-5 pack available.

Sweet, simple, and easy-to-use. No scripting knowledge required, even if you do want to customize a few things, since you can usually just type "rpg maker vx ace script" into google and you can find hundreds of scripts made by other people. Allows for heaps of customization, including music, sprites, battlers, battlebacks, tilesets, faces/busts etc. You can make your own skills, but if you're like me and can't find the patience to make 100+ skills, you can use the program's presets, alter them, add to them, rename them etc.
Heaps of resources, but you can import more from DLC packs, or certain websites.
For advanced users, there's the script editor (if you have any idea how to make scripts using Ruby) and you can also learn parallax mapping which looks really snazzy but is also really fiddly.
I definitely reccomend this program, especially for those with no idea how to make games. It's so simple and easy, that I started off with no idea how to even come CLOSE to making a game, and now I'm halfway through one!
Best of all, I've found it to be pretty much bug free, so I can spend more time on making games than pulling my hair out!
Definitely a program to buy, though, considering it's price, you might want to wait for it to be on sale first - that way you can get RPG Maker AND some of the DLC packs to kickstart you up.
Have fun everyone!

[TL;DR at the bottom]
Tales of Zestira is your typical JRPG - you've got your inconspicuous, a bit socially awkward protagonist, his childhood-friend who'd never leave his side, the nameless heroine whoiscertainlyofnoimportancewhatsoever *wink wink nudge nudge* and your set-up of "We're looking for a chosen one to save us from the demons."
Now then. How does ToZ manage to elevate itself into what is at least considered a highly-above-average JRPG?
Well - aside from the mundane story, we should firstly take a look at our cast of characters. Our protagonist, Sorey, is the first major factor. When we start the game, we can't choose his class, name, appearance or anything - which for some may very well be a negative, though it does enable the game to give him an actual persona. The player isn't meant to project himself into Sorey, but to emphasize with him during the game when the albeit few, yet very strong choices come up.
This is very important for Zestiria because although the story is as straight-forward and predictable as it gets, the characters are what makes it bearable. Your other party members all fit some sort of stereotype, as I already implied in the Opening, yet the game still manages to keep you interested. It manages to keep the cast on a level which is light-hearted, fitting with the story, yet tries to make you care for each and every member of your party.
This is were the first gameplay aspect shines: Skits;
Something I've not yet seen in many RPG's but may be compared to gameplay elements akin to the Camping of Dragon Age. Meaning: In Zestiria, if you for example explore a cave for some quest or even just to grind you can unlock "Skits" - or Dialogues between your characters by checking out different locations within that dungeon. These dialogues may only be humorous, may convey gameplay-explanations such as equiment fusion or may actually give some insight in the characters themselves. Though every single Skit is absolutely cleverly written and it is what always keeps the player hooked on the story and character progression, rather than violently seperating it's Gameplay from any form of party interaction.
The gameplay is not as in-depth as you may expect. What the game does is giving you a Rock-Paper-Scissors System which is called Artes. M. Artes > Mg. Artes > S. Artes and so on. Though this Artes System comes down to basically a combo system which you are expected to keep up with by learning needlessly complex Weapon Effects and how the different combat-aspects can be combined with one another.
You now might think "What is your problem with that? Sounds to me like a very in-depth system!" - This is only half true, really, as the game not only offers you a simple solution: You can spend AP (earned mainly by exploring) to unlock effects such as "Auto-Sidestep" or Control over your Partners or
<-- I've got a personal grudge against the last one, as the game arbitrarily locks many of your combat settings behind this AP-Wall. Want to move freely around the battlefield? No can do. You have to learn the Shortcut on your Pad and press it everytime you want to move as you like.
The thing that really kills this system though is that all this is not really necessary, as the difficulty of the game mainly comes down to micro-managing your party and if you're in a boss fight or not. Generally you can only control 1 character at a time + you can give vague commands to your teammates. Depending on your difficulty and on the enemy, this makes some bosses a nightmare. As the game requires you to learn patterns for bosses which may or may not result in 1-HKO's otherwise. Not being able to control the party AI properly is a big (-) in that case. Otherwise bosses tend to overscale horribly contrary to the laughable trash-mobs you encounter in any dungeon.
Is the combat system inherently bad though? Not really.. but it is definitely not the optimal mix between semi-strategy and action you might hope for, when thinking of buying this game. Many combat mechanics are just impractical, leaving the player to just stick with their standart-combos, which don't require you to learn some new shortcut, to rebind your new combos to any new button and so on. This of course also means, that players who want to get the maximum out of their character can still do so. It just requires a lot of getting used to and is in many cases just a wasted effort.
+ Great soundtrack
+ Clever character/party interaction
+ No separation between story/character progression and gameplay
+ In-depth customization (Gameplay + Characters)
+ Rewards exploration
+ NG+
- Generic JRPG Story
- Too much Info-dumping (Tutorial Messages throughout the game)
- Camera issues (Can somewhat be fixed by unlocking your movement in combat: See the next point)
- Some basic combat mechanics have to be unlocked first (e.g. Moving freely)
- Combat needlessly complex (at least when playing on anything below Hard-difficulty) and bad control over the rest of your party

Now many of these flaws are very subjective. I found myself enjoying the story despite its flaws, as Zestiria just presents itself so well - with the beatiful graphics and the outstanding soundtrack coupled with the character design of which I talked previously. The rest of the negatives are just my personal issues with the combat system which may very well not apply to you. Thus I recommend checking out a gameplay video on Youtube, before buying Zestiria.
All in all it is a very good JRPG for a reasonable price. Is it a must play? No. Certainly not. Fans of the genre will still have a wonderful time with it.

The basic gameplay allows for a variety of incredible movement options, which naturally open up to you as you get more used to its physics and controls. Co-op and the various gadgets available in the game extend these options further.
The difficulty of the game is also spot on. It gently introduces you to its mechanics, and then ramps up the difficulty continuously. By the time you reach the final (secret) level it throws some of the hardest challenges in any platformer I've ever played at you, but never feels arbitrary.

This is a fun little vertically scrolling schmup arcade style action game in the style of the early Raiden games. WOLFLAME differs from the early Raiden games though by giving you an infinite number of 'continues' which has the effect of making the game much easier and far less frustrating.
+Adequate, old-style late 1980's/early 1990's arcade game graphics with an extremely nice, nostalgic quality to them which is heavily reminiscent of the first few Raiden games (and other, similar styled arcade games from the early 1990s).
+Good, simple and responsive controls.
+Simple, easy-to-use menus.
+Good, though still fairly standard-feeling weapon upgrades.
+As you progress, the game's areas scale up in difficulty slowly but surely even on the easiest difficulty. This game features several difficulty levels for good replay value.
+Great game for the fairly low price of 6 dollars (and that's not even when this game is on a special sale).
+/-Enemies and levels are fairly standard for this type of game.
+/-Mediocre though not annoying sound effects and music. Mostly just generic sounding for this type of game.
-This game never gives you a great sense of speed. Indeed, the levels/areas scroll past fairly slowly.
-Certain bosses seemed underwhelming and a little repetitive (there are at least 2 levels which use some sort of tank or tanks as the main boss but that's still ok though because big tanks are cool, especially in this kind of game).
-There is only a single type of fighter craft which you can control.
-Perhaps the absolute worst thing that can be said concerning this game is that it may very well be a severe rip-off of the early Raiden games. That said, WOLFLAME is fairly well-done nonetheless and provides a great, nostalgic, classic arcade feel. If you collect vertically scrolling Schmup games (like I do), you should definitely buy this one too, at least when it goes on a special sale.

I picked up "The Long Dark" on a whim. I saw it on sale for ten dollars during the Steam Exploration Sale, and I thought that it wouldn't hurt to give it a go. Being a novice with survival games such as "The Long Dark", I didn't know what to expect.
What I can report is that this game is nothing short of excellent.
Currently playing on a save file where my character has survived for 77 days straight, I can attest to the fact that I have pretty much seen it all. The game starts with your player being dropped into a random location in either one of two predetermined regions. The regions are interconnected, however, so you do have the freedom to move between the two maps currently offered (that is, if you can find you way between them). Your only goal is to survive in the harsh Canadian wilderness, and that is something much easier said then done. You will have to be patient and use cunning in order to most effectively exploit the resources at your disposal. Looting houses for supplies and finding fresh water and food when your on the brink of death is one of the most satisfying feelings I've ever experienced in a video game that is as intense as "The Long Dark" is. Your character can only hold so many things, however, so learning to store some of your provisions in a safe place and carrying only what you need is vital to your survival.
Other environmental factors such as the harsh weather and wolves must be accounted for. There is a rifle in the game, but you will most likely find without any ammo (a resource that needs to be discovered separately). Until then, caution is the name of the game as you attempt both to avoid the unforgiving Canadian weather and try to slip past wolves undetected. Few things are effective in even scaring the wolves off temporarily, and their eerie howls and snarling growls that ripped through my headphones as I ran towards my safehouse contributed towards one of the most tense and scary experiences in any video game I've played. The wolves themselves may not seem to pose a lot of danger, but as you survive day after day and week after week, the thought of a single one of them attacking you (resulting in your permadeath and the loss of all of your save progress) can be a devestating thought. But sneaky maneuvering is of the utmost importance when encountering one of the beasts.
"The Long Dark" is one of the most impressive games I've played in a long time. It's atmospheric, intense, and very, very addictive. It breaks with traditional, forumlaic gameplay in exchange for a much meaningful respite from the big and brash gameplay of many AAA titles nowadays. The sound design is excellent, the art design feels purposeful, and the user interfaces are very easy to navigate. With the Steam Christmas sale arriving soon, I have no doubt that Hinterland Studios will be dropping the price on this masterpiece. And that's only one of many reasons you should pick up "The Long Dark".

Okay, so this is going to be a VERY, VERY,
deep review on the game, primarily listing ways the game can improve and become even more amazing.
Okay, so I look at the game and think 'well this is interesting'.  And it was very interesting.  A game that focuses heavily on realistic survival?  That was something I wanted to try (particularly for 'research' for my own game ideas but that's beside the point)
Booting up the game I turn down the settings to make it easier to run on my computer.  After doing that, I take the time to explore, gather a few supplies, and spend a bit of quality time with the project.
Allow me to explain why this game is so engrossing by example.
I open my eyes, and before me lies vast expanses of white, broken only by the occasional trees and the long grey expanse of road that lies before me.  Taking a quick moment to go through my supplies and check my condition, I set out on the street, not sure of where it will take me.  The only background to my journeying is the soft fall of snow and the crunch of my footsteps as I walk, alternated with the quiet 'tap, tap,tap' my boots make when I cross from snowy ground to concrete.
In the distance, I catch the sight of a small settlement, and make my way over, hoping I might find someone to clue me in on where I am, or at least where I should go.  Then, out of nowhere, I hear a howl to my left.  My head snaps in the direction of the noise, and right there in the distance the black outline of nature's embodiment of enmity stands on its four legs, ever so conveniently facing the wrong direction to find me.
I loose no time, even if I'm not seen, dashing inside.  Once indoors, however, I find that I'm completely alone.  There's no point in calling out, the building is too small for anyone to hide in.  Instead, I start looking around.  Maybe I'm stealing, maybe I'm not, but right now my stomach is rumbling and my throat is parched.  I need food and water.  Now.
Thankfully the tiny cabin is somehow warm enough to fight off the cold outdoors, so after I take a moment to stamp my feet and shake off the outside chill, I start sifting through the place.  In the crates I find a tin of sardines, some matches, and a can of condensed milk.  Not bad, but in the locker I find some small tools and, more importantly, soda and an energy bar.  Score.
Without a second thought, I rip into the energy bar and down the soda in moment, satisfying my empty belly.  A winter coat lies hidden in the other locker, and I immediately put it on, feeling the warmth of my body becoming more solid, more
.
And now, I make for the door.  Maybe there's someone in the next building.  But as I step outside and move on, the creeping feeling of loneliness begins to set it.  I cannot shake the idea I'm all alone out here, and, seeing the houses on the two islands in the distance, the howl of the wolves in my ear, the creeping, crawling feeling of the cold setting into my bones, the food turning to lead in my stomach, I grit my teeth in preparation for my journey to live.
My journey...into
This is what the game does to you.  As you play, you gain the sensation of being a part of someone's story.  Even without story mode (which honestly does feel a small bit unnecessary for this game, though some win goal of some sort would be cool) you begin to settle into the character's situation.  In short you BECOME the character.  His plight is yours, when he succeeds you feel like parading around in victory, and when he dies you beat on your desk with a cry stuck behind your teeth as if you cannot accept what just happened.  (BTW my first death was, pretty much literally, sleeping to death.  As stupid a move as it sounds.  Note to self: don't sleep past the fire going out.  Ever)
That said, there are several ways to improve this game.  It is by no means perfect, however it is still a fantastic game.
I will be focusing on the major, core elements that should be added/fixed for the game.  (primarily added)
First off, there needs to be an alternative method to create fire other than matches.  This puts a time limit on the sandbox mode that is COMPLETELY UNACCEPTABLE.  You should be able to craft a fire-starting kit (I mean everyone knows you can rub a couple sticks together, but there's also a way to make that method even more effective).  In addition you ought to be able to craft weapons and other gear you can use to help you survive.  A spear, a shank, just something other than a knife you can use to keep yourself alive.
You should be able to make bait for your snares to lure over animals.  This is something that, while not necessary, is incredibly helpful and makes getting animals a bit easier, as you can set your traps up to attract the creatures and make it easier to catch them.  Sometimes a bit more ease is also realistic.  You should also be able to salvage cars for parts like metal and such so you have more access to them, this in turn is also realistic, because you'd need a tool to do it, but on the other side this would allow someone to make more repairs on their gear.
Speaking of cars, we not only should be able to strip them for parts and supplies, but maybe also be able to fix them up and, after siphoning some gas from other vehicles and making sure they work right, ride them around to make travel a bit easier.  Or at least make them a bit warmer!
And, on the subject of gas, I would like to be able to fix up a house and power it up again with the proper resources.  But that ought to be a long-term goal, like a finishing objective or something.  A thing to actually PURSUE other than survive.
A side addition would be some form of multiplayer mode.  Think Dark Souls.  Communication through action.  That would provide a more engaging element for when people don't want to survive on their own, while not entirely depcretiating the core single player value.
Perhaps we could also add the ability to capture animals as pets.  Like a wolf.  If you catch an injured wolf or trap it, then care for it and keep it alive over a long time, eventually the animal could warm up to you and become your partner.  You have NO IDEA just how emotionally investing that would be.  Spending hours and hours in game befriending and working alongside your animal partner only to have him die defending you, or rushing to save him/her from an attacking wolf and being just in the nick of time, or even just having him laying at the foot of your bed waiting for you to get up and start your day.  That stuff is GOLDEN for this game!  I cannot emphasize just how much more engaging this feature would make the game.  (if you cannot tell, I really want this in game).
One thing you could probably fix is decay.  Food should be able to be preserved either by being frozen or using salt or something similar.  This would allow it to last much, much longer and give players a way to keep food around for longer periods of time, since they cannot really use all of it right away, and while this prevents some of it going to waste, it at the same time teaches players to keep around ways to preserve their food for later use.  Not to mention things cannot always be fixed, so if something gets too badly damaged it should be, in some form, irreparably damaged.  While this would make things more difficult, it would also force players to focus more on keeping things in good condition and making sure that they don't waste anything.  This would be a good thing to patch into the game.
Finally, there ought to be some way to craft portably.  This is not necessary, but being able to just sit down and make something you need is a very good thing.  It lets players be mobile, though other things like repairing your tools and making big stuff, like big traps or cages, should be limited to the crafting tables.
That is all, thank you.

A charming little game that shows that Kickstarter stories don't always end in failure. It matches it's own description of being a  "cute-as-heck 3D platformer" and still manages to pull ahead an possibly become one of my favorite 3D platformers of all time. As a longtime fan of games such as Super Mario 64/Sunshine and Donkey Kong 64; I can say for certain that A Hat In Time (AHiT) manages to encapsulate the essence of those games while still remaining unique on it's own rights.
The game does a fantastic job of creating large open ended mission based levels which engulfs you into those worlds and makes you want to wander off the beaten path and search through every nook and cranny for whatever secrets may be in the world. Either in the form of a collectible or a sly quip from one of the many characters that fill the large worlds of AHiT or simply to go off and jump and dive around the various areas of the worlds, AHiT's levels always seem to be briming with content and character.
As an aside, this doesn't mean the game isn't without flaws. One of the most jarring things to me personally is the voice acting. Not even that it is bad in general, just that there are some bad voice actors, especially in the beginning of the game from a certain mustachioed character. The rest of the voice actors do some fine work and as always the game has plenty of ways to ignore that either through simply disabling dialogue from the audio settings to buying the mumble badge that gives all the characters a Banjo-Kazooie-esque mumble sound. This game did do the mumbles very well mind you, unlike yooka-laylee's forced mumble that to be fair was quite horrid.
Another negative thing about the game would probably be the graphical fidelity of the game in terms of the character models. Some just don't look too good in and of themselves. The Mafia is a model that I may find in an older ps2 game or a very early xbox 360 game which looks jarring in comparison to the decent models on almost everything else. Thankfully the game's aesthetic does make up for it's shortcomings graphics wise thanks to the almost The Legend of Zelda: The Windwaker artstyle that makes the game feel very stylistcally sound and makes it a real beauty to look at.
Overall I would have to give this game a 9/10. I deeply enjoy most of the game. I adore the characters, I love the platforming and the levels for me are wonderfully constructed and I feel as if they had a lot of love put into them. The game does have some flaws and I do feel like they stop me from giving it another half a point or more.

I'm a complete sucker for Astro Port's stuff, but I'm particularly happy with Wolflame. I loved Satazius, their horizontally-scrolling homage to shoot-em-ups like Gradius, and Wolflame is the same level of homage to vertically-scrolling titles like Raiden.
Your ship can acquire two satellites, each of which shoots one of three different weapons and can be upgraded five times. When a power-up appears, it changes color as it moves around the screen, allowing you to switch each satellite's weapon type on the fly by grabbing it when it is the desired color. Having a fully upgraded set of satellites makes you feel powerful, but not invulnerable, especially at higher difficulty levels. My favorite aspect of the upgrade system is being able to recover your previous abilities after you die, if you are lucky enough to spawn the proper power-up icon and collect it with your new ship.
The graphics nail the intended retro aesthetic, and cover the usual variety of environments (land, sea, outer space). The game ran smoothly at 60 FPS on everything I tried, including a laptop with Intel 5000 integrated graphics. There are basic configuration options for resolution, controls, and difficulty. If you're looking for something to scratch a retro arcade shooter itch, give this a try!

I found this game after doing a simple Google search of 'Best City Builder' and this game did not disappoint. At first glance you may think this looks quite basic, but you would be wrong. There are not hundreds of buildings to choose from, there aren't that many at all really.
What makes this game so great is that it really is quite a challenge. If you think you'll start the game and just expand, expand, expand, then you are in for a shock. You need to keep a perfect balance to allow your town to grow without everyone starving to death, then once you have done that you focus on producing goods to trade for seeds and livestock until you have a fully self-functioning settlement.
Breakdown:
Graphics - 9/10 - Suits the game very well and allows for a very charming appearence
Gameplay - 9/10 - Build, Sustain, Trade, Expand. If you a die-hard city-builder fan. You'll love this gameplay.
Customisation - 8/10 - Even though there are only 2 types of basic house, not all of them look identicle, although they are random. When it comes to carving out room for your settlement, all the freedom is yours.
Longevity - 8/10 - The only limit to the size of your settlement is the edges of the map. And it will take you a VERY long time to grow a settlement to that size. You can lose hours in this charming game.
Worth the Money? - Absolutely
Overall - 8.5/10

You know, I imagine when Andy Warhol was a creator of art and released his Campbell's Soup Can piece in 1962 which was at the time a statement of how art in a capitalist society was becoming utilitarian, people who were in the know of the art movement were very divided about how they felt about it, just as how people are now divided over The Beginner’s Guide.
I thought for sure that Final Fantasy XV demo was going to be the weirdest thing I would have played all year but Davey Wreden of The Stanley Parable fame had to go and stealth release a game on steam.
I remember a bit in the Stanley Parable where the narrator, I think in a trailer or maybe, asks rather sarcastically “can games be considered art?” which was kind of the whole theme of the Stanley Parable where he was just kind of poking fun at these questions and exploring them a bit from a comedic angle and now having played The Beginner’s Guide a lot of that now seems pretty defensive, like Davey himself was making a joke about it because  he didn’t really feel comfortable about his own work, which is kind of sobering.
Which goes back to the campbells soup can thing. I think the utilitarian view of games, the review and press culture that hypes up games of being a certain gameplay hours per dollar ratio and lists features of the game like one would review a car or a mattress, is a large force behind the creation and releasing of this game. I think he feels like his games which are kind of these viewed as these “pretentious artsy fartsy walking sims” by many gamers really gets to Davey. I think he worries that people will think of him as a guy who makes weird games for the sake of being weird and that people will not understand his motivations.
I do genuinely think he is trying to push the medium forward, but after the Stanley Parable and after the critical acclaim it got from game critics, I don’t think he knows how. So now we have this which is sort of like an extremely personal, to the point of discomfort, cautionary tale for creators about the struggle with being recognized for your creativity.
And I really mean discomfort because while the game really did make me have a long hard think, it also was not an entirely always pleasant experience which is obviously the point, but I can really see people being turned off by it.
I’m still going to recommend the game even though I don’t know how exactly I feel about it because I think this is probably one of the most interesting games released this year. So if what I just wrote sounds like artsy fartsy ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t to you then yeah don’t buy it, but if you played and enjoyed the Stanley Parable or are a content creator yourself then I would say this is worth a look. But, this is also the first time I wish Steam had a neutral, in between, option for its user reviews, because that is closer to how I felt. Some of the negative reviews I’ve seen people put up I actually agree with in some respects. It’s a polarizing experience which might be all the more reason why it’s worth giving a look because that’s often what some of the most memorable art does.

I have to thank the DOOM 2016 open beta for introducing me to Unreal Tournament. I used to play DOOM 2 deathmatch over dialup when I was younger, and I was part of the Quake Alpha/Beta deathmatch trials back in the day. I loved online deathmatch, but went away from it for many years as FPS maps grew and gameplay slowed down. Playing DOOM 2016 deathmatch didn’t feel “right”, and the STEAM comments kept referring to Unreal as a much better online shooter experience. So I grabbed UT GOTY and the rest of the UT series. How right these commenters were….Unreal Tournament GOTY is one of the best games I have ever played. The graphics are amazing, the gameplay is action packed – so fast and adrenaline pumping. It is a pure Arena FPS, and in my opinion Unreal perfected the formula with UT GOTY. I’ve played the later games, which are fun in their own way – but this is just perfection. I loved the Mortal Kombat style voice over as the match went on…”Killing Spree….MULTI KILL” – and the tirade of smartass one liners from the bots, full of personality each one of them. The science fiction theme allows so much variety in levels, which are all full of colour and life…no brown and drab here. Musically, the tracks are all pumping electronica, that capture the essence of each level and the thrill of combat. The story, thin as it is, is all it needs to be – a couple of lines introducing the character or level, and the fact you are in an interstellar deathmatch tourney run by an evil corporation (cool!). The levels are awe inspiring, and I’d have to say the Facing World CTF map is up there with icons such as the Colosseum and Pyramids in its grandeur and online community reverence. No wonder it appears in all the sequels! Even if the online community dies off for this game (I can still get a match online today (2016) through the game which was released in 1999!) – I could always play with the bots, which are powered by the amazing Reaper technology which kept me hooked on Quake when I was younger. Thankfully I discovered this game late in life, otherwise I probably would have been hooked and not able to study or work or find a relationship. A masterpiece.

This game strikes a nerve. It dives into the mind of the creator of the many worlds you explore throughout the experience, narrated by the collector of these games, who is the creator of The Stanley Parable.
The games you play, big and small, are imaginative, beautiful, and intimate. They're experimental, unusual, and heavily metaphorical. The player begins to know the creator of these games after spending time with them.
So much of this experience needs to be left for the player to have firsthand. I highly recommend this game if you think about the creative process or what motivates you. I will say that to get the most impact from it you may want to be familiar with The Stanley Parable, not for any concrete gameplay purpose, but to understand the narrative.
The game goes beyond what you might expect, exploring emotional depths that left me pondering quietly for quite some time. It has a message, or at least raises questions, that I believe we all relate to.
It's important. It's valuable. Play it.

Soooo this game is hard to decide wether it wants to be a good platformer or not, purely because of development issues and/or oversights, I'll make it as simple as possible to explain...
I first saw this game on a Let's Play and instantly fell in love with the couch Co-op implication, as well as the aspect of the game itself, very inviting and intriguing to play. I downloaded this game without hesistation because I love playing adventure co-op games with the partner for hours of joyful fun, but after an hour or so, it started to go downhill, but I'll get to the issues as they come to mind.
Gameplay & Story - 7/10 - You drag a dead king in a box to lay him to rest in a suitable area, but sorry, your resting place is in another plot of land! That's the main plot of the story thus far for me, which looks like is the whole game, the gameplay is addictive for completionists, but leaves me frustrated when the game doesnt allow you to get that thing which is arms length away due to an item you get later on in the story, it's frustrating to not get the best score possible just because we haven't completed it yet.
Sound 8/10 - The sounds are okay, nothing special, the latch onto the coffin thing to save it from oblivion will be heard alot, and the caves arne't too bad, but it's nothing too noticeable, feels the same every level.
Visuals 8/10 - I would give this game a higher score for visuals, but I just cant when so many things look the same, no memorable landmarks and nothing that wows me, apart from the pretty plants that bloom from the chariot, and the glimmering lights alongside pretty collectable gems, which is a nice touch.
Issues - As well as what was mentioned in the Gameplay paragraph, there are technical issues that have made us quit the  game a few times, again, the concept is great and so is the game, but here are the things that should be fixed
- Controller jams up, and one player takes the form of an out of control chicken in Zelda, rendering the player useless to maintain control of him or herself, the "chicken" will fly around in the air whilst holding onto the chariot, this can only be fixed by disconnecting the controller and trying again, losing your stance if you are currently holding the chariot.
-Whilst climbing your own rope, you can glitch and fling yourself somewhere unexpected if you have the chariot in a tight position
-The physics of the game are not explained clearly, I know we shouldn't have hand holding, but some things punish you too much for falling off a ledge (Yes I'm looking at you Co-op challenges and platforms the side of a pea)
-The "maze system" and multiple paths are opinionated, some parts you can't get to can be annoying and having to pause just to see the map is a bore, halting the experience, mainly what was explained earlier, completing a level perfectly doesn't mean you did great, just means you're going to want to grab it all again when the story takes you back through the area.
Verdict 7-10 - I can't say it's a bad game, it's very pretty and feels good in my Steam Libary, but I also can't say it's great, I'm hoping to keep playing it but the issues are too frustrating to ignore, even after coming back fresh and ready to try again, I shall recommend The Chariot, but I'm skeptical about doing so, fix the issues, and everybody's happy

First I want to say do not take all the negative reviews as a critique on the game, they are mostly left from people who are angry at the company for the previous Godus release. You will find the discussions where people say I must play at least 0.1 hour of this so I can log in and give a negative review. I am not a person who cares about politics or the effects of past reviews of another game. Point in fact I played Godus, I liked Godus, I still like Godus, it just needs more work. ON to Godus Wars.
The game itself is slightly different from Godus because it relies on an unfinished combat system as opposed to simply collecting pink bubbles and trinkets and other stuff from Godus. Instead we have a map where you choose a God and fight an opposing God for world dominance.
Although the game will probably get harder later on, in this form it is very easy for anyone who plays strategy games, and by that I mean, make lots of archers and keep sending them until you overwhelm the opposing forces.
Now even though its very simple, and very easy in its present form, there is something here worth playing. I like style that they have built the game upon, and appreciate the 1v1 battles, though simple to win.
It's still early access and clearly they need to do a lot of work to make this more of a game, more warrior types, weapons, cards, etc, but what they have now is a good start,
The only thing I thought was bad, was the rolling random active rules that makes it look like a direct ripoff of hearthstone, but it could just be a placeholder for something later. The fact that it uses a launcher to open an additional window can throw you off at first as well, but someone who is used to playing games like League of Legends has seen this kind of thing before.
All in all a good start, needs work, but shows some promise. Is it worth what they are asking? That I don't know. As someone who purchased Godus and was given Godus Wars free, I can see why someone might think its not worth the $14.99 price tag in its current state and that's a fair observation. I like playing the game, and though this is clearly more mobile oriented in its current form, its still a good game. My final verdict is 7 out of 10. It could easily get a higher rating when more is added to it.

is very much in the spirit of Toaplan. The deal with Toaplan shootemups is that they excel at the fundamentals. When you play one of these classic games, you're not going to be dazzled by fountains of pretty bullets and thousands of shiny gold medals. Every moment of these games is a life or death struggle. The one tank that you miss just might be the one that takes you down. ASTRO PORT delivers yet another thriller that is sure to please any shmup fan.
Like most other shmups,
has no story to speak of. The goal is to destroy everything, collect a few medals, and try not to get shot down too often. The scoring system is pretty basic. All of the medals you collect in a stage are cashed in at the end for a lot of points, provided you don't die and lose them. Actually, you might as well try not to die at all, because spare lives are worth a ton as well. Unlike most shooters, there's no huge penalty for using bullet-clearing bombs. Even if you manage to collect a full stock, any extras are worth a measly 100 points each.
There are two kinds of bullets in this game, the kind that distract you, and the kind that kill you. The killer bullets are easy to spot. They're purple, thin, and fast. Most of the enemies that fire purple bullets are tanks, turrets, and so on. It's actually pretty sensible, since smaller ships don't have the power to maintain control, while firing such a powerful weapon. Typically, the killer bullets are fired when the enemy has you in their sights, so if you're not constantly moving, then you're probably going to die. As soon as a tank appears on-screen, either destroy it or get out of the way, because they're extremely deadly.
That's not to say there aren't any of the typical bullet-spreads we associate with STGs, but they're only a part of the threat. These slow yet plentiful bullets are there to catch your eye, force you into bad situations, and basically "herd" you into just the right spot. What happens next? If you guessed that a tank would appear practically out of nowhere and snipe you, then congrats! Your prize is a trip back to the last checkpoint.
Yes, Wolflame is a checkpoint-based shooter. That means you don't instantly respawn when you die. Thankfully, there's usually a nearby power-up that restores all of your lost weapons. The checkpoints are also a lot more reasonable than some of the earliest shmups. Still, getting kicked backwards upon death can be very punishing. Having to re-do bosses as well as brutal segments can chew through your spare lives pretty quickly.
One more thing: Like a number of vertical shooters, the screen shifts slightly to the left or right depending on your position. This can be useful, because enemies don't fire when they're off-screen. However, you also want to make a mental note of any enemies that are off-screen, just so you don't move over and suddenly get point-blank blasted by a killer bullet.
It's interesting that
is mentioned in the store-description for this game.
is the game that got me to fear tanks again. After several years of danmaku bullet-hells, where avoiding billions of bullets almost becomes effortless, I was re-introduced to the dreaded tank. Tanks in
only fire one bullet, but one bullet is enough in a shmup.
understands that same philosophy, and its legions of meticulously placed tanks and turrets are sure to confound and enrage a new generation of gamers.

Blues and Bullets is an adventure game that reminds me a lot of LA Noire and Telltale's The Walking Dead.
The game sees famed detective Elliot Ness, now retired from the police force and running a diner, pulled back in to solve a case of missing children, one missing child in particular.
It has quite a heavy focus on narrative, often times when in control of Ness you are limited to very small areas and can only walk around looking at a few items of interest before continuing with the story.
Conversation trees and dialogue choices are the main part of the gameplay, some choices more important than others but in a similar way to The Walking Dead you're often forced to make quick decisions and even when time wasn't a factor and I didn't feel the decision I made would really effect the story one way or the other I still found myself pausing to think, which to me is always a good sign.
Aside from that there are a couple of brief QTE sections and you'll get into a couple of shootouts, which are sort of on rail sections that I feel work quite well. Ness will move forward once you've killed the current enemies before stopping at the next piece of cover for you to repeat the process.
Combat involves aiming, popping out of cover and shooting. You can occasionally move from one piece of cover to another (there is no direct control though, you simply hit a button and Ness moves) but other than for a bit of variety there doesn't seem to be any point to this.
There are also crime scenes (or rather a crime scene in this first episode) for you to explore.
I hope that in future episodes more areas can be like this one was, a lot more open with a lot more to inspect and uncover.
You walk around looking at areas, occasionally zooming in to a specific location, like an overturned table, to look for more clues. These are all placed on a board and you need to match the right clues to the right heading.
For example, which clues tell you how the assault happened, which clues prove there was a witness, that kind of thing.
Nothing overly challenging and there's no penalty for choosing the wrong clue but exploring the environment and gradually piecing together what had happened kept me interested.
I really like the game's look, black and white with small dashes of colour here and there. It's very striking and fits the mood and theme very well. Performance was a little sluggish on the highest settings with a Radeon HD7800 series but absolutely fine on medium and the game still looked great, for the most part.
There are a few rough edges, animations are a little iffy in places, there's the odd graphical glitch and some people might find the pace a little slow but the story and the characters are pretty strong.
Voice acting on the main cast is very good and although this first episode is just kind of setting up the characters and the plot it's definitely got me intrigued.
If you can overlook the slow pace and some slightly rough edges I'd say it's well worth checking out.
If length is a factor I should note Episode 1 took me just under 3 hours.

RPG Maker VX Ace is a very powerful tool, especially when you know how to use it. While not as easy as it is advertised where you can simply pick up the program and go straight into making games ( actually you can, but there is a chance you're going to get stuck), it is one of the best tools that is readily available.  Though, admittedly, not much is really needed to start since you learn as you go through tutorials and good old fashion trial and error. The program comes with everything you need to make a straightforward enough 'classic' rpg game; graphics, music, special effects, the means to program and coordinate 'events', the ability to customize character classes, set abilities, even a character generator which does help when you're not familiar with spriting (I'm still learning! :D ), and so much more! The amount of customization is astounding, even further, the potential of your projects are limitless if you have the time and means to dedicate to your game. (Not to mention all the DLC which is now readily available!)
What I say I love best about RPG Maker is the community, they are more than willing to help provide resources such as tutorials, music, advice, graphics, scripts, and anything else you might need. So far from what I've seen, they are very welcoming and always happy to see new game makers on the rise. The community is supportive, but they also urge you to stand on your own and make your own mistakes.
I definitely would recommend this software to anyone who has wanted to be a game developer or just has a passion for the medium, whether you're doing this for the pursuit of putting out a commercial project or something you want to do on your down time rpg maker is worth it.

When I went into this game, I was initially surprised at the level of polish and style it had.  I thought it was going to be another simple yet endearing platformer with straight-forward mechanics and tranquil atmosphere.
Boy was I wrong.  The difficulty curve on this game is very steep, and goes near vertical at the end.  Never have a played a more unfair, un-fun, absolutely punishing game like this.  I made a steadfast attempt to complete this game, but the fact that you are locked out of 100% completion by a controller-throwingly hard hidden level is almost baffling.
I've gone through much of the game in both single player and co-op, and the results are roughly the same.  Initial levels are simple, and actually enjoyable.  After you leave the starting zone, the game kicks up the difficulty in all the wrong ways.  Slippery ledges, timed switches, needless enemies, weird flippy bridges. It makes this game an overall chore to play.
To add insult to injury, some levels are repetitive and excessively long.  A couple of the sections are more tedious than difficult, forcing you through five minute platforming ordeals, only for you to slip and fall to some unforeseeable physics glitch or auxiliary mechanic.  At which point, you have to pick yourself back up, and do it again a couple more times with similar results.  The game goes from enjoyable to unbearable very quickly.  You know something is wrong when you greet every checkpoint with a "God, finally".
It strains my brain to think why this was the intended difficulty.  Who is the target audience for this game?  Is this really supposed to be a casual buddy co-op game?  If so, it's far too difficult in its current state.
I can really only recommend this to the most masochistic of co-op players, or perhaps the most suicidal of single-players.

Let's get straight to the point - from what I heard from the negative reviews and criticisms, I thought this game would suck. "Typical JRPG dungeon crawler, graphics problems, crappy story, bad battle system"
I was greatly surprised, however, when I booted the game up for the first time. Maybe it's because of my i7 laptop, but the graphics were gorgeous. For those who are fans of RWBY, the animation style in-game is very similar to what Tales of Zestiria has, but with a bit more polish and attention to detail. As a fan of RWBY, seeing a similar animation made it so good for my eyes; but that's not what this game is about.
I'm 6.5 hours in, and I can say on normal, the game is pretty damn good so far. There's been some slight problems with syncing of character positions - but its very minor and happens rarely. That being said, let's talk about the battle system.
Like what has been said, there's a fusion system included within the battle mechanics that help to spice up the battles - because come on, what's better than beating up enemies than with shiny final attacks and combos that make your mouth water?
Also, the cutscenes between the major scenarios of the game are all in anime-quality, which I love.
In all honesty, I really do think - and expect this to be - an excellent game.

I've played for a few hours now, so I feel like I can give an honest review of Godus Wars.
To premise, I have play tested godus quite a bit back when it was actively being updated: about a year ago.  I put in 175+ hours, though probably 50 of that was leaving it on when I went to bed, since the first few interations had relatively slow belief respawn times.
I've seen Godus when it was new - lots of bugs, but relatively fun.  Then, cleaning the slate and beginning again.  I didn't like the second attempt as much as I liked the first, but I still play-tested and reported bugs here and there.  And then *it* happened - i.e. the game was released on mobile platforms and that was when **** hit 22cans.  The production of the game basically died, forums exploded in rage, Peter asked if he was pathologically a liar, etc.
Now, a YEAR since the last update, I can say I am pleased that this little game came out - *finally, something*.  I am going to base this game against populous, and against the previous Godus (which comes with this game if you want to play it).
Against populous:  This game is very simple in it's current form.  On the first continent there is only 2 units: the villager, and the archer.  Another unit, the catapult, appears for the enemy on the second continent, but I never was able to use it myself.  Compare this to Populous, which had 7.  From an RTS standpoint, having so few attack unit types seems silly.  They do level up, which makes for some differentiation between the different units, but their movement and attack patterns are the same.
In populous, you had a shaman who cast the powerful "god-like" spells.  In Godus Wars, you can sculpt land but your spells are limited to those you bring with you, in the form of cards.  You get 4 cards per match, and you gain cards as you progress through the continent. (I have completed second continent, so my review at this time doesn't deal with any continents after that).  I don't like this aspect of the game and I feel it needs work, or some sort of explanation or reasoning.  Why does a God have to choose only 4 spells?
One big thing - the sculpting is much more enjoyable and comfortable in Godus Wars than in Populous.  Also, I like the updated graphics.  In most ways, however, Populous beats Godus Wars from an RTS level.
Against Godus:  These two games are very different.  Most of the time you spend in godus is spent in a zen-like state or half-subconscious state where you are just doing things and clicking on things.  What is the goal?  It's hard to say... you are doing things for kinda whatever you want.  Back when you built roads to make settlement types, that was probably my favorite thing to do for some reason.  Anyways, Godus it's NOT a great revisioning of populous.  External threats don't present themselves for a very long time, and dealing with those threats is like dealing with pesky ants.  They are really just an annoyance, and can be very difficult to exterminate.
You are limited in strange ways in Godus.  Ex. Your villagers are dependent on you for all resource gathering (wtf).
Godus Wars does not suffer in this way.  Belief is automatically collected.  It is the only resource at the moment.  So, rescource management wise it feels much better and in-line with a god game for me.  I hope they re-add the resources for some purpose, and they are still auto-collected.  In general, more depth needs to be added to Godus Wars.
General review of Godus/Godus Wars:  I truely would personally like to see a true God Game where villagers make up their own minds, and maybe your actions determine behaviors or characteristics of the culture within your people.  Gods do not manually control people or cause wars.  They influence belief systems and THAT can lead to conflicts within differing cultures.  I think 22Cans needs to really reconsider what they have going here in general.  For more info reference the predestination forum thread in origional Godus...
So in conclusion:  Do I recommend Godus Wars?  I think it is close, but yes.  I find that when I finish a match I'd like to play another, and that is how I base if I am enjoying playing a game or not.
It is a milestone between Godus and Populous.  The game does not suffer from the click-fest of resource collections that Godus had, but as an RTS Populous has more depth to the strategy.  However, it has a LONG WAY TO GO TO BE A FULL GAME, but also HAS THE POTENTIAL TO LEAD TO A GREAT GOD RTS GAME NOW.  I would only recommend it to people with patience, and who are willing to really wait on the game.

I am consistently impressed with the games that Astro Port develops. They seem like a bunch of very talented people who really understand what makes games tick. Wolflame is no different.
If you're expecting a super innovative game that turns the Shmup genre on its head then this isn't for you. You have a shoot button and a bomb and that's it. It is built from the ground up to play like older shmups such as Raiden or any of the classic Toaplan titles, but without the arcade hard difficulty designed around milking quarters out of people. If you like those games you will love this one. It is challenging, but in a fair way, it keeps you wanting to play and overcoming the difficult spot you're in instead of giving up.
You have 3 different subweapon powerups, one is a powerful green laser that shoots slightly off to the side, a blue laser that locks on to any enemy it touches and a red spreadshot with homing laser. A cool feature is the ability to mix and match two of them, one for each wing, the powerup will show you which wing it is for with a direction, you can power each up to 5 levels, then you get 5000 bonus points for everyone you colect after that. I like to stick with dual green laser as it wrecks everything pretty hard.
It has checkpoints instead of instant revival, but unlike older shooters it is much easier to recover thanks to the ability to grab your previous powerups back contained in a single pickup, if you miss it then you may have a bad time :). Even if you get stuck with the peashooter starting weapon, the checkpoints are very well done, the game seems designed around having lower power weapons so if you're maxed out you will do serious damage, even to bosses. THe game is fairly long for a Shmup, expect to take around an hour to an hour and a half for a first run, it's even got a save and load feature. The scoring system is very basic, you find hidden medals and it tallies them up at the end of the stage, aside from that just kill everything you possibly can and don't die.
The game has many different enemy types and really good encounter design, they clearly put alot of thought into placement instead of just swarming you with enemies and bullets. This game isn't bullet hell, opting for simpler, easier to read but much faster bullets. Every single enemy in this game is deadly, you should fear even a lone basic tank which can easily snipe you when you least expect it and end your run. This combined with the checkpoint system makes the game very tense and exciting in a way that bullet hells can't touch. Bossfights are well done and memorable, though the first few die very quickly due to the stages being easy and your ship having full power. There are 10 stages in total with a nice difficulty curve throughout, there was no sudden spike in difficulty.
The graphics look nice, far better than the typical 2D game on Steam. Everything is very distinct and easily recognizable. The sound effects give it a nice punch and the music fits perfectly, though it isn't the sort of thing I would listen to outside of the game. You can change how loud the sound effects and music are seperately.
For video options you can switch between fullscreen and windowed, you can increase or decrease the size of the screen and the game supports TATE mode. Controls are fully rebindable with keyboard, cannot comment on controller support.
Great game overall, I highly recommend it. It doesn't do anything all that new, but excels at what it does set out to do, which is all you need.

I'm giving this a cautious thumb up. If money is tight there are better things to spend it on but it's a good solid game and worthy of the Total War title. I bought this game on sale some years back and it was sitting in my library. I was obsessed with Rome 1 in college and played Medieval II until my eyes bled and loved the modding community. One thing they pointed out was the games got worse and worse. I would say Napoleon is worse than Empire. It's just too focused on the one dude.
That said, Napoleon's conquests were remarkable and they were able to fit four campaigns and numerous historical battles in a game. What that man was able to accomplish is on par with Alexander, Belarius or Caesar any day. It's a complete game, don't get me wrong, but it's more narrow than Empire Total War. I think part of the problem is large studios like this feel the pressure to release their flagship games every year or every other year and the quality degrades. This really should have been marketed as a stand alone expansion to Empire Total War because that is what it is.
So much was borrowed from Empire from animations to text you name it. They improved some things though. I love shooting people off horses now and having the horses flee. However, there were some things that aren't as good as Empire. The main thing is stability. The game just freezes up during the battle phase and usually towards the end forcing you to replay sometimes really amazing battles. Also, the sound glitches after a battle. This can be fixed by alt tabbing.
One thing that they did, which I hope they do in the later Total Wars that I haven't played yet, is have a storyline. It's basic, you follow Napoleon. But Napoleon is such a remarkable character there was a lot to take from. I loved the King Arthur Roleplaying Games by paradox because it had a storyline. I was very pleased to see Total War (which gameplay is better) attempt to do the same and I hope future Total War projects go that route more.

RPG Maker has always been famed as being just about the best of the "Do-It-Yourself" Game Makers. With this, you don't have to master complicated programming languages or coding to make an awesome RPG. It's mostly point-and-click, and easy to define events and scenes.
And if you don't like the default characters, settings, enemies, etc., you can go ahead and draw your own creations. Same with the music and sound FX; or even adding videos to make awesome cutscenes. The sky's the limit.
RPG Maker VX Ace is reliably stable, and easy to work with. And for the more advanced user, if the default system isn't to your liking, the Scripting option allows you to alter the game's coding to suit your tastes.
Admittedly, the price tag is a little bit steep.
But, consider this: How many times have you spent $50-$60 on a single RPG game, with a strange, excessively philisophical, "over-your-head" kind of story? Or featuring a line-up of characters that your just simply don't like? And ultimately, at the end of the game, leaves you feeling cheated out of a good gaming experience?
But with this software, YOU can write a good story, one that YOU like! Create whatever characters that you want, and define their personalities however you see fit! Make the game (and the battle system) as easy or as hard as you want!

You technically can get/make MANY RPG games, all for slightly more than the cost of one regular, over-hyped $60 RPG. And, on Steam, you also get a fine community of fellow RPG game makers.

The Beginner's Guide is a surreal and immersive narrative about Davey Wreden's (Stanley Parable) developer friend, and why he retired. The way the game takes full advantage of what a medium like video games have to present is interesting, and smart.
So let me get this out of the way first and for most "Hold W to game". That's it. It's even less "gamey" than the Stanley Parable. I want people to understand this before even considering the Beginner's Guide. There's no mechanics, there's no real choice, it's very much a linear hour and a half trip being lead by Davey Wreden as the narrator. With that said, The Beginner's Guide really can't be told in any other form than through a video game.
Since the story is about Davey's developer friend, it takes you on an interactive tour through his friend's past games and levels. The game's aesthetics and concepts progressively get better and complex over time. The game is also very forth wall breaking, immersing the player into the narrative as a character in this story itself. Davey will often make reference to you, as you play through the game. It's a surreal experience, and it certainly breaks all sorts of video game norms.
If you're looking for a unique experience or just like really well told stories, The Beginner's Guide is an easy recommendation. However, if you're looking for a game, even for an off beat game, The Beginner's Guide might disappoint. As mentioned above, there's really no mechanics to speak of, other than hold W to game. In Gone Home you have to look for keys and can interact with objects all around. In The Stanley Parable you have a pseudo fail state and an Easter egg hunt for all the endings. Even in most other "Walking Simulators" you have some kind of puzzle, or obstacle along the way. Not in The Beginner's Guide. There's only 1 puzzle in the game, and that's solely there as a story element. There are dialogue choices to be made, but they have no significant (or any) effect on your game. It's very much a guided tour through an interactive narrative. It's also relatively short at an hour and a half (I finished it at exactly 91 minutes). But if you're able to focus on the quality of the experience the game tries to deliver, and willing to let go your previous conceptions of what to expect from a video game, The Beginner's Guide is top shelf material.
Overall The Beginner's Guide is a story that could only be told through a video game, yet ironically is one of the least "gamiest" game I've ever played. The story is surreal, immersive, and certainly something to be experienced for fans of great narratives, but the title of "video game" will be controversial to some on this one.
Pros:
- Amazing Story
- Good use of the medium
- Surreal and immersive

NOTE: I am not finished yet. I am working on it. At time of this update of the review, the final boss is defeated and I am merely doing post-game stuff on the first playthrough. The review will continue being updated over the course of probably multiple playthroughs. I will give some minor spoilers of the ending (such as if I thought it ended the story well, or of I thought there was more to be desired from it). I will consider this review probably less than 25% complete, based upon how close I am to doing enough in game to consider it done.
Now the actual review:
This game is a must have for those who are very much into the jrpg genre, but I would not suggest it for those new to the genre, as this is NOT a good intro. Pick up something a bit better.
PROS:
+Simple yet complex battle system
+Great gameplay
+Reasonable number of save points
+Quick save for when you are in a hurry to stop playing so you can get ready for work
+Very dynamic characters - You know, not one that you meet and 10 seconds later you know what type of character they are. I hate that...
+Overall story. I saw a lot of people saying they didn't like it, but I personally don't find it as bad as some people seem to be making it out to be. Sure it is a little cliché, but they did it in a pretty good way.
+Final boss is a hidden face for the first third of the game or so, adding to his mysteriousness.
+Optional bosses are plentiful.
+Dungeon puzzles are unique and creative, while providing a challenge for a moment.
+Each character has costumes they can put on, making each one unique in your own way.
+I can combine two of my favorite things into one fighting style: fire and swords.
CONS:
-Turn off subtitles turned off voices when I tried
-Will take time to get used to battle system
-My favorite character dies. I won't say who to avoid spoilers, but that one dies.
-Some parts of the battle system were so complex I didn't bother for my first playthrough. Might when I get to the second.
-Level difference between bosses and minor enemies around him/her can be quite high, as high as 20% by my estimate.
-Final boss can be a pain to deal enough damage to in order to beat.
-Optional dungeons (or "ruins") show no variety, just all of them basically "use the coorosponding power on each dead end with a symbol to unlock more, and find the way down as quick as you can."
-The ending left more questions than answers, which makes much to be desired. I did, however, like what I understood went on.
-Post-game bosses are EASIER to beat than final boss, despite being 13 levels higher at the minimum, and the most recent beaten was 25 levels higher, and still easier. No, I don't say this because I am a higher level, but because there is less strategy needed.
-Lailah has ADD
Disclaimer: These points are subjective. A person might like to grind to become a high enough level to match the boss. The last in each section are not serious, although they do exist.
Most recent rating I'd give this is 7.5/10, with it getting about 1-1.5 points taken off from the ending.
The ending is probably the most memorable part, after all.
