Tales of Zestiria is another installment of the "Tales of" series of RPGs, a series that's been standing since Tales of Phantasia on the Super Famicom in 1995. The series has 2 internal teams that make each game, and this was made by Team Destiny, who also worked on Tales of Destiny, and Tales of Graces, so this shares a lot of similarities with those games.
Story: The land has been corrupted by malevolance, and the Shepherd, working alongside beings called Seraphims can quell it, and purify it back to it's normal state. The Lord of Calamity is the main villain, carrying just
malevolance, and the main goal is to become strong enough as a shephard with the help of your companions to defeat him and purify the world.
When it comes to the characters, all of the characters are really convincing. Their personalities stick, and none of the characters feel too dumb or naive. Everyone in the group has a great since of humor, and if you like terrible puns then you'll love the skits and banter between the cast.
The gameplay focuses on the Linear Motion Battle System, a system in which you move on a line between you and your targets, initiating attacks based on what direction you input along with the attack buttons. You can hold down a button to unlock from the line, and move freely around the combat arena to reposition, and you can dash along the line and circle around your target to dodge. The arena is made right on the field map, rather than going into a seperate screen, so things like trees and walls come into count when dodging and running around (although this can make the camera bug out sometimes). Combos are basically put together for you in this iteration, so you can focus on just using the right weaknesses and whatnot. The item management is really intuitive, and once you get used to it it becomes very easy to put together exactly what skills you want to come out of your gear.
The dungeons and field exploration are a lot more open than what we've grown used to in Tales of Xillia. No longer is the world just a line, just going straight from town to town through copy and pasted valleys filled with recolors of the same enemies. With the adition of the on-field seraph actions, it even manages to intuitively push you in the right direction while still not feeling linear at all.
The only bad thing I can say about Zestiria is that the party feels a lot weaker when you don't throw them all in the same pot. Looking at Tales of Graces, every character had amazing strengths, and few weaknesses. There was even an option to go into fights with just the one character you're playing, without the other 3 members, because everyone could hold their own. In Tales of Zestiria, only Sorey and Rose really feel balanced out as strong characters, but the Seraphs are very clearly just there to cover weaknesses, and to buff the human characters. This kind of pushes you into sticking to Sorey the entire game, and throws the idea of maining any other party member out the window.
While not my favorite Tales game, it falls very close second under Tales of Vesperia. The mechanics are fun, the story is nice, and it's overall a great experience. Let's just hope they don't do it again. Everything feels great in Zestiria, but I really hope the next game is even more new things. The open field combat arena battles are cool, but it would be great if that was only a one-time deal. The same with how they managed the party setup and the field actions. Given the past couple games, where Xillia felt like Graces with a different camera angle, let's just hope Tales of Berseria brings something new to the table.

The steam recommandation system doesnt permit mixed reviews so I chose to
this game, but I hesitated for a long time.
Towerfall is a
like game where you can fight against a human opponent locally in arenas, solo play levels or play them cooperatively.
1/ The arena brawl mode is
It's the funniest game of this genre I have played locally since the bomberman sness one. It's that good, it's a masterpiece.
2/ There are long time technical issues that are not fixed.
3/ the solo and coop game are terrible.
It seems those modes have been put on top of the real game afterwards, as they are not properly designed. The levels are full of choke points, and the only challenge the game can throw at the player is overwhelming him with more entities, not clever enemy design, not clever mapping.
Timings are not properly tweaked, making use of the movement combos awkward and combined with the bindings the game isnt a fast flowing movement and fighting game anymore but an exercise in memory where you try to find the perfect way to beat every level by doing the same thing again and again.
And even that is defeated by the game choice to enter a little bit of randomness in the entities start position, which changes nothing but just add to the time you need to pass to know every pattern.
I understand that this game is a one man operation and came from an other platform. This could explain some of the technical difficulties or some bad design choice. As I said it is still one of the best game ever in local multi.
But those issues have been tackled to death by other games for a long time and they are resolved by other one-man games. Take a look at spelunky. Wether you like it or not, the timings of the entities, the reaction of the pad, everything is 100% precise and you can rebind controls.
The game could have somehow worked in solo mode too and warrant a recommandation if some of those issues had been taken care of.
In 2015, even if your game is an indie game with a retro look, we can't accept this kind of backward usability issues.

Bugs make this game unplayable. Avoid until fixed.
Edit> Clarity
Since installing this game I've gone through several iterations of it not working. I (very fortunately) have not experienced the graphical glitches experienced by the majority of people reporting bugs. I have, however, experienced keys randomly becoming unbound or rebound in weird ways (the escape key suddenly being swapped with the functionality of the space (help) key, the "cancel" button becoming unbound no matter where it was rebound to). Stuck save files. My issue isn't that there are specific issues with the game that have no fixes (although there are) it's that everyone seems to be having different issues with the game that cause it to break. The developers are very understanding and say they're working on these issues and stability, and I believe them. They released an emergency patch which some people claim saved their game within hours, but the fact is many games are still broken.
Because of the technical issues I'm having, I am probably not as far along as most people who are playing, but I get a slight sense of disappointment from the battle system and the lack of real sidequests. I wish the developers had put a little more time into optimizing battles for the PC. Support talents other than "prepare snack" are largely useless, and unfortunately some are necessary for forwarding the plot in ways that aren't immediately obvious.
On the flip side, the parts of the game I have been able to play (and replay, because the save system isn't so great) are very nice. They really take the classic Tales series storytelling to a new level and give fans some of that cross nostalgia. The battle system (despite my objections) is very visually smooth and pretty. They revamped the Arte system, so don't look for the same spells that have been used since before Symphonia, you probably won't find them. The cut-in final moves are pretty and unique, and you really get a sense of the character from them.
I'll probably change my recommendation in the next few patches. In the meantime, if you're thinking about buying, hold off and save yourself some headache.
FINAL EDIT>
It's official. I am unable to play this game anymore. I thought it was just me being grumpy about it's construction, but I am literally too bored of it to beat the final level. Sorry guys, this one is a major bust for me. Maybe you'll have more enjoyment.

Since this is hands down my favorite video game of all time ever, I feel it deserves a very heartfelt review.
+One of the most iconic and unique weapon sets ever. each weapon has a different use depending on the situation, and each one has an alternate fire mode making them more versatile then your standard shotgun or assault rifle.
+A multitude of complex maps. In an age where we pay 60 bucks for a bare handful of maps (looking at you Battlefront), Its hard to belive that you can get a game that has nearly a hundred maps to play on for $10, each one unique and hard to memorize. This game contains some of the most iconic maps in video game history, including Curse, Deck 16, and the amazing Facing Worlds.
+Silky smooth controls. This game revolutionized the way movement was handled in first person shooters, and the movement mechanics still rival some of today's triple A titles. Thise game takes dodging bullets to a whole new level.
+mutators! bored with your run-of-the-mill deathmatch? apply the low grav mutator for some mid-air combat, or the insta-frag mutator for one-shot death carnage.
+Programmable and customizable AI. If youre feeling like a challenge, you can crank up the AI level to godlike, or if you're
looking to blow off some steam, set the AI to average or novice and blow them to bits with your flak cannon.
-Graphics are of course not that great, but what do you expect from a game that came out in 1999?
-video settings can sometimes be a bit wonky. In order to get a resolution higher than 800x600, some messing around with the video drivers are required, as the default driver can't handle any more than that.

Honestly one of the most brilliant survival games i've played in a long time. The long dark is a survival game in its purest form and never manages to make you feel comfortable. In most survival games, its pretty easy to get supplies in the first day and within 2 you've pretty much mastered the game and the challenges you might have faced at the beginning are rendered nil. In The Long Dark you are never given that luxury and in most cases you never stay in one place for a long period of time. It's not the fear of zombies or wolves finding you, its down to what a survival game is all about: supplies. Once you run out food or tinder you have to move on if you want any chance of survival. The weather is your worst enemy, step outside in the middle of the night, you die. get caught in a blizzard, you better have warm clothes, a campfire and shelter or guess what, you die. The Long dark hits every mark and while it may be a little more complicated to understand all of the mechancics in the begining, any survival enthusiast will grow to love this visually stunning piece of art. 10/10

Napoleon Total War is a Tactical Wargame set in the Napoleonic Wars. Made by Creative Assembly ages ago, it was the first game I had, and the ultimate reason I ever got Steam. 3 years later it is still among my favourite games, and I still play it - though to a much higher quality than I used to.
Set in the Napoleonic Wars, as stated above, the main Campaign covers Napoleon’s Campaigns in Italy, Europe, Egypt, and the Peninsular. You are put in command of the French army, and in a certain amount of turns, must complete the campaign ending in a French victory. These campaigns are fun to play, and it feels good to replicate Napoleon's later military career, slaying his foes on the field, though I must be honest I do not think it is the best part of the game.
Alternatively, if you do not want to play as the French, there is the "Campaigns of the Coalition" option where you can play as any one of the 5 military superpowers of the era. Those being France, ♥ Great Britain ♥, Austria, Prussia, and Russia. Depending what type of campaign you play, they vary in length and difficulty, but you must strategically put your foes to the sword in your best efforts to meet all of your objectives, thus making your nation the very best it can be. Elite not only in Military and Navy, but also economy, and technological advancements. I wrote a campaign
(For Great Britain) which you can view here, showing and explaining in more detail what you can do in a Campaign, and things that may aid you, such as Spies, Gentlemen and of course your control over the Government, and how to use them effectively.
Napoleon really stands out from all other Total War titles in its battles, which are extremely well made. While I do not like many of the maps, and wish perhaps there could have been more, for the most part, games both multiplayer and single player require a lot of strategy and logic to win. There are varying difficulties, though with some experience, the AI soon becomes too easy for everyone, but each demand a more thoughtful approach to the tactic you use in order to ensure your ultimate victory. I've also made a guide on how I fight
, again as Great Britain. It was made a while ago, but my tactic hasn't really changed. Sorry if it's written badly in places, but I didn't want to edit it for memorabilia :D
This is my opinion, and many don't agree, but I believe Napoleon was the best Total War game. It's interface is simple and easy to use, but effective too, while still looking good. Graphically I think it walks all over the likes of Shogun 2 and Rome II, despite is age in comparison to the two. The combat engine is good, and fights, both shooting and melee, are fun to watch. The only criticism I do have are its musket sounds. They are quite bad, but this doesn't ruin the feel of the game.
Another reason I am so fond of this game is undeniably the era. I really like the Napoleonic wars, and oddly enough this game sparked my love for it three years ago, and so, to me, there is not another Total War like it. I've no interest in Roman or Medieval history, so perhaps my high opinion of it is partly because of that.
Overall, it is a great game. It's few small floors such as men charging the wrong way, and infantry not forming square in time for cavalry can be annoying, but they don't kill the game for me. I would give this game a proud 9.5/10. It's Creative Assembly's best work, and since then it's on a steady downhill decline for me, with their terrible interfaces and annoying camera restrictions in games such as Shogun 2 and Rome II, but that's for another review.
Thank you for reading my review :)

This is the kind of game I have been looking for ever since I got tired of Stronghold 2.  If you are looking for a city building game that tests your ability to organize your town into the most efficient/practical manner possible this is it.  You can't just make everything look pretty, you have to be concerned with the survival of your people.
For example, in a recent game I played I had laborers dying from cold and starvation even though I had plenty of wood and food.  Why were they dying then?  Because I had marked resources on the other side of a stream for harvesting without building a bridge.  They were taking so long to find a way around the river that they died before they could make it back to town!
If you have always dreamed of micromanaging a town, watching it organcally grow into a bustling town and knowing you  guided it there, this is that game for you.
My only complaint is that once you have reached a certain level of development there is little more to do except expand your town/population.  There is only two types of homes and a few survival related industries.  I would like to see the addition of more types of buildings and resources (luxury goods, service industies, etc...) so that you can continue to DEVELOP your town rather than simply growing it once you get past a certain stage.
All in all I highly recommend it, but you should probably wait for a sale to purchase (I got it for $6 on sale)

This game is great so far. I love how it not only does not hold your hand, but it also does not even give you a hint of how to survive. You are plopped somewhere in the bitter winter wilderness of Northern Canada with few supplies and not dressed appropriately for the weather. You must scavenge for supplies to survive.
This game does a great job of maintaining the fourth wall and fully immersing you into this harsh world. I feel as if I am truly fighting for my survival. The howling winds make me feel colder. The "wolves" send a chill throughout my body as my primal fight-or-flight response kicks in.
The UI could certainly use some work, but I have had no problems running the game despite its being in Early Access. I have not had one crash, and it is pretty well optimized even now so that it runs smoothly even on my aging gaming laptop from 2008.
Overall, I highly recommend this game to anyone who enjoys survival games or enjoys realism mods for their games.

First of all I just have to congratulate the devs for this record-breaking game. I don't think any game has ever received such a high percentage of bad reviews compared to good ones. Godus: Wars has even managed to beat Big Rigs: Over the Road Racing. It is the E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial (Atari 2600) of our time. Seriously this is so bad it may warrant a new "Do you recommend this game?" choice that is lower than "no". If you can think of the worst thing possible to ever exist and multiply it by 2, you would have this game. It's like when you go see a live performance that is so terribly bad you feel embarassed for even being there to behold it.
This game is a collection of gameplay elements that sound fun if done properly, but don't work well together or the way they were implemented. Some worked with Vanilla Godus, but some were still bad and were even worse when combined with combat.
All in all you have to be a real masochist to enjoy this game. It is frustratingly punishingly slow and annoying to the point of actual outright suffering. I can't think of anything at all in this game anybody in their right mind would consider fun.
There are so many annoyances in this game. I don't think there could be more annoyances if they were trying to pack as many in there as they could ON PURPOSE. I mean seriously, did none of this come up in the meetings? Did the developers even try to play this before they released it? It is so bad it is hard to say where I should even start.
First of all I have never liked the terraforming. It has been implemented in a way that just does not work well with a mouse. You end up clicking and dragging the same spot 500 times just to make a tiny area of land. This might not be so bad if it weren't such an important part of the game and if it weren't combined with the need to get it done fast because now you have an enemy doing the same thing but he doesn't have to ♥♥♥♥ around with a mouse. The terraforming♥♥♥♥♥♥implemented as it is now does not work well at all for a combat-oriented game where everything is time sensitive. Leave it for the casual game, not the war game. If anything, let the NPCs do it.
Secondly, the pathing is♥♥♥♥♥♥ The troops tend to run back and forth not knowing where they need to go, or run around in circles while being shot at. You are pretty much forced to control the warbands independantly because the pathing is even worse when you try to combine them into an army. They should replace the combat units with headless chickens, it would be more realistic.
One of the most annoying things about this game is the lack of any way to navigate the map with any convenience. Your troops are slaughtered so you need to make another army fast but your base is on the other side of the map so you have to slowly scroll there while your armies are fighting and dying. I guess Godus is too cool for a minimap.
Half the time when you add a new warband to your army it just sits there and doesn't bother trying to get to the rest of the army. I wouldn't give a♥♥♥♥♥♥either if I were them, it's not like they will do any good anyway.
When attacked by enemy troops, your army will shoot buildings and just let the enemy kill them. I guess I would be suicidal too if I were a character in this terrible game.
When the enemy is standing on the mission objective you cannot target them. Even when they are sitting out in the open with nothing near them it is STILL hard as ♥♥♥♥ to target them. It's like walking over to this building is more important than shooting something that is killing you.
You have to deactivate a god power before you can click on anything else. Very annoying, especially when you forget it is activated. One would expect it to be automatically deactivated when you try to do something else. God powers are pretty useless anyway. Might as well remove them completely. In fact remove the whole game and replace it with RTS elements that are already established that people expect to be in a RTS game becuase they work.
You can still squish houses to your base even after it is maxed. There is no feedback at all letting you know if it is even doing anything anymore. I liked it better when I could just use gold to upgrade a base. "Squishing" doesn't make anything more fun.
Each zone of each island is exactly the same. It feels like there is no progression at all. How can this game take up 3 gigs when there are only like 4 art assets?
Reward cards are terrible. Really I just spent an hour so I could get 4 extra followers for the next stage? Maybe if they were PERMANENT it would be sort of worth it.
If you alt tab out of the game and get back into it, the window is now slightly underneath the windows task bar. Congratulations now you can't see half your UI.
WTF 2 game windows? How does this enhance the game again?
It is a repetitive game of attrition. Make armies, go shoot houses until your armies have intentionally killed themselves, repeat (and hopefully you slowed down their army generation by at least 1%). How is this fun?
Peter, if you are going to try to be innovative, why not do it with something we WANT to see like a sequal to Populous or Theme Park? So bite the bullet and pay for licensing, it would be cheaper than total failures like these. I couldn't even tell you how to save this one, it is such a big failure I don't think anything can be done.  The only way to make this game more fun that it is now is if it did everything itself and all you had to do was watch.
Then again maybe I am wrong about all this. Maybe they were trying to make a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ game on purpose to win some 'worst game of the'.. EVER... awards. Well, "congrations, you winner !".

Power ups can be made by using A Machine For Pigs (meat grinder) if you'll pardon the bad pun; you make stuff by kicking pig parts into it.
This is also a survival game if you haven't guessed; it is a welcome twist on the genre to add humor. The most you could be terrified is when facing either the hordes of undead pigs, or bosses in the dark, with a flashlight. It's all good fun, but messy. :)

For those unfamiliar with the series, Tales (of) games tend to be heavily story loaded throughout the entire game. The newer games easily have 5 hours of main story dialogue at a minimum, and Tales of Zestiria likely continues this tradition. They all feature some variant of the original Linear Motion Battle System (LMBS) which is where primary combat occurs on a straight line, with moves resembling a beat-em up or fighting game. Aside from an early game or two, Tales games also pioneered optional bits of dialogue called "skits", used to flesh out the world or characters, though sometimes used for tutorial purposes. Stories tend to vary from game to game and are always on an epic scale. These are all core tenets of what makes a Tales game.
Of course, since
is what most people reading this will care about, I'll start with that. Out of 51 hours of gameplay, the port's quality is pretty strong. The most important aspect is that the game never once crashed -- something TF2 couldn't even claim given the extremely long individual play sessions. Like anything that dares to be 3D on the PC, there are spotted reports of folks having problems, but on an Nvidia 670 with 6 month old drivers, no problem.
, and both gameplay and wandering the world are smooth, responsive, and intuitive. The menus are also proper keyboard and mouse menus, but they're still ironing out some glitches. (a day one patch fixed some "last menu option can't be clicked" bugs, but there are other harmless but annoying glitches)
Oh, and you can opt to play with Japanese audio, or you can go with the English audio. I have nothing against the english VA's, but some people just love to have the option.
The story is somewhat run-of-the-mill to be honest. It's not bad by any means, but it lacks the twists and gut punches of many predecessors, especially games like Tales of the Abyss. You're straight up the hero who's saving the world. However, they do take a refreshing take on what would otherwise be a carbon copy plot -- Tales games tend to use humor, characterization, philosophy, fictional history, and fictional geopolitics to good effect, and Zestiria continues this tradition in a way that better lets the player empathize with this classic saintly hero. I do hope that Namco Tales Studio does give us another Abyss-level story in the future, though. The characters are...weird. If you're a fan of anime, you'll recognize many of the tropes and archetypes. The two playable female humans seem to stand out the most, while the rest are fairly formula. (with one almost seeming like a Persona ripoff)
Gameplay is where Zestiria shines -- perhaps even above all of its predecessors. This is coming from a reviewer whose last series game was Tales of Vesperia, but the LMBS changes could end up being a love-hate. Whereas older titles typically had you moving left and right, with 3D titles allowing free run, Zestiria has you running forwards and backwards. The two primary movement keys are even W and S instead of A and D, which I'm sure Symphonia will use. You can still free run, but they've added the ability to sidestep around enemies with the unused movement keys. These controls actually do seem to be an improvement, and is a smooth way to dodge enemy attacks and navigate the battlefield. Speaking of battlefield, having battles take place on the map is a pretty fun improvement. You can fight out on the open, or you can lure enemies into a corner or hallway and annihilate them with your team's AOEs. The movesets for both players and enemies are enormous, with many dedicated standard attacks joining the traditional artes and mystic artes. The game's difficulty curve is pretty smooth, and boy does it get hard. There's so much complexity and depth to the battle system that tutorial monuments litter much of the game, and tutorial messages will overwhelm you in the first 5 hours of play. That said, the game is still beatable without knowing even half of that's going on -- but you'll need all that info to master it.
It's worth noting that the nature of gameplay is pretty limiting in terms of what the writers could do with the plot. They refreshingly managed to make it so every playable character matters (especially on the overworld), and swapping out the Seraphs during a single battle is a core aspect of gameplay. You won't have to worry much about characters running off with your good gear, but the focused gameplay design probably made the story suffer.
Zestiria suffers in the graphics department, but I'm easily willing to forgive this one. The characters and towns look pretty good, the fields and dungeons -- not so much. Some of the dungeons look like they were mapped in a 2D editor and generated from said mapping, while the fields' textures are two generations old. That said, the series is the #3 RPG series in Japan and I can't imagine each game having what we currently consider a modern AAA budget. So what did they do? Pile most of the effort onto the gameplay, much on the story and characters, while the graphics are just there. If you can't look past this, though, it's not the game for you.
All said and done, it's a solid entry that probably wouldn't end up on many top 3 lists for the series. It sets a good PC precedent for port quality -- good job to the folks who managed said port and keep up the good work. With strong music and gameplay, solid story, and touch-and-go graphics, it's still an enjoyable Tales game, and hopefully the first of many ports to come.

Blues and Bullets is an alt-history game taking place in the fictional city of Santa Esperanza (Dunno why the devs didn't just make it take place in Chicago, there are really not many games set here, aside from Watch Dogs but that did such a♥♥♥♥♥♥job capturing the city it shouldn't count. The devs are Spanish so maybe they did it because they didn't feel comfortable enough to do Chicago, regardless its fine) where in Al Capone survived his time in jail and enlisted his old nemesis retired G-Man turned diner owner Elliot Ness to find his kidnapped granddaughter.
The game has a really nice atmosphere, they do a good job with the black and white aesthetic. It's also  been creative with the few twists on history it’s done so far, such as the Hindenburg disaster never occurring and the zeppelin getting bought by an eccentric millionaire to turn into a luxury hotel. The writing is good so far, Ness is likable and it’s overall interesting enough. The game is clearly going to be a mix of classic film noir with the first season of True Detective. The voice acting is solid as well, Doug Cockle, Geralt’s VA, isn’t far from home playing Ness.
Gameplay-wise it’s a little bit too railroaded for my liking to truly laud it, but so far the investigation segment was good enough to not feel braindead easy, but it still pales in comparison to Sherlock Holmes: Crime and Punishments. There are also shooting segments but these are solid enough to shake things up without ruining the pacing of the game. Adding to the railroaded feeling is that you can't really explore certain areas, you have to follow a preset path and you run into a lot of invisible walls if you don't, but on the flip side the devs take advantage of this to make some nice fixed camera angles, it lessens the game a bit but its not a deal-breaker. As far as choices go the game really hasn’t gotten into the nitty-gritty yet but you can at least roleplay Ness, whether this really affects character relationships is yet to be seen. There really isn’t any really complex dialogue segments yet either.
Overall it has better gameplay than Telltale’s recent fare, but I feel it needs more to really stand shoulder to shoulder with the current new adventure game greats. While it hasn’t instantly impressed me like Kentucky Route Zero and Life is Strange, it still got me to buy the whole season because if at the very least if it keeps up the quality of the first episode it will be a solid adventure game worth playing.

Greetings Everyone!  I’m not stranger to RTS games; they are my favored genre of gaming second only to RPGs and the two change places frequently.  I say this so that many will understand where I come from when deciding if I recommend this game.  At its heart we have a simple RTS that could find a good home on console or even a tablet, for the PC…well; it is a bit too slow for the average RTS gamer.
Uncontrollable:  This game was obviously designed with a controller in mind.  I don’t mean this disrespectfully; I feel these games were needed to allow RTS games to slowly transition as a viable genre for the consoles but I feel the entire game is a bit too simplified for a mouse and keyboard.  The game seems balanced over the intention you are going to be struggling with the controls and not have access to the precision of a mouse.  A small soapbox:  I really wish mouse and keyboard options would just become standard options for a console; shouldn’t be more than a software upgrade but I digress!
Childish:  I get the overwhelming feeling this game was meant for children, or at very least gamers who are not familiar with RTS as a genre.  If you are a veteran player of this genre you will get no challenge from this game.  You will also probably find the game boring.  The story is a bit silly and doesn’t really have any depth but is amusing at times.  I feel as they were trying to find an excuse to do a controller RTS with zombies and here you go; not necessarily a bad thing.
But will it blend:  Ultimately, you know what you are getting here.  About 4 hours of simplified RTS that would be great for a child or someone new to the genre and for $5 I can get behind that.  The game is old but does seem to keep up graphically, audibly but could use some updates for modern graphic options.
So, I’m going to say sure, why not.  For $5 and understanding that it would make a great entry to into the Genre then yes I’d recommend it.  This is the RTS equivalent of throwing someone Banjo for an entry into an enjoyable but approachable platformer.  So, if you have a child wanting to play games or never played an RTS here you go!

This review has no spoilers of the game or story
If you enjoy story-driven games of the kind of Life is Strange, Telltale games, or David Cage games you will probably love this game to death. This is a Noir/Detective game that has similar gameplay to Life is Strange and LA Noire. What you do is that you are a detective by the name of Eliot Ness, the former leader of the Untouchables as you look for clues as you uconver the mysteries of a missing girl.
VISUALS
The visuals are amazing in a indie Unity title. You might of never even knew it was a Unity game until you saw this post because even I had to do some digging to find this out. The game has a black/white look to it with a splash of red just like the movie Sin City. The game's overall design really reminds me of Bioshock 1 with its classic look but with it's own originality. The enviornment down to the models have been done beautifully. You would of never thought this was made by such a small team. This game is true art.
Story
The story is riddled with the mafia, murder, and mystery. What can I say? It is simply amazing. The first episode of the game as stated by developers took "150 pages" to write up. The story lets you chose what you want to say and how you want to act during certain situations giving the player choice and to be able to put themselves in the shoes of Eliot Ness. The story is filled with refrences to Film and video games, its just brilliant to me how well this was put together. You will be surprised what this mystery turns into as you play Episode 1.
SOUND
The voice actors do an amazing job in this game, never did I sit there laughing at a bad performance. The actors do a great job representing their role within the game world. The soundtrack is actually exclusively written by a blues muscian from my research into the game which is really cool. The opening track was written just for this game and honestly it sounds AMAZING.
Honestly I give it a 9/10 for Episode 1

About The Game: Zombie Tycoon 2 is a zombie RTS (Real Time Stratagy). Featuring both slow snd fast zombies. The slow zombies are big and tough and can take some hits. The fast zombies are skinny and weak but you usually get more of them in a unit. Both types of zombies take up jobs to help you get through puzzles. Hazmat zombies clean up damaging goo, Samurai zombies dash and slash their victims, and Engineer zombies operate machines to open paths for the mobil spawner. Humans arent a chooseable faction but are also your enemy in capaign mode.
Pantsu's Rating (out of 5)
Graphics: 4 It's cartoony graphics are clean and fit the world well. My only complaint is the lack of females, wether zombie, soldier, or survivor.
Playability: 3.75 The controls are okay but I found myself selecting a unit instead of one of my large creatures abilities. (Units 1234, Abilities QWER)
Fun: 3.75 Oh yeah it is fun. Taking over the neighborhoods house by house feels rewarding when you unleash the horde on the final gates. The leaders mobil spawner vehicle doesn't seem to have a way to reapair which kind of sucks since it can take lots of damage pretty fast.
Sound: 3.5 The music fits the scene of zombies rampaging around the city. Not very useful outside the game unless you want some spookyish music for a Halloween party. The groans and grunts of the zombies differs between type and even jobs.
Replay Value: 3 After the campaign mode, which teaches you how to play the game. There is multiplayer. You get to choose your faction, and your big moster then battle friends or strangers from across the globe.
Final Score: 3.5
Final Thought: A fun introduction to the RTS genre. At $9.99 it is worth waiting for a sale, but on a good note it is also sold as a 2 pack for a discount so you can get your friend a copy at the same time.

Beautifully rendered in "graphic novel" style, The Long Dark is a great addition to any library, even in it's early access state.  As Sandbox mode is currently the only way to enjoy the game, my review will stem from that.
Bearing in mind that many things can change, be removed, or are unfinished, the game is already excellent.  I'm hoping the items I am critical of get adjusted and/or changed for release.
You find yourself in the middle of the frozen Canadian north, near an unnamed coastline.  Your number one priority is to find shelter.  Number two, find warmer clothes.  Number three, water, etc.
The controls are the standard WASD keys and they are remapable.  The Tab key is used to bring up the central interface and this is where things are a little frustrating.  Common activites, like drinking and eating, require that you drill into this central interface each and every time.  So, say you wish to drink some water.  You either hit Tab and click on the Inventory Icon or hit "i".  Now, scroll down to Water (Potable) and click on the name.  Now mouse over to the "drink" button and click it.  You will take a drink.  If you don't have enough water to fulfil your needs and want to drink a can of Soda pop, you must do the same action again, only this time clicking on "Summit Soda".   Having to repeat this same activity time and time again to merely eat or drink causes one to wish for a different scheme, like right clicking on the item and click "drink" on a pull down menu.  With multiple needs and with an ever ticking clock, it gets old pretty fast.
There are other frustrations.  This is an open world game, without the ability to either jump or climb.  Thus you're limited in how you can move in a wilderness situation.  This is supposed to be a survival game and yet I cannot climb or jump up on the rock to avoid wolves, a rudimentary primate survival technique.
Clothing degrades . . . faster than armor in Diablo or Skyrim.  Apparently the wind is so strong that it rips the threads right out of your parka (Premium Winter Coat).  In all my years of playing in the winter wonderland that is North Western Wisconsin and Minnesota, I have never had the wind destroy any of my clothing.  I still have wearable jackets from 1984, yet in this game, after wearing my Premium Winter Coat for four days, it's in dire need a repair, and that's without being attacked by a wolf.
Speaking of wolves, they are to be feared, and with the latest update, if you do not have the ability to shoot the animal (like, you know, haven't located a gun or bullets) you are left with no good way to get away from them.  The latest build has changed the Wolves behavior when confronted with a flare and instead of keeping them away, after a bit the wolf comes back.  If you are encumbered, or tired, exhausted, or Freezing, you are generally toast because you cannot make sufficent distance.  Which is a great thing, because the player is forced to make serious choices.  The hardcore nature of the sandbox creates tension when the wolves come out and you've not found a firearm or the hunting knife.  And, it can be quite scary if you've found yourself stuck out of doors and a wolf comes lunging for you out of nowhere.
Much work remains on this project, but my hours with it have been both frustrating and fun.  I believe it deserves your serious consideration as an early-access title.

Personally, I've only played this for few hours, but I can already say its a solid game. It's surprisingly small for a game like this and runs smoothly despite my laptop not working as well as a proper PC. The designs are incredible and I felt a joy wandering around the worlds, finding secrets and collectives. The story is also solid and has a humour that made me giggle multiple times. Unlike some other platformers I've played, I feel the controls to be very responsive. I was worried of this the moment I started the game,  but I found it runs smoothy even by using keyboard!
I absolutely adore the voice acting and the marvelous character designs. They are one of the most unique ones I've seen in a while, which each one brings personality. The hats also are very well done, and I love the addons or 'skins' you can get for them as well. Their abilities don't feel too over powered, nor underpowered. They feel balanced.
My main problems are that there are things that aren't polished, things like text moving outside of text boxes and countless glitches, which so far have only once made me start over the level because I got stuck between walls. I also found the Mafia boss on world 1 be extremelly tiresome because of the 'Mafia ball' being glitchy. Not only did you get hit often when you were trying to get on top of it, you also got stuck often in a way that you are unable to hit the boss.
Update: I've now encountered a massive game-breaking glitch in chapter 2 finale in the boss. After a specific character does a thrust with a knife and goes for a new type of attack ( I assume), My camera glitched and so did the others. I couldn't die, so my only choice was to exit the level, only to find that I have to go through the same frustrating platform level to get to the boss. In general, I think the game should have a 'Reset to the last checkpoint' option in case of a gamebreaking glitch like this. Same chapter I also got stuck inside of a place I couldn't get out from.
I'd give it a solid 8/10 so far. I love it, but it just needs a little more polishing. Maybe the creators will find this out and maybe update the game with glitch removal.

First of all, don't buy this game just because you thought TSP was great. It doesn't mean you'll like this "game".
I put game in quotes because really, this is an art piece, or an exhibit. Criticizing this for not being "fun" or "interactive" is like criticizing a novel because it isn't choose your own adventure. This is an introspective art piece, that's all.
Now, it's definitely pretty short, but it's about the length of a movie and a couple dollars cheaper, so I think it's a good buy. Play through the whole thing, and don't try to just get to the end, think about what's being said.
If you like art that pushes into new mediums, or just modern art in general, you'll definitely love this.

I really, really wanted to enjoy LIMBO, but the more I played it, the more irritated I got. It's got that typical and extremely pervasive problem with puzzle-platformers of being overly reliant on timing-based puzzles rather than thought-based ones, meaning that the tiniest mistake can and will end up killing you in some gruesome way despite the solution being painfully obvious. Add to that the basically nonexistent story and storytelling, and it fails miserably as a game. But I get the feeling it's not meant to be seen as a game, but rather a piece of art, which it succeeds at brilliantly. The grim, oppressive atmosphere ingame is absolutely phenomenal and the artistic nature of it wanting you to come to your own conclusions is a massively refreshing change of pace. I'd say check out the demo, and if you like that then you'll like the rest of the game.

Godus Wars includes both the original Godus and its new RTS spin-off Godus War. Which takes the Godus art assetts and clunky controlls, adds some blood and a bare-bones RTS interface that is just as terrible as the basic landscaping interface of the original game. Which should come as no suprise, as the terrible interface was the inspiration for the RTS spin-off.
To quote Peter himself:
"We’ve always loved the landscape forming, changing and sculpting but quickly realised that it’s slightly more uncomfortable to do a lot of sculpting with a mouse. Really what it lacked was brutality, was war, was the ability to take on challenge and use your god powers and sculpting powers to fight, war and battle. And that’s where our initial concept of Wars started."
Yes, Mr. Molyneux thought that the interface was terrible, and his idea of improving on that was to do a completly different game with the exact same interface.
The RTS content is lack-luster and in the first missions it's just down to whomever builds the barracks first so he can kill the enemy barracks. Which is not really a challenge as the AI is rather lacking in aggression. This might change later ingame, but with the minimalistic approach to the RTS genre I couldn't get myself to play for long enough to see more content... or if there is even more content at all.
The game tries to freshen up the RTS mechanics by adding god-ability cards that you win in battles and than can use as one-time resource boosts or ingame abilities. Once used they are gone and you'll have to regrind them from the lower missions that you did before. You also get randomized extra-rules in each battle that might give extra damage for having a hight advantage or increase the cost of god powers... with all that thought going into how to 'freshen up the RTS genre' one wonders why there are so many basics just missing, like a mini-map for example.
tl;dr
minimalistic RTS that may be fun if you just want to see low-poly bow-men shoot at helpless farmers for 10 minutes between loading screens but doesn't offer anything interesting. This might change later on, as it's still early access, but if the original Godus is any indication I wouldn't get my hopes up.

Long review, so skip to the bottom, for the TL:DR
First off the PC port of this is amazing, while yes it only runs at 30 fps, it has all the other settings required of a PC port.
Now, for a year I completely remained ignorant to any of the story from the japanese release, as such, going in, I knew nothing, except for the alisha scandal. I can safely say, that Zesteria is a good game. Not a great game, not a bad one.
The Xillia games were a mess of incoherent ideas with no clear focus. Decent characters, but the motivations, story turns, and overall plot were far underwhelming and dissappointing for long time Tales of players, like me. But it had wonderful set pieces.
Zesteria on the other hand, is much the same. Except with a lack of memorable set pieces. So why do I consider it better? Zesteria is a sort of first for the Tales of series, an experiment to see if certain things work, and while some do, others don't.
In order to get the full experience out of the battle system, you are forced to play one of two characters, the rest of the playable cast will be used merely for buffs. So unlike previous titles, you can't really specialize with one character that aren't the two humans. Not to mention the party formation is NEVER saved. So you cosntantly have to switch to your prefered parties after every cutscene.
The characters, while enjoyable, are lacking in growth. It feels like the game is only 2/3rds of what it should be. The villains and heroes don't get the development needed to have a concrete emotional connection on why they do what they do.
It took me 29 hours to beat the main campaign, the first time. A decent length, but many of those hours were hollow, running around, trying to find where to go next. Searching every crevice just trying to know where to do. And there's two of these sections in the story. They give you a goal, you can do them in any order, go do it.
Vesperia is my favourite in the series, followed by Graces F and Symphonia. And I am one of the few that enjoyed Symphonia 2. All four of these games set up their characters and play out their stories in a natural and understanding way.
Even Xillia 1 did this, and for the most part it worked, until they introduced a character that made no sense within the context of the world. Xillia 2, well, It had a character so good, so well thought out, that it was amazing. Then they throguh it away.
Zesteria is lacking as a Tales of Game. Just as the Xillias were. And the only reason I consider it worse then Xillia 1, is because Xillia 2 is technically the second half of that story. Xillia 1 is better then Zesteria, but only because the plot is a tiny bit more coherent then this one.
The base characters, are good. They interact with each other well, and their skits and dialogue are spot on, but the lack of growth and compentant story, feels like they're jsut going through the motions.
And that's what this comes down it. Zesteria is bandai namco, going through the motions. It's a technical marvel at the technology for creating a battlefield from the terrain, but that's where it seems most of their efforts were laid.
There is a god awful lack of extra content. There is no hot springs side quest, no cooking challenge.
And what I cannot forgive, is that some side quests are locked off if you proceed with the story too much. Making them increable hard to complete without prior knowledge of when they're safe to complete.
Now. I've complained for a few paragraphs of why this game is lackluster, but it despite all this, Zesteria is a good game. My eyes as a Tales of fan, may be blind to the needs of a new player, and it's a solid game. I whole heartedly recommend it.
But there are better Tales of Games. Symphonia comes out next year, and it's a much better, more solid experience of a game.
TL:DR
A technical marvel as an experiment on Tales of technology. The story and charcters are lacking in  meaningful development, with a plot that contradicts itself.
The combat is fun, and later on deep with layers.
Recommended for the combat, but not the story.

This game is great so far. I love how it not only does not hold your hand, but it also does not even give you a hint of how to survive. You are plopped somewhere in the bitter winter wilderness of Northern Canada with few supplies and not dressed appropriately for the weather. You must scavenge for supplies to survive.
This game does a great job of maintaining the fourth wall and fully immersing you into this harsh world. I feel as if I am truly fighting for my survival. The howling winds make me feel colder. The "wolves" send a chill throughout my body as my primal fight-or-flight response kicks in.
The UI could certainly use some work, but I have had no problems running the game despite its being in Early Access. I have not had one crash, and it is pretty well optimized even now so that it runs smoothly even on my aging gaming laptop from 2008.
Overall, I highly recommend this game to anyone who enjoys survival games or enjoys realism mods for their games.

This is my first time playing a sandbox game and to be honest, I was kind of sceptical about how I would feel playing a game with no linear progression. I understand that the game intends to have a Story Mode once the game is completed from it's Early Access stage, but for now there's only Sandbox Mode, and for that you have to be content.
In short, this game is a absolute joy to play. Any game that can make me feel cold and desperate when it's warm and sunny outside (at least down here in Australia), should give you an indication at how immersed the player can get. Honestly, the scenery, the atmosphere and the distinct feeling of loneliness really adds to this game's realism, albeit if you were to imagine what it would be like being alone in a freezing cold environment doing everything you can to survive.
I will admit that it can feel a little tedious and boring in some parts, especially if you know that staying inside a house or hut is going to protect you from the extreme cold outside, but I guess this just adds to the realism of the experience. There is no electricity, no television, no one else to talk to, and so nothing to keep you entertained. You are surviving, and that is your only goal and purpose. With this realisation and understanding, it allows me to forget the lack of entertaining distractions, side quests, and all the other things that usually make games fun for me, and to want to continue playing the game.
In all honestly, I am kinda looking forward to the Story Mode being introduced to the game (old habits die hard) but for now I will be more than content playing it in its current state and trying to survive as long as I can and can recommend this game highly for anyone who enjoys the Survival genre.

**TL;DR VERSION AT THE END!**
Before I dive in the review, I must absolutely stress that this game is NOT like The Stanley Parable in pretty much any way other than its thougt-provoking nature. While TSP is an actual game with a cohesive narrative, The Beginner's Guide is more of what you could compare to a commentary about a particular game dev's life.
That being said, let's start. I went into The Beginner's Guide completely blind; the only thing I knew about it was that it is made by Davey Wreden, the person behind the EverythingUnlimited studios and the wonderful The Stanley Parable, and that it was about video game development. I bought the game without thinking because TSP holds a very dear place in my heart because of how it shows that video games have tremendous potential as an artform and I was sure that TBG would be similar. I was wrong, but not entirely.
As I've said, TBG is basically a commentary made by Davey about a game developper, nicknamed Coda (I say nicknamed because I have reasons to think it is not his real name, I won't give any arguments in order not to spoil anything, but think that Coda sounds a bit like coder). You will play through Coda's games and Davey will be commenting throughout by voiceover.
"Well that's great and all", I can hear you say, "but why not simply have us play the games outside of the compilation? Furthermore, why do we pay EverythingUnlimited the money that we would owe Coda?". Well, Coda has never released his games to the public. And that's why the story told by Davey is so interesting. I don't know if you are very familiar with litterature or even art in general, but there are many artists who create pieces and never show them to the public. They keep it to themselves. Why then? What is the purpose of their creation? This is one of the questions asked here in The Beginner's Guide.
Throughout TBG, Davey tries his best to explain Coda's games, how they show his personnality and how he was feeling at the time and confronts us with perhaps a vision not everyone will have had about video games. The goal of TBG is not only to have us play Coda's games, it's also to make us understand that a creator always leaves a trace of himself in his creations. In the end, The Beginner's Guide is the tale of a human journey, the one of a creator whose only way of expressing his thougts was through his games and his sorrow when he lost inspiration.
I would love to go on about the game, but I would risk spoiling it for you. It's really something to experience. You may still be asking yourself if you should get this game or not.
Well, in my very own opinion I think the price is a bit too much to ask for as a game. But look past the game aspect and you will have yourself something special that may change the way you see video games.
It also depends on what you expect from a game. You may have liked The Stanley Parable and not find any interest in The Beginner's Guide, as they have two very different approaches to making you think about its main topic, TSP being more metaphoric as opposed to The Beginner's Guide being direct. You could compare TSP to a philosophic tale and TBG to a philosophy essay. If you want something thougt-provoking and you're not afraid of sitting down for an hour and a half listening to someone talking while not doing much, this game is definitely for you.
tl;dr version:
You like thinking, consider video games as a possible artform and wish to support the dev with your money? Get it!
You want an "actual" game like The Stanley Parable that can be enjoyable without thinking too much? Forget it!

This is a great program to use whether you're looking to make a commercial RPG, or just want to mess around.
There's more than enough assets to make a game right out of the box, and it's incredibly easy to put your own assets into the game. It's as simple as just copying a file into the correct folder. And there are even generators out there that generate characters and other assets for you.
While it is fairly limited to just making RPGs with the default engine until you can script, there is quite a bit you can do without knowing scripting. For example, if you don't want to have random encounters, you can easily create wandering monsters instead. If you only want certain monsters to appear in certain parts of an area, you can do that. If you want to have different choices affect the story, you can do that too. Some of this takes a bit of practice and in-depth knowledge of the options, but it's not too difficult to learn with the many many video tutorials and help sites out there.
Once you've mastered the basic engine, you can then completely customized and change your game with scripts. Even if you don't want to learn to program, there are tons of pre-made scripts out there that you can use. For example, you can find one that increases the number of options in the menu, one that changes window size, and one that lets you skip text. All without ever having to learn scripting. Of course, if you do learn to script, the options are endless. You can do literally whatever you want with the engine, and then have the ability to sell anything you make.
So, it's a pretty good deal, especially if you plan on making commercial projects. Even more so considering other game engines are FAR more expensive, and some even charge you per game you put out. Even if you don't plan on releasing commercial games, it's a fun little tool to use to make games that you can share.

I love platformers but I don't consider this to be one of the good ones. It's a game where the main goal is to be relaxing instead of challenging which it does acomplish however it forgets what separates a good platformer from a great one. A great platformer is rewarding while still presenting a challenge to the player. Refunct doesn't do this. The game is far to short (beat it in 17 minutes) to even make the rewarding feeling even close to the realm of reality. Another thing that makes a great platformer is that the platforming comes first. Refunct brings a wall jump ability that is hardly used to get to the objectives and a cliff grab that makes the platforming too easy. The last ability is a slide that is used to slide under 3 areas to hit a objective point and to enter pipes that really don't fit the game that well and are only there to be there. There also is boost pads that just serve to add more verticality to the game without adding a actual challenge. The game focuses far to much on the music which is great but forgets the fundamentals of a platformer. There is no way to lose, which going back to my first point doesn't allow for any rewarding feeling to exist as there is nothing to overcome. The game has no story and the only objective is to turn the ground green by steping on a platform and to hit all the buttons while unlocking "new" areas every button you press. Overall Refunt is a shallow platformer with weak mechanics, no re-play value, no challenge, and nothing of substance. It may have great soundtrack but that doesn't mean much when the game around the soundtrack is mediocre at best.
I would give Refunct a 4.5/10 -Infinite

Last year, I heard about a program called "RPG Maker", something that had all the resources needed for me to fulfill one of my many, many dreams: Making my own game. Now, I am a huge fan of RPGs, JRPGs most of all. Pokemon, Final Fantasy, Golden Sun, you name it. There's just something about the turn-based battles and dungeon exploration that makes it just so much fun, and the thought of making a game in one of my favorite genres was incredibly enticing. And since I've logged in 100+ hours on it at this point, I think it's safe to say that I'm probably trustworthy enough to write a review. For those of you too lazy to read a full review, here's the TL;DR version:
It's awesome for goofing around with and making games, go buy it if you like either of those.
With that out of the way, let's get on with the review. RPG Maker is a very complicated system, and yet, it's very easy to use at the same time, and if you ever get confused about something, then there's probably ten different guides to using RPG Maker on YouTube. This program allows you to make just about every part of a game. Do you want to make a character who specializes in swords and uses lightning magic? Sure! Do you want to make a dungeon room that requires you to solve a puzzle to progress? Go ahead! Do you want to make a status effect that deals damage while lowering your defense? I don't see why not! Do you want to make an enemy that alters its elemental weakness and immunities every four turns? It'll take some time, but if you feel like it, then nothing's stopping you! Do you want to make a boss similar to Beldr from Shin Megami Tensei: Devil Survivor, who can only be hurt by a single weapon? By all means, even if you don't understand that joke, do it! In fact, if you want to take it a step further, then you can even customize the resources and scripts used.
Now, you may be wondering, what are resources and scripts? Resources are the sprites, music, and tilesets that appear ingame while playing your project. The game gives you numerous presets, but using them is considered to be the mark of an amatuer in the RPG Maker community, and they tend to take away from the professionalism of a project, although there have been examples of RPG Maker games that use the presets that are quite amazing. Scripts, on the other hand, are pages of Rubyscript code that control how the game and its mechanics work. Unless you know anything about coding, I don't recommend messing around with scripts. As I said, both of these things are indeed customizable. There are scores of custom-made resources and scripts for RPG Maker on the internet. In fact, not too long ago, RPG Maker opened up a Steam Workshop page for sharing your RPG Maker resources and scripts, as well as game projects. Look around there or on the internet and you'll find some good ones, I can assure you.
Now, there's one last thing I want to talk about, and that's commercial release, A.K.A. selling games. Now, stuff made with RPG Maker can indeed be sold so you can make money off of your games. However, resource and script creators for RPG Maker may not want you to use materials in your commercial release, and using licensed characters in your game(e.g. Mario, Cloud Strife, Gary M. F. Oak, etc.) is kinda sorta against the law. Others may be fine if you just give them credit for making the resources and/or scripts you used. The presets included with RPG Maker, as well as the DLC resources, are free for commercial use, however. Please keep this in mind if you intend on making your game to be sold on Steam or some other game distribution system.
All-in-all, RPG Maker is a very useful program for those of you who are feeling creative and want to make their own video game. The only downsides to this program, in my opinion, are the pricetags on both it and the DLC. $70 for the main thing and $10-30 for everything else? Seems a bit much to me. Even so, there's just so many useful tools at your fingertips that the pricetag seems to be worth it in so many ways. I for one am having so much fun making my own game, and I'm sure that you will too. So what are you waiting for? This is the perfect program for anyone who wants to make their own game.

Before we get started with talking about Arcane RERaise, I would strongly recommend you to check out my
for Arcane Raise, as a lot of my thoughts for that game are going to be carried on over to this one. This review is also probably not going to be as detailed as my usual ones, due to the number of similarities that this game shares with the original, so instead of just writing a review where I simply rehash the same details, I'll just make quick references to them and you can read into them in more depth in my Arcane Raise review.
So, Arcane RERaise is the sequel I'm not sure anyone wanted except for the developer to the game Arcane Raise. Calling the game a sequel is a bit of an overstatement though, I'd probably prefer the word "clone" of the first game.
The game follows the same style of gameplay but somehow manages to be worse than the original. The gameplay still has that grinding aspect where the whole game is you just wandering around in an area, waiting for random encounters to trigger so you can beat the enemy, gain experience and level up. However, in the original, you had a few different maps. You had your central hub area where you can rest, and then you had 4 areas with differing levels of difficulties. A somewhat logical method to make the gameplay leveled and balanced but still allowing players that wanted a challenge to go forward with it if they wished. With Arcane RERaise, you have your hub area, and then one room with random encounters inside of it, and that's it.
The game then goes on to literally copy from the original. The hub area is the exact same, the same layout, the same maps, the same items to purchase in there, everything is the same. There are even weapons for sale that none of the characters can use because the developer decided to not cut out items that could no longer be used by your class of characters that could be used by the characters from the first game. The goal is the same where you have to level up enough to beat a boss, and the boss lines of dialogue are copied as the boss makes reference to the 4 portals from the original game as being there, but they aren't present in the sequel. As a result of all of this, the game feels incredibly cheaply made and lazily put together, more than the original.
The only thing that I'll really say is an improvement over the original is the plot. There is an attempt at developing a plot to the series within this game. There's a castle under attack and you have to go in to rescue someone from the boss while also defeating enemies that stand in your way. It's not a great plot for an RPG as RPGs tend to have a heavy reliance on the story, but at least there is a plot to this one unlike the original.
There isn't really too much else to talk about now, if you want to know more details surrounding the game, check out my Arcane Raise review, as all the problems that Arcane Raise had are still present in the sequel.
In short, just stay away from the game.
Final verdict: 1/10

Ah, the "Godus controversy": releasing a mobile game onto PC, releasing slow and irregular updates, and then, a year later, re-releasing an update of the game as a new game to wipe out comments. I understand why most folks are angry. Personally, I'm a backer and I'm willing to forgive all this if the final product is
.
But is the game good ? No. Godus war tries to be a mix of a God game and a RTS, but it's a horrible RTS and a okay-ish God game.
- The ability to select multiple unit by creating a selection rectangle around them with a simple click of your mouse. The game kinda have control group but that's not enough.
- A minimap.
- Add more units type. I have only played one unit type (archer) in 4 or 5 battles, so the game started to feel repetitive.
- A move-attack order. But don't remove the simple move order, the game needs both.
- Production queue for barracks.
- Moving the camera by placing your cursor on the edge of the screen.
- Healthbar for units directly in the world. Okay, you have a list of every units on the top of the screen, but you can't read the health of units in a control group, and it's hard to know what unit in the world have how many health.
- Hover help text for powers and cards.
- (Rebindable) Hotkeys.
- Rally flag for barracks. You can rally a unit while it's under construction, but you can't rally every units ever build here.
- KEYS. Don't lock players behind arbitrary condition. I quit and uninstalled the game because after losing one battle, I didn't have any keys left, so I couldn't do anything. That's unbelievably stupid.
- Giving to the player a choice of one card in 3 is a good idea... if only I could know what card does what.
- The pathfinding is not great, although that's a minor issue considering everything I've written before.
- Buffs spells feels underwhelming for the moment. Maybe you should make them global ? (click on the buff and every units you control gain it while it last)
- Tone down the blood a little.
So yeah, until those complaints are fixed, Godus wars will be a bad game not worth your money (and I won't play it).

-If you're getting into this its safe to assume you've played JRPGs before and don't expect to get too much out of the story. While this ones isn't going to jump out at you either (at least not as of 20+ hours), there have been a few moments that I thought were wonderfully done.
-The combat system took some getting used to it. It starts out very easy to button-mash for a good amount of time, and makes combat kind of a chore. But, as you acquire more skills and run into stronger enemies, the combat becomes much more fluid and requires you to time your moves a little better in terms of evasion and arte placement in your combos. Overall, a slow and very boring start that makes its way into a new and very fun combat system.
-The equipment system is what really stood out to me the most. The types of armor and weapons you receive are very limited, but have
randomly generated skills (that you eventually have
control over which skills you receive). The skills have their own abilities, but are also placed on a skill map that stack in certain ways to make different or more powerful skills. Not going to bother getting very in-depth with it, but its an interesting system that makes you really think about how you fuse your equipment together and place skills at higher difficulties.
-Not much to say graphically. Beautiful, plenty of scenery to look at, some graphics glitching, and unfortunate its left at 30 fps.
Overall its been a very fun experience thus far. As with other Tales games, its a very slow start. Maybe more so than any other Tales game I've played, which is unfortunate because that is a big turnoff for some. But so far its been worth the wait because it becomes a very fun and unique game. So glad they brought this to steam as I haven't had the chance to play a new Tales game since Vesperia.

To make a lasagna u need :
For the tomato meat sauce:
2 x 28 oz. cans tomatoes - crushed or whole is best! If you get whole canned tomatoes just crush them in your hands.
1-2 tbsp tomato paste (this is my favorite kind!)
1 large onion
garlic, garlic, garlic - I always use a ton! I'd say two cloves minimum!
1 pound ground beef, preferably lean
1 pound Italian sausage - choose whatever spice level you like!
dried oregano
Italian seasoning
salt and pepper
fresh basil - dried can also be substituted!
olive oil
Keep in mind that if you can always just cook up some meat and then pour a couple jars of tomato sauce over it, so don't worry about it if you look at the ingredients and wonder what you've gotten yourself into.
For the rest of the lasagna:
1 package of noodles (should be around a pound in weight) - oven-ready or regular.
1 lb. mozzarella
1/2 lb. good quality parmesan
1 lb. ricotta cheese
1 egg
dried oregano + basil
Hardware:
large pan to make the sauce in
13x9 baking dish - I recommend glass
large pot for boiling pasta (if not using oven-ready noodles)]
Step 2: Making the Meat Sauce, Part One
Prep work and browning the meat!
Roughly dice the onion, and mince as much garlic as you want. I used quite a bit as you can see. :D
Once you've got the veggies prepped, film your sauce pan with olive oil. Heat the pan over medium and cook the ground beef and Italian sausage until browned. If a lot of fat seeps out, drain most of it. You need only a few tablespoons of fat to cook the onion and garlic in.
Once you've drained the extra fat, throw in the onions and garlic.
Stir this around for a few minutes over medium heat until the onions become soft. Then add in a few good pinches of Italian seasoning, a pinch of basil, oregano and salt, and a tablespoon or two of tomato paste.
Step 3: Making the Meat Sauce, Part Two
Now, open both cans of tomatoes and dump them in. Mix it around for a moment, and bring to a light boil. Watch out for splatters!
Lower the heat to a simmer and cover. Let the sauce simmer for at least a half hour while you do the rest of the prep work.
Step 4: Cook (or Don't Cook) Your Noodles
At this point, if you're using regular lasagna noodles, you'll need to fill a stock pot with water and cook those. I find it's best to cook them for the shortest time listed on the package or a minute or two under so they don't get soggy while the lasagna bakes.
Once they're done, rinse them with cold water using a colander and set them aside. Try to separate them a bit so they stick less later.
If you're using oven-ready noodles, you can worry about them later. :D
Step 5: Prep the Cheese and Finish the Sauce
Over the years, I've started combining all my cheese at the beginning - it makes for easier assembly!
Grab out a couple handfuls of parmesan and mozzarella and put them in a small bowl - this will be for topping the lasagna.
Place the ricotta into a large bowl, along with one egg. Add the rest of the parmesan and mozzarella, as well as a couple good pinches of Italian seasoning and basil. Mix this all together with your hands.
Once you're all done with the cheese, double check the sauce and adjust the flavors as necessary. You may need to add salt, sugar or more herbs - just keep adding and testing until it's good for you!
If you're using fresh basil, chop up a handful and throw it in now. Once the basil is in, stir the sauce well and turn off the heat.
Step 6: Assembling!
Preheat the oven to 375 degrees F / 200 degrees C.
Make sure your cheeses, noodles and sauce are all within easy reach.
Ladle just enough sauce to cover the bottom of the pan. Then place noodles on top of the sauce just to cover, slightly overlapping. (If you're using over-ready noodles, follow the box directions) If they're broken, piece them together as much as possible. Spread 1/3 of the cheese mixture over the noodles.
Now you'll put more sauce over the cheese and then noodles, more cheese, and then sauce again. You repeat the basic build three times.
For the fourth and final level, lay down your cheese mixture and top with the rest of the sauce. Now sprinkle the parmesan and mozzarella you set aside over it.
Now bake at 375 F for 40 minutes - if you're using a metal pan, check after 30 and make sure it's not too dark! If it's starting to get dark on top just pull it out. :)
Once it's done baking, pull it out and let it sit for a few minutes before cutting into it! Otherwise it will just be hot lasagna lava.
Serve it to a bunch of hungry friends and/or family with warm garlic bread and enjoy your hero status. :D
