Beautifully rendered in "graphic novel" style, The Long Dark is a great addition to any library, even in it's early access state.  As Sandbox mode is currently the only way to enjoy the game, my review will stem from that.
Bearing in mind that many things can change, be removed, or are unfinished, the game is already excellent.  I'm hoping the items I am critical of get adjusted and/or changed for release.
You find yourself in the middle of the frozen Canadian north, near an unnamed coastline.  Your number one priority is to find shelter.  Number two, find warmer clothes.  Number three, water, etc.
The controls are the standard WASD keys and they are remapable.  The Tab key is used to bring up the central interface and this is where things are a little frustrating.  Common activites, like drinking and eating, require that you drill into this central interface each and every time.  So, say you wish to drink some water.  You either hit Tab and click on the Inventory Icon or hit "i".  Now, scroll down to Water (Potable) and click on the name.  Now mouse over to the "drink" button and click it.  You will take a drink.  If you don't have enough water to fulfil your needs and want to drink a can of Soda pop, you must do the same action again, only this time clicking on "Summit Soda".   Having to repeat this same activity time and time again to merely eat or drink causes one to wish for a different scheme, like right clicking on the item and click "drink" on a pull down menu.  With multiple needs and with an ever ticking clock, it gets old pretty fast.
There are other frustrations.  This is an open world game, without the ability to either jump or climb.  Thus you're limited in how you can move in a wilderness situation.  This is supposed to be a survival game and yet I cannot climb or jump up on the rock to avoid wolves, a rudimentary primate survival technique.
Clothing degrades . . . faster than armor in Diablo or Skyrim.  Apparently the wind is so strong that it rips the threads right out of your parka (Premium Winter Coat).  In all my years of playing in the winter wonderland that is North Western Wisconsin and Minnesota, I have never had the wind destroy any of my clothing.  I still have wearable jackets from 1984, yet in this game, after wearing my Premium Winter Coat for four days, it's in dire need a repair, and that's without being attacked by a wolf.
Speaking of wolves, they are to be feared, and with the latest update, if you do not have the ability to shoot the animal (like, you know, haven't located a gun or bullets) you are left with no good way to get away from them.  The latest build has changed the Wolves behavior when confronted with a flare and instead of keeping them away, after a bit the wolf comes back.  If you are encumbered, or tired, exhausted, or Freezing, you are generally toast because you cannot make sufficent distance.  Which is a great thing, because the player is forced to make serious choices.  The hardcore nature of the sandbox creates tension when the wolves come out and you've not found a firearm or the hunting knife.  And, it can be quite scary if you've found yourself stuck out of doors and a wolf comes lunging for you out of nowhere.
Much work remains on this project, but my hours with it have been both frustrating and fun.  I believe it deserves your serious consideration as an early-access title.

Aren't sequels supposed to improve in some way upon the previous game in the series? Arcane RERaise, if anything, manages to be worse and more mediocre in every single way than Arcane Raise, even the obscure monetization: It ditches the tradeable Steam marketplace items and makes the cheat item pack be of fairly limited use, but doubles the amount of mutually exclusive DLC characters to 8, while making them even less useful.
Meanwhile, the game still has no original assets, almost no story, a bare minimum of mechanics (2 characters in fixed classes from the first game, all items available from a shop midway through the game), and is just over half an hour long with or without the booster pack, even picking up all chests, which I almost assuredly didn't need to do. At "best," there's one challenging fight, against a Succubus before you are able to access the shop, but noticing that Alex Oriana has Paralysis on his spell list is enough to make that a snap.
To similarly sum up the entire game as I did for the first: after a tutorial featuring mechanics that don't actually exist in the game (e.g. potential punishment for retreating from fights, vehicles), you are put in front of a castle, told that it's full of "Infected" and some NPC's brother is trapped inside (this is never mentioned again), walk up to the castle optionally fighting "Rates" (rats) and zombies on your way, as they're now immobile on-map encounters, fight a semi-difficult Succubus, then enter the castle, full of chests full of money and XP, shops selling all of the items in the game, and the exact same glitchy NPC from the first game which lets you fight the final boss at any point - including the same dialogue, which has no bearing on this game's supposed plot. So again: you grab all the chests, buy +attack items at 200 a pop / 99 for 19800, enjoy the sound of consuming items 99 times in a row, then hit the final boss for 4000 damage five or so times. Now you are not a Shade, but a Shade Alpha, despite that not, as far as I can tell, being the premise of the sequel. Also you can uninstall the game now.
Oh and you get 36 achievements, probably also all stock art, for starting the game. This time loading a "DLC character" savegame doesn't lock you out of the achievements and tutorial, though!
In conclusion, no. Irredeemable, and somehow worse than the first.

TL;DR - A Hat in TIme is a very good collect-a-thon game in which collecting the doo-dads is something you
to do rather then something you
to do by offering fun little rewards in return for collecting them through new abilities, Music, and Cosmetic flairs. The game is relentlessly cute with tinges of dark humor to keep things fresh, all while offering fluid and concise controls
limiting your ability to quickly traverse a level with ever dreadful stamina bars or ridiculous cooldowns.
ALSO the game WILL have steam-workshop-support in the near future!
A Hat in Time is a very fun 'collect-a-thon' more in line with those Mario games of years passed (Mario 64 / Sunshine)
As apposed to those of Donkey Kong and Banjo-Kazooie Offering more reason and story behind the areas in which the game takes place. The story is nonsensically whimsical and wears many of its inspirations on its sleeve but not so much so to detract from its own gameplay and style.
I cant speak for the overall gameplay of Yooka-Laylee but after the time its been out a general idea I can gleam is that much of its collecting doesnt truly leave much to look forward too and the enviroments seem, even from a spectator perspective, incredibly bare. In A Hat in Time in any given level you load into, even the Hub world spacecraft, the enviroment around you is always brimming with character and purpose. The game doesnt just drop you into a sandbox of an open level for you to collect meaningless doo-dads but gives you a fun enviroment for you to explore full of cute easter-eggs and other characters making the level actually feel alive.
The Controls of A Hat in Time also take after the Mario games of the past in that moving around the game feels precise and fluid and never feels too slow. The game doesnt artifically limit your movement capabilites with long cool-downs or stamina meters and simply allows you full reign of its base movement controls and unlocked traversal abilites to do with as you please as you explore the enviroments.
As far as the collection aspect of the game is concerned, as mentioned earlier, collecting all the items the game presents to you is quickly justified to you in the context of the game everything you collect leads either to a New hat (which provide you diffrent abilites) cosmetic pallete swaps for Hat kid, New remixed music (That can be swapped in place of the stages regular music during gameplay and not just played in a jukebox) and even cosmetic model swaps for existing hats providing a new look for the same ability, and unique collectibles based on the world/act its in given more background on certain characters.
The game exudes cuteness from its very being but balances it out with healthy doses of dark humor nothing extreme but enough to make the cuteness of the game remain fresh and throw the player a curve ball to keep them intrested.
Gonna put the 'controversial' bit at the end here as its REALLY not a big deal and it doesnt need anymore attention then necessary as its entirely a non-issue. Jontron IS still in the game as character voice overs and I absolutely do want to give the Dev's and even Humble Bundle (The games publisher) major props for not virtue signalling by taking him out or even really adressing it at all in the public sphere beyond Humble's comments saying they have no say in the devs artistic process in regards to the games they publish. Not even mentioning the controversy beyond what attention it has I feel is the best course of action and hope the dev team continue to brush aside the non-troversy and collect on their well earned praise for what is a dreadfully cute and fun game.
2017 has been a good year for games if I do say so myself.

-If you're getting into this its safe to assume you've played JRPGs before and don't expect to get too much out of the story. While this ones isn't going to jump out at you either (at least not as of 20+ hours), there have been a few moments that I thought were wonderfully done.
-The combat system took some getting used to it. It starts out very easy to button-mash for a good amount of time, and makes combat kind of a chore. But, as you acquire more skills and run into stronger enemies, the combat becomes much more fluid and requires you to time your moves a little better in terms of evasion and arte placement in your combos. Overall, a slow and very boring start that makes its way into a new and very fun combat system.
-The equipment system is what really stood out to me the most. The types of armor and weapons you receive are very limited, but have
randomly generated skills (that you eventually have
control over which skills you receive). The skills have their own abilities, but are also placed on a skill map that stack in certain ways to make different or more powerful skills. Not going to bother getting very in-depth with it, but its an interesting system that makes you really think about how you fuse your equipment together and place skills at higher difficulties.
-Not much to say graphically. Beautiful, plenty of scenery to look at, some graphics glitching, and unfortunate its left at 30 fps.
Overall its been a very fun experience thus far. As with other Tales games, its a very slow start. Maybe more so than any other Tales game I've played, which is unfortunate because that is a big turnoff for some. But so far its been worth the wait because it becomes a very fun and unique game. So glad they brought this to steam as I haven't had the chance to play a new Tales game since Vesperia.

While this game may be by the creator of the Stanley Parable, it is a whole different story - but, in many ways, after playing this game and thinking back to the Stanley Parable, I feel like I understand his original game more.
This game is short but it does well with the story it tells.  The narrator (Davey) creates the story talking about a friend named Coda who made games and then gave up on it.  As you play through each small game that Coda created, the games show similar themes and puzzles throughout.  One of the biggest theme is the theme of being trapped.  If you have never felt like Coda in the past, or even Davey, you may not get a lot of insight into this game and it may seem dull and uninteresting to you.  For those of us, however, who have felt depression, anxiety, and the constant feelings of being trapped and needing validation... this paints a picture which we can truly understand.
This is a wonderful game, and I truly do feel like it is another timeless idea in my mind much like the Stanley Parable was.

For those that have been following the Godus saga, it's been a year since the now-infamous RPS interview.  Many had presumed Godus was dead and buried, but to our surprise Godus Wars comes along.
This was the start of the long-awaited "combat" update for Godus - which is now being framed as a stand-alone RTS game.  The original concept for battles existed in the 2013 alpha builds, but was pulled with the version 2 "it's not free-to-play focused, honest" revamp. Unfortunately, the F2P ethos still lives large (as does the mobile-focused gaming engine, Marmalade) and this is more real time sculpting than it is real time strategy.
I've never seen a strategy game with such a linear path before...
I gave up after ten levels - which is handy as the first paywall would have kicked in soon after!
As with Godus, 22cans are eager to promote what functionality "will" exist in the future, and eager to blur the lines as to what is included in the base price of £10.99 ($14.99) and what is paid-for DLC.  At the time of writing, only the first continent is available in the base package, the second continent by DLC ($4.99), and the remaining five to be determined at a later date - it's possible the final game will cost more than $40.
When you add in the primitive enemy AI, the continuing game crashes from Marmalade and the pointless mechanics such as keys (which appear to restrict your ability to deviate from the intended path) - it's a concept that suffers as a mobile RTS game, and fails as a PC one.
Despite the "early access" label, three years on Godus Wars is no closer to an RTS game than Godus itself is to a "reimaginating of the god game".  It's going to need some serious work to achieve either of those goals.
If you are looking to spend £15/$20 on an RTS game - there are dozens of better alternatives out there, games like Rise of Nations and Age of Empires II have stood the test of time and I'm sure Steam can recommend plenty of modern classics too.

The game itself is terrible - there's very little for the player to actually do. In Godus Wars, you wait until you can build one of two types of unit, then click on the enemy, then repeat that until you move on to the next stage where you do the exact same thing. In Godus, the player waits until they can move small amounts of terrain around so buildings can be built, then they wait some more to do the same. There's apparently a victory condition, but there's a persistent bug that prevents players from moving on.
Speaking of which, the Godus Wars patch is a bug-riddled, slapdash mess that can barely keep one window functioning properly, let alone the two it currently requires.
Outside of the previous lovely art direction and momentarily interesting terrain manipulation, there's nothing about Godus Wars worth recommending. If it hadn't been in development for three years, I'd write it off as a bad game, but given its history, I can't believe it's anything but a scam.

I wrote a lengthy review for the original Godus, explaining what I didn't like and how they could improve on it. I even updated it several times so it reflects the latest changes to the game. But in the end, my opinion never changed: Godus was an epic failure. For Godus Wars I don't intend on investing a similar amount of time, it's just not worth it.
Just as the original game Godus Wars has some potential, but, in it's current state, is not worth the asking price. The sculpting mechanics are still not precise enough and the tacked on RTS elements are very basic. Even though they claim otherwise the whole game screams mobile port.
On it's own Godus Wars currently seems to be a nice 5-bucks time-waster. Neat graphics, simple gameplay and short missions are great for a quick session on your phone. As a PC game however, it still as a long way to go. There might be a good game here somewhere, but, given 22Cans history, I highly doubt that they will ever find it. This could have been the next "Populous: The Beginning" but at the moment it's just a shallow RTS with some sculpting mechanics clearly designed for mobile platforms. Avoid.

Overview: I recommend the Godus base game that comes with Godus Wars.
Update: Godus Wars itself is not being worked on, and is an incomplete game. If you're buying this, buy it for Godus, which has very little combat and is more of a decorating game.
==Why this game is panned by the community==
All of the negative reviews are angry about the messed up kickstarter that went down a few years ago. As a person who followed the Kickstarter but was smart enough to not pay for a game that was just a concept at the time and actually expect a decent product (or the exact product I paid for), I can't say I'm qualified to weigh in on that drama. The big upset was that 22cans went in on developing a mobile game, which was the primary focus of developement, when as far as I know that wasn't even mentioned in the Kickstarter. I've seen Godus panned again and again in video reviews, where the reviewer gave up in the tutorial, just because of the negative stigma; it's really quite unfair.
I will say that game developement takes more money than Kickstarter goals ever aim for. $1 million is NOTHING. $1 million for 'the best game ever' is IMPOSSIBLE. Look at Star Citizen. Almost a billion dollars down on that game, and it's barely a demo after like 2 years. I'd also like to point out that Planetary Annhiliation only delivered it's $1 million dollar goal in spirit. It also had to release an 'expansion pack' to cover all the promises made in the Kickstarter. And that game gets good reviews... and it's only a good game in multiplayer, if your PC can run it in multiplayer. At least Godus gave everyone the expansion pack who previously owned Godus, even if you only payed $2 for it.
==Godus + Godus Wars Summary==
Godus is a good game, though. There's a lot of complaints about waiting, but it's pretty much made to check in every few hours... Like a mobile game. But's it's much better than any mobile game I've ever played. It's very relaxing to build, sculpt, fill in oceans, name citizies, make building projects go faster, and ultimately take over the enemy settlements. It's a very pretty game, too.
It's very well optimized, but there are crash bugs and slow down every once in awhile. Godus Wars, though, opens several windows in the background.. which makes very little sense. That might be a placeholder for some online play feature? There was a map I couldn't play in Godus Wars, in the first release build, that was unplayable for crash bugs
The battles in Godus Wars are strategic enough, mostly focused on city building and planning to overwhelm or get the high ground. It seems like there's a lot of content to offer, and I'm having fun with it so far. It's not a waiting game at all, but it's a little annoying that at least in the starter island you don't get any of the powers you would have in the lategame singleplayer game. It's at the very least better than Populous (which sucks, imo) and that Flash game that everyone raves about based on Populous (which was okay). It reminds me of Age of Empires Online if that game had been enjoyable at all.
For the $15 price tag, the Godus portion of the game is well worth it. I put 47 hours into the base game, up until an island was introduced that was VERY mobile wait-timey. But all the fun I had in the starter world was well worth it. If you like building and tinkering and making your own civilization, with a moderate ammount of forethought, I highly recommend Godus.

This game is a passionate love letter to 90s beat 'em ups and it really shows in the little details and the references to classics like Turtles in Time, Final Fight and Double Dragon as well as 90s action movie stars like Steven Seagal.
It looks amazing, has snappy combat, fitting music, plenty of stuff to unlock and is really challenging, even on easy. At first it took me a bit to get into it, but once I started to get a bit better, I had a lot of fun stringing combo's together, parrying and dodging to get the best score possible.
The only thing I don't really like is that you need to finish the game in one setting as if you quit, your progress is lost. You only get your score converted to coins (the in-game currency to unlock things) if you finish the game or get a game over.
This used to be in many classics as well, but most of those classics weren't as difficult as Fight'n Rage and keeping focussed for an hour, hour and half can be quite taxing.
In all, it's hard to believe this game is made by one person. Hat off to him for making me relive my childhood!

Full Review:
Zombie Tycoon 2 is a comedic zombie RTS. Do not let the name fool you, this game has nothing to do with building an empire or formulating a grand strategy. There are 8 chapters, each about 30 minutes or so long. Each chapter consists of one map with a series of objectives that must be completed in order to advance.
The controls definitely make this feel like it was created with consoles in mind. You only ever have 4 units at most and each special character/monster will have 4 abilities. Good for consoles or just playing with a controller, rather limiting when you have a keyboard. Without all that many units, controls aren’t really an issue here. A minor complaint would be that there doesn’t appear to be a way to create groups, except by repeatedly dragging the mouse over the units you want. The game also offers multiplayer but I have not tried it and thus cannot comment on it.
Without going into spoilers the general plot is that you play as a mad scientist who is trying to wipe out humanity with your army of zombies. Fun and simple. The visual style is very Tim Schaeffer. While not laugh out loud hilarious, I found the game to be thoroughly amusing despite the fact that no character ever says a word. The entire story is given through various sounds, looks, and actions; no dialogue.
Overall, I enjoyed my 5 or so hours with Zombie Tycoon 2. If it sounds interesting and you can get it at a good price I think it would be worth your while.

Full Disclosure: I am a long-time consumer of the Unreal series, and a nearly life-long fan of both the Unreal series and Epic Games, the developer of said series. As such, I may be VERY biased, and my word might not be completely reliable, though I will try as usual to be as fair as possible.
Unreal Tournament is an Arena FPS whom is THE grandfather of the entire genre, of games which are entirely based upon combat in planned stages designed solely for combat, not story. It has fallen into obscurity since Unreal Tournament 2004's release, so allow me to try and show you how this game became such a staple of gaming.
These days, you've got games that run natively at 60fps, support resolutions for 4K monitors and ultra-wide monitors, and you've got games now which are nearly realistic for appearance. Unreal Tournament, came a bit late, but used it's engine well, Unreal Engine 1, which originated in the first Unreal game, which is an Engine that, even in the 90s, was the cutting edge of graphic fidelity and quality. It stands up even now, despite using polygons, lacking facial animations, but each weapon, and each character looks great even still. Levels still look gorgeous and cool, and almost falling into space still makes me very antsy even after 12 years later.
The game has only three modes. The Singleplayer Campaign, Multiplayer, and an offline skirmish-style mode titled Instant Action. The Campaign is of you, a new combatant in the newest deathsport known as the Unreal Tournament, where convicts have been turned into gladiators whom kill one another and win with the goal of becoming The Tournament Champion, effectively attaining a sort of celebrity-status. Multiplayer is smooth and reliable. There are no problems with the game itself that I've found, even with this re-release. Modes for it, are identical to Instant Action, only some maps function with people, as you don't need AI pathing with human players.
Instant Action's modes are Deathmatch, Team Deathmatch, Last Man Standing, Capture The Flag, Assault and Domination.
The only ones which aren't obvious and in other games, are Domination and Assault, so I will describe them.
Assault, is by far my favorite mode in virtually any game and it is a team-based mode with two teams. One team attacks a base, completing preset objectives and eventually aiming to complete them all, while the other team's objective is to stop the attacking team from completing objectives by any means.
Once the attacking team completes their objectives, they win the match, should they do all objectives and both teams switch sides, the defensive team becomes the new attacker, and vice-versa. At this point, the newly attacking team must match the completion time of the other team, or they will suffer a loss of the match. Though the sides switch even if the first attackers don't succeed, allowing both teams to attack and defend each match.
Domination, on the other hand, is a sort of variant of traditional King of The Hill gamemodes. Only there are multiple Hills, or Points, which either team (up to 4 teams, unlike other modes, save for TDM) must hold to win the match. Holding a point wil generate one score point for the team every 3 seconds or so, and holding more points will generate more.
It also has something no non-Unreal title has ever really adopted whole-heartedly; Mutators. Think of a mod, imagine how annoying it is that you can't just tick it on or off, or combine it with others witohut conflict for the most part. Mutators allow you to change parts of the game, like Low Gravity, and entirely different set of weapons, or powerful relics that change the game's strategies, or even classics like Volatile Ammo (ammo that is shot will discharge, resulting in hilarity from shooting ammo than the enemy) and Fatboy (Where your character model gets more "fat" or just wider, with obvious texture stretching, based on how well you're doing. Whoever wins, usually ends up being the fattest, while the one who did the worst, ends up like a skinny stick figure).
Due to the game being made in the 90s, the options menu isn't TOO varied, but it sort of gets hte job done.
It's got Video Driver settings, Resolution, graphics quality, texture quality (32 bit and 16 bit), A minimum FPS setting for video settings. It has the usual for audio, which technically hasn't changed for many games in years. You can alter the in-game auto-swap priority for different weapons, I personally have dual enforcers at the top above the sniper rifle. Input options are fairly varied with two different forms of sensitivity, and different mouse-based look options.
The game is difficult... if you want it to be. It has quite literally 12 different difficulties, from Novice to Godlike, there's almost no way anybody is too awful to play any difficulty of this game. With Novice, AI are painfully stupid, maybe even intentionally avoiding powerups in at least early singleplayer levels, whereas in Godlike, the AI become Kung-Fu gun masters, constantly know where you are and instinctually know when items respawn and always try to hog powerups aswell as having almost perfect aim and reaction, even mimicking players by spastically jumping around.
This game's soundtrack holds up today. In Unreal Tournament 3, most of hte songs are simply remixes of classic songs from this game, there's almost no single song that hasn't made it, and the music in this game are great for listenning when working out, writing, or even playing other games with.
The announcer is also very well voiced. It's dominantly used for custom content quite often, mostly in Gmod, though it's confused for the Announcer in Quake 3 Arena... which is actually more of a knock-off with 90% less recorded dialogue and announcements.
The game has barely any Story. IN the campaign, you are a newly brought-in convict in charge of your own team. Your goal? To climb the ladder of this tournament deathsport (which is canon as a sort of reality show to the human race) and to become the Tournament Champion by defeating it's first champion, Xan Kreigor... who is really hard to kill in-game. That's it though. You gain trophies though, and they still look cool!
The game comes with a decent amount of content, but given how some still play multiplayer, and that if you look in the right places, you can find over 10 GBs worth of custome content. Given how I once had only 2 gbs of content on my copy of the game in the past, that was over 500 maps, 7 game modes, 4 mods, and many mutators.
Some of these maps have neutral AI players which are super-powerful and are remixed versions of other official maps, using a different theme, or maps of such quality, you'd think
Some of these custom gamemodes is the wonderful Monster Hunt, like Assault, but the defending team is always the monsters, and the players are always attacking to get to the end before losing all their lives, or the chaotic 4-Team Capture The Flag. My second favorite is Jailbreak, bbasically Team Deathmatch meets Capture The Flag. Two teams aiming to kill one another and jail them, then watch them get executed, sometimes able to have prisoners of either team pit against one another in a 1v1 where the winner goes free, and it's possible to release your team by going into enemy territory.
This game is simply one of my favorites. It's always been one of my favorite as I can't remember a time it wasn't installed on my computer. Even just to play the Campaign, I've never forgotten this game, and I always have had a copy of it since I first played it when I was 10. If you like FPS games, or the idea of a gladiatorial arena-style game tickles your fancy, then pick this game up. There's more custom content than what I suggested like voice packs, models, even Total Conversions and far more.
I recommend this due to it simply being one of the best Arena FPS' to ever appear on the market. I don't think you'll regret your purchase.

Day 1: I have nothing but a box of matches as I huddle behind a pile of logs to stay out of the wind. I try to light a fire, but the blizzard keeps blowing out my tinder. I don't dare leave the relative safety of the logs and freeze in the storm, but I can see the direction of the snow being blown around me is starting to shift.. I don't have much time before I freeze, so I start sprinting through the blinding snow in hopes of finding shelter. After what seems like days, I spot something red whipping in the wind. It's the Canadian flag, and it's in front of a small cabin. Safe at last.

Day 8: I've recovered from the minor frostbite, and have been fishing through a hole in the ice for the last few days. Between foraging for wood and melting snow for water, I've built up quite an appetite. The salmon and trout have kept me full, but the axe I found in this cabin is almost about to break. So I stock up on fresh water and tinder, and I head out into the wilderness for another place to stay.

Day 10: I've found a hunting cabin with a rifle!! Sadly, I can't find any bullets.. But the weight in my hands give me a sense of security, false as it may be. But now I'm determined to change my fortune. I won't just endure the environment anymore... I'll thrive in it. I just need a few rounds to start eating some tasty wolf meat.
Tasty wolf meat.
Wolf meat.
Meat.
Me.
Day 12: There's a forest lookout on top of a mountain. Rangers and Mounties have guns, right? Probably bullets too.
As I start my ascent to the top of the mountain, I hear a wolf howl. God damn tasty wolf, all full of meat and♥♥♥♥♥♥.. It could be anywhere. What are the chances of it being on this pat--- OH♥♥♥♥♥♥it's turning the corner in front of me!
Now it's just me and the wolf. I slowly drop the rifle and bring out a flair. It lights and hurts my eyes, but it's the only thing I have to potentially scare it off.
The hair on it's back stands on end. I can hear the growls start to intensify. It's about to charge, but just as it leaps forward I throw my flair at it and hear it yelp in surprise. It runs away from the stick of life-saving white-phosphorous, and I am inclined to run after it. It won't be scared for long, and it can catch up to me if I run down the mountain. My only hope is to make it to the forestry lookout before it regains it's wits.
The sound of wooden stairs beneath my body weight was a welcome change.

Day 29: Well, I'm a master hunter now. I found bullets in the lookout, hunted that wolf, and ate every ounce of meat off his body. Tasty wolf meat.
Since then I've killed several more wolves, and have had the luxury of fast exploration now that my boom-stick assures me safety. I've found knives, hatchets, tools, and more clothing and canned food than I know what to do with. My run in with fluffy at the dam might haunt me for a while, but at the moment I'm far away from that place. Some kind of Coastal Highway. My current living conditions have been fairly pleasant. There's a garage with a convenience store that still had some snacks, but I've found plenty of bullets in the surrounding cabins, so deer and wold meat is never far away. I think I'll go get more of a stockpile from the other surrounding cabins.

Walking on the road I see a black shape over a hill, but it quickly dissapears behind a tree. I investigate, but come up empty. No paw prints, no wolf. But what's this? A dead deer on the side of the lake. I can still feel it's body heat residing in the carcass... but I didn't kill this deer. A quick 360 scan and no sign of a predator. Ah well! I got 12lbs of meat off this deer. I can eat happy for a week and make it to a full month!
But as I walk towards the garage, the wolf (presumably the one who took down the deer) turns the corner and charges at me. My rifle round pierces it's hip, but doesn't kill it. I feel it's teeth on my neck. I'm meat to it, and I know what hunger does to a living thing.
But my knife meets it's ribs, and it jumps off of my in fright. But this isn't over, you stupid wolf. You're full of calories that I NEED! But this deer meat is slowing me down, and the wolf is now too far away to risk shooting at it. I'll probably miss.
So after I drop the raw deer meat on the ground I start my pursuit. The wolf keeps it's distance, but I'm waiting for it to turn it's flank to me so I can get a larger target. It's been 29 days and 12 hours since this plane crashed, and with this deer and wolf I'll surely be able to make it to day 40 in that garage. The thought of turning away this wolf-meal is unimaginable right now.

Gun in hand, I bring the rifle stock to my shoulder. My cheek pressed firmly on the butt of the rifle, I aim down the sites. My cold finger begins to gently squeeze the trigger. I can't miss.

Something hits me. Big. Black. Hungry.
It's a wolf. That ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ had a pack with him.
Biting.
Wolf.
Meat.
Me.
Meal.
The Long Dark...

In 2291, the New Earth Government (NEG) legalizes "consentual murder" as a form of entertainment.  Due to an increase in reports of violence among deep space miners, the NEG sees the organization of gladitorial tournaments as a means of redirecting unrest among the working class for profit.  The largest mining corporation, Liandri Mining Corp. (LMC) begins providing arenas for the Tournament as well as broadcasting the event throughout the known galaxy.  LMC's profits soar as athletes, condemned criminals, mercenaries, soldiers, and regular citizens travel across the universe to compete.
The game takes place fifty years after the NEG's unprecedented decision.  As one character from a diverse roster of participants, the player competes in the Tournament's various events for unique reasons.  The ultimate goal?  Depose Xan Kriegor, the undefeated Tournament champion, and claim universal renown.
A first person shooter (FPS) in the truest sense, Unreal Tournament 1999 (UT99) sees players compete against AI and/or human opponents in a variety of game modes.  Deathmatch and Team Deathmatch have players racing to be the first to get a set amount of kills alone or as a team respectively.  Domination sees two teams fighting over control points, with every point controlled adding to the respective team's total; the first team to accrue a set amount of points wins.  Capture the Flag has the teams capture the enemy flag for points while defending their own at the same time.  Finally, Assault has one team in an offensive role while the opposite team plays a defensive role.  Maps that assualt take place on require the attacking team to complete a series of objectives while the defending team prevents them from doing so.  At the end of a round of Assault, the teams switch roles and the now attackers must either complete more of the assualt than the former attackers or complete the map in less than the time it took the former attackers to complete.  The singleplayer portion of the game involves playing through a certain amount of a particular gametype until the next Tournament rung is unlocked.  Each time you start a new rung, there is an optional tutorial level explaining how to play that particular gamemode.  Singleplayer is essentially matches against AI opponents who can be set to various difficulty levels.  The bot AI is one of the great things about UT99 because bots behave in a challenging, almost adaptive manner.
Each game mode features maps designed solely for that gamemode with the exception of a few overlapping arenas.  Assault maps are the most linear whereas Deathmatch maps are more open. Some arenas are symmetric while others asymetric and complicated.  A few arenas even feature a special condition, such as "Morpheus" which takes place atop a stratospheric skyscraper and features low gravity for huge jumps.  Filling these outlandish arenas is a plethora of futuristic and conventional weaponry.  Take the plasma rifle for example: primary fire is a straight beam, secondary fire is a slower moving orb, but if you shoot the secondary projectile with the primary fire, it detonates causing a small explosion.  Most weapons feature an alternate fire mode and can only be reloaded by picking up ammo scattered around the arena.  Steady aim is important as most weapons chew through ammo fairly quick.  Health vials and various armor pieces can be picked up to increase your longevity although respawning is instantaneous, giving gameplay a brisk and hectic pace.  There are also items scattered around arenas to pick up like the anti-grav boots for huge jumps and scuba gear for underwater breathing.  Finally, modifiers can be found in somewhat hard to reach places that can boost your damage with weapons, health, or even make you invisble.  Knowing arena layouts, the limitations of each weapon, and where modifiers spawn is essential to victory.
Unfortunately due to the age of the game, you should expect to only play UT99 in singleplayer as there are not many games to be found online.  Although sold as UT99: Game of the Year Edition, this version on Steam does not in fact include the game of the year content.  Ambitious players can attempt to track the extra content down however I have read that the missing content does not amount to much anyway compared to the base game.
Every match in UT99 begins in free roam mode.  This allows you to fly around the map and learn where all the weapon/item spawns are, where the enemy base is, and where conflicts are likely to occur.  Free roam is also nice in that you can see just how detailed certain arenas can be.  Built on the same engine as Unreal (Epic Game's 1998 title), UT99 is definitely an old looking game in terms of chracter and environmental models.  However, every arena feels unique in its tone and atmosphere.  From the lighting to the architectural theme of each map, the level design feels thoughtful as well as considerate of the type of game UT99 is.  Adding to the frantic nature of the game is a nice electronic soundtrack featuring lots of drum and bass.  Who can forget the music of "Facing Worlds"?  Characters are voiced appropriately over-the-top and the weapons sound sharp and distinct.  The game features a thorough list of options so players can tailor and mod the game as they see fit.
Long before I was a PC gamer, I played the Infogrames Playstation 2 port of UT99.  It featured updated textures and additional maps not found here on the Steam version, but aiming was clunky with an analog stick.  I purchased the steam version largely out of nostalgia and a desire to play the game as it was meant to be played.  In these respects, UT99 did not disappoint me even though I was retreading ground.  Unfortunately due to the age of the game, you should expect to only play UT99 in singleplayer or with friends as there are not many games to be found online.  From the soundtrack to fast-paced tone of the game, UT99 and its 2004 successor are

If the game's free or it costs <$3, I'd recommend it. Otherwise, I don't.
I played just over 80 minutes of it, and took my time. I didn't bother to attempt to scour every detail, but I didn't rush, either. Even then, that'd be fine, if the narrative or gameplay were more enjoyable.
If you've ever worked on an indie game while battling depression/anxiety, you might feel some resonance with the tale. However the point is kinda hamfisted, insistent, and even a bit self-phallating.
The final ~10 minutes of the game were the only things keeping me from being downright peeved that I'd spent money on this at all. Even then, there was absolutely nothing fun or too terribly interesting about the journey to that point.
Lastly, the overall final point of the game is also severely muddied by the fact that the dev put it on sale for $9.99. (Though I got it 20% off ... $7.99 doesn't change my mind). If you wanted the game to be a message instead of enjoyable, and have that message spread, then why charge for it at all ...? Makes the entire point seem made-up, like you've just done nothing for a few years and wanted to push out some unfinished stuff as a cash grab. Hopefully that's not the reason the game was made, but it should be rather clear what I'm getting at here.

Roughly a week in, and I've already poured hours into this title. It's one of those games where you look at the clock and wonder where the past 3 hours went. This is the city building simulator I've been wishing every other god game was for years. I've always resented my obligation to participate in combat, campaign modes, or politicking. When you take all of that out and focus on the city itself, the result is pure magic. In the end, this game is about balance. When one element gets out of whack the whole thing can fall apart. Carefully manage your resources though, and (barring unexpected disaster) you will be golden. There is a decent amount of micromanagement here, but it is not no overwhelming.

Such a fun game. I played a ton of this back when it was on Xbox 360, and I plan to put a lot more time into it now that it's on PC. It's an extremely cheesy, ridiculous, disgustingly bloody game where you run around shooting pigs, kicking their body parts into a grinder to buy ammo/grenades/milk/melee boosters/etc, and talk to a farmer with a close relationship with a pitchfork.
It starts off slow, but once you hit the Princess Blubbergut boss fight it all starts to get much, much more bloody and crazy. Early on you're only dealing with 10-20 pigs in a day, but after a while it'll crank up the difficulty with 50+ pigs at a time. Revenge Days are the best days of the week, giving you infinite explosive ammo and tons of pigs to gib for the grinder.
There's a decent amount of weapons, 100 days (levels), and three characters to unlock. There's a lot of content here for $1! I'd highly recommend it if you enjoy horde-style games, ridiculous gore, and a game that doesn't take itself seriously.
The only issues I've had with the game are not being able to rebind keys*, not able to edit the camera while using a keyboard (but you can with a controller by pressing Start), the black border around the screen no matter the resolution you use, some sound issues with gunshots, and sadly that co-op (which was on the Xbox 360 version) is not in this current PC port. However, the developer has said he's interested in doing it, but it sounds like it'll only be possible if the game sells well enough.
The rest of the issues I'm sure will be fixed sooner or later. The default keybindings are fine (minus X being use, instead of E), but I'd still like to be able to rebind*.
Also, the developer is extremely cool. If you have any issues, just hit him up, he responds really quickly and will try to help you fix any problems! I hope he'll bring some of his other games to Steam one day soon, I'd kill a thousand skeleton pigs just to play DeadKings (with the multiplayer included, hopefully!) on PC.
*Edit: Rebinding has now been added in the most recent patch. You just have to go to your game folder, find the KEYBOARD folder, then edit the KEYS_BU.txt to your liking. Once you're done rename that file to KEYS.txt and it'll work just fine!

Six hours in I'm already addicted. At first I as disappointed that there weren't that many attack options, but then I realized it's the right handful amount for all the combo possibilities you can connect. The graphics are nice 16-bit arcade style I grew up, the soundtrack rocks, and the gameplay is fluid once you understand what the characters can do.
Fight'N Rage really is an easy game to pick up as the controls are easy to learn, but learning how to connect them and discovering enemy strategies is where the challenge lies. I feel like the people who complain about this game's difficulty are far too used to AAA titles where flash takes presecedence over substance. Not that I don't like AAA games and their graphics. Of course there's amazing action set pieces found in stuff like Uncharted or the new Tomb Raider games and those are thrilling to play--but the CHALLENGE from games of yesteryear has been lacking in the AAA department and can mostly be found by indie developers.
Enter in FNR and you've got yourself a challenging and replayable game where there is no hand holding auto save, and each time you play you need to commit to the 1-2+ hours it takes to get through the varying paths you can take in the game. The time my vary based on how many continues you require, but if you're smart, you can easily learn how to use the combo system to your advantage and survive better when you figure out how enemies behave.

- How do you make the element of difficulty in an RTS unique and refreshing? Make the UI so cluttered and unnecessary that the main menu itself requires a strategy. Then, while the game has seemingly started, block out the "Exit Game" option in the menu screen.
-  Pathing is a quintessential aspect of all RTS games, which is why Molyneux knew he had to reinvent it to stand out. His solution? Use minimal programming, blame any problems on dynamic terrain, and then make it so that right-clicking is both the unit position command and the only way to move the camera fluidly. Didn't hold down the mouse button long enough after you clicked? Guess where your unit is going.
-  To give your games more close-to-home difficulty, losing even a single match inserts malicious batch executables into random string values in your client, disabling your Data Execution Protection and attacking your computer memory relentlessly.
- Essentially, Godus Wars is a reboot of Dune II, one of the greatest RTS games known to man. Molyneux's reinvisioning of the classic strategy game incorporates only its best elements with new standards in visuals and performance not capable in the early 90's.
- Important to every developing Early Access title is an active and friendly community of developers and moderators. Continuing the trend set by the original Godus, Godus Wars is host to exactly that. If the slightest problem occurs, your reported issues and concerns are
handled
by 22Cans and its moderators.

This is a fairly flexible software that will give you what you are willing to invest into it.
Let me explain.
Starting up a project takes a long time. A LONG time. You have to fiddle with the characters. You have to fine tune their stats and levels. You have to make a non-♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ inventory database. Monsters. Balance (omg). Mind you, you have presets to start with, but they sorta blow on many, many levels. Then you draw maps, you choose some music, etc. You can import things from sources, but it might take time to locate/download/import, while also not realizing if you can actually use those resources or not (at least mention the authors in some rolling credits somewhere).
Then you have to... uh... softcode. It's not a string of C+ gibberish mind you, and you don't need a degree in computers, but it still has a bit of a dauting logic and attributes you need to figure out. Nothing is so complex that you won't be able to. But putting it all together so it works like a charm takes time. Much time.
The end results? Varies based on how good you are at doing all the above-stated, and how good you are at actually making a game. It has to be fun. It has to be challenging. It has to be addictive. Is your game all this (after having done all the above-stated doodads)? I don't know.
Luckily, you can easily find out with the integration of Workshop/Steam community and online. It looks like thousands of people are trying to make RPGs.
If anything, it makes for a great hobby. For the rest, it's really up to you.

I first tried this game on the Xbox 360 months ago, and when I first tried it, I didn't like it. I'm not entirely sure why. As time passed, my interest in the Fallout series grew again and I finally purchased Fallout 3 for my laptop even though it's running Windows 10 and people were complaining about it not running or running properly on Windows 10.
I didn't have issues running the game for the first time, though it was crash-happy and did have trouble launching from time to time. I know it says I've only got 2 hours on the game. I'd estimate that I have closer to 20-25 hours because I installed FOSE (Fallout Script Extender, used for script mods), and I'm not sure if I installed it improperly but Steam stopped counting up my time spent and the Steam overlay disappeared.
The game was a lot of fun to play, however. I really loved exploring the desolate, abandoned, dead and creepy ruins of Washington, D.C. and I would recommend it to anyone who's just getting into the 3D Fallout games.
Unfortunately, there is a certain caveat with Fallout 3. I was not at all happy with the game's ending for a number of reasons and I'm pretty sure most other people were not happy with it either. I'm not going to spoil anything, but once you start the quest called "Take it Back!", a part of the main questline, make sure you've explored everything and done all the other quests you want to because once the questline ends, you can't go back and do everything you've missed with that save - regardless of the choices you make during that quest. You'll need to start a new save if you want to continue exploring the rather large map.
I'm pretty sure one of the game's DLCs changes the ending and allows you to continue playing after the main questline has concluded (I think it's called Broken Steel, but I'm not entirely sure) but I just thought it was important to mention that because I had no idea when I finished my first playthrough.
I also noted that Fallout 3 is not very mod-friendly, unless of course I'm doing it wrong. The game frequently crashed with almost any mods installed and other mods that didn't crash the game either didn't work properly or didn't work at all.
I would say that you should play Fallout 3 if you're looking to get engaged into the Fallout universe and lore, despite Fallout 3's problems and disappointing ending. I've started Fallout: New Vegas (released a couple years after Fallout 3) and it's better than Fallout 3 in nearly every way. It works well with its script extender (Steam overlay and counter appear to work correctly) and other mods I've installed seem to also work properly as well. Also, it is much more stable on Windows 10 and even runs a little better than Fallout 3 did.

Having backed this game waaay back in 2013, I can safely say A Hat in Time is well worth the wait.
Without spoiling much you have four worlds (with 2 more in the form of free DLC on the way) with about sevenish levels each, plus additional challenge levels. The game takes inspiration from Super Mario Sunshine in many aspects, from how Hat Kid handles to the nature of the challenge levels. The writing is very clever with some good jokes every now and then and the voice acting (which most of the game's dialogue is voice acted) is quite good. Missions are quite diverse, giving you a range of scenario's to partake in one world. The badges available in the game (which are equipable abilities such as the default grappling hook or the coin magnet) are quite varied, some don't give you abilities but can change the game slightly (such as one that reduces your HP to 1 for challenge runs or another that muffles all the voice acting so it's comparable to Banjo Kazooie's voice clips).
Plus the variety of available options in the menu guarantee you can run this game even on a pretty crappy computer (I use a Lenovo Ideapad which is more for business than video games)
Now, A Hat in Time isn't perfect, that's to be expected. But don't fret, the faults I had with the game were few and far between, and the blast I had with the game far outweighed the faults.
To be frank, we've had a lot of big name Kickstarter disappointments since 2013, but Gears for Breakfast delivered on their promise to give us a great 3D collectathon platformer, and although some features are coming post launch (such as co-op) I can fully guarantee this is a game that any fan of the 3D collectathon platformer genre will want to pick up.

Simply put: A Hat in Time is love letter to an era defined by Nintendo's 3D Platformers, which can be seen in the forms of Super Mario 64, Super Mario Sunshine, and Rare's Banjo-Kazooie duology.
It has all the makings of solid platformer, infused with colorful graphics, funny story telling, and unique & varied gameplay styles in levels throughout. DNA from other platformers such as Psyconauts, Rachet & Clank, and even Conker's Bad Fur Day can be seen through its unique story-telling, level design, and collectibles.
It's definitely the next "Mario Sunshine" in all senses, and I feel this will be a new age classic that will live down in history as the shining star of the resurgence of 3D Platformers. It will certainly be a darling of this era, which I suspect will live up to Undertale and other such titles.
In all, this is this studio's first title, and that's utterly imressive. It'f fun, charming, challenging, creative - all the marks, and I can't wait to see what Gears for Breakfast has to offer next.

Day 1: I have nothing but a box of matches as I huddle behind a pile of logs to stay out of the wind. I try to light a fire, but the blizzard keeps blowing out my tinder. I don't dare leave the relative safety of the logs and freeze in the storm, but I can see the direction of the snow being blown around me is starting to shift.. I don't have much time before I freeze, so I start sprinting through the blinding snow in hopes of finding shelter. After what seems like days, I spot something red whipping in the wind. It's the Canadian flag, and it's in front of a small cabin. Safe at last.

Day 8: I've recovered from the minor frostbite, and have been fishing through a hole in the ice for the last few days. Between foraging for wood and melting snow for water, I've built up quite an appetite. The salmon and trout have kept me full, but the axe I found in this cabin is almost about to break. So I stock up on fresh water and tinder, and I head out into the wilderness for another place to stay.

Day 10: I've found a hunting cabin with a rifle!! Sadly, I can't find any bullets.. But the weight in my hands give me a sense of security, false as it may be. But now I'm determined to change my fortune. I won't just endure the environment anymore... I'll thrive in it. I just need a few rounds to start eating some tasty wolf meat.
Tasty wolf meat.
Wolf meat.
Meat.
Me.
Day 12: There's a forest lookout on top of a mountain. Rangers and Mounties have guns, right? Probably bullets too.
As I start my ascent to the top of the mountain, I hear a wolf howl. God damn tasty wolf, all full of meat and♥♥♥♥♥♥.. It could be anywhere. What are the chances of it being on this pat--- OH♥♥♥♥♥♥it's turning the corner in front of me!
Now it's just me and the wolf. I slowly drop the rifle and bring out a flair. It lights and hurts my eyes, but it's the only thing I have to potentially scare it off.
The hair on it's back stands on end. I can hear the growls start to intensify. It's about to charge, but just as it leaps forward I throw my flair at it and hear it yelp in surprise. It runs away from the stick of life-saving white-phosphorous, and I am inclined to run after it. It won't be scared for long, and it can catch up to me if I run down the mountain. My only hope is to make it to the forestry lookout before it regains it's wits.
The sound of wooden stairs beneath my body weight was a welcome change.

Day 29: Well, I'm a master hunter now. I found bullets in the lookout, hunted that wolf, and ate every ounce of meat off his body. Tasty wolf meat.
Since then I've killed several more wolves, and have had the luxury of fast exploration now that my boom-stick assures me safety. I've found knives, hatchets, tools, and more clothing and canned food than I know what to do with. My run in with fluffy at the dam might haunt me for a while, but at the moment I'm far away from that place. Some kind of Coastal Highway. My current living conditions have been fairly pleasant. There's a garage with a convenience store that still had some snacks, but I've found plenty of bullets in the surrounding cabins, so deer and wold meat is never far away. I think I'll go get more of a stockpile from the other surrounding cabins.

Walking on the road I see a black shape over a hill, but it quickly dissapears behind a tree. I investigate, but come up empty. No paw prints, no wolf. But what's this? A dead deer on the side of the lake. I can still feel it's body heat residing in the carcass... but I didn't kill this deer. A quick 360 scan and no sign of a predator. Ah well! I got 12lbs of meat off this deer. I can eat happy for a week and make it to a full month!
But as I walk towards the garage, the wolf (presumably the one who took down the deer) turns the corner and charges at me. My rifle round pierces it's hip, but doesn't kill it. I feel it's teeth on my neck. I'm meat to it, and I know what hunger does to a living thing.
But my knife meets it's ribs, and it jumps off of my in fright. But this isn't over, you stupid wolf. You're full of calories that I NEED! But this deer meat is slowing me down, and the wolf is now too far away to risk shooting at it. I'll probably miss.
So after I drop the raw deer meat on the ground I start my pursuit. The wolf keeps it's distance, but I'm waiting for it to turn it's flank to me so I can get a larger target. It's been 29 days and 12 hours since this plane crashed, and with this deer and wolf I'll surely be able to make it to day 40 in that garage. The thought of turning away this wolf-meal is unimaginable right now.

Gun in hand, I bring the rifle stock to my shoulder. My cheek pressed firmly on the butt of the rifle, I aim down the sites. My cold finger begins to gently squeeze the trigger. I can't miss.

Something hits me. Big. Black. Hungry.
It's a wolf. That ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ had a pack with him.
Biting.
Wolf.
Meat.
Me.
Meal.
The Long Dark...

Such a fun game. I played a ton of this back when it was on Xbox 360, and I plan to put a lot more time into it now that it's on PC. It's an extremely cheesy, ridiculous, disgustingly bloody game where you run around shooting pigs, kicking their body parts into a grinder to buy ammo/grenades/milk/melee boosters/etc, and talk to a farmer with a close relationship with a pitchfork.
It starts off slow, but once you hit the Princess Blubbergut boss fight it all starts to get much, much more bloody and crazy. Early on you're only dealing with 10-20 pigs in a day, but after a while it'll crank up the difficulty with 50+ pigs at a time. Revenge Days are the best days of the week, giving you infinite explosive ammo and tons of pigs to gib for the grinder.
There's a decent amount of weapons, 100 days (levels), and three characters to unlock. There's a lot of content here for $1! I'd highly recommend it if you enjoy horde-style games, ridiculous gore, and a game that doesn't take itself seriously.
The only issues I've had with the game are not being able to rebind keys*, not able to edit the camera while using a keyboard (but you can with a controller by pressing Start), the black border around the screen no matter the resolution you use, some sound issues with gunshots, and sadly that co-op (which was on the Xbox 360 version) is not in this current PC port. However, the developer has said he's interested in doing it, but it sounds like it'll only be possible if the game sells well enough.
The rest of the issues I'm sure will be fixed sooner or later. The default keybindings are fine (minus X being use, instead of E), but I'd still like to be able to rebind*.
Also, the developer is extremely cool. If you have any issues, just hit him up, he responds really quickly and will try to help you fix any problems! I hope he'll bring some of his other games to Steam one day soon, I'd kill a thousand skeleton pigs just to play DeadKings (with the multiplayer included, hopefully!) on PC.
*Edit: Rebinding has now been added in the most recent patch. You just have to go to your game folder, find the KEYBOARD folder, then edit the KEYS_BU.txt to your liking. Once you're done rename that file to KEYS.txt and it'll work just fine!

You know, I actually didn't mind Godus. Sure, the clicking was annoying, but I did spend a fair amount of time in there building things up and exploring the lands. It wasn't terrible. But this? I don't even know what to make of it. There's only one reason I can think of as to why a company would release a game in this state, and that's money. They should simply call it, "Godus - We Need Money". Where to begin? I'm going to do my review backwards from what I usually do.
Why, in all the holy lands of Godus, does this application launch a second full screen application when I try to battle? I can't even fathom how this works. Are they using some sort of battle engine in Godus that they didn't want to port over to Godus Wars? What happens if I uninstall Godus (I may try this)? I'm completely flabbergasted on this. I wanted to ask in the forum, or maybe it's in the FAQ, but...
The forums are currently locked. Any time a company locks the forum and allows no discussion, right away you know it's to avoid negative threads. And this game, AS IS, will only be negative threads. They knew this was a pile of ... going in to it, yet they pushed it out anyway. Was there no way to simply wait a few weeks until the engine could be fleshed out? They put up absolute garbage and praised it, despite it being several orders of magnitude worse than Godus.
The battles themselves, when they work, are fairly simple. This (I hope) changes later on, but I haven't gotten very far yet because the game keeps crashing. Perhaps it's releated to it trying to run another process and getting confused somewhere inbetween. The few times it has worked, I had to manually select the second window it opens.
One of the major complaints in Godus was all the clicking. The clicking is still in this game, but luckily it appears you don't HAVE to do it. It feels more like a bonus click now. The game generates points on its own, but you can still click the rocks and trees to get additional points. I put this in the bad section because I fear it's going to feel like I still have to click all those rocks if I want to stay ahead.
Graphics-wise, the cards it shows me are blurry if I click on them. They don't appear to be very high resolution (I was running on 1920x1200). The rest of the engine in the battles looked fine since it was the Godus style, but the other windows that were tacked on for this just don't have a crisp look to them. Zombie Tycoon 2 is a real time strategy (RTS) that has you looking down on your small zombie army to command them against a rival zombie army, all with humans caught in the middle. It is not a zombie management game like the tycoon title would have you believe, you won't make a money making business of it. It is very easy to pick up and play (especially with a controller). Despite its zombie theme, it feels like it was meant for kids. Its pretty easy and instead of horrific blood and gore, there is a cute cartoony art style along with humorous animated skipable, cut scenes. Its like watching a cartoon with characters that convey so much without saying a word and I'm happy with that.
When the game starts, the zombie apocalypse has already happened. It seems to be a mutant zombie apocalypse that has turned creatures rather than former people. Your allies will even be a mutated badger, disfigured bear, some sort of creature car and a robot. Basically stated, there are two feuding factions of zombies, the green shamblers and the feral blues. The shamblers seem slower with more HP and the feral blues seem quicker with less HP.
Caught between the two feuding factions are the humans. There are easy to kill civilians, police officers with batons or guns, soldiers that take and give heavy damage. There are even thick bodied hill billies with shotguns that will insta kill lesser zombies with their double barrel.
The controls are simple and very controller friendly, since this was originally a console game. Left thumb stick to move the camera, right thumb stick to zoom in or out and rotate. Left bumper brings you to a map of the entire area and your objectives. The face buttons control your groups, two face buttons command two zombie squads. one group is your commander that if he dies, its a game over, but the game is very forgiving and lets you try from the last checkpoint. The commander will eventually be permanently upgraded to have a sentry gun with a wide radius and his vehicle will spawn zombies. The bottom 'group' is your 'hero' I'll call it, the mutant thing with powers and a lot of energy. The D-pad controls the special powers of the hero characters. The heroes gain experience to unlock these skills and there are brief cool downs when a skill is used. The heroes seems a little brainless and need your commands, while the zombies will attack enemies in range, but not buildings.
Through the campaign, you first play as the shambling zombies, then you will play the feral zombies at around chapter 4. They don't play any different really, but their stories are different. The feral zombie story begins before the shambling zombie story, so they are told out of order in the campaign. The objectives are pretty simple, go here, take over this, attack that. Its all marked on your map and there are arrows so you'll always know the general area where they are. There is fog of war of unexplored areas, so there is a need to explore.
Like many RTS, you can command your horde of zombies to take over houses, tool stores and towers. When you take over something other than a tower or house, you can command your zombies go in and the entire group of zombies will become a different type. Engineers come from tool stores and they can interact with objects on the map, but have no real difference. Flower zombies can be hidden, travel quickly and wait for someone to walk into their trap, brawlers have heavy HP, but less damage per second, Samurai have high DPS, but can't move as quick, throwers well throw things, damaging buildings more than anything. There are other types, but you get the picture. The game has an easy to use codex (bestiary) of monsters, factions and buildings.
When you take over towers, they give you more map visibility and throw items down on enemies. Finally, the homes are seemingly the most important, they spawn non controlled zombies that will just do their own thing. They'll take over other houses or attack other zombies for you. If you ever need to summon all of those non controlled zombies to one place, the right bumper will call them in a 'dead rush,' but there's a long cooldown and it rarely feels useful. The enemy faction can retake buildings, human soldiers and hillbillies can liberate buildings from zombie control, so there is a tug of war there.
Its not just the art style and humor that set this game apart from other RTS, it has different sections that I feel deviate from the normal RTS, such as one on one boss fights with patterns, so its not just two 'hero' characters knocking on one another. There are also chapters with stealth aspects, avoiding an enemy view radius and hiding in bushes as they pass by. On top of traditional RTS maps, there is usually something interesting happening, such as burrowing badgers that after a countdown will pop up to eat your zombies and a massive zombie straight laser that will go off every so often to cut through your troops. These are nice layers on top of a simple and easy to play RTS.
With all of that being said, I feel the art style might really hold someone back from getting this game. It is a cute and charming style that fits the cartoon humor. I can hope this studio gets a Disney game license in the future. Not everyone is into cartoon charm. Other than on the surface, this is a very easy, shallow RTS, better for kids, but is easy really so bad? In a $1 bundle its a great game and maybe for a younger audience its worth the $10 to play a 6 hour campaign, but there are better RTS out there.

Godus Wars. An attempt to sweep the reviews under the carpet, it still has the godawful sculpting mechanism that forces you to click and click and click and click, except now instead of running on a unified engine, it switches between Unity and I -think- WebGL (I can't be sure, but it's a pain in the rear because it bounces back and forth like a hyperactive kid who missed a ritalin dose). Every time I want to switch resolution, it needs time to think, every time I start a map, it needs a moment.
It reminds me of Battlelog. That's not a good thing. The RTS mechanics? Oh they're simplistic, you generate units, you send them forward, the pathing AI is terrible, with units unable to react if hostiles enter their firing vicinity, units pathbugging the moment they try to fire upon buildings. It's bad, oh god it's bad. It's like 22Cans thought slapping a REALLY BAD version of Divinity Dragon Commanders' RTS (and that wasn't even a particularly shining RTS example to be fair) on top of their already creaky god sim was a capital idea.
Unsurprisingly, GODUS was a splotchy mess. GODUS Wars is also a splotchy mess. Fable was a lovely splotchy mess. Most games that Molyneux has been involved in have been to some extent, a splotchy mess. There's a recurring pattern in among this. The successes have come about when the rest of the team have been able to refine the splotchy messes and turn them into something that resembles what is actually either going on in Molyneux's head, or a marketable game, or somewhere between the two. It's tricky to figure out where the magic is, when it hits, like Black and White, it opens up whole new ways of looking at games in general, but unfortunately, you wind up seeing a lot of splotchy messes between the rare flashes of inspiration.
Not that it stops him. Now this would be perfectly human and forgivable were it not for the fact that Peter has a ... well, an almost Steve Jobs like "Reality Distortion Field" that he projects. It's as if there are two different worlds in existence at any one time when Peter talks about his games, and when he talks, we're getting a glimpse of the game -he- sees, and not the one -we- see. Case in point would be "Curiosity : What's inside the cube". Peter called it a profoundly lifechanging experience. Pete, mate, IT WAS A GAME WHERE YOU CLICKED CUBES. IT WAS COWCLICKER FOR APPLE DEVICES. THAT IS NOT A LIFECHANGING EXPERIENCE.
The sad part is, the person who won Curiosity still hasn't got a single penny from the fund that was supposedly reserved for him, he may never see such a penny.
One day someone will tether Pete to the ground, and then we may once again see a return to form like the Bullfrog games of old, until then, we're going to see splotchy messes, infused with occasional strokes of genius, but often way, way oversold and far over marketed by Mr. Molyneux himself. Take anything that comes from him OR his dev team with liberal quantities of salt, and look up information about the game from other sources, then make your own decision if things like GODUS and GODUS Wars might appeal in the long run.
Right now GODUS Wars is barely a game, it's two very distinct halves cut and shut together into one ugly, frankensteined whole, and that's created a horrible, malformed monster baby out of code, and out of game. I wish I could describe just how terrible it feels, but the best description I can come up with is that it's the worst elements of Divinity Dragon Commander (which had a lot going for it, but the RTS -was- the weakest link), Battlefield 3's battlelog system (which made people invent new swear words), GODUS (which was frankly appalling), and the horror that comes from letting Peter Molyneux off the leash with nobody to force him to stick to a singular vision.
Would I recommend the package of GODUS or Godus Wars on it's own?
...
...
That would be asking me if I recommend Lutefisk. Only to the very worst of my enemies.

I see no reason to change parts of what I said then, as it's just as valid now. If Pete feels the need to recycle terrible mechanics like that horrific land shaping thing, then I shall recycle what I said about his work prior.

The Xbox Live Indie Market was quite possibly the closest thing console gamers could get to the boundless lunacy offered by some of the lower end Steam games or alpha swamps like Gamejolt or itch.io.
showed up on there in 2013 and although there are no noticeable changes in its jump to PC, this isn't really the kind of game you'll need an HD remaster to enjoy/despise.
Make no mistake,
is a shoddy game; the giant zombified pigs that you must spend each in-game day murdering range from acting suspiciously disinterested at you shooting them in the face to balls-out enraged, charging through solid surfaces and straight over the tops of buildings to crush you. It's an ugly, glitchy mess but it is also deeply entrenched enough in its madness to work.
Instructions are given to you by a farmer in a pitchless monotone, pinned to the barn wall by his own pitchfork, his eyes bulging and manic. You grow to look forward to Revenge Day, a weekly celebration of your survival where all of your guns are loaded up with explosive ammo and firing an AK-47 into a rampage of swine looks like a half ton of fireworks going off in a medical waste bin. Enormous pigs drop by once every ten days for an epic boss battle. There's a last stand mode.
I don't think I ever finished it the first time around; over a hundred levels of this madness is more than my delicate psychological balance can take quite frankly but you should easily grind some enjoyment out of it for the meagre asking price.

But if you want your (J)RPG game to set the standards for games in the future, then you need to learn how to code Ruby.
-Graphics:
Pixel and chibi, but changes for avatars and enemy battle sprites to anime.
==Overall Rating==
If you have the time, the additional programs to create the art and music, have the skills, and possibly some scripts to enhance your game, this is an amazing tool. After a while, you could even make non-RPG games (with heavy scripting.).
