Abso-♥♥♥♥in'-lutely worth your time. This is love letter to beat-em-ups of the 90s, and if you grew up with Final Fight, Streets of Rage and the like, this plays like a perfected, smoothed, updated version of those games.
Not only is the guy behind this (literally built by one dude, and I've never seen a game made by one man be so fluid, complete, and not-jank) is obviously a fan of the Street Figher Alpha series as well (as am I, which definitely helps my opinion, but I don't think it's necessary for someone to love this game), from the rotation decals on a spinning enemy being identical to the ones after an Alpha Counter in those games to charaters like Tsong Doo, the rooster who uses Muay Thai and stands on one foot with a mong-kon on, a perfect reference to Adon. Hell, there's a female ninja named Gal who has Guy's exact walk cycle (and F. Norris, the male ninja character, has his exact bread-and-butter combo). There's SF III as well, in the Doberman enemy who boxes you, including Dudley's exact Corkscrew Blow animation. Or the enormous water buffalo named T. Bison who does turnpunches. Or the cat enemy who is dressed exactly like M. Bison (Dictator) and attacks with slide kicks and scissorkicks. Homeboy is a Street Fighter fan, for sure.
There's three characters, Gal (the quick one), F. Norris (the all-arounder), and Ricardo (a bull with a penchant for wrestling moves, from powerbombs to lariats). The story is some kind of catastrophe went down and annihilated human technology while also mutating animals into sapient, humanoid forms. Suffice it to say, they are displeased with their treatment by people, and you are out to stomp 'em back out. Don't feel bad; they've enslaved and eaten loads of people. Stomp 'em back down to their places on the food chain!
Combat feels wonderful. Animations are smooth and buttery. Basic X-X-X-X combos give way to dash attacks, anti-airs and special moves. Everybody has a completely unique moveset and when you find out you can backfist-combo a dude into a roundhouse, then dash forward and slidekick him before he hits the ground to juggle him into a tatsu, or execute Gal's full basic  combo into a guy, cancel into her special move to launch the poor ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ straight up, bread-and-butter him again, THEN flipkick him until he EXPLODES INTO BONES, well, suffice it to say it is IMMENSELY gratifying. Dudes swarm you, but your verbset, while not particularly expansive, combos and interconnects so well, you can dish out pain commensurate with the enemy floods.
Unlockables are through the ROOF. Extra game modes like difficulties or speed settings, some eleven costumes for each character (I don't even have them all for my favorite character yet), and a battle mode where you can play as each of the enemy types, meaning you've got them to unlock, too. There's an entire grid of endings, with some 30 or so possible permutations. You can even unlock a CPU assist mode where you can play with an AI partner (or two!) to get the endings that require multiple characters, even if you don't have buddies who play beat-em-ups available.
I had a feeling I was going to like this game as soon as it pretended to the RAM check cycle that old arcade cabinets did back in the day. I was further convinced of the love and care of the dev when I saw that there are friggin' video modes to mimic the CRTs of days of old, even simulated GLARE, for Christ's sake. The music is great, the gameplay is so smooth you're liable to slide out of your chair, and the references are charming as all get-out. I cannot say enough good about it, and I legitimately believe it is impossible to go wrong for the price. Pick it up, for sure.

Jump scares. JUMP SCARES. So many of them. This isn't a hardcore horror gamer's game, but it's fun for the simplicity and the almost puzzle-style gameplay that you learn later on. Jump scares are only the basics of horror, and the ambience isn't enough to satisfy someone used to, say, Amnesia and Outlast, but the other mechanics make this pretty fun. The player has to check cameras and doors while carefully watching power reserves and learn how to balance everything, including which freaky animatronic thing to watch at which moment.
Graphics are not special and animations are rare, but that's not needed nor is it the point, so it doesn't detract much from the experience. The only issue I have is not being able to run in windowed mode. Pressing ESC also simply exits the game and there are no options to start with.
There is a little bit of replayability included as every time you start a night at Freddy's, each of the animatronics act somewhat randomly, so those who really enjoy the gameplay can do it more than once. Most will not feel the need to replay, however.
Overall this is well worth the budget price and great for streaming, but horror fanatics probably won't be as scared as the average, unless he/she has a specific fear of childhood toys or Chuck-e-Cheese.

First off, I'm going to begin by saying that I have been following the development of A Hat in Time literally since day one (back in 2012 when the creator first posted a video on an experimental UDK game he had just started on.) I managed to keep myself from any spoilers whatsoever (other than the one that he spoiled about the antagonist almost immediately after creating her) by not watching any videos of the beta or alpha builds that were out. So, now that I've got my hands on the game, what do I think about it? I think it's pretty good so far. The music is creative and fun to listen to, the characters are of an interesting and entertaining design, the gameplay is pretty solid and reminiscent of Super Mario Sunshine, Super Mario Galaxy, and a hint of the developer's mod for Team Fortress 2 that he developed, "Parkour Fortress." I haven't gotten a chance to check out too many of the levels so far, but I'm having a lot of fun. I would like to make a note, though, at the time of writing this review, I had noticed a number of simple yet noticeable glitches that are in the game. Firstly, and this is the most major one, if you walk into some objects and then open up the hat selection menu, hat kid will start floating up into the air and clip above the ceiling. So far, this hasn't caused any problems, as the walls seem to extend up infinitely, but it's definitely something that should be taken note of. This game became wildly popular recently, and I liked the visuals of it, so I got into it pretty fast - and I watched a LOT of videos of people playing it. The gameplay is pretty simple, but deceivingly so - I had to have watched at least ten different playthroughs of this game, and I thought I would be completely unphased once I started playing.
This is not the case, however. This game is about managing resources, surveying your surroundings while trying to defend yourself, constantly being on the defensive, all while the forces of RNG, programmed AI, and straight up paranoia cause this to be a much more daunting task than one would expect.
This game contains jumpscares, but honestly those aren't the scary part (and for those who have seen videos of this game, for some reason people turn the sound up to ridiculous levels... you can turn it to a reasonable level and the jumpscares aren't so dang loud.) I like them when they happen, because they're pretty well done and only occur when you've failed, but the really scary thing about this game is sitting, waiting, panicking while trying not to run out of electricity, and hearing something moving around, which could be any number of things, all of which might be close enough to kill you within seconds.
I like being terrified by horror games, and this one definitely gets to me, and I love it. I think playing this game is legitimately the first time I've ever been happy to be nauseous from how panicked I got.
(I also love the designs of the animatronics, they're fun to draw, but that's not exactly relevant to a video game review.)

If you're a fan of games that will unsettle you and scare you and cause you to never listen to Bizet's opera Carmen again in the same way, then this is for you. None of what I said is bad, though, as I thoroughly enjoyed this. The concept and execution are simple, in that all you really have to do is click a couple buttons to make sure some rogue animatronics don't kill you. Sounds easy, right?
That's the brilliant part about this game. Even though you stay in one room and really don't do much, the game can be incredibly difficult with the limited amount of power you have. As the nights progress, the animatrons get more and more aggressive, and your reflexes have to be up to the task. If you're not quick enough, then you'll be greeted with a horrifying scream as one of the abominations ends your life. The scream comes on both ends too - the surprise of the animatron sneaking up on you may cause you to scream in horror.
I applaud Five Nights at Freddy's for taking something so simple and making it a challenging, horrifying feat that keeps you on the edge of your seat.

I'm kind of OCD when it comes to building/sim games, and rarely do I get set up for failure. So, Banished has an awkward way of dealing with one of the game's biggest challenges - starvation. The way food works in this game is four-fold: Your citizens grow/catch/hunt/gather the food. They then move the harvested food to storage. Then, the food is gathered by storage and brought to the home. Once it hits this step, then it can be consumed.
I understand one might argue that this makes the game more 'realistic,' or 'challenging.' But in the same respect, if this 'elaborate' mechanic is applied to the harvesting and storage of food, why can't some kind of mechanic get triggered when someone is starving? Instead of sitting at home, staring at bare shelves, why not grab some corn from storage? I've seen my population go into epic famine-mode when I'm looking at stockpiles of food in the storage barn.
If the storage barn is located close to someones house, it allows them to quickly grab some rations when needed. However, if that person is a builder and working offsite, and goes into starvation mode on his way to the jobsite, they usually die on their doorstep upon returning home from their shift.
I admire their work ethic, but it's very frustrating.
This effect happens with other supplies in the game, but not as prevalent.
Overall, it's a good game. I'd like to see some future patches address these issues (and many others found in forums) sooner than later.
Also, Banished has much more potential than what it is right now. It feels empty in certain parts.
Again, despite all of this... and very, very frustrated, game-ending, Alt-F4 mashing nerd rage that it sends me into, I enjoy it.
Overall I'd give it a 7/10

Was doing great. The little town of Aviono, 20k food, 78 adults, around 12 children, and 15 years in. When the 16th year came around, it all went to hell. A fire started, burning one of the three storage barns stocked with food. I tried to get my little people to fight the fire with the wells nearby. They failed miserably and the other two barns caught fire, (this is about the time I realized putting all my food storages close together was a mistake). The fire started to spread to the wooden houses nearby, so I paused the game and looked up how to fight the damn fire. I figured out prioritizing the fire would help, so I did it and it did the trick. After the fire was put out, I checked out the damage. All my food gone and 5-6 houses destroyed. I knew my first priority should be to get my food back up to support my ever growing population of little people. This is where I realised I had made another mistake. Over 70% of my food was coming from potato farms, and guess what? All of my farms were right next to each other and an infestation started. Farm after farm were getting infected and loosing crops and I had no idea how to stop it. (I'm not one to go back and load and earlier save) So I paused it and looked it up, I couldn't find out how to stop it this time and I let it run it's course. Now the starvation began, and the graveyard began to fill up with little people's grave stones. It was too late to plant crops to get enough food to feed them all, so I basically gave up and watched everyone die a horrible death. I closed my eyes, mourning the loss of the little people that I had led around for so long. Then...I opened my eyes. I had three people still living! One 19 year old male and one 22 year old mother with her 6 year old male child. I had another chance to fix the broken city and save Aviono. This female was my last hope, unless I could get her with a female child, all was lost. So I set them to work tearing down the now unoccupied houses of the original Aviono, since I was almost completely out of materials.  I got them to live close to eachother and waited paitently untill....success! A female child was born. Life was good again. I set my new couple to tearing down everything not needed for materials and the future growth or Aviono. In the end, I had two stone houses, one of every type of resource production buildings, a town hall, and a cemetery (to remind me of the past mistakes). I got my population back up to 16 little people, and I sat back and sighed with relief. I had saved a town.
Then I realised that the new towns folk were all inbred children from the three survivors....

I like it and I would reccomend this but I would also like to go over a few things I like and dislike about this RPG Maker to make sure the person considering buying this will at least like it as much as I do.
First, the Pros:
1. It's somewhat easy to figure out and there is hardly any need to know scripting.
2. The Character Generator. This makes it very easy to make new sprites and there are quite a few options within the generator to create some original sprites. Also, if you know what you are doing you can draw your own sprites and put them into the generator for any new characters you create. For example, I made a backpack sprite for the accessories and I can create a person with a backpack whenever I need to.
3. The music in this is actually enjoyable to listen on itself (at least in my opinion) which is good since you want a battle with the right music to go with it.
4. DLC content is available.
5. Importing stuff outside of RPG maker is easy enough. Since I am an artist on deviantART and have some knowledge with GIMP, I can literally sketch out a monster, draw it, color and everything and put it in an RPG to fight.
6. There is quite a community base for RPG Maker so if you are looking for sprites, scripting help or whatever you need someone on RPG Maker forums, Steam or even deviantART might be able to help you.
7. Considering what you are given most game developers would pay three times as much just to get a program like this...
8. Events during battles. I can make a monster or a boss for example say something in the middle of the fight.
Cons:
1. ...but $69.99 is still a lot of money for most people these days. I actually got this for half that a couple months ago when it was on sale for at least half. Even some of the DLC is pretty pricey.
2. While there are a lot of sprites and the Character Generator helps, there are only a few monsters this game comes with. Back when I said I can draw my monsters on GIMP, I'll have to be doing that a lot for the game I am making. If you plan on having a large assortment of monsters to fight then you better know how to draw or at least have a few friends who do.
3. Chibi sprites. A major turnoff. As much as I like this RPG Maker I hate how they used these small sprites. Sure, Pokemon used them and this is just a personal thing but I would have prefered taller sprites. Now you can still use the taller sprites but putting an "!$" (ingore quotations) in the front of the name of the file but you would have to draw every single sprite by hand or go find them on the internet.
4. Small screen resolution. I mean very small.
5. For some strange reason whenever the monsters attack one of my party it doesn't show any lightning or fire hitting my characters. I'm sure with scripting it can be fixed but it shouldn't have to be in the first place. Speaking of scripting...
6. ...like I said there is no need for scripting knowledge to create a game. However, for the more advance graphical stuff such as seeing your characters beside their HP you MUST know scripting, otherwise you will be getting Earthbound style battles. Now that's not necessarily a bad thing but I would appreciate seeing my character's face by their health bar at least.
7. The battle message text goes by way too fast. Fortuantely with scripting it can be fixed very easily. Just go to the scripts and look for Windows. Look for Window_BattleLog and between line 191 and 197 change "20" to "30" and then save your RPG. The text speed should become more reasonable.
A lot of these Cons I was able to either get around or forgive but to some people, they might be too much. With that said I would still reccomend RPG Maker VX Ace because I use it, but I would also reccomend getting it while it's on sale like I did. It's good enough to buy but might not be worth it's current price.

This game is absolutely brilliant. The only things that drag it down are the technical issues, and given time, even those may be completely gone in a few months. Sure, this game isn't for everyone, but if you play it like it was intended - with collaboration - you will find one of the deepest shooter experiences around on the current market. Don't throw it away the instant you get killed fifteen times in a row… treat it as what it is - an intense, brutal, unforgiving (yet unforgettable) and realistic shooter with more than a few technical issues. Get back up, pick up your rifle and practice a new tactic. But even if you do learn the layout of certain maps, be prepared to have your most trusted strategies become useless when pitted against a good team.
To make things even better, a huge & free patch (carrying a hefty 5 GBs of new content) that was promised to the fans has been released by the developers. It separates the whole multiplayer experience into three main modes: realism mode (the game as it was before, with some expected fixes), action mode (or in other words: an attempt to appeal to CoD fanboys, which adds many unrealistic features to the game and feels like it detracts from the core game and what it stands for) and classic mode (which is exactly what veterans from the first game have been waiting for - the return of many realistic features from RO1, and probably the most powerful of the three modes).
Red Orchestra 2 is played best on realism and classic modes. If you want to experience something truly amazing, just ignore servers playing on action mode. Mind you, this action mode is still more realistic than many other shooters out there - but overall its existence is uncalled for. Among other new things included in this update are native language packs (that's right, no more English with foreign accents - you can now choose to play the game with Russian and German only audio) and the game seems to be even more optimized for better fps.
Finally, the "Rising Storm" expansion pack (originally a mod, but later supported by Tripwire Interactive throughout its development to become official additional content for the game) has been released. For a reasonable price, it gives us plenty of exciting new maps - each set in the Pacific theatre of World War II. The two new playable factions are the soldiers of the USA and Japan. These different playable troops come with tons of new content in the form of weapons, special abilities and tactics. The new factions and maps feel fresh & exciting enough to enhance the Red Orchestra formula, whilst staying true to the series' realistic and atmospheric core.

If you're a fan of games that will unsettle you and scare you and cause you to never listen to Bizet's opera Carmen again in the same way, then this is for you. None of what I said is bad, though, as I thoroughly enjoyed this. The concept and execution are simple, in that all you really have to do is click a couple buttons to make sure some rogue animatronics don't kill you. Sounds easy, right?
That's the brilliant part about this game. Even though you stay in one room and really don't do much, the game can be incredibly difficult with the limited amount of power you have. As the nights progress, the animatrons get more and more aggressive, and your reflexes have to be up to the task. If you're not quick enough, then you'll be greeted with a horrifying scream as one of the abominations ends your life. The scream comes on both ends too - the surprise of the animatron sneaking up on you may cause you to scream in horror.
I applaud Five Nights at Freddy's for taking something so simple and making it a challenging, horrifying feat that keeps you on the edge of your seat.

If you're an old Fallout fan you'll notice that this game lends more from the first game than the second. It's more serious, dark and gritty, and less slapsticky funny (it does lend from the second game but not as much).
If you're new to the Fallout universe and choose this as a starting point, you should keep in mind that even though this game is playable in first person, it does not have good shooting mechanics (no aim down sights) since it's first and foremost an RPG.
Either way, imagine a world where everything spiraled out of control after WW2, a world stuck in the art deco of the fifties, but withered down to ruins. A place where the few surviving people try to gather the scraps of what was once their society and rebuild it as best they can. A place where the nuclear fallout has made some poor souls mutate from the radiation, and where many people have simply lost their way and some have eventually gone mad. In this world is you, born in a safe vault that was built before the war, shielded from the harsh world outside.
If you like this game and want more of the same I can strongly recommend you pick up Fallout and Fallout 2 and play through those.

So I think The Marvelous Miss Take is a pretty slick stealth game but I would also like buyers to be aware of how the random guard patterns is not always a bonus. Yes, the randomness encourages you to be aware of your surroundings, but you probably were already. I feel like the main problem this randomness has is that it eliminates the puzzle-like aspect of most stealth games, where you have to map your way around obstacles without being spotted. Some of my favorite moments of this game come from finding ways to consistently dodge around early obstacles, attempting to beat the time limit. But this game hardly allows you to do that, because you never know exactly where the guards might be or where they're looking, making a lot of the speed strats simply to pray to RNGesus.
That's not to say the game is all luck, it isn't, but I still can't help but feeling I'm still the same player I was when I first started playing. I say this because even though I've completed more than half the levels, I would still be just as challenged to try and complete them again. That's my gripe with this game. The RNG elements rob you of some of your sense of accomplishment with the knowledge that anything you just did will be just as hard the next time, reassuring you that you haven't improved in the slightest.

The Marvellous Miss Take starts out as a wonderful game - tasteful visuals, great music and sound design, and slick, light-hearted gameplay. It was a nice casual stealth experience until Episode 3, where things got more serious(ly annoying), and then the last two episodes where pretty much a meltdown. I rarely feel like this, but I specifically regret the time spent on Episode 5 :(
I guess it's obvious from the above that the game stopped to be fun when the difficulty increased. It can of course mean that a) I s*ck at stealth games, but it can also mean that b) the game's mechanics are not good enough for more complicated scenarios. Unsurprisingly, I vote b). Some of my reasons:
- The environments are too small, there's hardly any room for maneuvering. This destroys most Daisy scenarios, unless you're of the goatherder persuasion. Especially if you want to work in full stealth, which would be my first choice.
- Controls are not accurate. That's not a problem early in the game until you don't have to round corners with a laser field right at your legs.
- Random guard movements. It's super fun early on, and super annoying when the game gets tough. You basically need to finish the late levels as if the computer was generating random numbers specifically to hamper you. I'm not saying the game is cheating, mind you - but it certainly feels so at times, especially in Episode 5.
There's more, but I don't want to dissect the game any further, and I'm giving it a (very reluctant) thumbs up anyway. The first two episodes were a blast, 3 and 4 were increasingly annyoing but bearable, so it's still a lot of worthy content. Just make sure you have nerves of steel for Ep5, or forget it altogether.

Even at this early stage in development, this game is brilliant. I won't deny that it can get boring fairly quickly, but that doesn't matter in my opinion. The few hours you spend playing the game before you get bored are magnificent.
I start a new sandbox game. Mystery Lake. I know a few locations, but I don't know the map. I immediately begin exploring, hopefully coming across a jacket to ease the icy chill in the air. The weather isn't too bad, so I'm able to relax a little. I follow the train tracks, making a few slight detours when I spot a wolf skulking around. Eventually I come across a derailment, red cars toppled in front of me. The winds picked up now so I think it'll be a good time to huddle down and get warm for a few hours before continuing to find some decent shelter. I step into the train car and stare into the corner. A frozen body is in the corner. I quickly check his inventory, feeling slightly guilty, but I'm going to need whatever he's carry more than him now. Discovering an energy bar and a soda, I retreat to the opposite end of the car with my prize. Huddling down out of the wind I study the body. Will this soon be me?
There's a snow storm outside now, and not even the car is protecting me. I need to move or die. I stumble out into the arctic temperatures and blindly pick a direction, praying to come across some decent shelter. Suddenly, I hear a howl. Black shapes materialise out of the snow and pad towards me. Wolves. I sprint now, the snow storm the least of my worries. I'm getting tired, hungry, and thirsty, but I can't stop. To stop would be suicide. I continue onwards, my vision starting to get blurry. My movements become sluggish. I'm going into the long dark.
Suddenly, I see it. Almost right in front of me, a hut on a small hill. Hope flares inside me as I try and sprint up around the path to the front door. I can barely walk now, I know my conditions frighteningly low. But I made it. The Trappers Hut. I'm safe.
Until the food runs out.

Stop. Think about what you are doing.
"Oh this game isn't scary. Pffft its just a bunch of jumpscares! I can handle it."
No. You are wrong, because that is exactly how I felt when I bought this game. I'd watched the trailers and the lets plays. Then I actually tried it from behind the keyboard and I couldn't even do it. Its not wrong to say that this game is mostly jumpscares, and jumpscares are widley regarded as the lowest incarnation at horror. However Five Nights at Freddy's does something different than other horror games. In most horror games the jumpscare is just a one-and-done, a little one trick pony to startle you and which is totally ruined if you see it coming, and ruined even further in the context that in games jumpscares usually don't kill you.
In Five Night's at Freddy's, the jumpscare is the lose condition, it is the game over screen. You know the jumpscare is coming, and the game has given you all the tools to prevent the jumpscare. Thats why this game is scary. Its not the jumpscare that gets you, its the anticipation, the stress and the anxiety that gets you. Ben Yahtzee from Zero Punctuation once said that most horror games can be summed up with "A man in a scary mask jumps out and yells 'Aboogiewoogiewoo!' while in a good horror game, the man in the mask is behind you. You know he's going to jump out and yell 'Aboogiewoogiewoo!' but he doesn't he's just stays behind you and lets the fear sink in."
Thats this game. This game isn't about the jumpscare at all. Its about the fear you feel when you know the jumpscare is coming and your frantically trying to avoid it.
So DON'T buy this game because you think it won't be scary, or because you think you'll impress your friends by showing how brave you are. Buy this game because its scary, because you WANT to be scared.
And if this game doesn't manage to freak you out even once, I would love to talk to you personally because I need to know your secret to managing stress and anxiety.

Giving someone who's a thief the surname "take" is an excellent choice. Meet Sophia, who only wishes to steal back what is rightfully hers. Along the way she meets Harry and Daisy; the 3 of them team up to find out what happened to Sophia's will (after the passing away of a close family member) and, of course, to steal a lot of paintings and other stuff from art galleries.
The "home" section shows your own gallery where you can launch a level. Each level has 2 floors to be completed. You can only control one character at a time: when Harry and later Daisy join you notice the already completed levels can be done by them, too. Naturally, this means a rather different positioning of guards as each character has a different playstyle.
With Sophia we steal most items. A lot of objects and paintings and each level has one object behind a window case. As the heist occurs during opening hours there are civilians in the galleries. They only notify guards when you smash this one particular window case. Your best bet is to immediately hide. Generally speaking, your job is to try to avoid the line of sight of guards, cameras and dogs. Later on wall-mounted lasers make your job more difficult. Sophia is a must for story progression - Harry and Daisy can only enter a level if it has already been completed by their friend.
With Harry running is not an option anymore as he walks with the use of a cane. He enters the galleries at night time and with him we need to steal fewer paintings only. In my opinion Harry's playthrough is the most difficult in the absence of running. If you run with Sophia or Daisy it can be heard if guards are close-by but in a distance it is an extremely useful feature. Back to Harry: he can drop a ball to emit noise and distract guards. You need to make sure you pick it up before leaving a level.
With Daisy I found the game the most exciting. Our job is to get close to each guard to steal a key so that a safe can be opened. Every opening triggers the alarm so make sure you have a plan for escaping as the guards will definitely check the area. While running Daisy emits a sound in a much smaller radius than Sophia.
Overall we have 25 levels to complete (beside the tutorial), so that's 75 times the fun considering the 3 protagonists. The game has great music; each level has a name of a street found in England. The graphics and the accompanying music indicate this must be the 1950s or 60s. Sometimes civilians comment on the thefts that all appear on the news; we can always read the latest headlines in newspapers between each stage.
The downside of Miss Take is that it has an uneven difficulty. The A.I. controlling the guards often gives them different commands. We can find it difficult to steal only one particular painting in a heavily guarded room. After a couple of attempts we notice even the other rooms are a bit more difficult to complete as you never know where a guard will be moving. This is especially true when it comes to starting a level: if they move to the opposite direction we know we are off to a good start.
Miss Take is a great stealth-based adventure game with a unique atmosphere. If you like challenges you can try beating all part times with Sophia and Daisy for extra achievements. With Harry, as he cannot run, the extra difficulty lies in not being noticed, at all, i.e. "ghosting" each level. I hardly play more than 10 hours with an indie game but Miss Take was worth every minute of it.

You're given very little to go on at first, and while some horror is the dogs-through-windows Resident Evil BOO! variety, much of it is in the suspense, the anticipation of what you'll be hit with from where next. Very much horror, in the best sense of the word.

Beat-em-ups like this just don’t come around that often anymore.
All too many nowadays try to basically be bad 2D fighters in disguise, focus so much on spectacle that the entire screen is nothing but a chaotic mess where you’re sure your character is in there SOMEWHERE, or just plain work too hard at reinventing the wheel while forgetting there’s a reason your tires don’t look like the squiggly blocks from Tetris.
But HERE… imagine a beat-em-up where the creator clearly loved the genre and plucked the best bits from the genre.
-You’ve got branching paths through the story that can bring you as long or as short an experience as you like, depending on the route you feel like taking.
-Enemies actually fight differently from one another, and there’s no situation you can’t control as long as you know what to watch for and how to play your foes off each other.
-Hell, YOUR CHARACTERS play very differently from one another, and while your move list for any given one is far more extensive than you might anticipate (and you can even buy a non-DLC training mode that lets you give them a test run), you CANNOT play either of the three heroes like you would the others (unless you like game over screens, of course).
-The combat engine is more robust than your average beat-em-up, but not so much so that it’s completely overwhelming and inexplicably requires you to memorize a giant list of complicated commands in order to make any sort of forward progress.
-You’ve got a very wide range of difficulty settings that do everything from alter the enemies’ health and aggressiveness, to making little alterations to the game’s rules – but it’s done in a way that subtly encourages you to step things up a notch once you think you’ve mastered your current difficulty, as opposed to just locking half the game’s playable content behind your difficulty setting.
-There’s an in-game shop that lets you buy a variety of game features, including new modes, new difficulty settings, new looks for your characters, and a number of other amusing little odds and ends.
-There’s a couple of cute little jokes about the genre and a few bits where the inspirations were a bit more obvious than most.
-You've got an EXCELLENT soundtrack that always feels like it matches the action on the screen.
-And hell, it’s just a damn fine rampage against the mutant hordes that could do with a bit of a bodyslam. ;3
Put it all together with an enthusiastic developer who clearly wants you to enjoy the game as much as he VERY obviously enjoyed making it, and you’ve got one of the finest beat-em-ups of this era - hell, this would’ve easily been among the highest tiers of the genre even in the best days of beat-em-ups!
The price may be a little on the steep side, but think of it this way - you’re buying one of the best games the genre has to offer, for a third of what you’d pay for a console port back in the 90s. It’s worth it. =3

Great new JRPG addition to the Steam Library and here's why:
Pros:
+ Equipment efficiency system for learning skills on your gear.
+ Cool fusion system to upgrade equipment with same name and get newer skills.
+ You don't mindlessly equip stronger equipment over your old, weaker ones due to equipment having synergistic skills that boost character stats or gives specific advantages in battle.
+ Character personalities and interactions are enjoyable.
+ Music and Sounds are fantastic to listen to- alot of wind instruments, drums, and an orchestra-esque style.
+ Scenery and environment are refreshing and nice to look at.
+ Action Battle system is fantastic (running around chaining combos and using magic).
+ Removing the TP system (MP in other JRPGs) and replacing it with a resource that all your attacks and magic use.
+ Combat is pretty fluid.
+ It feels rewarding to time attacks with allies to lock an enemy down instead of mindlessly attacking with your character alone (in higher difficulties anyway)
+ Encountering an enemy triggers a fight right there in the environment which adds great immersion to the gameplay.
+ Last but not least, the option of dual audio (Japanese/English) as well as English subtitles.
Cons:
- Because battles take place in the environment instead of a seperate battle screen, sometimes the battle camera derps and zooms in really close so its hard to see when fighting in small areas or backed against a wall.
- 30 fps locked (I personally don't find this to be an issue as the original was 30 fps and Namco Bandai has stated multiple times that they tried but the costs (gameplay performance) of upping to 60 fps outweighed the pros).
- Some graphical issues like a little screen tearing (can be fixed by tinkering with graphics card settings and V-Sync).
- Story is a little slow at the beginning.
My rating: 9/10

I have mixed feelings about this game. Overall, the game is extremely well polished. The graphics, sound effects, and game mechanics are outstanding. Multiplayer is really where this game shines. Up to four archers battling for chaotic supremacy. There's different "variations" of gameplay to choose from when playing multiplayer which really help mix it up when the stock gameplay becomes boring.
The somewhat crappy part about multiplayer though is that you have to unlock new stages and archers by playing the single player (or duo) "quest" mode. This is where things take a downward slope.
The difficulty is way over the top. Each mob has it's own unique abilities, which is great, but the AI is possibly the worst I've ever seen. Normally when people say "the worst" they mean dumb or too easy. TowerFall is the exact opposite. The AI doesn't really do anything 'on its own', it simply reacts to the user's input. Sure, there's some "dumb" enemies like goos or slugs that walk around the map and occasionally jump at the player but most of the mobs react as soon as the player it's the dodge, jump, or fire action. Like for example the second I press fire, the enemy archer dodges. Every-single-time. Like wise with certain flying mobs. The second I fire an arrow, they dodge. They will always dodge it. Likewise when they fire an arrow. If you dodge, they will fire a second arrow. If you jump, they will reaim and fire another arrow, hitting you everytime. The only way I've found to effectively kill an enemy archer is to unleash a barrage of at least 3 arrows. It's exceptionally stupid.
That being said, I think this is a really fun multiplayer game. While you have to unlock all the features through single player "quest" mode where you'll have to deal with the abysmal AI, the mutiplayer aspect is s great that I can ignore that.

A lovable cast of varied personalities, beautiful art direction and a robust real-time combat system make for a unique experience you shouldn't miss out on. It also has local co-op which is awesome!
I went into
almost entirely for the combat (I had played, and quite enjoyed,
), what I didn't expect was to fall in love with the Characters. From the visual design to the dialog and even the (English) Voice acting, I adore the characters (granted I've only met a few so far), I've even gone out of my way to talk to every NPC I can and have yet to be disappointed by dialog. Even minor characters seem to have plenty of personality and are worth talking to.
I'lll preface this by saying that
is
-by any means- the most graphically advanced game I've ever seen. Having said that, The art style, from the monsters to the backgrounds to the architecture are very well done and really help the world feel alive and grandiose.
Perhaps the greatest strength of the game, the combat is responsive, fast-paced and extremely rewarding, this is one of the few RPGs where I actively hunt down enemies to fight. There is a great, almost intimidating, amount of complexity to the combat system there are 5 elementes (Neutral, earth, fire, wind, water) every attack is either physical or magical (think
), has an elemental attribute, certain attacks are more effective against certain monsters types not to mention the rock-paper-scissor relationship between the three different types of attacks (Martial, Hidden and Seraphic). Different  from other
games, as soon as you come in contact with an enemy the battle begins with a much more natural transition. Though this may seem like a small feature, it really adds to the immersion to make combat even more enjoyable. On a side note, every enemy has detailed stats and some flavour text from the characters that is both informative and entertaining, I highly recommend giving them a read!
Nothing in this world is perfect, so it stands to reason I must bring to light some less than favourable elements of
. One of the greatest detractor from my enjoyment of the game is texture clipping. It's difficult to concentrate on the story is someone literally has their sword phasing through part of their body. Another annoyance is the sub par collision outside of the combat, quiet often you'll run into invisible walls where you would assume you could walk freely. while very minor complaints, it does break the immersion.
Whether you're looking for a rich, deep story-driven jRPG or just a fantastic combat system, I truly believe you'll find what you're looking for in
.

Overall this game's structure is pretty good for where it's at. The foundation is strong and has plenty of room for positive growth.
The upside and downside of this sort of game comes from its inherently social nature. The people are what end up making and simultaneously breaking it.
Ultimately I beleive it comes down to if the room has a good Host who can keep decent population control on the room. Such as keeping Mic-Spammers and repetative Memelords out of their room.
I recently held a small think tank on how the developers can give more tools to Hosts to help aid in managing their rooms.
--- Population Control/Filters ---
- Player Rating System:
Players rate others on their performance and overall behavior between 1 and 5 stars. After they get a certain number of votes they receive an average rating attached to their profile.
Admins can make use of this number by adding a rating filter on their room. Example: An admin starts a 3 star room. Players with 3 stars and above can enter no problem, but 1 and 2 star players will need to be approved. Similar to clubs having a bouncer at the entrance.
- Passworded rooms:
This would be more useful for Streamers who want to exclusively have their audience as guests in their club. They post the password to their stream and boom they have their audience. This solves the problem of having to constantly filter out random players or plainly setting the room as closed.
--- Customized Experience ---
-Custom Room Layouts
Similar to Tabletop simulator, adding the ability to change the appearance of your club to suit your style, a tool could be used to save different layouts and make a room stand out and be recognizable between sessions.
For instance, a streamer wants to stand out as a club. Upon entering, you know you've entered their stream by 1) the club name and 2) the effort they put in to change the appearance of their club.
There is the potential for steam workshop integration as well as microtransations to supply different style furniture and themes.
-Prompt Cards
For those that like to run Improv nights, what may help to keep things on track could be a prompt board that hangs off to the side of the stage. The admin sets up the prompt and text appears there for the audience and performers to reference without the need of the admin repeating themselves for newcomers.
-Timers
The option to add and adjust a timer for performers on stage. To keep the flow of the room moving as well as for when a Host goes AFK. Similar to the prompt cards, a clock hanging and ticking down off to the side of the stage.
-Clickable Objects
Similar to custom layouts. One player I spoke with thought that having things to click on and show some kind of small movement client and/or server side would be a fun add on. Along the vein of Hearthstone where it gives the player something to fidget with while they wait for their turn or just listen to the person on stage. Example: click the red lamps and they'll swing around a bit or turn on and off.

Refuct shows just how good an experience minimalistic design can produce.
Movement is really the only mechanic in Refunt, and it feels great. The controls are smooth. The music is both relaxing and inspiring. The sound effects give it just enough juice to engross the player. It's challenging in a very attainable way.
The flaws I find with this game are so minor that I don't even feel like mentioning them.
There are no explicit goals in the game. One third of the game is the implicit goal of reaching each sequential beacon to progress. The other two thirds are the player driven goals of getting on top of each platform to transform it, and collecting all the cyber cubes, also scattered about the tops of platforms. The way all three of these goals encourage and reward engagement with the main mechanic, movement, is brilliant.
I highly recommend Refunct.

Towerfall Ascension is most probably one of the best local multiplayer games ever created. It's a game that makes and breaks friendships.
The movement speed is insane once you become aware of the things that are possible. Catching arrows is one skill, but catching multiple arrows will dodging through the air, ending with sticking to a wall, jumping back into the open area to shoot your opponent with of the arrows you just caught, is simply brilliant.
Sure it will take you time to truly master this game, which is best played with an USB controller by the way, but the road to perfection is simply brilliant.
Just like other competitive arena games - take Super Smash Bros as an example - there are several extra power-ups available. These will spawn at the beginning of each match. Some power ups give you special arrows (laser arrows or bomb arrows for example), others will have an environmental influence (slow motion or rising lava). These power-ups are always a great risk to get, because you have to engage, but the reward can be big of course.
On the other hand there's the tactic to avoid shooting. You start with three or two arrows and when your opponent shoot and miss, you can grab that arrow. But of course, once again, these missed arrows can also be used as a trick. Those are just two examples of how arena control can work in your advantage of disadvantage.
Really, Towerfall Ascension is brilliant and all you need is this baby, four USB controllers, three friends and some drinks for an AWESOME video game evening!

Five Nights at Freddy's is probably one of the best point and click horror games I've played in a long time.
Pros:
+ The game keeps you on the edge of your seat, unlike a good percentage of indie horror games out there, you have an advantage to keep the potential threat away, rather than just standing there completely defenseless waiting for the threat to come and get you.
+ The idea of it being like an abandoned Chuck E. Cheese's, almost makes me scared to go back to Chuck E. Cheese's ever in my life.
+ The characters are likeable in the
kind of way.
+ The atmosphere itself is beyond creepy. A place that is going to shut down by the end of the year, children gone missing, more than likely murdered and stuffed into the animatronics (hence the foul odor emitting from the robots). Now they haunt the pizza parlor and pretty much kill anyone they see. Tell me that's not creepy.
Neutrals:
/ While the game doesn't exactly rely on jumpscares entirely, there are a lot of them if you don't time yourself right or just have crap luck. Once you get used to a loud "SCREEEEEEE!" in your face, it can get more annoying or frustrating, rather than scary.
Cons:
- The only negative thing I can say about this game, is that it spawned a bunch of Furries dropping down on it like a dog's fresh, warm, steamy dookie, on your just cleaned white carpet.
Other than that, I'd recommend this game to anyone that's looking for something to play for a few minutes, have a good scare, or laugh if you're making your friends play it. Was worth the $5.00 to me.

Last cycle, 5 days.
I had stockpiled tons of cans, wood, meat, cloth and a good knife in a nice house with a fireplace. I even had the luxury of having a can opener. Nearby was a workbench so I could make snares to fetch those juicy morsels. My condition for the past 3 days had been at its best. If I stayed at home, eat and sleep, I would've lived for another week without any incidents.
But that kind of life is boring.
There were at least 4 other houses nearby that I had yet ransacked. And being the wanderlust that I am, I just had to loot them. So what was the problem? Ever since I moved in, I had a pesky neighbour who wouldn't leave me alone! Bloody wolf scared me half to death, and I swear it's the same wolf every damn time! I had to make sure I wasn't encumbered whenever I ventured forth and trust me, the amount of times I sprinted for my life heading home were uncountable. In fact, I first encountered Wolf right before I moved in. He greeted me quite rudely but I had a knife and I managed to make it run. I bandaged myself up and applied some antiseptic and was forever wary of Wolf. On the 6th day, I had it.  I needed to set things straight with Wolf. *I had no guns.*
Right outside, once again, was Wolf after a routine chase. Me, behind the door, panting heavily and making a lifechanging decision. It's time to face Wolf, face him straight on and kill him. I've survived him once, I just might be able to kill it, and then, I could live in peace. I could try out fishing like I always dreamed of with the lake being right there. I could have nice walks down the road without perking my ears for a howl or a growl. No matter how many times I looked at it, facing Wolf only lead to many good things. If things were to go awry, I had bandages and meds, loads of them. I can do this!
I took a deep breath, calmed my heart down, and told myself that this is the time.
I stepped out onto the cold frigid snow, and there he was. He was waiting. I stared into its dark beady eyes for a long second, and I was no longer afraid. He was beautiful; a fierce wild creature of black standing on pure white snow. I feel respect for Wolf as I faced him that calm day. Without so much as a greeting, he jumped on me and started gnashing and biting as viciously as he could. With my trusty knife, I swung into his thin frame once to which he didn't flinch. I was on my back and at a bad position but I didn't lose hope. I swung at it again, and again, and again. It seemed to have gone on forever though I knew it lasted a mere 4 seconds. I had won. Wolf didn't die but he skimpered away with what must have been a fatal wound. I could see his blood marking his rout. Drunk, drunk with victory I was. I was relieved that Wolf hadn't died, it was a weird bond and only recently did I realize. Smiling to myself, I turned around to get inside and see to my injuries. And I fell, face first.
Blood loss.

Thankfully, you can switch to WASD keyboard controls, which have three problems.  First, they felt stiff and unresponsive; the number of times I failed after accidentally tripping a laser is too many.  Second, far,
too often I'd get stuck on the edge of furniture or doorframes.  Lastly, you still have to use the mouse to interact with things.  Which wouldn't be a problem, but you do this so rarely I found it more comfortable to use my off hand for the run command (Shift), and then had to scramble to reach the mouse when needed.  You also use the mouse to throw things, which is not convenient for quick responses either.
Second, the guard movements are random.  Which generally wouldn't be a problem except for the optional time challenges.  In my opinion, too many of those can only be beaten with luck.  It gets very annoying when you repeatedly start a level, then quit two seconds in as a guard you need to lure is looking the wrong way.  Even worse is when you get most of the way through and then get caught when a guard off-screen happens to look at you or wander in range of a safe alarm.  That randomness also means that the difficulty curve is all over the place; even late in the game levels can become trivial with just a little good fortune.
Third is that you need to press escape then make two mouse clicks to restart a level, for no reason that I can see.  That might not seem like much, but given how often I restarted levels, it really got on my nerves.  One click on 'Restart' should be enough to restart!
The game would also benefit from the ability to rotate the camera.  Perhaps that's asking too much of an indie game, but there where a few occasions when I couldn't see clearly thanks to my character being blocked by a wall, that interfered with my play.
Given all these problems, what kept me playing the game?  The basic gameplay is solid.  There are clear visibility and awareness cones for everything, so except for off-screen guards it's clear where's safe and where's not.  Once you understand how to lure the guards away from what they are guarding, the puzzles become the fun sort of challenging.  The different gameplay styles of the three PCs also add another dimension to each level.  The main character also gets to use a variety of different items as they progress through the game, which helps to keep things varied; it's just a shame something similar couldn't have been done for the other two PCs.
Also, I really like the game's art design.  It's simple but elegant and fits the mood quite well.
There's a lot of fun to be had from
, but also a lot of frustration.  I'd recommend it if you like stealth games and puzzle games, and like a modest challenge.

First of all: No, Peter, you didn't envision Godus as two different games, at least that's not what you initially said, so the first lie right at the start of the game.
To the review then: I will treat this game as Godus 3.0, or higher, because with every version came the promise that everything is better and this is still fully based on Godus, so you don't get the "It's a different game"-treatment. BUT as bonus difficulty you have to meet todays standards for RTSs, because now you want to be an RTS also.
Despite being in development for a very long time now, the game is very light contentwise. It's a bit of a backtrack to the first version of Godus, although you have to do less now.
You are there to level the ground, so that your people (which you can't control)
can build their houses on plots(which appear automatically)
to generate belief (which now gets collected automatically, one of the few positive aspects).
When you have enough belief, you build a fort (out of your houses that merge together automatically to a chunk with battlements) where you can recruit soldiers.
These soldiers are somewhat controllable, although their pathfinding is terrible and the mouse response is too, and you send them to conquer and destroy the enemy village.
Also the animations are clunky and ugly, the collision detection doesn't work that great resulting in corpses hovering above ground and blood splatters spread widely although the corpse is already gone.
That's it for the beginning, so at the moment the game is neither fish nor meat, as RTS it falls flat on its face because there are way better ones out there, and the god game aspect is mainly moving around dirt to make way for plots, not very interesting either.
VERDICT:
I gave the first Godus the benefit of the doubt, rating it positive, because it showed promise and I changed my rating to negative when the support ceased and the game died.
This time I will do it the other way round, so it gets a negative rating from the start (because it absolutely deserves this), BUT this version of Godus also shows promise, so if it gets way better and deeper than it is now, the rating might also change. As for now, NOT RECOMMENDED.
(PS: And dear developers, get rid of that cheap mobil-ish feel of the game, as long as your plan isn't to use PC gamers as beta testers for mobile AGAIN, this won't do you any good.)

I’ve been playing city builders and god games for years now, namely SC4 since release. My first impression of Banished was that it was a little dry in content, basic farms and buildings, no real 'wow' factor. This however quickly vanished as I began to play the game and started to understand that although it was basic, the underlying mechanics would take some time to understand.
Initially I failed at maintaining some cities for more than a decade. I blame this on my SC4 mentality where work is done automatically (construction etc) despite the number of people in a city or their particular job. Instead, this game is what SC2013 should have been based around in terms of having everyone being an individual in a city.
After reeling back and taking it slow (and putting it on easy) I began to see where I had gone wrong. My fatal mistake was forgetting that these are actual people in a village from centuries ago. What does this mean? I means everything takes more time and more effort. If you have ever been camping or backpacking you will know what I mean. You are limited by everything from the amount of light in a day (this game does not simulate that however), to the area you are working in (mountains, uneven terrain, obstacles) and not to mention the lack of modern conveniences or technology.
The above might seem obvious, but it really plays in to the game. As you watch your workers, they will have to walk to their job, manually bring resources, and do everything by hand. At times they will stop to go get something to eat (they go home since fast food did not exist) which causes another commute to and from work. All of this walking eats up time and slows production. It is your job to thoughtfully assign tasks as they are needed and not overwhelm the laborers and builders.
This game is meant to played slow, while it has the ability to play anywhere from 1x to 10x, I find that playing on 2x allows you to have ample time to spot problems(low resources, disease, etc.) and deal with them before it’s an epidemic.
Overall, if you like city builders and don’t mind being thrown back a couple hundred years to simpler, yet more labor intensive time, then you will like Banished.

I was pleasantly surprised to see Godus Wars pop up in my library today as it was only two weeks ago I'd been wondering what was going on with the development of Godus.
I didn't like Godus when I first played it a very long time ago, at all. I found it slow, heavy on clicking and just rather unenjoyable so I didn't play much of it at all. I didn't have the highest expectations for Godus Wars but despite saying that so far I'm really really enjoying the gameplay. It seems Godus has become a bit of a punching bag for people though.
Godus Wars is Godus meets a very, very, very basic Age of Mythology style gameplay. In the original Godus the your aim was to build belief from your followers to be able to sculpt your world and find treasures and such. Godus Wars takes the sculpting and belief elements and combines them with some RTS features. The aim of Godus Wars seems to be defeating the enemy God by controlling the whole map which you do stage by stage. Each map stage is unlocked using keys and rewards you at the end of each with more keys and a random card. Cards are used within each map stage to buff your followers/soldiers/belief/cooldowns and you are able to select up to four cards per map stage. Some are reusable spells such as 'shield' to give your soldiers a shield boost and others are consumable such as '+8 followers'.
Each map stage requires you to capture the enemy belief tower to win and this is done by building up belief to buy soldiers and destroying anything in your path.
Since this game is in Early Access I have come across a few bugs as expected. The game opens up a second process for the map stages and this seems pretty unstable. I've had it crash on me three times so far. It seems that the developers know about this though as there is a failsafe to still reward you with some keys or to allow you to replay the level upon this crash. However on one of the crashes it would not let me replay the level and gave me no keys. This left me completely out of keys and forced me to replay an earlier level just to proceed. A few other minor bugs involved followers not being able to find a route until I unsculpted and re-sculpted it, but this didn't cause much trouble at all.
Ultimately I've only played two hours but I really am enjoying the premise of the game and I am glad to be able to finally get a feel of how Godus was mean to be made. I look forward to the future updates and it's good to see the developers still working on Godus along side this rather than just abandoning it like I've seen often in Early Access. I'm not sure if it justifies the full £10.99 price tag but as a counterpart to Godus it's 100% worth it.

Refuct shows just how good an experience minimalistic design can produce.
Movement is really the only mechanic in Refunt, and it feels great. The controls are smooth. The music is both relaxing and inspiring. The sound effects give it just enough juice to engross the player. It's challenging in a very attainable way.
The flaws I find with this game are so minor that I don't even feel like mentioning them.
There are no explicit goals in the game. One third of the game is the implicit goal of reaching each sequential beacon to progress. The other two thirds are the player driven goals of getting on top of each platform to transform it, and collecting all the cyber cubes, also scattered about the tops of platforms. The way all three of these goals encourage and reward engagement with the main mechanic, movement, is brilliant.
I highly recommend Refunct.

Zombie Tycoon 2: Brainhov’s Revenge is a Real Time Strategy game. Great twist to a RTS game,  you as a mad scientists control faction of zombies and monsters that you created. Frima Studio have done a great job bringing a unique RTS with zombies.
You control the game with four different “units”, two of which are groups of zombies. These two are primary units for attack or defence. Leader Tycoon or Brainhov along with monster form the other two units. The basic objective in multiplayer games is to kill other leader in his mobile HQ while protecting your leader in his mobile HQ.
You also command a special power of rush attack. The power of rush attack depends upon how many houses you captured on the map. Each house you capture results in increase in zombie counter present at the screen at all times. Greater the value of counter, more powerful the rush attack will be.
The rush attack summons all the zombies to a specific locations. Best to use this attack to demolish rivals HQ or capture key buildings on map. There is a cool down period after every rush attack to recover lost zombies, so use the attack wisely. Multiplayer is loads of fun but here is lack of online players , so you have to wait quite a while to get a match.  Also more multiplayer maps would have added to the enjoyment factor of online matches.
The game has a great single player campaign, and, although it may have been short. The story is also interesting with well timed humour to keep you entertained. The story begins with Tycoon taking over a Human Colony and suddenly Brainhov comes back for revenge against Tycoon. Campaign Story is divided into chapters . All RTS elements are perfectly utilised in the campaign.
Based on unreal engine, the game provides great visuals for a RTS . The cartoon styled graphics are a perfect match for humour filled story. The background music and sounds work well but nothing to write home about here. Overall all aspects of game work well in cohesion and provide a great RTS game. HGunified recommends Zombie Tycoon 2: Brainhov’s Revenge to all RTS fans who enjoy a good RTS game with fun-to-play multiplayer coupled with well written story. Totally worth your time game . (7/10)

TowerFall is a game that is timeless. Don't let it's looks decieve you. This is a skill based, reaction heavy, action platformer that is best played against your
enemies (friends). This is best played with 3 friends. The only warning I have is to prepare for a noise complaint because you
be yelling.
This is very skill based. You are an archer equipped with a finite number of arrows. There are upgrades and different TYPES of arrows to try to reach before your most hated foes (friends :)). You must be the last man standing, yet the game is based on SCORE. Therefore you must choose between going all-in or hanging back and playing defensive.
You have the highest score. A flurry of arrows fly in your direction. What do you do?! Evade into the arrows, catching them! Now not only do you have more arrows than your enemy, but you're above them as well. You wall slide gracefully and plop on your friend's head almost in slow motion. Splat. Two more to go...
That all happens within a second's time. TowerFall is ridiculously intense and thrilling. Arrows missed will be left pierced into the ground or wall, waiting to be picked up. There's so many things I can say about TowerFall but I just highly recommend buying it and doing a good old fasioned party night with your friends. You'll see the value immediately.
Note : Make sure everyone has a controller. I've been the one person playing on a keyboard and it's torture and just feels plain unfair.
There are a few multiplayer modes:
-Last man standing
-First to "#blank" kills
-Team deathmatch
As well as probably about 100 game modifiers.

If you are a fan of beat em' ups, brawlers, or fighting games in general; do yourself a favor and pick this little gem up. Its like where to start? First off the graphics and art are outstanding, lots of the character/enemy sprites for the most part have fluid animations, especially the females...they have bits that jiggle so much that it puts the jiggle physics of DOA Volleyball and Senran Kagura series to shame; some might find it off putting or a nit pick, but me, I enjoy this man's work, attention and detail to those parts; with that aside the other enemies you ecounter in game have unique and interesting designs each with different fighting styles that are heavily influenced by Street Fighter (like come on, there is an enemy that dresses and fights like M.Bison).
Next is the controls and combat, Fight'N Rage has this down to a tee; it's a simple three button layout you got your attack, jump, and a button for you special attack. It's one of these easy to pick up hard to master sort of combat; you got foward attacks, down attacks, jump attacks, running attacks, grabs/throws, parries, cancels, combos, big combos the list goes on. The dev was clearly influence by the Street Fighter combat mechanics and it works so well in a beat em' up so big props to them.
I got not much to say about the music, but I know good music when I hear it and this game totally has it. The main menu music hypes you up for beating up these ♥♥♥♥ing furries; and track after track keeps the blood pumping. So yeah, compliments to the composer very well done. Might as well also mention the difficulty, this game is pretty rock hard and I will admit with no shame that I havent beaten it yet, it gets to Cuphead levels of hard, maybe a bit harder than that; so just a fair warning. There is an "easy mode" but you need to unlock it first with points.
As for everything else I havent mentioned, like the story; its just there to be there, nothing too deep or a meaning behind it; You as the humans (or the only furry that fights along with the humans) have to fight through stages of "mutants" (they are anthros) to get to the boss. Simple and straightfoward yeah, but truth be told, there are branching paths in certain stages that will change the game's ending, so there is high replayability to have here. Along with story mode you got a shop where you can buy a plethora of things from main character skins, game modes, and new characters for your battle mode. And dont worry, no microtransactions on this. Its just a matter of scoring high on story mode to obtain coins and thats how you buy things, so thats another plus there, no lootboxes or microtransaction ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t.

Fight'n Rage is a love letter to beat 'em ups of the past, a genre not really seen anymore. This is inspired by games such as Streets of Rage and Final Fight, games I really enjoyed when I was younger!
During my first playthrough I didn't really catch much of the story: Think it's that mutants are running amok and on a genocidal rampage against the humans. Enter you, the protagonist, to beat up hundreds of them. You can unlock a lot of extra characters but you start with 3:
-Gal, a lady who's all about speed, combos, and jiggling---I mean, juggling. And jiggling.
-F. Morris, a strategic fighter with numerous strategies.
-Ricardo, a minotaur with massive strength to crush foes.
I played through as Gal the first time, and the fighting felt really good. Pulling off crazy combos while surrounded by enemies feels amazing, and the enemy variety is large enough to the point it never really feels boring. Combine that with an awesome rocking soundtrack and you got all you need for a fantastic beat 'em up. Not to mention very well animated sprites for both the characters and the enemies: Game looks really good.
The way it differs from many others is how it has multiple routes and endings. You can take different paths to go to different stages, and fight different foes. This gives the game a ton of replayability, and I'm looking forward to my next run!
I played on Normal, and for the most part the game was reasonable in terms of difficulty! There's some REALLY rough stretches in the end stages but with a little strategy you can make things a lot easier for yourself. There's only one stage which started to test my patience, and that was a raft stage where you fight a lot of enemies on a small raft. You can knock them into water, but the same can happen to you and you take a chunk of damage when that happens. It gets worse when you start fighting enemies that cannot fall into the water, and there are zero health drops during this entire section.
This raft stage ended with a really bad boss, and that leads to one of my bigger complaints: The boss design is kinda inconsistent. This particular boss could not be harmed by anything but jump kicks and special attacks as they were often floating over the water. Most of the fight had me just doing jump kicks as he dove for me, and...It was really bad.
Still, there's a number of enjoyable fights, it's just some weak bosses thrown in there.
Overall, if you loved the beat 'em ups of yesteryear, you'll love this game. The game took me 2 hours to beat the first run, and now that I have a run under my belt I can probably annihilate that time. You also have a ton of unlockables, a ton of modes, a lot of customization...You get a whole lot for $20!
I give this a hearty recommendation.

If I had to say, I'd probably say that I'm a Beat Em' Up novice. I viciously and without remorse cheated to get max stats in Scott Pilgrim, I played Red knight in Castle Crashers and grinded my way to becoming an invincible wall of lightning and in Guardian Heroes I couldn't beat the game without getting that extreme buff from the magic sword. About the only "real" beat em ups I ever won were ones that got re-released with infinite continues.
So why then, did I buy this? Well to be blatantly honest, I had heard about it on a minor gamming site thought to myself "yeah that looks cool" and bought it once I had the available cash. My total regrets since then have been negligable. Sure, my first run basically ended in failure, but this time, this time I truly fought the game. I didn't just go "well time to grind up exp or find an easier route". Nope. I just went and said "fine, I'll buy easy mode". I then proceeded to try again(I won that time), get some practice in the training room, and read a helpful guide. After that, I truly started enjoying the game by blasting hundred of poor rats into thin gruel as Ricardo and my first "true" run ended up being my first single credit clear.
Welp, that's my little "backstory talk". Let's talk actual game design stuffs. The game is just one big chunk of eye and ear candy. Amazing sprites on amazing backgrounds all while listening to a godly soundtrack. It's just pure nerve pleasing goodness. for gameplay, well, it's bog standard beat em up. You can move around in a "3D" envirnment, you have your basic combo button, jump button, and special button(or Lariat button for Ricardo) so you shouldn't have any problems figuring things out. This is the game that drew me into the Fallout Series and I cannot recommend it enough. To me, it perfectly captures the feeling of a classic table top RPG in video game form. The character stats are diverse so as to allow many different types of play and the absolute openness of the world allows you to experience whatever it is you want while keeping you on your toes with random envounters.
Before you begin playing, I would reccomend downloading the Fallout Mod Manager as well as unofficial patches in order to add stability to a game that was never designed to be run on current hardware. However, I don't think mods beyond patches and aesthetics are essential to have a grand adventure in the Post-Apocalyptic wasteland. The quests are smart and center around interesting concepts or conflicts and can be tackled in many different ways depending on the player's play style and character's build.
The setting is unlike others in the genre in that the fall of society didn't happen in neo-futuristic world, but rather a retro-futuristic world. Much in the way steam-punk sees the use of mid 1800's technologies that could have been if the combustion engine never caught on, Fallout's universe is one in which the micro-chip's development was delayed by a century and the world continued in its effort to harness the atom.
The setting allows for a revisiting of classic sci-fi staples like giant insects, alien life, laser guns, and cold war tensions while seamlessly marrying those tropes with the tropes of fantasy games. For example, the "super mutants" in the game are visually and functionally the same as the Ogres of fantasy games; and yet, they are distinct enough (with their own science fiction origins) that they don't **feel** like an adaption of existing archetypes.
The combat in the game is a mixture of first person shooter and turn-based combat, giving the player the option to either play it as an FPS or, at any time, pause time to plan out their attacks with a given number of action points. The dialogue system is incredibly deep, allowing players more than just "yes" or "no" interactions. Players can use their aquired skills to solve problems or make speech checks that have an impact on the rest of the interaction. The only problem with these interactions is that the characters themselves are, for the most part, one dimensional due to the aforementioned reliance on archetypes seemingly as a holdover from it's tabletop roots.

First off, I'm going to begin by saying that I have been following the development of A Hat in Time literally since day one (back in 2012 when the creator first posted a video on an experimental UDK game he had just started on.) I managed to keep myself from any spoilers whatsoever (other than the one that he spoiled about the antagonist almost immediately after creating her) by not watching any videos of the beta or alpha builds that were out. So, now that I've got my hands on the game, what do I think about it? I think it's pretty good so far. The music is creative and fun to listen to, the characters are of an interesting and entertaining design, the gameplay is pretty solid and reminiscent of Super Mario Sunshine, Super Mario Galaxy, and a hint of the developer's mod for Team Fortress 2 that he developed, "Parkour Fortress." I haven't gotten a chance to check out too many of the levels so far, but I'm having a lot of fun. I would like to make a note, though, at the time of writing this review, I had noticed a number of simple yet noticeable glitches that are in the game. Firstly, and this is the most major one, if you walk into some objects and then open up the hat selection menu, hat kid will start floating up into the air and clip above the ceiling. So far, this hasn't caused any problems, as the walls seem to extend up infinitely, but it's definitely something that should be taken note of. Secondly, I found that during the first level of the game, when moustache girl asks you to climb up to her and the game shows you the button that allows you to do so, if you instead climb up the rock face onto the construction site-esque building next to you, and then double jump + slide from the edge to reach the top of the belltower that moustache girl is in, she won't move, as, for some reason, the developers didn't think that the player would find their own way of making it up to the top and didn't include a backup trigger or even a simple temporary player clip so that this could be avoided.
In conclusion, I'm liking the game so far and think it's been worth the 5 year wait watching it be developed, even though the game has a number of day 1 bugs. Also, tell people if you're going to include a pack that has the game bundled with the soundtrack for less than both individually, I bought the two seperately at the same time and I could've saved a few bucks :p.
p.s. I liked the prototype theme for mafia town, bring it back!

Hat Girl traverses fairly quickly with double jump, sprinting, and diving -- which makes her very nice to just move. Paired with an actually good camera makes her incredibly satisfying to just travel and explore.

The developers of The Long Dark have created something that other early access titles should aspire to: a clean, playable experience with room for expansion.
The game, at the present moment, is absolutely fantastic. Survival is a challenge at all times, and death is always around the corner. Even when you've spawned in a great place with everything you need at your fingertips, you could be faced with a sudden and unexpected wolf attack or fall through thin ice to your certian death. You could also spawn in a horrible place and freeze to death before you even reach any supplies.
Yes, the game has room for expansion, but ultimately, it delivers a well-streamlined and essentially great product, free from noticable bugs. Unlike most other early access games I've played, the game doesn't turn me away until a patch is introduced to fix glaring problems, it invites me back for more fluid and addictive gameplay.
So, if you like the survival or exploration genres at all, do yourself a favor and pick up this excellent game! Support good game developing practices!
