The Marvelous Miss Take is a stylish stealth game which focuses on distraction and dealing with randomly wandering guards as its primary mechanics.
The game stars the Sophia Take, an heiress whose aunt’s fortune (and more importantly, her art) is all stolen (via a forged will) by Ralph, an evil megalomaniac whose focus seems to be hoarding the art for himself rather than sharing it with THE PEOPLE. Sophia’s goal is to steal all the art back and expose Ralph for what he is.
Joining her on her quest are Harry, an older thief with a bum leg, and Daisy, a young, seemingly orphaned pickpocket who joins the team.
The game’s stealth gameplay is very simple – click to walk to a location, hold down the mouse button to run there, and use the right mouse button to throw a device (which varies by character and level) to distract or get around the guards. Ducking behind obstacles is automatic as long as you aren’t running, and the fields of view of all the guards are displayed via very simple and easy-to-understand visual displays.
The levels are all viewed from a top-down isometric perspective which is pretty heavily constrained around your character, meaning you’re exploring the level as you’re penetrating it. What makes this game unusual for a stealth game is that, contrary to most such games, the guards – both in the form of men and dogs – wander randomly through the level, meaning that you cannot rely on them to turn just the right direction or walk just the right way. This also means that waiting around can get you trapped between randomly wandering guards, so it pays to move quickly and to distract the guards to get them to go where you want them to go, either by showing yourself to them, making some noise, or by throwing a noise-making gadget.
Sophia’s goal in each level is to collect all the golden art pieces, set up on walls and pedestals, and then make it to the elevator or exit. Every level has two independent floors to it, and if you fail on the second floor, you start over at the start of that floor, not at the start of the level. On top of that primary goal, she has two secondary goals – she can break the glass around a special statue which appears once per floor, which attracts the attention of the nearest guard, or she can try and do a speed run through the level, completing it within a certain amount of time. In most of the levels, Sophia finds an item lying on a pedestal near the entrance that helps her clear the level – a noise-maker that can be thrown to distract guards, glue to stick them in place, a smoke bomb to obstruct their view, or a teleporter to skip past them.
If Sophia is spotted by the guards, she has to go hide before they catch her; if they catch her, you must start the floor over. Unfortunately, even if you are not captured, Sophia will drop her (very stylish) hat, which must be retrieved before she can complete the level.
Her two allies have slightly different gameplay. Harry always has the same item – a noise-making ball which bounces off the walls – wherever he goes, but as it is his lucky charm, he must collect it back up before completing a level. His missions take place at night in the same rooms that Miss Take’s missions take place in, but with a different setup of guards, and various barriers put in place to obstruct his route through the level. Unlike Sophia, he can’t run, but on the upside, he only has to collect three paintings per floor. His alternate goal is to make it through levels without being spotted by any guards or cameras.
Daisy has no special items at all to help her, but on the upside, she can walk right up behind guards without alerting them, and is the fastest character in the game. Like Harry, she plays in the same stages Sophia does, but with barriers up (though different ones than Harry, oftentimes), and with different guard setups. Daisy must pickpocket keys off the guards to unlock safes and retrieve deeds. The safes are alarmed, so Daisy must run away quickly after avoiding a safe to avoid getting caught. Her levels tend to be the most frustrating simply because the guards must be approached up close, and the safes always create intense situations. Like Sophia, her goal is to speed-run through every level, which is the hardest goal in the game due to the random movements of the guards, and can sometimes lead to extreme frustration.
Indeed, the game’s greatest flaw is its randomized nature. At times, the enemies will turn around and completely screw up your quickly thrown-together plan, and there are occaisions where you will simply be forced to reset a stage because guards randomly wander in through both ends of a hallway. Such events are sometimes your fault, but at other times, the random nature of the game can be quite annoying – especially when doing speed-runs as Daisy, who is pretty dependent on a good guard setup at times to complete her run in time.
The game’s other flaw is its repetitive nature. There are 25 stages, and all but one of them is played through by all three characters, leaving a total of 73 stages in all. However, there are very few mechanics in the game. There are the basic guards who wander around and are the only thing which can actually catch your character. There are security cameras which move automatically back and forth over a field of space, but which have blind spots which can be taken advantage of to sneak around; if you move into their field of view, they will alert the guards to your presence. There are dogs, who will sniff out your character if you are close to them, but which have a very restricted field of view; these canines will at time track you throughout the level if you don’t throw out something to distract them, and can at times feel very frustrating as they home in on you. If the dog catches you, it will bark at you, alerting the guards. Finally, there are lasers which periodically turn off and on, which set off an alarm alerting the guards if you stand on them.
That’s all there is, and it really shows, as the games’ levels don’t really exhibit much variety. Once the mechanics have all been introduced, you’ve seen all the game really has to offer, and the final levels are hard simply because they throw a large number of things at you all at once. While they’re interesting enough, they’re also the place where the random movements of the enemies are the most frustrating, as the large numbers of enemies populating many of those levels means there is more opportunity for you to get cornered. Thus, the game varies from kind of samey to kind of frustrating, and Sophia’s levels are by far the most enjoyable, as it is the first time through a set-up and her broader skill-set and larger number of objectives just feel like they flow better.
Overall, the game is pretty mediocre. The story is flimsy and not particularly interesting. The art style is quite nice – very deco – but isn’t enough to carry the game on its own, and while the core stealth gameplay is alright, it also starts to feel the same after a while.
Ultimately, this is a game best eaten in small bites – none of the levels are very long, with speed run times of four minutes or less which are readily achievable, and completing everything the game has to offer is likely to take only 12 hours or so. When the odd level is played here and there, it doesn’t wear on you so much, but when a lot are played consecutively, it tends to get kind of boring (or frustrating).
Really, though, I wouldn’t recommend it - it isn't a very substantive experience. While the game encouraging you to move quickly and distract foes actually gets rid of one of the worst parts about stealth games – boringly waiting around for a guard to walk by on the right portion of its pattern – it replaces it with the frustration of the RNG occasionally spoiling your run.

Story-focused game: Fine.
Story-focused game with minimal interactivity: Fair enough.
Story-focused game with minimal interactivity where the dialogue is delivered in audiobook form: Ok now you're putting me off.
But no; what we have here is a story-focused game with minimal interactivity where the dialogue is delivered in audiobook form AND is just a developer waxing lyrical about how they feel in what might as well be their own diary.
I'm going to spoil the hell out of this thing right now because it is NOT damn sacred like everyone saying "play it, don't read up anything on it or it'll spoil it for you!" No, all we have here is a classic trick developers use where they give their work to someone else whilst saying "Hey, a friend of mine made this and I think it's kinda weird but I'd like a second opinion." That's it. The narrator, Davey, talks about "his friend" Coda and the various surrealist pieces he made as you walk and occasionally click through them (virutal art gallery is the technical term but this is Source engine; hardly that pretty) and the unspoken TWIST is that they're the same person. (If you're doubting this, there's literally a level with an ending where the player has to make a phone call to their past self. It could hardly be more blatant about it.) And the narrator abuses this because by pretending that they're an observer rather than the creator, they can make pretentious statements about metaphorical meanings of the quirky features present. Something which they'd NEVER do when talking as the creator of that level because they KNOW that it was just a bug.
The entire thing is a smokescreen. It's framed as one man apologising to another when in reality it's just 1 guy feeling sorry for himself. It's one guy saying the most vapid and meaningless garbage to himself, but because most people think it's a conversation they get emotionally invested. And what higher meaning is there to the narraive, what lessons can we learn from it? Such things as "You grow creatively by letting others see your creations," and "Isolation is painful and debilitating," and "No human being is perfect." You know, things most people learn in ♥♥♥♥ING PRIMARY SCHOOL.
And this comes from the creator of The Stanley Parable. A game that manged to defy the expectations of walking simulators by making the player's actions into the most powerful kind of commentary. And it's on sale for £5.59. No chance son, this guy ain't fooled. Try harder next time.

Let's call this what it is: Davey Wreden, the creator of the really funny and unique game "The Stanley Parable", talks us through "games" that some acquaintance of him has made throughout the years.
From the description for this game: "it tells the story of a person struggling to deal with something they do not understand". Cryptic description, I know. What it essential means is "Davey talks about what went through his acquaintance's head when making less than 5 minute long games without any true plot, and you as the player gets to press W and listen". This is all fine if you're looking for that experience, but I was expecting something different, something similar to "The Stanley Parable". As the description for this game (for some reason) was written in such a cryptic way, it's hard to know beforehand what you're buying. In my case, I was disappointed.
As this isn't what I thought the game was about and what the description entailed, I can't recommend it. My suggestion would be to simplify the description on the Store Page and make it more clear to the customer what he/she is buying. Furthermore I think it's outrageous to ask for ~8€ when Davey Wreden did not even create these games himself.
So yeah. You're paying ~8€ to listen to Davey Wreden and to press W. If you think that's worth it, be my guest.

I came into this game as a visual novel player. I am not sentimental about symbolism or get emotionally attached to the words that I choose. I choose consistently and logically with my desired outcome in mind. Most importantly, I expected my choices to not be illusions. I played "Beginner's Guide" because of multiple sources claiming it to be dark and have multiple twists. The biggest draw in for me is that it would "make me feel depressed" after playing it. I love gut-wrenching stories. This was not one, and the hype has surely disappointed me.
As a proud introvert and skeptic, I was unimpressed with most of this game since the narrator irritated me. I disliked his enthusiasm and the overanalyzed answers he had for everything. As an uncreative person, I could not relate to the "artist's struggles" that riddled the game and thus it failed to draw me in. Honestly, are these first world problems really that traumatic? Life goes on regardless of tedium or success. I also did not buy the backstory that this "Coda" (the coder) was a real person. A supposed recluse developing quirky game scenarios by himself  is believable, but if he is so socially awkward, how did he obtain the rights to the bg music with vocals in it, along with the female voiced murmurs and crying? Am I supposed to believe he's all lonely and detached from the world, ya know, aside from his presumed sister that voice-acts his game for him? And how exactly did that fated meeting between the narrator and Coda go down? My speculations were rather ridiculous... and it seems, perhaps half valid.
It wasn't until the Tower chapter that I finally felt "Notice me, senpai" the (barely interactive) game got my attention. I was very interested in seeing a certain character being portrayed in a way I laughingly pretended he was from the start. I was excited for the bloodshed and tragedy that was to be revealed next- but all I got was a vague sentimental ending. Spare me your scenery and feels music, it does nothing for me. All in all, this game did not immerse me in its environment. It did not have an emotional impact on me. I did not feel that the mental condition of any of the characters were on a harmful or abnormal level of obsession. Word, situational, and color symbolisms were blatantly apparent throughout and made me roll my eyes more than anything. This was not dark or scary. I would like to say the game is dull- but I can't because it most definitely is thought provoking. While exploring why this game didn't work for me, I discovered a lot about myself. While this game was largely about relating yourself to the characters, which I failed to do, the main goal was to get the player to think about themselves- their own goals in life and their own personal struggles. This game is about introspection, and on that front, it succeeded.

As I read about the game, the idea just got me. I'm kind of an outdoor person myself an enjoy hiking through the local woods at least twice per month.
When I played the game for the first time, it gave me the experience I had watching "Into the wild" for the first time. You really get the feeling of survival, despite the quite rough graphics in this alpha version (but that's why it's called early access).
## MYSTERY LAKE REVIEW ##
Unfortunatly, the survival experience gets a little bit to intense in my eyes.
Most of the time you are running around without orientation, find a hut or two containing about 20% of the equipment you would actually need to make it to the next day, and then die either from exhaustion or from being attacked by one of the many wolves wandering around everywhere.
This is of course just as realistic as surving after a plane crash in northern canadian winter would be, but on the other hand you are not able to craft stuff out of the items inside the huts (not even a mace from a chair to stand SOME chance against the wolves) or even wrap yourself up in the blankets from the beds inside the huts to prevent freezing to death outsinde while trying to forge some hardwood to keep your fire in the oven alive while resting a bit.
And thats the point - I payed 10 € for this game.
If I want to experience what it feels like to die alone in the nature, I would buy a bus ticket for 3 €, ride to the next forest and run around naked till I collapse.
IMHO, dying over and over again is not the point of playing a video game (except you're playing VVVVVV, but that's another story).
At this time, I cannot recommend the game as you end up wandering around frustrated - wondering behind which corner the deadly wolf attack will lure this time - way to soon.
Hopefully they'll get it fixed in the story mode of the final version - if we'll ever come to see the final version as the game seems to be in alpha state for two years now...
## COSTAL HIGHWAY REVIEW ##
After spending almost three hours playing the *Mystery Lake* Sandbox-Level, I just wanted to try out the *Costal Highway* Level before I was about to uninstall the game.
I just played the game for five minutes, ran down the first hill, enterd the first house and found more stuff inside than I managed to aquire in all the attempts that I took on Mystery Lake.
Seriously, WTF? This is kind of the definition of imbalanced level architecture...
Dear developers, would you PLEASE be so kind and add a brief notice at the start screen that tells TLD-inexperienced players to best start with the *Costal Highway* Area? That would be great. -_-

The feel of real survival game I missed from WC3 maps, specifically Wilderness Survival. A godsend for open-world survival genre being saturated with zombies. It's you against nature, minus the other crap. As this is still in early access, I expect more features in the already good game.
+ Fun survival sandbox, without zombies.
+ Lots of areas to scavenge.
+ Awesome environment
- There's nothing much to do in the later part of the game( 20+ days) but sleep, gather meat and eat & drink. Well, there's the occasional gather wood and tinder to melt some ice for water but that's it.
- Knowing the temperature accurately without some sort of aid is like having a built-in geiger counter in your brain. You could at least make it somewhat general perception of weather (warm, cold, colder, freezing) and/or make a thermometer lootable.
-At day 40, I'm almost bare naked. A blizzard tore most of my clothes off.I am left with nothing. The game could make use of surprise events (random heli crash/supply drop) to counterbalance the game's crescendo.
Overall, I can recommend this game to everyone I know. A little tweaking will make the game the best open-world survival game on Steam.

These colorful sprite graphics lend personality to the eight character skins, but are almost painfully primitive and depend on nostalgia for the early days of 2D platformers for appeal. That simplicity makes it especially surprising and fun when a screen-warping visual effect triggers mid-match to set off panicked reactions during battle. My friends often flailed and shouted trying to avoid incoming arrows, creating some of the most hilarious moments.

Just started messing around with RPG Maker VX Ace, following along with some tutorials on youtube
by a great user called Venthros.  If you're into old school RPG games in the vein of the original Final Fantasy and are interested in making one of your own, this is the best tool for you.  It has tons of included assets you can build a complete game with, or if you've got the talent or resources you can create your own assets - everything from sprites, to tilesets and music - and really make it your own. I can see how addicting this program could be, though, and there's a chance I'll go farther down the rabbit hole as I continue to learn and get better at using it.
When you start up the program, it just drops you in, so it can be pretty daunting at first.  The software does provide extensive tootips on everything to help you out, but if you're new to game making, you'll need to find a tutorial somewhere.  I hightly recommend Venthros at the link above.
In any case, a great tool for the money.  Grab it if you're at all interested in game making, or even just being a Game Master.  Especially if there's a sale again and it gets discounted.  Definitely worth the money.

I bought this on a whim during the big sale and I am not disappointed. Zombies get a little overdone these days, so it is nice to see a real survival of the fittest game come around.
The art style works fine as it allows a wide variety of machines to play The Long Dark, and while the interactivity is partially static, it doesn't really take anything away from the experience. Gameplay is just what I was looking for, tense and can be a real challenge depending on where the game plops you down to start. I have done well at times, others not so great. My best record so far is right at 5 days. I always slip up at some point and become wolf bait.
The wolves are your biggest fear next to providing for yourself. You can't be too certain just where they will show up and it makes you hesitant to lollygag around, as it should.
One thing I would like to see added is the ability to find a basic club or sturdy stick to defend yourself early on. Even as a kid this is the first thing I would think of if I felt threatened; you need something other than your hands to defend yourself against sharp teeth. Other than that there are not too many things that stick out as a problem.
Might be nice if wolves close to the building you are inside at the moment would make a certain amount of noise so you have a chance of detecting their presence before blindly going out to your death.
Having a blast with TLD and have already reeled in one friend so far based on my recommendation.
Don't wait until the sale is over, this is worth the full price. Just do it!

Banished is one of the best resource managing simulations out there. If you liked playing Age of Empires and prefered to simply focus on putting up buildings, harvesting resources, and developing every square inch of land you can instead of raising an army then this game is for you. now instead of fighting in wars, you are fighting the elements. That said, there are some major flaws that the game can improve on.
First off, this game has a huge learning curve. Unless someone is helping you learn the game, your first few villages are going to fail. There's no tutorial in-game to teach you how to play. Luckily it's easy to learn how to play, the issue is learning what judgement calls to make.
Second flaw, starvation. I don't know what it is, but your villagers are hell bent on starving to death if they can help it. I've had villages where there is one woodcutter for firewood, and everyone else is in food production yet I STILL lost because everyone starved to death. If ever you feel safe that you have enough food, don't believe it.
Another flaw, population. Sometimes population is very slow, other times it booms. The issue occurs when everyone gets old and dies before reproducing, or when population exceeds food production and everyone starves to death. You need to be careful building houses or people will have kids and fill them well beyond what you can handle, then the whole civilation crumbles.
Final flaw, no direct interaction with the civilions. If your herdsman decides he wants to go cut some trees instead of mind the cattle, you can't select him and tell him to go do his job. If your woodcutter isn't making firewood and everyone is freezing to death, you can't direct him to work. The game works on priorities, and you can increase priority of tasks in an area, but not specific tasks. If you need a specific building built, your builders may decide to work on one of the other not-as-important buildings.
I love the game and can't stop playing it, and if you think you would like it you probably will. just be mindful of the flaws when you play, or you might have some missed expectations.

Pros and cons of this game.
Pros are that it is graphically polished and optimized and that there are no staggering and unfinishness like in Empire Total War. The map is tighter and encompases Europe from the Spain to the Moscow and from the Mediterranean to southern Norway and Sweden. Single player introduces the option that was missing in Empire TW and that is looting of conquered towns which brings you money or option of making puppet states of selected conquered national regions. So you can essentially be an European puppet master who forms huge puppet states dependent politically of you which give you money and with whom you can trade and have steady income. 2nd huge thing different from Empire is that your troops automatically replenish losses in friendly or allied teritory. Also now you have expanded diplomatic options where you can ask your allies to join your wars or you can give them proposal to stop trading or breaking alliances. The AI often gives you similar propositions which are usually to their own gain and your loss.
Cons are typical for most recent vanilla total war games - vanilla AI is criminally stupid, battles are arcadey, soldiers die too fast, firepower is buffed to the degree where bayonet attack is pointless. Also there are only 5 playable factions and number of Napoleonic era troops is limited to few generic groups like ''militia'', ''line'', ''elite'' etc., with pretty much similar stats. And game engine cannot endure modding or unit multiplier that adds more soldiers to the units, and that is where all recent total war games stagger. It doesn't help even if you have a beast of a PC with huge amounts of ram.
All those things can be fixed and given depth by installation of mods. This game is practically worth of investment because of mods who give it depth and complexity. Personally, I played vanilla limited time and dissapointed by its usual arcadey SEGA style for casual majority of bored gamers I switched to mods. Now once you have tried mods for this game there is no turning back to vanilla and you would be sattisfied.
Same goes for Empire TW or Shogun 2 or Rome 2 or Attila - the engine and battle mechanics are pretty same, despite latter games being without firearms - soldiers still die too quickly and it completelly ruins those games. Now with mods, some of them supporting multiplayer, installed this game is worth investing into and I have no regrets.

The Marvelous Miss Take is essentially a stealth game stripped down to its core elements, with a top down camera, vision cones reminiscent of early Metal Gear Solid games, and the slight flavouring of a puzzle game on top. This is wrapped up in a slick presentation, which is sadly the game's greatest strength.
Sophia moves at a fairly slow pace and will automatically crouch behind waist-high objects--it's better to think of any waist-high objects as walls, since they effectively block vision cones in a similar way, though also preventing Sophia from running. Running produces a noise radius that alerts guards to your location, so it must be done outside of a certain distance from a guard. Additionally, Sophia occasionally collects gadgets, and can earn additional uses for these gadgets by looting art. This is a fairly smart system that rewards skilful play.
The problem, then, is the game's randomized AI. Randomized AI does not work very well for a game with light puzzle elements and time trials. Guards move in random directions, sometimes leaving the rooms they are stationed in. This randomized AI can put you in very unfavourable situations, sometimes (if you are extremely unlucky) as soon as the level starts. Often, they can put you in unwinnable positions even after collecting all the trophies, or waste a lot of your time. Completing heists can require several attempts to get lucky. Getting under par time also happens because you were lucky; the AI didn't put you in any strange situations, or you restarted each floor until you beat it with time to spare.
Dogs suck up all the fun with their presence. Their scent radius is huge and they will follow your trail around the entire map if you let them, putting you in unwinnable situations that force a restart. Dogs are very often placed in rooms with security cameras, which further reduces your mobility options and makes dogs a nightmare to deal with.
Miss Take isn't a very good stealth game. There are much better stealth games out there. Miss Take doesn't innovate, and it doesn't even iterate, either. It doesn't really have anything new to offer to the genre. Its presentation is its only redeeming quality. Get it on sale, if you're curious.

Don't go in with expectations past the blurb at the top.  It's not The Stanley Parable 2, but what it is is just as amazing in its own way.
As a fan of theorycrafting, the act of Davey curating and commentating on his friend's portfolio of games felt natural-- I could imagine a friend showing me in a similar manner the games they were passionate about as well as what they believed the game communicated to the player.
Conversations like this with friends-- I love to listen to them as they speak more to the reviewer than the content being reviewed.  Maybe the author just like creating games where there is no win-condition-- maybe that reflects inner frustration?  Maybe, maybe not.  You'd have to ask them.
With that said, I naturally empathize with others.  I want my friends to know that they aren't alone, that they're going to be okay, that we all experience some period of darkness, but that we all eventually move past it.  I want to be a support and a resource-- but through experience you find out when to draw a line, when to just let things go.  People aren't problems that you're assigned to fix, and respecting personal space is integral to all relationships.
The Beginner's Guide is a character study and, for the (perhaps stongly) empathetic, an emotional rollercoaster.  I would guess that it will touch creative individuals in its own way, but it certainly isn't limited to just impacting those who create.  I don't create games/art, but it's stuck with me for multiple days now.
Completely worth the price of (actually cheaper than) a movie ticket.  It will stick in your mind for much longer than the 1.5 hour playthrough time.

Pros/Cons
+ Snazzy jazzy soundtrack
+ Simple clean visuals
+ Daisy’s heists are generally quite fun
+ Open solutions, levels can be cleared in different ways using different paths
+ Lots of optional levels
- Levels all look and sound the same, repetitve
- Most optional levels are just reskins of campaign levels
- Very standard stealth gameplay, nothing really stands out or feels new
- Character abilities are very limited
- Successfully completing a heist often feels like the result of chance rather than skill, leading to frustration
- This chance leads to frequent failure, meaning having to replay missions again and again
- Harry’s missions are tedious and dull
I wanted to like The Marvelous Miss Take. I love stealth games, it had an awesome upbeat jazzy soundtrack, cool visual style, minimalist gameplay that’s quick to get into and quick to complete, and as cardboard cutout and cartoony as they were, I liked the characters. But the more I played the more I had to admit to myself that I just wasn’t enjoying the game. It’s a bizarre mix of frustrating and boring.
What I enjoy best about stealth games is two things. The first is the patient methodical observing and memorizing of guard movements and behaviors, exploring and finding the best paths to the goal, the trial and error of taking a risk, getting caught, revising strategies, and trying again until I get it right. I love the feeling of having finally outwitted, out snuck, outrun every guard by the end of the level, the feeling of having conquered using wits instead of brawn. The second is gadgets. The stealth genre is great at giving players all sorts of toys to play around with--noisemakers, sleep gas, night vision, zip lines, disguises, hacking systems, teleportation, invisibility.
Marvelous Miss Take is a stealth game. The goal of each ‘heist’ is to sneak through an art gallery, avoiding guards, cameras, and trip wires in order to steal and escape with various pieces of artwork. Levels are very small, consisting of only a few rooms, two floors, and a handful of guards. Most can be beaten in just a couple of minutes.
The thing is, the guards don’t follow any set paths, more or less randomly wandering about the level. On the one hand, this is cool, because it leads to every playthrough of a level going a bit differently. There is an unpredictability to guard movements that’ll keep you on edge the whole time, as no area is safe. They can find you anywhere. Unfortunately, this also leads to frustration. Finishing a level is almost always dependent on luck. At the end of a heist, I almost never felt like I’d expertly outwitted a group of guards, because beating levels depends on things as trite as Guard 2 just happening to not patrol the room full of trip wires this go around, or maybe because one of the guard dogs happened to get stuck in a corner.
All the other times you fail often have less to do with mistakes you make and more to do with getting unlucky with where the guards decided to wander. The player doesn’t have many options for escaping when cornered. Besides a few limited use noise makers and smoke bombs, Sophia, the main character, has nothing in the way of cool gadgets for players to play with (with the exception of a teleporter that unfortunately only appears in a couple levels), and most levels don’t even have those. Difficulty ramps up pretty quick, and you’re going to fail heists, and you’re going to fail them over and over. Levels are very short, so you won’t end up replaying much. But when every level has the exact same visuals, guards, dogs, cameras, and goals, the game is repetitive enough already. Everything is very expected, all as per genre. You won’t find anything new here.
The developers do try to inject some variety into the gameplay with two other playable characters. Both are able to replay heists already completed with Sophia, but with some added challenges and abilities. The first is Harry, who is much slower than Sophia and has nothing to show for it except a noisemaker that is made useless because it has to be picked up after thrown. With Harry, you’ll be playing through the exact same level as with Sophia, stealing the same sort of artwork, except more slowly. It’s beyond tedious.
The third playable character is Daisy, whose heists are easily the highlight of the game. Daisy is both faster and quieter than Sophia. Her heists strip down most of the extra fat in randomly wandering guards and dogs from Sophia’s missions, and instead involve her pickpocketing just two or three guards, and then using the keys to open alarm-rigged safes. I had a great time sneaking directly behind and beside guards to get their keys, and using strategy to draw them away from safes long enough to get in and out before the safe alarm sent the guards charging back to my position. It’s a shame her missions are so much shorter than Harry or Sophia’s. It’s the only time I felt like a professional cat burglar while playing.
At the end of the day, I’m not sure who this game is for. It has a cool style and soundtrack, the minimalism and bite-sized levels makes it easy to jump in and out of. But it has none of the things I usually look for in a stealth game. I expect casual players will be put off by the frustrating chance-laden levels, but I also expect fans of the genre will be disappointed by how limited the stealth gameplay is. And twenty dollars is an awfully steep asking price for the amount of content you’re getting.

Dungeon Defenders 1 and Eternity were a blast to play. When I learned Dungeon Defenders 2 was coming, I was excited. However I saw that they were trying to change the formula and make 2 versions, which I wasnt happy about. But I saw it on Steam again as a F2P game, so I tried it out.
Its good to see Trendy go back to the true formula of what made Dungeon Defenders so much fun. I literally play it every day.
Pros
+ Item fusing/Enchanting: This is a great feature. I completely forgot you could power up items in 1 and bringing it back like this is refreshing. By taking items you dont need and fusing it with your weapons and armor to make them more powerful is very simple and easy to understand. Your fighters can become super strong with Hero Damage and your tower builders can put more damage and health into your defenses.
+ Enemy Paths: In the first game, they showed the gateways to where enemy minions would spawn, but for multiple cores to defend and multiple spawn points, sometimes you had to guess where they were coming from. Showing the exact paths where they would travel from makes big maps a lot easier to do. Just pray that your defenses are strong enough. :P
+ Increased difficulty: Dungeon Defenders 1 was almost too easy on Hard and once you got better, Nightmare was not that hard either. 2 has more balanced difficulty based on your iPWR, your Item Power. If youre not at the right level, youre bound to get crushed. I learned that the hard way.
+ Graphics: A nice upgrade from Dungeon Defenders 1, but still keeps that lovely pastel and colorful style.
Cons
- Not enough content: Its still in alpha so it does get kinda boring doing the same levels over and over. But thats understandable too since its still in alpha.
Overall, I recommend Dungeon Defenders 2. Its so much fun and has so much more to offer. Just remember, its still in alpha.

So I got this game once it became free, and it's brilliant. Like it's predecessor, DD2 does an excellent job of making a tower defense (one of the most boring game-types in my opinion) into a much more involved and fun experience. Everything from the original and more.
However, it still has some problems that I assume the devs already know about and may or may not do anything about while still in EA. Some problems are...
-Always Online. (From what I've seen) This is an idea that only works with MMORPGs and the AAA Multiplayer FPS's. A tower defense game that focuses on grinding (not a bad thing here) and has things in place for people that like to play solo is great, but Solo-players are forced to have a private session that's still connected to the internet. If your ISP decides to kill your connection or your wireless connection is♥♥♥♥♥♥ then you get kicked out of your private, SOLO match. It's not TERRIBLY awful, just a feature that shouldn't really be there.
-Length of the Game so far. Not gonna lie to you, this game is grievously short. Yes, I know it's EA, it's gonna have more stuff, yadda yadda yadda; but it won't hold your attention too well after the campaign is over. After the story is done you essentially just screw around on the maps with tougher monsters at higher difficulties.
-"Hard Difficulty" This is something alot of games honorably fail at. It's difficult to up the difficulty of something, sometimes it's simply made unfair (MGSV:PP, Iwannabetheguy, etc.) other times it's not that much harder or maybe it's easier (Legend of Zelda games, Metroid Prime, etc.). DD2 kinda flops in this regard as "Hard" mode is simply just a♥♥♥♥♥♥ton of enemies that hit harder. Sure, that makes it harder, but not by much. It would be nice to see a new mechanic introduced to make the challenge more of one. But what it should be, I dunno.
Aside from the problems, this game is in EA, and it's free as far as I'm concerned. It's worth the look.

When I first started to play this game I had a pretty rough start - Issues with my resolution, frame drops, I even managed to softlock the game twice in the first thirty minutes of gameplay, wrote it down as a bad indie game, gave it a bad review.
Then I stopped being a ♥♥♥♥ing ♥♥♥♥♥ and actually played the game.
The next 7 and a half gamplay (at this moment) was nothing short of magical. Its rare that I even want to play the same game for longer than an hour, so its something else when this game kept me stuck to it constantly and had me thinking solely about the next time I would get to play.
As it stands, the only issue I have with this game still is that I cant play it at the proper resolution and get that crisp HD. And thats it. The atmosphere of this game is just perfect, each chapter is an adventure all of its own and shows just the raw love and hard work that went into making this game. Every time you select a level, you get the good Mario Sunshine showing you the basic idea of the level, and the objective. Is it nolstagic? Yes, but is it still good? Hell yes.
Controlling Hat Kid is just like, what, how- Honestly I havent had controls this good on my character since Super Meat Boy. At first, it can get be a little wonky, but the moment you get it, that moment of 'Aha!' it just fits and works so perfectly. Its percise and fun to use and gives so many options while maintaining the simple concept but also adding a layer of skill and extra thought that can be used.
The camera isnt half bad. It definitely isnt bad on its own, but ever so often theres segments where it locks itself into a place or angle - And then it can start to freak out, but even then I never found it to be too frustrating to use.
To be honest, I really hope everyone read down this far because this is the most important part of the game, and my last point: The charm. I havent seen a game so... Damn, I cant even find the word - Mystical? Amazing? Immersive? - Im not really sure what the proper word is. The characters are so full and unique, the locations are impressive and fun to explore, even Hat Kid, this mostly-mute little girl is just bursting with fluid motion and emotion.
30$ is a little expensive for a game, yes. Usually I go by the rule that for each dollar I paid I should get an hour of gameplay in return. But this game is an exception - Because one hour of gameplay is just so full, so constantly exciting and fun, that the experience is worth more than one dollar. Im sure Im going to get a good 10 hours out of 100% this game and so many more from replaying it and just enjoying it. Do yourself a favor and purchase A Hat in Time.

This game is simply amazing.
When I first saw this game, I was worried that it would be more slow paced than I would like. Then I got 3 friends over and boy was I wrong!
The pace can be frantic and down right insane at times. Trying to take out one opponent when another is hot on your tail can make for some intense matches. Nothing can beat the yelling that goes on when one person misses with an arrow only to be taken out by the person they were attacking. Or watching a one-on-one match from the sidelines and shouting for who you want to win.
The variety in this game is truely astounding, and frankly, something I wasn't expecting. The variants you can add to the match (such as laser arrows that never go away until they hit a person or another arrow, or corpses that can explode on command) really add a layer of depth that a game like this benefits from. The fact that you can save up to three pre-set variation packs makes these options work extremely well. So you don't have to go into the variants menu every time and select each modifier one-by-one, you can just save your favorite to a pre-set and reload it whenever you want to use it. The group I play with use this every time we play and it is wonderful.
The single player (Quest Mode) starts off more slow-paced than its multiplayer conuterpart, but does not stay there for long. The boss fights (yes, there are boss fights) take on a whole new level of gameplay and test your skills learned thusfar. The ability to play the "Quest Mode" with a second player really helps on  the more difficult matches, and I was only able to defeat the last level with a friend helping me. It really is a value add for something that could have been a multiplayer only experience.
The trials were something I never really got into. I'm sure they are fine, but I'm not a big fan of trying to speedrun stuff like that so I can't speak much on it.
Lastly, the hidden unlockable characters add a nice incentive to try the other game modes. There are four characters and I believe the same number of levels that can be unlocked in various ways. Each character has their own unique look. I would highly suggest getting all of these, as they are not too difficult to find and unlock.
All in all, this game is insanely good. Fast paced, frantic, screamingly good fun for a group of friends. Highly reccomended!

As someone whose main interests are Megaman, Castlevania and oversaturated arcade brawlers, I'm a gamer who hasn't had much to smile about in recent years. Even going back to play those old beat-'em-ups is only halfway satisfying because I realize as an adult what I didn't as a kid: that they were cynical money-grubbing cheap shot factories that drew me in with pretty graphics and catchy music to drain as many quarters as they could get out of my acid wash jean pockets.
When my husband gifted me this game, I was cautiously optimistic because of the stellar retro style graphics and the outstanding soundtrack... and my trust was rewarded in a way I never would've expected. Fight'N Rage is the rarest of all: a difficult but fair brawler that's beatable not just by one player, but on one token, provided you're good enough. And no, that doesn't mean constantly jumpkicking or using some stupid rotation exploit! The movesets of the three playable characters are so shockingly robust that it felt at times like a fighting game that had its characters imported into a brawler vis a vis Guilty Gear:Judgment. The single developer- yeah that shocked me too- made sure that each character had enough moves that there are (with a very few exceptions) really no situations they can't get the upper hand in no matter how saturated the screen is with enemies.
The graphical and narrative style of this game is peak 90s. Roided-out, angular men, ugly mutant furries, dank alleyways, and HUGE bouncing breasts everywhere with the frequency of a sexploitation film... and I don't say that as a negative! I could see the gonzo visuals and adherence to retro style storytelling- "The evil bad men captured and/or killed these scantily clad ladies, IT'S TIME FOR REVENGE"- making some roll their eyes, and fair play to you if that's too high an entry fee, but if you're willing to part with your higher cognitive functions and 20 bucks, I can promise you this is the single most satisfying, rewarding, challenging and deep brawler experience of your life. This game is really, REALLY GOOD.

If you have ever played a town/city or basicly any builder game, you know the drill: build efficiently and keep people happy (and alive). Banished was never intended to revolutionize the industry, which I think is a good thing considering all the games which started to rethink the basics and squeezed under it's own weigth.
Following the minimalist path, there is a very short list of buildings you can build. You start with a cart and two families, it's your job to build them everything they need before winter. The graphics is great, I really love it, perfectly fits into the theme. The first hours are also awesome, understanding the UI and examining the possibilites took about 5 minutes. Than the winter came...
...And nothing happened. My town turned white, and people used firewoods to keep themselves warm. This was the part when things started to stink. Where are the extreme snowfalls you read in medieval books? Why people are not shivering or at least give a damn about the freezing cold in their unheated wooden house? Of course, when you run out firewood, people can't heat and eventually they die but somehow I expected a more complex behaviour.
Okay, well, still playing hours with this game, After a few winter, suddenly a text box appeared: one of my villager was ran over by a boar. A textbox? You serious? WTF? Is the village mourning (as 30 people lived in my village at that point), or at least his family? Ney, Banished ignores all these community thingies. Oh, I almost forgot the merchants who are only willing to come by boat, after you have built an expensive harbor.
Well, still playing. I have every resources to live happily, but the population is not growing. As I read in the forums, it is because I didn't build houses. They make children only if you build houses before (you read it right). In addition, the quality of the house really counts: in shanks, a couple can have one child only, while in a brick house more is allowed. (Not speaking about new-born children living in a house alone)
At this point, I was really worried, but insisted on playing. My town grew and grew, and eventually, I've found my ultimate problem with this game: this game has no porpuse at all! Of course, build your town and stuff like that, but there is no achievement in this whole game. You built a school? Good. Now, you'll have educated workers, who theoretically works better.  Have a church? Now a guy can work there. Asking a townsman about his thougths? Rofl. A basic diplomacy (e.g. like in Tropico) would have been a good point but it was never in the cards.
Banished stands on strong legs. The concept is great, but it is full of half-solutions. While playing I thought maybe after a certain size it will be more diverse and exciting, but no. It might become harder if you plan wrong, but not more exciting. Using the workshop you can put a lot of buildings in it, which are really great, worths a try, though they cannot fix the big problems with this game. There is not a single point where you can bind to your townspeople (I think they don't even have a name), or your town. This game is not that good, and not bad either but it is a real time-killer for sure. If you have a lot of free-time I recommend it, because it makes the hours fly, but if you play one or two hours only a day, maybe you should keep looking.

This game feels like a mix between Super Smash Bros. (particularly Melee) and the 8-bit Kid Icarus as far as gameplay and singleplayer campaign goes. Each part is more noticable depending on whether you're playing multiplayer or campaign. And, let it be known, this was the game that, alongside Bombsquad, led me to purchasing an Ouya.
It's upgraded appearance on the PS4 and on Steam are very much welcomed by me, though I have some qualms for the Steam version.
The PC is, unless you hook it up to the TV, not built for local multiplayer couch parties in mind. Overall, the PC mainly focuses on online multiplayer with the likes of Quake, TF2, and League of Legends. Towerfall does not have online multiplayer, and though arguments have been made supporting its non-support (and I agree with most of them), you essentially have to get things hooked up and working properly to get a decent couch multiplayer experience with Towerfall. Best thing I will say is that the Singleplayer is a bit easier on the PC.
Because, in my opinion, playing Towerfall with friends on the couch is THE best way to play it, I vastly prefer the Ouya and PS4 versions to the PC version. And, aside from these minor qualms, I think that Towerfall is one of the better combat-platformer (combatformer?) games on the market, outside of Super Smash Bros. itself. If you do not have a PS4 and want to play your PS4 game with friends, Towerfall alone is a solid reason to buy one, though at this point it's somewhat difficult to truly recommend it (hard to say with all these games getting delayed), but if you don't have one and do not intend to buy PS4 or Ouya, get it on Steam. If you have an Ouya, you need Towerfall. If you have a PS4, I will instantly recommend Towerfall Ascension. It's that good of a combatformer game.
Pros: VERY Solid gameplay, neat character design (My favorite's the Thief), a unique concept that by all means may be a steep learning curve (1-hit KO on most attacks) but ends up being easy to pick up anyway. Great soundtrack, and interesting take on the pixel art aspect.
Cons: If you're not familiar with the game, you may get steamrolled by other experienced players. The music, while still great, can get repetitive in the campaign. PC version is, by design of PC, hard to get that multiplayer experience without online multiplayer built-in (which is why I recommend the PS4 and Ouya versions over the PC version, at least for now). Ouya version was what got me hooked on Towerfall, but last I checked did not get the Ascension version that PS4 and PC had.
Overall: 9.5/10 for PC and Ouya, 10/10 for PS4.

The Marvellous Miss Take is a lighthearted stealth game about a young theif stealing from an evil art collector to restore her mother's gallery. It has some political overtones and a bit of that pandering feminist flavor BUT the game at its core is pretty fun, and the story is what it is. There are 25 galleries with two floors each ( the final mission actually has three floors), and the 3 playable characters have a different objective to perform in each mission so there is plenty to do.
The characters are ok, likeable but underdeveloped.
The game is charming but lacks variety.
There is no way to go back and review the story if you accidentally skip over something. "Cutscenes" are one and done.
Progression is fairly balanced, you have to do everything as the main character and a smaller number of levels as the two other playable characters.
The controls are a bit sloppy which can make a good run turn disasterous in a frustrating instant. You will probably find the use of a gamepad to be to your benefit.
The game is locked at 60fps which is ok but not great if you have a higher refresh monitor.
There are not a huge number of graphics options, but the game is simplistic enough visually to not need a ton.
Levels are well laid out and fun to walk around in.
There is very little motivation for getting all the side-acheivements unless you are trying to get every single one for the achievement in Steam. The DRM-free players will gain nothing from accomplishing the side missions which is disappointing. Unlockable costumes would have been a PERFECT reward for collecting these
You can learn the levels and improve based on skill for the most part, occasionally a random walking pattern from a guard will throw things off, but such is life.
Levels are easy to fail, but they are short enough that you can attempt them in quick succession.
There are only four types of enemies (guards, guard dogs, cameras, and lasers), but the level design makes sure that these are all you need for enough variety. Some gamers WILL find it repetitive, while others will not.
The game is probably about 4-6 hours in length and probably 10 or so if you are trying to get all the acheivements. It may be much shorter if you are really great or decently longer if you are kind of bad.
TMMT is a fun and lighthearted stealth game with simple mechanics that are easy to learn but difficult to master. If that sounds like what you are interested in, and the little bit of political griping isn't going to bother you (it's not as bad as I am making it sound) then this may be a game for you. I'd probably recommend the multiplayer Monoco over this, but Miss Take has a nice game on her own. At $20 the game is probably a little overpriced. I picked my copy up in a Humble Bundle, but in a Steam sale for around $5-7 I would say Miss Take is worth the price of admission.

[NOTE: While I have very little time logged for RMVX Ace on Steam, I have used RMVX Ace and RMXP to a much greater extent on my old computer and am familiar with both.]
While I do recommend this software overall, there are a few things that I feel should be addressed.
- The software takes a bit of time to get used to. It took me several days to learn the ins and outs of RMVX Ace, and the mechanics are a bit complicated for new users.
- Scripting. It's a pain. RMVX Ace does cover a lot of stuff that won't need scripting, but for the things that do, it's often a hassle. (Like vehicles.)
- The tilesets, characters, and sprites that RMVX Ace comes with are pretty basic. But it IS meant to be customizable, after all, and you can create your own material or search around the RMVX community. The community is huge, and there are a lot of people out with great resources who are willing to help.
- It's too expensive, in my opinion. While this is fairly decent software, I think $30 would be a far more reasonable price. I did manage to catch it on sale, which was why I got it, but I wouldn't have bought RMVX Ace at the full price of $70.
All in all, I think this is good software for creating a basic RPG. It's certainly capable of creating more complex games, but there's a lot more work involved. Personally I do like using RMVX Ace, but it's not for everyone. I do recommend XP over VX Ace.

Unreal Tournament is one of the granddaddies of online team-based first-person shooters. It may have aged, but only in graphics, because the gameplay is still fast and exciting. And with its many game modes and high quality maps, it’s a game that you’ll never get bored of.
First-person shooters weren’t always the on-rails, self-healing, cover-to-cover interactive movies they are today. This genre was a scene of highly competitive players who were constantly searching for the next game to test their limits. And in 1999 they got two of them, one being Unreal Tournament.
The game featured a bundle of innovative weapons with two fire modes; memorable map design that is copied even today; game modes that finally showed something innovative beyond the same old death matches; and finally, bots which may feel a little dumb and predictable today, but back then they were topped only by Half-Life 1.
UT may have been designed as a multiplayer game, but it is also enjoyable in single player. It has an actual campaign mode, where the “plot” may be simple as a doornail (you play in a futuristic gladiator tournament) and most participants only have a single-paragraph story, but it is still enough to build the foundation of a world you can immerse yourself in and make you care about your team. Because despite the popularity of free-for-all death matches, this game is all about team play.
With the ever-increasing issues with the game engine (which was one of the best of its time) and the even more successful sequel, UT2004, UT ’99 faded into obscurity, but if you ever want some really old-school FPS action, you can always rely on it.

Just finished my first major project with RPG Maker VX Ace.
Overall, there's a lot to recommend here, and the good tends to outweigh the frustrating.
Pros:
* Standard old school RPG elements -- such as text blocks and portraits, basic cut scenes and inventory/skill management -- are quickly and easily implemented once you know what you're doing
* You can code you own Ruby scripts to extend game mechanics, and all the code for the RPG engine (battles, menus, etc.) is exposed and editable. I added a stealth system and a twitch-based chase sequence almost entirely in-engine, with minimal Ruby tweaks
* Makes resource management for characters, portraits, enemies and UI elements a breeze
* Lots of built-in assets included, from character sprits to portrait art to some pretty decent background music
Cons:
* It's a bit overwhelming at first, and some of the more useful elements (built-in event scripting, the "features" system, etc.) aren't adequately explained. A quick trip to the forums usually solves this, but it's still annoying
* If you're a coder, the Ruby dev environment is woefully inadequate. It's basically a text file, with no syntax highlighting or basic testing capabilities. The fact you can alter the game code is still cool, but don't expect to do a full overhaul of the code without investing hours and hours and hours
* Struggles to make anything that's not a standard JRPG. Of course, if you're spending money on a product called RPG Maker, you shouldn't really be surprised.

Secret of Magia is a curiosity in that it's a wonder it made it onto Steam at all.  It obviously has a lot of ideas going into it, but none are brought to fruition and little of the game feels finished or satisfying as a result.  The game features weapon crafting, but the weapons you make are useless compared to what you can buy by the time you can craft them.  It features potion crafting which requires gathering items from defeated monsters.  However, defeating monsters means gaining levels and gaining levels is more of a drawback than a plus.  You rarely feel that your character is getting stronger since monsters level up with him and they get stronger faster.  The game has side quests, only five in total, and not all of them give rewards.  Money is too easy to come by, so you might as well spend it all on potions and armor to make the game more bearable.
This is not the kind of game that you pay for and I'm sorry that I did, even though it was on a massive sale.  This is the kind of game that someone puts on the Internet for free so he can get feedback about what to do betterin his next project.  This is an amateur's first attempt at an action RPG and the creator must have a heck of a lot of audacity to think he can sell this.  Don't make the mistake that I did.  Don't buy it.  It's not worth the few hours it will take to play through.  At least, it's not worth money.

If you're comfortable enough with first-person wall-jumps (the hardest part for me was wall-jumping upwards between two walls somewhat like in SM64) it won't be that much of a challenge. It's worth a look if you want a quick, casual platformer that you can take at your own pace and has decent visuals/sounds and simple gameplay.

TLDR: The game has horrible keyboard and mouse menu controls. Like they're really bad. Enemies become invulnerable because you combo too good and you don't get to know it until you attack them and do nothing. Gear system is confusing. Besides that, normal Tales game. Cheesey characters, story, and ideals, very anime, pretty involved combat.
After finally finishing the game and restarting with new game+, I have a few complaints. If you're playing with keyboard and mouse, you're going to realize the controls, especially the menu controls, are incredibly inconsistent, and the ones they tell you on screen are just bad. For example, say you're looking through your inventory. You want to switch from consumables over to your prepared food tab to give yourself a good boost for the big battle you could see coming from a mile away. The controls say to use like the Insert and Home buttons. You know, those buttons nobody uses. Sometimes, though, you get to just click the tab icon, like in every other RPG with reasonable controls. In ToZ, though, about half the time, it'll make you try and use an apple gel on somebody. If it were consistent, I'd just leave it at bad controls (since if the game makes you pick up your hand and move it to the other side of the keyboard just to navigate part of a menu, I think it's half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥in the design). But the fact that sometimes they do let you makes me a bit more annoyed. How can the controls be so inconsistent? May as well just hit escape and exit the menu. Oh wait. Sometimes escape works to close the menu, but other times, you have to right click to exit the menu. Also, Page Up is used to check the next page of descriptions for anything with more than a few words of description, and also it's the button to switch seraph in the menu to decide who's where in the next battle.
Controls in battle are alright, even if it can be hard to make mystic artes actually trigger sometime. But what isn't alright in battles are the enemy invulnerability frames. I get and really appreciate that they don't want you to be able to stunlock enemies. That would ruin the majority of the game. However, to fix it by punishing you for large combos by giving enemies several seconds of invulnerability that you can't see when it begins or ends is not the way to do it. Keep in mind, there's nothing to stop the player from becomming stun locked, and if you accidentally hit them while they're invulnerable they have a huge window to hit you,  and depending on the enemy and number of them, that could really make for a bad time. If you could armatize or dearmitize to break it, I'd have been happy. But all you can do is mash buttons while the player character makes an awkward pose over and over because they got hit.
Also, several times in the game, they give you 0 direction. "Go find the bad guy. He's somewhere probably. Good luck." I like that it's not a matter of "follow the quest arrow" that some games use, but I don't know, I don't like having to just search the world for a lead. Like I'd like to have an idea where I need to go, which fortunately most of the game provided.
The gear system is overly complicated, and this is one of those cases where I feel it wasn't broke but they had to try and fix it. In a way, it punishes you for getting new gear, since you lose those symbol things on them and the bonuses that come with them.
The game's not horrible overall, mind you. It's still a Tales game at core. Standard cheesey characters with the same cheesey ideals, same cheesey anime plot and overall world design. I like that the game doesn't use mana but instead a replenishing resource pool for all attacks.
Armatization is a fun mechanic, but it's easy to rely too heavily on it. I almost exclusively used it for the last 20+ hours of gameplay. After starting a new game, I've been much less intensive with it, and it adds more depth to the game when you're not just immediately hitting shift then clicking rapidly to kill everything.

As someone who has played a lot of Cadillacs & Dinosaurs, Golden Axe, Streets of Rage and Final Fight, I can vouch that Fight'N Rage is a remarkable example of beat-em-up craftsmanship. The game offers 56 possible endings based on routes and character combinations, a crapton of unlockables and a very deep fighting system. Enemies can be juggled into insane combos and if you have a friend with you, you can even kill certain bosses in one well-coordinated combo.
Beating the game several times doesn't just net you different endings, but you get to unlock new costumes and even regular enemies as characters to play with. Oh yeah, and if you are worried about not having friends to play with to get all the endings, the game lets you unlock a CPU partner mode to help you with that!
What's even more impressive is that it was made by just two developers, one of which only did the music.

I was so excited for this game when it was announced. It's exactly the sort of thing I usually enjoy - introspective, visual, thought-provoking. I'm really sad to say that it did not deliver. I considered refunding it - the first time I've ever considered such a thing - but since I did play through it, I'm going to leave a review instead.
I won't go into spoilers or dissection of the plot. My biggest gripe is that when you create a game that is specifically designed to pull volatile emotional strings - decidedly NEGATIVE emotional strings - and you leave things unresolved, that doesn't make for an enjoyable experience. I walked away from this feeling miserable. I've seen sad movies, played games that made me cry, that's not what I'm talking about here. If you compare the game to a balloon, it kept inflating, inflating, inflating, and I kept waiting for it to pop, for something really important to happen, for some brilliant conclusion... and it just never happened. The balloon was simply released, and it went PFFFFFT everywhere, and I realized that all this "deep" discussion was really just a lot of hot air. I felt like I got emotionally jerked around for no reason. It was not enjoyable, there was no justification for all the unpleasantness. Why in the world did I just pay $8 for this experience?
Secondly, I'm a big believer in "walking simulators." Most have exploration elements along with their narratives. Sometimes, they have minor interactions that make them more than just videos, and that, in my mind, justifies playing them as games. You can often find your own way through, re-visit things. With this game, the doors are constantly getting closed behind you, and several times, the scene was simply switched on me without warning when I was trying to line up a screen shot. It's way too linear, you can't go backwards, there is no variation in the story, nothing to miss and come back for. For that reason, it has no replay value. This doesn't even feel like a walking sim because there is literally no difference between playing it yourself and watching someone else's Let's Play.
I get that this is probably a very personal thing, and for that reason, I really hate being a critic about it - but it's one thing to share your feelings on a blog or a YouTube video, and quite another to charge people so much money, especially without being extremely clear up front about exactly what this is. I'm also very concerned that because there is such a glaring lack of closure, it could have very real consequences for people who are suffering from severe depression, social anxiety, and who knows what else. My advice is to save your money and watch someone else play it - but turn it off if it starts to get to you.

This game is a love letter to all the great 3D platformers of the past. Here you'll find a mish-mash of ideas found in games like Super Mario 64/Sunshine/Galaxy, Banjo-Kazooie, and Sonic Adventure. The protagonist's movement and combat techniques take a little getting used to, but once you do, you'll see how they each complement each other leading to a very fluid player experience. Each world has lots of things to collect, and as you beat each chapter, even more items to collect appear, giving you yet another reason to revisit a world. Customization options are rewaded to real treasure hunters and explorers alike. Did I forget to mention how cute the protag Hat Kid is? Because she is. A few cons for this game are the lack of a cohesive art direction; the enemies seem to have not as much thought put into them as the protag, lots of flat textures, and less than stellar voice acting. But don't let any of that stop you from playing one of the few kickstarted games that actually live up to and exceed expectations. Buy A Hat in Time!

A Hat in Time is a prime example of how to do a Kickstarter correctly. Gears for Breakfast maintained excellent communication throughout the development process and have delivered an amazing game, not to mention the free DLC worlds that will be added later. Overall, A Hat in Time looks beautiful, sounds wonderful, and controls perfectly. Every level is something unique, and you never know what gameplay style will be featured next (exploration, combat, stealth, mystery, horror…) The myriad of styles aren't half-baked either: each one works great and adds tons of variety. The game is filled to the brim with personality, much of which comes from Hat Kid, who is an absolutely adorable protagonist! If you love games like Super Mario 64 or Banjo-Kazooie, you'll be delighted with A Hat in Time. Support Gears for Breakfast for delivering on their promises and making such a wonderful game!

I really wanted to like this game. From the outset the presentation is delightful. The mechanics are simple but neat. The control is a little wooly (click on a destination and Miss Take will walk there - hold the button down and she'll run), meaning that you sometimes get spotted by a guard because you clicked one pixel too far around an object so you end up on the wrong side of it.
And that gets to the meat of why I couldn't get on with this game. It's a problem not unique to this game, but to many stealth-based games. Random patrol patterns - the guards move at random, giving you no means to plan your approach or escape. What this means is that one of two things happens - you wait around forever for the guards to move in such a way that opens up an opportunity for you to sneak through, or, you get caught becuase all of the guards randomly converge on the exact place you are.

I want to write something about the Beginner's Guide. Something poetic, something brave, or clever, or emotional. I want to be angry, or judgemental, and I feel like these are things that I should feel. But I can't. This is the single hardest game that I have ever played. Maybe it's because I see myself in Coda. Or maybe I see myself in Davey. I can't get over the overwhelming feeling that I have played a game that was never meant to be played. At least not by me. This is actually art. I don't mean in the pretentious "Video games are art," way. This is the only game that, to me, actually conveyed emotion. I'm not really sure whose emotion, or what emotion is even being conveyed. I hate to sound like an English Literature teacher, but this game actually and deeply conveyed an indescribeably complex and dark part of the human expierence.
This game hurts.

The video/screenshots do not do it justice! This game is awesome. The gameplay above all is
. It's built in every way to be easy to start but hard to master. The Arrows are extremely well done. They go straight for the most part but will quickly fall after a little distance which allows it to be easy to hit most things but allows the expert player to use that quality to their advantage. Dodging has many uses, it's perfect for a double jump or a dash across a short gap and doubles as a way to catch arrows from the air and avoiding damage. Having to retrieve arrows is a great move in my opinion because often times just managing how to get them amid all the enemies takes the most skill.
The enemies are pretty smart. They all will attack as soon as they have the opportunity and many will dodge or block your arrows if you attempt to take an easy shot at them.
The screenshots are quite sad because they really don't showcase how beautiful this game really is! There is so much detail put into the different parts such as arrows catching on fire as they pass through torches, Dead enemies will often be stuck to walls with your arrows and will fall once you remove them. Also I'm a sucker for local co-op games because that's what I used to play as a kid.
Great noir brainteasing adventure! Sometimes lack of colour conveys atmosphere better than full-color Hollywood FX...

I would reccomend, as others in the reviews have been, that you ask someone else that has played if you would like it. I think it takes a certain type of person.
On a more critical note, I do agree with other reviews that it tends to be self indulgent, and might not quite have been worth the actual money just to listen to what some might conclude to be simply venting by the author. But, I don't want to say this. Because sometimes that's what you need. You need to vent, you need the attention, you need the validation. And certainly, I would say we all need the money. And this game hit in a spot near my heart that I can't help but support it. So I hope it's not just a money grab, intended to pull in profits from previous success. I really hope so. I'll try not to feel so cynical about it.

You are a woman - even if there are other secondary characters to play with during the game - you should inherit your aunt's art gallery works, but other art galleries take them from you and expose them, so you decide to steal them all to refill your gallery with what should be yours. I mean, you want to create an art gallery with stolen works, you can see how silly this idea is, but, well, the game want to set a nonsense spirit? I can be ok with it.
I could, at least, but everything else keep being silly and unsophisticated. In the game, you have to select a rival art gallery and raid it to steal everything inside it, in freaking full day,
. Every single gallery has two floors, you enter the first floor, empty it, take the elevetor to the second floor, empty it, and take the exit door on the back of the second floor: the most unrealistic art gallery architecture I can imagine, even I could think of one better. They decided for this silly one and used it for every single level of the game.
You steal things while visitors are loking at them, they are ok with it, but don't you dare to steal the masterpiece of the floor or they'll call the guards! All the rest isn't important, just take it, they don't care!
So, immagine this woman getting in an art gallery, buying a ticket, putthing on a mask, and start stealing things inside the place while people are looking at them, then take the exit with a cargo of stolen works of art in her arms. I mean, how immersive can this be?
Feminists seem to like this game because, you know, strong female protagonist! Yay! What I want to ask is: if everything this thief woman does in the game is silly and unrealistic, maybe this is how the developers see a female thief, silly and unrealistic. I don't know how much feminist this can be.
By the way, I think something about the gameplay has to be said:
.
For starters, it's a gameplay suited for a touchscreen device, and, I mean, this is not a plus. Everything is repetitive, you do the same two things over and over in the same environments, the only thing which spice it up is the guards placement. I really don't believe that a difficulty only created by a different placement of enemies can make a game fun.
Do you ever dream about going in an Art Gallery during opening hours stealing everything that's inside it? Too silly? Well you can do it in this game! Yay!

As I read about the game, the idea just got me. I'm kind of an outdoor person myself an enjoy hiking through the local woods at least twice per month.
When I played the game for the first time, it gave me the experience I had watching "Into the wild" for the first time. You really get the feeling of survival, despite the quite rough graphics in this alpha version (but that's why it's called early access).
## MYSTERY LAKE REVIEW ##
Unfortunatly, the survival experience gets a little bit to intense in my eyes.
Most of the time you are running around without orientation, find a hut or two containing about 20% of the equipment you would actually need to make it to the next day, and then die either from exhaustion or from being attacked by one of the many wolves wandering around everywhere.
This is of course just as realistic as surving after a plane crash in northern canadian winter would be, but on the other hand you are not able to craft stuff out of the items inside the huts (not even a mace from a chair to stand SOME chance against the wolves) or even wrap yourself up in the blankets from the beds inside the huts to prevent freezing to death outsinde while trying to forge some hardwood to keep your fire in the oven alive while resting a bit.
And thats the point - I payed 10 € for this game.
If I want to experience what it feels like to die alone in the nature, I would buy a bus ticket for 3 €, ride to the next forest and run around naked till I collapse.
IMHO, dying over and over again is not the point of playing a video game (except you're playing VVVVVV, but that's another story).
At this time, I cannot recommend the game as you end up wandering around frustrated - wondering behind which corner the deadly wolf attack will lure this time - way to soon.
Hopefully they'll get it fixed in the story mode of the final version - if we'll ever come to see the final version as the game seems to be in alpha state for two years now...
## COSTAL HIGHWAY REVIEW ##
After spending almost three hours playing the *Mystery Lake* Sandbox-Level, I just wanted to try out the *Costal Highway* Level before I was about to uninstall the game.
I just played the game for five minutes, ran down the first hill, enterd the first house and found more stuff inside than I managed to aquire in all the attempts that I took on Mystery Lake.
Seriously, WTF? This is kind of the definition of imbalanced level architecture...
Dear developers, would you PLEASE be so kind and add a brief notice at the start screen that tells TLD-inexperienced players to best start with the *Costal Highway* Area? That would be great. -_-
