Smaller things like mouths not moving during cutscenes - although this is likely a key design choice which I understand and respect, although it gives off that older style of genre that doesn't seem to fit.
Very straight forward story as to why you're collecting stuff in the first place creating for a stale and dull game play, meaning I'm not given a reason to be attached to the character's story at all.
The game's controls are very wonky and feel out of place. It's almost like I'm playing an older game from the ps1 era with how jank the camera work is. Alongside very clunky fighting mechanics and almost "brain-dead" like game play for the first 30ish minutes.
There was no reason for me to continue playing after the "tutorial". There's no indicator as to whether or not I can do X or Y actions at the start of the game. I'm just put into the game. The only bit of a tutorial you're given is that you can double jump if you decide to talk to an NPC early on. On top of the clunky controls you're thrown into the game and baby sat without being told how to actually play.
As far as progress in the game goes it's very straight forward and simple. It was probably intended for younger audiences unfortunately it has an issue of not having a straight path from Point A to Point B. It seems very easy to get lost in this game and be overwhelmed, almost like a free roam Wind Waker with broader, more expansive and more fleshed out map design.
The map design seems fantastic, unfortunately it feels out of place as stated above. You're given little direction as to where to go, even cutscenes don't aid you that well.
For being given 1/3 of a million backed up on this game it's team did put hard effort into this game I'm sure, unfortunately it lacks a lot of elements and contains a lot of issues that make me not want to play this game - even after backing it since day 1.
I'd rate the game (30 minutes worth I guess?) a 2/10.
Another major turn-off was the price to game ratio. $30 game that I expected to be around $15-20 due to the length and how much effort was put into it as a kickstarter project.

I picked this up in a Humble Bundle and decided to mess around with the program to see what options are available. Turns out it's pretty easy to make a functional game, so I quickly became a lot more immersed in RPG Maker and bringing a world to life.
The learning curve isn't all that steep and there are a LOT of resources online if you need help - forum posts, blog posts, youtube tutorials, etc. RPG Maker is easy to use but the program doesn't give you quite as many options as you might want. This is unfortunate but most issues can be gotten around by adding custom scripts to modify how your game works. It's fairly easy to find something you'd like and adding scripts is incredibly easy.
It may seem a contradiction in terms, but RPG Maker VX Ace is both limited and versatile. It's still a very good program though - maybe not for full price, I'm not sure on that - but if you've ever wanted to make an old-school JRPG then this program will do that for you. You can crank out a workable game in a day or two, but for something good it will take a long time. That's pretty much expected though, considering you're making a game. More effort = better product.

The feel of real survival game I missed from WC3 maps, specifically Wilderness Survival. A godsend for open-world survival genre being saturated with zombies. It's you against nature, minus the other crap. As this is still in early access, I expect more features in the already good game.
+ Fun survival sandbox, without zombies.
+ Lots of areas to scavenge.
+ Awesome environment
- There's nothing much to do in the later part of the game( 20+ days) but sleep, gather meat and eat & drink. Well, there's the occasional gather wood and tinder to melt some ice for water but that's it.
- Knowing the temperature accurately without some sort of aid is like having a built-in geiger counter in your brain. You could at least make it somewhat general perception of weather (warm, cold, colder, freezing) and/or make a thermometer lootable.
-At day 40, I'm almost bare naked. A blizzard tore most of my clothes off.I am left with nothing. The game could make use of surprise events (random heli crash/supply drop) to counterbalance the game's crescendo.
Overall, I can recommend this game to everyone I know. A little tweaking will make the game the best open-world survival game on Steam.

Want to play Dungeon Defenders 2? I hope you aren't in a hurry. Actually getting on to the server is like gambling.  You feel that high each time you roll the proverbial dice to log in and then your heart breaks when you get that blasted error message again.  Want to play in a private Tavern with friends? Be prepared to wait even longer. If you're patient enough to try, try, try again what you'll experience is an okay game that leaves you wanting to replay Dungeon Defenders 1.
Tho Good:
Manna collection and item pick up are now more convenient.
New bad guys are different and imaginatively reminiscent of DD1.
The Bad:
Gameplay in general feels less fleshed out than the first game.  There doesn't seem to be as much of a strategic element to tower placement.  Place the towers wherever you want, make sure you have a DPS character, and shoot everything until you're bored.
Costumes and character customization are non existent unless you want to pay a ridiculous amount of gems (i.e., real money). Then again, the game is free to play, so I suppose that sort of nonsense is to be expected.
To sum up: My friends and I enjoyed it for a weekend, and it was free. For me, I can't say the game has replayability.  When we finished I was left feeling “meh.” Glad I didn't pay anything for it. If you liked DD1, give DD2 a shot. Just don't expect to be as enthralled as you were with the original Dungeon Defenders.

Gameplay is just what I was looking for, tense and can be a real challenge depending on where the game plops you down to start. I have done well at times, others not so great. My best record so far is right at 5 days. I always slip up at some point and become wolf bait.
The wolves are your biggest fear next to providing for yourself. You can't be too certain just where they will show up and it makes you hesitant to lollygag around, as it should.
One thing I would like to see added is the ability to find a basic club or sturdy stick to defend yourself early on. Even as a kid this is the first thing I would think of if I felt threatened; you need something other than your hands to defend yourself against sharp teeth. Other than that there are not too many things that stick out as a problem.
Might be nice if wolves close to the building you are inside at the moment would make a certain amount of noise so you have a chance of detecting their presence before blindly going out to your death.
Having a blast with TLD and have already reeled in one friend so far based on my recommendation.

Also some of the things that made the first game incredible are not to be found in this second edition. For example I LOVED how versatile Huntress weapons were. Some projectiles pierced, some shot webs, some shot bombs, etc... That versatility is completely gone now. Even though some weapons have different projectiles and shooting speeds, every weapon virtually feels the same. Also the way leveling is atm is way too grindy. The grind to max level will take you longer than the grind for good gear at max level.
In conclusion, it's a great game so far (it's not completely finished yet), but don't expect it to be miles ahead of its predecessor.

Secret Of Magia is an action RPG with a hack and slash combat system and approximately 3 hours worth of gameplay.
The world map contains a sequence of areas which lead away from your home town, with enemies becoming more difficult, the further you go. Levelling up is pointless as enemies level up with you, but the further flung enemies have fancier moves that make them more formidable. The map is open world, and you can easily retrace your steps.
The main mission consists of capturing the souls of four different bosses, then defeating the final boss. To get to each of the bosses, you must enter a cave, then find and defeat a powerful enemy which holds a key to the door where the boss is found. Defeating that boss will reveal its soul.
There are several areas and towns to explore, and a handful of quests to complete. There is enough content here that it's possible to make it through the first two hours, without ever realizing that you've overlooked the main mission.
As for the main mission, it is not well explained at all, being only vaguely hinted at by some of the NPCs. The only way you'd know what to look for, is if you read up on the game beforehand, or stumble across the key by randomly killing the enemy that drops it.
The story is virtually non-existent, as the side quests are given in the most blunt way possible, and the ending is equally lacking in fanfare.
There is extensive customization of your character in terms of class, equipment, magic, and craftable items; however, this is largely wasted, because most of it is unnecessary to beat the game, and you can easily earn enough gold through combat to buy the strongest equipment in the shop, and more potions than you'll ever need.
This game has a little bit of action and a little bit of adventure, but probably not enough of either one individually to satisfy its prospective fans. The hack and slash gameplay might prove too easy for its hardcare fans, while for adventure RPG enthusiasts, the story is somewhat lacking. There are five achievements, however, which are relatively easy to accomplish, if you prefer something more basic.

There have been a few indie beat'em ups that came out lately that came so close to being good but tripped at the finish line: Mother Russia Bleeds and 99 Vidas come to mind. These two I didn't feel made the cut because of aggrivating stage design along with too many annoying enemies to fight. They both like to overwhelm the players with so many enemies that they fill the screen if you choose to play the games with 3 friends. Add to the fact that there isn't an icon showing where the players are, it's easy to lose yourself in the on-screen mob. You get a sense that the developers thought "Hey, classic beat'em ups were coin eaters so our game should be just like that in terms of difficulty". Meanwhile the really memorable ones like Final Fight 3 and Streets of Rage 2 had you on fair grounds with your enemies.The playable characters in those two games are way too samey as well. Little to nothing in terms of mechanics that separate the playable characters and just end up feeling like palette swaps.
All these problems I had with those games aren't present here. Fight'n Rage's developer seems to really understand what makes a great and fun beat'em up, something that's easily lost on others. You get 3 characters to use in the story mode and they feel very different from one another to play as. Each having their strengths and weaknesses in more aspects than something shallow like one being stronger and one being faster (ala Mother Russia Bleeds). They have unique combos and unique ways to perform combos as well as their own special attacks.
If you choose to play the game with 2 friends, the game won't try to just fill the screen with monsters in a futile attempt to balance the difficulty. There are a few more enemies but at a moderate degree so it's not unreasonable. The game compliments multiplayer as you can help each other extend combos which is incredibly satisfying as you're all making enemies explode into piles of bones.
The stage design is pretty to look at and very rarely incorporstes an annoying gimmick to insert a "challenge". 99 Vidas and MRB liked to do this a lot and those games suffered for it. Only one small sequence comes to mind that was bothersome, which was the bit on the raft. But it doesn't last very long so it didn't sour my enjoyment of the game.
Something I was exceedingly thankful for was that boss fights were done well. 99Vidas had terrible boss fights that forced you to fight them a specifically limiting way or you had to throw your extra lives at them because they have no hit-stun and attack frequently. MRB had gimmicky fights that also forced you to play in a limiting fashion. In Fight'n Rage you are welcome to combo the hell out the bosses and most allow you to grapple and throw them for added enjoyment.
The only criticism I and my friends have about the game is that you aren't able to use unlockable characters in story mode; they're only for use in the battle arena mode. We really wanted to go through the game as the Doberman, Muay Thai Birds, and the Bruce Lee monkeys. Hopefully an update will allow this to happen in the future. One other criticism is that there's no online play at the moment but I'm glad the developer spent the majority of his time making sure the core game was complete and well made first-and-foremost.
There are multiple endings in the game that depend on which path you take, which character you select, and which combination of characters are present during co-op. So at the price of $20, there is plenty of conent to unlock and enjoy for this great game

Fight'N Rage is incredible. For a one man shop, this game is absolutely amazing. One of the mechanically strongest arcade style beat-em-ups out there.
But I hate its guts for two simple reasons: It runs way too long and it's too damn draining to play. A clear demands at least an hour in a single sitting, no saves. And the game drags that out with endless enemy waves at the end that goes well beyond "YES! A TEST OF MY SKILLS!" and into "Oh great not this bull$#!@ again!"
And Fight N Rage WANTS to kill you, too. The game is balanced to make completing a run successfully hard, even with infinite continues (That restart the zone and then the stage on higher difficulties.) So it's tough, which is good... usually... except here it's an hour long run and all the game has to do is knock you in the water or sneak one BS attack through a hitbox it should not have been able to penetrate and you can lose an incredibly rare life and sink your run 30 minutes later.
I realize all of this is pronounced in damn near every other arcade beat-em-up, but the screws in FnR are tightened so tight that all of this comes to the front. So I end up hating a game that is mechanically and graphically outstanding in every way because I end up furious at the game every time I play it. SoRR has nearly the exact same pacing issues (As it should, FnR is a love letter to SoR2 in many ways.), but it gets around this with saves, with 8 difficulties, and you pretty quickly raise the funds for stage select so if your run bombs out you can just stage select to practice or cheat your way to see the end. FnR doesn't have any of this, sadly, and runs afoul of problems we were able to ignore in earlier beat-em-ups but can't here by being a more hardcore product.

This game is a very pleasant surprise!  I decided to try it on a whim since I have not really played a good beat em' up since Castle Crashers and Dungeon Fighter.
This feels very good to play, hits have impact, there are zoom-in and explosion effects during big combos, and backgrounds and characters are quite colorful with smooth animation throughout.  To think this was made by only two people is really impressive.
Fighting has depth, with an excellent combo and parry system that is reminiscent of a 2D fighting game like Street Fighter (Which is referenced a few times throughout the game).  Good crowd control and use of your entire arsenal is needed, as the game is quite challenging.  I beat it on Normal but it took some effort.  There are many unlockables, branching paths, and endings, enough to keep you busy for quite a long time.
Originally, I was offput by 20 dollars for a beat em' up, but after playing it feel the cost is justified.  Highly recommended to all beat em' up fans.  Tip for the developer:  Advertise where you can and get the word out about this fantastic game!

I rate this 7 of 10. This is initially a very good game with great stealth mechanics that, after its first half, actually feels too long and becomes a chore if you want to complete it. The global achievement stats are a testament to that,
(normal "story mode" completion, not with all the extra stuff you can do in the game). That compares to
, which is not a trivial one. All this is almost one year after its release. Many people seem to like the game (for good reasons) and play it to a considerable extent, but only very few finish it. (The phenomenon is ofcourse natural and can be seen with other games, too, but much weaker. This game makes most people give up on it, much more than other games.)
Also I don't like how the game never stays at a smooth frame rate (probably for everyone, check the forums), even though I'm far above the system requirements. I'll have to assume this is due to bad programming and misuse of middleware. When you're running on too many layers of software, performance and timing problems are likely to happen. The slight stuttering doesn't ruin the game though.
Finishing with the positive things, this game has nice stylish graphics, and great music that fits the style. And the gameplay is really nice, the stealth mechanics are well done and you are never unclear about what's going on and why a guard has "caught your scent". The difficulty ramps up smoothly, so the point where it starts to become tedious will depend on your tolerance and skill. But that point will come for most people, so know what you're getting into.

Miss Take is a stealth game whereby you play one of 3 characters attempting to complete one of the 25 missions.  You play from an isometric-ish standpoint and must sneak around the levels and steal stuff. While each character share the same levels as the others, the levels for each character have different layouts and challanges and merit playing as each characters.
PROS:
- Amazing art style. Really, really great.
- Great sense of difficulty. It is never too easy or throw-your-controller difficult.
- All 3 characters have their own play styles.
------Take is the "normal" character and must steal around 12 paintings/objects per floor.
------Hector cant run and has a ball used to bounce off walls to distract guards and dogs, but he must get it back.
------The third charcter must pickpocket guards to get keys to open safes (which WILL cause an alarm).
- Each mission has multiple floors per building.
- A good amount of missions.
Cons
- It is minor, but the menus are confusing as to what option you are actually choosing if using a controller.
- Unlike Volume's 100+ levels along with an editor, this only has 25 missions x 3 charcters. Not really complaining though.
All in all a fantastic stealth game. Plays best with a controller i found.

I look forward to getting frustrated as hell at the next Zachtronics game I pick up!

Unreal Tournament is a game that people play. People generally enjoy playing this game, this game named Unreal Tournament. Out of the set of all people, this tiny subset called me is going to review the game. Are you ready for this subset? I hope you are.
OK. So, this game is like a really good spiritual successor to Combat for Atari. But imagine instead of random pixels, you had people with guns. Now imagine it's not just a 1 and 1 and it's like a whole bunch of people together, running, running around the room.
Imagine bullets flying and you have to dodge them. Then imagine sometimes not dodging them and then that's when you die.
I bought this game twice. Once when it was the jam (1999), and once when it wasn't the jam (Steam). If you really think about it though, both purchases cover the two states of jamming, both jamming and not jamming.
Please note, that there are better Arena shooters (for example, Rush 2: Extreme Racing USA), however this one holds a special place in my heart as being the arena shooter that really got the "feel" of what is now known as ":unts: :unts:" music, what we now know as Steve Aoki.
There is some talk about a new Unreal Tournament coming out that is crowd funded, but I think Shovel Knight took all the crowds money so everyone's poor now, so you might want to start coding your own. Alternatively, you could just put on "groove is in the heart" and shoot nerf darts at your friends. It's up to you. It's your money.

My jaw dropped when I saw a Tales game, and for PC no less!
If you've played any other bandai tales games and enjoyed them, you're in for a treat with this one. Same innovation, memorable characters, interaction, and action based RPG combat (lotta button mashing but there is strategy and it's fun!)
If you haven't played the Tales series, it's a hard explanation of what to expect but in short form:
- Anime characters (duh you saw the pictures above..)
- Voiced character dialogs
- Plays perfectly with an xbox 360 controller and has native support like most new games (e.g - it tells you hit "Y" in yellow instead of JoyButton4 or something.
- Good music
- Cutscenes
- Engaging storyline with a lot of character development, each character feels dynamic and they have specific interactions with each other throughout the game, which develops a better sense of who you are and who your party members are.
- Unique combat system compared to other RPGs, it's fun too unless you don't have a controller or have a bad hand or something.
- Combining equipment to upgrade it to a stronger version.
- Achievement system
- Skills level based on your decisions, train in a specific direction for a certain set of skills, replay the game and train in a different direction for another style (common in the tales series, adds replay value.)
By far one of the most under-rated RPG franchises, probably because they were spotty with releasing their games on specific consoles in the past. I really hope they remake more of them for the PC, as they're doing with Symphonia (included with this purchase) in 2016.

This game is a love letter to all the great 3D platformers of the past. Here you'll find a mish-mash of ideas found in games like Super Mario 64/Sunshine/Galaxy, Banjo-Kazooie, and Sonic Adventure. The protagonist's movement and combat techniques take a little getting used to, but once you do, you'll see how they each complement each other leading to a very fluid player experience. Each world has lots of things to collect, and as you beat each chapter, even more items to collect appear, giving you yet another reason to revisit a world. Customization options are rewaded to real treasure hunters and explorers alike. Did I forget to mention how cute the protag Hat Kid is? Because she is. A few cons for this game are the lack of a cohesive art direction; the enemies seem to have not as much thought put into them as the protag, lots of flat textures, and less than stellar voice acting. But don't let any of that stop you from playing one of the few kickstarted games that actually live up to and exceed expectations. Buy A Hat in Time!

I should start by saying that I've really only played around with the software. I've never completed a project or done anything too complicated. I have this recurring desire to make an rpg, but I don't have the stomach for really doing it. And it is in that way I recommend RPG Maker VX Ace. There is something so intuitive and comfortable about working with it. Even doing more complex eventing is actually enjoyable. I haven't touched scripting yet, but will probably, because the rest of my experience has been rather pleasant and I hit limits even with my light use. If the feature you are thinking of including is not in an SNES-era rpg, then you would hit that wall as well. It is very specific. But for years I have looked for other options to scratch that nagging make a game itch, and never used anything that is as easy to get into. Unity, the open source rpg makers, the modding tools for Torchlight and Driftmoon and Neverwinter Nights 2, the ToME engine, all of them turn me off due to the intital learning curve and lack of the same immediate gratification I get from this. Now to make a game, or even to do serious fiddling, RPG Maker VX Ace may not be ideal, I would imagine, and for people who are serious about game development, learning code or working with a more robust engine is probably the way to go. But to fool around and see your idea take shape without tremendous investment, this is the best tool I've picked up. In addition, there is a huge community and some of it's members seem very serious about the software. There are a ton of resources, tutorials, scripts, and support, so if you do want to try something more advanced with RPG Maker, you would be able to find answers to questions fairly easily. It is a bit pricey, but it's on Steam, so it will go on sale periodically. I picked it up at 66% off, I think. Have gotten my money's worth and then some.

At the top: the single greatest problem with giving random gamers an anonymous platform upon which to speak to an audience of real human beings is that the worst of humanity will be more than inclined to take advantage of it. If you are easily offended by racism, sexism, xenophobia, transphobia, or the exploitation of appalling tragedy for its own sake, this game is NOT for you. If you are not a cisgendered male and are made very uncomfortable by strangers asking to expose your naked body or belittling you on the basis of your gender identity in general, this game is NOT for you. In fact, ANYONE who has substantial faith in humanity’s overall goodness would do well to avoid this game.
The unfortunate fact about Comedy Night is that, more often than not, the things you will be exposed to will not even resemble comedy. Quite the opposite — for every player you encounter who has any interest in entertaining you, there will
be at least a dozen misguided sociopaths who will derive sick pleasure in making you feel angry, uncomfortable, bored, abused, or any combination of the four. Use of the N-word and many other slurs is despicably common, particularly in asinine contexts that don’t even bother with the pretense of comedy. Just as often, their use takes the form of a player taking the stage, yelling a slur, and then getting off stage. Micspam is rampant and sometimes extreme. And, since players in the audience have the ability to broadcast their voice while another player is on stage, you run a substantial risk of being drowned out by racists or various other lunatics if you take the stage. Although each lobby has an admin who has the ability to kick and ban players, many of them are uninterested in discouraging trolling, or are trolls themselves.
And yet, despite all the grating micspam, misapplied racial “humor,” and sickening reliance on dead memes and hackneyed  clichés (i.e. ground beef), there are still funny people and well-administrated rooms to be found. And when you do find one, you may very well have an excellent time making good-hearted people laugh and being made to laugh by such people. Every so often, you’ll come across players who are legitimately hilarious — I would be unsurprised to learn that there are professional comedians who sometimes queue up Comedy Night on their Steam account. To my mind, these positive experiences easily overcome the gargantuan roadblock of finding a needle of comedy in a haystack or poorly raised preteen boys.
In essence, Comedy Night is not just a silly experiment in multiplayer game design, even though I suspect that such a thing is exactly what the developers had in mind. But even if they did set out to design a game with the intention of making a virtual /b/ in the Unity engine, they have managed to create a fascinating microcosm of the gaming community’s sense of humor. Any reasonable person knows that gaming has serious problems with a lack of tolerance and inclusivity, but the same person knows that there is a black sheep in every flock — in this case, a cool person who tells funny jokes and makes everyone laugh, even if those laughing are the brunt of a joke.
Now, if this game was a $60 major release from a major publisher, not only would I not recommend it, but I would personally pray that whomever greenlighted it would know nothing but suffering and poverty for the rest of their days. Although this is a silly little Unity game made by a small team of clever nutcases, and there are more than enough laughs and good times to be had to justify the relatively tiny price tag. Again, if you are easily offended or otherwise made furious by ignorant, unenlightened lunatics whom you cannot hold accountable at all, then this game, even more than most other games populated by such maniacs with a microphone, is one to avoid. But if you’re willing to sift through the mania a bit, I can almost guarantee that you’ll enjoy yourself.

I asked several people whom had played Tales Of games, and asked them if they were any good. I received the response that if I had /not/ already played a Tales Of game, I should bash my own head in, and then play a Tales Of game.
So I bought Tales of Zestiria, the vibrantly livid JRPG. And oh, how I mean 'vibrant'. Everything's so damn colorful, you can be forgiven easily for wandering around just to look at the shading on the rocks. Even the gloomy dungeons take you out on the finest date to skull♥♥♥♥ you with its art. So yes, it's very visual. The saving factor from all this being a meaningless gesture is how much of it you can interact with. Most of the skybox is like OoT, where all the massive artworks in the back are used as indicators for landmarks and places you can visit. So it goes as said that the art is indeed functional and appealing.
Combat is fairly interesting, if slightly cluttered as can be from having four heroes, six enemies jumping around casting hidden artes. It's real time, so at no point do you have to stand still and let an enemy take their turn doing a jig on your face, which is rather nice. It offers combos, damage scaling in terms of how much SC you and your enemy have, combo damage, so it really lets you optomize combat, provided you can see what you're doing.
Ready to talk cutscenes? No? Too ♥♥♥♥ing bad, kiddo. They're goddamn everywhere. You'll sit through a cutscene to take five steps into another, longer cutscene! That's not an exaggeration, it's hell.
Voice acting is done alright. Character model work while trying to mimic the voice acting, however, is a smelly poo. If you watch lips while words come out, the only face you'll be making is one of general confusion and/or disgust.
The characters all fit into their niche, each given enough time to show off what they're about and portray it without being terribly hamfisted. Unique looks easily distinguish which is which, and customization, while further distinct, is silly.
In conclusion? If you have /not/ played a Tales Of game, allow me to polietly tell you to bash your head in with a cutscene, and then play this game.
Oh, and hard mode will dunk on you if you don't use the exp boost. I mean, cheat.

Music is excellent.  I'm don't really care for music in video games, but the soundtrack in this game sticks out a lot to me in a good way.  It has the "pumped up" feeling which makes you want to go berserk and destroy everything in the game.

Definitely do put it at the top of your wishlist and wait for a sale, you really do not want to miss out on this game.

This is one of those games I wish I had read the reviews a bit more thoroughly. Banished was exactly what it promised to be, once I had paid attention to what it was really supposed to be. I actually found this to be nice though, as a lot of times "city-builders" don't really require much thought in strategy form. The game is very good and well worth the money once you get past the learning curve. Go ahead and pick it up if your into city-builders, or even standard rts games. You'll be happy you gave it a shot.

For an Early Access Game, this game shows some promise. An interesting take on survival games, no zombies or really life of any kind. Just you vs nature. Story mode (as of this review) is not yet active, but just the basic sandbox is pretty fun. You spawn in a random location on a map (which is static and not randomly generated) and must fight against nature to survive. Wolves roam the countryside and to date I have only barely survived one attack (with the help of my trusty crowbar...) and they should be avoided at all cost. Otherwise cross your fingers -> smash your LMB till the bar fills up, and then press RMB and hope for the best. This was really confusing to me, especially when a wolf is eatting your face...
Game mechanics are pretty simple, find food/water, shelter and warmth. There seems to be some hunter aspects to the game such as fishing, setting snares for rabbits or hunting deer, however I have yet to acquire all the necessary items to do any of the above before death...  On that note, game mechanics are rather final. If you die, you're dead - game over. There are saves/loads, but only if you're still alive upon exiting the game. If you die, the save game deletes itself and you're back at square one. While some might dislike this aspect of the game, I think it furthers the games plot of a survival game - there are no "undos" in real life.
Graphics are kind of borderland-ish, that realistic mixed with cartoony. Weather adds an interesting aspects to both visuals and survival. I've been stranded out on a lake in a complete whiteout, just stumbling around hoping to find something to take shelter in.
It will be interesting to see where this all ends up. I'd recommend grabbing it before it exists "early access" status.

I bought this game within minutes of it coming available, but I wanted to wait until I got a good gist of the game before I put out a review. Hopefully this will help you make the decision if this game is for you or not.
First off, a little about me, because it's very important as to why I picked this game up after only becoming aware of it the day prior to it's release, and why I did so for the $20 price tag, which seemed to have generated a little negative buzz from people who thought $10 was a better price. I'm 31 years old. I was born the year Super Mario Bros. was released, and I grew up with classic 80s leftovers and early 90s 2D pixel hits. I remember playing Final Fight 2 and especially Final Fight 3 on my SNES, and playing Streets of Rage 2 on the Genesis that belonged to the kid across the street.
Two days prior to my writing this review, I was randomly searching upcoming titles, just to see if there were any gems that weren't given much hype. This game popped up. I looked at the graphics, I looked at the gameplay and I watched a little video on it, and immediately placed it on my wishlist. Why? Because this game looked like it was an homage, or the torch bearer of these old pixelated beat em up classics. So when the game dropped for $20, I bought it - without hesitation - as soon as Steam sent me the alert. And you know what? I was exactly right about this game.
From the introduction, I knew this would be a love letter to games I played in my youth. The game opens with the filter set to imitate a tube television already on (scanlines included), and you're treated to some "technical text" overlaying a black background. Anyone who waited for the local arcade to turn on the machines in the morning will recognize this instantly as the old arcade startup screen, specifically the one used in Capcom games.
From that point on, you are treated to a game that has so many homage or inside joke references to older beat em up and fighting games of this era that you can't help but feel the nostalgia dripping off the screen - provided, of course, that you ARE nostalgic for that period of gaming. There are honestly so many "old school references" that I can't remember them all to put down. Firstly, the name of the game - "Fight'N Rage." While not confirmed, it wouldn't surprise me if the developer deliberately crunched the titles Streets of Rage and Final Fight together to come up with this one. The primary character, Gal, has a name that is deliberately a nod toward Guy from Final Fight. Gal's walk animation is nearly identical to the stiff walk that both Guy and SOR's Axel have. Your first boss is an enemy dressed like M. Bison from Street Fighter, who also happens to have the iconic slide move Bison has retained all these years, and his animation frame while doing it identically copies Bison's frame from Street Fighter II. The list goes on and on, and it's best not to spoil everything here. It's strongly recommended you save any other old school references for your playthrough of the game.
So while this game IS in many ways a torch bearer for the old beat em ups, it does have it's own improvements over these older games. Obviously, controls are far superior, as are the animations of the characters. As with the old beat em ups, your character has a special move (multiple ones, actually), and like the older games of this genre, performing it will decrease some of your health. These moves have always been crowd clearers and escape effort attacks, and beings as they are stronger than standard attacks, the loss of health is justified, lest everyone just mash the attack through the whole game without penalty (Axel's "Bare Knuckle" in SOR2 is a good example of this). However, Fight'N Rage offers a decent balance - your character has an additional meter that fills up automatically over time. Once this meter is filled, your special attack is consequence-free. You will not lose health by performing it. Important to note, this meter is NOT a slow meter. It doesn't fill up exceptionally fast, nor is it a slow turtle. It's got a really good balance that means you'll see specials often in a level, but not so much that enemies can't touch you. This whole setup is great, as performing these specials not only help in garnering some breathing room or taking down enemies, but also in "destroying" an enemy, netting you additional points as their body explodes into bones. Points are crucial, as you gain a life for every X amount of points.
That is not uncommon in beat em ups, but the points are more crucial with this game, as it does tend to be on the harder side, and lives do not come easily. The difficulty is something that has garnered criticism for this game. Yes, it is difficult, but when you consider just how closely this is linked to the old beat em ups of yesteryear, it shouldn't be much of a surprise. This game is built like an arcade game set to free play. It's not the easiest walk in the park, and the game doesn't hold your hand for long. Still, I don't think it's the hardest thing out there. In truthfulness, I have yet to beat the game, but I have reached the final boss, and simply lost because of a numbers game with near zero life. Thing is, I KNOW where my dilemma is - it lies with a certain fight right before the final room - and so I know that I have to learn how to counter this enemy in order to save health for the finale. I don't in any way feel stuck, and know it won't be long before I DO beat the final boss. (To give you an idea, my first playthrough only lasted through the first stage of the second level, and in my death, I barely racked up enough points to hit 70 coins [more on coins in a moment]. 3 playthroughs later and I can get to the final stage on the same "quarter" I started with)
Despite the difficulty, this game is incredibly accessible. It has enough to it to learn the game and get the gist of it quickly without feeling overwhelmed. I will give an example: as much as I love River City Ransom, and the modernized sequel available on Steam, these games can be far less accessible. RCR has a number of RPG elements to it, and don't me wrong - that's fine; I love River City Ransom - but this means to start out, these games require more effort into getting acustom to everything. River City Ransom: Underground is even moreso like this. Again, that's not to say the game isn't good - it IS a lot of fun, from what I've played of it - but this is the reason why, despite have RCR:U for months now, I've already invested more time in Fight'N Rage. It's ease of gameplay is reminiscent to Streets of Rage, Final Fight, Double Dragon, etc., and it makes this game a classic "pick up and play." For someone like myself, sporting a 9 to 5 office job and a family to boot, I don't have as much time to play games, so I'm going to gravitate toward something I can get right into.
The game features in-game currency, which you receive by automatically trading in your points every time you die or beat the game. There is a lot to unlock here, including enemies that can be used in a versus battle mode, and alternate costumes [primarily color designs] for the three main characters. I think this certainly increases the replayability of the title.
There are 7 or 8 stages to this game, depending on the various paths you take (multiple paths, another plus), and I would say the length of a playthrough is about the same, maybe a little longer than the old school beat em ups. In other words, this is a game beatable in one sitting that won't make you feel like your entire day is gone afterward, which is important considering there's no sort of "save now, play later" feature.
Final note, Gal and practically all the women in this game are nice eye candy, even if they are sprites, meaning this game gives you cheesecake to factor in as well, if that rocks your boat.
Overall, if you like 90s nostalgia and a game that sits on the more challenging side, PICK THIS UP. NOW.

What initially drew me to this game was its overall style. After all, the main character wears a hat so cool that you literally can't complete levels without it. But what kept me playing it, all the way to the point of 100% achievements, was the gameplay. For the most part, the levels are designed really well, and the game's use of shadows to display when you are and aren't in an enemy's line of sight is both cool and instantly-understandable. The three playable characters each have their own unique feel to them, and the fact that each one steals a different set of loot really makes you feel like you've cleaned a level out completely once you've beaten it with all three.
Overall I really liked this game! It had a good amount of content, and the story is a great example of something that's kid-friendly without feeling childish (which matters a lot to some people and can be very hard to do). If you're in the mood for a light stealth game, check it out.

At the top: the single greatest problem with giving random gamers an anonymous platform upon which to speak to an audience of real human beings is that the worst of humanity will be more than inclined to take advantage of it. If you are easily offended by racism, sexism, xenophobia, transphobia, or the exploitation of appalling tragedy for its own sake, this game is NOT for you. If you are not a cisgendered male and are made very uncomfortable by strangers asking to expose your naked body or belittling you on the basis of your gender identity in general, this game is NOT for you. In fact, ANYONE who has substantial faith in humanity’s overall goodness would do well to avoid this game.
The unfortunate fact about Comedy Night is that, more often than not, the things you will be exposed to will not even resemble comedy. Quite the opposite — for every player you encounter who has any interest in entertaining you, there will
be at least a dozen misguided sociopaths who will derive sick pleasure in making you feel angry, uncomfortable, bored, abused, or any combination of the four. Use of the N-word and many other slurs is despicably common, particularly in asinine contexts that don’t even bother with the pretense of comedy. Just as often, their use takes the form of a player taking the stage, yelling a slur, and then getting off stage. Micspam is rampant and sometimes extreme. And, since players in the audience have the ability to broadcast their voice while another player is on stage, you run a substantial risk of being drowned out by racists or various other lunatics if you take the stage. Although each lobby has an admin who has the ability to kick and ban players, many of them are uninterested in discouraging trolling, or are trolls themselves.
And yet, despite all the grating micspam, misapplied racial “humor,” and sickening reliance on dead memes and hackneyed  clichés (i.e. ground beef), there are still funny people and well-administrated rooms to be found. And when you do find one, you may very well have an excellent time making good-hearted people laugh and being made to laugh by such people. Every so often, you’ll come across players who are legitimately hilarious — I would be unsurprised to learn that there are professional comedians who sometimes queue up Comedy Night on their Steam account. To my mind, these positive experiences easily overcome the gargantuan roadblock of finding a needle of comedy in a haystack or poorly raised preteen boys.
In essence, Comedy Night is not just a silly experiment in multiplayer game design, even though I suspect that such a thing is exactly what the developers had in mind. But even if they did set out to design a game with the intention of making a virtual /b/ in the Unity engine, they have managed to create a fascinating microcosm of the gaming community’s sense of humor. Any reasonable person knows that gaming has serious problems with a lack of tolerance and inclusivity, but the same person knows that there is a black sheep in every flock — in this case, a cool person who tells funny jokes and makes everyone laugh, even if those laughing are the brunt of a joke.
Now, if this game was a $60 major release from a major publisher, not only would I not recommend it, but I would personally pray that whomever greenlighted it would know nothing but suffering and poverty for the rest of their days. Although this is a silly little Unity game made by a small team of clever nutcases, and there are more than enough laughs and good times to be had to justify the relatively tiny price tag. Again, if you are easily offended or otherwise made furious by ignorant, unenlightened lunatics whom you cannot hold accountable at all, then this game, even more than most other games populated by such maniacs with a microphone, is one to avoid. But if you’re willing to sift through the mania a bit, I can almost guarantee that you’ll enjoy yourself.

Only 3 hours in and I am hooked already. If you've never played a Tales game before and are an RPG fan, you owe it to yourself to pickup one of the best RPG series you've probably never heard of. The Tales Of games are a series similar to Final Fantasy but have never reached the same level of acclaim due to many of the games not being localized in English or only being released for specific consoles. Despite that, the Tales Of series has been going strong since the SNES days and is one of the greatest RPG series of all time. Combine the action-oriented combat with deep character customization, great narrative and plot, and for the first time ever, branching storylines with choices that impact the game as you play along.
If you are a Tales fan, you are about to experience one of the best games in the series. I have not beaten the game, and as I said am only 3 hours in, but I will update this review as I progress. But I can already tell this is THE defining game in the series. Want the best of Tales of Graces without the quirky combat, the cool and memorable deep characters from Xillia, the unique story of Phantasia, the epic feeling of Symphonia, and the awesome graphics of Vespiria all in one game? That's what I'm getting from Tales of Zesteria, and at only 3 hours in. There is so much depth to the battle mechanics, titles, equipment, collectibles, skits and more.
You need to play this game. Technical issues will be ironed out, this is the first PC Tales game... EVER. So they are surely developing on a new platform they haven't worked with before. Please support the game and encourage this great series to cater to PC gamers in the future.

Fight'N Rage is a rare example of a retro-styled game that knows what made the games of the time it's emulating so memorable, while also innovating and adapting to the games that have come since. As soon as you boot it, you're taken to a different time in gaming history -- in the good way -- and put into the mood to put your boot to the opposition.
Good thing, then, that the gameplay that follows is satisfying, challenging, and delightfully brutal, and while the characters' movesets are a bit simple, if still more robust than most such games, the ability to string damn near any attack into another onto a reeling enemy provides an additional layer of skill, incentivizing you to use your toolset to produce spectacular results. Even with the assortment of palette-swapped enemies typical of this genre coming at you in waves, you're constantly trying to maintain impressive juggles with your hapless opponents and keep your combo count up, offsetting potential monotony and giving way instead to white-knuckle, palm-sweating excitement. Timing windows to combo your attacks feel good, and there are several opportunities to cancel and reset your combos mid-way, a la fighting games -- try dashing or jumping in the middle of a combo once you've stunned or lifted your enemy off the ground, and chasing after flying or wall-bounced enemies! -- allowing you to pile on major damage. The touchy commands themselves can cause some occasional accidental chaos, but it generally doesn't cost you too badly, and sometimes even amusingly works in your favor.
The visuals are also up to speed, with expressive, animated characters and lively backgrounds perfectly framing your path of destruction, itself punctuated with great feedback as you lay waste to the opposition. The style well imitates the times it draws from, but also has lots of polish to bring the game to life in a way that wasn't possible back then. The music is solid and appropriate, if not particularly memorable, and the sound effects are great, with your most vicious hits providing an equally glorious earful. The female characters are a little over-the-top with the thrashing breasts, and thongs apparently being the only lower-body wear in the universe, but it's in good fun, so whatever. There are also several cases of sprites that are outright lifted and adapted from other games, but you won't care about the cut corners too much once the action gets properly underway -- assuming you even noticed them in the first place.
Another thing the game remembered from the days of yore was the difficulty, and the game definitely provides a meaty challenge that requires you to adapt to your opponents and find openings to safely deliver punishment; even as a veteran of the genre, and a quick study of game mechanics, I met an inglorious end and my first Continue screen midway through the fifth stage of Normal difficulty. But for the more ham-fisted or simply less experienced among us that may struggle sooner and find themselves frustrated, consider taking a breath and adapting to the game before asking that it adapt to you; any enemies in the air or currently hit-stunned is an opportunity to continue your combo, and you can maintain or finish them with your SP gauge, not to mention use it to get yourself out of trouble, so remember to use the tools available to you; they're no good to you if you don't utilize them. Also remember to hit the Extras menu and buy the training mode to get an idea of what you can do with the game's engine; it'll give you some bread and butter combos, as well as some ideas to come up with your own, although I would argue it should've just been available in the first place.
Speaking of the extras menu, it also contains a suite of other unlockable content and small customization elements, bringing to mind the shop of the fan-made Streets of Rage Remake, and like that shop, more play means more currency to find out what else the game has tucked away, which is additional incentive to dole out some more knuckle sandwiches.
On the whole, Fight'N Rage is an example of a game that knows what was great about an era of video games, but also knows what needed refinement, and it delivers both to great effect, largely succeeding in its bold mission statements. There are a couple of snags -- flying enemies are as annoying as you remembered them in Streets of Rage, for instance -- but overall the presentation is great, the action is thrilling, and the challenge is fair... mostly. This is a modern classic that doesn't just hang with the best of a bygone era -- it surpasses many of them. If you have any fondness of this genre, or even just its era, and aren't afraid to do more than relentlessly pound your character's basic combo, strap on your gloves and hit the streets!

Fight N' Rage is a classic style beat 'em up game.
The game has fun gameplay and responsive controls, great pixel art visuals, and the story has several paths and endings, so there's replay value. You'll collect coins and unlock all kinds of stuff. Music is all right too, personally I didn't find it to be that memorable, but maybe that's just because I don't listen that much metal. Most of the time the game has a great "game feel", you really feel the power of those attacks. As far as I understand, the entire game was made by one person (not counting the music), so the work is very impressive and clearly a lot of effort went into making this game.
There's just one thing that I don't agree with. The game goes for that arcade experience and you can't save the game between levels. You have to beat the entire game in one sitting, and I am not a huge fan of that. The game is quite short, but I could imagine it can still be too long for some people to finish in one session. The game is very much fast non-stop action and it may get a little exhausting to play it all at once. And I haven't even mentioned that the game throws huge amounts of enemies at you as you make progress, and it won't be easy for those playing in single player mode (in normal mode, at least). I haven't played in multiplayer, but at least I'd think this problem isn't that bad when playing with a friend or two.
I can understand that this is how it was in other retro arcade games back in the day, but I don't see how having the option to save would hurt the game. After all, the game already has infinite continues, so it's not like saving would make finishing the game any easier. The only problem might be that save scumming could be used to cheat and get more coins than you should, but even that could be easily fixed by having it so that saving always resets your score to zero. Naturally this save feature would be completely optional and purists could disable it. Well, this all is just a suggestion. I'm just saying that the lack of saving effectively prevents Fight N' Rage from being a pick up and play -kinda game for shorter sessions. (if you don't wanna play the first levels again, that is)
That aside, there's a pretty good training mode that will help you to learn the moves and combos. Every character plays differently and it's fun to learn them. Weirdly enough, you start with normal and hard difficulty modes, but easy mode is something you have to unlock by collectiong coins (maybe this was done to encourage people to not play on easy so that their skills would improve more?). I very much recommend all new players to unlock the easy mode as soon as possible and then finish the game once with it, and then try the other difficulty modes after you get better.
Still, very much recommended for all fans of the genre, I've had a lot of fun with this game.
+ Fun gameplay and "game feel"
+ Responsive controls
+ Three main characters play differently
+ Great pixel art visuals
+ Different routes and endings that give it more replay value
+ Generally it's a well polished game
- No saving between levels, requires you to finish it in one session
- Some unlocks require you to finish the game in harder difficulties, that may be really hard for some players
- I would have liked to see just a few more special moves per character, or even more playable story characters (to be honest this may be unreasonable, as this game must have already been a lot of work for one developer)

First of all, let me list the awesome parts of this game.
+ Great soundtrack - needs to be buyable via DLC
+ Humor - the bones flying everywhere when an enemy is overkilled is one example
+ Deep battle system - purchase the training mode to get a feel for this
+ Creativity in character design - chickens that use Muay Thai and a fat cat in a samurai gi, for example
+ The idea of unlockables - more games need to do this
+ The idea of an easy mode - a stride in the direction of supporting those with average gamer skill
+ The idea of SP is great. It allows the player to be able to use a special move (with a cool-down timer) without sacrificing health.
+ Fighting technique options for the gifted gamer - this is a great idea for those gamers that can actually make use of those said options. I just read a tip in the extras section that said that parrying restores SP. That is a GREAT thing for gifted gamers.
+ Fighting technique options that increase score - this is a great idea for those gamers that can actually make use of those said options. One example is the up-down attack that F. Norris and Gal can do. Gifted gamers can use that attack to "crush" enemies and increase their score.
+ Multiple game paths are a great idea for increasing replayability. One example is going left to "escape" at the beginning of the first level. That provides a different experience than those that charge full steam ahead.
Second of all, let me list the parts of the game that need work.
- Easy mode should really "make you feel like a boss" as opposed to barely making the game playable for those with average gamer skill. One simple way of helping that along would be to provide more food in Easy mode.
- Unlockables need to be unlockable for people of average gamer skill. For example, Gal's outfits should be unlockable by everyone. I have only been able to unlock one outfit for Gal, and if I select the other oufits,
How about making the outfits so that X number of hours played with the character would open up extra outfits instead of game objectives that belong in Steam Achievements (such as beating the game in normal mode, hard mode, or score attack mode with an S)? If gamers can do that stuff, great. But average gamers should not be penalized with something as important as unlockables. Or, you know what, penalize us. Make it so that we have to spend 5000 coins for the outfits instead of 500 or 1000.
- Unlockable characters should be available for a normal play-through of the game (even if gamers can't earn coins while playing as enemy mobs). For example, I unlocked the whip girl, but the only thing I can do with her is fight her in the practice mode. Really? I used 500 coins for playing with a character in practice mode?
- Gamers need to be able to adjust the number of lives given to them at the start (even if doing so disables achievements).
- GET RID OF THE <expletive> DOBERMANS and the other mobs that abuse invulnerability frames! They have no business being in the game...particularly when the enemy can abuse invulnerability frames WITHOUT sacrificing SP or health. This would be a different story if SP regenerated MUCH FASTER on Easy mode.
- The Raven boss (the bat boss) is beatable, but it requires a drastic change in fight style from what I use everywhere else in the game. Since I couldn't practice with the boss in practice mode without beating him X times, I had to find out how to beat him from other gamers. Here is what I have learned.
- Training mode needs to include a demonstration of the things that actually need to be done. The timing of some of the combos is not intuitive. If the gamer can see the combos being performed, then the gamer has an idea of what is expected.
- Either disable the area timer or provide a way for average gamers to increase their SP in boss fights...particularly in Easy mode. Bosses like to abuse invulnerability frames. The best counter to that is SP attacks which counter most invulnerability moves. The problem is that bosses can use invulnerability attacks 3-5 times more than players can. That is only a problem for patient gamers due to the problem of the area timer that prevents players from walking around until their SP meter is full.
- Multiple game paths is a good idea when all paths have similar benefit. As the game stands, the multiple game paths is a tool only for unlocking characters you can use in practice mode. Once players learn about the "escape" and "bike" path (
), players will ONLY use that path once they learn how many more points they can earn, which then leads to more extra life awards.
- What about parrying? I continue to read forum posts where people ask for changes to the game's parrying system. Some people want a bit of wiggle room. Other people want a separate button programmable for parrying. And if parrying is the developer's solution to the bat boss and to the dobermans, then the developer should think about the suggestions provided for parrying. As things currently stand, the timing required for parrying is just brutal. And the fact that the d-pad must serve as both the parrying mechanism and the movement mechanism doesn't help matters.
Thank you.
Here's one more thought. If a gamer buys the Sega Genesis Streets of Rage games on Steam, they can also download mods. Kind modders made it so that average gamers can play Streets of Rage 3 with 99 lives if they choose to do so. And they did that for free. I would actually PAY to get a game mode I can enjoy of this game, since on so many levels it is better than the old arcade brawlers.

First off, this game has a fantastic soundtrack, if you're a long time fan of the Guilty Gear series you'll feel right at home from the first note.
A quick note before delving into the visuals, if you don't like the CRT mode you can turn it off in the settings, though I loved it, it can be a little distracting at times.
The visual design of this game from what I've seen of it so far is superb. The stage tiles are given life by a healthy mix of colors with good shading techniques, detailed background and foregrounds (The foregrounds are just on screen enough to give detail, but not enough to block the screen. I love it.) with animated effects such as raging fires, or down pouring rain with ripple effects, that all come together without making it difficult to navigate the screen.
Enemy and character design follows suit, I've yet to ever lose myself or the enemy on the screen, even when there's a ton of stuff going on. On that note, lets talk about gameplay.
The game will give you a short, brief little tutorial on the controls at your disposal, how to walk, inputting a directional button twice for a dash or a dodge, and your jump, attack, and super button. As you progress through the stages you'll beat up some dudes and earn points that'll turn into coins you can spend on new characters, costumes, and other cool stuffs.
Real quick note, first thing I strongly advise anyone gets it's the training mode. There's some hidden depth behind all of the characters movesets and this will take you through them all (as far as I know thusfar)
The game is challenging without feeling entirely unfair (though it looks like Ricardo has a tougher time on his own given that he doesn't have a dash/dodge) by yourself, and is a blast with a friend or two.
Getting through to the end will take practice, this isn't just a smash attack to win styled beat 'em up.  learning how the various enemies and their AI's function, and most importantly who to prioritize when, and how you can string your combo's together in combination with dashes/dodges, jumps and kicks to avoid damage. (You can jump again when ever your character is above an enemy sprite! There is no limit far as I can tell on how many times you can do this.)
Big thing to note, you have a decent amount of delay time you can make use of between each attack, sometimes hitting one guy as fast and hard as possible isn't the best play at your disposal, but rather drawing a hit string out so that you can get the really dangerous guys into the combo, worst comes to worst, dodge, or super out of it if things look iffy.
The various different paths are a nice touch I feel, some good examples that come to mind, in one of the stages (on a diversion from the standard path already) you have the choice to either escape upwards down a path, or to continue on facing a seemingly endless horde of enemies. Or, in the first stage, you can flee the burning town to the left just like the rest of the townsfolk are doing. And the final example, for saving a hostages life, before the boss can do them in.
Now, real quickly. I'd like to go over some stuff that would be nice quality of life improvements. If you could map a button to be a context action for dash/dodge, so for example, I use a playstation controller. X is super, O is jump, Triangle is attack, I'd love it if I could map it so that I could press, or hold square, and tap any directional button to trigger it's respective dash or dodge. Just something that would take some pain off my left hand and make the gameplay feel a little less frantic.
Second thing that would be nice, and might already be in the game, I don't know. (as of yet, I have not beaten the game on normal, just so you know.) It'd be awesome if there was a way to see a roadmap of the stages you've seen, and the possible exits within them, and how many of them you've seen.
Again, these aren't stuff that are needed, just feel like it would improve the game a little.
All in all, I put this right up there with Double Dragon Neon for one of my favorite beat 'em up games and hope to see more from SebaGames! Please keep up the fantastic work!
Edit: Stage 8 is made of nightmares and hopelessness. my hands know only pain. But I won't let this beat me. may want to throw in just one more food drop at some point in that stage, also might want to include a save at level start/check point feature for those of us with hand issues, so we can take a break and come back later when the pain has died down.

Making a functioning society at the time when people were the most important commodity, and I'm not talking about the slave trade.
Literally, you're a group of banished individuals who have chosen a plot of land to make your own town where all you have to rely on is the people who live in the town. You want them to live and prosper, so they can make more children of their own and essentially continuing the life of the town.
It's actually quite difficult to control the birth rates and have a steady increase over time as you steadily increase the amount of resource you're required to consume. Too few of people, and you won't be able to harvest all you need. Too many people, and you won't have enough resources to sustain the current population. New births don't just start working immediately and there's a waiting period as they come to adulthood. But do you extend that waiting time by sending them into school so they are more proficient at their job? Or do you put them straight to work and fill the current need, but ultimately losing out on precious time and resource in the long run.
It's a balance and requires planning with a dash of patience. Thank you developer for the 10x time warp! Oh♥♥♥♥♥♥ houses are on fire.
It's a fun game if you like the simulator style city manager without all the bulk and fluff of a Sim City. It's straight forward and doesn't require charts, or graphs, or a calculator. Manage your life-force of a precious commodity with care. As soon as is dips, be prepared for a sweeping number of deaths before it bottoms out with only a few remaining survivors to repopulate the now vacant township.

Initial impressions:
-overblown CRT/Chromatic Abberation effects on by default, thankfully it's possible to dial this down
-the core mechanics are very fleshed out in this 2d beat em up on a traditional 3 button layout (attack, jump, special)
-closer to Final Fight than Streets of Rage i.e. target combos into back throw/forward throw
-does still feature the walk up grapple system from Streets of Rage
-backgrounds vary in quality (some are really barebones, some are very well drawn)
-branching paths in  stages akin to Dungeons and Dragons (Capcom) / Dragon's Crown, seems to lead to distinctly different playthroughs
-Tons of homages to 2d brawlers/fighters (M. Bison's c.HK, Guy's Bushin chain into throw, the Ultimate Warrior from Streets of Rage, E. Honda's sumo buttslam, etc)
-Streets of Rage 3 power gauge system where you get a free use of a panicked, invincible clearing move on a cooldown; if used during cooldown, docks a significant chunk of your own HP
-Just Frame/Parry System from Street Fighter 3/Garou in which you can tap any horizontal direction at the precise point of getting hit to go invulnerable and negate hitstun/blockstun, allowing you to squeeze in attacks
-Very satisfying grab tech/throw escape mechanic - tap jump on reaction to getting grabbed to avoid being thrown, leaves enemy in a throw whiff state for you to counterattack
-Flying enemies are still a pain, much more so when it comes to flying bosses.
-Decent unlock system akin to Streets of Rage Remake, earn coins in main campaign (purchasable modes, costumes, difficulty levels (easy mode), playable enemy characters (only in Duelling Arena VS. mode))
-darn flying enemies
-training mode where you... whoa... this is combat depth closer to the likes of a fighting game. Combos challenges to be done (i.e.jump in down+attack and land into 3-hit target combo into run cancel into running attack into 4hit chain cancel into flash kick cancel into air special)
-there are also air movement options available in the form of walljumps and launching yourself off successful jump-in attacks (Smash Bros style)
-you can air recover by pressing the jump button to avoid getting juggled
-yo, flying enemies, why?
-must be the path I chose through the story, but I had tons of difficulty with the flying boss on the raft.

Fallout 3 : Great Shooter Terrible Rpg
Overall Fallout 3 is a good shooter game . It has relatively good mechanics ,plenty of weapons to use etc. but I genuinely think it is a bad role playing game –to be hones I am not sure even you should consider this game one .
Hey hey hey! Before pressing dislike I would like to say that Fallout 3 Is a great game overall what I am going to criticize is the lack  of rpg elements in a rpg game . Unlike Fallout New Vegas and fallout 1 &2 the game has little to offer regarding storytelling . It lacks depth , has plenty of plot holes and the character you have simply doesn’t have a great effect on the universe you are playing in . Main story is weak . It is about your character leaving his vault and  finding his father On the paper this is a great idea ;having that Father son relationship affecting the interactions between your character and other people  , but in the first five minutes of this game you do realize that this is not a role playing game this is a rail shooter . Because unlike other Fallout games whether you do something or not doesn’t affect the game at all and game doesn’t let you create a free independent character who makes his own decisions and has his/her own ideas.It is all about do you want to be nice or a f*cking maniac who blows up a city for no reason?
In fallout new Vegas Caesar’s Legion is presented as the bad guys . But more you learn about them the more you learn about their ‘’IDEOLOGY’’-a word that has nothing to with fallout 3-   you start to think that they might have a point even though they are genocidal rapists and when you confront their leader Caesar for the first time he talks about the need for Totalitarianism and militarism in such a sensible manner that you might think that he is right –and the funny thing is he is right- so in this situtation what would you do ? Would you respect old world values such as democracy or would you bend your knee to a smart dictator … Or would you use the trump card and destroy both of the factions despite the possibility of failure . As you can see game had choices whereas here you have kill or be killed .
Game only has 3 different endings which only depends on the last mission and these are simply
A)You are a good guy you repaired the purifier
B)You are a coward you made lions activate the console
C)You are a bad dude because you intoxicated the purifier and the entire water resources with it .
(I am excluding the minor faction endings)
No matter what your justifications are  these are the only  endings you can get while in Fallout:NV and Fallout 1&2 you could get dozens of endings  in addition to minor faction endings  owing to how you play the game . If you are a good guy but sided with legion this actually causes legion to abandon some of its barbaric ways but if you sided with NCR as a bad guy the opposite happens  and this is not due to  some stupid karma system on the contrary it is related with the side quests you do during the game and as you can see these side quests actually affect the ending  and this is what makes a role playing game .
Also skill system is such a mess  lockpicking , hacking and Speech are totally useless since you can always bypass them somehow  and the game actually encourages you to do so .For the example ın the Overseer’s room (at the very beginning)  you need to hack  overseer’s computer and guess what  the password for the computer is in the footlocker next to computer  While it is okay for these kind of stuff to happen from time to time  this is the case with entire game and such level building destroys the roleplaying .
And to be honest  I can only remember only names of three characters : These are Moira , Lyons and Liam Neeson ( Ok I have forgotten our character’s dad’s name but funny fact it was voiced by liam Neeson I think this is a great )
And Also ai is terrible all they do is running in a straight line like they want to die . Unless you have downloaded a mod that makes them harder I don’t think they will pose such a great problem .
Of course I have some stuff that I like about this game . I loved the mission where you have to handle two superhero wannabes –and possibly get their outfits- I loved the camp littlelight – a little village consists of only children. I loved the Vats system I appreciated the repair system but it could have been better . But as you can see these don’t have anything to do with  story telling .
Overall I would give this game 3/5 for its solid fps mechanics and being a stepping stone between Fallout 2 and New vegas
Also if you guys want a review about rpg aspects of this game I would recommend you to watch hbomber’s Fallout 3 review I have to be honest I have been influenced by him .

"Just Cause 2" is a stellar effort.
First off, it actually delivers on the premise of having freedom of movement. That's right - this "open world" is actually open, and it's also reachable. If you want to grab a plane and fly across the island, the only thing stopping you is actually finding a plane. Nothing artificially stands in your way.
"Verticality" is another huge victory on the part of the developers. Other games promise a lot of verticality, but this is the title that actually does it. If you want to go straight up a mountain, you can. Just deploy your grappling hook. I can't remember ever hitting an "invisible wall" while playing the game, which was incredibly refreshing. If you see something, you can get there.
Alongside the above, another great feature of the title is that "getting there" IS actually half the fun. Parachute slingshotting is an entirely viable method for traversing a fair distance, and it keeps you engaged while you're making the run to your waypoint. There were a number of times where I passed up the fast-travel system in favor of just flinging myself around with the hook and the chute. It's a perfect example of a "gameplay loop" that has been flawlessly executed. It never stops being fun.
"Just Cause 2" isn't quite perfect, though. The difficulty vs reward ratio is a little bit weak on the reward side, especially when it comes to race challenges. A race challenge with a land or sea vehicle is usually pretty darned easy, whereas the aircraft-based races can be a real bear...but they all pay the same. This also connects to your character development, of which there's very little. You can upgrade vehicles and weapons, but there are only a few that really matter. This hurts the reward element of "seeing and doing everything," especially when the locations start to get samey. You'll eventually see enough towns and military bases that the "patterns" start to become noticeable.
Don't get me wrong! The treasure-hunt-blow-things-up loop is really well done, and can stay fun for tens upon tens of hours, but there's a point where you suddenly tire of it. There aren't any super-nifty weapons or jaw-droppingly amazing vehicles to find...not really. So, at some point, you're just picking up upgrade parts and money that isn't really useful. Exploration loses its importance at that point. There's no real novelty to be found at a certain point.
Also, the endgame seemed very thin and anticlimactic to me. What you do in the "sandbox" to get there doesn't seem to tie-in very well, and there's very little buildup with the campaign. It suddenly spikes to the final confrontation, and then just stops in its tracks. There's no winding up of tension, no sense of stakes being raised, and no real emotional payoff for saving the day. Sure, there's story exposition that's meant to do that, but telling me that "really important stuff is happening!" is never as good as truly showing it.
The weaknesses in the game are significant, but they're also handily eclipsed by the sheer fun of tearing around the island. That bit of the game, which is the true core, is expertly handled.
So, you really ought to try this thing out.
