Alright, this game is a hidden gem. I know some people have said that but I want to drive that point home. In my time playing the game I have not had any bug encounters except one which was annoying I will admit but it was avoidable. The game itself has got a lot of variety to the game play that it will keep you amused for hours. They have a risk type mode, scenario mode, dungeon mode. All of these have different rules that go with them and you will need to become familiar with each if you want to grow in strength. There is also a unique tetris type system to upgrade your robots that gives you quite the intricate customization. Overall the game is well done, if you like turn based strategy games this is a game for you. The only thing that might turn people off from it is there is the element of grinding involved. I haven't found it obnoxious, sure it kind of stinks if you run a dungeon hoping for a piece to drop and don't get it. But, I have found other games far more bothersome in their grinding.
Also I want to point out that the plans seem random and a lot of people don't like that. I feel the element of surprise is worth it and also once you have the previous plans created it will be taken out of rotation and then you will be able to whittle it down from there. Really it takes some guesswork, not any different then other games where you guess what recipes will make what.

This is a really cool game with a bunch of issues, but still really worth the money. I think it really deserves more attention than its getting.
The Good.
* cute graphics
* the units you play with are really different and really encourage you to use different play styles
* 3 games in one, and each game type lets you earn different types of  resources (money, parts, and chips
* the campaign mode is pretty much a full game all by itself, with both a strategy map and tactical maps whenever there is a fight
* chips allow for great customization of individual robots
* i frequently complain that games dont have enough tracks, but at least the tracks here are catchy enough that it doesnt bother me. i am listening to the menu music looping as i write this, which i normally cant tolerate.
* devs are really freindly and eager to improve the game
* quest system - not sure if this is a good or bad - its cool, and it does help you find out a bit more about the game, but it could be developed a bit more
* it even has auto-farming in infinity mine and scenarios! once you have plenty of bots you can send one team to farm while you go play with another team
The Not-So-Good.
* the tutorial is very brief and only covers a small part of the game.
* because of the short tutorial, large chunks of the game are a complete mystery, and have to be worked out by trail and error
* there are a number of bugs, sometimes preventing you from accessing buttons, menus, scrolling etc... Hapily, most of these can be busted out of if you know what to do (eg when scrolling/panning is broken. clicking on 'reset camera' usually fixes it)
* the three game types are really cool (scenario, infinity mine, and campaign) but it isnt really explained that you need to be switching from one to another to advance.  A number of reviewers complain that the infinity mine gets really hard around lvl 5. I'm guessing thats because they didnt discover how to get more units or how to upgrade them.
Summary:
A really cool little game that will reward you for your patience in struggling to work out all the info for yourself. I bought this on special, but knowing what i know now i would have happily paid full price ($9.99 USD at the time of writing). i already have 20+ hours in this game and i am pretty sure i will get plenty more. It does play a little like an EA title some times, but a good EA, one which the devs care about,

TL;DR: If you can overlook the unpolished UX, you'll get a great game for your money.
This game is very "indie." By that I mean it definitely lacks a lot of the polish that big-name funding provides. There are copious grammatical errors, although little typos, which leads me to believe it's more of a translation issue than a proof-reading one. However, everything is understandable, it's just occasionally a wonky read. Other than that and the unintuitive HUDs, the balance of the game and some of the mechanics feel a bit odd, especially with the multiplayer aspect. I don't think this could ever have a robust competitive player-base, but it might be enjoyable to play with a friend from time to time.
Once you get past having to dig around for certain things (again, with the unintuitive UI), you'll find it's actually a pretty great game. It's obvious a lot of work went into the core of the game, and the battle system itself is great. There are countless ways to configure your team, and the different abilities and attributes don't feel cheap or gimmicky -- afaik there's no way to stack a single skill or effect and munchkin your way through the game. There are many different game types, and a fair portion of your progress (i.e., robots and upgrades) persist across all your games (weird for campaigns/skirmishes and multiplayer, but good for singleplayer progression). The 3D art and animation is great, and the music is decent enough that I haven't muted it yet.
After about a week of playing, I'd say it's a very satisfying turn-based strategy, and recommend it even at its full price.

It is something to be experienced--made by a creator, for creators. It is, at different times, uplifting, dreary, uncomfortable, and oddly reassuring. The Beginner's Guide offers perspective, at the terrifying cost of opening all the doors into your darkest closets.

There's a fandom about this game, and no I don't mean the furries. although they've been doing a bunch of art.
The game's got interesting mechanics, combining research manangement and critical thinking; and like most good horror games, it has a nice balance of showing you something scarry, while at the same time letting your mind make the horror. You might find it hard to get further in the game whether it can be the robots destroying you or your own will to progress further.
The robots design of uncanny valley-esq looks combined with their AI, the sounds, the subtile changes you might only notice flipping through the cameras, camera 6 being an audio only camera, and even the hallusinations occuring on later nights really hammer a scary enviorment. You will never ever ever know a greater joy hearing the 5-6AM song.
And of course, for the interested, there is a story within the game, and like most good stories, you can take what you want from it.
I'd recommend it for any fan of horror. It might seem like jump scares from the Let's Plays, but there is soemthing about it when playing that play against your parinoia. Try the demo, and then play it yourself.

This is a game that is enigmatic and hard to describe. I feel the need to write about it and tell people about it and yet, I can't really say anything or go too deep. It would ruin the experience.
Basically, you are playing through bite-sized, mostly unfinished games ostensibly developed by a person named Coda. These games are narrated throughout by Davey Wreden, and he provides the backbone to these otherwise loosely connected series of games. You play one, Davey talks about it a bit, you move on to the next.
But it's not that simple.
There's a deeper meaning here that I can't go into. I don't even know if I really understand it, but I can't get this game out of my head. It's like having food stuck between your teeth; you consistently feel it, but it's hard to get rid of. Not that I want to get rid of it in this instance, mind you.
Do I recommend this? Yes. Absolutely. I love games like "The Stanley Parable" and "Gone Home" and if you do too, this is an obvious recommendation. This game will stay with me long after it's over, and I'll probably go back and play it again just to peel back the layers a little deeper, whether those layers are real or imagined.
I don't understand "The Beginner's Guide". But I love it so very much.

Just a quick note on port as I play. So far seems decent, better than most of the ports of recent times.
That said there are some issues I find annoying, some will be fixed, some won't.
Thankfully keyboard/mouse work, and they actually play overall smoothly and well. Although I have a controller, I am thinking of not bothering with this title, as I do like the feel of K/M in it. That said there are some issues.
Most problematic is that instead of actually taking a good look at the UI and figuring out a decent control scheme, they just went for the brute force approach. Notably it does have reasonable mouse driven functions. However when using the keyboard every option is mapped to varying keys, in no logical way. Plenty of options could have been reduced to a single common set of keys, but aren't. In this sense keyboard layout for game menus is horrendous. It does thankfully display the keys to use at all times, but it is still annoying given it uses the full spread of the keyboard, when it is not a keyboard only game.
Apart from that I would recommend to save often. There are currently some game breaking bugs with no way out, so if you get trapped in one without a recent save, arrrrrrrrggggghhh... One I just experienced was where on opening the merchant sell screen some key bindings failed. So that although I could sell stuff, I couldn't exit the screen and get back to the game. Who would have known a merchant was the final invulnerable boss.
On the graphics side I have had no particular problems apart from reasonably bad screen-tearing which is fixable. The game has otherwise run fine and smooth at maximum on my 750ti.

This was one of my favourite games to play as a child (I was like 6 or 8 the first time I played) and it was my introduction into FPS games. It is very fast paced, spontaneous and action packed. For it's time it was something different and new, it was futuristic and exciting. Everything from the various maps / locations. To the many characters to play as and battle against. Nothing is more satisfying then the announcer screaming "Mo-Mo-Monsterrr Kill!" whilst you completly destroy your opponets with a rocket launcher. It differs from the Unreal Titles, with less story and more action, it gives you what you want - futuristic weaponary, unqiue and exotic locations, sexy characters and dance music. The diverse game mods mmake game play fresh, however if like me, playing the vanilla maps over and over again can be repetitive and boring. Hence why I downloaded new community made maps which keep the game fresh. My favourite game mode is Monster Hunt (or Team Monster Hunt), which combines both the Original Unreal Game with the Unreal Tournament Game. I've since gone on to play the Original Unreal Games and the other Unreal Tournament Titles. It will be one of my favourite Series of games and I will always be a FPS fanatic. Defianetly recommend this game to anyone who wants to expereince a blase from the past, an original and classic FPS game (Or any of the Unreal or Unreal Tournament Titles for that matter).

just to contrast (in order of importance):
Really, that's it. Despite what people say though, this is not really a very challenging game. It's just not very forgiving either, which are different things. It's fairly easy to not screw up completely if you think about what you are doing but the consequences of a screw-up can be harsh.
For reference, I'm fairly used to tycoon games and to playing the likes of OpenTTD in very stringent economic settings. After the tutorial I've started my first Banished town with all on Medium difficulty (I thought it'd be a challenge). All went well and smooth, no hiccups, the town is packed with resources and only growing. I can't wait for a hard game but I fear it won't be really hard.
On the other hand, the
are many and quite convincing:
An absolute must-have. If there's any chance you might like the genre and you haven't gotten this game yet, get it. Right now.
The 9/10 score is solely because of the lack of a proper challenge in the long run. Things I'd like to see are more consequences for the lack of a balanced diet (there's not that much incentive for diversification as it is), or things like a super harsh winter every 5 or 10 years that may get you off-guard, that kind of thing. Anything to
, to throw you a curve ball to deal with every once in a while. Maybe the classic citizens becoming unhappy if the town is too big, or if they need to walk too much to stock their households (beyond the lower productivity "penalty"), I don't know. Just more mechanics to make the game interesting and challenging in the long run instead of "if you're producing a little more than you consume your are safe forever" current mechanic, which is a bit too easy to beat and a bit too stable/predictable.

They were all huddled around the storage cart for a time and they started wandering around aimlessly but wondering how they were possibly going to make it after being banished from their town. Many of them had little understanding of the world outside their former homes walls and started to fear the worst. It started raining and people were getting cold and hungry.
And then one person named Trist picked up an axe and started building himself the best house he could. People watched him in shock for a few minutes, and then one by one others started following his inspiring example and before they knew it they had a home, food, and a job.
They were happy. But not for long.
Winter came and the snow started falling lightly at first and soon blanketed the lands as far as the eye could see. But it was a dangerous beauty and people soon died of hypothermia and hunger. This is everything the store page claims and more. The influences are evident - Street fighter, Streets of Rage, Golden Axe, Battletoads, Final Fight - the sole programmer seemingly combed through every game you could conceivably call a "beat em up" from the 90s, and cherry picked some of the best elements from each. Better yet, he managed to wrangle a surprising amount of depth out of it without having to resort to a "lane" system, or requiring you to press a button to toggle which direction you're looking, like some other games in the genre have leaned on in order to shoehorn more fighting-game-style inputs in.
The presentation is top notch. From the moment you launch it, the CRT filter and arcade cabinet overlay make it clear exactly what kind of game you're getting in to. The musician that was hired gets his own intro, and it's off to the games title screen proper, and you're greeted by the games logo as a tune practically plucked straight out of Guilty Gear blares in the background. Pressing start brings up a neat menu, making it immediately obvious that this game has plenty of secrets to unearth.
My first foray into the game was by myself, and the pre-game tutorial (which is very arcade appropriate, by the way) tells you just enough to get you going. In the path that I decided to take, new enemy types were slowly introduced, usually by themselves or in pairs, to give you time to figure out how to defeat them. Once you've had some time to practice against them, they start coming in greater numbers, or combined with other enemy types, to create a mental challenge that demands you keep track of all of them. They all telegraph their attacks, but it's up to you to make sure that you can either get out of the way, or throw something into them before they connect with you.
The game is quite challenging, even on Normal. I found myself falling into button-mashing habits very early on, and got a game over on stage 2. Determined not to credit feed this game, I let the timer run out and gave it another go from stage 1. Everything I'd learned up to that gameover point, and a new-found level of caution got me up to the 6th stage before running out of Steam again. It wasn't until I parked my wife next to me and we played together that we were able to defeat the final boss, using a single continue. After seeing one ending, the game unlocks a new menu item that shows you exactly how much "progress" you've made. I won't spoil it for you here, but suffice to say, the game has plenty of replayability.
Since this game is rooted deeply in the days of old, where you buy a game and you own it, and extras are something you unlock and not just fork money over for, there's plenty for you to unlock. Alternate costumes, new colors for any costumes you already have, new playable characters, new modes, and more. Scoring points in Arcade mode and beating the game or getting a game over converts those points into coins, a currency used to unlock things in the extras shop. With the rate that you earn coins, and the number of branching paths available to you, there's plenty of incentive to play the game again and again, including higher difficulty modes that present more of a challenge as you gradually figure out the combo system and how to deal with the enemies.
If I have any major gripes, it's the absence of online play, and lack of a manual. Only being able to share this experience with local friends is not entirely out of place for the 90s arcade atmosphere the game is promoting very thoroughly, but as a modern title, it's moderately disappointing that I can't share it with my online friends too. I'd also have liked to have some sort of documentation that explains how to pull off the extra moves and combos that, occasionally, I'd pull off entirely by accident. Perhaps this is revealed to you later with the "tips" system available in the Extras shop? Still, after having played through once and having familiarized myself with the controls and how to effectively use the one "combo" they teach you, I wanted to know more, and was prepared to read for it. Perhaps they're taught to you in the training mode, which is something else you can buy in the Extras shop...but I'm not yet certain, as I haven't bought that extra yet.
The controls are tight, the overall presentation package is superb, and the length of the game is just about right to casually whip this game out in front of a friend, sibling, or partner and force them to play it with you. Some may protest the price tag, but I think it's a silly notion to expect a game with this much content on offer to be any cheaper than it is. Do yourself a favor and pick this one up!

Fallout 3 is a welcomed addition to the Fallout family, but is not without its flaws.
I'll start with the positives: I thoroughly enjoyed scavenging the wastes in search of rare loot, conversing with unique characters, completing challenging quests, and going toe-to-toe with frightening creatures. Fallout 3 is brimming with content, and will surely offer you dozens of hours of enjoyment.
Now for the negatives: at the time of writing, Fallout 3 is nearly nine years old, and it really shows in some areas--low resolution textures, odd facial animations, and an overall "janky" feel to many of its mechanics. The gun-play feels weak (no iron sights to be found in most weapons), the game as whole is prone to crashes, and the story ending is surprisingly underwhelming.
Despite showing some age and sporting a lackluster conclusion, Fallout 3 is great fun. However, I still hold true to the notion that Fallout: New Vegas is the series' pinnacle. Regardless, Fallout 3 offers hours upon hours of entertainment, and I highly recommend picking up a copy.

I always loved arcade games, sinking many quarters whenever I came across a cabinet. Beat 'em up games always held a place in my heart though as one of my favorite genres.
It's a simple, yet solid arcade beat 'em with great pixel art and rocking music. If you ever enjoyed a beat 'em up like Streets of Rage, Final Fight, or Captain Commando, you'll feel right at home with this one. The story is simplistic, but has a surprising amount of depth to it, and won't interfere with the massive thrashing about.
The spritework is amazing and fluid, with quite a bit of bounce (really, take a look at any of the girls) to the action. The game also has options to emulate old CRT TVs or monitors, in case you wanted that really old feel, but no matter which options you pick, the game looks fantastic.
The game is simple, with three major buttons (attack, special attack, and jump). Like a lot of arcade games, it's got hidden commands to do some fancier moves, and it helps raise the excitement. Like many old school beat 'em ups, there's also multiple endings depending on which paths you take.
Also, if you're like me, you get a strangely powerful feeling of catharsis when you kick a furry in the face so hard that they explode into bones. If you like beating up furries and looking at bouncy babes, then this game is for you.

Surprising amount of depth to this little 2d fighter! In just a few hours of gameplay I have discovered how to parry, special input attacks, combo strings, mix-ups, and combo-string mixups that turn into juggles. Wall juggling is very entertaining, and if you build a super before you launch into one of these, you can pretty much one-shot any bad guy. Do enough overkill damage and they'll explode into blood and bones! This is the side-scroller you played in the 90s, but without the limitations from 90s hardware. Often times there are darn near 20 enemies on screen and the well optimized game handles it all like a champ.
If you were a fan of Streets of Rage, Final Fight, or even Street Fighter you are in for a surprise. There are nods to these great games and probably more packed into every level. You see where bosses draw inspiration from your favorite characters when their movesets come out. One boss is based off of Zangief from Street Fighter, in a level that appears to be based off of Vega's level. But there's plenty of unique enemy types to the game as well. I particularly enjoyed the flies armed with boxing gloves.
What else does this game have besides great combat and great level design? It has a fantastically scored musical track to carry you through your journey. Speaking of your journey, while you're on it you will be collecting in game currency to unlock TONS of extra goodies. It looks like you can unlock the entire roster of enemy fighters for the 1v1 battle mode. Want to use that Zangief-like character to smash your friend with command grabs? Unlock him and use him! This game has no micro-transactions, so all of your unlocks will come via rewards for playing.
In an era of cookie-cutter triple A games that have stagnated our market, Fight'N Rage is both a breath of fresh air and a fantastic dopamine-induced Nostalgia trip. Grab one of the three unique story characters and dive in.

A DAY IN THE WORLD OF FALLOUT 3
As you open the door out of Moriarty’s Saloon into the broken-down city of Megaton, the sun blinds you, reminding the inhabitants of the Wasteland of the power of radiation. You walk down the rickety old stairs and into the heart of the town. People greet you as you pass, and you can almost smell their respect for you, as you have shown your resolve many times by defending their lives. Your laser rifle bounces on your Vault-Tec armored jumpsuit, and your trusty 32. Caliber pistol hangs at your side. As you are about to leave the rundown town, a tall man in a hat and sheriff’s badge approaches you. He tells you of a group of Super-Mutants that has attacked a nearby village. He offers 700 caps for you to eradicate them, a handsome reward. You pull out your Pip-Boy on your arm, and mark the destination on your map. You nod your thanks to the sheriff, and set out, your loyal dog at your side. The doors out of the city open, and the strong smell of death and smoke fills your nostrils. You resist the urge to guzzle your bottle of whisky in your pack, knowing that you will need the ability to perceive all you can in the battle ahead.
As you reach the war-torn village, you hear the cries of the Mutants and the screams of the people, as they flee in terror. A Super Mutant notices you, and grabbing his club, he runs at you, yelling murderous threats. You calmly take out your rifle, aim, and blow his head off his shoulders. You feel the acidic blood spray your skin as the giant topples to the ground in a heap. You walk over to the corpse and feel his pockets for stray caps. None. You grunt, drawing your pistol and shooting the arm off an incoming Super-Mutant. He falls to his knees, yelling guttural cries at you. You walk over to him and, brandishing your brass knuckles, punch him in the face so hard that you feel his bones break. As his limp body crumples to the ground, you see who you came here for. Over twelve feet tall, brandishing an assault rifle and nail-board, clad in Kevlar armor was the chieftain, the Super-Mutant Brute. He roars, firing round after round at you, as you try to find cover. As the bullets pierce the bunker that you hide behind, you ready a bottlecap mine. As you hear the gun click and the cursing stop, you know that the creature is reloading his weapon. You quickly stand up, and diving for cover, throw the highly explosive mine at his feet. Too preoccupied with filling his gun with more rounds, he doesn’t seem to notice it. You aim your pistol at his feet, thinking to blow the mine where he stands. The Brute lets out a raucous laugh, reaches down, and picking up the bottlecap mine, he hurls it at you. Your vision blurs in a burst of light, and searing pain covers your entire body. Your eyes burn and you can only see a hazy sight of a hulking creature walk over to you. It raises a large object, and brings it down on your head in a flash of bright light, then, everything goes dark.
Fallout 3 is a gritty, atmospheric, open-world RPG that has you exploring a post-apocalyptic wasteland crawling with both friendly and combative inhabitants. With a cast of interesting and unforgettable characters, along with the most unique locations to explore, and a deep and brutal combat system to bind it all together, the world of Fallout is a masterpiece. With its immersive sound and visual design, you will soon start to feel the effects of radiation on your body as you enter the world Fallout 3.

I pre-ordered this game since I was unable to back the kickstarter back in 2013.  I did end up backing Yooka Laylee, which I personally regret.  I do not regret pre-ordering A Hat in Time however.  This game blew me away with charm, great music, a decent amount of variety, heart-pounding boss battles, and excellent control.  The only issue I had were the more precision based platforming where you had to jump on thin lines or up on small ledges since it's not as tight in those areas.  I cringed every time I had to do them or do them over and they were almost the sole reason I died more times than I'd like to admit.
I 100% this game, which I haven't done in a long while.  I don't think I'll be going for the achievements.
NOTE: There will be a free expansion coming at some point to this game.  An entire new world to explore.  There's also a ton of mod support which adds more hats, planets, and more.  So while that free expansion is brewing, the creative community should be able to tide us over.
I whole heartedly recommend this game to platforming fans, kids, adults, people just getting into video games, basically everyone.  Buy it.

As an avid Turn based tactical games, there's a lot of great things in this game. The RPG part feels rewarding in solo, and most of the game mechanics are fun.
From specific skills to each unit that you can upgrade during the battle, a speed stat for dynamic turns, dynamic terrain, a heat system when you use your skills too much, there's a lot of interesting mechanics here to play with.
Aside from the good things, the game still needs a whole lot of polish. On the top of my head:
- Resolution handling is really messy. You cannot have lower than 1280/720px res, and anything higher than that will clip the loading screens and UI.
- The general UI design is, honestly, bad.  A bunch of things work correctly, and that's generally usable, but it's clearly not at the level of the models and especially their artistic direction.
There are other usability issues, but nothing preventing you from playing, and I'm sure they're going to fix most of them.
Overall, I just wish there were more players to be able to play in multiplayer online as I crave for it.

I'm in my third play through currently.  My first game was nine days (eaten by wolves), the second play through was 20 hours (also eaten by wolves), and my third and ongoing game is right at nive days (survived one wolf attack so far).  I am very impressed with this game.  Any time outdoors is anyways exciting.  You can only be outside a few hours before the cold sets in, so movments need to be thought out ahead of time.  Wolves are frequently observed, though I am getting the hang of managing their AI.  Seems that there is plenty of loot in the various structures.  Wood and tinder are easy enough to find, through you only have a finite amount of matches.  Snow can be melted and boiled for water.  Food is probably the biggest challenge.  I've yet to hunt.  Stabbed a few wolves, then later scrounged meat from those.  I also scrounged from deer and rabbits already killed by wolves.  Fishing is productive, but wolves get attracted to the fishing huts so exits are exciting.  Overall I'm getting the hang of it.  I really like the dynamics behind this game....looks great in a Team Fortress kind of way.  You always have to think and plan ahead...not too much room for error, especially early on when you have nothing.  I would recommend that the developers look into fashioning improvised weapons like spears or primative bow and arrows.  In a real world situation, I think the first thing I would do after finding a knife or axe would be to sharpen a stick.  The wolves may still win over time, but I would make them pay for their efforts with a quick stab/swing in their direction.  Highly recommended!

PROS:

-parkour elements are easy to learn and feel pretty smooth. a good introduction to parkour games for beginners. more advanced players might find them repetitive.

CONS:
-objectives are not easy to follow and I found myself aimlessly searching around more than once
-the storyline has a lot of potential, but seems stunted--it's unclear why the hero needed to collect the items he did, how he ended up where he was, and why the other characters introduced are significant. finding "pre-apocalypse items" was a nice addition, but could easily be expanded
-similarly, the game finale seemed rushed there is a warning that the finale is coming, I just expected something more in terms of plot once it was finished and left unsatisfied. I also found the mechanics of this final level quite frustrating. it did tie in the major elements of the main story, but whether I was able to successfully interact with key items seemed completely up to chance

This game is interesting, and I'd say I enjoyed it, but I can't get over how very, VERY pretentious it is. If it were a statement on the difficulty of creative endeavors or the boundaries of friendship or existential ennui, etc., which THEN OFFERED an empowering perspective or even just a thesis statement of some kind, I could see myself getting behind it. Instead, I'm genuinely irritated that by the end of this experience Davey can offer no meaningful commentary besides a near maudlin plea for acceptance and respect. It screams in anguish, but doesn't take a break from self-pity to reflect.
The game is so specific about the relationship of its characters it seems out of place in a fictional story. I even find myself holding some legal qualms. Never before had I felt as though I should have signed a Non-Disclosure Agreement before playing a game. Perhaps I've missed a disclaimer somewhere clarifying "The Beginner's Guide" as a fictional meta-commentary on fandom, or more specifically the occassional failure of fans in discerning the difference between genuine friendship and excessive adulation, but if this mysterious "CODA" person indeed exists, I could see him preparing a lawsuit against Mr. Wreden for pricing his games and releasing them to the public without his permission or knowledge.
If CODA doesn't exist then, well, you've covered your butt legally, Davey. That sure was an elaborate, schizophrenic ruse. Well done.
Better yet, I'll be able to hold out for the hope that you're not a completely insane, approbation-dependent jerk seeking the friendship of other, equally unpleasant human beings. Maybe you're a great guy, but seriously: this game is not flattering to its characters.

The main feeling the game left me with was frustration, not enjoyment.
Parkour games are about going fast. To go fast, you need to figure out where you need to go in just a couple seconds. You need to see what obstacles and potential paths are around without much fuss. Mirror's Edge did this by giving you a lot of color contrtast. The Valley did it by putting real paths everywhere and studding them with glowing collectibles.
Downward gives you very dark areas so you can't see where you're going. It's kind of bad at giving hints about where to go next.
In order to go fast, you also need large areas in which to move. Mirror's Edge gives you spaces with multiple city blocks. The Valley gives you huge sections of the valley to just play around in. Downward gives you small, constrained areas.
And if you want to go fast, the game can't slow you down unexpectedly at random times. Downward does. Usually it's just frustrating, but at least once I've fallen to my death because it decided I should only be able to slowly shuffle instead of running.
Beyond that, Downward is supposed to be a puzzle game. I got fed up with a "puzzle" of hunting for a hidden object in a small area that was horribly inconveniient to navigate. I'm pretty sure I went through the whole area multiple times. I suspect I found the artifact it wanted me to find, but the game didn't register it. Conidering this was only about twenty minutes in, that's kind of egregious.

This is only the fourth Steam game I've written a review for. This is simply because this is one of very few games I have played on Steam which I feel strongly enough to write a review for.
The Beginner's Guide is a game by Davey Wreden, as a sort of spiritual successor to The Stanley Parable. But where The Stanley Parable was comedic in tone, The Beginner's Guide is surprisingly melancholic and introspective. It's a game about making games, and about what it's like to make games.
Beyond that, I cannot say much without spoiling the game. It's one of those games where by the end of it, anything you really have to say about it would ruin it for someone who hasn't played it. But what I can say is that it's a game that will make you think, long after it's over. And that's good given how short it is; I took my time with it and still only clocked in at about 115 minutes. I can honestly say that despite the short length, this is the best $8 I've spent on a game, or on any fictive experience, in years.
Of course, if you take advantage of the fact that it's under 2 hours long, and get a Steam refund once the game is over despite having enjoyed it, you're a monster.
Don't be a monster.
But I digress... Buy The Beginner's Guide. You won't regret it. Trust me.

It doesn't matter if you like this game or not. This game is not for you.
I relate to everything this game has to offer more than I wish I do.
I feel, judging solely on the reviews, that this is a love it or hate it kind of game, much like most games in this vein do. Games like Dear Ester and Gone Home, "walking simulators".
That I won't delve into, because I know it's a topic that's been beat to death, both sides stubborn in their views.
I don't really care about that.
What I care about are the following:
1) Should this game have been sold for money?
Say what you will, but in my eyes, it really comes down to the type of society we live in today. Sure, Stanely Parable was a big hit. But you have to take into account that it was more of a cult hit more than anything else. So, I think that it's fair to come to the conclusion that Davey is probably not riding off a golden river from its profits, so to speak. So what do you do when you want to put a lot of effort into something, something so time consuming as making a game (albiet out of other already made games)? What do you do when you want this piece of work to be spread around? You want it to be talked about- you want the game to be popular by any means: by press, good or bad.
I think the easy solution would be to sell it.
2) Should Davey had made the game despite Coda's explicit wishes otherwise?
I will say first and foremost that as an artist, what you create is like an extension of your being. It is among the most personal and vunerable things you can share with another. It is not unlike putting yourself out on a limb when you ask someone to date you. What Davey did was absolutely wrong. Coda's work is obviously very personal.
And yet here I sit, telling you my thoughts on this collection on these secrets that weren't kept.
I'll say this: dealing with loss is never easy. Having to still deal with loss after four years is also never easy.
I can only imagine that Davey was at his wit's end. He wanted to desperately reach out, still, after all this time. And, it just so happens that he recently had a game success. So, he saw an oppurtunity, and he took it.
My initial reaction was that what he did was awful. It was wrong, and this game should have never existed.
But then, I put myself in his shoes. I asked myself, would I have taken the risk? Would I have bet it all, just for a slim chance at reconciliation? I, selfishly, would have.
But, it doesn't matter if I like this, or what I think of it. The only two people who matter are Davey and Coda.
I don't know what will come of this game. I can only hope it is good for the two of them.

Towerfall is an exceptional multiplayer game. I have yet to have a friend play it who did not instantly fall in love with it. It's mechanics are simple, making it easy for anyone to pick up and immediately have a lot of fun. My friend gifted it to me for my birthday, and that was definitely one of my favorite presents. That afternoon my tiny dorm room was filled with about 8 guys playing and spectating, all yelling and laughing.
This game is great fun in party settings, but it can also be extremely intense in a 1v1 match. A couple of my friends and I got really good and it started to become a sort of mind game where whoever had the upper hand was the one who could predict what the other player was going to do next. It was crazy.
If you're a casual gamer or not really a gamer at all, you will love this game for its simplicity, its openness, and the hilarious positions rounds find themselves in. If you are a more serious gamer you will love the tight controls and depth of combat the game provies.
Two more notes:
> This game balances extremely well--making it so people who are really good can play with people who are new and everyone will still have a lot of fun.
> This game is extremely polished. If your arrow flies through a torch, it will catch on fire. If your arrow nicks somebody's head, their hat will fly off and be off for the rest of the game. If the round is in a cold setting, you can see the characters' breath (even if they are invisible). This and more show the care the developers put into every detail. It is phenomenal. You should get it.
*note: buy cheap logitech Xinput controllers.

Infinifactory is a very challenging but fair 3D puzzle game. The goal is to take the component blocks supplied and construct/deconstruct them as the 'end goal' displays. This game is not unfair, as the only true obstacle between you and completing the puzzle is your own ability to make the production line between point A and point B. While there is one single puzzle from my memory that has 'RNG' applied to it, the rest of the puzzles are predictable and do not throw anything unexpected or unpredictable at you. The puzzles do ramp up in complexity rather fast, but the goal of each puzzle stays the same, only with more blocks added in to the solution. There is no point where you should feel like you’re fighting the game to complete a puzzle, and each finished level gave a strong sense of satisfaction.
The story isn't remarkable, but not unwelcome. When it comes to puzzle games I don't expect story as I am only there for the challenge the puzzles provide, but what was added to this game felt entertaining enough for me to enjoy. The setting as well adds variety to the environments you work in, changing things up just when the surroundings might start to feel same-y. The art style has a cartoon-y feel to it that I enjoy and has been fairly memorable, but I attribute that more to the unforgettable difficulty the game provides rather than the art style itself. The soundtrack is good, the kind of music that plays in the background and does not distract the player while getting rid of any uncomfortable silence, but is also something nice to listen to when you need to step back from a puzzle and think about it without intense focus.
Another small feature that adds to the challenge of the game is the scoreboards of ‘Cycles’, how fast you can complete the goal, ‘Footprint’, minimizing the area your factory takes up, and ‘Blocks’, minimizing the utility blocks added in to your factory. There are no scores by the game that you’re expected to beat, but each puzzle shows a chart of scores other users have received on the same puzzle. It adds an extra, but entirely optional, challenge in for you to try and optimize your factory as best as you can.
Ironically I have not beaten this game, but this is due to my own shortcomings rather than the game. Despite getting stuck I still have a fair bit of time logged and found the game to be highly addictive. The difficulty near the end is very high, and while I do know the solution exists, my own perfectionism and impatience has made me take a bit of a break from the game. That being said, I still think the game is fantastic and unfortunately very underrated, as there isn't anything I can really complain about when it comes to Infinifactory. Zachtronics knew what they wanted to do, they set out and did it, and everything about it feels right. Come to the game for the puzzle, and enjoy the sci-fi worlds they added in while you're bashing your head on your desk trying to figure out one of the level solutions.
The only reason this game is not a 10/10 is because they decided to add in a story that was average, but without the story or variation in level environments, I do not think it would be worth the current price tag.

Warface used to be a decent F2P FPS when it first came out. Since
took over the game from Crytek, the game has really gone downhill especially with the nerf to the ingame economy system. I started playing Warface in 2013 when I got accepted to the closed beta and this was when the game used the Gface launcher client. I'm not one to judge the microtransactions and pay-to-win aspects of the game because Warface is free and the developers need some way to make money. Being the cheapskate I was, I mainly used the default weapon kits with some health regenerating armour to play both PVP and PVE, in order to make as much ingame currency as possible and to reduce equipment repair costs. I was okay with this. However,
at some point significant reduced the amount of ingame currency and experience gained per mission. Players, such as myself, often lost more money than they gained for completing PVE missions if they used any equipment outside of the default gear. It got to the point where even completing the mission with the first-win-of-the-day bonus could get a player to lose money; failing missions completely punished the player for even attempting the missions. Essentially, the only way to gain ingame currency was to pay real money for XP and money boosts. That being said, free-to-players (most of the playerbase) should stay far away from this game until
decides to revert the economy changes (which will pretty much never happen).

A lot of games make a big deal out of player choice, but few in recent memory offer so many intricate, meaningful ways of approaching any given situation. You fulfill or dash the spiritual hopes of an idyllic society, side with slavers or their slaves, and decide the fate of more than one city over the course of your postapocalyptic journey through the Washington, DC wasteland. Your actions have far-reaching consequences that affect not just the world around you but also the way you play, and it's this freedom that makes Fallout 3 worth playing--and replaying. It's deep and mesmerizing, and though not as staggeringly broad as the developer's previous games, it's more focused and vividly realized.
Welcome to the wasteland.
Welcome to the wasteland.
This focus is obvious from the first hour of the game, in which character creation and story exposition are beautifully woven together. It's an introduction best experienced on your own rather than described in detail here, but it does set up Fallout 3's framework: It's the year 2277, and you and your father are residents of Vault 101, one of many such constructs that shelter the earth's population from the dangers of postnuclear destruction. When dad escapes the vault without so much as a goodbye, you go off in search of him, only to find yourself snagged in a political and scientific tug of war that lets you change the course of the future. As you make your way through the decaying remnants of the District and its surrounding areas (you'll visit Arlington, Chevy Chase, and other suburban locales), you encounter passive-aggressive ghouls, a bumbling scientist, and an old Fallout friend named Harold who has, well, a lot on his mind. Another highlight is a diminutive collective of Lord of the Flies-esque refugees who reluctantly welcome you into their society, assuming that you play your cards right.
The city is also one of Fallout 3's stars. It's a somber world out there, in which a crumbling Washington Monument stands watch over murky green puddles and lurching beasts called mirelurks. You'll discover new quests and characters while exploring, of course, but traversing the city is rewarding on its own, whether you decide to explore the back rooms of a cola factory or approach the heavily guarded steps of the Capitol building. In fact, though occasional silly asides and amusing dialogue provide some humorous respite, it's more serious than previous Fallout games. It even occasionally feels a bit stiff and sterile, thus diminishing the sense of emotional connection that would give some late-game decisions more poignancy. Additionally, the franchise's black humor is present but not nearly as prevalent, though Fallout 3 is still keenly aware of its roots. The haughty pseudogovernment called the Enclave and the freedom fighters known as the Brotherhood of Steel are still powerful forces, and the main story centers around concepts and objectives that Fallout purists will be familiar with.
Although some of that trademark Bethesda brittleness hangs in the air, the mature dialogue (it's a bit unnerving but wholly authentic the first time you hear 8-year-olds muttering expletives) and pockets of backstory make for a compelling trek. There are more tidbits than you could possibly discover on a single play-through. For example, a skill perk (more on these later) will enable you to extract information from a lady of the evening, information that in turn sheds new light on a few characters--and lets you complete a story quest in an unexpected way. A mission to find a self-realized android may initiate a fascinating look at a futuristic Underground Railroad, but a little side gossiping might let you lie your way to quest completion. There aren't as many quests as you may expect, but their complexity can be astonishing. Just be sure to explore them fully before pushing the story forward: Once it ends, the game is over, which means that you'll need to revert to an earlier saved game if you intend to explore once you finishe the main quest.
Thus choices are ruled only by your own sense of propriety and the impending results. For every "bad" decision you make (break into someone's room, sacrifice a soldier to save your own hide), your karma goes down; if you do something "good" (find a home for an orphan, give water to a beggar), your karma goes up. These situations trigger more consequences: Dialogue choices open up, others close off, and your reputation will delight some while antagonizing others. For example, a mutant with a heart of gold will join you as a party member, but only if your karma is high enough, whereas a brigand requires you to be on the heartless side. Even in the last moments of the game, you are making important choices that will be recounted to you during the ending scene, similar to the endings in the previous Fallout games. There are loads of different ending sequences depending on how you completed various quests, and the way they are patched together into a cohesive epilogue is pretty clever.
Fallout 3 remains true to the series’ character development system, using a similar system of attributes, skills, and perks, including the S.P.E.C.I.A.L. system from previous games for your attributes, such as strength, perception, and endurance. From there, you can specialize in a number of skills, from heavy weapons and lock-picking to item repairing and terminal hacking. You will further invest in these skills each time you level, and you'll also choose an additional perk. Perks offer a number of varied enhancements that can be both incredibly helpful and a bit creepy. You could go for the ladykiller perk, which opens up dialogue options with some women and makes others easier to slay. Or the cannibal perk, which lets you feed off of fallen enemies to regain health at the risk of grossing out anyone who glimpses this particularly nasty habit. Not all of them are so dramatic, but they're important aspects of character development that can create fascinating new options.
The VATS system makes for some awesome-looking battles.
The VATS system makes for some awesome-looking battles.
Although you can play from an odd-looking third-person perspective (your avatar looks like he or she is skating over the terrain), Fallout 3 is best played from a first-person view. Where combat is concerned, you will play much of the game as if it is a first-person shooter, though awkwardly slow movement and camera speeds mean that you'll never confuse it for a true FPS. Armed with any number of ranged and melee weapons, you can bash and shoot attacking dogs and random raiders in a traditional manner. Yet even with its slight clunkiness, combat is satisfying. Shotguns (including the awesome sawed-off variant) have a lot of oomph, plasma rifles leave behind a nice pile of goo, and hammering a mutant's head with the giant and cumbersome supersledge feels momentously brutal. Just be prepared to maintain these implements of death: Weapons and armor will gradually lose effectiveness and need repairing. You can take them to a specialist for fixing, but you can also repair them yourself, as long as you have another of the same item. It's heartbreaking to break a favored weapon while fending off supermutants, but it reinforces the notion that everything you do in Fallout 3, even shooting your laser pistol, has consequences.
No matter what platform you own, you should play Fallout 3, which overcomes its issues by offering a deep and involving journey through a world that's hard to forget. It has more in common with Bethesda's Elder Scrolls series than with previous Fallout games, but that is by no means a bad thing. In fact, Fallout 3 is leaner and meaner than Bethesda's previous efforts, less expansive but more intense, while still offering immense replay value and quite a few thrills along the way.

Before I get into my opinion of the Game please be aware that I am writing this Review while Ground Breakers is still in Early Access, so it is not completely polished yet and things might change before the official release.
With that being said, most of what I have to say about Ground Breakers is very positive. Let's get to the most important part for a game like the first, the Gameplay:
Ground Breakers is a turn-based strategy game where you fight with Robots on a randomly generated Grid of varying size. While this sounds simplistic, it gives the game a surprising amount of depth and I'll do my best to elaborate why. The grid itself is nothing new of course and they way United Indie implemented this cornerstone of turn-based gaming is very good. It gives you a good battleground to fight on without feeling too small and restricting, but also not so big that there is much downtime.
Where Ground Breakers shines is the implementation of height differences and the individual robots. Being on High Ground gives you and advante in combat, but it is more costly to move to a higher position. So moving one of you Robots onto a good high ground position is a big commitment, but also with a good reward attached to it, if you can pull it off!
Now let's talk about the Robots, which is of course what this game is all about. I'll get to the artstyle in a moment, let's focus on the mechanics for now. There is a surprising number of different Robots available, that you unlock gradually and randomly (the order in which you get them) as far as I can tell. Each Robot comes with 3 Skills. This in combination with the general Attributes (like Movement, Damage, Health or AttackRange) make for very unique Robots and they all have a very distinct feel to them. There is also a big reward to unlocking a new Robot and being able to use him for the first time in combat.
All in all, Ground Breakers gets a lot of the Gameplay bascis right, which makes for a very solid foundation to build upon. Let's move on the the Graphics:
Art Style and wether or not you like it is a very subjective matter. I personally really like the style they are going for. It is simplistic and very fitting with the Genre. The Robots themselves are designed with a lot of care and once again they managed to created something that not only handles uniquely, but also looks the part. United Indie did an amazing job of creating a package that at least for me works very well. From the choice of skills to the design of the individual Robots it comes together in a very fitting way.
The Main Menus background is a bit bland at the moment, but I assume they will change that before the game comes out of early access. Aside from that there I not much I could criticize.
Let's move on to another aspect of the game that could make or break a game like this, and that is the A.I.:
From what I have seen of the A.I. it is very good. They make smart choices and use their skills. They attack weakened units and make good choices in their priority. I am playing on normal most of the time (as long as you can choose the difficulty), so it should get harder on a higher difficulty. That being said, it never really feels unfair. If you have a good grasp on the game mechanics, you can appreciate the fair fight that the A.I. is putting up. I don't know too much about the mechanics behind A.I. in general, but in my opinion it looks like solid work that will be challenging, but not entirely unfair.
Now that I have covered the cornerstones, let's talk a little bit about the game modes you have available. First up, there is the Campaign mode. It's not really a sort of Story mode but a way to take what the game does, so the individual battles and put it in a more complex setting. In the campaign you choose the difficulty, the amount of opponents and the size of the map. You then try to conquer areas (so squares on a gridded world map) and try to eliminate your opponents, who are doing the same. This is rounded out by a round system. So you have only limited actions per turn and once you have used them up, your opponents make their move. Then the whole thing starts over again. It's a nice way to give your battles a bit more meaning then just the short-lived battles.
There is also a layer of economy in the campaign that is absent from the rest of the game, which adds in another interesting layer to work with.
Next up you have the Scenarios. Here you get thrown into specific settings you have to win. For example you have to defend a Crystal from the enemy until you either destroy them all or the time runs out. The enemy Robots will be respawning though, so it is harder than it sounds. Admittedly I haven't gotten too far into the Scenarios yet, but what I have seen so far looks good. It is more about working with your ressources to win a single battle, than an overall campaign.
The next game mode is the Infinity mine. At this point there are 100 levels of the Infinity Mine and they get gradually harder. Something I haven't mentioned so far is the option to customize and upgrade your Robots. With that you can modify them or just make them overall better. You will have to do that to progress in the mine, as the enemy does not match you strength, but works of a set difficulty. You can upgrade you Robots a lot and if you want to make progress you will have to do that. Even though this means grinding out items to upgrade your Robots, I like the mine. It's an awesome feeling to be really challenged, because you might be a bit too weak for the mine and still win. They also use the Mine to implement a simplisitc Quest system that allows them to teach you a bit about the story and history of the world they have created. Although personally I wouldn't necessarily need that, it is a nice added bonus.
So before I come to and end here, let me explain the customization of the Robots a little bit more. What you need to know first is that even though there are several game modes, the Robots you unlock and their upgrades stay in every mode. So you don't need to start over in every mode, but can share your progress throughout them all!
There are two ways of upgrading your Robots. The first one is the improvement of the quality of materials in the Robot. You start on the Iron level and if you have the correct Silver parts, you can upgrade your Robot to a higher level. Next will be Gold (I think) and so on and so forth until you reach the end. It can be a bit frustrating if you can't find the right parts to upgrade a Robot, but once you do it feels very rewarding and the increase in power is noticeable enough to make a difference.
The second way is to insert Chips into the Robot. You once again have a Grid where you can insert Chips to get varying effects, for example a small healthregain on every normal attack. So even though two Robots might be same Level, they could play differently, depending on the Chips used.
The last game mode is Multiplayer, but as I did not get a chance to try that one out yet, I can't say anything about that.
With that said, let me come to a conclusion. This review did run a bit longer than I initially anticipated. Even though Ground Breakers is an Early Access game, it feels and plays very good already. In my opinion the found the right mix between game modes and progression to keep you motivated and invested in the game. It is a lot of fun to play and once you grasp the concept and figure out how to use the individual Robots and how their skills can synergize with each other, it gets even better.
If you are into turn-based strategy games you can't do anything wrong with Ground Breakers. They chose the scale of the game very carefully and created a very good game!
That's it and I hope you found this Review helpful and informative :)

A little background on the story: You are a journalist that has dealt with irregular stories and this is your next one. You were emailed by a person who goes by the name of whistleblower and you find your self in asylum were it apparantly has gone crazy. As you adventure through the game you find even more disturbing stuff than you would ever imagine... and the worst part you can't turn back and escape. You must film everything you can with your video camera and show the world this place.
The campaigns: Both the DLC and the normal campaign have really good story lines to them. They very nicely linked between eachother with the storyline. The campaign really is a winner from this game and it seems pretty believable to. Not many horror games can really have a great balance of horror and storyline but these guys got it just right. So it keeps the tension high and doesn't fall short for each stage of the game as you find out about the Asylum. Just keeps you on the edge of your seat the whole way through the game and sometimes you even fall off your seat. You never know whats around the next corner. I would recommend this for both the great thrilling campaign and for those unscarable people who would like a freight.
Now the actual scare factor: This game envolves mostly jump scares and very intense chases (mostly chases). But as you encounter new characters and enemies you have to use the environment to your advantage not many horror games do this very well but this game achieved this with ease and nicely. The jump scares arnt cheesy either, which is a good thing, so it is very orignal with its jump scares. The chases are all ways very intense and have lots of tension for you to survive. Some times you must be chased to escape a zone which may seem hard for some players but adds another challenge to the game for me. Escaping can envolve being chased and moving objects at the same time.
Controls: The crontrols are very straight forward wasd keys to move around and mouse to look around. Tab can bring up a menu allowing to access collected files and your personnel diary that you log into whenever a significant event is caught on camera. Hold left shift with wasd keys is to run. spacebar to jump and Ctrl is to crouch. Clicking can allow you to interact with objects like document and doors etc. Right click allows to record with the camera and pressing the f key while in this mode allows you to turn on night vision and waist battery life. Only in night  vision mode you can consume battery life so in theory you will have to find batterys to power night vision which is used a lot. Clicking on a battery interacts with it and picks it up to be stored. Pressing the r key can replace your current battery with a new battery (only do this once battery is out of charge).
Graphics: The graphics really toped off the game and made it look really nice and sweat. As long as you have a great cumputer with a good graphics card and enough ram, like me, you can play with all of the settings to the max for a stunning looking game. With the graphics settings to the max the game flourishes visually and looks divine. Even with a less great computer you can get maximum settings with a little bit of lag. Normally even with the settings at about medium it can look just as good. Maximum settings just makes the image look crisp with the tiny details. Depends how you would like to play with your computer.
Summary: Excellent game with a divine campaign and the scariest characters. Also with graphics that look stunning anyone would enjoy this game. I highly recommend this and would give it a score of 9.5/10.

First, I know that I checked "No" to recommend this game. However, if there were a "Possibly" button, I would check that instead.
What I liked about it: Graphics are pretty decent, music is dramatic and fitting. Right from the start I am intrigued. Wandering about this asylum with many people of questionable sanity (some of whom do not attack you, some of whom do) can be quite dramatic, it is that not knowing what a patient will do as you walk right by them that adds a certain suspense to the game.
What I didn't like: This is not the first game to have you run/hide from enemies rather than fight them. A good concept for a horror game, however, this game does not execute it well. You should get familier with the inside of a locker (the typical hiding place) Seeing a locker instantly tells you that you'll probably encounter an enemy nearby. The AI is both irritating and predictable. It irritates by having enemies consistantly blocking the only paths to objectives. It is predictable by the nature of flipping virtually any switch or button acting as a trigger and spawning an enemy following a path blocking you to your next objective. The high level of scripted mini-scenes also become formulaic and predictable, while the larger ones simply become disturbing, not frightening.
While darkness is also a significant factor in horror games, this is also not executed well, there are parts in which the game is so unfathomably and unrealisticly dark, your night vision can only see the floor about one step ahead of you. I understand that not seeing something can add a level "fear of the unknown" but when you can't see the next step in front of your feet with "night vision" on, it becomes too much.
Next, the type of "Horror" this game chooses to be. To be compared to Horror movies, this is the "Saw" of Horror games, not in the half decent story with a twist way either.
This game is all disturbance and no substance, with a hint of senseless gore. For instance, if you find people impaled on spears telling you to "Get out of here" and inmates having gay sex with other beheaded inmates to be "Horror" then this is for you. The story also takes a drastic and pointless turn mid-game for no real reason.
If you are looking for a game that leaves you hunched in your chair and whispering "Oh♥♥♥♥♥♥ he's right there, he's going to see me." Then don't look here, look to the Amnesia titles.
Overall, this game is more "Eww" and "Damn it's really dark in here" than actually attempting to scare you. If the game is on sale and you are looking for a game to play and want the gross factor at a 9 out of 10, then consider it a decent buy. If you want to be tensed up on your keyboard, hunched in your chair, and occasionaly jumping out of your seat in a way that sends your cats running for the hills, then go to the Amensia pages.

[Please note that this game was provided to me free of cost to review.]
Ground breakers is a turn based strategy combat game from United Indie currently in early access.  You fight on randomly generated maps with your robot army in an attempt to eliminate all of the opponents, capture tactic points, protection missions, and other objectives.
You collect spare parts to upgrade your robots and enhance their abilities.  The special chips that you collect can be pieced together like tetris pieces to add additional bonuses such as stun modifiers and health gain per attack among many other options.  The robots level up throughout the matches and allow you to spend points during the matches to unlock their powerful special skills.
The game is visually appealing and plays well for its stage in development.  There are a few gameplay bugs that I have encountered and I wish that there was more instruction or pop up tips that explain mechanics and areas like the shop more thoroughly.  If you really enjoyed the gameplay and the visual style I would recommend that you pick it up, however I would suggest that you wait a little longer in the development cycle so that the developers can work out a few more bugs and improve the systems.

The Beginner's Guide is a game by Davey Wreden, as a sort of spiritual successor to The Stanley Parable. But where The Stanley Parable was comedic in tone, The Beginner's Guide is surprisingly melancholic and introspective. It's a game about making games, and about what it's like to make games.
Beyond that, I cannot say much without spoiling the game. It's one of those games where by the end of it, anything you really have to say about it would ruin it for someone who hasn't played it. I can honestly say that despite the short length, this is the best $8 I've spent on a game, or on any fictive experience, in years.
Of course, if you take advantage of the fact that it's under 2 hours long, and get a Steam refund once the game is over despite having enjoyed it, you're a monster.
Don't be a monster.
But I digress... Buy The Beginner's Guide. You won't regret it. Trust me.

It doesn't matter if you like this game or not. This game is not for you.
I relate to everything this game has to offer more than I wish I do.
I feel, judging solely on the reviews, that this is a love it or hate it kind of game, much like most games in this vein do. Games like Dear Ester and Gone Home, "walking simulators".
That I won't delve into, because I know it's a topic that's been beat to death, both sides stubborn in their views.
I don't really care about that.
What I care about are the following:
1) Should this game have been sold for money?
Say what you will, but in my eyes, it really comes down to the type of society we live in today. Sure, Stanely Parable was a big hit. But you have to take into account that it was more of a cult hit more than anything else. So, I think that it's fair to come to the conclusion that Davey is probably not riding off a golden river from its profits, so to speak. So what do you do when you want to put a lot of effort into something, something so time consuming as making a game (albiet out of other already made games)? What do you do when you want this piece of work to be spread around? You want it to be talked about- you want the game to be popular by any means: by press, good or bad.
I think the easy solution would be to sell it.
2) Should Davey had made the game despite Coda's explicit wishes otherwise?
I will say first and foremost that as an artist, what you create is like an extension of your being. It is among the most personal and vunerable things you can share with another. It is not unlike putting yourself out on a limb when you ask someone to date you. What Davey did was absolutely wrong. Coda's work is obviously very personal.
And yet here I sit, telling you my thoughts on this collection on these secrets that weren't kept.
I'll say this: dealing with loss is never easy. Having to still deal with loss after four years is also never easy.
I can only imagine that Davey was at his wit's end. He wanted to desperately reach out, still, after all this time. And, it just so happens that he recently had a game success. So, he saw an oppurtunity, and he took it.
My initial reaction was that what he did was awful. It was wrong, and this game should have never existed.
But then, I put myself in his shoes. I asked myself, would I have taken the risk? Would I have bet it all, just for a slim chance at reconciliation? I, selfishly, would have.
But, it doesn't matter if I like this, or what I think of it. The only two people who matter are Davey and Coda.
I don't know what will come of this game. I can only hope it is good for the two of them.

The Long Dark is a thoughtful, exploration-survival experience that challenges solo players to think for themselves as they explore an expansive frozen wilderness in the aftermath of a geomagnetic disaster. There are no zombies -- only you, the cold, and all the threats Mother Nature can muster.
Okay, this game has to be one of my favorite, if not my favorite, survival games of all time.  The games visuals are stunning, especially indoors with the light beaming through the windows, and I also enjoy the cartoony artstyle that they went for.  The survival mechanics are great, making you survive the cold, hunger, and thirst.   The game also has windchill, and blizzards that can randomly occur.  Let's say you're walking down the road and all of a sudden a blizzard hits.  If you can find a car, you can get inside and it will prevent the windchill from the blizzard, making your character much warmer.  There is no randomly generated world.  The maps are all customly made, so there isn't as much area to explore, but alot more detail than you would find in a game with random generation.  Also, all the maps are connected, so when a new map is realeased, you can go to it, and the older maps.  The developers are updating this often with gameplay improvements, new maps, and new items   I would definetly recommend this game to anyone who enjoys survival games.  That also reminds me, this is just a survival game.  You are surviving nothing but mother nature, no zombies, aliens, nothing like that.  Just pure mother nature.

This game is a great classic shooter. Out of all the Unreal Tournament games, this is probably my favorite game, and it isn't just nostalgia talking there either.
Unreal Tournament is pretty fast-paced. The guns are also different; you have your standard bullet-firing Enforcer and Sniper Rifle, and you have more exotic types like the plasma-firing Pulse Gun and the bio-sludge firing... Bio Gun.
The modding community behind this game is immense, and is still alive even today. Installing mods is as easy as grabbing the right UMOD, and installing it, or in the absence of a UMOD, you just drag-and-drop files to the right directory.
This game offers a story-line too, but as with other games in the series, it's mainly you vs bots on known multiplayer game types (CTF, Deathmatch, etc). Bots have various levels of difficulty, and make great practice.
Mutators are also a fun way to spice-up matches. Tired of the old weapons, and want a match with more insta-kill shenanigans? Throw on Instagib and get a modified Shock Rifle that delivers red beams of insta-death :p New mutators can also be delivered through mods.
A really popular recommended mod to get is ChaosUT, and I believe it even came with original Unreal Tournament GOTY discs back in the day (but is strangely absent from the Steam version).
The graphics may look a bit dated, but guess what? You can also fix that easily through mods :) Original GOTY discs also used to ship with ST3C textures to enhance the game's textures. These are nice and all, but the site UT Textures also offers even higher-quality textures for low-end (still better than the original ST3C textures), high-end, and extreme-end computers. Pair that with a newer renderer (like Marijn Kenti's D3D10 renderer, or the D3D9 or updated OpenGL renderer on Chris Dohnal's site), and you'll have yourself a very nice-looking classic! ENBSeries has nothing on those modifications.
Audio can also be updated. The easiest way to do this is to grab the updated multimedia package from Oldunreal's site. This allows for updated audio backends, like OpenAL and FMOD.
This game is a real treat, and it's really hard to find a reason on why not to buy it. If you've never played an Unreal Tournament game, haven't tried the classic version, or even if you want to re-visit a classic gem, get this.

I didn't have any prior knowledge to what this game was about before playing. While I love the effort put into RPG Maker for these sorts of games, unfortunately I just don't feel like I can recommend this one.
It feels unfinished, like this was a build to get things balanced before the story was fully written, and unfortunately the balancing just didn't happen either. As others have said, the enemies level up with you, which would have been fine if the shops did too, but once you have the basic equipment you run out of things to spend money on other than health potions, of which you will be using a lot because the armor is quickly outpaced by the damage of enemies. Your own damage does comparatively less as you level, and enemies take longer to kill the more you play, until it takes a minute to bring down a basic enemy by knocking them back into a wall to stun-lock them in place.
The achievements are simple and easy to get, and the game elements like harvesting flowers as impromptu potion materials can be quite charming, but ultimately the game fell flat on the one thing most important to gaming. It just wasn't that fun. I didn't have to finish it to get the achievements, and unless I have a pretty dull day at work on this dusty laptop, I probably won't ever see where the story was heading. It was just too lacking to keep me invested.
This survival horror is definetly on its way to becoming one of the greats but still needs lots of work to reach that point.
