I'm normally a bit generous towards low budget indie RPGMaker games but I really can't recommend it.  It has a number of problems:
-The game needs a proofreader.  There's spelling, grammar and punctuation mistakes all over the place.
-Features are introduced early on in the game and then forgotten.  The hookshot is used about a half dozen times in the first 15 minutes, then never again.  Crafting is the same way.
-Enemies level alongside you, making fighting largely pointless.
-The plot and world is bare bones and mostly generic.
-Bad scripting in some places.  In Oblivia, I stayed  at the inn.  When I left the inn I found myself back at the inn at the beginning of the game.
-Very underwhelming ending.  The final boss says "Well Done" when you defeat him and then dumps the player back to the title screen
-The player can choose one of several character classes, but it doesn't seem to have much of an impact on anything other than the weapons you can use.
On the other hand, the game is very short so speedrunners might like it, and the achievements are easy.

Counter-Strike: Source retains its team-based objective-orientated first-person shooter style gameplay. The aim of playing a map is to accomplish a map's objective: defusing the bomb, rescuing all hostages, or killing the entire opposing team. The ultimate goal of the game is to win more rounds than the opposing team. Once players are killed, they do not respawn until the next round, though this depends on which server people play on. This gameplay feature distinguishes Counter-Strike from other first-person shooter games, where players respawn instantly or after a short delay.
Shooting while moving dramatically decreases accuracy, and holding the trigger down to continuously shoot produces severe recoil. The severity of damage induced by weaponry is dependent upon the specific locations of hits, with hits to the head being most lethal and shots which make contact elsewhere causing lesser loss of health. Damage is also affected by the distance, and if the target wears protection.

Banished. The title of this game describes everything pretty well.
You're an outcast, thrown out of your old home to start over from scratch.
You and some few other settlers will face the many horrors of a young civilization.
Stay one step ahead at all time, and prepare for next year. Will the firewood last? How much food will your citizens eat, and can you survive a year without crops if it was destroyed by locusts?
This game goes one step further than all those other AAA-simulators that focus on giving you an easy start to get you hooked.
The creator of this game does the opposite! You plant your crops and chop your wood, or you'll be witness of how 90% of your population dies in a matter of seconds. Be prepared to start over plenty of times to get that perfect village going!
I bought this game the day it was released, in 2014. Since then I've starved. Frozen to death. My village burned down. Refugees coming and sucking my resouces until we all died horribly.
But I have also watched few become many. Villagers turned nothing but a forest into a beautiful flourishing city, and when I finally got everything under control and my city is complete.. watched it all burn down and start over.
10/10 Would buy again.

I'm impressed, positively. This game it's a fusion beetween an rpg, mirror's edge and the talos principle, everithing with a strong platform taste. You go around free in this wasted lands, parkouring and "fighting enemies" (you can avoid most of them if you want), collecting objects and improving your character. If you go far too soon there are stronger enemies that kills you, wich is nice, being a platform-parkour game I like that combats are avoidable, and useful only if you need artifacts to explore more.
Level Design: I love that you never know if a passage brings you in a small room or in another different "world", it gives me a great sense of exploration like dark souls 1. Also the quality of the graphics enhanced the desire to explore.
Voice Acting: Nice voice acting, I was in love with the woman's voice that guides you, (spoiler) at least until I saw who she was. The old man its great.
Parkour: it is less fast-oriented than ME and more relaxing, more platform. This works ok with metroidvania level design. The difficulty of the parkour is well-balanced, never frustrating and the mark it's an ingenious add, a lot like POP but faster and more useful than the time-mechanics
In conclusion: I feel that this game it's something that the market needed, it has some small bugs but it seems that the devs are open to feedback and being their first game it's a very good start for me.
Worth the price if you like exploring, platforming or the visuals of the game, but don't expect a AAA game for this price (in both negative and posirive meaning)

I got this game, I have not played it very much, but I do have one story for you. Gather round children.
I though, "Yeah, I've studied the Napoleonic wars, I'll be good at this game!" so I hopped on multiplayer.
At first I thought I would be good.
I lost all of my Cavalry and most of my Infantry within fifteen minutes. The only reason I was still alive was because of my artillery.
Then I realized something: I was going to be Wellington. I was going to recover and route all of his infantry.
With the rest of my Line infantry, I ran, leading them into my artillery on a hill. With a combination of cannister shot and Volleys, they were breaking. Then, his cav charged and killed most of my infantry.
But I have forgotten about three units.
Three units that I had moved into the trees at the start of the round and forgotten about.
My rifles.
I quickly moved my rifles into position. They quickly killed many of his militia, causing a route. His cav tried killing them, buy my riflemen were not fazed. They killed almost all of the cav as they charged. When they met my brave riflemen, we lost one man. His cav was dead by my brave riflemen.
Then, in a last ditch effort, he sent in his Grenadiers. His elite infantry against my rifles. They outnumbered them, and they were stronger.
But my Brave riflemen did not run. They fired on them from afar, then, without giving the grenadiers a chance to recover, the brave riflemen, who were full with energy, charged against the tired, wavering grenadiers.
My brave riflemen killed all of the Grenadiers.
The brave riflemen, the last men on the battlefield, the only men to have not routed or died, had won the battle.
Heroic Victory.
10/10, would forget about riflemen then say ♥♥♥♥ it and charge again.

This game really embodies a struggle that many of us go through. Who are we? What do we want? How are we supposed to fix our problems? Wouldn't it be nice to share our feelings, our ideas with someone?
Sometimes, its uncomfortable to admit or witness the truth. We surround ourselves with friends, media, work, or in this case, video games to avoid the truth, to keep everything the way it is, to keep away from change.
On the flip side, it is nice to get to know someone, know what they're feeling, know how they see life. What is more beautiful than perspective? We all have our opinions, our experiences, but it gets awkward to share them in a serious environment. Frequently, we change details to give people a good opinion of ourselves. We lie.
This "game" is the naked truth, however hard it might be to admit. It shows that no matter what side we're on, we believe what we are doing is right. We may never know the issues we create. Many times, we don't know how to solve our own either.

Just noticed I never reviewed this game.
Prior to this game there was Empire: Total War, another game of the Total War series that took place during the 1700-1840.
Cannons and muskets are the dominant force on the field.
As the title suggest the wars you will see and take part in, will be between Napoleonic France and his Allies vs. those that oppose the little Emperor.
Pros
-You enemy is clear for the most part, you do not need to spend so much time in diplomacy.
-The Tech tree has been re-worked and has been dumbed down to focus on Military recruitment, tactics and nation moral. The only part of the tree that still gains technological benefit from research is the Naval Tree, which unlocks better ports and ships.
-Battles are not just about cannons. Calvary has been given a needed boost, making them the fierce opponent they would have been historically.
-Each nation has a respectable and historical (In a sense) start when it comes to regions owned, and troops deployed.
-Very long story campaign.
-Challenging
Cons
-A very annoying sound bug can occur that potentially results in the game crashing. Luckily it tends to only happen on the campaign map.
-France has a Light Calvary unit that has bugged stats, which make it superior against all other types of Calvary. The AI knows this and will field massive armies of this unit if appropriate funds are achieved.
-Ships feel more brittle and will sink with much more ease. (A pro for some)
- Cannons still determine the battle out come. Being that one well placed explosive shell can completely turn the tide of battle.
-Limited number of playable factions to about six.
However there are many mods and online fixes out there to get the game working to the degree you want it too. I do not use mods, and still have fun when I get the Napoleon itch.

Napoleon: Total War is always that one game that I'll remember with nostalgic feelings and how much I love this game. It hooked me for the Napoleonic era and well more history in general.
For the complete newcomers - total war is a turn-based strategy with real time tactical battles between the armies, usually composed of 20 units max. each. During the battle you give commands to each of the unit or more of them at the same time, while applying tactics. Results of the battle, obviously, reflect on your strategy on the turn based campaign map. Easily the most popular ones are Rome: Total War and Medieval II: Total War.
One of my favourite Total Wars definetly. It took what Empire wanted to create - a new environment of a new kind of warfare with gunpowder and bayonets - and turned it gloriously better.
My favourite aspect of the game was in fact the storytelling - surprising from a strategy game - as it told the story of each of the Napoleon's campaigns while retaining it's sandbox values allowing you to do much more than what Napoleon accomplished.
It also has many of Napoleon's famous historical battles that you can play outside of the campaign (like Waterloo, Borodino, Austerlitz...), with Waterloo being the expection because you can play it from the British perspective as well, while others are from French perspective.

“The oldest and strongest emotion of mankind is fear, and the oldest and strongest kind of fear is fear of the unknown” - H.P. Lovecraft
Outlast scares me! Thus far I have been able to play it in 20 minute sessions, not for a lack of time, oh no, I am limited to 20 minutes because I lack the nerve to continue. Alone in a dark room, late at night, my nerve is quickly whittled away.
Last night I sat down at 8:45 Pm. I can reasonably play until 11:30. This time I leave the lights on in the room. My wife is sitting on the couch only six feet from me. I can do this!
The game play is simple. Walk around pick stuff up, click on buttons and open doors. Oh god, opening doors! I don’t know what’s on the other side, it could me nothing… but it could be… something! If there is something behind the door, I will run and hide… because… those are my options.
Run or Hide.
I have no gun, no strength, and no Fighting chance! I’m not Marcus Fenix, or Master Chief, hell I’m not even as tough as Luigi. I’m a reporter, a writer, an average Joe. This helplessness it what makes Outlast truly terrifying, helplessness in the face of the dark unknown.
The atmosphere is tense and the visuals are clean… well, not clean but crisp, or… Horrifying… Yah, Horrifying. For example, after I walk through a puddle of blood, I trail bloody footprints on the floor behind me.
I move through Mount Massive Asylum, carefully traveling from dim lamp to dangling florescent light. I’m forced to travel in the darkness. Terrible, terrible darkness, filled with the ruinous remains of the hospitals contents… and the hospitals staff… and the hospitals Patients…  Patients, some dead… some living. Living patients, pushed past the point of insanity. They are now prone to mindlessly inflicting Violence on anyone they can find. If they can’t find anyone… then they will inflict violence on themselves. Violence has become their total being, and their only form of expression.
Darkness is an ever present pressure, forcing itself on me… an inescapable weight on my mind and soul. I’m given one tool to combat the darkness. My ever trusty video camera, with a built in night vision setting. At least… it’s trusty as long as I have enough batteries… which I don’t. I never have enough batteries. I am always looking for more, but while I look, I must conserve the precious juice I have. So when approaching a long dark room, I click my night vision camera on, take a quick glance around the room to get an idea of the layout in my mind. Then I turn off the camera… and I run. I do this again and again, always panicked, always terrified.
But it’s not just me that is terrified, it the reporter, the character…he becomes overcome with fear. As we run through the darkness we hear the splash of a puddle at our feat… oh god... It’s blood… we push forward his breath intensifying, becoming erratic… Short gasps, punctuated by trembling exhalations… we stumble over something lying in the blood… We don’t stop to see what it is, because I know what we’ll find… the source of the blood, and the reporter knows it too. His breathing is becoming so intense that it is affecting our vision; the screen sways with each rise and fall of his lungs.  The world around us seems to tremble with a terrible fear.
Fear overcomes us. Both the reporter and I are paralyzed with it... unable to face the shadows at the end of the hall. We stand motionless for an eternity… unwilling to move forward… unwilling to face the horrible unknown that fill Mount Massive Asylum… I can’t take it.
I save the game and quit. The reporter is on his own. I abandon him to wait in that ever oppressive darkness… I look at the clock…
It mockingly displays the time as 9:04 Pm.
Sigh…

I can only half recommend this game.  I fully recommend it as a puzzle game, but I can't recommend it as a physics-based puzzle game.
As a puzzle game, it's got a lot going for it:  it's challenging without being too difficult (so far), it's logic-based, the controls are mostly intuitive, and it's even got sort of a story/lore with some decent humor.
However, this game must take place in some alternate universe where the laws of physics aren't applied evenly, and that bugs me.  Since you're scored on how many blocks you use for your solution (with fewer blocks being better), you often have to come up with solutions to the puzzles that would not work in real life to get a good score.  For instance, if you need to make a structure that is three blocks wide, you only need to support one of those blocks with a conveyor belt, and it doesn't matter which one.  That means you could have a conveyor under the leftmost block with nothing supporting the middle or right blocks, and the whole thing will keep moving along the conveyor as though the center of mass is supported when it clearly isn't.  That diminishes the game somewhat for me, but I realize that's a personal preference and that not everybody will care about that, hence the split recommendation.

Banished. The title of this game describes everything pretty well.
You're an outcast, thrown out of your old home to start over from scratch.
You and some few other settlers will face the many horrors of a young civilization.
Stay one step ahead at all time, and prepare for next year. Will the firewood last? How much food will your citizens eat, and can you survive a year without crops if it was destroyed by locusts?
This game goes one step further than all those other AAA-simulators that focus on giving you an easy start to get you hooked.
The creator of this game does the opposite! You plant your crops and chop your wood, or you'll be witness of how 90% of your population dies in a matter of seconds. Be prepared to start over plenty of times to get that perfect village going!
I bought this game the day it was released, in 2014. Since then I've starved. Frozen to death. My village burned down. Refugees coming and sucking my resouces until we all died horribly.
But I have also watched few become many. Villagers turned nothing but a forest into a beautiful flourishing city, and when I finally got everything under control and my city is complete.. watched it all burn down and start over.
10/10 Would buy again.

Banished... well it's a simulator.
This is not a "game" so much as a ... well a god game, you plant some ideas in the form of buildings, tweak some production numbers, plant a couple fields and sit back and hope for the best, and trust me, there will be a lot of sitting back if you play on normal speed, but it's oddly relaxing, and at times hilarious.
However, you plant too many ideas at once, forget to structure a decent food supply/ firewood supply, etc, then the logs all go the wrong places, and your little peasants freeze and starve to death : Game over.
Not assuming of course a freak tornado wrecks everything you've spent two weeks building or a fire burns it to cinders :P
Other than that, the game's pretty peaceful, nice relaxing experience, so long as you have the patience, if you're someone who likes something more upbeat then this will likely not be for you! There's no multiplayer feature, although a co-op city building game would be pretty damned baddass in the way of a rewarding experience... but, as it's a simulator, I doubt it'd happen.
There's some nice mods to add extra content, and plenty of room for you to make your own, but my advice would be to get this little game on a sale, then at least you can say you get your monies worth.
A good 7/10... if I'm in a good mood :D

Dont get me wrong, I love explosions as much as the next guy, but after the first 100 fuel tanks you strafe with an attack chopper the magic starts to loose its luster.  The same sound effect, same animation, and with the scale of the game world, you blow up a LOT of stuff.
Yes, the map is HUGE.  There is a staggering amount of things to find, and then blow up.  And it keeps track of them.  1020 fuel tanks, 90 statues, 320 broadcast towers, 185 SAM sites, 220 water towers, 490 gas pumps, and more.  There is never a shortage of things to blow up.  Or collect, because there are 3,000 separate collectables.
Where it falls flat is in the gun play.  So far there isnt a single gun in the arsenal that has a good feel.  You spend SO much time shooting at mooks, and until you unlock the ability to upgrade the machine gun, there just isnt a truly satisfying weapon.  Even the explosives, as much fun as they can be, lack that wow factor.
But I DO like it.  And now that its... older and cheap, your entertainment dollar will go a long way.  Kind of like this game world.
Also... there is the small issue of its amazingly badass multi-player mod...

Start off good, this game is currently unfinished, but it is by no mean unpolished. This small group of 3 people from Rome have blown me away with their amazing word, and fine eye for detail. I refund a lot of games, and after my first 5 minutes I knew I would be hooked! The character controller feels very smooth, and apart from a couple game breaking glitches that make you have restart your file (game is early access, what can you do) this game is well on it's way to being a full release. This game feels like it draws heavy inspiration from Mirror's Edge on it's parkour mechanics, yet it's cues are a little more subtle. Given the open world, you may find yourself going off track to explore, and does this game ever let you. Now let's talk about the bad, because there is a bit. The parkour is a little unrefined. Don't get me wrong, most of the time you will find it being flawless, however there are currently a few early access bugs that cause the character to react automatically to some wall cues and mess up your input (This never bugged me too much on my playthrough). Another flaw is the open world itself. The quest cues are a little confusing, at least they were for me until I explored just about the entire map and found my way into areas I shouldn't have been yet. Although it was really fun finding extra areas before completing the first story arch.
If you enjoy parkour style games, don't mind a bit of added action, and love exploring well thought out world, I would highly recommend this game to you.

If your having a problem with a code [NUMBER] then here it is. Some guy found the correct way to do this and I am now playing this on very high without any lag :D here it is:
"PART 1: This is to get Just Cause 2 to launch
1. Right click Just Cause 2 in your Steam Library and select PROPERTIES.
2. Select LAUNCH OPTIONS, and type in "/dxadapter=0" without quotes.
PART 2: This is to get your graphics card to render the game
1. Download Nvidia Inspector from:
2. Open Nvidia Inspector
3. Click the button to the right of DRIVER VERSION.
4. From the PROFILE menu, select JUST CAUSE 2.
5. Scroll down the window until you find: Shim Rendering Mode Options per application for Optimus.
6. Click the text to the right, scroll to the top of the dropdown, and select SHIM_RENDERING_OPTIONS_DEFAULT_RENDERING_MODE
7. Click APPLY CHANGES in the top right-hand corner.
8. Run your game"
-- Checked by me, it works.
UPDATE: When updating nvidia drivers, make sure you restart your computer and then redo these steps (without redownloading the inspector obviously) and reapply the correct settings. The game should then run normally again. this is due to the fact that after an update, those settings are reset to the default values and yo have to restart your computer because otherwise the nvidia inspector will not recognise your version of nvidia drivers.

I can't remember the last game I played that was this much pure fun. And I don't think I've laughed and screamed at the TV with any game this much outside of Smash. Towerfall is a fast paced brawler/platformer/shooter game. It guess it kind of defies genre classification. I suppose you could file it under party game? It plays best multiplayer, that's for sure.
Towerfall is kind of like Smash, except every hit is a one hit kill. And the levels wrap around Pac-Man style. And every player has projectiles. So I guess not really like Smash then, but it's similarly as fun. It's easy to pick up and play, the only buttons are jump, shoot and dodge. Moving your character around and learning the game is quick and easy, but like any good game, there's a deceptive amount of depth. You don't always want to shoot when your opponent is expecting you to because then he will dodge and catch your arrow. You also don't want to mindlessly fire away arrows at your opponent because ammo is limited and your opponent can pick up any stray arrows that miss and fall on the ground. You also have to be mindful of opponents that get up close to you as jumping on an enemy's head is also a one hit kill.  You also have to be aware of the edges of the screen and remember that the level wraps around. It's possible to get easy kills on unaware opponents by shooting back across the screen at an enemy on the other half of the level or jump down the bottom of the stage to head stomp somebody on top
There are also powerups that appear throughout the match that can give you arrows that explode on impact, bounce off walls or cut through the stage. Matches are quick, usually averaging about 30 seconds per round, so you'll want to race to pick up powerups as you see them. There are also powerups that can grant you invisibility, flight or trigger arena traps to try to kill your opponents. There's usually a lot happening on screen all at once and matches can get a little hectic, but I mean that in the best way possible. At the end of each round, there's an instant replay system that shows the final kill of the game. This is actually a pretty cool feature because things often happen so quickly that you'll miss how someone died. There's also a good variety of levels that have different powerups, different layouts and different terrain. You can also randomize the rules of Towerfall each round for maximum ridiculousness. One of my favorites was playing under a rule that doesn't show you how many arrows you have left combined with another rule that instantly kills you if you try to fire an arrow when you have no ammo left. The amount of customization and variety in Towerfall is a huge plus
As stated before, Towerfall definitely plays best with friends. The single player is alright for what it is I suppose, but if you're buying Towerfall, you're getting it to play with other people. Towerfall supports up to 4 simultaneous players and I found that 4 seemed to maximize the fun, hilarity and craziness of the games. Towerfall doesn't support online play of any kind which is really unfortunate because I think a game like this could really be fun online. At the same time though, this game is really fun to share with other people in the same room, yelling, laughing and screaming at the TV and at each other. I wouldn't be surprised to hear that this game eventually gets some sort of online support though, I would imagine that's going to be an often-requested feature. The only other thing that might be limiting this game is the hardware. This game plays best with 4 people. I happen to have 4 USB controllers for my PC, but I'm pretty sure I'm in the minority. And I don't think a whole lot of other people have 4 Ouya controllers or 4 PS4 controllers lying around either.
But if you've heard the positive buzz about this game, it's true. Believe the hype. This game is well designed, fun and fast paced. It's the early leading candidate for my 2014 game of the year. Yes, I know this technically came out last year on the Ouya. But now it's out on platforms that people actually widely own and use, so I hope this game gets lots of exposure in the near future. Check it out if you want a good, fun party game to share with friends

The camera, on the other hand, moves way too fast and jerky, so that when you're moving you just have to guess whether you're doing the right thing. Also falls prey to the problem of trying to platform when you can't see your feet.
Also, the game has a really stong "Made in UE4" vibe that the devs haven't tried to overcome.
Probably would be okay for someone who could put up with this, but I'd rather play something with a little more nuance in the design.

dares you to play it, comparing it to RPG greats such as the Legend of Zelda and Secret of Mana.
Do you have what it takes to delve into this story's mysteries?
Are YOU ready for ADVENTURE?!? Are you looking for fun?
Then look somewhere else.
Concept & Story:
Secret of Magia is standard Japanese Role-Playing-Game fare. There is nothing new brought to the table. Some may be fine with this approach, as was I. However, there is hardly any story at all. The game opens with a monstrous bird that threatens to kill you if you do not return with four crystals... at least it appears to threaten you. Significant grammatical errors are made immediately. While these can be sludged though and understood because of context, they persist throughout the game, sometimes making sentences nonsensical. This problem never alleviates. There are portions of text that lead completely off the screen, leaving the player to guess what was being said.
After leaving the introduction, our hero is set on a set of sidequests. That's it: five sidequests that aren't really tied in any way to the plot. The plot, of course, does not exist. It is only revisited at the end of the game and very, very briefly at that. While it is typically considered in bad taste to spoil the ending of a game or film, I cannot do so, though I am sorely tempted to. You see, the ending... it doesn't exist. As the boss lays dying, you are returned to the title screen. No credits, no "Thank you for playing", not even "Game Over"; there is absolutely nothing following this. This isn't just unexpected in story-based games, it's just downright rude.
Concept & Story - 2/10
Gameplay:
This sort of title has many expected mechanics in gameplay style. It is clear what the developer was aiming for, it just misses the mark in each and every way. Full controller support is claimed, but this is false. Movement, with a control pad, is only permitted with the analog stick, not the directional pad. This sort of game would have played much better with the latter. Giving players the option of either or best would work for everyone. Instead, the developer chose otherwise. The buttons used for play are odd in placement and incredibly awkward throughout the game. It is not unusual for them to be nonresponsive. Sometimes, there is a significant delay between pressing buttons and having a chosen action take place. This is inexcusable.
Navigating menus is slow, tedious, and excessive. Early in the game, the player is asked to equip items that aren't even present. They come into existence only when suggested by the interface. Other portions of inventory are completely unused, specifcally charms and accessories. It is as if something were planned and then completely forgotten. Evidently, the forgetfullness persisted through alpha and beta testing, if there was any at all.
The game utilizes class systems, levels, and crafting. This would seem a good idea. Class choice makes little difference as they play nearly the same. When leveling, your character becomes stronger. Unfortunately, the enemies gain in strength, health, and resistances to your attacks... and very disproportionally so. In other words, "leveling up" not only does not help you, it is an extremely bad idea. Under no conditions should the player consider grinding for experience; they may find the game unfinishable. Crafting is introduced to upgrade weapons and to create potions. In fact, one entire town in the game is dedicated to the industry of alchemy and potions. This system is never flushed out and developed. It suggests itself to have great promise and then proceeds to be completely ignored. There is no reason to bother with crafting weapons of any sort.
There are more concerns about things that would never be discussed if it were not for the fact that these normal mechanics are broken. Sleeping in village inns poses the slight risk of waking up in another town. It would appear that the screens that the interiors of the Inns are not reliably linked to the screens of the towns. As such, about one out of three nights spent will leave you across the world. When fighting certain enemies, the player can be stunned. This, in it of itself, is normally not an issue, but menu access is also locked. Any attempts to access the Game Menu or otherwise Pause are also "stunned". The entire game locks until the Effect wears off. There is no reason for this. Frequently, the player will become stunned even if not hit with a stunning attack. There is no way to predict when this will happen. Furthermore, progress through the four key dungeons is dependend on acquiring unique keys held be mini-bosses. Sometimes they drop them upon death... sometimes they don't. If not, pray you did not save, as the required Key is now and forever inaccessible. The only solution is to reset or load from a previous save file and try again.
For what should be simple and casual play and control, The Secret of Magia fails even at this minimal task.
Gameplay - 3/10
Sound & Music:
The sounds are fine and what would be expected for this sort of game. While voice-acting is a nice feature, it is not neccessary. Music is acceptable. It isn't awful, but it isn't memorable either. It is the sort of thing one would expect if a developer snatched up a few royalty-free music tracks and tossed in the ones that sounded best. Actually, this is exactly what developer, Lunatiod, did. The exact same music can be heard in other games as well. Even if they chose to use synthesised MIDI tracks that someone composed with this title in mind, it could have added more substance.
Sound & Music - 5/10
Graphics:
JRPGs have a typical look to them and this title attempts to keep up with the look and style of these. It is light and whimsical, with a touch of cartoony adventure. This being said, it is expected that things are consistent. Windows appear out of the edges of the walls of a church. Players walk right over gates. The player can even walk into and through some walls. Frequently when moving, the player will appear to be using their "Hookshot" item, when no such device is in use. These realatively easy fixes persist.
Most striking is the fact that the game does not appear as shown in the presented screenshots and advertisment video. It is extremely clear that the developer or publisher used photo and/or video editing software to make the game appear to have a very different asthetic than is actually present. In short,
. This sort of practice is loathesome and completely disqualifies this aspect of the game.
Graphics - 0/10
Enjoyability and Replay Value:
Secret of Magia showed a certain amount of promise. Each promise suggested was carelessly broken. Even if one sets their expectations low, this particular title fails to meet even that. This was an attempt to be a game without any intention to put in effort. It is hours of constant frustration dealing with glitches and broken game mechanics, a lack of story. and a complete absense of any fun. They entire game plays out as if "fun" is going to be right around the corner; it never comes.
Since all characters are virtually the same, despite what their names suggest, there isn't a reason to try these variations out. There is not much in the way of secrets, so outside of a hidden dagger (with coordinates that mean nothing), there is nothing to go back for. It isn't even the sort of game that one can enjoy the story once more, because there is practically no story and what little is presented is certainly not enjoyable. It isn't fun or remotely interesting. It offers absolutely nothing.
Enjoyability and Replay Value - 2/10
Final Thoughts:
It is obvious that the publisher and developer were interested in creating something that could be called a game, on paper. At 49 cents for this and three other titles, I feel ripped off. A waste of two hours. Avoid.
Overall - 2/10

This is probably the first time i'm not recommending a game, so it pains me to do this :(
I can see some potential but this is nowhere near production ready; do not put money towards it. I got a copy in a pack of 4 RPGs i wanted to try for ~60p, thankfully.
Obvious problems:
You get direction for what to do for the first 5 minutes ('Go to the well'), after that, you're free to wander the entire map (and good luck finding a map so you can squint and get an idea of where the hell you are or what you're supposed to be doing.) Quests have no markers - if it says 'go and kill blah', and you don't know where blah is, then so begins a wild goose chase.
After you save the miner...you can go back to the mine with the dungeon key and have a go at the fire boss...but not if you can't equip a shield.
It might just be because i picked the mage class, but i couldn't equip a shield despite buying everything possible (currency is nowhere near balanced, items cost ~30 gold and you can earn 1000s in minutes). No shield? No hope in hell of beating the elemental bosses. Was i supposed to buy 99 health potions and spam those instead??? (for shame)
While normal attack damage is ok and different weapons do different AoE areas (the combat system is quite interesting actually), magic is realllllly weak :/ like not even worth having. It's good for long distance but not when it does 10 damage against an enemy with 1000s of HP - who doesn't always stay STILL - who has time for that?
Enemies are all overpowered - i got to ~lvl 16 and even the wasps were taking off ~1/5 of my health per attack. Only the rats in the well at the very start of the game seem like they're at the right level for your character, and if you go back down there, they can divebomb you to hell and back in seconds.
The screen is littered with annoyance after annoyance and they don't scale with you nor drop anything significant. You're thrown in at the deep-end and get nothing for not drowning.
You can only save at the green flames and not the barely-existent menu, which i thought was a bit annoying because you have to backtrack to the last village and hope you can remember where it is in that village/town - some sign posts really wouldn't go amiss.
NPCs are pretty lifeless - if you ever even find one, chances are they'll just talk about their house (i found books in ONE house, all the other houses are window dressing :/) Ok, Sir/Madam, your house is nice and all....(not if there's nothing to loot lol) but how about some lore or something? Why go on???
I don't hate the game, but it really needs a lot of work. Tone down the difficulty (there doesn't have to be an enemy everywhere), scale enemies to class and level - battles are supposed to be FUN. Put in more 'where to go if you're stuck' (signposts!) . Know your characters - do we get a party at some point?? Why are we being forced by some flying bird to collect all the elements? Because it will 'reap our soul' otherwise? Well that's very nice of it???? haha

In the end of the game (yes, less than two hours) the story is more about the narrator then the developer.
Now, I'm not blaming the developers of The Beginner's Guide for trying new things. Hell, The Stanley Parable was an experimental game that I really, really liked. But don't release a game that looks like a string of amateur, private test games that are supposed to have hidden meanings behind them all, and then proceed with telling us those hidden meanings. It sorta beats the point, right?
You are being told (directly to the player) why these levels are deep and what everything symbolises, leaving nothing to discover yourself. When you try to explore, the game plainly states that there is nothing over there and that it would just be a waste of time. The player is never an active part in the experience, meaning that there is no reason buy it if you can get the same experience looking at a let's play of it.
This game should have been an experimental, free mod for Half-Life 2.

I purchased this game when it came out nearly a year ago, being a little more excited because it takes place in Colorado, and I just moved to a creepy mountain town here called Manitou Springs.
But I had yet to play it.  It sat there in my library, daring me to enter.  So I finally loaded it up:
First impressions:
Fantastic atmosphere - your character is a reporter, and therefore, they find papers, do research, and use their camcorder - yet they are investigating a facility filled with nightmares.  The whole experience feels like a nightmare from the get go, forcing you into creepy situations you would never choose to do normally.  Your character meanwhile, breathes and chokes as he encounters increasing horrors.
Despite the tension, exploring the game, with it's nearby creaks, thunder, and whispers in the dark - is oddly relaxing.  The simplicity of the game makes the experience very pure - Explore, Hide, Discover - that allows you to really get into being this helpless reporter in way over their head.
Don't be scared - it's a very good game, unique and well worth getting.
Highly interesting in its all simplicity. All hail the indie games!

UPDATE: So, it's been a little over two months since I last played The Long Dark, and there have been a LOT of changes. And as near as I can tell, all of them are for the good.
With my progress removed from the previous builds, I had to start over in the Mystery lake area and (with a couple of deaths) I've been making my way to the Coastal Highway, where I now make my temporary home, and eventually to the new Pleasant Valley area.
Some of my previous problems with the game have been entirely solved with the addition of difficulty levels. Before, in what I assume was the hardest difficulty (or perhaps they've changed some variables?) it was nigh impossible to find both a rifle and ammunition in the same area. Now, I've found both and have a decent amount of ammo, hopefully enough that I can survive the inclement wolf attacks, and eventually the bears of Pleasant Valley. In addition to that, I've survived many wolf attacks, given that I have some sort of defensive weapon on me. Before, that was absolutely impossible no matter what I did.
The Long Dark is definitely on it's way to being a game I can sink a lot of time into. With a few more tweaks, it'll be perfect.
ORIGINAL REVIEW:__________________________________________________________
After putting in a little over seven hours into this game, I've come to my verdict (in it's current state). At the moment, I find the game annoying at the worst of times and nerve-wracking (in a good way) at the best of times.
Once you learn the ins and outs of how to survive in this cold, dark world, reapiring your gear, making sure you're warm, and ensuring that you have enough food is an everyday occurance in this game. Honestly, that is exactly what you'll be doing 100% of the time you're playing. I would have done some hunting too, and probably a little more surviving than I have been if I had found a hunting rifle and some rifle rounds more than the handful of times I've found them se[erately. Though the exploration and survival elements already implented are fun, there needs to be more of both, especially the latter, for it to be a complete and playable game.
As it stands, the game is just too annoying for me to play for huge chunks of time. Every single time that I've died while playing has been due to run-ins with wolves. The only way you have to defend yourself against them is but madly mashing on the left trigger to get the power of your attack up, and then hit the right trigger repeatedly until you either 1) die or 2) get away with 1% or 2% condition left, from there either dying a few seconds after or act quickly enough to apply antiseptic and a bandage to your wound. If you have a weapon of some sort on you (like a hatchet or hunting knife, but those are as scarce as the hunting rifle), you can use it to fend off the wolf more ably.
This game has promise, and a lot of it. I will definitely give it more credit as it's in early access at the moment, but it and the Hinterland Studio team has a lot of work ahead of them in making it a fun and playable game, rather than annoyingly loveable one.
Sorry guys, but for the moment you aren't getting my recommendation. Hopefully you will after a few updates, but not now. Not in this state.

Limbo will creep you out.  It will leave you satisfied at that one challenge you've been scratching your head over for five minutes.  And, I do not use this phrase lightly, it'll have your soul stirring at its most crucial moments.  Limbo uses visuals and sound so artistically you'll likely see nothing like it ever again.  Music is sparse but when you hear a sombre piece float up, typically after or before something significant happens, it has a deep effect... if you're into that sort of thing. Secret of Magia is an ARPG made in RPGmaker. It is not like other RPGmaker game, as it is not turn-based... It's more of an action game.
The pathing of monsters and their attacks are quite frustating to play against, some just dash to you in zigzag kinda patterns and are almost impossible to dodge. On the other hand, with anything but a dagger or a bow, you can sit next to monsters and kill them to your side. With a bow, you can just kill them from afar without them trying to kill you.
It could have been a great game, but there are too many flaws. Mana regen is slow, leveling-up actually makes the monsters harder to kill overall. Classes are a little meaningless and have no really specific skills. There's also no abilities to unlock as you gain levels.
There's no maps, so you have to keep the layout of the map in your head and the game is just pretty, bland... In the first 2 dungeons anyways, all you have to do is kill the unique monster inside the zone, get his key and then unlock the door that leads to the boss room, that's not very original!
The music is not too bad, but I heard it wasn't composed for this game, so I won't praise it too much. The graphics are fair enough for RPGmaker, but they could be way better. There are some game breaking bugs (just pressing f12 for example, it crashes your game). The game is also very short.
The game is really cheap, about $1, but even there, it's not a game I would really recommend playing. If you are a fan of RPGmaker games, then maybe this is for you, otherwise, I did not enjoy it very much, it is a bit too clunky and unfun to play.

I really enjoyed this. Cool gameplay, quite an interesting story and the playable character is well written.
Gameplay
Yes, this is a Diablo clone, and Diablo has done quite a lot what this game is doing. But that is a popular and effective mode, so use it. Also it is cheap compared to Diablo.
The game consist of a few maps, each with its own challenges that you can try to complete before finishing it off with a boss fight. The game is kind enough to allow you to scour the map to complete the challenges before moving on to the boss fight that will lock the map. Once completed you can replay the map as a raid or hunt, allowing you to farm for xp or loot.
Story
The story takes you on a campaign of revenge, blazing through Norse and Celtic mythology and (for want of a better word) history, and have you (grudgingly) attempt to stop Ragnarok. Along the way you meet well written characters and some interesting cameos of some legendary figures.
A nice touch is that your character has a personality; typically brusque and antagonistic as you would expect from a vikingt, but more than that, your comments through the game stays unique to the situation and that map. Its not (always) the same 5 generic comments on each and every map, but specific to the type of enemy, to the environment, to the part in the story etc.

I can't remember the last game I played that was this much pure fun. And I don't think I've laughed and screamed at the TV with any game this much outside of Smash. Towerfall is a fast paced brawler/platformer/shooter game. It guess it kind of defies genre classification. I suppose you could file it under party game? It plays best multiplayer, that's for sure.
Towerfall is kind of like Smash, except every hit is a one hit kill. And the levels wrap around Pac-Man style. And every player has projectiles. So I guess not really like Smash then, but it's similarly as fun. It's easy to pick up and play, the only buttons are jump, shoot and dodge. Moving your character around and learning the game is quick and easy, but like any good game, there's a deceptive amount of depth. You don't always want to shoot when your opponent is expecting you to because then he will dodge and catch your arrow. You also don't want to mindlessly fire away arrows at your opponent because ammo is limited and your opponent can pick up any stray arrows that miss and fall on the ground. You also have to be mindful of opponents that get up close to you as jumping on an enemy's head is also a one hit kill.  You also have to be aware of the edges of the screen and remember that the level wraps around. It's possible to get easy kills on unaware opponents by shooting back across the screen at an enemy on the other half of the level or jump down the bottom of the stage to head stomp somebody on top
There are also powerups that appear throughout the match that can give you arrows that explode on impact, bounce off walls or cut through the stage. Matches are quick, usually averaging about 30 seconds per round, so you'll want to race to pick up powerups as you see them. There are also powerups that can grant you invisibility, flight or trigger arena traps to try to kill your opponents. There's usually a lot happening on screen all at once and matches can get a little hectic, but I mean that in the best way possible. At the end of each round, there's an instant replay system that shows the final kill of the game. This is actually a pretty cool feature because things often happen so quickly that you'll miss how someone died. There's also a good variety of levels that have different powerups, different layouts and different terrain. You can also randomize the rules of Towerfall each round for maximum ridiculousness. One of my favorites was playing under a rule that doesn't show you how many arrows you have left combined with another rule that instantly kills you if you try to fire an arrow when you have no ammo left. The amount of customization and variety in Towerfall is a huge plus
As stated before, Towerfall definitely plays best with friends. The single player is alright for what it is I suppose, but if you're buying Towerfall, you're getting it to play with other people. Towerfall supports up to 4 simultaneous players and I found that 4 seemed to maximize the fun, hilarity and craziness of the games. Towerfall doesn't support online play of any kind which is really unfortunate because I think a game like this could really be fun online. At the same time though, this game is really fun to share with other people in the same room, yelling, laughing and screaming at the TV and at each other. I wouldn't be surprised to hear that this game eventually gets some sort of online support though, I would imagine that's going to be an often-requested feature. The only other thing that might be limiting this game is the hardware. This game plays best with 4 people. I happen to have 4 USB controllers for my PC, but I'm pretty sure I'm in the minority. And I don't think a whole lot of other people have 4 Ouya controllers or 4 PS4 controllers lying around either.
But if you've heard the positive buzz about this game, it's true. Believe the hype. This game is well designed, fun and fast paced. It's the early leading candidate for my 2014 game of the year. Yes, I know this technically came out last year on the Ouya. But now it's out on platforms that people actually widely own and use, so I hope this game gets lots of exposure in the near future. Check it out if you want a good, fun party game to share with friends

So, after over 1200 hrs of playtime, it seems to be appropriate time for the review.
5 Most notable features:
1. Four classes; rifleman, engineer, medic and sniper with their class specific abilities you can find more info about from Internet.
2. Three in game currencies; warface dollars (in game money), crown points (will tell you later), and kredits (real world money).
3. A dosen gamemodes every first person shooter game has, for example; plant the bomb, team death-match and the newest addition, battle royale mode.
4. Weapons (primary, secondary and melee) with attachements and armor gear for your character.
5. Maintenance system for weapons and armor, repaired with warface dollars.
For new players, the honest recommendations:
- It's free, you don't have to pay to play the game but you won't either get access to all content available in the game. These things can range from "Random Kredit Box weapons" (and their achievement stripes) to "Global Operations" (DLC like events).
-It has both Versus (PvP) and Coopperative (PvAI) modes. Versus mode includes quickplay, ranked mode, and custom games. Co op mode also has longer missions called Spec ops which are more story driven experience rather than fast paced, straightforward coop missions.
- It has good ESports potential with all the allowed weapons and armor avalable for every player in Tournament server, which makes the competitive play fair and balanced.
- It has a progression system for player, known as "vendor" system and generic "rank" (not to be confused with ranked-versus mode). Vendors include unlockable weapons, armor pieces, and attachements, which of all you can unlock by just playing the game.
- Runs on Cryengine 3 with DirectX 9.0c, meaning the optimization and graphics are very good, but also support for older hardware and laptops. Some AMD (GPU) users are rumoured to encounter freezes in game but I cannot confirm that as Nvidia user, go ahead and give a shot.
Then the critique:
- The game is indeed P2W because most random kredit box weapons are statistically better than free ones, with the exception of SAI GRY AR-15 assault rifle. There are "crown weapons" that are better versions of kredit box weapons, but they cost rare ingame currency known as "crowns" that can only be earned from coop mode. They are rentable meaning that once they expire, you have to buy them again.
- Random kredit boxes are loot boxes that contain timed weapons, xp, progression boosters, and ultimately the main prize; a kredit box weapon that is generally better than any other free weapon. However, the odds to get the main prize permanently is super small 1%, and 0.1% for golden variant some weapons might have! As the boxes' name tells you, you have to buy the boxes to have a slight chance to get the main prize, which is GAMBLING in its purest. Fortunately boxes with golden variants will grant you the gold version once you have bought 1000 pcs of that particular box! Unfortunately this golden gun has cost you over 500€ if dropped from the 1000th box...
- Inaccurate in-game statistics for weapons, attachements, armors, ect.
The in-game stats don't represent the real performance of most guns for example there's no accurate values for recoil, reload speed, weapon swapping speed, min/max spread, damage drop, minimum damage, pellet count (shotguns), random box odds, or repair costs. Also some attachements have "hidden" stats such SIG Sauer P266C's "Custom Pistol Silencer" (that reduces the nowhere mentioned damage drop by 50%) or "Advanced SMG Scope" from rare vendor attachement category (that reduces the nowhere mentioned min/max spread of smg by 20% while aiming).
Some community members have hacked into the game files to find us gamers the real stats for each of weapons, which are available for readers in the community maintained wiki of Warface.
- Cheaters
The game uses the CIS side publisher, Mail.RU's private anti-cheat aka MRAC which effectiveness is unknown since possibly banned cheaters are cencored for the sake of their privacy. If someone cheats, he/she almost certainly won't get banned immediately from the game but the players are forced to report the cheater via in game report tool (which effectiveness is questionable at least), or by submitting a ticket on publisher's support-page with proper proof (a dosen screenshots or a video).
- Repair costs
There are still weapons and armor that are too expensive to be used by free2play players; every profit they make will drain to gear maintenance, which forces them to buy progression boosters only available via kredits.
- Lack of regional servers
Players who connect from the other side of the globe to EU server will make the matches go nuts due to unnecessary complexity of lag compensation and hit registeration calculations to also favor laggers. In worst cases, players teleport all over the place, and back to where they stood, or tank point-plank shotgun blast without showing any hit markers.
- Bugs which still haven't been fixed, yet being reported. The Steam version of the game which is basically EU/NA server, is very buggy due to the previous publisher's (Crytek Frankfurt) changes in the client compared to RU server which is apparently Crytek Kiev's main development/test platform with numerous PTSes available for russian players. Possible reason for this propably is because the debugging/bug tracking being also done with RU version despite bugs existing only within EU/NA server client.

Just can't recommend this. It looks nice, and it moves smoothly, but it's just not engaging for long. Yes, it's a first-person parkour game, but it fails to capture what made Mirror's Edge's best moments so great. There's very little depth to the movement. The character doesn't need to accelerate; he runs at full speed right away - this kills what made doing well in Mirror's Edge so rewarding. There's no sense of momentum or buildup as you move fluidly through a level, which makes doing well less fun and screwing up less meaningful.
It's missing mechanics like skill rolls or turning around and jumping out of a wallclimb; I'm not trying to bash this game just for not being Mirror's Edge, but it doesn't introduce anything new to bring back that depth and creativity. You've got your anomalies, but even they don't do a whole lot; by adding skills like super jumps or slingshotting but restricting them to particular locations, you're not really creating more depth. It's a glorified springboard; it's a tool placed in the environment that's clearly meant to be used in one specific way. That's not depth; it hardly qualifies as gameplay. It doesn't make you think; all it really does to "deepen" the game is force you to backtrack once you've unlocked a given anomaly so that you can get all the stuff that you couldn't before. That's not gameplay. That's more walking.
It's not just anomalies that suffer from the issue of being very clearly placed for a specific purpose. The whole environment has this problem.  If something has wooden beams hanging off of it, you climb it. If it's got that floral pattern (and, frustratingly enough, ONLY if it's got the floral pattern), you can wallclimb/wallrun. The levels are very telegraphed; you can tell at a glance exactly what the dev wants, and this is problematic because the only option is what the dev wants - there is no room for creativity. It makes the game really easy and linear.
The devs saw the number one complaint with Mirror's Edge, the lack of player freedom, and attempted to fix it by creating an open world and a skill tree and anomalies. But with little depth to the movement and painfully linear level design, Downward is far more restrictive than Mirror's Edge ever was.
Downward is early access, so maybe I'm passing judgment too soon. But seeing as the early access blurb mentions nothing about deepening the mechanics, I'd give this one a pass. It's too shallow to be entertaining for long.

This is basically a Far Cry clone, but with a few interesting twists.  Silly physics leads to some crazy action and absurd stunts (riding on top of a jet at top speed flight and then jumping off to parachute to the ground).
It's a completely open world with tons of cool places to find and explore.  The missions are fairly varied, but still seemed a bit repetitive at times and without a strong driving plot to link them together.  I went through the main mission and have still only done 33% of  the game so you can read  that a couple of ways: the plot and missions weren't leading me to explore that much; or, the world is so big that even the main story and associated missions wasn't enough get close to seeing it all.
There is a bit of an RPG element accomplished through slowly granting access to more weapons and vehicles through the black market.  You can also improve these items by spending vehicle or weapon parts  which are acquired through completing missions and finding them in the various locations.  My complaint was that I couldn't really tell the difference with a fully improved weapon vs the basic one.  Maybe that's because a headshot is an instant kill against anything but a main boss and getting those wasn't that hard.
I'm probably not going to go for 100% completion, but I  do see myself going back and playing more to do some of  the remaining optional missions so I can see more of the world and the many crazy locations I've seen from a distance or spotted on the map.
7/10.  If you are a fan of Far Cry, pick this up.

A deceptively short, deceptively ugly game about a man who drove his friend away, The Beginner's Guide is an interactive love note to a lost friend, and a desperate, screaming cry for help at the same time.
All of which is fine, except you're being charged for the priviledge.
From the man who is banking very, very heavily on the fact that The Stanley Parable will let him coast for a little while longer, comes a collection of Source Minigames from a completely different person. The Narrator, presumably the Devolper of the Stanley Parable, guides you through the source minigames, explaining how things work, makes his observations, and occasionally hacks the games to be functional. The Designer we meet only through the games we play through.
To spoil the ending, The Narrator drove his friend insane by stealing his work, modifying it, and showing it to others, which drove his friend to abandon him and game design. It's a lovely little drama, told in an admittedly unique way. The tone grows darker and darker as the designer's mind is poisioned and the narrator's desperation for reconciliation grows. Would have been a fine subject for a video game.
Except this isn't a video game, it's love letter, and you paid $8.00 for it. ON SALE.
There's something inhumanly ugly about that. Something above and beyond the ugliness of the Narrator confesses to towards the end, something beneath the bile The Designer displays for his tormentor. The message is ♥♥♥♥ed by the price point, frankly, and if this was anything but an attempt to make a cheap cash-in and a cry for help at the same time, it sure doesn't show it.
The Beginner's Guide is neither a Guide nor really about beginning anything. It's about lonliness, desperation, and the mistakes we make when we think we know what's best. And if it had been released for free, I would have believed every word of it.
Now all I can think about is if this is just an attempt to prompt a lawsuit.

If you've never played any UT or Quake, there's a good chance that this'll feel fresh as can be, and there's a good chance you'll never play anything like it again. While UT2004 (and 2003 and 3) are all great, the three are all their own entries, and this is probably the best. Nearly 15 years later, Unreal Tournament still remains an outstanding first-person shooter with some of the best FPS design (along with Q3A).
Nothing about it feels dated, and arguably first-person shooter game design as a whole has regressed from this and Q3A's high-level mental gaming and high skill ceiling shooters. Incredible pacing, maps designed to facilitate movement and area control, weapons with utility and balance, skillful gunplay all lead to the high-level mental games that really make the challenge and high skill ceiling the time.
Epic really struck gold with this in every way, and I'd highly suggest that everyone give this game a weekend to start that spark within them. It's not particularly casual, but the bots are still plenty fun (especially for non-pros) and if that and the excellent design aren't enough to sway you, there're plenty of mods and custom maps for it as well (though I think UT2004 really is the best of the series for mods).

This is my first time playing a Tales game. The battle system is semi-action based. The combos aren't complicate but the focus is more about the timing of guarding, side stepping (bonus effects from doing it just before an attack), guarding, etc. The game doesn't focus on free movement as much as other action RPGs.
The battle system and movement are kind of similar to a 3D fighting game where you can side step, block, etc (though there is free movement too if you want).
So, Tales isn't like Star Ocean exactly in terms of battle system.
The PC version is capped at 30 FPS but besides that, the game is has decent graphical options, mouse and keyboard support, etc.
You can switch characters early on (press "E" to go to the menu, then "E" again to switch player 1 or player 2 characters, then you can set the character you want AI to control to Auto, Semi-Auto, or Manual, use Manual or Semi-Auto for the player character you want to control). Finally for DLC costumes, you can unlock them by going to Menu > Items > Look at the far right and there should be a wireless looking icon button, click it, then click on the things you want to redeem.
It's probably best not to redeem skits though until you finish the game (to avoid spoilers) (the DLC skits are dialogues between characters). Another thing regarding DLC is, when you use an alt costume, it might enable an alt music. You can disable or enable alternative battle music by pressing E in the fashion list while highlighting the costume (If you are using Alisha's Cheria costume, highlight the name and press E to turn it on/off).
Finally I have it set to English voices. So far, I have found the English voices to be really good. The first few cutscenes didn't do it for me at first but within 2 hours, the voices have grown on me and I love them.
Overall, I am only 2 hours into the game but everything seems to run well. Take a look at the discussions and the sticky topics though if you find any issues. The PC version of Tales of Zestiria seems good so far.

I kinda gave up on this game after a while. It felt like Bandai/Namco were fighting the fans of this game, first we had a intro with lyrics then they blocked that, then outright forced PCs to erase the file. There's a work around online but there's other issues with this game. The game runs at 30fps without a mod and the combat is a bit wonky in so many ways. Nevermind the story which I couldn't get behind.
They push the combat as seemless, you see an enemy on the field, you bump into it, your party members rush out of you and you're in a fight instantly ....then you go to a victory screen and a screen wipe later you're back on the field...so it's not seemless as they make it out to be. This presnets a problem since you fight were you stand meaning the maps have to be built overly large and look awkward, like out of a MMO with super tall ceilings or just overly giant hallways/rooms.
The mechanics of battle irk me too, they encourage you to block to regain your action points (what you need to attack) meaning you'll do a combo, and hold block and with a power up later you're encouraged to block a bit more till you get a pulse effect meaning your next attack is powered up.
The game's story also makes it difficult to play as other characters, they really want you to play as the main character Sorey and I much prefered ......"a later character". But you're often forced to use him instead, and some charcters you straight up can't use because of ...'backstory/spoiler reasons' that work into battle mechanics.
The other issue is, co-op in this game? It's impossible. I played a bunch of Xillia on PS3 with a friend and it worked nicely! ...But due to how the camera operates in this, it's impossible. It focuses on player 1 so much that the other player will often be off screen, unable to see what's going on. While to some this isn't a deal breaker, it's notable to me and should be stated in the review.
The game isn't bad but it just didn't catch me. The technical reasons are modable if you want to do that and the game runs on lower end video cards such as what was in my Surface Pro 2. If your machine is beefy enough, look for the 60fps fix as the game will run MUCH smoother and will feel much better and responsive over all.

Even after just a few hours play, I can see that this is an excellent Action RPG.  The graphics are amazing, and the music excellent.
The player can choose and customize their character at the beginning, with class specifying which type of weapon the player will gain passive bonuses while using.
Players will find that their character is particularly vulnerable to environmental conditions (on some maps or just parts of some maps), such as snow, so will have to seek out campfires and/or shelter.  Luckily there are many items of armour that you can find, that will increase your resistance to exposure to the environment.
Many maps also require puzzles to be solved, in order to gain access to new areas, or areas containing hard to reach loot chests.   The player will find exploring maps in completion very rewarding.
Many weapons and armour items have sockets, which runes can be fitted into, (once the player has unlocked the relevant NPC).
I really like the features that set this isometric view Action RPG apart from other games in the genre.  The character class selection alone, increases replayabilty immediately, with each character benefitting in specific areas.
I bought this game in the sale, and have to say I am very pleased with it.  Even at full price it represents good value.
The inventory screen and UI in general feels solid and well made, as do the graphics with amazingly well animated character models and really beautiful environments.  In screenshots the game looks good, although when you see the snow in-game, and the maps in general, the graphics really are amazing.
Combat mechanics seem spot on, with a bit of thought required in the timing of attacks, although not so much that it detracts from the ability to fluidly dispatch hordes with a few slashes.  Very enjoyable action.  Xbox 360 controller works very well!
Highly recommended for Action RPG and/or Vikings enthusiasts, or anyone looking for a deep involving atmospheric game.  10/10.

INTITIAL REVIEW:  After a couple of hours of playing this game I can understand how people can find it both interesting AND boring.  The scenery is realistic and the act of finding random items is fun(Ive never been so excited to find a wool peticoat before), but after both of those get old, so does the rest of the game(and it happens rather quickly, sadly to say).  The wolves simply add a very annoying obstacle to deal with while looking around and finding things.  I say annoying because you are attacked or chased by wolves just about every 10-15 seconds.  Its a little much and completely unrealistic.  I wish I had spent my money on something else.  I just cant imagine where all the "great" reviews came from.  There just isnt a whole lot to do in this "game".
PS: They say that there are no zombies but there are.  They just look like wolves.
AFTER PATCH REVIEW: Wolf aggressiveness and spawning issues seem to have been resolved(thank you!).  Now that there is a decent chance of avoiding wolf attacks, the game is more fun to explore.  You are still looking over your shoulder for where the wolves might be all the time, but they sound off before attacking which quite often gives you a chance to run for a building or car.  This seems a little more realistic.  I am sure that some people will say that it takes the challenge out of the game but the way the wolves were before, you may have just as well bought a zombie survival game.  I bought this one because it was not supposed to be a zombie survival game.  So thank you for fixing the wolves.  I am POSITIVE that the developers can and will come up with other threats to make the game challenging.  After all, surviving in a bitter cold, isolated and abandoned wilderness is not supposed to be easy even without wolves.  There would also be bears(probably more in the woods), falling from a height while walking around in the dark(They've already got that one in the game as I very recently discovered lol), and lots of other challenges.  The developers seem to be right on top of things judging from their frequent updates which fix important issues and the fact that they actually read and respond to reasonable reviews of their game.  I have high hopes for this game now.  I will be playing much more and anticipating updates.

The story mode feels like a survival run through New Vegas where your character is a diabetic. It's kind of a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥and I am not a big fan of where the hunger/thirst/fatigue/temperature balance ended up, it seems more demanding than the last time I played the beta. That means you spend a lot of time clicking through radial menus and performing inventory management instead of, say, hunting, or exploring, or playing the game.
That's part of the biggest problem. Most of The Long Dark doesn't happen on screen, the developers kind of ask you to use your imagination for way too much of the gameplay. If they were doing that to quickly skip through some tedious tasks it would otherwise be boring to simulate, fine. But every little thing necessary to do to gather resources or complete an action comes with a boring menu to click through, a slowly advancing time bar to watch deplete, and the added consequence of depleting your satiety indices, forcing you back into inventory management after every little thing you do.
The actually fun parts of the game are difficult, especially towards the beginning. On the plus side, that makes things tense and leads to a lot of interesting situations where you have to be kind of creative to get out of a jam, but the save system can also make things like that kind of annoying. You can't save just anywhere, there are chapter checkpoints and arbitrary auto saves, so if one of those trigger when you're in a tough situation, you stay in that tough situation, and can potentially lose a lot of good progress before you stumble into the next save area if you die along the way. And dying is easy.
One final gripe about the gameplay: No autorun. When you're not messing about with resource menus and figuring out what piece of gear you need to drop to skirt the encumberance limit, you're usually pressing W. There's enough other stuff to do to avoid calling this a walking simulator, but it's bad enough that I set up a macro on my keyboard.
The story is engaging and well written, but I think we all know why we're here, the reason I am still recommending this game, despite being disappointed in most of its mechanics. We're here to ♥♥♥♥ up wolves, with Commander Shepard starring as Liam Neeson. Well, that's a bit facetious. The real reason I'm still recommending The Long Dark, is that it's a beautiful game with a unique art style, and there really isn't anything else like it. If you like adventure games, this is a great take on that genre, I'd just like to see the more tedious aspects of it tweaked a bit in future efforts.

One of my favorite games of all times, Banished gets you in the situation of a group of families determined to start their lives again from scratch by settling down in a new, unknown virgin land to them.
There are no objectives in this game; just lean on your couch, sort out the best way to start building your city and watch how your settlers begin to work. No instant building; before even a simple house can be lifted, you must make sure that you are in possession of the required materials for it. Though it may become really relaxing for some players, don't get me wrong; this game, without mods, is as challenging as could be.
In short terms, this is (at least for me) just the perfect game to relax; the gameplay comes with a smoothing music selection for you to enjoy, mixing emotions such as what the settlers may feel while facing the inclemency of the harsh weather or when they look at the future with a positive lens, working hard to earn their keep and contribute to the growth of their new hometown.

This game is absolutely addicting and fantastically fun at the same time. I kind of enjoyed mirror's edge which is the only other game like this on the market and this outshines it by miles! This game takes a free running genre and combines it with an open world in a fantasy setting. Love it. But thats not even the greatest part of this game, puzzles. Literally every segment of this game is a puzzle and they are all very well crafted and put together in a non obvious way that has many paths to completion. When I hit the end of the developed part of this game (as its still in progress) I wanted more right away!
Another part of this game I absolutely love is that they don't take a linear approach to anything. There is a main storyline but you don't have to follow it for a long long time if you don't want to. Instead you can say no thank you to the voice in your head, go explore, find hidden treasure and fun obstacle courses, earn coins and buy upgrades, decorate your hideout, on and on and on!
My final thoughts here are for the developers on where they can take the rest of the 2/3rds of the game that has yet to be released.
I personally would really enjoy it if you keep up what i love about it so far (as stated above) but add in a few layers of psychological confusion. The wanderer hears a voice in his head so make it trick him/not be real/ make him doubt reality. The sheer level of mind games you can do with this storyline is astounding and I would really like to see something along those lines.
I would also really like to see the game develop more perks whether they be less fall damage scaling to no fall damage, or one perk you can level infinitely that increases your run speed by 1-5% per level purchased. I love the idea of a perk system and in a game with no combat you can really get creative on the things to offer the player.
Summary: Amazing graphics, great physics, amazing storyline, very addicting, recommending to everyone I know.

A great multiplayer party game needs to be immediately accessible, but also deep.  It needs to reward skill, but have an element of luck as well.  It has to allow for incredible comebacks and crushing losses.  TowerFall Ascension does all this and more.  It has quite a retro feel, set up for a 4:3 screen and with SNES-era graphics.  It also has a ton of customizable options, great level variety, a really nice replay set-up for final round kills, works great with Xbox 360 controllers... I could go on and on, but I won't.
This game has that "thing" that makes you say "one more round..." about 30 times before you actually turn it off.
There are two drawbacks that came immediately to mind.
One, couch multiplayer only.  Not a problem if you have friends, controllers, and your PC is set up for gaming.  Not great if you typically play games at a desk on a monitor.  This isn't much of a single player game, so this is going to limit its audience, which is really unfortunate.
Two, per the store page, minimum specs for integrated GPU solutions call for Intel HD 4400, which I believe starts with 2013 Haswell chips.  I don't really get that at all.  Intel HD 4000 is able to run The Darkness II or Bulletstorm on medium settings at 720p at 30FPS.  How on earth this game would be so poorly optimized as to not run on that chipset is beyond me.  Note that in fairness, I haven't actually tried it yet, so who knows, it may run.  I just find it bizarre.  As a comparison, games in a somewhat similar space like Nidhogg and Samurai Gunn run flawlessly on an Intel HD 4000 chipset.
EDIT:  Haven't tested multiplayer yet but the quest campaign mode ran flawlessly on my Surface Pro.  Inten HD 4000 probably runs this game fine.
Outside of that, I'd give this game my strongest possible recommendation.  It is an instant couch multiplayer classic like Mario Kart, Smash Brothers, Rock Band, etc.
