I've tried many Early Access Games and I have to say that the developers of this have done a phenomenal job. Being a fan of games like Dying Light and BioShock, This game has several features I love such as the Parkour and abilities to aid the player in getting around and using the environment to progress.
The visuals are simply breathtaking. I adore the bright sunlight against the panoramic landscape, Though It can get a bit hard to see here and there. Thankfully, The developers don't overdepend on effects such as Bloom to hide visual artifacts and everything is extremely detailed. There is the occasional pop-in but overall, I think this is a beautifully crafted world.
In terms of enemies, The Golems are really well animated and initially could prove to be a slight challenge to newcomers.
However, Once you learn their attack moves then they do become rather predictable. It then simply becomes a dodge game where you just wait for the Golems to reveal their vunerable cores. I would love to see more tactics added. Perhaps using the environment to stun Golems while trying to avoid getting hurt yourself? Maybe knocking down crumbling pillars to make several heavy rocks rain down on the area. The turrets and drones are neat too and I like the very basic Stealth system to avoid being spotted by them as you try to deactivate them. I adore Stealth and I hope this gets expanded on, If possible.
The voice acting is pretty decent. Nothing spectacular but not too grating. So props to the developers for creating a protagonist not too serious and not too annoying. It's rather balanced. I also do hope that the Old Man gets more than one laugh.. :P.
Sound work is nice though I have noticed times where the music or sound effects, Such as the Artifacts, Will cut out occasionally. I hope that some sounds will gradually fade out as you move further away as It would help In trying to locate them slightly easier. I have also noticed that when I am looking at an Artifact, The whispering sounds can be heard through either my left or right speakers through my headphones which can feel a bit weird. But It isn't that much of a problem.
Gameplay is great. I really do love the Parkour in this but It can end up feeling a bit " floaty " here and there, Especially when falling. As for the Magic [ Or Energy? ] skills such as being able to Slingshot around or leave behind Marks that you can quickly teleport to, They are very fun to use but at times, I haven't been able to leave Marks as pressing the button often does nothing. Hopefully, This will get fixed in later patches.
I am very interested to see how the story progresses. The mix of Fantasy / Sci-Fi really gives me a somewhat " Assassin's Creed " mixed with " Halo " feeling. It does leave you wondering what is yet to come.
Overall, A brilliant job by the developers. I highly recommend this, Especially at such a great price. You are sure to get your money's worth. I wish the developers of Downward all the best with this project and any future ones that they may start. The amount of potential here is extremely high.

An intriguing premise constantly at odds with Davey Wrenden's subpar writing ability.
A character study of a hobbyist game developer told through the exploration of his games is a really compelling idea. But this premise is completely hamstrung by its underwhelming execution. Taken as a work of fiction, the story is clumsy and unsure of how to develop itself past the first 30 minutes. Taken as a work of non-fiction, the narrator comes off as an unsympathetic, self-centered/self-pitying, uninteresting jerk. The emotional aspects of the work lack subtlety and border  on melodrama. The narrator's lack of voice acting talent makes the weak script come off as overly whiney.
The visuals and "set design" are fantastic, though. Exploring some of the areas without narration was a delight. The messy house level was definitely the high point of the game.
But excellent visual design can't save this overwhelmingly flawed game. Not recommended.

There is an IRL writer, who goes by the name of Borges. At some point, he wrote a short story, called "House of Asterion". Where knowingly or not, this game tries to touch on the same themes that exist in that book. Especially in its last scene.
The operative word being: tries.
The simple problem with this game is that it starts off selling you on one premise, and then pulls off a bait and switch. You won't see this premise fulfilled. Instead, you will see it denied. And it won't be denied in any meaningful sort of fashion, it will just be a "cold stop, you are done" kind of denial. It is a bit like selling you an adventure novel, only to turn it into a closed-room horror midway, with little to no explanation - or even foreshadowing.
Which is sort of acceptable in something like a fanfic, but is certainly a step down from the brilliance of Stanley Parable.
Now, there obviously is some novelty here. The narrator not just talking directly to you, but actually directly altering the gamestate to his whims, is a bit new. An attempt to elevate the use of mechanics as metaphors is also apparent.
Neither really works, though.
The intrusive narrator is the most interesting case. He rather quickly wrests the game away from the player's hands, but for a while it is not hard to be essentially okay with it, because he is both genuinely useful in showing you some features of the world that you might have otherwise missed, and shows to have gone through some impressive character development in the past, the fruits of which he is very willing to share. Essentially, the intrusive narrator acts as a benevolent "i have already played this, let me help you out" kind of character, and it is actually pretty good to have him around, given the largely experimental, fundamentally unstable and inherently player-unfriendly nature of games being played.
However, at some point, we start playing games that cause significant emotional distress in our narrator, utterly ruining his "i am pro at this" qualification, which is the only reason the player agrees to suffer his presence to begin with. The fact that said distress is, in itself, not very believable, is not helping either. This effect makes the narrator character rapidly deteriorate, to the point where he even begins to act in a way that is incompatible with his own past character development. As the narrator deteriorates, the narrative crumbles.
As for "mechanics as metaphor" attempts - they also suffer from two issues. First, they are simply bland, but second - they are constructed in such a way that you can't really play with them. Which kind of kills the whole point of having mechanics as a metaphor, as opposed to actual metaphors in your everyday simple text.
"House of Asterion" took its place among the literary classics, because it succeeded in actually creating an infinite maze that you really could believe the story's focal character could actually live in.  The failure of "The Beginner's Guide" is that it promises to show us a believable infinite maze of human mind, only to fail to really show it to us, because the narrator is an idiot.
"Stanley Parable" succeeded because, for all its walker-simulating narrative-drivenness, it still afforded, to an extent, actually playing with its mechanics. The failure of "The Beginner's Guide" is losing this defining aspect of games as a creative medium. Or rather, throwing it away for the sake of an intrusive narrator gimmick that didn't pan out.
So yeah. Really cannot recommend this game to anyone, but scholars of game design. And even those should tread lightly.

I kinda gave up on this game after a while. It felt like Bandai/Namco were fighting the fans of this game, first we had a intro with lyrics then they blocked that, then outright forced PCs to erase the file. There's a work around online but there's other issues with this game. The game runs at 30fps without a mod and the combat is a bit wonky in so many ways. Nevermind the story which I couldn't get behind.
They push the combat as seemless, you see an enemy on the field, you bump into it, your party members rush out of you and you're in a fight instantly ....then you go to a victory screen and a screen wipe later you're back on the field...so it's not seemless as they make it out to be. This presnets a problem since you fight were you stand meaning the maps have to be built overly large and look awkward, like out of a MMO with super tall ceilings or just overly giant hallways/rooms.
The mechanics of battle irk me too, they encourage you to block to regain your action points (what you need to attack) meaning you'll do a combo, and hold block and with a power up later you're encouraged to block a bit more till you get a pulse effect meaning your next attack is powered up.
The game's story also makes it difficult to play as other characters, they really want you to play as the main character Sorey and I much prefered ......"a later character". But you're often forced to use him instead, and some charcters you straight up can't use because of ...'backstory/spoiler reasons' that work into battle mechanics.
The other issue is, co-op in this game? It's impossible. I played a bunch of Xillia on PS3 with a friend and it worked nicely! ...But due to how the camera operates in this, it's impossible. It focuses on player 1 so much that the other player will often be off screen, unable to see what's going on. While to some this isn't a deal breaker, it's notable to me and should be stated in the review.
The game isn't bad but it just didn't catch me. The technical reasons are modable if you want to do that and the game runs on lower end video cards such as what was in my Surface Pro 2. If your machine is beefy enough, look for the 60fps fix as the game will run MUCH smoother and will feel much better and responsive over all.
If you're looking for a good JRPG, they released a new title Tales of Berseria which I'm 5 hours into at the moment and I recommend that more. At time of writing it needs an update to fix a bug but they insist it's a priority fix so keep an eye out for that.

As someone who played the hell out of the first Red Orchestra, I was excited for RO2. A rocky launch dampened that, despite some fun I had from it.
The GOTY edition solved a lot of launch bugs and optimization issues, but it still doesn't really fix a few major things - namely, wasted potential and some seriously harrowing bugs that still persist. Red Orchestra 1 had dozens upon dozens of brilliantly-made custom maps (Black Day in July and Hedgehog still beats my fluttering heartstrings!), a very large assortment of armored vehicles, and lots of weapons to choose from.
RO2, on the other hand, is lacking widely in terms of content compared to its predecessor, despite being bigger and better looking. It added more depth to infantry combat, including slow death, bandaging, adjustible iron sights, and a low-impact customization/proficiency system. These sound great on paper, but over extended play these become nuisances (slow death), kind of superfluous (iron sights), or disappointingly obtuse balance-wise (the upgrade/RPG system). It's really disappointing to have something as interesting like being able to suppress nearby enemies while sprinting in close proximity with friendlies - like a 'charge' effect - go to waste when 90% of battles are pub rifle camp fests.
I loved the first game, I've tried RO2 and Rising Storm through their launches, and maybe I just have rose-tinted glasses, but I don't feel like RO2 was able to deliver on what potential it had.

Rather than writing a deep expansive review that will probably just bore you within the first paragraph, I thought I would change it up by just simply get down to the brass tacks.
This game was made using the RPG Maker VX Ace Engine, therefore it presents the same problems that just about every other RPG Maker game presents. Sadly, these issues are just simply the mechanical limitations of RPG Maker, not developer errors, therefore I cannot fault the game on these issues.
Putting the issues of RPG Maker aside, I really wanted to like this game, however it does have its problems. The first problem I had was a very noticable drop in FPS while in larger open areas. This FPS drop really slows down movement and becomes a quick nuisance. This issue is fixed when entering a building or cave, etc however presents itself again when re-entering the large area.
Second problem I have are the controls. The controls are really bad in my opinion and have somewhat of a learning curve as you cannot change them. Granted you can remap controls using Xpadder or another re-mapping program if you have a controller, I feel I shouldnt have to use another program to get the controls you want.
As I said previously, I am not going into a great amount of detail with this one. The two problems are my main issues, as of right now, therefore you want to know about other game issues or gameplay mechanics, check out some of the other reviews. They are chalk full of plenty of information.
I gave this a prositive rating becuase I believe this game had potential and with some issues aside it really isn't all that bad for the price, especially if you pick it up in a bundle on sale.

I am a fan of this franchise since I played Tales of Symphonia in 2003 on the gamecube. I was a tiny bit disappointed with some titles of this series in the past (Xillia and Graces). However for a few reasons this was not the case with this title. This title is far from perfect, but this time I enjoyed my time with it.
Positives
- The first Tales of game on pc! (I know, not exactly a ingame positive).
- The Characters (I like this cast so much more than some other tales of games. Yes I am looking at you Tales of Graces).
- The battle system (it's not perfect, but it's fun).
- The music (Most tracks from Go Shiina are great).
- A good port (Yes, I was a bit afraid for this one).
Mixed
- The presentation (I thought some scenes were odd).
- The graphics (It's nothing special but does the job most of the time for a game with presumably a tight budget. It really helps that this game is on pc though).
- The story (The story is meh).
Cons
- The camera (Sometimes the camera angle is odd (like behind a wall) when you are in battle).
- The world (When will developers learn that a big world is fun if it's not empty).
- The 30 fps lock (A mod is available to fix this. It's not a dealbreaker for me, but still a big negative).
I am happy with this port and playing this game was fun. It's by far not the best tales of game, but I can still recommend it.

RPG Maker VX Ace is a great piece of software that enables users with little to no programming knowledge to create fully fleshed-out RPGs. Most facets of game development are customizable, allowing you to make your game as small or as epic as you want it to be. Want to create 500 unique items? Done. Want to import external sprites and music? Easily done. RPG Maker is so versatile that some games made with this software have found commercial and critical success and are available on Steam to download.
As with most software like this, there is a learning curve. Previous users of RPG Maker should have no problems adjusting to VX Ace, as it uses the same event-driven structure that all of the other RPG Makers have. For new users, there will be a learning curve. This is a massive program and it will take a while to figure out what each item in the menu does and how to troubleshoot various issues that arise during the game development process, such as understanding why a parallel process event is freezing the game or why an event does not trigger when it is supposed to. It's intimidating to a first-time user, but you'll get used to it before too long.
VX Ace also addresses some of the problems associated with the previous VX release, such as script issues, lag, and limited tilesets. In addition, it includes a highly customizable character generator which produces not only a sprite of your custom character but a portrait to use on the character menu and in cutscenes. This version also features a new soundtrack and an upgraded RTP. I highly recommend it - it's a definite upgrade over the original VX.
Despite this, RPG Maker VX Ace has some of the same limitations of its predecessors. Events do not always interact with one another the way that they should, and you may have to use some creative thinking or find an external script to achieve the desired result or reduce lag issues. Turn-based battles have always been a staple of the RPG Maker series, and VX Ace is no exception in this regard; you can get around this limitation with scripts. As mentioned, it does have a steep learning curve, so prepare to do a significant amount of trial-and-error while you are adjusting to the program, and maybe consult some online help if necessary.
On the plus side, RPG Maker is a great introduction to game making. You won't realize it, but you are learning to program through a graphical interface. I've just started learning programming languages, and I attribute my success and understanding to having tampered with older versions of RPG Maker during my childhood. Do yourself a favor and get this software if you are looking to start creating RPGs - try to get it as part of a bundle because its standard retail price is fairly high. You absolutely won't regret it.

This way I only had to use 1, 2, middle mouse, and two buttons with my right thumb so I didn't have too many buttons to press with my left hand.
PROS
What is thwackiness, you say? Well, in real life weapons have a solid thwack when you hit enemies or objects, so I really got that feeling from this game. The game didn't spawn a horde of enemies at me and kept them manageable. The graphics were also very stellar.
The enemies were fleshed out very well. I won't give any spoilers but I liked fighting the ... let's say ... undead. Hey, you can read some of the types of enemies you will face in the future when you hit C to view your stats in the game anyways, so I'm not spoiing anything.
Pillage away, because there are a good variety of supernatural enemies in this game. You aren't really pillaging helpless people though, so no worries. No evil Vikings today, because these Vikings are a clan proving their might.
I didn't spec into every character class. I had one save file and I think I can save enough gift points (gifts are the name for skills here) to equally use a sword and shield, and wield a bow and arrow. And wow, the arrows really whistle through the air and thwack into enemies and objects like they should, instead of feeling fake like in some games. You are not bound to class in this game, so don't worry about being stuck. You can't respec skill points as far as I know, and I'm about level 15 now, but just think wisely. You can't respec your high school education or your math tests just because you don't like them, so why should you be able to do that in a game? Odin's beard!
By Thor's hammer, this game is smashing! Even though each class only has five gifts/skills and you can't exchange them if you don't like them, I actually liked that. The game didn't overwhelm me with way too many choices of skills like some games do, and you can actually craft good weapons instead of wasting time looking at useless loot in your inventory, so that's a plus.
There is an exposure mechanic in this game and wearing heavy, light, or cloth armor really gives you the feel that they are each special in their own way. The exposure mechanic, such as having to go near campfires before getting really cold and being damaged by it, kept me on my toes, but it wasn't so bad that I kept on dying. I didn't die once from exposure but it was pretty realistic and worth it.
I liked the story and the main character. The main character really felt like an arrogant Viking, and the story really did the Viking mythology and culture justice. I'm not an expert on Vikings but this felt very realistic and gave me a window into what a Viking epic would be like.
You can also upgrade certain parts of your base, which helps you feel like you are really living in a Viking village.
CONS
I can't think of any cons. As for bugs, there was a moment when I dashed or rolled behind a rock and got stuck between "a rock and a hard place (the wall)". I had to exit to the main menu, but luckily there were enough checkpoints so I didn't lose much progress.
The game crashed twice just now actually. It wasn't a big deal though. Developers should look into the cons here but so far two crashes are not a game changer (literally). I also defeated an enemy and afterwards a copy of the enemy was just frozen in place there for some reason. I kept on moving but that's weird...
You don't really get to interact with your village or with people from other villages too much, making the other characters forgettable. Even shieldmaidens and warriors from other villagers who fight with you who die are very forgettable, so this is one aspect the developers could have worked on to make us feel more connected with our home village.
This game's plot was easy to understand at first but got confusing mid-game and end-game. I couldn't remember who was on who's side. I would like to see the developers add some sort of way to see who's who and what's what (friends and foes).
I wrote the most of this review before I had gotten to the middle of the game, but the more I play the more bugs I find. Not many, but my game froze once so I had to restart at a checkpoint. There are enough that it doesn't set my progress back much, but fighting enemies that have too much health becomes a drag.
9/10.

What a brilliant puzzling platformer. Up there with Braid, this simple yet fantastically arty experience is not one to miss. Every step of the way had me thinking, and every puzzle had me in awe.

This game is the gold standard for Early Accessgames, economy games, modding support, you name it.
Gameplay is a challenge, your colonits will starve, they will freeze to death, they will die from illness, storms, fallin rock's, wild boars, etc. You will learn from your mistakes and get better, it never feels like you were cheated. But it is free of any bugs that I can tell. It does not have a combat or defense element to it, your only adversary is mother nature and starvation. But it specializes in economy, It really makes any other economy based game look like childs play.
Modding support is crazy good, you can shop, download and install MOD's directly from the games main menu. They are not all winners, but you can easilly double the number of buildings, professions and commodities via mods.
My only gripe is that this game is so good at what it does that it makes other games in it's genre just seem so easy and pedestrian. Even ones that incorporate a combat element.
TIPS: Build supply chains in this order for success. FOOD (LOTS OF FOOD) start with gatherers and hunters. FIREWOOD (people will freeze in the winter if they do not have wood).TOOLS (a villager's productivity drops by 75% if he/she does not have a tool). CLOTHING (again with the freezing business) once you have the basics get a DOCK built so you can trade firewood (your first commodity) for SEEDS. FARMS give your more food with less hands, but you need to first acquire seeds from traders. Then you can get your individual REASOURCE chains up and running, Start with Wood, instead of clearing away swaths when wood gets low a forrester will put people on making wood renewable, then move onto stone and iron and coal production when you have enough hands, or when you run out of surface reasources. The real secret to food production is variety, if you have alot of different kinds of food then people consume a little bit less and no one source is over stressed. Another big deal is the market, if your villagers are busy running all over town to get firewood and food and clothes and tools then they spend less time working and gathering reasources. A market has employees that get all of those things and bring them into one place.
Good Luck!

At the time I'm writing this review, I have 480 hours on this game. This game is good and bad, but I like it. I'm playing this game since Q2 2015, of course not everyday, and I like and dislike that game in many ways. So I will make a list of good and bad features down below.
Good:
1.	Free2Play
2.	A lot of weapons, maps and game modes
3.	Game is updating every month at least once
4.	ESL
5.	Challenges
6.	Pretty much skill based game
7.	Very good sound effects
8.	Very good graphics for F2P game
9.	Game is automatically kicking out high ping players
10.	There are codes which you can redeem to get something in-game (after every match on their YouTube live stream, they give one code)
11.	Items in shop aren't very expensive
12.	Special points for unlocking items which you get for free after unlocking
13.	Christmas, Easter, Halloween and other traditions in Warface (new weapons, maps, items, …)
14.	You get decent rewards for leveling up
15.	Various cash and XP boosters
16.	CO-OP missions (normal and special operations)
17.	Great support for connecting to game rooms with your friends (you and your friends will, in most cases, be in same team)
18.   Daily rewards (coins and lootboxes, sometimes items)
Bad:
1.	Pay2Win
2.	Lootboxes
3.	Team balancing
4.	Optimization
5.	Cheaters
6.	Anti-cheat system
7.	Lot of players lost their accounts after Warface moved to
8.	If you want to unlock a lot of items, you really need to play game very often
9.	There aren't many servers and they are very bad (high ping, packet loss, …)
10.	Skins for weapons are very rare (you need to buy them with real money, but I've seen some skins that sometimes appear in the shop and you can buy them with in-game money)
11.	Repairing system (Weapons lose about 1-2% of their „health“ per match and repair costs about 100-300 in-game money)
12.	New battle royale game mode isn't balanced (weapon you find has only one magazine of ammo, only 16 players, map not big enough, …)
That is all I can say about Warface with my 480 hours experience in this game and I hope it will be helpful for new people who are interested in playing this game. Personally, I recommend this game to everyone who want to play pretty much skill based first person shooter game that is Free2Play. Also I really hope that the game is going to be even more good and the bad features will disappear in future.

It's been brought to my attention that there is a code for unlocking all the characters and stages in the game.  One of the main reasons I could not recommend this game at all on release was that, as far as I knew, it was not possible to unlock all single-player content without multiplayer modes (versus), which requires an extra controller. My outdated review can be seen below
---------------------------------------------------------------------------
If you can gather 1 to 3 people for local multiplayer, then feel free to buy this game.
However, if you plan to play this game by yourself, make sure you have a spare controller before purchasing this game.
Why?  Because even with a keyboard, a controller is required to play Versus mode, and certain content (at least 3 map sets and all 4 extra characters) can not be unlocked unless you can access Versus mode.
If you do not have a controller, you will not be able to unlock all single player content.
If you do not have a controller, you will not be able to unlock all the content in a game you paid for.
I would change my stance on this game in the future if either:
1)  The ability for a single player to fight against the AI in "versus mode"  is added
or
2) An online mulitplater mode is added
The second option may be a little unreasonable, but the first isn't.
Either of these would allow players to play versus mode without a controller, thus giving them the ability to unlock game content that is currently unaccessible with just a keyboard.

Rogue is a top-down dungeon crawler which, in 1980, spawned a whole genre with its then unheard of gameplay style, but the way the players of it and its spiritual successors such as Hack and NetHack see it is "D&D for lonely people". The sole objective of it as well the other games mentioned is to find the Amulet of Yendor at the lowest dungeon level and make it out of the dungeon alive, though the game is extremely challenging making some players simply want to achieve a higher score. Just like Dungeons & Dragons, classes (or "roles") in NetHack in particular are a very important feature. NetHack was released in 1987.
Obviously, this is not the first instance of classes in video games, but this was just over 5 years before the release of Wolfenstein 3D, a first-person shooter which could easily be played with a top-down perspective, that is too influential to the genre for 1 review to describe.
Fast forward to 1996. Quake, a fully 3D first-person shooter is released, and soon after a modification for the game called Team Fortress.
Team Fortress is, because it is a Quake mod, a first-person shooter, putting it into the same bunch as Wolfenstein 3D and the DOOM games, which again, might as well be top-down (and if not for advancements in technology, this would also apply to Quake and Team Fortress). The game has several classes to choose from, each having their own unique strengths, weaknesses, abilities, and uses on a team of players expected to complete clear cut objectives, such as capturing the enemy team's flag. This game has been remade on newer engines such as Goldsrc (in Team Fortress Classic) and Source (I'm not going to bother listing even a sixteenth of them), as well as even "demade" on some older engines.
These days, the servers of the games created before the direct sequel, Team Fortress 2, are mostly empty aside from a handful of highly populated ones, forcing you to play on your own if you have anything against those servers.
Now wait a minute... Classes? Clear cut objectives? Playing on your own? Tossing in the unfunny joke about DOOM being top-down?
That's right, Team Fortress is a complete ripoff of NetHack.
You TF2 players can ♥♥♥♥ off with your whining about Overwatch, the whole series is just a reskin.

There is only  one for now, but i am pretty sure that two more are coming. Even though, the world is not huge, you will get the chance to play it in (once again i assume) 4 different settings, each time unlocking few more secrets.
There is also practise and challenge area. This is the wolrd you enter when you meditate. Area itself is simple and not interesting, but the challenges are very welcome. It is always nice to put the skills to the test.
As for the story, i can't really say much as it is far from complex or engaging. It will definately be interesting to see what happened to the world and the few characters that we meet, but i don't expect mind blowing twists or deep backgrounds. I don't even know who am i playing and why.
We might get to see two different endings depending on collecting certain items for certain "person". Some betrayal possibly... That is just my mind doing some random thinking :D
Anyway, the story exists and it's not crap.
And finally, the gameplay and the actual parkour. Well, hmm. The moves are there, walls, gaps, edges, but i just don't feel like i am doing that much. You can chain some serious moves only in the challenges. Not only that, but no skill is even needed through the story. You can pass the obstacle, stop and do the next one almost from standstill. Also, it is all done with one key (which is making it even worse since i can't chose between wallrun and walljump which results in ocasional fails) and timings are way too easy. Reaching the destination is not a matter of skill, but time.
Dash is fairly useless outside challenge.
One obvious contender in the genre is Mirror's edge, but lets not compare these games. The one game that i think should be compared is Deadcore. When i bought Downward, this is the style i expected. Combining multiple dashes with jumps and boost and double jumps, creating impressive moves and passing areas in different ways.Honing the skills and owning the leaderboards. When i reach the top i want to feel like the freeclimber filled with pride and excitement.
In summary, i enjoyed the game. Had a lot of fun with care free exploration of a beautiful world. Unfortunately, one of the selling points is actaully one of the worst aspects and that is the parkour. I will still highly recommend this game to every casual gamer and explorer.

This is the first and probably only review I will write on steam. This game was about as close to perfect as I have seen yet. It's not a run of the mill pop-up-scare genre, this game will haunt you in ways you have never seen in any horror game to date. In the main storyline, you play Miles, a journalist following up a mysterious email with claims of foul play in an unusual asylum. Unlike most of the horror genre, this game has a story and it makes you feel closer to the world that Miles' has been thrown into. Most of the game is avoiding as much interaction with twisted individuals lurking throughout the asylum and obtaining your objectives received after a series of what could be described as bad luck. Some people may find this game to be repetitive, however I personally found each experience unique and as equally frightening as the last.
If you decide to try out this game, I highly suggest playing in a darker room with a good pair of headphones, it will heighten the experience exponentially! Also, avoid playing this when there is a lot of background noise that could draw you out of the game and kill the environment that the game provides.

As someone who played the hell out of the first Red Orchestra, I was excited for RO2. A rocky launch dampened that, despite some fun I had from it.
The GOTY edition solved a lot of launch bugs and optimization issues, but it still doesn't really fix a few major things - namely, wasted potential and some seriously harrowing bugs that still persist. Red Orchestra 1 had dozens upon dozens of brilliantly-made custom maps (Black Day in July and Hedgehog still beats my fluttering heartstrings!), a very large assortment of armored vehicles, and lots of weapons to choose from.
RO2, on the other hand, is lacking widely in terms of content compared to its predecessor, despite being bigger and better looking. It added more depth to infantry combat, including slow death, bandaging, adjustible iron sights, and a low-impact customization/proficiency system. These sound great on paper, but over extended play these become nuisances (slow death), kind of superfluous (iron sights), or disappointingly obtuse balance-wise (the upgrade/RPG system). It's really disappointing to have something as interesting like being able to suppress nearby enemies while sprinting in close proximity with friendlies - like a 'charge' effect - go to waste when 90% of battles are pub rifle camp fests.
I loved the first game, I've tried RO2 and Rising Storm through their launches, and maybe I just have rose-tinted glasses, but I don't feel like RO2 was able to deliver on what potential it had.

TL/DR:
fun, educational, more to it than meets the eye. Easy to get into but a lot to learn along the way before you'll be producing a half decent game of your own. If you have got the ideas for a retro RPG type of game, this is the tool to get you started. Steam workshop is very well supported. Try the Demo/Lite version.
Review:
They claim "a child can use it"...  So after having the Lite (free) version for ages I can say the basics can be mastered in literally half an hour but to get the best from it you'll certainly be needing some youtube or steam community tutorials, then downloading scripts and addons of which there are hundreds, almost all are free and then you might want to start to write your own (and share them on steam workshop of course)
Lots of youtube tutorials, and a friendly  community around it on and off steam, 99% of whom are helpful.
The community made up of all ages from elementary/primary school age to grandparents and everyone in between, this software really is for people of all ages to make games for people of all ages.
This software is long established and well developed, and it's capable of helping you turn your ideas into solid games in the popular retro RPG Genre.  Some RPG Maker games are for sale on steam and on Kickstarter which goes to show how useful this tool can be in the right hands.
Lots of full-price DLC, also masses of free content, so unless you have a lot of money to burn play smart and wait for humble-bundle or bundlestars deals which are DRM free with a steam key as well.  And keep an eye on steam sales. In the meantime there is the enormous amount of free content outside of steam, plus lots of useful scripts etc to keep you going. Any games you make in the lite version seamlessly import into the full verion, so really there is no reason to rush into buying this unless its on sale at a price you can't resist, hopefully with a bundle of DLC.

The interface is simple dropdown lists, these lists basically do all the 'programming' for you. I don't even need to script much to make my game, but you can do so much more when/if you use scripts. The best part is you don't need to script at all. (I only use a persistant event positions script to be safe) The layout is simple as well, and it's not hard to find what you're looking for. Pretty much every bit of programming is boiled down to "point and click at this, type that in please, select okay and you're done" and fixing errors is easy as well since you can playtest right in the program itself. There's a little bit of a learning curve, but nowhere near as heavy as other tools I've tried, such as Game Maker.  For the price you pay on the program (by the way, it's on sale this month at Humble indie Bundle) it's a powerful tool for making your games with.
It's lacking a few features though(I would love to be able to check if an actor's health is ABOVE a certain percent, I would love to have more weather effects too, and well I'm just nitpicky about certain things.) but to be honest if you want an easy way to make an old school RPG you can certainly use this software to get the job done. My only complaint is that the help document doesn't really explain how to do certain things with the program but there's tons of youtube videos and the steam community is usually pretty friendly. Would I give it a perfect rating? Probably not, but it's worth at least a 9.5/10 for the effort and the ease. Especially since you can sell your games and you own all the rights to the content and dlc you buy.

I've been a true blue Tales fan since I popped a Symphonia disc into my Gamecube and encountered what may just be my favorite RPG of all time. None of the Tales games that cane afterwards however, regardless of how good they were themeselves (yes Xillia, I'm lookinh at  you), have given off the same charm that symphonia did. Symphonia made me tear up. Symphonia made me feel very attatched to my companians. Symphonia did what so many other RPG's have attempted to do, flawlessly.
But this isn't a review about Symphonia. This is a review on what seems to be the closest thing to reliving that experience I did so long ago. I have been waiting for this game to release for so long now. The protagonis is nongeneric. The story is so into depth you can tell how much time and effort was put into it in the very few minutes you play it. The environment is rich and filled with detail. Even the enemies are fun to fight because they look so darn nice! Having said that, I must admit a few minutes into gameplay before my first encounter I  thought, "Wow spider webs. Spiders are so original", but then later encountering the spider my jaw dropped. they managed to actually put some originality behind such a cliche enemy.
The one thing that doesn't compare to Symphonia is the coive acting. Not to say Symphonia had the greatest voice acting ever, but if you decide to buy this game about 2 minutes into gameplay I'm sure you'll realize exactly why I had a good laugh at it. Sometimes the voices are emotionless leaving a bland feeling of discomfort and confusion as to how exactly the character is feeling. Think of the notorious film "The Room" to get an idea of what I mean.
All in all? This is bound to be one of the best, if not, the best RPG of this year, and is definitely on my top three Tales games already. Combat is fluent, the game looks cool, and there seems to be a lot of promises with character progression story wise. If you like RPG's? Get it. If you want a new experience? Get it. If you're not sure, you only have enough for one game and  it's between this game and another game currently or soon to come out? Get THIS game. You won't regret it.

RPG Maker VX Ace is a decent version of RPG Maker. I started up with RPG Maker XP, and few things are annoyingly different, some no loger possible, but than again, new options were added.
All editions look and handle similiar though. All it takes to learn the basics is an hour or two, with many many tutorials available everywhere.
Basic functions are easy to master, but it offers way more past that. So it essentially depends on YOU and how much effort you want to put into it.
Most games look similiar to each other, unless you decide to work harder on it, import your own tiles and textures, sound, etc. but with generic materials you can still do quite a lot, depending on your imagination.
Even more with the DLCs.
Most of all, the process of making the game from tile sets and simple events is both very simple and really entertaining itself.
The extra stuff involving content creation and scripting is possible for those who have even more time on their hands :)
Everyone can do something with it, regardless their skill. Highly recommended.

Wow! That's the first thing that came to my mind moments after I fired this up. For such a small footprint, this game nails what it sets out to do...to provide an immersive survival environment in which you can't help but be pulled into. To begin with, this game is absolutely beautiful aesthetically. Beyond this beauty lies imminent horror, as you quickly grasp the reality of your situation in game. There is no hand holding here, but that’s what you would expect given the “survival” moniker stamped on its front cover. The Long Dark succeeds at an extremely high level where other games that fall within this genre have sorely missed the mark. Yes, it’s frustrating once you recognize that there’s only one end game in your demise, but I believe therein lies the genius at the root of its design. TLD will invoke many emotions throughout your short time in its environment. Bouncing between depression, despair, elation and achievement is all part of the dance. I recommend you dress warmly before taking the leap into TLD, as the lines between reality and fantasy will quickly become blurred. All this, and we are still in early access. I cannot recommend the experience waiting for you inside enough.

In some ways, the game seems simple enough to be a throwback to earlier "Sim" type games.  Specifically SimCity or SimFarm.
Yet in a lot of ways its newer, fresher like the indie title it is.
So far it is a beautiful, gentle game.  I thoroughly enjoy building my tiny little village.  It is at once peaceful, but also challenging.  Because instead of trying to manage my tax base, I'm trying to keep people alive.
Honestly, it's sort of hard to explain.

Banished is a fantastically atmospheric, albeit barebones, city builder set in pseudo-colonial times. You start off with a handful of ragged outcasts thrust into the wilderness with a mission of building your own civilization from the landscape.  Because of its small scope, Banished is also much more personable than more robust city builders; instead of managing multiple cities or even a nation, you start with four to six families and grow to a few hundred people (or more, depending on how long you wish to play a map). This isolation combined with little charming touches, like knowing each citizen's personal info, excellent ambient sound design, and a slower paced game speed, makes Banished the most atmospheric fictional city builder I have played.
Although there is a rough "progression" to what you can build via resource requirements, any building can be built at any time depending on what your city needs. Real strategy comes in properly timing and planning your construction; While Banished is a pretty laid-back game, a sudden influx of nomads can bring diseases or cause starvation if your city isn't prepared and construction takes significant manpower and cross-profession coordination. This flexibility can be overwhelming for a new player trying to survive their first winter but thankfully Banished's tutorials are well constructed and actually worth playing through even for veterans. Your city's growth (and essentially the game's difficulty) is tied to how much or how little you want to build, leading to a more relaxed game than most city builders.
Even though I loved most of this game, I spent a lot of time fighting with the villager's AI. While Banished strictly doesn't have win/lose conditions, it is heart-breaking to watch your citizens die from starvation while they are harvesting crops or gathering fish. Other AI issues emerge much earlier in the game, like farmers acting like laborers and not tending their fields during the summer. Laborers also seem to act erratically; when you assign multiple removal tasks, they seem to work in arbitary priority. Constructing multiple buildings is a huge pain with trying to coordinate the laborers with the builders; I eventually resorted to laying down a "building plan" and mass-pausing construction, unpausing one building at a time to be built. Maybe I don't understand all the intracies of the AI but 50 hours in and I'm still frustrated and often resorting to using the "Increase Priority" tool.
Banished is also missing many things that add challenge and depth to other city builders. This is essentially the "kiddie pool" of city builders with no crime, polution, budget balancing/taxation, or non-essential buildings. With 31 construction options, everything you build is for managing food, housing or supplying citizens, or transportation needs. There are some minor trading elements but its mostly there to keep your city growing once you run out of certain resources. Once you have a stable city running all there is to do is make it bigger while avoiding starvation or disasters. The same could be said of many games but I always look forward to building a sports stadium in SimCity... here it feels like it's just food, food, and more food.
If you haven't played a city builder before, Banished is a great place to start. Veterans looking for a more laid-back experience will get a few dozen hours out of this while alt+tabbed with something else. Nothing here is groundbreaking but what there is is a great change of pace from playing certain other sims at Cheetah speed.

This is a really interesting and fun puzzle game.
The game also has a lot of replay value because the first time you play you are just trying to solve the problem. That solution may or may not be the most efficient possible. So once you have solved other problems you may find yourself tracking back to old problems to solve them in a more efficient manner. In the game each solution is evaluated using number of cycles, footprint or number of blocks. Your solution is compared to the other submitted solutions from the other players. This is really useful to know how good your solution actually is. In my case i spent a lot of time trying to beat the scores of the other players in each category.
A lot of the time problems have no perfect solution. You usually have to make a compromise on what you want to optimize what you want to optimize. Luckily you can save up to 3 solutions per problem. So if you want to optimize for each characteristic you can also save the solutions to improve them later if you want.
I recommend this game for people who like a good challenge and efficient solutions.

Few games take you back to your roots as does this 'classic'.  TFC was the beginning of my PC gaming life and opened new doors to gratification, imagination, competitiveness, and friendship.  This game helped get me through my college years and when I needed a break and time to reset, I could always count on this game.  It was through TFC that I learned about leagues and clans and how a game can create a whole new universe of possibilities to bring people together to compete in league matches, practice on skill maps, and even unlock secrets about the games engine that could change the entire way the game was approached (bunnyhopping) years after it's release.  To think of my first ever clan, [4H] (the four horseman) and how using tools like Roger Wilco and IRC/MIRC in addition to playing a game was something I had never experienced before and was such an amazing experience.   This game to this day, which has grown old and slowed down quite a bit, still sparks dedication and follow through to it's fan base with servers like Drippy's 2 Fort (a lot of hours logged there :) still up and running to this day.  There have been a lot of games in this genre releaesd since, but even with the newest graphics and fancy engines, nothing quite seems to bring me home and have that same gratifying appeal, or should we say taste.... like sitting down to a 'steam'ing plate of Mom's spaghetti.

About sums up the quality of the voice acting, and my opinion on the game, to be honest.
+
* The game looks very pretty.
* The levels seem well designed
+/-
* The general mechanics and control systems are... "okay". There's nothing inherently wrong with it, but it's also not exactly the best, either.
-
* There doesn't seem to be much of a story. Nothing grips you from the moment you start playing. You're just this guy in a brand new world. That would be fine, however, if your character was either more engaging or just shut up. This brings me onto the next part.
* The character. Man, what a load of drivel. He just wouldn't shut the f*** up. "Ugh." "ooh". "OOH". And any other ways of expressing a minor grunt type comment. That was accompanied by rather unhelpful "tips" like "that's not how you do it"... well if he already knew, he could damn well tell us. He could fall off a huge pillar and you'd hear a "ugh" as if he'd tapped his leg on a shrub.
* The game does a poor job of teaching the mechanics. It's very haphazard and random. It'll introduce some mechanic like the marks, then say "oh you need an artifact to use that" then mention nothing about artifacts for ages.
* The quality from the developer(s) in regards to grammar, punctuation and spelling is atrocious. My God just run your text through a spell checker first. Multiple, easy words are misspelled, small case 'i' at the start of a sentence etc.
* There's no quality in the character development from the NPCs you meet along the way. Everything seems very generic and bland.
* The voice acting sounds like some bored teenager got coerced into doing it as a favour. You hear more enthusiastic voicing on a soap opera...
Overall - do not recommend...

Honestly:
Cons first:
I was a little disappointed in terms of how linear it was. I was hoping for more of an exploratory, multi-pathed thing with lots of places to explore but it's kind of straightforward, with really obvious goal markers, and single paths. This can, of course, all change when it moves form EA.
However the biggest issue is... the main character's voice-acting. Not the actor themselves exactly, but it seems really awkward and forced given the context- it's also slightly too loud cmpared to ambient sounds (haven't looked into adjusting the sound yet if I can change the different levels but at default) and sort of tears me away from the immersion at times. A few lines are really sort of unnerving:I mean, if the main character's lived in the world for however long he has (the main character is an adult); he obviously cannot be as ignorant of things as the tutorial-style intro makes it out to be. He gets confused about finding artifacts and is like ?!??!! WHAT ARE THOSE whenever he runs into a new enemy (which seem to be fairly widespread- really, he's never seen one of them before?). Also, some things are never even explained but he totes knows what's up with those guys. It's a bit contradictory. This is also coming from the fact that he is already on a 'journey' and probably has some goals in mind. Honestly, I feel like I'm playing an absolute idiot most of the time. I haven't gotten too far yet; but he seems really, really ♥♥♥♥ing stupid. Not to mention that he talks about how rare people are; yet he can speak a language that everyone understands. Where did he learn it from? He had to have parents or an origin or something, they must have taught him some other things! Why is he so stupid when he's talking?
I'd highly suggest them re-writing and re-recording most of his dialogue, because it just seems really weird. I do really enjoy the lines he says when you find an artifact though- those are hilarious. Some folks here (after reading the other reviews and editing mine a bit) complain about his lack of emotion- hoenstly I find the deadpan execution quite funny. However, they are right- he should be a little more invested when it comes to the actual storyline. VERY IMPORTANT: The voice-actor himself is GOOD. It's not about him- it's just.. the dialogue lines themelves are really awakward and umeotional.
Also, for being a parkour game, the grab-edges are kinda.. awkward? and it's really easy to miss things for really stupid reasons. Maybe I am just bad at games, but it's hard to tell where the cut off point is. And, with it being first-person (and not third person like assasin's creed), it's hard to tell where your feet are when running - and you can't look down because you tend to move whereever youre looking towards).
Lastly, ****[early-game spoilers begin here], when finding the shrine for the first time, and the first door gets opened, I was really confused because of how far away it was in the end. It was really awkward to run all the way across the map and having to get down from up ther ewas really awkward (pipe-passage shortcut I did not go to, as I thought the door would be somewhere else so I went past it a little). Also, I was not too sure what exactly I accomplished going through that first area.
[spoiles are over]****
Pros:
This game actually reminds me quite a lot of old-school Playstation and Gamecube games- like Spyro. The nostalgia's really strong with the way it's been developed and played. Honestly, I'm really digging that. Modern games have gone in the wrong direction at times, and it's mnice to see a straight-forward, item-collecting-y type thing to play. It's something I just enjoy. I'm not very good at developing good battle strategies or complex fights- like Dark Souls at the worst. This is so simple and just has these really nice basic elements to it; but with the modern graphics. It's really nice for me to play it. It's just something I could pick up and gothrough. Maybe this is a con for some people, but I really like it. It gives me a break ffrom really hard-core RPGs and complex stuff. It's just nice to play, though I wish the storyline was a little darker.
The landscapes are also amazing! I actually find the world really beautiful, though some of the foliage could use an upgrade (specifically in the frozen area).
Lastly for pros, I really like how progress is saved. I really like finally getting to an object, and even if I die I still retain it. I'm not sure if it's intentional, but it takes off a lot of stress about falling. Losing SKypieces really isn't an issue, but it's nice to see that all my collectibles save regardless of where I go.
All in all, I'm actually enjoying it quite a bit, thouigh don't go into this expecting a really deep complex game juuust yet.

Unlike most of the horror genre, this game has a story and it makes you feel closer to the world that Miles' has been thrown into. Most of the game is avoiding as much interaction with twisted individuals lurking throughout the asylum and obtaining your objectives received after a series of what could be described as bad luck. If you decide to try out this game, I highly suggest playing in a darker room with a good pair of headphones, it will heighten the experience exponentially! Also, avoid playing this when there is a lot of background noise that could draw you out of the game and kill the environment that the game provides.

Banished is a fantastically atmospheric, albeit barebones, city builder set in pseudo-colonial times. You start off with a handful of ragged outcasts thrust into the wilderness with a mission of building your own civilization from the landscape.  Because of its small scope, Banished is also much more personable than more robust city builders; instead of managing multiple cities or even a nation, you start with four to six families and grow to a few hundred people (or more, depending on how long you wish to play a map). This isolation combined with little charming touches, like knowing each citizen's personal info, excellent ambient sound design, and a slower paced game speed, makes Banished the most atmospheric fictional city builder I have played.
Although there is a rough "progression" to what you can build via resource requirements, any building can be built at any time depending on what your city needs. Real strategy comes in properly timing and planning your construction; While Banished is a pretty laid-back game, a sudden influx of nomads can bring diseases or cause starvation if your city isn't prepared and construction takes significant manpower and cross-profession coordination. This flexibility can be overwhelming for a new player trying to survive their first winter but thankfully Banished's tutorials are well constructed and actually worth playing through even for veterans. Your city's growth (and essentially the game's difficulty) is tied to how much or how little you want to build, leading to a more relaxed game than most city builders.
Even though I loved most of this game, I spent a lot of time fighting with the villager's AI. While Banished strictly doesn't have win/lose conditions, it is heart-breaking to watch your citizens die from starvation while they are harvesting crops or gathering fish. Other AI issues emerge much earlier in the game, like farmers acting like laborers and not tending their fields during the summer. Laborers also seem to act erratically; when you assign multiple removal tasks, they seem to work in arbitary priority. Constructing multiple buildings is a huge pain with trying to coordinate the laborers with the builders; I eventually resorted to laying down a "building plan" and mass-pausing construction, unpausing one building at a time to be built. Maybe I don't understand all the intracies of the AI but 50 hours in and I'm still frustrated and often resorting to using the "Increase Priority" tool.
Banished is also missing many things that add challenge and depth to other city builders. This is essentially the "kiddie pool" of city builders with no crime, polution, budget balancing/taxation, or non-essential buildings. With 31 construction options, everything you build is for managing food, housing or supplying citizens, or transportation needs. There are some minor trading elements but its mostly there to keep your city growing once you run out of certain resources. Once you have a stable city running all there is to do is make it bigger while avoiding starvation or disasters. The same could be said of many games but I always look forward to building a sports stadium in SimCity... here it feels like it's just food, food, and more food.
If you haven't played a city builder before, Banished is a great place to start. Veterans looking for a more laid-back experience will get a few dozen hours out of this while alt+tabbed with something else. Nothing here is groundbreaking but what there is is a great change of pace from playing certain other sims at Cheetah speed.

The Team Fortress series started out as a popular Quake mod, but was then picked up by the then young Valve, who had the TF team convert the game into their Goldsource engine to promote their development kit. The result was this game.
𝐆𝐚𝐦𝐞𝐩𝐥𝐚𝐲: 𝟖/𝟏𝟎
In Team Fortress Classic, you play as different classes, each with their respective role, and fight over an objective (Carrying a bomb to a point, control points, CTF, etc.) If you're looking here, you probably know what a class shooter is, so there isn't too much to say about that. There is a learing curve to this game, with several techniques, and the game has its pitfalls (grenade spam, one-sided maps, very confusing to newcomers, etc.), but the gameplay is solid overall, with many options.
𝐆𝐫𝐚𝐩𝐡𝐢𝐜𝐬: 𝟔/𝟏𝟎
As an old game, the graphics haven't aged too well. It can be hard to notice the different classes looks, and the demolition man's grenades just look like s***. Not much to look at.
𝐒𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐝: 𝟕/𝟏𝟎
Not much to hear. Generic sounds, the rampant "Excuse me, I'm in need of medical attention!", and the boring monotone announcer. However, the sound gets across what's happening on the battlefield, so it's serviceable enough.
𝐑𝐞𝐩𝐥𝐚𝐲 𝐕𝐚𝐥𝐮𝐞: 𝟔/𝟏𝟎

𝐅𝐢𝐧𝐚𝐥 𝐒𝐜𝐨𝐫𝐞: 𝟔.𝟕/𝟏𝟎
The game is deep and fun to play; however, the graphics haven't aged gracefully, the audio is monotone, and the replay value is lacking. I would only recommend this game to those who are coming back from playing this before, and those who don't care about the lack of servers. I don't recommend this to the average consumer.

Team Fortress Classic is a surprisingly retro first-person shooter game, released in 1999 as a follow-up to the original Team Fortress Quake mod this game uses Valve's Half-Life engine. In TFC you take the role as one of ten different classes, each with extinct and somewhat unique abilities. TFC isn't as fast pasted as something like Counter-Strike which released around the same time as TFC and also is a mod for Valve's Half-Life game, but it's still fun in my opinion and is different enough from Counter-Strike even to be enjoyed to this very day. With different community made maps and game modes the game also still holds up in 2017, and that shows since the game yet has a massive cult following and it shows when you see how many people are playing on the online servers. If you enjoy the Team Fortress 2 game, then I recommend you try this game out, it's quite different from the sequel, but I'm sure you'll enjoy seeing how the Team Fortress franchise evolved into what it is today. Zachtronics has a history of creating highly acclaimed conveyor / programming logic puzzles, ever since their cult hit SpaceChem. Their other games have been 2-dimensional, but Infinifactory brings the same formula into 3D.
The addition of 3rd dimension adds a whole lot more space for creating solutions, which can be both a good and a bad thing. Having more space can make solutions turn rather messy towards the end, where the conveyor belts can zigzag wildly among multiple levels of elevation, whereas 2D map restrictions forced a certain level of optimization to make the most of limited space. On the other hand, 3D offers far more possible solutions to any given puzzle, so wider range of players are able to find an answer eventually.
The campaign difficulty is decently challenging but not too hard. For the most part the game leaves you to figure out your own tactics and favourite setups with the blocks you're given, which you earn gradually while progressing in the story. The story is rather weak though, and only starts to open up later in the game. The game's also rather visually simplistic, which worked just fine for the 2D puzzle games but sticks out a little bit more in the 3D environment. Still, neither really bothers anyone who's simply absorbed in the puzzle solving.
The game tracks how well your solution was optimized, based on time, blocks used or how much space your factory takes. You can compare scores with your steam friends, or see where your score lands among the entire playerbase, so you can always go back and optimize your solution to compete for best scores. If you'd prefer more tangible goals besides score hunting, there's a good handful of achievements which require a certain score within certain levels, which often requires you to fully rethink your entire setup to complete.
This game is a solid entry in their library and I have no problem recommending to fans of puzzle games, but in my opinion this isn't quite as good as their other titles. Give it a try, if you're in the mood for a puzzle game.

Five Nights at Freddy's is an indie horror game that has gained a lot of poularity recently for being one of the scariest games ever according to a lot of people. When I look at Five Nights at Freddy's I don't see the scariest game of recent memory, far from it. What I see is the potential to be the greatest horror game ever made. For those of you that don't know in FNF you control a security officer working the night shift at Freddy Fazbears Pizza, a pizza parlor renowned for its animatronic robots. The reason they need a security officer at night is because they have a tendency to wander around the building and someone needs to keep an eye on them. As you are playing you find yourself in a rather small office equiped with security cameras dotted around the building, lights by your doorway, two huge security doors(one on each side of the room), and limited electricity. The way the game works is all the robots want your head on a silver platter and they are headed towards your room to basically kill you. Now here I will give the game some credit. The developer nailed the paranoid feeling in this game. You see you would naturally want to sit with the doors closed all night to defend yourself, but you have a limited supply of electricity and closing the doors drain power so you can only close them if absolutley neccisary to survive. I love this idea. Having the game dictate you need to leave your guard down when you know a killer robot is right down the hallway is really genius and the opposite of what you would typically expect out of a horror game. Anyways when you look through the cameras at the, rather creepy I must add, robots that particular robot you are looking at(there are four) will not move, but of course using the camera takes energy too. Another fatal weakness of the camera is that you aren't able to see everywhere. There are two blind spots, one by each door. You can use the lights next to the door to catch any robots before they try to get into your room. If you see a robot with the doorlight thats when you need to close that specific door, or you will lose. Again this is a good idea and was executed well like all the other ideas. Now you may be asking why I don't find it scary if all of those scary sounding ideas are,according to me anyway, well implemented. The problem is once you make it to the third night you are focused like a laser performing the same exact method of robot prevention over and over again with no margin for error. It means the game isn't scary anymore because you don't have time to be scared, and if I'm being truly honest the scares  get stale either way. I must admit the sound design is phenomenal, playing this game with headphones was terrifing the first night,but then as I said earlier it loses it's touch by night 3 at least. I commend the developer of this game for not only coming up with all of these brilliant ideas, but for the setting too. Freddy Fazbears Pizza was a real place with real robots, and a lot of nasty stuff happened there that you should look up, and by that I mean watch the game theory episode on it. In the end though the game didn't live up to its full potential. I heard that the developer is making a sequel. If that turns out to be true I'll be sure to play it, because I'm expecting a lot form the developer now. In the end Five Nights at Freddys scores a 5.8/10 and with a $5 price tag I reccomend it to anybody who thinks they are ready for Freddy.

After playing this game for a while, I will be playing no longer.
The game IS pay-to-win contrary to what people say. This is especially true for ranked matches. You can join in with, say the R4 SMG, and maybe get a kill or two before being popped by some person with a paid sniper rifle due to some BS quickscope. Another problem is ranking; lower ranks like I are put up against HRs, which is extremely unfair and ruins the game.
Some ways this game can improve are to do away with Kredits and do something like Black Squad; make the paid items cosmetic only. It works for Black Squad and CSGO (which, while still a paid game, has made a lot of money off of skins), and it will gain more approval in the long run.  The game should have to be skill based, not money based. A game should be fun to play, not fun to pay. A game should be to the roots of enjoyment - kills and wins should be earned by sheer skill rather than cash, and like I said they can still make a decent amount of money off of cosmetic items such as knives and skins.
Overall, the game itself is good, but the in-game economy and matchmaking is below mediocre. Another bugging but minor problem is that the FOV cannot be changed. I hope the devs, while very unlikely, will take this into consideration.
EDIT: The ranked matches are also very broken, as I am typically pitted up against high-pingers in South America rather than people from North America, and the matchmaking isn't skill based at all, which ruins the game for newer players looking to get into competitive. As for the high-pingers, they have the high ping advantage as their hitbox is delayed and most likely not on their body due to their high ping.

Few games are as important to me as Napoleon: Total War. This video game represents some of my most favourite hours spent playing video games. Every battle I fought in this game felt realistic and intense, capped off with an insane artillery mechanic that will leave you with your heart stopping every time your enemy fires a barrage. This is truly a fantastic game.
As far as critical concerns, this is unlike most Total War games. If you have just started with the series, you might be very happy with this game and Empire: Total War. Both are solid games, but unrepresentative of the Total War series as a whole. If you are a diehard Total War fan, with your Medieval II: Total War poster on a shrine above your dresser, then you probably will dispise this and Empire very much. It is very much a conscious decision that your units walk towards an enemy, stop, stare, and then fire at quizzically odd rates.
I'm not going to argue the attention to detail the developers had for history here, only say that this is about as perfect a representation of 18th-19th Century warfare as we can get with our slow processing power. If it is on sale, I highly recommend this game. If not, consider how frequently things appear on sale, and debate whether that money burning a hole in your wallet can be used for more constructive purposes. Either way, I believe this is a sensible purchase. Who knows, you might just like it as much as I do...

I'd been walking for hours, completely out of food, and freezing after being unable to start a fire in the blowing wind. I hear the familiar howl of wolves in the distance, and down to my last 3 rounds, I ready my rifle. As one spots me and starts running in my direction, I take aim, wait until he's a bit closer, and fire. He drops immediately, and his companion runs for the trees. Finally, I've found something to eat, now I just need to find a way to cook it before I starve to death.
Luckily, I was able to get a fire started behind some turned over rail cars, and I cook and immediately eat a chunk of meat from my fresh kill. As I sit and warm myself by the fire, cooking the remainder of my kill, I think to myself "I might actually make it through this".
It's colder out than normal, and I huddle as close to the fire as possible to get my core temperature up as quickly as I can. That's when I found out that fire in this game is just as dangerous as it is in real life, and in my already terrible condition from almost starving and freezing myself to death, I immediately burn to death. F*ck.
I didn't even hesitate starting a new game. Easy 8/10 now, and they haven't even added the story yet.

Napoleon: Total War is the 6th game of the Total War Franchise and is released at 2010. Napoleon: Total War is a historical turn-based strategy game. The game is really fun to play and with your volume button it sound more realistic. I am a great fan of historical strategy games. I've played a lots of strategy games and I must say; Napoleon: Total War is one of my most favorite (for now). Napoleon was one of the greatest emperor and general in history. The game lets you play a lot of generals and even Napoleon in his campaigns.
At the beginning I've started with the tutorial, but after a several minutes I got bored so I started with the Italy campaign on easy mode. When I played the Italy campaign I started with recruiting soldiers for the France Empire, but you need to wait several turns. In the main time the enemy was approaching my lands. When I sent all my armies to enemy countries to capture them the crisis started for France I lose more money then I get. Because of the bankruptcy I couldn’t recruit more armies or upgrade buildings to make profit. I've started the campaign over and tried it again but with better tactics.
After I finally completed this campaign I started to play multiplayer, but I can say the multiplayer is dead except you’re a high rank. I tried to find online campaign games for the achievement, but there wasn't any except some locked servers. So I started to host one after some minutes someone joined and I started it, but there was one problem: the game crashed and windows said there was some unexpected error and closed it. I were not able to achieve the achievement.
My impressions of the game.
The game is sure fun at single player, but I can't say if you get the same fun with the single player campaigns. I sure liked the sound it gives you the feelings to play more and more.....
Pros and Cons.
Pros.
- The game is fun
- The game isn't easy to complete, even on easy mode
- The sounds gives you more feelings to complete the whole game (at least for me)
- The game has trading cards
- Amazing graphics
- Choices you make decides your empire
- Variety in historical characters, like generals and soldiers
Cons.
- Multiplayer sessions are hard to find
- Multiplayer crashes
- Achievements are hard to get

This is another of those times that I'm having so much fun with a game, that I feel the need to sit down and share why it is that I feel this way. I first tested DD2 very, very early on, before it was redone to be much closer to its predecessors, Dungeon Defenders, and Dungeon Defenders Eternity. Team Trendy was still deciding on the direction they wanted to go with the project. At the time it was PvP, and I for one am extremely happy that they went back to the tried and true formula that makes the series great. After trying the game again, post-redesign, I bought into the Defense Council, and it's not often that I feel thrilled to have paid $70 for a game. Here are the things this game does SO right:
Dungeon Defenders at its finest:
DD2, even still in alpha, trumps the first 2 games already. The tavern is bigger, better, and packed with things to unlock and discover as you play. The game features quests, NPC's, mad amounts of loot and items, a solid campaign, and once beyond that, multiple new game modes to dive into. For an Early Access title, there is a tremendous amount of content here already, with more updates pouring in every 6 weeks or so. I do look forward to plenty more maps coming in in the future, those are pretty limited currently, but not so much so that you get bored.
Trendy!
Trendy Entertainment, once again, shines in their interactions with the community, in addressing bugs and issues, and in building a great experience. These guys GET IT. I mean REALLY get it, when it comes to how to treat the community, and even in alpha they're right on top of things. You'll see them reply to nearly every thread, and for a game with around 14,000 concurrent users at the time of writing this, that's impressive to say the least. They've gone above and beyond the call, even compensating the community when issues arise which reset quests or cause the players to lose progress. This is an alpha, we will ALL lose progress at times, but these guys still know how frustrating that can be!
Immersion
One of the big surprises for me in DD2 was getting into the campaign and seeing more than just the same crystals to defend. There are interactive traps on the map, and other things to defend besides just the main crystal. In one case, there were even NPC's on the map, cowering up near the throne while you defended them and kept them alive. Tel ya what, having actual characters there made it feel so much more worthwhile! Who wants to defend an empty throne? I love the added depth they've brought to DD2, it brings so much life to the game!
F2P done RIGHT!
Trendy has done a perfect job with the cash shop. There is absolutely nothing pay to win in DD2, and never will be. It's a promise they made, and have stuck to like glue. You can buy costumes, bags, things like that, but never boosts, or anything that changes the way the game is played. You can't go to the cash shop and make your game any easier, or make it impact the experience. You can sure look great though! The costumes for each character are quite cool, and worth a spend for people looking to support the development of the game.
Additionally, even with an already bustling community, I LOVE the option for private taverns/friends only gameplay. Let's face it, most people don't want to play with "that guy", who presses ready before the towers are even placed, or who afk's mid battle. There are plenty of players around, and getting into a public tavern/game is definitely easy to do, but if you want to chill alone or with the best friend, being able to do that is a huge plus for me. The game has taken the best of what makes a free to play game fun, and added in the way to play the way you want to play.
To sum up:
Pro's:
-The game is already head and shoulders above previous games in the series
-The development team is ROCKING this!
-The game has depth, immersion, and a ton of fun, even for an alpha release
-It's Free to play done beautifully right
Cons:
-It is an alpha, so you are going to find the hiccups and bugs that come along with an Early Access game
-Maps are still limited this early on, but there are enough to keep you going for hours even now
