It's a quickly-played, quickly-made RPG Maker action RPG game.  RPG Maker notoriously handles anything but the turn-based actions it was made to handle quite poorly, so the game can be clunky at times, but it's not QUITE as bad as most action RPGs on RPG maker is.  Still, I would suggest looking to something made in another engine for any substansive action RPG fix, because this game is anemic in content, and has no interesting gimmicks to make it stand out compared to the hundred other Zelda-wannabes on Steam.
Pros:
* Dirt cheap, so you won't regret it long even if you don't like it.
* It's fairly fast-paced, and you level up quickly with relatively little grinding.
* It's possible to just run past most of the enemies.
* Six possible classes.
* If you aren't going for cards, you can beat the game fast enough to return it for a refund!
Cons:
* The enemies are rubber-banded to your level, while your stat-boosting equipment is based upon how far in the plot you have progressed, meaning you lose power relative to your enemies as you gain levels.
* The enemies meander around until it's time for their attack, at which point they fly at you at mach 12, clip through your own attacks, and keep chasing you even if you do hit them in the middle of their attack.
* You have a shield button, but except for the archer, you have to be a melee class to get it, and there's no wind-up animation to warn you to raise your shield before they start running at you, so you need to use psychic precognition to tell when to use your shield when you're standing only 1-2 tiles away.
* The enemies deal about 1/5 your total health per hit.
* The enemies have about second-long invulnerability after being hit, and can attack immediately after that.
* The enemies can stun-lock you in place with spammed ranged attacks
* The classes are not described in-game at all, and have unintuitive effects.
* The classes are not balanced at all.
* The archer class relies upon arrows, can only carry 99 at a time, I shot 50 getting from the first town to the second, and the second town doesn't have arrow vendors.
* The spells deal 1/6th the damage a physical attack does no matter what your magic stat is, so mages are useless.
* All other classes are melee classes, and any melee class besides Paladin is just plain weaker than the Paladin.
* Bugs galore! Walk through walls! Don't walk through objects that look the same as ones you can walk through! Enter one house, leave out a different one!
* The writing is as utterly barebones as possible.  "Go kill this thing for me." "Thank you for killing it.  Here's the ___ I promised."
* The plot consists of your character having a dream where a bird tells you to go kill four bosses and bring it their souls or it'll eat your soul.  You find these bosses literally just sitting out in a field, and after you're done killing all four, you get a final boss, then, BAM, credits, game over.
* You will finish in about an hour if you don't grind, and the game punishes you for grinding, anyway.
It failed to keep my interest to continue playing the game.

This game feels like it's trying to do the Y Chronicals or Link to the Past thing, where combat takes place in real time, rather than in the typical random enounter way. The problem with this is that the RPG Maker engine wasn't meant for this type of combat. Developers, I congratulate you for making the game do it... but it's a shame you didn't do it well.
I learned that this game uses a system where enemiew level up with the player. A novel concept, but it utterly fails in practice. Developers, I'm sorry. But you picked the wrong genre to include such a feature, because doing this punishes the player for grinding. When you have a game that rewards players for killing enemies with exp, money, and crafting items, chances are we're going to be encouraged to fight as many things as we can see. And the combat system you developed makes it really easy to kill a ton of things early on. But as you level up, enemies will start to take more and more hits to kill. And then you'll reach level 5 during the first notable quest, only to get gored by a bee on the way back.
Killing 20 slimes doesn't turn the rest of them into liquid iron. Not in a logical world, anyways.
Writing is extremely poor early on. Who am I? Why do I down a rat infested well to train? What "training" do I get done by beating up on an archery target with a knife? How did guy from the guild see me training on the cliff side? I never say any other spot in town where someone could get that kind of view. The moment I'm done with that training, he comes to me and says he'll give me a weapons license and a guild membership. Is it really that easy to join this guild? I wouldn't mind if the writing wasn't handled so clumsily. If you have a guild with criteria to join, it's typically best to have the player go to the guild, and be given some sort of minor adventuring quest to join it. Not saying you have to fit the generic mold; but either make joining the adventurers guild some sort of major feat for the character, or have them already in it. Otherwise, joining feels meaningless. Another protip would be to think of catchier names for towns and people. I know that seems like nitpicking. But it helps your world to make it memorable.
And here's a protip for using the RPG VX ACE maker. I noticed this when I stepped on a patch of tall grass, and it looked like I was floating on top of it. If you go into your tilesets, where most tiles have like an X or O on it, there should be an option that looks like 2 wavy lines. I don't have it pulled up right now, so I can't give the actual name for it. But it'll make it to where characters get their lower half shaded when walking over a section. This creates the illusion that your character has the grass coming up to his waist. Just apply it to the tall grass sections and you're good.
Overall, it's a game I fell if I do complete, it'll be by force. Sorry guys. This just wasn't your game.

The NPC voices are terrible, the story is shallow, the vehicles are poorly tuned, the gunfights lack feedback, the goals are repetitive, and the DLC is too granular.
And I love it to bits. This is a feel good game, standing out from a bottomless pit of soulless sandboxes with at best mean-spirited or insufficient premises. Ultimately that sums up why I love it: Rico has a just cause. And despite the obvious pun, he pursues it as a mostly well-meaning hero, not a chaotic blank slate. Never has wreaking unfettered havoc on an island paradise been so pleasantly justified. It also has the trappings of an action spy thriller, providing an appropriate thematic backdrop for the action and paying affectionate homage to the genre, but toning down the typical byzantine plot in favour of uninterrupted carnage and exploration.
Even lacking polish in multiple areas, JC2 is conceptually superior to many similar titles. Much like the peerless Metroid Prime, it begins with a solid gameplay concept and builds a story around it, not vice versa. Unfortunately the plot is more or less a straight shot to the finale with few memorable twists or diversions, but on the other hand, it's harmless to the experience. Throughout the story and into the endless Mercenary Mode, Rico's personality and motivation is reinforced through small quips he dishes out in response to certain events. For instance, although there's no real punishment for harming civilians, once you hear Rico complain about "aiming for the other guy", you might prefer to avoid them. Happily, these quotes trigger sparingly and are still fresh after 100+ hours of gameplay.
Here's hoping Avalanche Studios can create the perfect implementation of this formula in Just Cause 3. Until then, part deux remains a unique beast offering many hours of childish fun.

Just Cause 2 is like Michael Bay redesigned Grand Theft Auto after playing Red Faction. If you liked either of those games, this game is bigger, easier to move around in and has MOAR BOOM. And yes, "MOAR BOOM" is the best way to describe this game. Sure, the story isn't quite as deep as the aforementioned games (at least in the 9 or so missions I've played so far), but that's not important. Just messing around in it for hours is more fun than plot. And I'm usually a sucker for a good plot.
Also, the missions can be frustrating sometimes, but that is made up for by the fact that I just blew up a rocket with a fighter jet that I had grappled into. It might have been on try number three, but it was still epic.
There is no other game that I've played that is so rediculously fun and explosive. The map is also deceptively huge, which means that there always tends to be something for you to make go boom in a hail of bullets and missiles from a fighter jet. I got this game on sale for like $4, but it's easily worth three times as much for just the pure fun of it. It's also a MUCH better port than GTA IV, by the way, so it will run on a variety of computers. It may be 5 years old, but until Just Cause 3 comes out, this is the king of explosive open-world games.

This is a fantastic example of a problem-solving puzzle game.  If you're familiar with Zachtronics' other titles and liked them at all, stop wasting your time reading this and run-do-not-walk to the "buy" button.
If you're not familiar with the genre or the other titles, let me put it like this: you're building a factory.  You get some collection of stuff in, and some tools (conveyor belts, welders, etc) which you arrange into a production line to build a specific requested product.  You have essentially infinite freedom for what to build, and the _first_ puzzle is figuring out how to make what you want.
Then things get a little OCD.
Every solution you build to a puzzle is scored on three factors: how fast you solved it, how many pieces you used, and how "big" your solution was (for a measure of bigness that is not worth trying to define here.)  And it shows you how well yours scored compared to other users who have played the game.  Even if you're not the competitive type, it's awfully hard not to look at the fact that someone else solved it in half the time, think "That's impossible!  Well maybe if I..." and look up 4 hours later from the ruins of your civilization to realize that you are now addicted to this game.  Often times optimizing your solution one way will make it hilariously inefficent according to one of the other two scoring factors, so you'll end up solving the same problem many times.
The game is also set in a quirky-but-dark setting with a nice touch of humour.  It doesn't impose on the gameplay much (yet) but it does add a nice tone.  The interface is quick and intuitive.  The music and art assets are well-done, and the support is nothing short of phenomenal - I emailed Zachtronics with an issue and got a response from the developer within minutes (not that you should expect that every time, but I was still impressed... especially since the issue was actually User Error.)
Thanks Zach!  Great game!

Amazing and addictive puzzle game. I have played several other Zachtronics games before, so I knew this would be hard, but it is not as hard as I feared. I have played it about 20 hours now and I am through most of the first campaign, but I know that there is more to come and it will get more difficult. So far I had very few moments of frustration, though I had to take a break sometimes and think about a problem. I never felt the need to use online solutions, though it might be helpful to look at some of the user guides with some tips and tricks. In contrast to other Zachtronics games, I felt that the levels are quite large, so there is a lot of room for unelegant solutions, which still do the job.
Due to the 3D the game is much more immersive than other Zachtronics games and I like that it feels like you are constructing factories to manufacture actual stuff, like spaceships, tanks and packaged meat. It runs very smoothly on my non-gaming notebook, looks pretty enough and the backgrounds are gorgeous. The music is nice and not distracting, good for long periods of concentration. The story or setting reminded me of "The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy". It is funny and bizarre, but also sad at times. I really makes me want to know how it continues and I actually care for some of the characters (Floyd). However, I cannot judge how it will be in the later part of the game.
In the game you get different inputs and have to build a factory to create something as an output (for example a Sattelite). Otherwise you are given total freedom, so you can get really creative and in the end you are really proud of your own, personal solution. It is not a puzzle game in the sense that there is a predefined solution that you have to find, which is what I like about Zachtronics games. The puzzles (at least in the first campaign) feel all quite different, so it does not get repetitive. In some way it is like programming, because you can use sensors for kind of "if then" instructions: "If there is a block at this position, active that pusher in that other location". But you don't have to be a programmer, it is just some logic thinking. It's fun.
For the moment I will stop playing this game because I have an exam soon, which is why I am doing the review now. But this will take me some effort, I really want to continue playing it.

Welcome to Freddy Fazbear's Pizza. The date is May 5th, 2015. You needed money for the upcoming Steam Summer Sale, and  you started looking for a summer job on the newspaper. The one job that caught your intrest was Freddy Fazbear's Pizza and it looked like a simple job to just watch the cameras and keep the building secure. You pay the admission fee of $5 for the job and started to work at your first night, until suddenly you got a voicemail message on the phone. The guy that used to work at your position told you instructions, and also the distubing thing about the robots. He said that these robot mascots tend to roam around the building complex between 12AM to 6AM and if they see any human being, they will misinterpret it as a robot without its costume and will forcefully put the person in a costume (which leads to death). After the message you thought that this guy was just blabbering nonsense since the robots usualy go off when the building is closed. As you checked the cameras the first place you seen was the stage, but you noticed one of the robots is missing. You checked the other rooms and found the missing robot just standing there and not doing anything. You wondered how it got there, and suddenly the cameras only show static for a couple of seconds. As soon as you saw the room again, the robot was gone and as you check the other rooms, you saw that the missing robot moved and this time it was closer to the security room. You were scared and you started to believe everything the Ex-employee told you in the message. Can you survive Five Nights at Freddys and get the money for the Steam Summer Sale, or die trying? The job experience features: Simple point and click navigation, the feeling of being paranoid and afraid, and $120 after the week is over.

Five Nights at Freddy's. A game that has grown more controversy than Donald Trump himself. (That's not even a joke. It's actually true.) It's a game that when you observe the source code and basic algorithms used to plan out the game, is really and truly random generators and timers glossed over with a creepy and unsettling art scheme. Such a simple concept, but I must admit it is done very well. Especially considering one person is behind it. However there are flaws. The first is that the game itself is not very complex. You must conserve power, but the more you conserve, the more you become paranoid, and the more paranoid you are, the more you look for enemies, and the more you look for enemies the less power you have. The game relies on you being scared and clueless as to what's going to happen and scares with the classic jumpscare. horror games I respect like 'silent hills' scare you on a deep psychologically torturing level. But that's apple's and oranges. The next flaw, is the replay value. Scott Cawthon is a good marketer for his game. And he knows how the populus operates. From giving free early copies to populer youtubers, to getting this game on steam early, he is clever indeed. In addition to this he announces his sequels JUST as he figures his last one is losing interest. And to add to that, he is incorperating a vague and unexplained storyline to add to it. Which is how the FNAF controversy, and Scott's fortune was born. That clever rat.. Anyway the next flaw would have to be the simplicity. Once you get used to the game, it really gets boring until around night 4 or 5 difficulty. Cause by then you don't know for sure if you will win. The difficulty is what makes a game good. Letting you be able to customize your difficulty was a good move. To end, the game is good but simple. The scares can get you if you don't pay attention, the concept is beyond creepy and the frantic micro-managing the damn cameras to keep freddy and foxy in their place is strangely fun and annoying. I'll give this game an okay 77/100 for it's uniqueness

Vikings: Wolves of Midgard is a hard game to recommend. But I've played more than 20 hours of it and mostly enjoyed my time with it, so recommended it I will. Know, though, that it's very rough, with many questionable design decisions and an overall... lack of ambition is maybe not the right way to put it, since a lot of work was put into it and it shows, but let's say it doesn't set its sights particularly high. The TLDR version would be to get this in a sale if you like ARPGs, and not at all if you don't care for them.
What it is is an action RPG, with an emphasis on the action. You play as the leader of the most shiftless tribe of vikings (Wolves of Midgard(tm)) ever commited to game. As such, you're forced to venture out on missions to single-handedly save their sorry arses while they stay back and do nothing. Which sounds historically accurate to me; I don't remember Hagar the viking (not a Wolf of Midgard, as far as I know) ever actually doing anything. So you're basically fighting to preserve the viking (Wolves of Midgard(tm)) way of life.
Your character will even bemoan this lack of support, which is a slightly amusing and a whole lot aggravating. This practice is called lampshading and it's just... basically trying to cover up a shoddy aspect of something by calling attention to it for humorous effect. Instead of, you know, trying to do something about it. Ugh.
Anyhow!
So you use your tribe's hometown as a base hub (with traders, crafters and all the amenities) and launch incursions into discrete levels that function as either story missions or simply raids for experience and loot. It evolves over time, which is a neat touch - I really liked how your hall slowly fills with trophies from vanquished bosses. The maps you go a-viking to are simple but sprawling, with a decent amount of variety in both environments and enemies to fight, and some secrets to reward exploration, and they always end in some form of boss fight. There's always a story mission available, though sometimes they'll be above your character level to nudge you to replaying one of the maps you've already completed as a story-less hunt for monsters. Yes, you will have to grind at least a little.
Combat is completely action-based. The game feels like it should play like a twin-stick shooter, but doesn't, using the right stick as a directional dodge instead, and mapping normal attacks to the A button. This never sat right with me (especially since I chose the bow as my weapon), and using the same button attacks and interactions seems like a rookie mistake since I often found myself opening chests or worse, drinking one-use health cauldrons in the middle of a fight.
It's fun-ish rather than fun, with the difficulty on the average setting being pitched a little bit low and enemies taking a bit too long to die, especially if you're underlevelled. So your character isn't really in any danger of dying most of the time, but progress is a bit of a slog. There's also an environmental exposure mechanic - you're almost always freezing, being poisoned or... overheating? to death, and need to find safe spots to bring the danger gauge down. This adds some sorely needed urgency to your forays, but also hurts the flow of the game even further as you're forced to retreat to a shelter and wait to recover.
This may be fixed with higher difficulties or different weapons - I didn't enjoy the game's fundamentals enough to give them a try. Combat feels ponderous, even though it tries to focus on mobility with shielded enemies that need to be surrounded and heavily telegraphed attacks to dodge. It felt to me like they didn't get the balance right.
There's a fair amount of character customization; you've got equipment, stats, and perks. there's... five? types of weapons, each one associated to a god with His or Her own skill tree consisting of passive and active skills. Pretty standard stuff, but solid. Everything ties directly to combat or survival, though a little too much of it consists of slight percentage increases to your stats.
It's got graphics. Yup. Lots of them. The music is rather nice.
The story is fun and completely forgettable. It for some reason casts the Vanir as angels, with the Romans serving them, and the Celts as a different tribes of Vikings (non-Wolf of Midgard division). Like much of the rest of the game, it's happy dumbing things down and being serviceable rather than kicking things up a notch. And that, sadly, is the final impression I took from the game. Really liked how the story ends, so there is that, though the final boss fight was absolute rubbish.

I wanted to address several points that I have seen  posted about this game. I feel as though perhaps some of the negative comments that are aimed at this game stem from a misalignment of expectations. To be fair I didn't read anything about this game (in terms of marketing material) before I bought it. I read a bunch of the steam reviews as well as some random found on google.
To me, first and foremost this is a hack and slash (button masher) that has some semblence of a story behind it. If you are looking for an actual RPG this isnt for you. However, it reminds me a bit of games like Gauntlet. A game you play with a friend and just run around and beat the tar out of things. I think that viewing it as anything else will lead to disappointment.
With that said there is a lot to like about this game
* I absolutely love playing this with the steam controller. The default button layout is great for me. (more on this in the cons)
* you can switch back and forth between keyboard and controller by just using them, no toggling of settings
* There does seem to be a difference in game play style depending on which character you play. I have used the dual wielder and a character with hammer and shield. I have found that they tactically play differently which makes the game interesting
* Upgradable smithies (i.e. you can upgrade the armeror, weaponsmith, enchanter and trinket dealer). I personally enjoy having a target to shoot for. Some people complained about excessive grinding, which could be true if you are trying upgrade everything all the time
* I actually really like the roll mechanic for dodging, especially with the steam controller
* I enjoy a lot of the animations
* the game is very graphically pleasing
* I like the fact that you have to get to fires from time to time. It adds some strategy to the game
* There are definitely terrain bugs. From time to time in multiplayer either play may get stuck on the terrain. Once in a while someone may need to disconnect/reconnect to get free
*  I personally cannot play this with the controller alone. I find interacting with inventory and shop keeps inferior. Its not even about the controlls themselves, the actual interface changes depending on which device you use. The interface when the keyboard is active (to me) is the most sane
* Some of the material drop rates could be much better
* Have encountered what appear to be lag issues even though playing on the LAN
* I had trouble establishing/hosting games over the internet (UPnP is strongly recommended by the devs)
Overall, I have zero regretts with this purchase. I would recommend it to anyone looking for an action/hack and slash style game that has some "rpg" elements. The story telling is decent, and so far I haven't found any parts that are not voice acted which is nice. I would return this game if I could.  For such a small game, it's hard to imagine the developers possibly finding any /more/ ways they could screw it up and render it unplayable.
Expect ear-splittingly loud audio when you first start the game.  Setting volume at 1/10 makes it bearable, but expect a repeat performance every time you come back.  If you're unlucky like me, you won't even be able to play anyway, because the game speed is up by at least an order of magnitude - you won't even be able to navigate the menus.  If you get that fixed, still expect random timing glitches based on whether you have vsync on.
But those are all bugs, and one presumes that if the developers have any shred of decency or respect for their consumers, they'll at least fix those.  No the real deal-breaker is the controls.
Control mappings are backwards (jump/confirm swapped with shoot/cancel) and can't even be customized.  Countless side-scrollers that have come before have trained us to expect a competent layout that puts your most spammed inputs (movement) closest to the base of the thumb, and conversely your limited use controls further away.  But no, Towerfall went way out of its way to make it as hard as possible not to hit the wrong button /constantly/.  This and this alone renders the game an unplayable exercise in frustration just with the inputs.  The actual gameplay doesn't even factor in.
Don't expect to be able to pick up their slack either.  Mapping controller keys to other controller keys is pretty much impossible or just not worth the exhorbitant effort depending on what hardware you have, and just mapping to keyboard keys won't work either - the game will then read both.
I feel like an incredible sucker for buying this game on two steam accounts before I actually tried it - never even considered it could be this messed up, not when the reviews are so positive and only focus on gameplay and the lack of online play.  This wouldn't pass muster for a PC game in the 90s and would make a sub-par free flash game today.
When did developers lose all respect for their customers?  We're humans, not programmable money machines.  Software conforms to us, not the other way around.  To not even bother allowing any way to remap keys - even if the default mapping weren't ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ - is just a slap in the face.  I cannot imagine in what world falling short on even this baseline effort could possibly be considered acceptable and worthy of my money.  I want mine back, and barring that, you can at least be sure the developers responsible for this game will never swindle a penny from me ever again.

Great game though, cannot wait to see how it develops!

I loved SpaceChem, so I expected I would enjoy this game too. I wasn't wrong. Infinifactory is, simply put, SpaceChem in 3D.
Pros
+ Challenging Gameplay
+Finishing levels gives a great sense of satisfaction
+The audio logs are very interesting
Cons
-Game doesn't seem to know quite what its tone is supposed to be. The times when you interact with the aliens are funny and goofy, but the audio logs you find on the bodies of your predecessors are pretty dark and haunting. There's even a
within the first few levels. The uneven tone of the game doesn't take away from the gameplay, but I wish they had gone either serious or silly all the way/
-Visually, not great. The visuals seem pretty utilitarian in their purpose. They show what you need to see with no bells and whistles. Lighting isn't great, either.
-Music gets old fast, especially when spending a long time on a level. I usually play my own music unless I find one of the audio logs.
In spite of the cons I've listed, I would still highly reccomend it. The gameplay is just so incredibly good that it makes up for the other shortcomings.

Wow! That's the first thing that came to my mind moments after I fired this up. For such a small footprint, this game nails what it sets out to do...to provide an immersive survival environment in which you can't help but be pulled into. To begin with, this game is absolutely beautiful aesthetically. Beyond this beauty lies imminent horror, as you quickly grasp the reality of your situation in game. There is no hand holding here, but that’s what you would expect given the “survival” moniker stamped on its front cover. The Long Dark succeeds at an extremely high level where other games that fall within this genre have sorely missed the mark. Yes, it’s frustrating once you recognize that there’s only one end game in your demise, but I believe therein lies the genius at the root of its design. TLD will invoke many emotions throughout your short time in its environment. Bouncing between depression, despair, elation and achievement is all part of the dance. I recommend you dress warmly before taking the leap into TLD, as the lines between reality and fantasy will quickly become blurred. All this, and we are still in early access. I cannot recommend the experience waiting for you inside enough.

I love this puzzle game because it gives you complete freedom in how you go about solving each level. Every challenge gives you a set of building blocks and asks you to build a factory line that puts them together into a specific structure. The different factory parts at your disposal are so multifunctional that there's tons of ways to go about it. This doesn't make it easy - on the contrary, it's all about combining simple parts to perform complicated procedures! You feel like a genius engineer every time you solve a level.
The learning curve is exquisite. It starts off really gentle with a few levels just to get familiar with the mechanics, and slowely introduces new blocks throughout the game. It nudges you slowly towards realizing how the simple parts you're given can be combined to form incredible contraptions to solve even the most complicated engineering challenges. The later levels
challenge you and will have you spending multiple hours on a single problem. You'll size up the challenge and decide it's best to divide the puzzle into puzzles, assembling parts of the final structure on several separate conveyor belts so you can tackle one problem at a time and put it all together at the end. There's nothing quite like the satisfaction of getting your own idea to work and then watch it go in a beautiful harmony of interlocking mechanisms of your own design.
Took me 50 hours to complete every single level, and I haven't even started on the Steam Workshop content. Plus, if you like, you could go back and try to improve on your old solutions (you can compare your score with other players).
This isn't a game for people who like to fill in sudokus - this is a game that challenges you to find your own solution and think like an engineer. If that sounds like your cup of tea, this game will keep you busy for a considerable amount of time.

PROS:
-Easy to expand with new graphics, sounds, music and scripts
-Quick to create events, characters, enemies or even animations
-With a good knowledge it's even possible to do a own level system without any script
-Testplay function easy to use (not in every editor easy to use, tried many others too)
-Ingame character creator
-Extended sound settings (like how fast or loud the BGM, BGS is)
CONS:
-Only 544x416 screenresolution, no matter if fullscreen or windowed. With a script you can expand to 640x480, with an .dll file you can go up to 1920x1200 pixels. But 2560x1440 is too much. But the game becomes laggy.
-No support for Anti Aliasing
-No shadows or lights without a script
-No limitless numbers of variables, switches, items, weapons, armours, levels (never reached the limit so far)
-Maximum Map size from 500x500 (never reached it, but if you plan to do a open world game, this could be a hurdle)
RESULT:
I can recommend it to everyone/everypony, who wants to make easy and fast a RPG. It's not done in minutes or hours, still talking about days. But in comparison with other editors it's way faster and easier. From character sizeses is no limitation, you only need to look that they are ordered like the original set of characters or marked with "$" to make it a single character sprite. If more animations are needed, there are scripts for that. The only thing who really bothers me is the really low 4:3 screen resolution of 544x416. I think at least there should be a HD and FullHD option. Ultra HD or 2560x1600 are not really that common, because you need a good graphic card anyway.
After all I can say if you want a easy to use tool, I can recommend it, but if you want to make the ultra complex, god like game, then not. For me it's the best game maker tool. (\s/)

THEN there is the other currencies, the ones you find in mobile "games" that cost real money to acquire. The extra currencies and VIP   bullsh*t allows you to progress much quicker. It took me around 12 or so hours to save up for a good helmet..for one of the 4 classes. That helmet costs 12K and too many hours of grinding.
In short:
- fun for the first 13 ranks (about 10 - 15 hours) but then you get all the people who pay and have god weapons against your gun which is a pea shooter by comparisson
- advancement system is slow and complete bs
- repetitive grind
- if you still get this game, DO NOT BUY ANY OF THE CRATES (the loot box system for this game). They are a huge waste of money
Bottom line:
The game has lots of flaws, but is kinda fun for a while. They need to fix the advancement system and costs for certain things. Change up the matching system so you don't have level 15s against level 25+ because the higher-ups have stupid good gear and cut down on the mobile game formula (I get it they need money, but this is absurd)

After being gifted this game, I really really want to recommend it, but I just can't. Here's why:
Pros (+) :
1. Pleasant and fitting music though it feels... Not so original.
2. Strong monsters (for those of you who like strong enemies in games) that scale with your level, including their loot.
3. Six different classes to choose from.
4. The character art is pretty, but everything else is what you would expect of a game of that genre, nothing special or unique here.
5. It's possible to upgrade your weapon as well as craft your own potions.
6. It's a fairly cheap game.
Cons (-) :
1. Classes are way too similar to each other. In fact, it doesn't matter which one you pick as they hardly differ from each other at all as there are no special abilities or talents. All of the classes can use the two OP weapons I will mention further down in this review.
2. Unfixed bugs are present in the game. Several of them. You can literally walk on the walls inside the church, an innkeeper won't allow you to enter the room you paid for and you can't walk behind a really tall building.
3. Hardly any balancing in melee fights: Enemies have more hp and hit harder as you level, while you hardly become any stronger. In fact, it wasn't unusual for enemies to be able to kill me with 2-3 hits once I leveled up just a few times. And that was indeed as a melee class with a higher defense stat than mages and archers. Also, there are two swords that can be used by ALL classes, and those swords can kill just about every monster without them ever being able to hit you as you hit them diagonally, while they can only harm you when you are in their path.
4. Spells are useless: only 2 spells and they don't really do any major damage. Also, enemies apparently have a 2 second or so invulnerability after being hit, which isn't much of an issue when using melee weapons (as a melee weapon takes about equally long to charge the attack), but it's a major issue when using spells as you have to time the spell right so you don't waste mana nor get hit while waiting for their invulnerability to wear off. Unnecesarily hard and really bothersome.
5. Very few quests for a game of that genre: I could only find 4 in the game and I literally looked everywhere and talked to every single npc in the game. Oh and they don't really give any directions so you more or less have to guess where to go for x quest.
6. Lacks content: Like I wrote above, enemies become stronger the higher level you are, and so it would be nice if you could buy or acquire better armor, but there isn't anything meant for mid-game fights and above. Also, why is there a random guy living in the middle of nowhere when he does nothing important? Why does everyone talk about the king and all when he actually proves to be completely irrelevant to the story and is, in fact, impossible to interact with?
7. Incomplete (or feels so) things: why are there guard towers with instructions on how to use smoke signals if you don't ever get to use it yourself or see it happen? Why are there so many locked doors?
8. Doesn't really have a lot of different weapons to offer: Again, no need to acquire any other weapon than one of the two swords mentioned above.
9. The crafting / upgrading system is more or less useless. Once you acquire either one of the swords (again with the swords…), you can literally just kill monsters without them ever being able to hit you, and only standard weapons sold by npcs can be upgraded, and the upgraded weapons are FAR inferior to those two swords. As for making your own potions, well, using OP swords will give you so much money that you will easily be able to buy more potions than you could ever need. Oh and if you really want to make your own potions, farming the ressources is a major pain and nearly impossible to do, as nothing says where to acquire them (apart from those blue butterflies). Just farm gold kay?.
10. No "fast travel" or "teleport to x city/town": It's really annoying to travel through several zones 10 times while trying to avoid monsters (in EVERY zone) that can almost kill you with one hit.
11. It's a fairly short game (fortunately?). I beat it first time as a ninja (the slow and long play-through to explore everything the game has to offer, and ninja is a melee class) in four hours, second time was to test the mage class and I completed it in aprox. 2, and the third was a speed run as an archer, which I completed in about an hour. I tried to beat the game using only magic and arrows, but I eventually gave up on both and just went the OP swords "route", which made the game A LOT easier.
Final Verdict:
Is it worth buying? Not really. I would probably recommend it if it had fewer bugs and more content, but right now it just feels empty content-wise after 30 or so minutes.

Secret of Magia is a game that takes hints from several 2D adventure titles such as Ys, the Mana series, and Zelda. What it fails to do is execute these well and the game just turns into a giant mess. In Secret of Magia, you'll experience game breaking glitches, awful hitboxes, poor English, and a game that just isn't very long at all. The game has a grand total of five dungeons available, though only four of them are actually required to beat the game.
One of the things in Secret of Magia that made absolutely no sense to me was why the enemies scaled with your level. I very quickly decided to not even bother with killing anything but what was required to even proceed. When it comes to the bosses, it doesn't even really matter if you're underleveled. All you have to do is stand to the side of where they can hit, and so long as they don't have some sort of area of effect skill they just can't hit you. One NPC remarked that you needed a shield to beat a particular boss. This boss was actually one of the only ones I couldn't abuse this hitbox effect on and I still never even used the shield (playing as a Paladin).
Secret of Magia holds some good promises but completely fails to deliver on them. Many glitches are being left unchecked, such as being locked out of dungeons forcing you to restart the entire game and the Scythe just not being upgradeable. There are much better games in this style out there, so my suggested is to just play those instead and pass on Secret of Magia. Unless, of course, you don't mind smashing your head into awful English and poor hitboxes.

I was quite willing to agree with Davey on his verdict about Koda. The games he made did seem a little like a cry for help. I was okay with the starting premise that it was okay to show these games to people, because I thought the games would be a little more conventional. I did not expect each of them to be a somewhat harrowing personal journey. There were many moments where I had to take my hands of the keyboard and think about what had just occured. I was duly shocked towards the top of the tower. I can only begin to imagine the intense hurt those remarks and accusations caused, mainly because it is a thing that I fear myself.
(Original written in 2015)
EDIT (2017): In retrospect, there's no way that this game is not a work of fiction. Koda is more likely some sort of inner demon of Davey's and the narrative of the game compounds from an internal dialogue of the author. But whether the story is real or not is yet another discussion the player will have to have with themselves as they question the morality of the narrator, and more importantly, themselves.

Ok, so this game is not really that good. But it does get way too much flak for things many other releases get away with. And that's downright unfair.
It's an ok game. Soundtrack being an exception it ticks all the boxes, but with no more than a satisfactory mark. Reminds me of Dungeon Siege III that way. In fact it suffers very much the same fate.
Environments are rather pretty and also tick almost all the boxes required for the genre. I for one very much like the exposure mechanic. It requires a bit more thinking than slashers are usually known for, fair enough, but that doesn't make it bad. Also, this game (like many other single-character slashers) is best played with a controller. You can switch to keyboard/mouse at any time (for example, for inventory). Loot is mostly filler, even legendary items and even the Ring of the Nibelungen! In fact everything else - stats, skilltree, crafting and item upgrades is just there and that's about it. The long and short of it is spamming attack, abilities and rolling away in time. Isn't that why people play these kinds of games? I don't know. I do.
The major league sin here is the issue of overall balance and progression. The first couple levels and more so the bosses are very hard (up to impossible) if you do not have proper equipment. And you most definitely do not if you do not run through a fair few of the starting levels at least twice hitting everything living and not living in sight and looking for treasure just to save up enough moolah. In fact it's encouraged. That stretches the gameplay, reeks of MMOs and makes the lack of variety in monster types and their attacks and general lack of content very noticeable. So yeah, that's the big downer that brings down everything with it.
Main character is a single-minded tool with severely bad attitude. The game very liberally borrows concepts from Norse, Germanic and Celtic mythology and plays the bloodthirsty viking trope straight as a longsword. The story is just an excuse to go and kill things, everyone else is incompetent and rather content to sit on their thumbs. And the main character actually makes it known to everyone else all too often. Well, I'd imagine that's the only kind of person that *can* save the gala... err... Midgard! Nevertheless, some of the lines are delivered with a comedic deadpan ("I'm becoming crispy." in a forge level). And I just laughed out loud hearing the Shieldmaiden say "I'm sick. I hope I'm not with child.". Yeah, that would be inconvenient! That maiden part in your name is a major cokc-up, isn't it? Hurr durr.
There's two things that this game does right, though. One, its soundtrack. Dynamedion has done an outright excellent job. They often do, but this is one of their best. I wish it was also available on Steam. Two, this game has a demo. Just like the good old days, you can play through the first level and decide for yourself. And for what it matters, I think you should. Reviews and... uh... internets in general are such a cesspool that only Mjolnir could possibly banhammer them all to Hel. In fact I'll go play this game some more and imagine that I can.
P.S. Mirkhrafn. If you can pronounce it right quick ten times out of ten, there's probably a place for you in Valhalla.

Ah Five Night's at Freddy's, I don't think this game needs a introduction with the massive popularity it has gotten. but for those on the fence of buying the game and don't wish to spoil themselves on the dozens of let's play videos of it out there, this game is a resource-management nightmare-fuel inducing horror ride.
You play a newly hired security guard at Freddy Fezbears pizzaria, sounds like a boring job right? well in till you start your job at midnight and a recording left by a previous guard tells you the animatronic characters like to move around by themselves, and consider you stuffing for empty costumes full of crossbars, wires and animatronic parts mostly around the facial area. and would cause some discomfort and a minor case of death having your face forcefully pushed inside.
Scared yet?
The moment you start you realize you cannot move, the entire game takes place in the eeriely vulnerable security office where you have a set amount of electricity per night. turning on the door lights, closing the doors and even checking the security cameras all use up this limited power and if you run out, well. . .you don't wanna run out. as this sounds the atmosphere is so terror inducing, as you look into the camera and see the animatronic characters peering at you with their soulless eyes sends a sense of dread through you that few games have managed. not even mentioning the sound effects, which are BRILLIANT. from the children music and singing, to the subtle footsteps of them approaching the room or them rumaging through a empty room every sound will send you scurrying to close the doors in panic.
Now to talk about the big problem many people seem to have with this game, calling it nothing but a "Jumpscare" game. this statement is both true and false, yes there are jump scares, but such events only happen when you die. in till you get caught there are absolutely no jumpscares and it is pure atmosphere but sadly once you get exposed to this game for 2-3 hours, you learn the events and how to avoid them so the game loses some of it's scare. but for 5 dollars, it's hard to find anything wrong with this game at all and it stands tall as what I call will be a classic horror game for generations to come.

TL;DR: It's like trying to tell jokes in a YouTube comments section.
This game provides a quirky and fun platform for people to take the spotlight with a small audience. The premise is very unique and I really give the developer props for making something so original. If you can get a large enough group of your friends together, this has the potential to be a fun game. I've had a few good moments with a few decent audiences. My favorite time was when three of us changed our profile names to different U.S. Presidents, dressed our characters like them, and did political jokes. Hilarious!
I'll say this first. I've done real life stand up and improv at comedy clubs when they have amateur nights. People in 'real life' will generally be respectful and let a person tell their jokes. The best that can happen is roaring laughter and people buying you drinks for making them smile. The lack of laughter or throwing up drunk usually would be the worst thing that can happen. So in that case everyone can still have a great time tossing around new jokes without worrying about too many unruly people, whom are always promptly asked to leave.
However, that's not what it's like in this game. At no fault of the developers, there is one fatal flaw...  The other players.
It's a shame that it only allows 14 people in any given session, but it's also a blessing in disguise. In great contrast to real life, the majority of random players that you find in Comedy Night sessions are not respectful at all. It's a roll of the dice if you get an audience that will listen to people's jokes, or rather just boo and heckle every person that gets on stage because they want their turn to make noises in the mic. Usually it's the latter. Most admins don't police their sessions, and let audience members be loud and boisterous to the point you can't hear the person on stage. In most rooms, if you take longer than 30 seconds to tell a joke, "get off the stage" is often shouted. I don't have to participate to witness all of  this. They do it to everybody.
The majority of people telling jokes are reading them from websites, so you'll hear jokes repeated quite frequently after an hour or so. If they aren't doing that, they're mostly spewing some of the most vile garbage you'd ever hear just to get an edgy response. This includes badly delivered jokes about racism, sexual assult, pedophilia, sexism, holocaust denial, 9-11, cats and dogs living together. Mass hysteria. Others like to play loud sounds from YouTube, scream, fart, or make any manner of strange noises into the mic. The community for this game became cancerous very quickly. I told myself that if I have to hear another 12 year old yell racial slurs at the stage, I'll uninstall this game... and I did.
This game requires more features for controlling the crowds. As admin you can kick or ban them, but due to the low player count, you wont be able to fill up the 14 seats if you keep banning people. I'd like the ability to mute the entire audience so everyone has a chance to perform without interruption. However, when it comes down to it, playing Secret of Magia makes you reminisce of Zelda and sulk over how inferior this game feels in comparison.

CONS

Really fun and interesting puzzle game with familiar yet somewhat unique mechanics.
The player takes the role of a human who has been abducted by an alien spaceship and is tasked with constructing a variety of different production lines (for lack of a better term) to make equipment and machines for the aliens across a variety of levels. The player will unlock more machine parts and mechanics as they progress.
The games interesting story is initially told through tape recordings that the player will find in different levels.
The levels seemingly easy but quickly get more difficult as the game progresses. There are many different ways in which to construct the different production lines in each stage and the player is rewarded for making their factory as efficient as possible. This game is sure to frustrate any player but they will be rewarded for their determination.
This game has elements from, and can be compared to, other games such as Factorio and Minecraft, but it is also very different from those games in other ways and is more than capable of being considered independent from those games.
+Fun and interesting puzzle mechanics.
+Excellent soundtrack.
+Freedom to solve puzzles in different ways, with more efficient ways being rewarded.
+Good story, however, the story does not
have a central role in the game.
+Very relaxing, yet difficult gameplay.
+Workshop support for creating new levels.
+Nice aesthetic.
+Good learning curve.
+Longer that it seems.
~Online functionality limited to leaderboards and the workshop.
~No performance issues.
-Levels may get repetitive after a while.
-Players may get bored of the game's mechanics.
-Some players may not like the games linear progression.
-Price is perhaps slightly too high.
Overall, I like this game. I would recommend this game to anybody who likes puzzle games. It is a very good puzzle game and it is relaxing and fun to play. The game will require alot of determination to complete and I would not recommend it to people who are looking for an easy game or to those who are not interested in puzzles.

This is a gem of a puzzle game. If you enjoy building contraptions in block-based building games, then you'll absolutely love this. It even has a surprisingly decent story to boot with a satisfying ending.
The relatively simple building blocks are set up to allow for pretty impressive emergent gameplay.
There are a few things I would like to see improved however. Blocks can only be rotated in the X/Y plane, which means that a lot of the functional blocks have two variants for side/top (but no bottom) which leads to some annoying building restrictions (Why can't my piston push up? Why can't my welder weld from below? Why can't my laser/eviscerator aim down?), but if full 3D rotation was present these extra blocks could be removed, and we would have a lot more options for building things.
Also, the tutorial is pretty much non-existent, and there's a lot of advanced building techniques that the game doesn't even hint about. Some players enjoy the trial and error of discovering this on their own (I do to some extent, but eventually it just got to be annoying when some of puzzles expected you to know an advanced technique, but didn't actually give you any hint whatsoever on what it might be), for everyone else, there's plenty of online guides.
The only real flaws I've seen are some performance issues (stuttering) and occasional crashes. The autosave system saves frquently enough though that I never really had any problems with losing anything.
Overall, despite a few small issues, this is a great puzzle game and easily recommended.

Red Orchestra 2: Heroes of Stalingrad. A hidden jewel amongst the vast array of FPS out there.
Where to start? The game either has you play as German or Soviet during Operation Barbarossa: the German invasion of the Soviet Union during WWII.
Multiplayer is the vital component. While there is a singleplayer part I have yet to get to it, mostly because the multiplayer is the very epithome of fun, balance and technical brilliance. The latest patch added a beautiful netcoding tweak: player side hit detection. You can play with 220 ping and it does feel as if you have 20-40.
BEAR THIS IN MIND, THOUGH: This game IS HARD. You are not meant to withstand an insane ammount of punch, nor are you able to survive against truly insurmountable odds. Expect realistic bullet trajectories, realistic sound effects, realistic hit detection and thus realistic healing.
To sum up, it is a hard but deeply rewarding MP experience, one you should not pass up.
COD & BF killer. Get it. 5/5.

I randomly found a trailer for this game about a year ago, and even then when it was pretty under the radar I was stoked to see it come to fruition.  I was very hopeful that this title would turn out well, but equally worried that it wouldn't be up to my expectations.  This game finally did it for me.  Survival at its core.  A harsh environment can be the most dangerous thing out there.  Some of the situations you encounter will catch you completely off guard.  You'll feel quite comfortable with your current setup and then something will go horribly, horribly wrong.  I made it to seven days so far, and even that was pretty impressive for me. My character was constantly freezing everytime I went outside for a large portion of my run, and towards the end I had finally found some warm clothes to replace my nearly broken clothing; and I also managed to find a sewing kit to repair what I did have on!  I had just entered a fishing hole to search for items and knew where my destination was after I left there.  But fate chose to laugh at me, and moments later before I had a chance to look outside a monstrous storm began.  Incredibly short draw distance and incredibly low temperatures left me too my demise.  I was walking in the long dark, lost completely.  It was saddening, yet satisfying.  I had come so close to dying so many times, and just barely made it through it and found myself getting comfortable with my new set up each time.
Positives:
+ Feels like almost every moment can be your last.  Each decison you make counts.
+ Amazing art direction
+ Good graphics, yet small file size
+ Tons of replayability
+ Crafting is not overly-complicated, and straightforward
+ Constantly changing meta due to Early Access changes as well as randomized locations for events; it makes the game feel like the environment can be harsher or more forgiving at times.
There's just a few things I'm still hoping for from this game that would bring it to perfection:
- More animations, less loading bars.  I'd much rather see myself making the fire than seeing a loading bar as it progresses.
-  Ability to use more items as weapons.  If I have a prybar, a hatchet, and a hunting knife, it's going to break immersion if I can't use any of these to help fend off the wolves.  Noise can be used to scare off wolves, and I'd love to also be able to use these weapons to create enough noise to scare them off as well.
-  I love the number crunching for staying alive, but to be honest it kind of ditracts from the immersion.  If I just knew the character was hungry/thirsty that'd be good enough and probably better for the overall game.  We can't quite number crunch in real life unfortunately.  We don't know how many calories are in products unless labelled, and we don't know how many calories are currently in us.  These numbers matter, but that feels like it should be back-end and something the developers really know about and the players don't.  As a solution, perhaps if the player becomes severely dehydrated they end up becoming delerious, and can even go far as passing out? There's plenty of potential in removing the number crunching.
- More interactivity with the environment.  I'd love to chop down a tree myself rather than clicking on a 'forage' button.  I'd also like to be able to incorprate plants/bushes for tinder
- More options for hunting animals, more trap types, larger animal variety,
- SHOVEL, seriously, there's so much potential!!!  Imagine you could stack up snow and create an igloo or snow fort in case of emergency.  There are real life situations where you can dig yourself into a hole, cover it, and survive; I'd love to see that implemented.  We've got to be able to create our own makeshift shelters.  Perhaps small leather tents we can construct as well.
- This game screams co-op experience.  It may be ideal to only have one friend available for the current set up, but I'd love to see a team of four as well.  Something about trying to survive together just feels right.  Of course for the sake of balancing issues I would suggest only certain maps be available to co-op.
- This one seems stupid but it's just a given, it's a survival game, and I don't think it detracts or makes the game silly or less serious by adding it; they should definitely allow you to drink your own urine.  Were in desperate need of fluid and on the verge of death, yet were too good to drink our own urine?  Come on.
- Fall damage is a bit high in my personal opinion
- On warmer days, have randomly placed thin ice
- Raw meat seems to be okay with sitting out for days, while convienent for balancing, it's not exactly accurrate.  At the very least there could be containers outside of cabins to place them in to freeze, but not completely freeze over.
- RARE Hostile/friendly AI human
- Skiing poles as rare items to help scale steep heights,
- Snow shoes as rare item to traverse deep snow with less fatigue.
- Ability to carve wooden weaponry like a club or spear
- Perhaps this is nitpicky, but I want to be able to see my feet/arms
Overall: As an early access title this game easily earns an 8/10.  I'd love to give it a higher score, but it needs to keep expanding and have more content first.  There's a lot of promise in this game, loads of potential.  I'm already having a ton of fun with it. They've tapped into a lot of it already, but I'm really hoping they manage to keep this up.  I hope it takes them a long time to feel satisfied enough with the project to consider it a full release.  But in the mean time, support these devs, buy their game and enjoy!

Do you know what an action rpg is?????  You do!  Well, guess what .  This is not like Diablo.  Nor is it like Grim Dawn.  Nor is it like POE.  You will not have a golden shower of magic items every time you kill a mob of enemies.  There are magically items, but it is more subdued.  You will not have a dilemma of do I pick the Axe of the Fox, with regen of 2 hp per hit or the Axe of the Walrus which is 10 more damage.  Simply in Wolves there is not that much loot.  Which is a good thing so you are not bogged down with loot management.  This of course is a matter of preference.
Wolves leans more towards action with dodging, blocking, and taking more damage if you get too close to some non-boss enemies.  There is one boss per level which can be challenging, but is not rage-quit challenging.  If you lose against a boss, you can try again because you magically are resurrected on that boss's doorstep to fight another day.
The enemy variety is almost alright; the game likes to recycle enemy types.  But then again most games do this.
I picked it up on sale for around $13.  I do not think it is worth $40.  My opinion again.
If you do get the game, one thing we can all agree with is that the damn mini-map is mapped  badly on the controller.  Maybe, some day the devs will fix this.  Don't hold your breathe.  Although fustrating, you can live with the mini-map popping up in the heat of a battle.
One more thing.  You can see your footprints in the snow, but you cannot make snow angels, nor snowmen.  Nor can you have snowball battles.  Once again, I think I can live with this missing omission.

As someone who loves couch cooperative games and owns a fairly large collection, I am happy to say that Towerfall is one of the best. Towerfall has that "pixel-perfect" movement that makes simply running around and mastering each map a joy. The level of polish present far surpasses that of many other indie games and the inclusion of quest mode makes this release substantially more complete than the OUYA version.
Compared to the recently released Samurai Gunn, I would say that Towerfall offers more complexity and a higher skill cap, not to mention more content and customization. Among my friends Towerfall is already the clear favorite. However even without multiplayer, I have played 5+ hours of singleplayer and still have many more trials and secrets to unlock. If you enjoy classic arcade games and are without nearby gaming friends, I would still highly reccommend purchasing Towerfall. Improving upon times in Trials mode and beating High Scores in Quest Mode offer an endless challenge, while simply clearing all the levels on diamond and hardcore will take most people atleast 8 hours!
That being said, this game truly shines when you and three of your buddies gather around the same television. With thousands of possible game variants, easy to learn but hard to master gameplay, and short enjoyable rounds I don't see myself playing any other game with my friends for a long time.
A classic

The Long Dark, even in early access, ranks as the best survival genre game I have played to date.
Open world games are often mired by easy exploration that centers on repetitive locales, loot and achievements.  The Long Dark transforms exploration into a struggle for survival that's consistently rewarding and filled with satisfying discoveries across spectacular, frigid landscapes. Despite the wolves, harsh weather, persistant need for calories, water, heat and rest, there's a peaceful serenity here that one can get lost in for hours. Apart from some balance issues and missing content, The Long Dark is already a surprisingly polished experience and one of my favorite games of the year.

This punishingly hard medieval town sim will have you managing not only building materials, but also food, tools, and items to survive winter.  Don't plan effectively, and your town will fold like a cheap suit at an origami expo.  Not enough food from your farms prior to winter?  Everyone starves.  Did you forget to have your woodcutter working this summer?  Prepare for you populous to freeze to death.  Did your blacksmith die of old age, and did you forget to replace him with a young apprentice?  Prepare for your production to slow to a crawl when you run out of tools.  You will manage workers, food sources, renewable building materials (read as: trees), and even housing vacancies.  Ignoring any of these metrics could spell the end of your fledgling colony!  Players are challenged to not only gather resources to survive, but to do so in such a way that is sustainable.
While the base game is very good for those of a management mindset, Shining Rock Software has made a smart decision by integrating steam workshop support.  The player community has added a number of resources, such as different crops and livestock, and new buildings as well.  Banished really shines when you add the Colonial Charter mod by [Black Liquid].  Colonial charter adds a large number of resources and new starting options, allowing new players an easier way to learn, and offering veterans numerous options to challenge themselves.
Beyond the fun and challenging gameplay, the graphics are also quite nice.  With a multitude of building and road types, your eyes will soon feast upon the robust hamlet you have created, and the sight is both pretty and something to be proud of.  If you like city builders and are looking for a challenge, look no further.  Banished is for you.  You'll be mismanaging (and likely inadvertently killing) your loyal followers in no time.

I've only had the program for a little more than a week, but as my playtime suggests, I've managed to cream out a lot from it.
So I figured I'd summarize my current feelings towards it:
Pros:
* Easy, light-weight and simple event structure for those who lacks Ruby Programming knowledge. So it isn't difficult for someone who have NO experience with programming to do a easy RPG game with cutscenes and events.
* Simple program structure. Simply by starting it up and playing around for a little, you'll find out how to access the various tools available, and how to use them.
* Due to its large modder potential, there are plenty of mods that change how the entire game is played. Even turning it into something else than an RPG. Say, a platformer. Or even a horror game.
Cons:
*Lack of tile textures. The base game offers a few sets of different textures (including ground, furnite, walls etc.). However, most of them are made in such a way that it is difficulty to set them up in the actual game, without it looking unnatural. (The lack of textures that shows a side-view of an object, or behind one comes to mind. All furniture textures etc. are taken from the front.), leaving a lot to your imagination and creativity, IF you are good with sprite modelling however. You could create your own and use those.
* Some features from previous installments are not included. Such as the "layer" system from RPG MAKER XP, that allows you to place texture over each other, but on different layers, without removing the object underneath it.
* There are basic functions that are unnecessary complex, but once you learn them, you will never be troubled by it again. It is just slightly inconvenient and time consuming.
Verdict:
Nothing is without its flaws, and despite having its own, RPG Maker VX Ace has shown to be worthy of calling itself a software tool for RPG creation.
It is simple and easy to use for all the newbies. And for the programming and coding savvy, it allows full customization of its engine, allowing you to create completely new, original things from your own hard work.

This is brilliant. I love the way that the in game video camera and it's night vision effects are so life-like. The graphics are very believable, while the brass stabbing music and sound effects add to the already tense atmosphere.
I also like the way that you can hear the characters heartbeat and heavy breathing when he gets scared or runs for his life. Your character can also peep around the corners and look behind him while he is running. Very realistic indeed.
This is NOT a monster mash up - In this game... You are trapped inside a world of hurt. All that you are armed with is a video camera with night vision capability, and the strong urge for self preservation. You have objectives to complete and no way of defending yourself.
YOU... Are now the hunted. The only way to survive is to run for your life when you have to; creep about quietly sometimes, and also hide inside cabinets or underneath beds, and I find this approach extremely refreshing and very addictive.

Takes some tweaking to get your mouse functioning properly (more on this below)
*Mouse Setup Guide*
1. Grab the Direct3D9 Renderer from
.
2. Put D3D9Drv.dll and D3D9Drv.int in your "Steam\steamapps\common\Unreal Tournament\System" folder
3. Use your graphics card control panel to disable v-sync
4. Use your graphics card control panel to limit your fps to your monitors refresh rate (i.e. 60Hz monitor = 60fps cap) this prevents the game from running in superfast mode. If you aren't sure of your monitors refresh rate, just cap it at 60. A useful program for doing this with Nvidia cards is
.
5. As always, make sure you have Windows built-in mouse acceleration disabled. Go to your control panel>Mouse Properties>Pointer Options and uncheck "Enhance pointer precision" because in reality this hinders your precision by applying OS-level mouse acceleration! This last step is essential for all FPS games.

Ah Five Night's at Freddy's, I don't think this game needs a introduction with the massive popularity it has gotten. but for those on the fence of buying the game and don't wish to spoil themselves on the dozens of let's play videos of it out there, this game is a resource-management nightmare-fuel inducing horror ride.
You play a newly hired security guard at Freddy Fezbears pizzaria, sounds like a boring job right? well in till you start your job at midnight and a recording left by a previous guard tells you the animatronic characters like to move around by themselves, and consider you stuffing for empty costumes full of crossbars, wires and animatronic parts mostly around the facial area. and would cause some discomfort and a minor case of death having your face forcefully pushed inside.
Scared yet?
The moment you start you realize you cannot move, the entire game takes place in the eeriely vulnerable security office where you have a set amount of electricity per night. turning on the door lights, closing the doors and even checking the security cameras all use up this limited power and if you run out, well. . .you don't wanna run out. as this sounds the atmosphere is so terror inducing, as you look into the camera and see the animatronic characters peering at you with their soulless eyes sends a sense of dread through you that few games have managed. not even mentioning the sound effects, which are BRILLIANT. from the children music and singing, to the subtle footsteps of them approaching the room or them rumaging through a empty room every sound will send you scurrying to close the doors in panic.
Now to talk about the big problem many people seem to have with this game, calling it nothing but a "Jumpscare" game. this statement is both true and false, yes there are jump scares, but such events only happen when you die. in till you get caught there are absolutely no jumpscares and it is pure atmosphere but sadly once you get exposed to this game for 2-3 hours, you learn the events and how to avoid them so the game loses some of it's scare. but for 5 dollars, it's hard to find anything wrong with this game at all and it stands tall as what I call will be a classic horror game for generations to come.

I've been a fan of Total War for a good few years, but Napoleon slipped past my radar until a year ago when I bought it on sale and for some reason I just couldn't get myself to play it. Well, today, with a bit of free time, I decided I was going to start a campaign. I never would have guessed that today I would also finish it.
I'm by no means a great Total War player. It takes me around 100-200 hours to take over every province on the map in most games in the series. Most of these games have early hours of figuring everything out, building up a bit of a base so I can afford to expand out and carefully picking out weaker targets that I can claim without upsetting our larger, more powerful neighbors, trying to create the best armies that can adapt to varied situations and create new tactics on the fly, winning some hard fought battles with bare-minimum units, establishing a pattern of stretching my borders and then building up infrastructure to support the expansions and taking a little bit to restock my armies and pacify the locals before starting the cycle all over, each time a bit bigger and a bit more efficiently until what begin as a bunch of dudes in tshirts with sticks has become an armoured, trained fighting machine backed by a growing culture and economy and somewhere a point comes towards the end where my economy really starts booming beyond what I can even spend and suddenly countries are falling left and right to my juggernaught of economic and military might as I storm across the rest of the map, so powerful that even if everyone banded together they could not stop me. It's a culmination of a hundred hours, hundreds of turns of planning and pacing and careful execution that feels cathartic as I realize the whole world belongs to me.
That final push is what Napoleon is all about.
A big part of the Total War experience is the struggle at the beginning: starting from nothing and building up, but Napoleon gave me everything to begin with. I didn't really have to put any work in. The units you start out with are fantastic. Indeed, my first recruits were winning my final battles. There aren't many upgrades, and it's debateable whether the new units you can research are even better at all, and there's very few technologies to research either, further giving the impression that you've begun at the end with all the build-up completed for you. The building in this game is also incredibly restricted to the point where it felt token and unnecessary, like how some FPS games give you the opportunity for a health upgrade or two and call themselves RPGs. There's generally only one, maybe two options that you can build at any given place, so even in this area the game has set up everything for you. You just have to click the picture to build what they've decided should go there (you can also set the computer to manage the building automatically, which at this point might just remove some of the tedium, though I never tried it for fear something interesting might pop up at some point. Nothing ever did.). You begin with such a strong infrastructure that it's more a matter of holding the unbeatable hand you were dealt than fighting your way to the top.
That's not to say the game is all bad, though. The fights look and feel intensely cinematic right from the start, with muskets and rifles and canons blasting and smoke filling the air and men dying by the hundreds from battle #1. It was awesome to watch the fights unfold, and the game is beautiful both visually and in terms of audio. That's great, because there's really not a lot for you to do during the fights besides watch things unfold. Every battle I partook in I won easily with the same simple strategy. Every fight went the same way. The enemy always reacted exactly the same. Every faction used basically the same units and fought in exactly the same way which meant that the country divisions were basically meaningless and every battle melded in my mind so that I can't describe any single battle, but rather just what "the Napoleon battle" is. My PC really didn't like the naval battles for some reason, so I just ignored it, and yet still came away with the strongest navy in the world: it was, according to the game, twice as powerful as the next strongest navy on the map. Likewise, my army was composed of basic units throughout the entire game that all used the exact same strategy for every single battle and always won, even though some units, especially cavalry, would decide not to follow orders but instead to make up their own galavanting across the map instead of taking a few steps to the side, or charging at enemies to the left instead of ones on the right I had targetted. My spies never failed in their missons, my gentlemen always won their duels (though the effects your spies and gentlemen can have are so insignificant and unnecessary that it wouldn't matter had they all lost), everything always turned up my way. It felt like someone else had played the first hundred and fifty hours of the campaign and then decided to let me have the last 10 once they felt like it was too far gone for me to mess anything up.

And that's all it took. 10 hours to beat my campaign, and a good part of those 10 I wasn't even at my computer, though really it felt like the game should have just played itself while I was away for all it expected of me. When I looked at the "prestige" screen to find that the only nations left were my unnecessary allies and that I was more than twice the prestige of the next strongest group even in areas I had given no thought to, all I could think was that there really was no other way this could have gone, and that was a disheartening thought. Even Napoleon himself fell while I watched a video on YouTube after setting up my men in their basic formations, assured that they would win without my help.
If you love the endgame of Total War and find the early- and mid-game a chore, you'll love this game because it really is just a ready-made endgame set up and waiting for you. But for me those early stages are where the challenges really lie and the necessity for thought and strategy and planning is what entices me to keep playing. For me, the endgame rush is only satisfying in light of the beginning, and with that gone it feels pointless and hollow. I struggled to find motivation to keep playing even for one day, where before these games have lasted me for months. I tried other campaigns as well as the historical battles and was met with more of the same, easy, mindless victories.
I could see potentially how this could be a good starting point for people looking to get into strategy games or the Total War series because it does a great job of holding your hand and leading you down the path to victory, but for those who want a challenge I cannot recommend this game. The victory of a Total War game rests on the knowledge of the struggle you went through to get there, and this game takes out the struggle. It delt me a pair of aces, and as I watched the dealer some how turn over 5 more aces, I couldn't feel accomplished or proud of myself when none of my opponents could beat the hand I'd done nothing to win.
