I have a genuine question here: is this the same developer team that has presented us
? Because both games carry the banner of 8Floor, and if so, this game is an unacceptable decline in quality compared to their previous title, coming as a mediocre and bug-ridden disappointment.
Here, we take the role of Kathleen Wilson, a young lawyer whose boyfriend; Danny has the obscure hobby of collecting and researching occult artifacts. One evening, Kathleen receives a phone call from Danny, explaining that he's been accused of murder by the police! As you rush to his side to prepare a defense, Danny tells you that he is being set up by an unknown perpetrator who also stole a set of ancient Indian totems from him. At this point, you prefer to go back to Danny's hotel room to investigate the phenomenon and flush out the perpetrator in hopes of helping Danny, rather than staying by his side to actually prepare a defense like a sensible lawyer. So, this murder investigation turns into a paranormal yet obscurely constructed, absurd little journey as soon as you step into Danny's room. Soon, you'll be dealing with Indian curses, generic eerie little girls, mad researchers, agoraphobic pilots and murdered cabaret dancers.
First mistake: the story construction is completely malformed. Sure, I've seen worse in HOG genre, but the story is so full of holes, it fails to present a consistent story altogether. One moment, you are in the hotel room, in another the protagonist mentions travelling in time, and in the next chapter you are helping a pilot. If you go back and read your journal carefully, you manage to come into the conclusion that you are somehow going through time depending on the former actions of your perpetrator. But while the story unfolds, you are rarely given the reason WTF you would be doing there. Plot resolutions are sloppy, characters are nearly cardboard and the ending is a new level of ridiculous.
The previous game from the developers was surely no award winner, but its display qualities were exceedingly good. Here, it feels like that they didn't even try. Artwork is generic, character designs are forgettable and there is no voice acting at all. There is not even a single scene that you'd particularly enjoy. The narrative both in dialogues and in the journal are so dry, that it bores you. As someone who'd especially enjoy fictional settings and character designs, this was the first time that I genuinely got bored of a HOG.
Gameplay is on the low side within the genre too. HOG scenes are amateurishly matched stock pictures, with many item labelling and even logic mistakes. In one scene, there are 6-7 lightbulbs within the picture, yet for some reason the game expects you to click on a particular one without giving any indications. Most puzzles are dreadfully simple, yet some fails to give you decent explanations so you keep clicking around until something happens. The backtracking is also horrendous.
Oh, and the achievements in this game are bugged, be warned. Even though you wouldn't click on the hint button it recharges every time you start the game, and if you are to accidentally leave a HOG or puzzle scene to look around, the game registers you leaving as if you've used a hint! If you want all your achievements you gotta wait for the button to charge completely before clicking on anything. It is purely ridiculous. I've been lucky enough to check discussion forums before starting my playthrough but many others who wouldn't would be annoyed. This issue is yet to be resolved.
Got the game in a bundle and feel like giving it a try? My condolences. You'll be either bored or annoyed with this one. There are truckloads of other great HOGs to check out here on Steam. Make yourself a favor, pass this one.

A very nice puzzle platformer in the vein of Braid. But where Braid had swirly pastel painting colors and a Celtic soundtrack, this is gothic black and white and has an eerie thriller music and a pulsating grainy silent movie-era filter. Both games have a unsettling feeling that creeps up on you. Some people complain at "unfair" deaths you can't predict, but really, you are only moved a few seconds back in the game to the latest checkpoint so I don't see the problem with it. I think the constant dying is meant to reinforce the horror. Only a few hours long, which means it doesn't outstay it's welcome, but look for mood rather than plot.

I've got a real love for procedural generation -- no actual UNDERSTANDING of it, mind, but a real love for it -- and while this game, or non-game, or whatever may share some things in common with similar generate-it-and-watch experience Mountain, it has way more variety and none of Mountain's pomposity. It lets you generate strange, alien structures and examine them from every angle, all the while grooving on the exotic, offputting tunes they generate. During my first few minutes with the game, I explored:
- the glowing, dismembered skeleton of some vast, spacefaring beast
- a thorny, plantlike entity that waved gently in the solar wind
- a whirlwind of oddly flattened stones
- an enigmatic alien pyramid that glowed red like some infernal forge
- a colony of twisting worms flitting to and fro, occasionally meeting nose-to-nose as though exchanging information
I'll be coming back to Anomalies. It's not a game; it's a trip.

I exited this game feeling torn. I want to relish Limbo, as it has one of the most arresting visual aesthetic styles I've seen. However the gameplay and puzzles are more of a trial and error theme than my tastes generally tolerate. There are a couple perplexing moments that may slow you down a minute, but on the whole it really boils down to dying a few times before you realize where you're supposed to go. Beyond this there is the horror aspect, which rivals the likes of Amnesia. There are few things more disturbing than watching children take on a Lord Of The Flies approach to dealing with life, or more appropriately, Limbo. I can't say more without giving away too many spoilers, but rest assured you will be creeped the ♥♥♥♥ out at some points. The story and visuals will have your utmost attention, while the average puzzles will diminish the impact of those qualities. Engage at your own risk. 8/10

TL;DR: It's like trying to tell jokes in a YouTube comments section.
This game provides a quirky and fun platform for people to take the spotlight with a small audience. The premise is very unique and I really give the developer props for making something so original. If you can get a large enough group of your friends together, this has the potential to be a fun game. I've had a few good moments with a few decent audiences. My favorite time was when three of us changed our profile names to different U.S. Presidents, dressed our characters like them, and did political jokes. Hilarious!
I'll say this first. I've done real life stand up and improv at comedy clubs when they have amateur nights. People in 'real life' will generally be respectful and let a person tell their jokes. The best that can happen is roaring laughter and people buying you drinks for making them smile. The lack of laughter or throwing up drunk usually would be the worst thing that can happen. So in that case everyone can still have a great time tossing around new jokes without worrying about too many unruly people, whom are always promptly asked to leave.
However, that's not what it's like in this game. At no fault of the developers, there is one fatal flaw...  The other players.
It's a shame that it only allows 14 people in any given session, but it's also a blessing in disguise. In great contrast to real life, the majority of random players that you find in Comedy Night sessions are not respectful at all. It's a roll of the dice if you get an audience that will listen to people's jokes, or rather just boo and heckle every person that gets on stage because they want their turn to make noises in the mic. Usually it's the latter. Most admins don't police their sessions, and let audience members be loud and boisterous to the point you can't hear the person on stage. In most rooms, if you take longer than 30 seconds to tell a joke, "get off the stage" is often shouted. I don't have to participate to witness all of  this. They do it to everybody.
The majority of people telling jokes are reading them from websites, so you'll hear jokes repeated quite frequently after an hour or so. If they aren't doing that, they're mostly spewing some of the most vile garbage you'd ever hear just to get an edgy response. This includes badly delivered jokes about racism, sexual assult, pedophilia, sexism, holocaust denial, 9-11, cats and dogs living together. Mass hysteria. Others like to play loud sounds from YouTube, scream, fart, or make any manner of strange noises into the mic. The community for this game became cancerous very quickly. I told myself that if I have to hear another 12 year old yell racial slurs at the stage, I'll uninstall this game... and I did.
This game requires more features for controlling the crowds. As admin you can kick or ban them, but due to the low player count, you wont be able to fill up the 14 seats if you keep banning people. I'd like the ability to mute the entire audience so everyone has a chance to perform without interruption. There are nearly a dozen buttons for audience reactions like laughing, cheering, clapping, booing, and even crickets! This should be more than enough to gauge how good or bad everyone's jokes are. This game is doomed due to being filled with people that would be kicked out of any REAL comedy club in a heartbeat.
Edit #1: I'm happy the devs responded to this review. I stand corrected that the game has a feature to mute the entire crowd. Still wish that this wasn't nessesary. They have promised future changes in the coming weeks. I'll still take a break from using this game, but will keep an eye out for improvements made. I'll rewrite my review if there is better crowd control in place than simply client-side muting or blanket muting the room. Might I suggest a banlist that is stored on each player's account? That way it would remember who you banned and auto-add them to sessions you create.

If this game was in early access I would highly recommend, which honestly most of these high reviews are from when the game was in early access. The problem? This game is NOT a finished game, and if it is then it is grossly overpriced.
Premise of game: this is a city builder, simple as that; no storyline, no RPG elements, etc. With that in mind "building your city" because paramount as it is the only thing your game has. The game has you start with a couple of families and three different starts of varying resources (having houses already built, nothing built, ect) and just basically tells you to build and survive. Playing through the teaching you how to play missions is a must but still doesn't prepare you for what is to come. You have the option to play "with disasters" or not, but it really should read "more/less disasters" as you might not have fires and tornados but you will still have terrible sickness outbreaks and other disasters. This brings me to my first real problem,
1. The game is unforgiving: yes, once you figure stuff out you are okay but when you just start out your people will die and die and die and you will have to restart city after city as you figure out what the hell is going on. The game is designed to have you frantically in this order "not freeze to death, then everyone will start to starve to death, then freeze to death again, then your tools will run out so you will freeze and starve to death" so you will have to frantically build houses and then frantically get food (gathering hut- I'll get back to this in a second) and then build a firewood cutter so your people don't freeze in their houses and finally a blackmith. At this point (if you have survived to this point) things begin to settle down and you switch from frantic to terrible AI and disasters. You will watch as a single member of your clan takes 300 of your food and stashes it in his house and watches as everyone else around him starves; which is hilarious, flat out a laughing stock that people defend this as "PEOPLE DO THIS IN REAL LIFE!" like they are experts on when civilization falls apart- you are right, people do horde when times get hard, but do you not know what also happens? People get killed sitting on their horded pile of whatever right before they have it taken. You really think in a population of 17 people (less then ten being adults) someone could hide all the food in his house and have no one know about it and then have them starve to death before rushing in and stealing this dudes horde of food? There are no kings in this game, these are all old school people living an old school connected life; no one in this time period would horde and watch their neighbors die (hell, they were all banished TOGETHER right?). Regardless, the point is this is a failure of AI and it repeats over and over and over again. People defend the bad AI like people defended ME3 ending saying that it wasn't bad it was a brilliant ending of indoctrination and tried everything and everyway they knew how to try and cover up bad game making with "that's what happens in real life, darrrr, realism, darrr". Like I said above and will again, if this was in early access I would believe some of these problems would be fixed and improved on, but for 20$ complete package this is unnacceptable. The game tries (with bad AI and disasters) to keep your population down as best it can and turn the game into a "how long can you survive city builder" whichs brings me to the next point.
2. City lags as cities grow: so you overcame the disasters and terrible AI and are growing into an amazing city, good times right? Wrong. As soon as you hit around 200-400 population the game levels out, you can overcome a lot if not all disasters easily/with time and you are starting to trade away and get new seeds and animals for your bustling city- basically things are good and you for the first time get to stop focusing purely on survival and get to switch to "how do I want my city to look". After you realize that there is nothing to build (wonders, statues, gardens/parks, etc) to really say "I survived being banished and my city rocks" you begin to realize the game is lagging. At around 600-800 population the game is unplayable on 10x speed (which speeding up time is a must in this slow game) and then between 800-1000 combined population 5x speed becomes unplayable and after 1200 population 2x speed isn't working. People have reportedly made it to around 2k population combined before calling it off on normal speed before game crashes, Basically their engine sucks and they knew it and insted of fixing problem they created maps and disasters DESIGNED to keep you from ever really getting cities to be 'amazing cities'. For a 20$ finished game I personally expect more than that and so  this fact alone would keep me from recommending to any real friend. But I have one more point, and that is
3. Simply not enough: one wood house, one stone house, one school, one hospital, dirt road, stone road, stone church (no wood church), stone cemetary (no wood), one blacksmith, one tailor, one wood cutter, and a forrester/herbalist (i think I might be forgetting one or two others) and about a dozen ways to get food but most are grossly underpowered so you basically just use two. Fishing is terrible, farming/orchards/animals are hard and expensive to get running but pay off in the long run- but you can't use them early on or you will starve to death waiting for them to pay off. So basically you learn to build a group of buildings close together (a hunting lodge+gathering post with herbalist+forrester) early on in your learning curve and honestly never need to build anything else; you build and do other stuff because there is nothing else to do in said game. The game isn't modular, you can't build a wood house and upgrade it to a two story or even really upgrade it to a stone house (they tear it down and rebuild) you can't build a school and then a high school and then higher education to progress and watch as your people graduate from school and move on to higher levels of school, etc etc. You don't have a "nurses station" that can be upgraded into a hospital and you need a doctor to run it which has to be educated, etc etc, you just build a hospital and someone just can become a doctor. Honestly (and sadly, so very very very sadly) Keflings had more depth and heart than this game had. Once again and finally I will say if this was in early access I would hope there would be much more depth added (at least to rival Keflings for crying out loud, and that game had COOP!) but in its current state and current cost it is asking too much and giving too little.
TL:DR
Bottom Line: if you are the kind of person that enjoys Nazi Zombies (CoD), a game where there really isn't any story and you will never win- you will die- it is just a matter of "how long will I endure this game?" then this game is very much for you. It is a game based around very little actual substance (get guns, get bullets, shoot zombies, survive as long as possible- 16 guns total) and very similiar concepts (build house, get firewood, kill deer, survive as long as possible) in which you will either watch as you city all dies out (a real possibility, almost a 100% probability the first half a dozen times trying the game) or you will watch as your game lags out and crashes when your city gets too large (which isn't very large, 1,200 combined population) which is a garentee. If you are the kind of person that would rather play Left 4 Dead, a game with actual story that you can actually win with much more depth across the board then this game is so, so, so, so very not for you- Keflings had more depth and content than this game did (plus COOP, so sad!).

Unfortunately, this is the game that I will forever use as a standard for other city building games. Banished is marvelous, an absolute thrill to play. The in game economy is very complex and diverse and can quickly screw you if you aren't careful. The city building aspect is difficult, time consuming and very believable.
In order to survive, you need only provide houses for population growth, diverse food stores for consumption, clothing to keep the cold off, firewood to warm houses and tools to work with. With each new house, 2-4 children are born that need to be fed, clothed and educated (potentially). Each new citizen requires a rethink of food stores, clothing and tool supplies. If you build too many houses at one time, your people will risk starvation or dying from exposure. These things happen before you can even begin to consider a solution. If your people start dying, you will lose much needed workers. If you don't have enough farmers, even more people starve. If you choose to make all your tool makers farm for a season, you will run out of tools, resulting in extremely slow crop production and people will starve. If this wasn't bad enough, you also have to provide your citizens with a variety of food products to maintain ultimate health. People can't live on cabbage alone, they also need grains, protein and fruits to remain healthy.
This is by far my favorite city building game. It has unlimited replay-ability and will keep you entertained for hours, even if half of your time is spent screaming at the screen in an attempt to make your farmers work more quickly, or trying to figure out how one of your builders got stuck in an icy tundra in the middle of winter with no clear path home (I mean seriously how does this keep happening??)

If you took Quake II's CTF mode and injected it with steroids and liquid cocaine, this game would be the outcome. If you want to know where TF2 sort of started, then you're in for a fun time. It retains all of the classic Quake sound effects, the wacky physics of the GoldSrc engine, and the classic class-based gameplay that Team Fortress is known for. I've owned this game for a long time (in fact, I've owned this since I created my Steam account,) but I never got around to writing a review for it until now. The classes have COMPLETELY different weapons and playstyles compared to the sequel's counterparts. The spy has a "feign death" option, but no invis-watch, so you need to have good timing and hide in the shadows when playing Spy. Every class has a shotgun or nailgun of some kind, sometimes even both. Every class has grenades, so every class can jump across the map just as their heart desired. Just imagine a Medic jumping across the map with a Nailgun, completely obliterating people. Oh, did I mention that the Medic can infect a player on the opposing team with a deadly virus? No? Well, he can. Here are some other pros and cons about this game:
PROS:
*A whole butt-load of fun
*A relatively inexpensive game
*Graphics are still decent for today's standards
CONS:
*Has a sequel
*The sequel is free
*The sequel has hats, weapons, and a NEW UPDATE that came out a few days ago.
To be honest, I think if you're buying this with the rest of the Half-Life Anthology, you'd be getting a very good value. But, I don't think you should get it standalone. Although the game is fun, it stopped getting updated at around 2004 with its Steam Update. The sequel is free, so if you want to play Team Fortress, play the second one. I still recommend this to people who either want to get the entire Half-Life Anthology or are just curious about what Team Fortress looked like during the Early 2000s.
Final Score:
9 Flying Medics out of 10

Dropped in the middle of the Canadian wildness due to a plane crash (but strangely, there isn't a plane anywhere that I've seen lol), you'll start in sandbox mode (single player will be made available once the developer's have gotten that far) in a randomly generated spot within two areas you can choose from. Don't worry about which one you pick, although Coastal Highway is a lot easier as a starting area due to an abundance of resources.
You are your only friend out in the woods, with prowling wolves that seemingly are unkillable without a firearm (so far I've never been able to get both a firearm and ammo in the same playthrough, lol) which will require you to either light a flare and throw it at them to scare them off, or if you're unlucky and can't outrun them, fight for your life (90% of the time you end up dying) and live to treat the wounds and hopefully be close to some shelter to escape the cold, other wolves, and have time to rest.

After playing "Secret of Magia" for over 10 hours I must say that it has its good moments and unfortunately lots of bad moments as well.
-I like the fighting system, since it makes the gameplay more arcade-ish compared to the turn based RPGs.
-It has a male and female character selection, classes, armors, weapons, gathering, alchemy, blacksmithing, trading and    even gambling!
-The hookshot is a nice plus!
-The quest system is great as well!
-The graphics are cute, especially the character close ups.
-Audio-wise it has a decent soundtrack that fits perfectly to the game's concept.
-A couple of bugs to ruin your gaming experience... For example:
-The enemies are leveling up according to your level! That alone actually destroys the point of leveling...
-Your character's speed gives you the impression that everything goes in fast forward.
-You are basically on your own. You do not get a lot of help from the game, in order to progress.
-I found myself spending most of the time wandering around the areas in order to find out what's next. Although, there's an in game map in certain places, that doesn't help so much. I would rather have it accessible everywhere in the game after pressing the M key.
-There's a quest where you get the following coordinates "X33 Y24", but there's not any coordinate indication in the game to get an idea where you have to go.
-You cannot save the game anytime and anywhere you want.
-I wasn't able to switch into windowed mode until I found out in the game's discussions that you have to press the F5 key to do so. Also, Alt + tab doesn't work.
-Minor spelling issues.
-Lazy ending...
Overall it has a lot of potential to become a great game and I would love to see improvements and bug fixes as soon as possible! Until then I cannot recommend it.

Initial Review (bear in mind I only played for an hour before deciding I wouldn't like it):
1. Introduction was quick enough.  However, my interest wasn't piqued much.  A strange bird tells you to get all four elements or he'd reap your soul.  You get to choose your gender and class (assassin, archer or mage).  That's it.
2. You wake up in a city and you're being told what to do next exactly.  The game pushes you in the direction you have to go.  Not much thought process involved at all.
3. The combat system is Zelda-like; Secret of Magia is an action RPG where you press Z to swing your weapon, S to block with a shield, A to cast a spell.  Easy enough at first, but you can be one-shot by some enemies as melee rather easily if you don't act quickly enough.  The shield that I bought from the weaponmaker after receiving the license in town didn't seem to be working either (and I made sure to equip it, too).  And the monsters really do move too fast for you to avoid them sometimes.
4. There are background bugs everywhere.  Cliffs and walls are passable when they shouldn't be, etc.
5. No proofreading has been done for this game, apparently.  Dialogue is full of typos and misspellings - you'll be talking to plenty of 'Gaurds,' for example - and even with that fixed, it's not particularly memorable.  Many of the NPC's lines are nothing special.  "I love my nice house!"  One guard said that they couldn't drink in the watchtower and giggled as he said it - which seemed weirdly out of place.
6. Quests are discovered by talking to NPCs with an exclamation point or by examining books or so on - they seem to be straightforward but there was one quest that pointed out a location of a dagger while giving you coordinates.  I'm not sure how that would have been accomplished without an add-on telling you X and Y coordinates of the map you were on.  Granted, I didn't play long enough to try to figure it out.
7. Did I mention you could be one-shot rather easily?  Now there aren't enough save points to really help you avoid a lot of experience and gold loss if that happens.  I decided not to risk entering the mines and try to find a save point because of it in the next town up.  This isn't really a criticism.  I like the challenge, but it can probably be discouraging to some.
8. The Dash function is default (and essential in avoiding monsters); however the game's frame rate doesn't seem to be very smooth when you're dashing.  I've seen this done better in other RPGMaker games like Labyronia.  It's a bit distracting in this game.
9. There are two different ways you can use items: through equipping them, and by using the Q-W quick item equipper.  I think the item equipper could have probably been removed to simplify up the UI a bit in that respect.
10. There was a map inside the training hall in the first city that showed you the first few areas as if they were zoomed out.  I play RPGs to explore areas myself, so that map kind of took away most of the mystery of the first few areas for me.
All in all, unfortunately I wouldn't recommend this game.
EDIT: I bought it on sale ($1) and still feel ripped off - and now I find out from reading other reviews, if I had kept playing, I would have completed it in 2.5 to 3 hours anyway... I feel like there are a lot of better games for your money's worth.  Labyronia for one, which I mentioned.

Almost anyone who has gone to a Chuck E Cheese's has looked at the animitronics and thought, "What pit of hell did those things crawl out of?" This game has taken those robots that kids love, and created a straight-up nightmare.
Five Nights at Freddy's is amazing. It is a unique horror game that is simplistic yet so satisfying to play. This game has you responding to a local newspaper ad for a security guard at Freddy Fazbear's Pizza, a place that is very similar to Chuck E Cheese's. With singing robots, pizzas, and parties, it should be a place that brings much fun. Freddy's has a very dark and mysterious past and has one feature that keeps it from being a pizza-filled paradise: the animatronics tend to "roam around a bit at night". Normally this wouldn't be much of a problem if it wasn't for the fact that these robots will recognize you as a metal endoskeleton without a furry suit. This is strictly against the rules at Freddy Fazbear's and these robots will gladly obey the rules by shoving you into a suit. This wouldn't be bad either, if it weren't for the fact that these suits already have endoskeletons, so you won't survive the plunge. You must survive each night of the week as you manage security cameras, large metal doors, lights, and a dwindling power supply that will certainly spell certain doom for you if it diminishes completely.
With gameplay mechanics never seen before and an extremely creative setting and characters, Five Nights at Freddy's earns a solid 9/10 from me.
My only wish is to see updates bringing new content to a wonderful game and I hope to see more from Scott in the future.

This game is very poorly named: there are neither witches nor warlocks here, just some limited time travel (magic!) having to do with "totems" of some sort.
Also note that the achievements are a bit buggy: this counts for many of the negative reviews here, and the developer deserves them for as long as they aren't fixed. However, the game itself is fine and can be played to completion.

I really like the premise of this game, and... once again, its a game I want to like. But it simply can't make the grade.
Result: 4/10
THE GOOD
* Beautiful game : Neat bridges crossing winding rivers, beautiful snow blanketing log houses in white while chimneys keep it all cozy.... its just gorgeous
* Random Seed Level Generator : Lots of random levels, which allows for endless replayability... which you will need because your villages will die off constantly.
THE BAD
* Citizen AI : This is really the one great failing of this game, but its so pivotal to a simulated villiage like Banished, that the game simply cannot be good without a passably competent AI for the characters. Seriously. Citizens putting down crates of fish to go to the market and have a meal, and then waiting there until starving to death because there's no food. W-T-F. Citizens going home because "they're cold" (in early autumn with new clothes) and not harvesting and letting the frost kill the crop. W-T-F. In real life, a society like this would never occur. Humans are smart enough to understand that if you don't collect the crops before the frost... they will die. This is not a mystery, but the AI in this game is not clever enough to comprehend these simple game mechanics.
* Traders : $2000 for 2 cows? Seriously? I'd believe that if it weren't for the fact that that's about a billion tools or coats. These traders would never succeed in the real world. Their prices are too absurd for anyone to make deals with them.
* Difficulty : Taking into account that all of your citizens are apparently imbeciles, its virtually impossible to get a village to succeed. In the rare cases that you do, you will find yourself frustratingly stagnated by lacking some minor resource without the ability to get more of it, or exhausting the local area's resources until you can't build new tools and everybody dies.
* Supply exhaustion : While I realize they were going for realism, they missed their mark. During the game, you need to rely on surface resources like wood, stone, and iron. That's fine. Some can be replenished, such as the trees. But stone and Iron are completely exhaustable. After the surface resources are consumed, you can build mines and quarries, but their resource production is slow, and they only give you a few thousand resource throughout their lives, and then they can never be removed. The result is whole swaths of unusable eyesores just to keep your colony alive. Which is also stupid from a realism perspective because IRON DOESN'T GO BAD. If a tool breaks, your blacksmith should be able to take the iron and make something new. But the game-makers obviously didn't consider that.
* Frustrating as hell because your people are so stupid. Its clear to me now why they got banished: because they are imbeciles undeserving of survival.
* Also: nothing is documented. They don't tell you why you need certain things, or what they are for. You just have to learn the hard way, often by your villiage being wiped out and having to start over.. again.
CONCLUSION
Game should be renamed Starvation Simulator, or Frustration Tycoon. Despite 22 hours of trying, it deserves to be BANISHED into my trash bin. Good riddance.
